‘I’ll be first in line to buy your bonds’: how Zhu Rongji put steel in Hong Kong’s spine
Tributes pour in for former premier Zhu Rongji from senior leaders in Hong Kong’s political and business circles
In late 2002, former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji visited Hong Kong and sought to put steel in the spine of the city’s establishment that was floundering under an economic slump and a ballooning deficit.
“Even if you spend all your fiscal reserves three years from now, what is there to fear?” he asked his dinner guests at Government House in a famously unscripted speech.
“If you issue 50-year long-term Hong Kong bonds on the mainland, I will be the first in line to buy them. I believe the mainland people will follow me and buy them too!”
His show of unreserved confidence lifted their spirits, Tsang said of the former premier who died at age 97.
“Visiting Hong Kong in person, he galvanised our confidence in combating fiscal deficits, high unemployment, and widespread negative equity, that prevailed at that time,” he recalled.
“His candid and inspiring words continue to resonate in the hearts of many people in Hong Kong.”

UK Officials Call for Military Dialogue With Russia to Be Restored
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:09:16 UTC
23:09:16 KST

British defense officials are calling for direct contacts between the military leadership of the United Kingdom and Russia to be restored amid concerns about escalation.
The Times reported the matter.
The situation has escalated following a series of incidents involving British and Russian military personnel.
The last known conversation between Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov and his British counterpart took place in September 2022. At the time, Gerasimov spoke with the then-Chief of the Defence Staff Adm. Sir Tony Radakin.
Radakin subsequently tried several times to contact Gerasimov, but the Russian side did not respond to his calls. After Richard Knighton was appointed Chief of the Defence Staff, he also tried to establish contact with Gerasimov, but without success.
In June, the Russian frigate Admiral Grigorovich fired warning shots from small arms at a British yacht in the English Channel, after which the crew changed course.
Another incident occurred near the aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales in the Norwegian Sea. The Russian Tu-142 Yuri Malinin approached the ship at an unsafe distance while flying at low altitude. According to the British side, the aircraft also dropped a large number of surveillance devices into the water near the British aircraft carrier.
Former UK defense attaché to Moscow and Kyiv, John Foreman, said that Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting and Chief of the Defence Staff Richard Knighton should restore direct contacts with the Russian military leadership.
According to him, even in the absence of a political agreement, the military should maintain communication channels to resolve dangerous incidents.
UK Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting, July 21, 2026. Photo: Jack Taylor/Reuters
The lack of direct communication is not the only problem. In 2024, the United Kingdom expelled a Russian defense attaché, accusing him of working for Russian intelligence. In response, Moscow expelled the UK military attaché, Adrian Coghill.
The two sides previously maintained a dedicated hotline between the UK Ministry of Defence and the Russian Presidential Situation Center. It still exists but is used less frequently than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The UK government says London is ready for dialogue with the Russian military leadership, but Moscow has so far shown no willingness to restore that dialogue.

Heatwave and jellyfish: a fifth of France's nuclear capacity offline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

France generates about 70% of its electricity from nuclear power. This year, output has been disrupted by repeated heatwaves and droughts.
France recorded on Wednesday a shortfall of more than 20% of its nuclear power generation capacity, a new record for outages due to "environmental constraints" or "external causes linked to the environment": drought, extreme heat and a jellyfish invasion.
Nuclear power provides around 70% of France's electricity. This year, output has been disrupted by multiple heatwaves and periods of drought.
According to AFP calculations based on data published by energy group EDF since 2015, 20.4% of generating capacity was unavailable.
Between 9:45 and 10:00, EDF's nuclear fleet hit a new peak in unavailability for reasons described as "environmental constraints" or "external environmental causes", both in terms of the number of reactors shut down or operating at reduced power and in terms of lost generating capacity.
In total, 13 of the 57 reactors in the French nuclear fleet were affected. Eight were completely shut down (Bugey 3, Cattenom 1, Chooz 1 and 2, Golfech 2, Gravelines 2, 3 and 4) and five were running below capacity (Saint-Alban 2, Tricastin 1 and 4, Gravelines 1 and 6).
Eight reactors were completely offline, while five were operating at reduced power.
A large share of the lost nuclear capacity was due to full or partial shutdowns of five of the six reactors at the Gravelines power plant, western Europe's largest, after a mass of jellyfish clogged the pumps used to cool the facilities.
"Several tonnes of jellyfish" surged into the seawater pumping stations, clogging the filter drums, an EDF spokeswoman said.
Units 1 and 6 have since returned to full power at around 10 am on Wednesday, while reactor 5 is in a scheduled maintenance shutdown. Currently offline, Gravelines 2 is due to be reconnected to the grid at 11 pm on Wednesday.
Gravelines, which draws water from the North Sea to cool its installations, had already faced the same problem exactly one year earlier.
According to experts, overfishing, plastic pollution and warmer waters linked to climate change have created conditions favourable to the proliferation and reproduction of jellyfish.
Apart from the Gravelines plant, the largest in western Europe, shutdowns or reduced output at other reactors are linked to extreme heat and drought, which deprive power stations of the water they need for cooling.
In periods of drought or heatwave, lower river flows and higher water temperatures can force EDF to cut back or even halt production in order to protect the environment and biodiversity. In such cases the operator cannot discharge chemical or radioactive effluents, nor further warm rivers with its cooling water, which is returned at a higher temperature.
"But there is enough leeway for this not to cause supply problems" in the short term, stressed Nicolas Goldberg, an energy expert at consultancy Colombus Consulting, quoted by CNews. In August, a month when electricity consumption is lower, France was still on Tuesday a significant net exporter of electricity, after posting a record net export balance of 51 TWh in the first half of the year.
In the longer term, however, "particularly if the lifespan of reactors is extended to 70 or 80 years, adapting them to climate change will be a real stress test over the next 20 to 30 years, in a warmer climate," the expert said.

23:05:25 KST

MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. The Kalashnikov AK-12 assault rifle is more reliable and easier to operate than similar foreign assault rifles, Alan Lushnikov, CEO of the Kalashnikov Group, stated in an interview with TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov.
"In terms of reliability and ease of use, the assault rifle surpasses its foreign counterparts, and in terms of weight and dimensions, it is on par with them. We market this weapon internationally as a high-quality, top-tier assault rifle. Not many [countries] manufacture such a product. The AK-12 is represented in export markets by the 7.62mm and 5.56mm caliber AK-15 and AK-19 models," Lushnikov noted.

Portugal boosts maritime surveillance with Portuguese-made long-range drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:00:36 UTC
23:00:36 KST

The Portuguese Air Force will boost maritime surveillance using AR5 drones from Portuguese tech firm Tekever, which supplies autonomous systems to Ukraine. Delivery is due in early September.
Portuguese technology company Tekever is to supply AR5 drones to the Portuguese Air Force (FAP) for maritime surveillance missions. The autonomous platforms are scheduled for delivery in early September.
In a statement, the company, which has become an important player in the unmanned systems industry, especially when it comes to exporting drones to Ukraine, announced the signing of a contract with the FAP that also includes "operator training, as well as the supply of the Ground Control Station and the ATLAS mission system".
With a wingspan of almost 8 metres and weighing close to 200 kilos, purpose-built for maritime missions thanks to its robustness and ability to fly at higher altitudes, the AR5 will enable the FAP "to strengthen its operational autonomy on long-range missions".
These missions include "maritime surveillance, security and defence, monitoring of the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and support for missions in the public interest", which in turn covers "the Special Rural Firefighting Device (DECIR), coastal security and environmental protection".
Portuguese-made drones
In the statement, Tekever explains that in the first phase, it will train Air Force personnel until September so they can operate the systems as soon as they are delivered. Then, from October, a "second phase of training" will take place to consolidate "full operational readiness and the development of new skills within the operating teams".
Tekever has not disclosed either the scope of the contract or the amount invested by the FAP. However, an order from the Ministry of Defence (source in Portuguese), dated November last year, authorised the Air Force to purchase an unmanned aerial system for maritime patrol with an overall maximum budget of just over 7.79 million euros, to be financed through the Military Programming Law.
Quoted in the statement, Lieutenant Colonel Luís Henriques, Operational Coordinator of the AR5 Working Group of the Portuguese Air Force, argues that "the integration of the AR5 system represents a significant improvement in the operational capabilities of the Portuguese Air Force."
"This platform meets current surveillance, security and defence requirements, offering greater range, endurance and operational flexibility," he says, stressing that its integration "will strengthen the nation's ability to monitor the Exclusive Economic Zone and support a wide range of missions in the public interest, contributing to an Air Force better prepared to respond to current and future challenges."
For his part, Pedro Petiz, Director of Strategic Development at Tekever, points out that this contract "puts an autonomous capability developed and produced in Portugal" to work protecting the country's airspace and maritime territory. "In addition to supplying the aircraft, we will work with the Portuguese Air Force to consolidate and develop its own operational capability, which will strengthen national autonomy, readiness and responsiveness," he adds.
'Information-gathering' missions
The company describes the AR5 as a "fixed-wing unmanned aerial system, medium-altitude and long-endurance, designed for information-gathering missions over large areas". With a flight endurance of up to 20 hours and able to carry up to 50 kg of payload, the system "incorporates satellite communications (SATCOM), enabling operations beyond radio line-of-sight (BRLOS)."
Tekever systems have been gaining prominence on the market, having logged thousands of flight hours on coastal patrols, persistent surveillance, border protection, detection of suspicious activities, environmental protection and search-and-rescue missions.
The company has been signing contracts with various national and international entities, including the United Kingdom Home Office and the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA). Tekever systems are also currently in operation in Ukraine, where they undertake surveillance and reconnaissance missions in an operational environment.
Recently, one of the company's drones made headlines after managing to catch Russian forces off guard in the border region of Bryansk. The Portuguese-made AR3 reconnaissance drone, operated by the Ukrainian army, was shot down by Russian forces, then recovered and transferred to a research institute, where its technical and engineering features are expected to be studied.

What time will the eclipse be visible in my city? Solar eclipse times for 12 August in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:00:27 UTC
23:00:27 KST

The total solar eclipse will sweep across Spain this Wednesday at sunset, peaking at about 8.30 pm. Check when it will be visible in each city, where it will be total and when it will reach its maximum in Madrid and Barcelona.
Spain has a date with the sky this Wednesday, 12 August. The total solar eclipse will sweep across much of the country in the last hours of the afternoon, and millions of people will be able to watch one of the most eagerly awaited astronomical events of recent years.
But there is one key question before heading out to find a place to watch it: What time will the eclipse be visible in my city?
There is no single answer that applies to the whole of Spain. The Moon's shadow will move from west to east and the moment of maximum darkness will change slightly depending on the locality. Broadly speaking, the most eagerly awaited moment will arrive at around 20:30, although in some cities it will happen a few minutes earlier and in others, a little later.
And not all of Spain will be able to witness a total eclipse. The band of totality will cross parts of the northern and eastern mainland before reaching the Balearic Islands. Outside that band, the eclipse will be partial, although in many places the Sun will be almost completely covered.
What time will the eclipse be in each city?
These are the approximate times of the phase of totality in the main Spanish provincial capitals that will lie within the track of the lunar shadow:
- A Coruña: from 20:27 to 20:28. Totality will last approximately 1 minute and 18 seconds.
- Oviedo: between 20:27 and 20:28, with nearly 1 minute and 48 seconds of totality.
- Santander: between 20:26 and 20:28. Total darkness will last for around 1 minute and 2 seconds.
- Bilbao: at around 20:27, although totality will be much shorter: about 27 seconds.
- Vitoria-Gasteiz: between 20:27 and 20:28, for approximately 1 minute.
- Lugo: between 20:28 and 20:29, with 1 minute and 25 seconds of totality.
- León: between 20:28 and 20:30. Totality will last for around 1 minute and 45 seconds.
- Burgos: between 20:28 and 20:30, for approximately 1 minute and 43 seconds.
- Logroño: between 20:28 and 20:29, with around 1 minute and 19 seconds of totality.
- Palencia: between 20:29 and 20:30, for approximately 1 minute and 42 seconds.
- Soria: between 20:29 and 20:30, with 1 minute and 41 seconds of totality.
- Zaragoza: between 20:29 and 20:30, for approximately 1 minute and 23 seconds.
- Lérida: at around 20:29, with a totality of barely 24 seconds.
- Tarragona: between 20:29 and 20:30, for about 58 seconds.
- Zamora: between 20:30 and 20:31, with about 24 seconds of totality.
- Segovia: between 20:31 and 20:32. Totality will last approximately 1 minute.
- Guadalajara: between 20:31 and 20:32, for approximately 1 minute and 8 seconds.
- Teruel: between 20:31 and 20:32, with around 1 minute and 35 seconds of totality.
- Castellón: between 20:31 and 20:32, for approximately 1 minute and 34 seconds.
- Palma de Mallorca: between 20:31 and 20:32, with around 1 minute and 36 seconds of totality.
- Cuenca: between 20:32 and 20:33, for about 57 seconds.
- Valencia: between 20:32 and 20:33, with approximately 1 minute of totality.
What time will the eclipse be in Madrid and Barcelona?
Two of Spain's most populous cities will lie outside the main band of totality.
In Madrid, the eclipse will be partial and will reach its maximum at around 20:32. The situation is particularly unusual because the edge of the band of totality passes very close to the capital and reaches areas of the municipal boundary near Barajas.
In Barcelona there will also be no totality. The moment of maximum obscuration of the Sun will be at approximately 20:29.
That does not mean the event will go unnoticed. From both cities a very deep partial eclipse will be visible, although there will be no brief period of darkness experienced by locations lying within the band of totality.
The shadow will cross Spain in just a few minutes
The time differences between cities are explained by the route of the Moon's shadow. The zone of total darkness will enter from the west and will cross Spain heading towards the Balearic Islands.
That is why, while in places such as Santander, Oviedo or A Coruña the decisive moment will arrive at around 20:27, in eastern areas such as Valencia, Castellón or Palma it will take place several minutes later.
Everything will also happen with the Sun very close to the horizon. The eclipse will coincide with sunset, a circumstance that makes it especially important to choose a place with good visibility towards the west, without buildings, mountains or trees blocking the Sun in those crucial minutes.
An eclipse that will be visible throughout Spain
Those outside the band of totality will also be able to follow the event. The eclipse will be visible, at least partially, from all Spanish territory, including the Canary Islands.
The big difference will be those seconds in which the Moon manages to cover the solar disc completely. Within the band of totality, the sky will darken rapidly and it will be possible to observe the solar corona for a brief interval.
Outside it, a small part of the Sun will remain visible even at the maximum, so the sky will not take on the characteristic appearance of a total eclipse.
And one final warning will be crucial regardless of the city from which it is observed: you must not look directly at the Sun without certified protection during the partial phases of the eclipse. Ordinary sunglasses are not suitable for observing the event safely.

There is no single answer for the whole of Spain. The Moon’s shadow will move from west to east and the moment of maximum darkness will vary slightly depending on the location. In general terms, the most eagerly awaited moment will come at around 20:30, although in some cities it will occur a few minutes earlier and in others a little later.
What is more, not all of Spain will see a total eclipse. The path of totality will cross parts of the north and east of the peninsula before reaching the Balearic Islands. Outside that path, the eclipse will be partial, although in many places the Sun will be almost completely covered.
What time will the eclipse be in each city?
These are the approximate times of the totality phase in the main Spanish provincial capitals that lie within the path of the lunar shadow:
- La Coruña: from 20:27 to 20:28. Totality will last for approximately 1 minute and 18 seconds.
- Oviedo: between 20:27 and 20:28, with close to 1 minute and 48 seconds of totality.
- Santander: between 20:26 and 20:28. Total darkness will last for around 1 minute and 2 seconds.
- Bilbao: at around 20:27, although totality will be much shorter, at about 27 seconds.
- Vitoria-Gasteiz: between 20:27 and 20:28, lasting for roughly 1 minute.
- Lugo: between 20:28 and 20:29, with 1 minute and 25 seconds of totality.
- León: between 20:28 and 20:30. Totality will last for around 1 minute and 45 seconds.
- Burgos: between 20:28 and 20:30, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 43 seconds.
- Logroño: between 20:28 and 20:29, with around 1 minute and 19 seconds of totality.
- Palencia: between 20:29 and 20:30, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 42 seconds.
- Soria: between 20:29 and 20:30, with 1 minute and 41 seconds of totality.
- Zaragoza: between 20:29 and 20:30, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 23 seconds.
- Lérida: at around 20:29, with a totality of barely 24 seconds.
- Tarragona: between 20:29 and 20:30, lasting for about 58 seconds.
- Zamora: between 20:30 and 20:31, with around 24 seconds of totality.
- Segovia: between 20:31 and 20:32. Totality will last for approximately one minute.
- Guadalajara: between 20:31 and 20:32, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 8 seconds.
- Teruel: between 20:31 and 20:32, with around 1 minute and 35 seconds of totality.
- Castellón: between 20:31 and 20:32, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 34 seconds.
- Palma de Mallorca: between 20:31 and 20:32, with around 1 minute and 36 seconds of totality.
- Cuenca: between 20:32 and 20:33, lasting for about 57 seconds.
- Valencia: between 20:32 and 20:33, with approximately one minute of totality.
What time will the eclipse be in Madrid and Barcelona?
Two of Spain’s most populous cities will lie outside the main path of totality.
In Madrid, the eclipse will be partial and will reach its maximum at around 20:32. The situation is particularly unusual because the edge of the path of totality passes very close to the capital and reaches parts of the municipal area close to Barajas.
In Barcelona, totality will also not occur. The moment of maximum obscuration of the Sun will be at approximately 20:29.
That does not mean the phenomenon will go unnoticed. From both cities it will be possible to observe a very deep partial eclipse, although there will be no brief spell of darkness such as that experienced in towns and cities lying within the path of totality.
The shadow will cross Spain in just a few minutes
The time differences between cities are due to the path of the Moon’s shadow. The area of total darkness will enter from the west and cross Spain on its way towards the Balearic Islands.
That is why, while in places such as Santander, Oviedo or La Coruña the decisive moment will come at around 20:27, in locations further east such as Valencia, Castellón or Palma it will occur several minutes later.
All this will happen with the Sun very close to the horizon. The eclipse will coincide with sunset, a circumstance that will make it especially important to choose a place with a clear view to the west, without buildings, mountains or trees blocking the Sun in those crucial minutes.
An eclipse that will be visible across Spain
Those outside the path of totality will also be able to follow the event. The eclipse will be visible, at least partially, from all Spanish territory, including the Canary Islands.
The big difference will lie in those seconds when the Moon completely covers the solar disc. Within the path of totality, the sky will darken rapidly and it will be possible to observe the solar corona for a brief interval.
Outside that path, a small part of the Sun will remain visible even at maximum eclipse, so the sky will never take on the characteristic appearance of a total eclipse.
And one final warning will be essential, regardless of the city from which it is observed: you must not look directly at the Sun without certified protective equipment during the partial phases of the eclipse. Ordinary sunglasses are not suitable for observing the event safely.

How Africa is becoming a ‘strategic hub’ for Chinese industrial expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:00:07 UTC
23:00:07 KST

How Africa is becoming a ‘strategic hub’ for Chinese industrial expansion
Countries including Zimbabwe and Guinea are ending the pit-to-ship model that saw them exporting raw minerals with limited local gains
Today, nations such as Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Ghana and Guinea are dismantling that system – by banning exports of raw materials and enforcing local processing rules. These measures force international mining firms, including Chinese companies, to invest billions of dollars in domestic processing plants.
Now, instead of simply shipping out ore, Chinese firms are building local facilities to transform Zimbabwean lithium into its sulphate or carbonate forms, Guinean bauxite into alumina, and Mozambican graphite into battery materials.
According to Carlos Lopes, a professor at the University of Cape Town’s Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance, the shift runs far deeper than resource processing. “China increasingly sees Africa as one of the few remaining large-scale spaces where industrial expansion, urbanisation, infrastructure deployment and consumer growth can still unfold simultaneously over decades,” he said.
The continent was becoming less a peripheral supplier and more a strategic hub between fractured economic blocs, Lopes said, with Chinese firms more likely to localise where governments ensured policy clarity, reliable energy, domestic demand and regional scale.
“Bans on unprocessed exports will not necessarily deter investment,” he said, adding that the African countries imposing the bans could actually improve investment quality by forcing longer-term commitments.
However, these policies were only successful when states possessed negotiating discipline and institutional coherence, Lopes warned – otherwise, bans risked becoming blunt instruments that fuelled smuggling, policy volatility and elite rent-seeking.

Russia Produces 3,000 Geran-4/5 Drones a Month, Ukraine Says

Russia’s defense industry is producing around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 kamikaze drones per month, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (DIU) told Militarnyi in an inquiry published Wednesday, Aug. 12.
According to the Militarnyi, the serial production of the drones has been established at a facility in Russia’s Yelabuga, within the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, while other Russian companies supply components for the production chain.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The growing use of the drones is linked to improvements in their flight characteristics, particularly their ability to overcome Ukrainian air defenses, according to the DIU.
Russia expands production in Tatarstan
Despite the current production rate, Russia’s Defense Ministry is seeking to further expand manufacturing capacity at Alabuga.
Large-scale construction of new facilities was observed at the special economic zone in July 2026, according to satellite imagery cited by Militarnyi. Construction reportedly began in May, although the exact purpose of the new buildings remains unclear.
The expansion comes as Russia prepares to increase its use of jet-powered attack drones.
In June, then-Ukrainian Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrsky said jet-powered drones could eventually account for 50% of Russia’s attack UAVs used in attacks against Ukraine.
The latest DIU information provided to Militarnyi supports the assessment that Russia is increasing production of jet-powered variants of the Geran drone family.
Kremlin Removes Even Weak Opposition as Ukraine War Takes Toll
At the same time, the intelligence agency said Russia has halted production of the Geran-3 jet-powered kamikaze drone.
Geran-4 is faster and has a longer range
The Geran-4 is based on the concept of the earlier Geran-3 but has a more powerful engine and an airframe optimized for higher speeds.
The drone has a wingspan of around 3 meters and is approximately 3.5 meters long. Its maximum takeoff weight has increased from 350 to 450 kilograms.
The Geran-4 uses a turbojet engine producing 160 kilogram-force of thrust, roughly twice the thrust of the Chinese Telefly JT80 used by its predecessor.
According to Militarnyi, this allows the drone to reach a cruise speed of 350–500 kilometers per hour, compared with 280–330 km/h for the previous version.
Its reported range has also increased from 600 to 850 kilometers.
The Geran-4 can operate at altitudes between 100 and 5,000 meters and remain airborne for around 2.5 hours. Its warhead weighs at least 50 kilograms.
Geran-5 resembles a missile
The Geran-5 has a substantially different design from earlier members of the Geran family.
Instead of the delta-wing configuration associated with Shahed-type drones, the aircraft has a fuselage shape more closely resembling a cruise missile.
Militarnyi therefore describes the Geran-5 as a “missile-drone,” a category also being developed by Ukrainian defense manufacturers.
The Geran-5 carries a 90-kilogram warhead and has a reported attack range of around 1,000 kilometers.
It can also reportedly carry R-73 (NATO: AA-11, “Archer”) air-to-air missiles equipped with infrared seekers.
According to the DIU, the Geran-5 can be launched from aircraft, including Su-25 attack aircraft.
The growing production of Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones suggests Russia is seeking to supplement its large-scale Shahed-type drone campaign with faster and more capable systems that are more difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
On Aug. 12 Kyiv came under a second Russian drone attack, with air defenses engaging jet-powered drones approaching the capital from multiple directions. Kyiv Post team members across the city and surrounding villages reported hearing loud explosions as Russia continued its near-round-the-clock aerial attacks against Ukraine.
Earlier Russia targeted a shopping center in Zaporizhzhia overnight. The attack caused extensive damage to an Epicentr store, while overnight Russian attacks also killed two women in Kherson.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury has permanently eliminated beneficial ownership reporting requirements for domestic companies and individuals under the Corporate Transparency Act, gutting a major federal anti-money-laundering disclosure program for American small businesses.
The rule effectively exempts U.S. citizens operating domestic businesses from disclosing their beneficial ownership information as was mandated under the Corporate Transparency Act, a landmark anti-corruption law enacted in December 2020, aimed at combating money laundering and illicit finance.
Under the update, foreign companies must still report beneficial ownership information for foreign individuals to FinCEN. However, foreign companies are exempt from reporting ownership information regarding U.S. citizens, as well as details about Americans who assist them in registering to conduct business within the U.S.
FinCEN also announced that it will delete all previously collected information regarding U.S. business owners from its beneficial ownership database.

Retired Bundeswehr general says Nord Stream pipelines could have been legitimate target for Ukraine
Klaus Wittmann, a retired Bundeswehr brigadier general and lecturer in contemporary history at the University of Potsdam, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"I am prepared to go so far as to say that, from a military-strategic and moral perspective, this was a legitimate target," Wittmann said, commenting on whether Nord Stream could be considered a legitimate target if the German investigation's theory of Ukrainian involvement is confirmed.
At the same time, he stressed that he was not offering a legal assessment of the case and was not questioning the independence of the judiciary.
"I am not a lawyer and, of course, I do not want to question the independence of the judiciary. But if you look at the background, I was among those who strongly opposed Nord Stream 2," the retired general said.
According to him, the decision to build Nord Stream 2 was made after Russia had already occupied Crimea, despite warnings from Ukraine and Central and Eastern European countries.
"The decision on Nord Stream 2 was made when Crimea had already been occupied for a long time. Despite this, people continued to believe that Russia could be relied upon as a reliable supplier of cheap gas and called it a purely economic project. At the same time, they turned a blind eye to what the Baltic states, Poland and, of course, the Ukrainians had repeatedly told us: from Russia's perspective, it was a geopolitical project," Wittmann said.
He also recalled the position of Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
"Here I would like to quote Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who said that the problem was the construction of Nord Stream 2, not its destruction," Wittmann said.
At the same time, he acknowledged the seriousness of destroying someone else's property but urged that the case also be viewed in the broader political context of Russia's war.
"Of course, destroying someone else's property is a serious matter. But we also need to look at it from a political and psychological perspective and ask whether it is in Germany's interests for the first conviction for a 'war crime' in the war in Ukraine to be handed down against a Ukrainian – and in Germany, of all places?" Wittmann said.
He noted that he did not know how much room for maneuver Germany's Federal Prosecutor General's Office had in the case or "whether it was obliged to seek extradition."
"But given the scale and horror of Russia's war crimes, I do not consider it acceptable for the German justice system to focus primarily on a 'Ukrainian war crime,'" Wittmann said.
On September 26, 2022, explosions damaged three of the four pipelines of Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 in the Baltic Sea. In June 2026, Germany's Federal Prosecutor General's Office charged a Ukrainian citizen, identified as Serhii K., a former Ukrainian serviceman, with, among other offenses, aiding and abetting a war crime through an attack on a civilian object. According to the prosecution, the group acted on the orders of Ukrainian state bodies, with the aim of halting Russian gas supplies and depriving Russia of revenues that could be used to finance the war. In July 2026, Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office said that its investigation had found no evidence of involvement by Ukrainian state bodies or officials in organizing the explosions.

Lebanon passes a controversial general amnesty law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:53:02 UTC
22:53:02 KST

Lebanon passes a controversial general amnesty law
BEIRUT (AP) — Lebanon’s parliament Wednesday passed a controversial general amnesty law, a day after a majority of legislators voted to formally abolish the death penalty.
Lawmakers who backed the bill call it a beginning to correcting past overreach by the judiciary and security agencies and help reduce prison overcrowding, but critics say it is skewed and largely benefits Sunni Islamist prisoners.
The initial proposal, debated since 2019, has exposed sectarian tensions among the country’s multitude of Islamic and Christian sects.
A sweeping law that has exceptions
The last time Lebanon approved a similar amnesty was in 1991, when the majority of the country’s combatants and militia leadership were absolved of any atrocities and possible war crimes following the country’s devastating 1975-90 civil war that killed about 150,000 people and left 17,000 missing.
The new law replaces death sentences with long prison terms, reduces life sentences, and frees some convicted militants and drug dealers. It excludes rape, trafficking, corruption, terror funding, and premeditated murder, but reduces sentences for killing Lebanese troops. Some detainees will be released immediately.
Repeated drug offenders and Lebanese who have been convicted of collaborating with Israel were excluded from the amnesty.
It also remains unknown if the amnesty applies to Lebanese families who took refuge in Israel after occupying Israeli forces withdrew from southern Lebanon in 2000 but who were not involved in military operations against Lebanon.
Released foreign prisoners, mainly Syrian Islamist militant prisoners, would be transferred to Lebanon’s General Security intelligence agency that is responsible for enforcing immigration laws. It wasn’t immediately known if they would be deported.
Concerns rise over the fate of extremist Islamist prisoners
While the law was debated in parliament, lawmakers from various sects made different demands.
Sunnis wanted the release of Islamist militants while Shiites demanded drug dealers, mostly from Lebanon’s eastern Baalbek region where cannabis is planted, to be freed. Christians required amnesty for hundreds of Lebanese who fled to Israel after the Israeli withdrawal. Many have links to the Israeli-backed South Lebanon Army militia, which collapsed following the withdrawal.
However, the most controversial point in the yearslong debate was the fate of extremist Islamist prisoners, including firebrand cleric Ahmad al-Assir.
Al-Assir gained support in southern Lebanon for his vocal criticism of the powerful Shiite militant Hezbollah group’s involvement in Syria’s uprising that turned into civil war. In 2013, clashes between his supporters and opponents killed 18 Lebanese soldiers. He was sentenced to death in 2017.
His fate remains unclear, but Lebanese lawmaker Waddah Sadek, a Sunni Muslim and supporter of the law, told The Associated Press al-Assir could be released “between a year and a half and two years.”
Some celebrate while others feel wronged
Sunni legislators largely celebrated the law passing.
Bilal Abdullah, who represents the Druze-led Progressive Socialist Party, said the amnesty law is not intended to benefit just one sect.
“We are turning a political page where (Sunnis were) targeted, justly and unjustly,” Abdullah told reporters in parliament. “Targeted by a regime, security agencies, and unfortunately the military tribunal with some of its unjust convictions.”
Supporters of detained Islamists claim their sentencings came at a time when the Shiite Muslim Hezbollah militant group had greater political power in the country and larger sway over its security institutions and judicial system, directly targeting the country’s Sunni Muslims.
They also said the detainees weren’t allowed a fair trial and some were held for too long in pretrial detention due to Lebanon’s swamped courts.
Videos circulating on social media showed Islamist prisoners in the notorious Roumieh prison chanting “God is great” in celebration once the law was approved.
The families of the killed Lebanese soldiers have called the law a grave injustice, saying that the perpetrators behind the death of their loved ones should remain behind bars or even be sentenced to death.
Civil society and reformists have largely been critical of the move.
Activist and lawyer Nizar Saghieh, who co-founded the watchdog group Legal Agenda, said justice “comes through accountability and building institutions, not a general amnesty.”
Saghieh criticized lawmakers who called the amnesty a form of justice due to what they said were unfair trials in military and civil courts. However, they haven’t made any real structural reforms, he said.
“They talk about injustice in military courts, but they are still functioning as before.”

The empire’s last aces: Russia in the skies of World War I
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:52:07 UTC
22:52:07 KST

The empire’s last aces: Russia in the skies of World War I
When we think of WWI-era aviation, what usually comes to mind is the ‘Red Baron’ and Zeppelin raids—in short, most people think of the Western Front in all its fury. However, few people know that during the First World War, Russia was waging its own aerial war, full of challenges and drama.
Dreaming of the skies
Aviation pioneer Igor Sikorsky didn’t plan to build a bomber. What he designed was a luxury passenger airliner—a flying hotel with four 100-horsepower engines, a lounge and bedroom. The interior of the plane was heated by an ingenious design that channeled exhaust gases from the engines into a special pipe. The plane even had balconies.In 1914, the aircraft was stripped of all its luxury and transformed into the Ilya Muromets- type long-range bomber. War broke out and Russia repurposed everything for the needs of the army.
The development of Russian aviation started even before WWI. In the fall of 1911, a dozen aircraft and an airship took part in exercises in the Warsaw Military District (Poland was then part of Russia). The aircraft were used for reconnaissance and communications. The result was quite impressive: the aviators accurately reported the location of the simulated enemy. Soon enough, they had to fight a real enemy. In 1912, the Russians sent a detachment to fight the Turks jointly with the Bulgarian forces. Experiments with light aerial bombs were carried out at this time. In short, a foundation for the development of aviation was laid.
In general, aircraft development progressed quickly in Russia. Foreign aircraft were assembled under license, and later, Russians began experimenting with constructing their own aircraft models. Russian aviation was very lucky to have an influential lobbyist. Grand Duke Alexander Mikhailovich, the first cousin once removed of Russian Emperor Nicholas II, was very fond of aeronautics and actively advocated for the establishment of aviation schools, the purchase of aircraft, and the development of aviation. Before the war, the Russian Imperial Air Force had 244 aircraft and 300 pilots; this was the largest air force among the belligerent powers.
Russia’s main problem during the time (and in fact, this challenge persists to this day) is that it had plenty of bright minds capable of understanding the benefits of aviation; it had original designs and small-scale production of unique aircraft. However, it lacked the industrial base to create a large, continuously replenished air fleet, one that would be resilient to losses and that could decisively influence the course of military operations.
At the beginning of the war, the Russian air force was organized into corps-based aviation detachments. At first, airplanes had to compete with aerostats: the army command considered the latter the primary means of aerial reconnaissance. In fact, there was initially a prejudice against aviators. One of the tragedies of the early days of the war—the defeat of the Russian 2nd Army in East Prussia—was partly due to General Samsonov’s mistrust of aerial reconnaissance. Having received a warning from pilots about a German force on his flank, he ignored it and instead chose to believe the intelligence, which did not confirm this information. The outcome was tragic; despite possessing a formidable new weapon, the commander failed to utilize its capabilities.
However, aviation firmly established itself in the battle formations. The Russian army quickly adopted aerial photography and less conservative military commanders made good use of it.
Specially-designed fighter aircraft did not yet exist. If pilots from hostile nations met in the air, they could only fire at each other from pistols. Staff Captain Pyotr Nesterov became a landmark figure in Russian aviation for achieving the first aerial ramming. Nesterov hoped to survive this feat, but the airplanes of the time were too fragile; as his landing gear hit the wing of the Austrian Albatross aircraft, his plane’s engine broke off. Aleksandr Kozakov was more fortunate. This pilot attempted to attach a grappling hook to his aircraft: it dangled beneath, posing a danger to the plane. However, Kozakov managed to hit the enemy with the propeller and then made it back to the airfield. He became the first pilot to survive an attempt to ram his aircraft into another airplane.
The primary losses were due to the rapid wear and tear of the aircraft. The planes were unreliable and often malfunctioned even without any contact with the enemy. The weakness of the industrial base also took its toll: in 1915, factories supplied only 157 aircraft to the army. Because of this, repairmen had to resort to tricks to get existing aircraft to fly, and, when possible, pilots used captured aircraft.
Being a Russian pilot at the time was, to put it mildly, no sinecure. By the beginning of 1915, 33 pilots had died. Due to their design and low ceiling, the aircraft were often hit by artillery or even infantry fire.
In the midst of battle
In 1915, the resources of the Russian air force were stretched to the limit. The Germans shifted the bulk of their efforts to the Eastern Front, and the Russian army was forced into the Great Retreat. The army suffered heavy losses and abandoned Poland and Galicia, retreating eastward. Aviation softened the blow and helped predict the site of the attacks, thereby at least preventing the encirclement of ground units. By this stage, the war had turned into a never-ending series of trench assaults, and the cavalry was no longer useful as a reconnaissance force. Pilots, however, could detect enemy defenses from the air and track movements in the enemy’s rear.
There was a shortage of pilots, and the air force was replenished with some unusual figures. For example, the only black Russian aviator, Marcel Pliat, served on Ilya Muromets bombers. He was born in Polynesia, came to Russia by chance, and settled in the country. When the war began, he became a mechanic and gunner on a bomber. Several times, the agile Polynesian climbed onto the wing right in the middle of the flight to repair damage to his airplane, and in the fall of 1916, he shot down two German aircraft in a single battle. By the end of the war, he was awarded two St. George Crosses – Russia’s highest awards for bravery in combat.
Air combat was still rare at the time. Most often, a pilot carried a pistol or carbine. Ilya Muromets bombers were the only exception – these heavy bombers could carry heavy loads. They weren’t agile, which could prove fatal during combat with fighter aircraft, but the crew carried several light machine guns. Equipped with Lewis and Madsen light machine guns, the Russian bombers turned into flying batteries. During the war, Ilya Muromets bombers brought down an impressive number of enemy aircraft while only one bomber was destroyed directly by enemy fire.
Around the same time, Lieutenant Pokrovsky and Cornet Plonsky scored a victory reminiscent of the Indiana Jones films or ‘TaleSpin’. The duo approached an Austrian airplane and began firing at it with Mauser pistols. The Austrians surrendered shortly afterward and landed within Russian-controlled lines. This is an extremely rare example of victory in aerial combat achieved by means of a pistol.
1915 saw the widespread installation of machine guns on airplanes. That summer, a notable air duel occurred between Ensign Ivanov accompanied by observer Lieutenant Alekseyev, and an Austrian aircraft over Ternopil (present-day western Ukraine). The pilots approached each other, exchanged fire, and retreated; during the pauses, the Russians and Austrians exchanged greetings. Finally, the Austrian plane caught fire and crashed over Russian-held territory. A day later, the Russians dropped a photo on an Austrian airfield: the fallen Austrian pilots were buried with full military honors, and, according to military aviation custom, with propellers placed on their graves.
The Russian air fleet remained small. By the end of 1915, only 322 operational aircraft were at the front. There were significantly fewer airplanes than in the West, and the Russian pilots bore a heavier burden of war, since the planes were expected to provide as much support as possible to the bleeding ground forces.
The Ilya Muromets bomber vividly demonstrates both the success and failure of the Imperial Russian Air Force. The four-engine long-range bomber, converted from a comfortable passenger airliner, proved to be a very capable aircraft. The Ilya Muromets performed well, and this prompted the Russian army to form the Squadron of Heavy Aircraft. Muromets bombers could fly at an altitude of about 3,000 meters, were out of reach of the anti-aircraft fire of the time, and bombed large stationary targets, from railway stations to airfields. It was very difficult to shoot the bomber down: the crew was armed with machine guns, and the aircraft flew at a high altitude. Moreover, it could survive even serious damage. Only two bombers were lost to enemy fire. However, technical malfunctioning due to wear and tear and other flight accidents were much more common. Repairs proved challenging, and only 80 Muromets bombers were produced during the war. Often only a dozen remained in service at the front, while the rest awaited repairs. Moreover, the majority of Russian aircraft were of Western design, and the aviation depended on supplies of components from Britain and France.
The last aces of the empire
1916 was marked by a massive offensive on the Southwestern Front. In Galicia, the Russians managed to shake the entire southern section of their front. The plan was to launch a simultaneous attack on several Austrian armies. One of the tactics that proved very useful to the Russians was aerial photography. The Russians had an artillery group, which wasn’t large enough to break through such an extended front. However, what they lacked in striking power, they made up for in accuracy. The positional front allowed them to devote considerable time to their work and make detailed, high-quality photographs of the Austrian positions. Accordingly, the artillerymen fired directly at well-known targets. The 1916 offensive was the Russian Army’s greatest success during the First World War, and in general one of the largest victories on the battlefields during WWI. And aviation played a huge role in this success.
The era left its mark on everything that concerned aviation. In those times, the pilot could not count on ejection, and the airplanes were easily damaged. On the other hand, pilots often made repairs right in the air. For example, during reconnaissance, second lieutenant Georgy Kovenko was attacked by a German Fokker aircraft and his plane suffered damage. Kovenko managed to plug the hole in his radiator pipe with a glove and tie it with a binocular strap, and made it to his airfield.
In 1916, fighter aircraft groups became a separate combat detachment in the Russian army. At the same time, a progressive organizational idea was implemented. Russian aviation was divided into air squads, and each squad was assigned to a formation of ground forces. In 1916, three air squads were joined to form the Combat Aviation Group (BAG). This fighter group was dispatched to dangerous areas. The group received new planes with machine guns capable of firing through the propeller. This made it much easier to fight. Gradually, Russian aviation adapted to the requirements of the time. The peculiar features of the Eastern Front remained the same: both sides had fewer airplanes compared to the Western Front, and the front was much longer. This meant that the role of the individual pilot was higher and a good aviator was often irreplaceable.
Biplanes were very unreliable. Over half of all the pilots who died perished due to technical aircraft failures; about a quarter died due to piloting errors and only about another quarter of the pilots were killed as a result of enemy actions. And yet, each day, these pilots rose into the sky to fight. Alas, it turned out to be a swan song: in 1917, the revolution broke out in Russia.
A characteristic episode occurred in the fall of 1917 between the best fighter pilot in Russia, Alexander Kozakov (the one who rammed into the enemy aircraft and survived to tell the story) and his colleague Ivan Pavlov. Kozakov congratulated Pavlov for taking down a German airplane, and said that if it had been in his power, he would have immediately promoted him to officer. Pavlov coldly replied, “No, thank you, officers are not in fashion now.” Pavlov soon joined the Red Army Air Force, which at first tried to completely abolish the old military hierarchy. Kozakov served in the White Army, and died as a result of an air crash that resembled suicide.
The Imperial Russian Air Service was established and effectively dissolved in the course of WWI – the only war in which it participated. In the next war, it was up to others to rise into the air and fight.

Syria slams Colombia for recognizing Israeli 'sovereignty' in Golan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:50:00 UTC
22:50:00 KST

Syria has formally protested Colombia's recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights, sending letters to the U.N. secretary-general and Security Council president, state media reported Wednesday.
According to SANA, the letters conveyed Syria’s protest, condemnation and categorical rejection of Colombia’s recognition of what it described as "Israeli sovereignty" over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights.
Earlier Monday, Colombia’s Foreign Ministry announced its recognition of what it called Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, citing continuing regional instability in the Middle East and the plateau’s strategic importance to Israel’s security.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar welcomed the decision, making Colombia the second country after the U.S. to recognize Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights. Washington took the same step in 2019 during U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term.
Earlier, Syria’s Foreign Ministry rejected and condemned Colombia’s decision, saying it was based on security justifications inconsistent with international law.
The ministry said the Colombian position contradicted statements by U.N. chief Antonio Guterres affirming that the Golan Heights are Syrian territory and that the U.N. unequivocally recognizes them as part of Syria.
It also said the decision violated the principle prohibiting the acquisition of territory by force and U.N. Security Council Resolution 497 of 1981.
The EU reiterated Wednesday that, in line with international law and U.N. Security Council Resolutions 242 and 497, it does not recognize Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights.
In remarks to SANA, the bloc called on Israel to respect the demilitarized buffer zone in the Golan and comply with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
It also reaffirmed its support for the U.N. Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF), which monitors the occupied territory, and stressed the importance of Security Council Resolution 497.
The EU also urged Israel to respect Syria’s independence, sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity and to refrain from actions that would undermine Security Council Resolutions 497 and 2799.
It further called on all parties to exercise maximum restraint, avoid further violence and comply with international law, including international humanitarian law, while expressing support for diplomatic efforts aimed at preventing further escalation, including dialogue between Israel and Syria.
Israel has occupied most of the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967 and annexed the territory in 1981, a move rejected by the UN as "null and void” under Resolution 497.

New Ebola variant linked to unknown animal source – study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:49:39 UTC
22:49:39 KST

New Ebola variant linked to unknown animal source – study
Scientists have identified a new variant of the Ebola-causing Bundibugyo virus behind the 2026 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) and Uganda, according to a study published in Nature Medicine on Monday.
Bundibugyo strain is not new: variants of the pathogen caused outbreaks in Uganda in 2007-2008 and the DR Congo in 2012. However, researchers found that the strain circulating in 2026 began with a new transmission of the virus from an animal to humans, rather than the re-emergence of strains responsible for previous epidemics in the region. The animal source remains unknown.
The conclusion is based on an analysis of 22 viral genomes obtained from infected people in the DR Congo and Uganda, which formed a distinct genetic cluster separate from variants linked to the previous outbreaks.
The researchers called for broader local diagnostic capacity and expanded genomic surveillance to detect future outbreaks earlier.
Bundibugyo virus, or BDBV, belongs to the same group of viruses as the better-known Zaire ebolavirus and can cause severe Ebola disease. That form of the virus is carried by fruit bats and spreads through direct contact with infected animals or bodily fluids from infected individuals. Symptoms of Bundibugyo strain include fever, severe headaches, muscle and body pain, weakness, fatigue, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, and loss of appetite.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has described the current virus as the largest Ebola epidemic ever recorded in the DR Congo, surpassing the 2018-2020 outbreak. The agency’s Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned last week that the disease was spreading faster than efforts to contain it.
The outbreak had spread across 53 health zones in five provinces of the DR Congo as of August 10, with Ituri remaining the main epicenter, according to the country’s Health Ministry. The authorities have recorded 4,449 confirmed cases and 2,061 deaths, putting the fatality rate at 46.3%.
Neighboring Uganda, meanwhile, declared itself Ebola-free last month after recording 20 cases, 15 of which were imported from the DR Congo. Two people died and 18 recovered.

Lebanon passes a controversial general amnesty law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:48:24 UTC
22:48:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon passes a controversial general amnesty law
Lebanon's parliament Wednesday passed a controversial general amnesty law, a day after a majority of legislators voted to become the first Arab state to formally abolish the death penalty.
Lawmakers who backed the bill call it a beginning to correcting past overreach by the judiciary and security agencies and help reduce prison overcrowding, but critics say it is skewed and largely benefits Sunni Islamist prisoners.
The initial proposal, debated since 2019, has exposed sectarian tensions among the country's multitude of Islamic and Christian sects.
A sweeping law with exceptions 
The last time Lebanon approved a similar amnesty was in 1991, when the majority of the country’s combatants and militia leadership were absolved of any atrocities and possible war crimes following the country's devastating 1975-90 civil war that killed about 150,000 people and left 17,000 missing.
The new law replaces death sentences with long prison terms, reduces life sentences, and frees some convicted militants and drug dealers. It excludes rape, trafficking, corruption, terror funding, and premeditated murder, but reduces sentences for killing Lebanese troops. Some detainees will be released immediately.
Repeated drug offenders and Lebanese who have been convicted of collaborating with Israel were excluded from the amnesty.
It also remains unknown if the amnesty applies to Lebanese families who took refuge in Israel after occupying Israeli forces withdrew from southern Lebanon in 2000 but who were not involved in military operations against Lebanon.
Released foreign prisoners, mainly Syrian Islamist militant prisoners, would be transferred to Lebanon’s General Security intelligence agency that is responsible for enforcing immigration laws. It wasn't immediately known if they would be deported.
The fate of extremist Islamist prisoners 
While the law was debated in parliament, lawmakers from various sects made different demands.
Sunnis wanted the release of Islamist militants while Shias demanded drug dealers, mostly from Lebanon’s eastern Baalbek region where cannabis is planted, to be freed. Christians required amnesty for hundreds of Lebanese who fled to Israel after the Israeli withdrawal. Many have links to the Israeli-backed South Lebanon Army militia, which collapsed following the withdrawal.
However, the most controversial point in the yearslong debate was the fate of extremist Islamist prisoners, including firebrand cleric Ahmad al-Assir.
Al-Assir gained support in southern Lebanon for his vocal criticism of the powerful Shia militant Hezbollah group’s involvement in Syria's uprising that turned into civil war. In 2013, clashes between his supporters and opponents killed 18 Lebanese soldiers. He was sentenced to death in 2017.
His fate remains unclear, but Lebanese lawmaker Waddah Sadek, a Sunni Muslim and supporter of the law, told The Associated Press al-Assir could be released "between a year and a half and two years."
Some celebrate while others feel wronged 
Sunni legislators largely celebrated the law passing.
Bilal Abdullah, who represents the Druze-led Progressive Socialist Party, said the amnesty law is not intended to benefit just one sect.
"We are turning a political page where (Sunnis were) targeted, justly and unjustly," Abdullah told reporters in parliament. "Targeted by a regime, security agencies, and unfortunately the military tribunal with some of its unjust convictions."
Supporters of detained Islamists claim their sentencings came at a time when the Shia Hezbollah group had greater political power in the country and larger sway over its security institutions and judicial system, directly targeting the country's Sunni Muslims.
They also said the detainees weren't allowed a fair trial and some were held for too long in pretrial detention due to Lebanon's swamped courts.
Videos circulating on social media showed Islamist prisoners in the notorious Roumieh prison chanting "God is great" in celebration once the law was approved.
The families of the killed Lebanese soldiers have called the law a grave injustice, saying that the perpetrators behind the death of their loved ones should remain behind bars or even be sentenced to death.
Civil society and reformists have largely been critical of the move.
Activist and lawyer Nizar Saghieh, who co-founded the watchdog group Legal Agenda, said justice "comes through accountability and building institutions, not a general amnesty."
Saghieh criticised lawmakers who called the amnesty a form of justice due to what they said were unfair trials in military and civil courts. However, they haven't made any real structural reforms, he said. "They talk about injustice in military courts, but they are still functioning as before."

Colombia declares three days mourning for quake victims as EU pledges assistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:46:52 UTC
22:46:52 KST

The quake overwhelmed parts of the health system, turning the rescue effort into one of Colombia's largest disaster responses in years.
Colombia declared three days of mourning on Wednesday for the victims of an earthquake that demolished buildings in the west of the country, killing more than 200 people.
At magnitude 7.4, Monday's quake was the strongest to hit Colombia in a century.
The government said flags would be lowered to half-staff on official buildings, as well as at Colombian embassies around the world, "in honour of all the dead."
Frantic attempts to find survivors continued, as authorities revised the death toll down to 216 after local officials in Cali corrected earlier figures.
In Pereira and in Cali, emergency crews used cranes, dogs and heavy machinery to search ruined buildings while volunteers formed human chains to clear debris by hand, hoping to reach people still trapped beneath collapsed structures.
The first two days after an earthquake are crucial for finding survivors under rubble, with some experts saying there is a 72-hour window, after which hopes quickly tail off.
There was joy on Tuesday when rescuers pulled out 32-year-old Daniela Largo.
"We were losing hope and then we received a call," said her mother Sandra Milena Perez in Pereira.
Perez said a local resident heard cries for help beneath the rubble and joined neighbours in removing debris before professional rescuers arrived.
From the air, neighbourhoods in Cali appeared flattened, with piles of grey rubble replacing entire blocks of homes and apartment buildings.
Nearby, cars lay crushed beneath fallen walls and concrete slabs.
The quake overwhelmed parts of the health system, turning the rescue effort into one of Colombia's largest disaster responses in years.
Many survivors spent the night outdoors, either because their homes were damaged or because they feared aftershocks.
One park in Pereira was transformed into a makeshift shelter with tents and mattresses.
"We lost everything, but we're alive," said 23-year-old John Tabasco, who was camped there with his wife and seven-month-old son.
In Cali, part of the Hospital Universitario del Valle collapsed during the quake, forcing doctors to move patients into a parking lot and treat some in the open air.
Thousands brought water, food and supplies to affected neighbourhoods, while long lines formed outside blood donation centres.
"It's about wanting to help your community, your city and your country," said blood donor Ferney Cabrera.
President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a state of emergency and promised rent subsidies for affected families during a visit to Pereira on Tuesday.
Help from Europe
Meanwhile, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday that the European Union would provide €2.1 million to Colombia to support its most affected areas.
“As search and rescue operations continue, the EU is supporting Colombia wherever possible,” she said in a statement posted on X.
The funding will provide health, water, sanitation and hygiene material, as well as shelter, food, protection and cash assistance.
The president of the EU executive added that Colombia has activated the bloc’s civil protection mechanism, which is designed to pool resources from the 27 member states to effectively provide assistance to the nation that triggered it.
Von der Leyen previously said the EU had mobilised Copernicus, the bloc’s satellite service, to help with rescue operations.
EU support is already operating on the ground, with the bloc's humanitarian partner, the German Red Cross, reallocating €100,000 from an EU-funded project to meet the immediate needs of 2,500 families affected in Choco and Valle del Cauca.

2026-08-12

Blue Bird Airways will significantly expand its Israel-Italy operations in September, offering direct flights from Tel Aviv to four Italian destinations, the airline announced.
The Greek carrier will add Rome, Bologna and Naples to its schedule, alongside its existing service to Bergamo, near Milan, which has been operating since May 2026.
The expansion will make Italy one of Blue Bird Airways’ main markets from Ben-Gurion Airport, with some routes operating daily and others several times a week.
New routes connect Tel Aviv with Rome, Bologna and Naples
Flights to Rome are scheduled to begin on September 3 with three weekly services. From September 13, the route is expected to operate daily.
Flights to Bologna will begin on September 2 and operate three times a week, on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.
Service to Naples is scheduled to launch on September 16 with two weekly flights, on Wednesdays and Fridays. From September 25, a Monday flight will be added, bringing the route to three weekly services.
Blue Bird’s existing Bergamo route will continue operating daily, giving passengers access to Milan and northern Italy.
Blue Bird and TUS Airways to operate Italy flights
The flights will be operated by Blue Bird Airways and TUS Airways. Both airlines are owned by Kavei Hufsha, also known in English as Holiday Lines, which is owned by Arnon Englender and Ami Cohen.
Tickets are available through the airlines’ websites, travel agents, and flight-search platforms in Israel and abroad.
“Italy continues to be one of the most popular vacation destinations for Israelis, as reflected in both demand and Ben-Gurion Airport statistics showing a rise in passenger traffic to the country,” Englender said.
He said operating flights to four Italian destinations would give travelers more options for reaching different parts of the country.
“Expanding our operations to four destinations allows us to offer a broader response to travelers, whether they are planning a vacation in northern, central or southern Italy,” Englender said.
He also pointed to the timing of the new routes ahead of the autumn travel season and the Jewish High Holidays.
“Autumn is one of the best times to travel in Italy, featuring pleasant weather, fewer crowds, and coinciding with the Jewish High Holidays, allowing for longer and more flexible trips,” he said.
The company said round-trip fares would start at €270.
“We believe the combination of diverse destinations, high frequencies and competitive round-trip prices starting from €270 will drive continued growth in passenger traffic between the countries,” Englender said.

Chinese manjha is generally made using synthetic or plastic material.
NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has found a rather unusual way to join the viral ‘kuchu-puchu’ Gen Z trend, using internet humour to deliver a serious warning about kite-flying strings.In a recent social media post, the police urged residents to enjoy kite flying but stay away from banned Chinese manjha and plastic-coated strings, which can cause serious injuries to people and animals.“Dear Kuchu Puchu, Patang Udao but Say NO to Chinese Manjha, Samjhe?” the police wrote, giving its usual safety messaging a more playful, social media-friendly tone.The message comes as authorities step up action against the banned string in Delhi. The Crime Branch recently seized more than 1,300 rolls of Chinese manjha during an enforcement operation. In a separate action, Central Delhi Police recovered around 120 rolls.The post quickly drew reactions online, with some users poking fun at the police for adopting the language of Gen Z.“Gen-Z mode of Delhi Police”, “They are updating”, some comments read. Behind the light-hearted presentation, however, is a serious safety concern.
Chinese manjha is generally made using synthetic or plastic material and can be coated with abrasive substances. Because of its sharpness, it can cause deep cuts and injuries.
It can also become particularly dangerous for birds, which can get caught in the string while flying. There have already been fatal consequences in Delhi.Recently, a 32-year-old man travelling to Mundka for business suffered a cut to his neck after coming into contact with Chinese manjha in southwest Delhi's Uttam Nagar.
In another tragic incident in 2023, a seven-year-old girl died after being injured by Chinese manjha while travelling with her father on a scooter in west Delhi's Paschim Vihar.The police's latest post therefore carries a straightforward message beneath all the social media humour. People can continue flying kites and enjoying the activity, but using banned synthetic strings can put lives at risk.The campaign also reflects a broader change in the way police departments communicate with the public, with serious safety warnings increasingly being delivered through the language, trends and humour that dominate social media.

South Korea’s media regulator on Wednesday concluded that Google and Apple have violated the country’s telecommunications law by abusing their dominant positions in their respective app marketplaces.
The Korea Media Communications Commission reached the decision during a regular meeting, while the level of sanctions against the two US technology giants will be determined later, Seoul-based Yonhap News Agency reported.
The case centers on a 2021 revision to South Korea’s Telecommunications Business Act aimed at preventing major app marketplace operators from forcing developers to exclusively use their proprietary in-app payment systems.
Under the change, Google and Apple allowed customers to make purchases through third-party payment systems.
However, the companies imposed transaction fees of around 26% on purchases made using alternative payment methods, prompting criticism that the charges effectively undermined the purpose of the legislation.
South Korea became the first country to impose legal restrictions on major app-store operators over mandatory in-app payment systems.
In October 2023, the country’s media watchdog warned that it planned to impose the maximum possible fines on Google and Apple over their payment practices.
The regulator, however, has yet to carry out those penalties.

Ukraine Spots One of Russia’s Main Self-Propelled Guns—and Takes It Out Almost Immediately
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:42:33 UTC
22:42:33 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Spots One of Russia’s Main Self-Propelled Guns—and Takes It Out Almost Immediately
Ukrainian drone operators needed only minutes to locate and destroy a Russian 2S19 Msta-S self-propelled howitzer, with released footage showing the artillery system bursting into flames before its ammunition began detonating.
The strike was carried out by pilots from the Northern Eagle drone unit of Ukraine’s 151st Separate Mechanized Brigade, the brigade reported on August 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the unit, Ukrainian aerial reconnaissance first detected the Russian artillery system before strike drones were immediately sent to engage it. Only several minutes passed between the initial sighting and the destruction of the vehicle.
Footage released by the brigade shows the Msta-S being hit and catching fire, followed by secondary detonations from inside the vehicle.
The 2S19 Msta-S is one of the Russian military’s main 152mm self-propelled artillery systems and is regularly used to strike Ukrainian defensive positions, logistics routes, and settlements near the front line.
The system entered service in 1989 and was developed at the Uraltransmash plant to replace older Soviet self-propelled artillery. It uses a tracked chassis incorporating components from both the T-72 and T-80 tank families and is powered by a V-84A diesel engine.
Its steel armor is designed to protect its five-person crew from small-arms fire and artillery fragments.
The Msta-S is armed with a 152mm 2A64 rifled gun equipped with a semi-automatic loading mechanism. When firing ammunition stored onboard, the system can reach a rate of fire of up to eight rounds per minute.
The vehicle carries as many as 50 artillery rounds.
Its ammunition options include high-explosive fragmentation, smoke, illumination, radio-jamming, and other specialized 152mm projectiles. The system can also fire Krasnopol laser-guided precision ammunition.
With conventional high-explosive shells, the Msta-S can engage targets at ranges of approximately 24.7 kilometers, or about 15 miles. Rocket-assisted ammunition can extend that reach to roughly 29 kilometers, or 18 miles.
For close-range protection, the vehicle also carries a remotely operated 12.7mm machine gun mounted on top of the turret.
Previously, Ukrainian FPV drone operators tracked down and destroyed a Russian BM-21 Grad carrying a full ammunition load, triggering an explosion so powerful that only a single wheel was left behind.

Russia Has Built Up 6,200 Shahed Drones—and Its Biggest Barrages Could Reach 1,000 at Once
Russia has accumulated roughly 6,200 Geran strike drones of various versions as of August 2026, Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence told Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi on August 12.
The stockpile is intended to support large-scale combined attacks against Ukraine, allowing Russian forces to unleash much heavier drone waves after periods of accumulation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, Russia’s current production capacity is still insufficient to sustain its highest launch rates over the long term. Instead, Moscow has to build up large reserves of strike drones before carrying out its biggest attacks.
That means periods of lower launch activity do not necessarily indicate a decline in Russia’s ability to strike Ukraine. In many cases, they may simply reflect an effort to rebuild inventories ahead of another major barrage.
Ukraine’s intelligence service estimates that Russia’s most intense drone attacks could involve between 600 and 1,000 UAVs in a single wave.
During periods when Russia is replenishing its stocks, Russian forces typically launch around 150 to 200 drones per attack, while heavier strikes during those phases can rise to roughly 300 drones.
The estimated 6,200-drone reserve gives Moscow enough inventory to prepare multiple large-scale attacks even if its factories cannot replace the weapons at the same pace they are fired.
Geran drones have become a central element of Russia’s long-range strike campaign against Ukraine, often used alongside ballistic and cruise missiles in attempts to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia’s defense industry produces approximately 3,000 Geran-4/5 strike drones each month.

German inflation reaches 2.8 pct in July as economists warn of further rise
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
21:41:33 CST
22:41:33 KST

BERLIN, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Germany's inflation rate accelerated from the previous two months to reach 2.8 percent in July, official data showed Wednesday, while economists warned that record-low water levels on the Rhine could add further price pressures in the coming months.
"Energy prices continued to increase at an above-average rate and therefore remained the key driver of inflation," said Ruth Brand, president of the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis). Germany's inflation rate stood at 2.3 percent in June and 2.6 percent in May respectively.
Brand said the sharp rise in motor fuel prices was driven by higher oil prices resulting from the ongoing war in the Middle East as well as the expiry of the government's temporary fuel tax cut at the end of June.
The German government introduced a two-month tax cut on petrol and diesel in May, reducing taxes by around 17 euro cents (0.2 U.S. dollars) per liter. The measure helped cushion the impact of higher oil prices on consumers through June.
Energy prices rose 8.3 percent year-on-year in July, significantly faster than the 3.4-percent increase in June and 6.6-percent rise in May, when the fuel tax cut was in effect, according to Destatis.
Germany had already experienced a sharp energy-driven inflation surge earlier this year. In April, disruptions to global oil supplies by the war in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent oil prices sharply higher, pushing German inflation to 2.9 percent, its highest level since January 2024.
Meanwhile, persistently low water levels on the Rhine, caused by prolonged drought and extreme heat across Europe, are creating fresh inflation risks. Water levels at Kaub, a key shipping choke point on the Rhine, have fallen to record lows, severely restricting cargo transport along Germany's most important industrial shipping route.
Simon Gerards Iglesias, an economist at the German Economic Institute (IW), said low river levels could eventually feed through into higher energy and goods prices and directly affect consumer prices, as vessels are forced to carry less cargo and transport times increase.
He also warned that refineries along the Rhine could struggle to receive sufficient crude oil in time, affecting the production and distribution of petrol and diesel and adding further upward pressure on fuel prices.
Felix Schmidt, economist at Berenberg Bank, estimated that persistent low water levels on the Rhine could temporarily add as much as 0.5 percentage points to Germany's inflation rate. ■
