MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. Ukrainian nationals liable for military service will be automatically registered with the military when applying for consular services abroad, the Strana news outlet reported, citing new rules for checking the documents of draft-age men, approved by the cabinet.
"Those with no entry in the database will be automatically placed on the military register and a digital military document will be formed," the document reads.
The document authorizes consular services to be provided to men who do not have a military registration document, but only if they "update their personal data by registering with the consulate." Meanwhile, the electronic consular system and military register will be interconnected.
Men will not be required to travel to Ukraine to undergo an examination by a military medical commission. They will be placed on the military register based on their registered address in Ukraine, while those without one will be processed by a local recruitment office designated by the General Staff.
The media outlet pointed out that, under the new regulation, information on conscripts, those liable for military service and reservists would be stored in the digital register throughout their period of military registration and for 75 years thereafter.
In February 2022, Ukraine launched a general mobilization, which has since been extended repeatedly. The country's authorities have taken various measures to prevent draft-age men from evading military service. Videos showing violent mobilization efforts and clashes with military recruitment officials regularly emerge on social media from across Ukraine. Amid critical troop shortages, recruitment offices have stepped up raids in public places, while draft-age men are doing all they can to leave the country, sometimes risking their lives.

Mount Etna eruption: Catania airport closes and ash cloud reaches as far as Libya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:00:41 UTC
22:00:41 KST

The eruption of Mount Etna continues to bring air traffic in Sicily to a standstill, forcing Catania–Fontanarossa airport to close temporarily as ash reached Malta and as far away as Libya.
The eruption of Sicil's Mount Etna volcano, now in its sixth consecutive day, continues to disrupt air traffic in the island at the height of the summer season.
On Wednesday, Catania–Fontanarossa Airport was forced to suspend all arrivals and departures until 6 pm.
According to data from the airport's tracking system, around 55 outbound flights have been cancelled, on top of roughly 388 departures scrapped between the start of the eruption and the previous day.
Dozens of other flights have been rescheduled or diverted to other airports in the region, notably Palermo, Trapani and Comiso.
At the latter airport, operations were halted for several hours on Wednesday morning, until 10 am, because of volcanic ash.
The airport later resumed operations, with both departures and arrivals restored.
Etna causes disruption beyond Italy's borders
Etna is Europe's most active volcano, located around 220 kilometres north of Malta. The impact of its activity has spread beyond Italy's borders.
Ash clouds have forced some aircraft arriving in and departing from Malta to alter their routes.
The disruption has also affected some local celebrations on the island. The Socjeta Muzikali La Stella Levantina of Attard postponed the fireworks display scheduled for Tuesday, the Feast of Santa Marija.
The organiser explained that the fireworks launch site is close to the runway approach path and that, after consulting with authorities, it decided to postpone the display for as long as operational restrictions remain in force at the airport.
The Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre in Toulouse (VAAC) has noted that the volcanic ash cloud continues to drift south and southwest.
According to a VAAC bulletin issued on Tuesday evening, the highest concentration of ash remains over Sicily, while lower levels have been reported between eastern Malta and as far as northern Libya.
A political issue
Catania airport, just a few kilometres from the volcano, has been forced to close several times in recent weeks, with numerous flights cancelled or diverted to Palermo at the height of the summer season. The repeated shutdowns have reignited a political and infrastructure debate.
The Minister for Civil Protection and Maritime Policies, Nello Musumeci, has weighed in on the issue.
"What has been happening in recent days at the airports of Catania and Comiso, with cancellations, delays and serious disruption for thousands of citizens and tourists at the height of the summer season, brings back to the fore a problem that Sicily has known about for a long time," the minister said.
The minister said this is an issue he had already highlighted during his time as president of the Province of Catania, when he put forward a plan for the Sicilian airport that failed to win support.
"As far back as 1999, as president of the Province of Catania, I had pointed out the limitations of the Fontanarossa airport and its particular vulnerability linked to its proximity to Etna," he said.
"We did not stop at raising the issue: we included in the provincial spatial plan a proposal to relocate the airport. We also commissioned a preliminary study for a new airport on the plain between Catania and Enna, designed to serve seven of the island's nine provinces."
"That idea of mine did not receive any backing," Musumeci added, explaining that he returned to the issue when he was president of the region, only to encounter opposition from the airport operator and indifference from local authorities.
"The events of recent days show just one thing: it is not the volcano that is in the wrong place, but the airport."

Fund backed by China memory giant YMTC invests in push for alternative chipmaking route
Guangzhou-based SOI Micro is developing a low-power logic process aimed at easing reliance on overseas technology while strengthening domestic chip capabilities
A venture capital fund backed by Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp (YMTC), China’s top producer of NAND flash memory, has taken a stake in domestic semiconductor manufacturer SOI Micro, adding a high-profile investor to the country’s push for an alternative chipmaking ecosystem.
Led by a prominent figure in China’s semiconductor industry, SOI Micro is focused on developing fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FD-SOI) technology – a low-power chipmaking technology that offers a complementary route to mainstream processes.
SOI Micro completed a shareholder change on Thursday, according to a recent update on China’s National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System. The company’s registered capital increased to 2.53 billion yuan (US$375 million) from 2.39 billion yuan, with the Wuhan-based Changcun Industry Investment Fund appearing as a new shareholder.
The size of Changcun’s investment and its specific stake were not disclosed. SOI Micro did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.
The Changcun Industry Investment Fund was established in 2023 by YMTC alongside the Hubei Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, a state-backed vehicle in Wuhan. While its investment mandate has focused heavily on memory-chip supply-chain players, this latest move extends its reach into specialised logic manufacturing.
SOI Micro, founded in Guangzhou in 2022, is led by Ye Tianchun, a veteran semiconductor technologist who previously headed the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Microelectronics. Ye also served as chief technologist for China’s high-profile “02” project, a major state initiative to advance domestic chipmaking equipment and fabrication capabilities.

Ukraine wants foreign investors to buy its state assets. So far, they’re not biting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:59:07 UTC
21:59:07 KST

Ukraine wants foreign investors to buy its state assets. So far, they’re not biting
Specialists of an emergency recovery team inspect and shut down a damaged pipeline near the state-owned Ocean Plaza shopping mall in Kyiv, Ukraine, on May 14, 2024. (Yurii Stefanyak / Global Images Ukraine / Getty Images)
Ukraine's government wants to sell thousands of state-owned assets that are overwhelmingly unprofitable, inefficient, or nonoperational — sometimes all three. But it's facing a problem. Low prices aren’t enough to attract the foreign investors Ukraine wants most, particularly those from Europe.
As Ukraine positions itself as an investment opportunity rather than a charity case to foreign partners, the country's State Property Fund, the government body overseeing privatization, is advertising state-owned businesses as an easy and secure path for foreign investment.
"It is probably one of the safest ways to enter the Ukrainian market," Dmytro Natalukha, the chairman of the fund, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The whole process is very straightforward. You take part in an online auction on the Prozorro platform (Ukraine's transparent public procurement website), meaning that there cannot be any infringements whatsoever. You have the possibility to access all the data beforehand, to sign a non-disclosure agreement, and even do a site visit," he added.
The fund currently lists 18 large-scale projects and 157 small-scale projects on its website, with around 1,200 projects in the pipeline from a pool of more than 3,000 state assets in total. The auctions have attracted local investors, with 168 small-scale sales bringing in over 1 billion hryvnia ($22.3 million) in the first half of 2026.
But in late June, Natalukha stood on stage at the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Gdansk, saying that no European investors were interested in bidding for state assets. This is despite there being a plethora of privatization opportunities in Ukraine, from an ammonia plant in Odesa to a bakery in Chernivtsi, he told the audience.
People involved say deep-rooted problems are turning off foreign investors. Poor communication by the government about viable projects and ongoing war risks are major roadblocks, as well as staffing issues at the fund, particularly with English-speaking employees, a person with direct knowledge of Ukraine’s privatization program told the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity.
"From what we have seen, many of the assets currently being offered require substantial restructuring and additional investment."
Ukraine also bars the government from disclosing an asset's financial details before announcing an auction, leaving investors just two to three months for due diligence checks. Meanwhile, the assets are often saddled with debt, in poor condition, or — if the asset was confiscated — in the firing line of potential lawsuits.
"From what we have seen, many of the assets currently being offered require substantial restructuring and additional investment," German Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine CEO Reiner Perau told the Kyiv Independent.
read also
After the conference, Natalukha told the Kyiv Independent that the government has poorly advertised projects to foreign investors in recent years. The fund was even headless for nearly 18 months before he took the reins this January, putting privatization on the back foot while the government courted large financial institutions to other investment projects instead, like new industrial parks.
But he also says Brussels, despite pushing Kyiv toward privatization, could make it easier for European firms to enter the market by providing derisking instruments. Most investors, especially from Europe, don't have the risk appetite to take the plunge without insurance, which is hard to access for small and medium-sized investors.
In the case of German companies, the lack of participation in privatization auctions isn't necessarily an indictment of the process itself, according to Perau, but rather reflects investors’ reluctance to commit capital while the war and its risks persist.
"We want the buyers to be strategic and to be present not just in our economy, but physically on the ground, and to be willing to protect the assets that they have invested in."
Natalukha said that companies from more venturesome countries such as the U.S., Turkey, Israel, and Azerbaijan are inquiring about and visiting state-owned assets in agriculture, mining, and chemicals. But even then, only one foreign firm has bought a state asset during wartime — Azerbaijan's Neqsol, which purchased the UMCC Titanium mine last year for 4 billion hryvnia ($95 million).
The tide could turn later this year. The U.S. Development Finance Corporation (DFC) announced a partnership with the World Bank's Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency at the Ukraine Recovery Conference to expand political risk insurance for American firms investing in Ukraine, covering government overreach as well as war risks.
According to the person with knowledge of the privatization process, the DFC is ready to provide political risk insurance to American investors willing to bid for the Odesa Portside Plant Facility — an inoperative ammonia plant that comes with its own port — which goes to auction in October for the sixth time since 2009.
Kyiv is more optimistic it can sell the plant this time around after the last attempt in 2025 collapsed because no one applied for the auction. According to Natalukha, the plant has attracted significant attention this year from American, Turkish, and Israeli companies after Iran strangled ammonia supplies by blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
But investors will have to face the same issues that plague so many other state assets during wartime. It's laden with heavy, swelling debt — $193 million — as the plant ceased operations in 2022, and it's located in a region frequently targeted by Russian missiles and drones.
Nonetheless, it remains a key asset in the government's large-scale privatization push this year, which aims to raise a total of $295 million by the end of 2026. The plant's starting price will be Hr 4.3 billion ($100 million), five times less than the 2009 auction. That would increase if more players join the auction.
"It's a trade-off for us because we are selling these assets for a discounted price for obvious reasons. But we want the buyers to be strategic and to be present not just in our economy, but physically on the ground, and to be willing to protect the assets that they have invested in," Natalukha said.
With one or two standout privatizations, cautious European investors could come round to bidding in auctions, Wojciech Kostrzewa, president of the Polish Business Roundtable, told the Kyiv Independent. But the first step for the fund should be improving communication with European firms, which have traditionally stuck to safer investments, he added.
"The leadership of Ukraine's privatization authority should do a proper roadshow with business associations in Europe," he said.
"Get out of Kyiv and visit Warsaw, Berlin, Paris, London, or Stockholm, and meet leaders of organizations to explain why investing in Ukraine now is attractive."

Lithuania expands border defences, extends timeline for counter-mobility measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:58:00 UTC
21:58:00 KST

Lithuania’s government on Wednesday amended its plan for counter-mobility measures, establishing a new defence zone along the country’s borders with Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region.
Under the revised plan, a 20-meter-wide counter-mobility strip will extend from the border patrol road into Lithuanian territory. In areas designated by the military for operations, the strip will be widened to 150 meters.
The changes come as Lithuania expands its network of defences intended to slow or prevent the movement of hostile forces and military equipment in the event of an attack.
The government has pushed back the deadline for completing engineering equipment parks at designated military sites to the end of 2028, from the original April 2025 target.
The Defence Ministry said the extension was necessary because the number of planned parks has increased from 27 to 50. The expanded network will require additional time to implement, while state-owned rail infrastructure company LTG Infra has also been tasked with providing storage facilities for the engineering equipment.
The deadline for installing reserve obstacles on national roads and approaches to bridges, as well as fitting bridges with structures for explosives, has also been extended to the end of 2028.
The revised plan shifts the focus of some measures from planting tree barriers to creating marshes. Those projects are expected to be completed by the end of 2030.
According to the ministry, restoring swamps in selected areas should make them impassable for heavy military equipment within several years.
Plans to build defensive drainage ditches and stream networks in the Marijampolė municipality have been dropped. The ministry said more suitable locations for such measures had been identified in the Vilkaviškis and Šakiai districts.
The changes could require an additional 50 million euros from Lithuania’s State Defence Fund between 2026 and 2030.
The government originally approved its counter-mobility plan in July 2024.
Lithuania began developing counter-mobility parks in 2023, drawing on lessons from Russia’s war in Ukraine. Last year, the Defence Ministry introduced a unified three-tier defence line, with defensive measures planned at distances of 3, 20 and 50 kilometres from the country’s border.

HAIKOU, /China/, August 12. /TASS/. The southern Chinese province of Hainan is developing a new tourism model emphasizing wellness vacations and training in traditional medicine, Sanya Ribao reported.
According to the newspaper, the resort city of Sanya on the island’s southern coast plays an important role in developing this tourism sector. The city is home to the Sanya International Friendship Traditional Chinese Medicine Sanatorium, which attracts visitors from Russia and other countries.
The services and disciplines offered to foreigners, primarily students, include acupuncture, herbal therapy, and massage. Sanya Ribao noted that the Hainan Free Trade Port is promoting the internationalization of traditional medicine practices in this way. The 10-day courses are designed for aspiring practitioners from around the world.
Many students visiting Sanya for the first time have taken advantage of this new model, which allows them to combine training with tourism. The organizers provide favorable conditions to ensure participants gain as many practical skills as possible and are not limited to theory.
In particular, foreign specialists learn how to diagnose conditions and select treatment regimens and master traditional methods that have not yet become widespread in Europe, the Americas, or Australia. According to visiting specialists interviewed by the newspaper, this experience will lay a solid foundation for their professional careers. Some are already working in clinics abroad and aim to "address the shortcomings of European education" in this field.
The Sanya Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital regularly organizes internships. Experienced medical professionals teach students treatment methods and popular cosmetic rejuvenation practices.
Wellness programs
Sanya offers foreigners the chance to learn traditional medicine techniques and improve their health. According to Sanya Ribao, more and more people, including Russians, are coming to Hainan specifically for this purpose. Some tourists prepare for these trips in advance and choose a personalized program.
One benefit of Chinese medicine that attracts vacationers from around the world to Sanya is its emphasis on natural treatment methods that help regulate metabolism and restore vitality. China's visa-free policy with several countries, including Russia, has also played a significant role in increasing the number of tourists coming to Hainan for wellness purposes.
According to Sanya International Friendship Traditional Chinese Medicine Sanatorium Deputy Director Kou Zhixiong, the level of acceptance of these methods among foreign patients has risen from “trying it out for the experience” to “targeted treatment.” “In the past, we did our best to promote our services, asking people to come and give them a try. Now they reach out for consultations on their own, wait in line to make appointments, and come to us specifically,” he noted.
The doctor stressed in 2025, his clinic treated approximately 10,700 foreign patients, marking a 42% increase. From January through June of 2026, the medical institution has already treated over 8,000 foreign patients.
Kou Zhixiong emphasized his clinic has branches in Kazakhstan and Canada and provides remote consultations through international platforms in countries such as Australia and France. This network of traditional Chinese medicine services is expected to grow.

It also said the decision violated the principle prohibiting the acquisition of territory by force and UN Security Council Resolution 497 of 1981.
Israel has occupied most of the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967 and annexed the territory in 1981, a move rejected by the UN as “null and void” under Resolution 497.

AI generated
PARIS – France on Aug 12 recorded a more than 20 per cent shortfall in nuclear power production capacity, a record deficit caused by environmentally related outages linked to drought, extreme heat and a jellyfish invasion.
France uses nuclear power to generate around 70 per cent of its electricity. The country has seen nuclear power production disrupted by multiple heatwaves and droughts in 2026.
According to AFP calculations based on data published by energy group EDF since 2015, 20.4 per cent of generating capacity was unavailable.
Between 9.45am and 10am local time, EDF’s nuclear fleet recorded a new peak in outages due to “environmental constraints” or “external environmental causes”, both in terms of the number of reactors shut down or operating at reduced output and in terms of lost generating capacity.
In total, 13 of the 57 reactors in EDF’s nuclear fleet were affected. Eight reactors were completely shut down while five were operating at reduced power.
Much of the lost nuclear generating capacity was due to full or partial shutdowns at five of the six reactors at the Gravelines nuclear power plant after a swarm of jellyfish clogged pumps used to cool the units.
Experts say overfishing, plastic pollution and warming seas due to climate change have created conditions allowing jellyfish to thrive and reproduce.
Outside the Gravelines plant, the largest in Western Europe, the shutdowns or production reductions affecting other reactors are linked to extreme heat and droughts, depriving the plants of the water they need for cooling. AFP

Turkey's Erdogan seeks expansion of 'Mecca Defence Agreement'
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday he hoped more countries would join a defence agreement signed last week between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan aimed at stabilising a region wracked by conflict.
The so-called "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement" was signed on Friday as the regional grapples with fallout from the US-Israeli war on Iran which has dragged in regional players and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
"Our vision for it is not limited to the three countries," the Turkish leader told the London-based Asharq Al-Awsat daily. "Rather we aspire for it to grow, and perhaps appropriate conditions will emerge one day for all countries of the region to gather under its umbrella."
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Saturday said Turkey expected Egypt to join the pact "in the next stage", telling the Anadolu state news agency only "a few technical issues" stood in the way.
Egypt has not commented on the agreement nor on the remarks by Fidan, who will visit Cairo on Thursday and Friday.
Cairo has robust military cooperation with Ankara, but has given no indication it intends to sign up to the new security alliance, which contains a NATO-style clause saying any attack on one would be seen as an attack on all.
The five-month US-Israeli war on Iran war upended the security architecture in the region and forced a rethink of decades of conventional wisdom rooted in US military supremacy.
Erdogan said the pact emerged out of the "new circumstances" in the Middle East with regional players seeking to assume greater responsibility for their own security and stability.
"Regional issues should be resolved by regional actors, and with this action, we consider that we have taken a first step toward achieving that goal," he said.
"Resolving regional issues must be carried out away from formulas imposed from the outside. We know very well that solutions imported from abroad only bring disasters," he told the Saudi-owned newspaper.
The pact, which consolidates three major US allies into an alternative security architecture that rejects Israel's hegemony, seeks to boost security cooperation, while also opening the way for "developing joint projects in the defence industries", Erdogan said.
Since the onset of the war, Saudi Arabia has grown closer to Turkey, with whom it previously had fraught ties, with Erdogan saying Ankara and Riyadh would "take steps that will elevate relations between the two countries to much higher levels", without giving further details.

Consumer prices rose 0.1% in July, as expected, putting the annual rate at 3.4%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:54:09 UTC
21:54:09 KST

A key inflation reading Wednesday showed prices moderating across a range of goods and services, possibly taking the urgency out of an imminent interest rate hike.
The consumer price index, part of the Federal Reserve's inflation dashboard, showed a seasonally adjusted increase of 0.1% during July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Excluding food and energy, the so-called core CPI rose 0.2%.
On an annual basis, the inflation rates were 3.4% and 2.5%, both down 0.1 percentage point from June.
All of the readings were line with the Dow Jones consensus forecasts.
Though the levels held well above the Fed's 2% target, the tame monthly readings, coupled with similarly moderate levels in June, indicate that the energy-fueled burst earlier in the year is easing, though prices remain volatile and subject to constantly changing conditions in the Middle East.
Stock market futures rose following the release while Treasury yields were negative across the board. Traders further cut the probability for a September rate hike, lowering the odds to 42%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge of futures prices.
Energy prices dropped another 1.5% for the month following a 5.7% decrease in June. Still, the sector saw an annual increase of 14.7% following sharp gains in prior months, including a 10.9% surge in March just after the attacks against Iran began.
Both food and shelter saw 0.1% increases in July. Shelter costs had been stubborn and a key contributor toward keeping the inflation rate above 2%. Even with the modest gain, shelter accounted for about two-thirds of the headline increase, the BLS said. The index was held in check by a sharp 2.8% decline in lodging away from home costs. A key measure that asks property owners what they could get in rent increased 0.3%.
New vehicle prices rose 0.1% while used cars and trucks increased 0.4%. Medical care was up 0.4% and airline fares accelerated by 2.2%.
The Federal Open Market Committee, the central bank's rate-setting body, does not meet again until September, so it will have an additional month of inflation data to digest before it has to make a decision.
"In-line inflation will keep the 'no need to hike rates' narrative that took hold after last week's jobs report intact," said Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management. "There will be another round of inflation data before the September FOMC meeting, so the storyline could still change. But unless those numbers tell a much different story, the Fed will likely still be in a position to leave rates unchanged next month."
Up until a week or so ago, markets had been pricing in a strong likelihood of a hike at next month's policy meeting. However, renewed concerns about the labor market following a net job loss in July combined with gyrations in the energy sector have taken the immediacy out of a rate increase.
At the July meeting, the FOMC voted 9-3 to hold its key interest rate steady, with the dissenters all voicing support for a rate hike. Markets now are pricing a stronger chance for a move in October or December.

Meanwhile, OPEC maintained its 2026 forecast for non-OPEC+ liquids production growth at 0.6 million bpd. The main growth drivers are expected to be Brazil, the United States, Canada, and Argentina, the report noted. For 2027, non-OPEC+ production growth is also expected to hold steady at 0.6 million bpd, with Qatar, Canada, Brazil, and Argentina driving the increase.

Putin threat pushes Germany to give spies major new powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:52:17 UTC
21:52:17 KST

A policeman stands guard next to the logo and name of the German Federal Intelligence Service (BND) in Berlin on Feb. 8, 2019. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government is moving to turn the country’s foreign intelligence agency into a more potent weapon to counter mounting threats from adversaries including Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Under the proposed reform, spies working for Germany’s foreign intelligence agency, the BND, could carry out acts of sabotage, conduct offensive cyber operations and pursue more aggressive espionage operations. Until now, those spies have been limited to information-gathering operations due to intentional restraints put in place after World War II to prevent a repeat of the abuses perpetrated by the Nazi spy apparatus.
Advertisement
But with the threat of sabotage and influence operations from Russia growing — and concerns that U.S. President Donald Trump could halt or leverage the intelligence sharing Germany heavily relies on — Merz’s government has moved to push through a historic strengthening of the country’s foreign intelligence apparatus.
“We are daily targets of espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks and covert actions by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany, at harming our country and at bringing about political and social changes within our country,” Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters after the cabinet meeting in Berlin.
“Our mission is to continually adapt the state’s protective mandate to these new threat scenarios,” he added.
The reforms must still be passed by both chambers of parliament before going into effect by 2027.
Nina Warken, the chancellery chief overseeing the BND reforms, suggested Germany can no longer afford to rely so heavily on foreign allies for sophisticated intelligence operations it has long been unable conduct itself.
“So far — and this must be stated objectively — we have relied too heavily in too many security-related areas on our partners to help ensure our security,” Warken said. “In short, we are simply too dependent on the support of other countries’ intelligence services. And in too many areas, this assistance is a one-way street.”
Advertisement
Germany’s postwar foreign intelligence service was founded in 1956 with far more legal constraints than intelligence agencies elsewhere. Those restraints have had the side effect of making Germany particularly dependent on the U.S. for intelligence gathering.
In view of the growing threat from Russia, leading politicians now argue that it is time for Germany’s spies to be given the ability to hit back harder. That argument took on new urgency following the sighting of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany last week that was found near a Ukrainian Antonov plane used to transport munitions.
Dobrindt, in remarks after the incident, stopped short of naming Russia as responsible for the drone incursion, but said that “a hybrid threat is evident” and that such perils do not originate from amateurs but are “often linked to foreign powers.” On Wednesday, he said results of an investigation into the drone incident were still pending.
Germany’s security “worsened significantly” in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to a report by the country’s domestic intelligence agency last year.
Germany’s intelligence reform would allow authorities to actively respond to hybrid threats such as the Leipzig drone incident. Measures could range from exposing those involved or destroying their property to sabotaging explosives before an attack or feeding adversaries false intelligence afterward, according to the proposed reform. Any response would have to be directly linked to the original incident and could not endanger life or physical safety.
“We are expanding the technical capabilities of the intelligence services and granting them active, operational powers,” Dobrindt said. “This is not just about enabling the services to see and hear better in the future and analyze information more quickly. Above all, it is about being able to take active measures against our attackers and adversaries.”
The BND will also face fewer data-protection restrictions, allowing it to make greater use of tools such as AI and facial recognition and to store data for longer periods of time, according to the proposed reform. The agency is also set to receive more funding in the coming years. Merz’s government increased the agency’s budget by about 26 percent to €1.51 billion this year.

Interview: UAE banker says financial connectivity to power UAE-China cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
20:51:43 CST
21:51:43 KST

by Xinhua writer Xia Xiao
DUBAI, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Growing financial connectivity between the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and China, driven by the wider use of the renminbi (RMB), digital payments and cross-border financial services, is set to become a key driver of bilateral trade and investment, a senior banker in the UAE has said.
"As more Chinese companies establish themselves in the UAE, financial infrastructure will become increasingly important," Raheel Ahmed, group chief executive officer of the National Bank of Ras Al Khaimah, also known as Rakbank, told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Over the coming years, RMB internationalization, local currency settlement, trade finance, capital market connectivity and digital finance will be the main pillars of China-UAE financial cooperation, he added.
Founded in 1976 and headquartered in the northern emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, Rakbank is one of the UAE's longest-established banks and has served Chinese clients for more than two decades.
"In the past, the UAE was primarily a trading hub and a distribution center for Chinese companies," he observed. "Today, we are seeing more and more Chinese companies using the UAE as a regional platform for growth, investment and innovation."
Additionally, Chinese companies are increasingly looking beyond traditional economic hubs such as Dubai and Abu Dhabi, Ahmed said, noting that around 400 Chinese companies now operate in Ras Al Khaimah, drawn by its competitive operating costs, well-developed industrial infrastructure, strong logistics connectivity and supportive government policies.
As Chinese companies deepen their local presence, banks are increasingly expected to provide broader financial services.
According to Ahmed, Rakbank now serves about 6,500 Chinese clients, including more than 2,400 companies. Its localized proposition includes 17 Chinese-speaking colleagues across the bank.
The bank also supports RMB settlement, connects with Chinese mobile payment platforms to enable instant remittances, provides RMB liquidity and treasury services to other financial institutions, and offers trade finance and project finance solutions for Chinese companies investing in the UAE, he noted.
"Digital payment infrastructure creates significant opportunities," Ahmed said. "It enables near real-time cross-border payments, lowers costs and improves settlement efficiency, making international trade faster and more reliable."
China has remained the UAE's largest trading partner, with bilateral non-oil trade reaching 111.5 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, up nearly 25 percent year on year.
Against that backdrop, Ahmed said demand for RMB settlement had risen rapidly.
"Our RMB settlement business grew nearly tenfold in 2025 compared with 2024, reflecting rapidly growing market demand," said Ahmed, adding that he expects the RMB's role to expand as more Chinese companies establish regional operations and manufacturing facilities in the UAE.
Looking ahead, Ahmed looks forward to closer cooperation between the two countries in trade finance, treasury services, capital markets and digital finance.
"The relationship between China and the UAE is evolving beyond trade. It is increasingly about investment, finance, technology and people-to-people connectivity. As those links continue to deepen, I believe the opportunities for cooperation will become even greater," he said. ■

In addition, the project will support the accreditation and upgrading of food safety laboratories by providing standardized equipment and technical capacity building. This will strengthen the ability of Lao laboratories to meet international standards and issue internationally recognized certificates for processed agricultural products destined for export.
Through these efforts, the project is expected to expand access to finance and technical services, strengthen agricultural enterprises, improve food safety and quality, and contribute to a more competitive, sustainable and climate-resilient agri-food sector in Laos. ■

German rights group files criminal complaint against Meta over AI glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:50:32 UTC
21:50:32 KST

Dilara Hamit
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
A German digital rights organization filed a criminal complaint Wednesday against Meta and several companies involved in selling its AI-powered smart glasses, alleging that the devices violate the country’s privacy laws.
 
The complaint targets the management of Meta Platforms Technologies Ireland, eyewear brands Ray-Ban and Oakley, as well as retailers Fielmann, Apollo-Optik, Mister Spex and MediaMarkt.
HateAid said the sale of the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses, particularly the Wayfarer Gen 2 model, violated Germany’s Telecommunications-Digital Services Data Protection Act.
The law prohibits the manufacture or sale of communications devices disguised as ordinary objects and designed to record images or private conversations without consent. Violations can carry a prison sentence of up to two years or a fine.
HateAid argued that Meta’s glasses are difficult to distinguish from conventional Ray-Ban products and that the small light indicating when the camera is recording does not provide sufficient warning to people nearby.
“There is nowhere people are safe from smart glasses,” HateAid Managing Director Josephine Ballon said, warning that people could be filmed at any moment and later exposed online.
 
Growing cases of image-based digital violence
The organization said it had documented a growing number of cases involving image-based digital violence, particularly against women, and accused smart-glasses manufacturers of disguising surveillance technology as an everyday product.
HateAid called for the sale of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses to be prohibited in Germany and demanded mandatory “safety by design” measures, including more visible and tamper-resistant camera markings.
Germany’s Federal Network Agency, or BNetzA, has previously said smart glasses are prohibited when optical or acoustic signals do not sufficiently alert people that photographs or videos are being taken.
The regulator said ownership, import and sale of smart glasses are not automatically prohibited as long as the recording function is clearly recognizable. It is monitoring the market but has not opened a formal investigation into possible violations.
The Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information has separately been examining the Ray-Ban Meta glasses since 2025, focusing on the visibility of recordings, the processing of images and audio, AI functions and the possible use of collected data for training Meta’s systems.
The authority has said the glasses’ small white recording light may not be visible from every angle, distance or under all lighting conditions, potentially leaving people unaware that they are being filmed.
Mister Spex said it had not been formally notified of the complaint and that it took privacy protection seriously. There was no immediate public response from Meta or the other companies named in the complaint.

Andrus Kaarelson: If we do not act fast investments will go to Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

Andrus Kaarelson: If we do not act fast investments will go to Latvia
Estonia's government has failed to attract foreign investment. Companies are choosing our neighbors instead. Now we cannot even distribute major investment support because there are simply no investors, Andrus Kaarelson writes.
Everyone who has been at the helm of the state in recent years should take responsibility. Our NIMBY culture ("not in my backyard") has grown beyond all reason. It is impossible to make any major energy or industrial investment in Estonia without years of disputes with a local municipality or even in court.
You cannot even build a poultry farm. A few years ago, when interest in building the Väimela large poultry farm faded, OÜ Lõuna-Eesti Talumuna leader Tõnu Vetik summed up Estonia's investment climate well: "It is not possible to build anything big in Estonia, whether wind turbines, poultry farms or pulp mills."
Investors are rational and prefer countries that welcome major investments instead of tripping them up at every turn. The state has had years to change this attitude. Officials talk about making planning easier, but real steps have been few and investor trust has not grown.
Problems with actually completing investments have been made worse by the unstable economic environment created after the 2023 elections. Constant and wide-ranging tax changes — always upward — have led foreign investors to look past Estonia. They prefer countries where taxes remain stable between drafting a business plan and completing an investment, so the plan still works.
This leaves Estonians poorer. Fewer competitive jobs mean lower wages and more unemployment. Unfortunately, the governing parties do not seem to understand this.
While neighboring countries are receiving foreign investments worth billions of euros, Estonia is trying to scrape together small investments to save what can be saved.
Recently we learned that the application threshold for support of up to €20 million — previously meant for companies investing at least €100 million in Estonia — was lowered by several tens of millions to €70 million. For defense industry projects it was lowered to €20 million, and for priority technology (which includes food production and renewable energy) to €30 million.
The government essentially admitted it has failed to attract major investments and now must lower the €100 million bar because applicants simply did not come. Under the previous conditions, the roughly €40 million available for support this year cannot be distributed. Major investment support should not be scattered randomly, and the government must start working seriously to find large investments.
This comes at a time when Germany's Rheinmetall alone is investing about half a billion euros in Lithuania, Finland is building data centers worth billions, and Poland is building a nuclear plant worth billions. Even Latvia received slightly more than €1 billion in foreign investment in 2025. Estonia's figure was nearly twice as low, between €500 million and €800 million depending on the source.
We should not forget that several Estonian entrepreneurs have made their biggest recent investments in Latvia or other nearby countries. These include Frankenburg's €10 million investment in the Ādaži rocket factory and Fibenol's decision to invest €700 million in a Latvian biorefinery.
Skeleton Technologies also did not choose Estonia. Last year it launched super battery production in Varkaus, Finland, and in late November opened supercapacitor factories in Germany and Poland.
Yes, Estonia still has more foreign investment overall than Latvia and Lithuania, but our lead has shrunk sharply in the past year. If the trend continues, our southern neighbors will soon pass us. To prevent that, Estonia's business environment must again become attractive to foreign investors. That requires breaking the NIMBY culture and ending constant tax hikes. Only then can our economy start growing strongly again.
Parempoolsed do not believe that high taxes and large subsidies will bring foreign investment to Estonia. The government has not created a competitive business environment in the past decade. Estonia lacks affordable electricity, fast internet access is still unresolved, and the state's erratic tax policy and heavy bureaucracy drive foreign investors away. It is high time to start improving Estonia's business environment.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

====================================================================================================

Jason Arday’s life may be a warped fantasy. But so is this conversation around DEI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:49:35 UTC
21:49:35 KST

Few stories have dominated discourse and headlines like that of Jason Arday. The University of Cambridge professor, now resigned, was accused of plagiarism, and appears to have made up an awful lot of fantastical stories about his life. But weeks into the affair, it feels that there has been an additional layer of reality-distortion: this time, by the rightwing press and in broader public discourse. This week, I try to unravel some of the falsehoods that have taken hold around the matter.
Debunking five myths around the Jason Arday discourse
The stories told by Arday about his life are outlandish, but so are some of the stories we are being told about Black people’s position in professional life. Increasingly, a number of fantasies are being spun by the media and wider public as they attempt to make an example of Arday.
Here are the most egregious:
1. Academia is dominated by DEI appointments
While Arday was in a senior position at Cambridge as the university’s youngest Black professor, he was still in a significant minority. The proportion of Black professors in the UK remains at around 1% of the total cohort. In the last academic year, only 75 of Cambridge’s 6,180 academics across all levels were Black, according to the Higher Education Statistics Authority. The university has serious questions to answer, but can this one case really be taken as a broader comment on the erosion of academic standards in favour of diversity? Arday was a high-profile appointment precisely because he was not the norm. For Black people, the path to academia is not a smooth ride greased by wokeness, but a bumpy one, hampered by persistent under-representation. And crucially, the percentage of Black professors in the UK has remained broadly static over the past few years, indicating that post-Black Lives Matter DEI measures, of which Arday has become symbolic, are actually not changing academia across the board.
2. DEI has taken over the world
Critics of DEI (Diversity, Equity and Inclusion; EDI in the UK) have framed the Arday case as evidence that diversity initiatives have taken over certain elite institutions and white-collar professions. Let’s zoom out a little, and survey what the real world looks like. In the UK civil service, there have been measurable improvements in racial diversity in entry-level roles – but diversity up the ranks remains largely unchanged. Sector statistics suggest that there is a glass ceiling firmly in place for Black civil servants. This glass ceiling also exists in media jobs: a recent survey of broadcast newsrooms found that journalists from all ethnic minorities are still locked out of top jobs. One respondent described their workplace as an “apartheid newsroom … You look left and there’s disproportionately too many people [of colour] because everyone’s on the lower rung. And you look on the other side, it’s like, [almost] everyone’s … white.” In 2015, Black journalists in the UK were “under-represented by a factor of more than 10”, a figure that has barely changed. The story is the same among Britain’s top firms, where Black directors remain under-represented, even as overall ethnic minority representation increases. In addition to this persisting lack of advancement, Black people now have to worry about a growing perception that they are “diversity hires”.
3. DEI is about race (and mostly Black people)
It’s striking just how much “DEI” has become a straight swap – a byword for “Black” in conversations about employment and representation. DEI is also about much more such as disability, class and gender. There is something instructive in how it has become collapsed into race, because it seems that it is only race that triggers outrage – the sense that these minorities are cheating their way in. The Arday case itself proves, rather than negates, the fact that resonant DEI themes go beyond race. One can see how his story weaves in all strands, and would not have been as compelling if it was one of a typical middle class professional. In Cambridge’s own announcement of the appointment, their narrative centred neurodivergence, Arday’s delayed speech, his class. He epitomises, the statement says, “the significant barriers that neurodivergent individuals, those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, and Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic people face when trying to build careers in the sector”.
4. Black people aren’t critical of DEI
The fallout around Arday has landed in the middle of a fraught and nasty public debate about DEI, which has pushed Black people into a particular rhetorical position. A post-BLM backlash has argued that attempts to redress systemic imbalances against people of colour are not only discriminatory, but unsafe. Donald Trump has legally challenged DEI initiatives in the US by executive order, and has gone so far as to blame air traffic accidents on DEI, due to the alleged lowered hiring standards under his predecessors. These interventions have created an environment in which it is impossible to have reasoned discussions about DEI, and its value, application, flaws and benefits. The Arday case is troubling on its own terms, but it also feeds into an image of a world held hostage by “wokeness”, one that has been amplified by motivated, cynical actors.
But there is a difference between rejecting such hysterical notions and universal denial that there is nothing to see here. Several Black analysts and writers (myself included) have long been critical of DEI. We have warned that a focus on “representation” over material change will do little to genuinely address the harms that Black people face due to their class, employment status, housing, policing and immigration. But it is the right, in politics and the media, that has dictated the terms of the debate.
5. We live in a meritocracy
Public discussion of Arday’s case would have you believe that elite institutions reward skill and aptitude alone. This is fiction. It is a mundane fact of life, for example, that US higher education admissions have a formal preference for “legacy students” who have family ties to a given university. Between 10% and 15% of Ivy League students are legacy, and are favoured in order to promote donations and alumni networks. In 2019 Harvard’s acceptance rate of legacy students was almost five times that of the general rate. These students are overwhelmingly white and wealthy. While things are not codified as such in the UK, one Cambridge student newspaper survey found that more than 27% of its undergraduates had an immediate family member who attended Oxford or Cambridge. One first-generation student recalled being asked in the first week which Cambridge college their parents went to. And the sort of informal networks that mean that a British royal and his sibling – the future king – can gain admission despite not attaining the results required, are evidence that there are systemic biases towards the connected, the rich, and the predominantly white circles from which they come. Yet that is not perceived by the same people scandalised by Arday. The outrage around perceived preferential treatment only seems to extend to certain demographics, which tells us a lot.
None of this is to say that Arday, and Cambridge, have not failed to live up to the academic standards required for such a role. But so much reality has been warped in the fallout, the story flattened into an account of a world in which Black people and their gullible enablers have created a society plagued by a fixation on identity, to the detriment of quality and fairness. Arday, by all accounts, appeared to tell many untruths. But we should be careful that in our eagerness to draw grand conclusions from his story, we don’t end up concocting another lie.

12:49:25 UTC
21:49:25 KST

Estonia's e-Governance Academy ranks Albania and Czechia as the world's most cyber-secure nations, with major attacks often forcing the top-to-bottom overhauls that push smaller, easier-to-coordinate states ahead of larger powers like Germany and the US.
Albania has the world's strongest cyber defences, according to a global index that puts the Balkan nation ahead of tech powerhouses including Germany, the UK and the United States.
The ranking, from Estonia's e-Governance Academy (eGA), scores 155 countries and territories out of 100 points based on their readiness to prevent and respond to cyber attacks.
Its top two, Albania and Czechia, are not the names one might expect to top a global security league table.
Meanwhile, some of the world's largest economies rank surprisingly low. Germany sits in 13th place, the UK in 42nd and the US in the 31st — all trailing considerably behind Moldova, Jordan and North Macedonia.
At the bottom of the table are Micronesia, Palau and Timor-Leste.
The National Cyber Security Index (NCSI) is built from 49 indicators grouped into 12 capacities across three categories: strategic, preventive and responsive cybersecurity.
It covers everything from legislation and dedicated cyber units to crisis response plans and international cooperation.
As geopolitical tensions rise worldwide, cyber security has become a national priority for governments seeking to protect critical infrastructure, from power grids and hospitals to transport and financial systems, against escalating attacks.
Beyond the ranking itself, the NCSI also functions as an open database of evidence and official documents, helping governments identify gaps in their defences and build capacity where it's lacking.
Why is Albania top of the table?
Albania scored 98.33 out of 100 — a striking result for a country not typically associated with cyber security leadership.
It posted a perfect score across all its strategic indicators, including cyber policy, international cooperation, and education and research, and again across all preventive indicators, covering critical infrastructure protection, threat analysis and data protection.
Its only shortfall came under military cyber defence, where it scored two-thirds of the available points.
Every other responsive indicator, including incident response, crisis management and cybercrime enforcement, hit full marks. The gap traces to a single missing element: Albania has no published military cyber doctrine, the document that sets out the armed forces' rules for conducting cyber operations.
For Albania, the top-tier score followed a 2022 cyberattack by Iranian state hackers — so serious that Tirana severed diplomatic ties with Tehran over it — which forced a clean, top-down legal overhaul.
Rather than a setback, the crisis triggered rapid modernisation: legal frameworks were overhauled, defence operations centralised under the National Authority for Cyber Security and partnerships forged with the EU, the US and major tech firms. The government also moved to secure e-Albania, the digital portal that hosts 95% of the country's public services.
Czechia: Legislation and enforcement
Czechia matched Albania's score of 98.33, with a stronger digital development level than its Balkan counterpart.
Like Albania, it scored full marks everywhere except military cyber defence, where the same single gap applied: no published military cyber doctrine.
Its resilience rests on a centralised national strategy, close public-private coordination and a dedicated regulator, the National Cyber and Information Security Agency (NÚKIB), backed by EU and NATO alliances.
Czechia regularly updates its national cyber security strategy to address emerging threats, and imposes strict, tiered compliance requirements on critical sectors including energy, health and finance — pushing companies well beyond basic IT defences.
Canada: Strong, but two clear gaps
Canada ranked third with a score of 96.67. Unlike Albania and Czechia, its shortfalls were more varied and specific.
On digital enablers, Canada lost points because it has no nationally recognised electronic identification (eID) scheme for citizens to use in secure online transactions.
On crisis management, its gap was a missing operational cyber reserve — a formal mechanism to call on extra cybersecurity specialists during a large-scale incident. Every other category scored full marks.
The country's underlying strength lies in an integrated defence model built around the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, paired with deep public-private collaboration, a strong cyber talent pipeline and a sharp focus on data sovereignty.
Estonia: The pioneer
Estonia tied Canada on 96.67. Its gaps mirrored the pattern seen elsewhere: no formally adopted national crisis management plan for large-scale cyber incidents and,as with Albania and Czechia, no published military cyber doctrine.
Estonia underwent a similar shift after a 2007 assault widely attributed to Russia, though never formally proven.
The country pioneered a decentralised, whole-of-society model built on foreign data embassies and public-private partnership.
Its X-Road data exchange platform and KSI blockchain now underpin the digital economy, alongside heavy investment in public cyber awareness.
Finland: Strong across the board, one coordination gap
Finland rounds out the top five with a score of 95.83 and unlike the other four, it scored full marks on military cyber defence.
Its two shortfalls were narrower: no single body clearly tasked with coordinating national cyber awareness campaigns, and, as with Canada and Estonia, no operational crisis reserve.
Finland ranks first in the world on a separate measure, the Global Cybersecurity Index, reflecting its "Comprehensive Security" model, which brings together government, business and citizens.
That approach is sharpened by decades of vigilance living alongside Russia and one of the world's highest levels of digital literacy.
Energy and telecom operators work directly alongside the National Cyber Security Centre Finland to coordinate national defence.

Europe’s new border system is causing huge airport queues as EES wait times double
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:48:31 UTC
21:48:31 KST

The EU’s new biometric border system is causing waits of up to two hours at major airports, with Frankfurt, Amsterdam and Munich among the hubs reporting the biggest delays.
Europe’s new border system is turning passport control into a serious headache, with peak queues at some of the continent’s busiest airports as much as doubling.
New data shows wait times have doubled at major hubs including Frankfurt, Amsterdam and Munich, as the Entry/Exit System (EES) scheme struggles to cope with the sheer number of non-EU passengers passing through.
Data shows that the biometric EES, which requires non-EU travellers to register fingerprints and facial scans, has seen queue sizes soar, as well as passengers missing flights.
The study by UK-based newspaper the Financial Times and travel analytics group Qsensor shows that in Frankfurt, the average wait time reached 120 minutes in July, up from 60 minutes the same month last year.
At Munich airport, waits are up to 60 minutes from 31 last year and, in Amsterdam, maximum waiting times have rocketed from 80 to 120 minutes in the same period.
While these times are shocking to see, it’s unpredictability which has made the situation so difficult.
Peak periods can mean queues of up to two hours, wait times are much shorter outside the busiest times.
Since the system was fully launched on 10 April, every traveller from outside the EU has been required to scan their passport and do a facial scan, as well as registering their fingerprints on the first occasion.
In practice, passengers have had to give fingerprints on multiple trips, due to glitches in the system.
EES kiosks have been malfunctioning and travellers have needed more assistance than operatives initially thought.
The chaos has drawn criticism from across the travel industry.
Ryanair’s chief executive Michael O’Leary poured scorn on the system, saying it had been “misdesigned”.
“Only the Europeans would invent sh*t like this,” he said in July, referring to the fact that his airline had witnessed large queues at some 15 airports across the continent.
Some airports have been deciding to temporarily turn off parts of the EES checks – including not collecting fingerprints during peak times – to ease the strain on passengers and workers.
That policy is due to come to an end in September, though – a fact which has seen eight EU member states and Switzerland ask the European Commission to extend it.
In a statement, the Commission says they are considering the possibility of continuing the practice.
“When it comes to the time after the summer, we are in close and constructive contact with those few member states where there are challenges at certain border crossing points,” a spokesperson said.
They added that EES wasn’t disastrous everywhere, and that registration takes an average of 70 seconds and that “in most cases” the impact on non-EU travellers has been limited.

‘I had planned to stay for life’: last villagers prepare to leave Cha Kwo Ling
‘There is no need for so many mega-events in Hong Kong to create something new ... better if we could retain something unique,’ resident says
Nestled within thick, verdant foliage in Cha Kwo Ling is one of Hong Kong’s last squatter settlements, where a handful of remaining residents are staying until a government deadline to move out for redevelopment of the area for public housing.
Mrs Lam, one of the last villagers living among the juxtaposition of makeshift metal dwellings and stone houses complete with wooden window frames, said she had until August 25 to clear her belongings.
“I’m going to miss my medicinal herbs so much,” said Lam, in her sixties, who declined to give her full name. She pointed to the plants at her door that she inherited after moving to the village more than a dozen years ago, saying she would not have space for them when rehoused.
The plants, such as Chinese fevervine, are a source of income for her as she dries them for medicinal use. Lam said that redevelopment work deprived her of space to regularly sun-dry them to keep the plants from moulding, causing her to forgo more than HK$400,000 (US$50,980) in potential earnings.
Her letters to the Chief Executive’s Office asking for compensation for her products have not yielded a substantial response so far, but she revealed her family of three had received just under HK$80,000 from the government for the forced relocation.
“Of course, it is a shame to have to vacate. I had planned to stay here for life,” Lam said, pointing out that she and former neighbours who had already left the village would regularly get together for dim sum.

MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has revised down its forecast for global oil supply in 2026 by 0.6 million barrels per day (bpd) compared to its previous report, according to the organization's data.
Consequently, global oil supply is projected to fall by 4.3 million bpd this year, dropping to 102 million bpd.
Meanwhile, the IEA expects global supply to bounce back in 2027, growing by 8.3 million bpd to reach 110.3 million bpd.
According to IEA estimates, global oil supplies rose by 2.4 million bpd in July to 101.5 million bpd, as Gulf countries continued to restore oil production. The IEA added that Gulf producers increased shipments by 600,000 bpd in July to 13.7 million bpd, but exports fell sharply during the month amid worsening shipping bottlenecks. Total volumes transported through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes fell by 2.1 million bpd to 15 million bpd.
By mid-month, the volume of oil stored on tankers in the region had returned to its lowest levels since February, but began to rise again by the end of July as inventories accumulated on vessels arriving in the area. Despite the partial resumption of production, total supplies from Persian Gulf countries in July stood at 23.9 million bpd, remaining 8.3 million bpd below pre-conflict levels.

Israeli troops clash with settlers besieging Palestinian homes in West Bank

The incident on the outskirts of the Palestinian village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank marked a rare confrontation between settlers and the military and comes amid a sharp increase in settler land seizures and attacks on Palestinians.
The military has come under increasing pressure to halt rogue land seizures by settlers emboldened by the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, which has spearheaded a rapid expansion of settlements in the territory.
Offering some of its sharpest criticism of such land seizures to date, the military in a statement late on Tuesday described the Qusra outpost as "illegal, reprehensible, and unacceptable activity that harms the residents of the areas and disrupts their daily lives."
However, when troops deployed to the area to attempt to disperse the settlers on Wednesday morning, clashes broke out between the settlers and the troops, who deployed tear gas against the settlers, witnesses said and video reviewed by Reuters showed.
The army removed the cover of one of the outpost's tents and then withdrew from the area, after which the settlers tried to break the gate to one of the Palestinian homes, witnesses said.
Aysha Hassan, a Palestinian woman who lives in one of the three besieged homes, said settlers set the outpost up four days ago and that the Palestinians have been effectively trapped there since.
"They tried to break the gate," to the house, Hassan said, "and started throwing stones at us, cursing and insulting us."
"We (are) dying of fear, extremely terrified."
The military said in a statement on Wednesday that border police forces "evacuated the tent and are working to evacuate the civilians who were staying there," referring to settlers.
"The incident is still ongoing and security forces are currently at the scene."
The military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on any clashes with settlers. The Israeli police did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The West Bank, territory Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war, is home to some three million Palestinians and 500,000 settlers. There are some 146 settlements in the West Bank, as well as 390 smaller outposts, according to the Israeli settlement watchdog group Peace Now. REUTERS

In Russia’s Orenburg Region, fueling is being introduced based on vehicle number plates: what the situation is in other regions of the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
In Russia’s Orenburg Region, restrictions on fuel sales have been introduced following a UAV attack on the Orsk Oil Refinery. Vehicles will be refueled based on even and odd numbers, and limits on the amount of fuel have also been introduced.
Fuel dispensing at all filling stations in Russia's Orenburg Region will be carried out according to even and odd numbers, depending on the vehicle's number. This was reported by Orenburg Region Governor Yevgeny Solntsev, UNN reports, citing DW.
Details
The day before, Solntsev reported a fire "at one of the industrial enterprises" caused by a UAV attack. According to the ASTRA Telegram channel, the target of the strikes was once again the Orsk Oil Refinery — PJSC "Orsknefteorgsintez" — one of the largest oil refineries in Russia, with a processing capacity of about 6 million tonnes of oil per year.
According to the Russian governor, filling fuel into canisters is also prohibited. Limits are being introduced on the amount of fuel dispensed. Petrol (AI-92, AI-95) will be dispensed in quantities of no less than 15 litres and no more than 30 litres per person. Diesel fuel will be limited to 60 litres in populated areas and up to 200 litres at filling stations on intermunicipal, regional and federal highways within the region. Ministry of Internal Affairs personnel and volunteers will be deployed at the filling stations.
We should add
In at least 12 regions, as calculated by the publication "7×7", filling stations are once again seeing queues for fuel lasting several hours. Journalists name Krasnodar Krai, and the Voronezh, Kaluga, Rostov, Ryazan, Tambov, Tula, Saratov, Smolensk, Penza and Ulyanovsk regions, as well as Primorye, among these regions.
Russian media note that restrictions on the amount of petrol dispensed to one person have also returned. On August 11, the Sochi administration announced that limits had been introduced at filling stations in the region "due to logistical disruptions in supplies." In addition, local residents and tourists were asked to "refrain from travelling by private vehicle where possible" in order to reduce the burden on filling stations.
A system of separate refuelling on even and odd days has also been reinstated in Lipetsk Region. It will take effect on August 13, Governor Igor Artamonov announced. At the same time, limits were introduced in the region — up to 30 litres of petrol at filling stations operated by the "Gazprom", "Lukoil", Teboil and "Rosneft" networks.
In addition, regions are reporting complaints about petrol shortages and the closure of some filling stations — residents of Krasnoyarsk Krai and Bashkortostan are talking about this. Rising prices are also being noted, as evidenced by some indirect signs — in particular, in the regions that Vladimir Putin visited in recent days.
In Krasnoyarsk, one day before Putin's visit, petrol prices at some filling stations of the regional network fell sharply (by 24 roubles per litre). The filling-station network itself attributed the price reduction to a "temporary improvement in logistics" and the "receipt of an additional volume of fuel directly from the oil refinery." However, immediately after the president's departure, prices returned to their previous level.
In Novosibirsk, which Putin visited next, his motorcade stopped (whether accidentally or deliberately is unknown) next to an empty filling station. Children were waiting there for the president, and he spoke with them. These images, filmed by Kremlin pool reporter Pavel Zarubin, were widely circulated by many media outlets. They show that the price display at the filling station was switched off.
Russian media note that there have so far been few reports from Moscow and St Petersburg. However, a Business FM subscriber said that she encountered a lack of AI-95 petrol at several Rosneft filling stations on her way to her dacha along Dmitrovskoye Highway.
We should add
The Russian authorities have not officially reported a new wave of the crisis. On August 11, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the fuel industry, held a meeting on the situation in the domestic market. Following it, relevant agencies, regional authorities and oil companies were instructed to "continue coordinated work to supply the domestic market with fuel," monitor price dynamics and guarantee the "uninterrupted delivery" of petrol to consumers.

Ukraine has updated its approaches to bullying and violence in schools — what is envisaged
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:43:52 EEST
21:43:52 KST

Ukraine has updated its approaches to bullying and violence in schools — what is envisaged
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Education has approved updated procedures for responding to bullying, introducing a single commission and clear deadlines. The fact of bullying is now established only by a court, and institutions must create their own prevention systems.
Ukraine is updating its approaches to preventing and responding to bullying and violence in educational institutions, the Ministry of Education and Science reported on Wednesday, UNN writes.
Details
"The updated Procedure for Responding to Cases of Bullying and the Procedure for Applying Educational Measures have been approved," the statement said.
The documents were updated in connection with changes in legislation on protecting children's rights. In particular, the approaches to defining bullying have been aligned with the Law of Ukraine "On the Protection of Childhood" and the nationwide system for responding to cases of violence and cruel treatment of children.
What is changing
The MES explained what has changed in the updated procedures:
-  A single commission has been introduced to consider cases of violence and bullying. From now on, instead of two separate response mechanisms in educational institutions, there will be a unified approach: one commission will consider all cases of violence and cruel treatment of children, including reports of bullying.  
-  A list of signs that may indicate violence has been established. These include economic pressure (including deprivation of property or obstructing access to educational services), psychological violence (insults, threats, humiliation, harassment, intimidation), unwanted verbal, nonverbal or physical behavior of a sexual nature (gestures, jokes, nicknames, distribution of material of an intimate nature), and any unwanted physical actions, from pushing to striking.  
-  Clear deadlines for responding to reports of violence have been established. The head of an educational institution must consider a report within one day of its registration. If signs of violence are identified, the head is required to immediately, but no later than within three hours, notify the National Police and the children's services. 
-  Only a court establishes the fact of bullying, not the commission. Instead, the commission assesses the circumstances of the case, identifies the child's needs, organizes the necessary support, and makes decisions guided by the principle of the best interests of the child. 
-  The range of people covered by the procedure has been expanded. Whereas previously the document applied only to participants in the educational process, it now covers the broader concept of members of the community, which includes students, employees of the educational institution, and other people involved in the educational process. 
-  Mandatory monitoring of the implementation of commission decisions has been introduced. If the measures determined do not produce the expected result, the commission must review them and, if necessary, adjust them. 
-  Children's rights during the consideration of cases of violence have been strengthened. The updated procedure guarantees a child's right to be heard in accordance with their age and level of maturity. The child's position must be recorded during the consideration, and the hearing takes place with the participation of the parents or their representatives and a practical psychologist or social educator (or without the parents, with their written consent). 
-  The criterion of systematic violence has been clarified. Violence is considered systematic if it is committed two or more times within 12 months from the day a report of the first case was registered or from the day it was committed, even if the first case was not officially reported. 
-  Every educational institution must create its own violence-prevention system. Educational institutions must approve internal regulations on preventing and combating violence, designate a person responsible for receiving and registering reports, provide various channels for submitting complaints, and keep records of all reports. In the near future, the MES will propose methodological recommendations to help implement these changes in practice. 
-  Reporting violence will become easier. Educational institutions must provide several ways to submit reports, including via email, telephone hotlines, or special boxes for written submissions. In addition, reports of possible cases of violence may be submitted anonymously. 
You can read the full text of the order at the link.

2026-08-12

MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. The phenomenon of the Kalashnikov assault rifle, which has gained worldwide fame, lies in the personality of its creator, as well as in the weapon’s reliability, simplicity, and exceptional effectiveness, Alan Lushnikov, CEO of the Kalashnikov Group, said in an interview with TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov.
"I think the reason lies first and foremost in the personality of the man who created the rifle. Mikhail Timofeyevich was a simple soldier who designed the rifle for himself. He spoke about this extensively in his interviews and books. That is why the rifle turned out to be reliable, simple, highly effective, and inexpensive," Lushnikov said, answering a corresponding question.
The Kalashnikov assault rifle (AK) is a line of automatic small arms developed by Soviet and Russian designer M. T. Kalashnikov. The first assault rifle, a 1947 model, was adopted for service in the USSR in 1949.
