Number of children injured in e-scooter crashes in England surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:36:25 UTC
19:36:25 KST

The number of children involved in crashes on e-scooters has soared in recent years, with some as young as nine involved in collisions, research has found.
Researchers carried out a review of injuries among the under-16s at three specialist paediatric trauma centres – Alder Hey in Liverpool, and Sheffield and Royal Manchester children’s hospitals – between January 2019 and December 2024.
They found the average age of those involved in e-scooter collisions was 12, and almost 65% of those injured were male. The most common injuries were to the limbs, followed by head and facial injuries. Fewer than 2% of patients had been wearing a helmet.
Half of the children injured were between 10 and 13 years old, with the youngest only nine. The three hospitals had recorded a total of 477 e-scooter injuries, with a significant increase in numbers since 2019.
More than 80% of the injuries were sustained on private e-scooters, which can only be ridden legally on private land. The majority of the accidents had happened on public land, roads and parks.
Up to 1.2 million people in England are believed to privately own e-scooters, which are available to buy from many high street retailers. “Clearly, reporting these accidents is important to influence and change policy,” the researchers told the Emergency Medicine journal, adding: “There must also be an onus on retailers to clearly advise customers of the law, and policymakers to regulate private e-scooters, such as with speed limiters, or mandate helmet use.”
Rented e-scooter are legal to ride on public roads. The rider must be 16 years old or older and hold at least a provisional driving licence. Rental scooters are typically speed limited to 15mph, and companies must have appropriate insurance.
In June, a 15-year-old boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was sentenced to a youth referral order and a driving ban, after earlier pleading guilty to causing the death of his friend Jacob Calland, 14, who was a passenger on the back of his e-scooter when it collided with a car in Wythenshawe, Manchester.
After her son’s death, Carly Calland launched Jacob’s Journey, a campaign that aims to raise awareness about dangerous e-scooter use and the legalities around riding them.
“No words will ever be able to describe the pain caused by Jacob’s death,” she told the court in a statement as his friend was sentenced. “My heart has been smashed into a thousand pieces and there is nothing that can be done to fix it. My life is a living nightmare.”
DC Steve Pennington from Greater Manchester Police’s serious collision investigation unit said: “E-scooters are not harmless toys and they can lead to horrific consequences when used by inexperienced riders and without the due care required. I would urge parents to check what their children are using and to ensure they are educated about the risks of using them on the road.”
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads. It is illegal for private e-scooters to be used on roads, pavements or in other public spaces, including by under-16s, and we’re bringing forward new laws to make their use safe and legal, including consulting on requirements like helmets.”

International humanitarian law requires combatants to adhere to the principle of distinction between military personnel and the civilian population.
Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions stipulates that combatants must distinguish themselves from the civilian population during military operations, including by openly carrying weapons during combat and while visible to the adversary during deployment prior to an attack.
Wearing civilian clothing to conceal one’s military affiliation during an attack may violate the norms of international humanitarian law.
At the same time, during the full-scale invasion, the Russian army repeatedly violated the norms of international humanitarian law, both during combat operations and in its treatment of prisoners of war and civilians.
In addition, Russia systematically attacks civilian infrastructure. In settlements near the front lines, Russian troops are deliberately targeting people with FPV drones.
Militarnyi has previously reported that a Russian drone deliberately pursued a man selling vegetables in Kherson and exploded right next to him.
According to the victim, he used hand gestures to signal to the drone operator that there were only vegetables nearby. However, this did not stop the operator.

BRUSSELS, August 12. /TASS/. The Kiev regime has asked NATO for underwater demining equipment, including autonomous underwater vehicles, underwater metal detectors and remote detonation systems, allegedly for "humanitarian demining" purposes, according to a NATO document.
"The State Emergency Service of Ukraine has submitted the following request to NATO for <...> assistance in enhancing capabilities for humanitarian demining and transportation of explosive ordnance," the document reads.

NATO, in turn, has asked member states to provide the requested equipment to Kiev and published the contact details of a liaison in Ukraine.

At least 44 dead after overcrowded ferry capsizes on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:34:40 UTC
19:34:40 KST

At least 44 people have died after an overcrowded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, police said.
The boat had a capacity of 90 people, but was carrying 114 adult passengers, five crew members and an unknown number of children, Zimbabwe’s civil protection unit (CPU) said earlier on Wednesday, citing ticket sales.
A crew member told the national broadcaster ZBC that there were 153 people onboard when the ferry overturned on Tuesday after it hit large waves. A passenger told ZBC that the boat began taking on water about 30 minutes after it left the lakeshore town of Kariba, heading for islands and fishing camps.
A specialised underwater team was flown to the area, the CPU said, as search and rescue continued on Wednesday. At the time, the CPU said the death toll was 15, with 27 known to be missing.
Zimbabwe’s police updated the death toll on Wednesday afternoon in posts on X twice in the space of 32 minutes. In the first post, it said the death toll was 38, adding: “The bodies have been retrieved from the lake.” Then it said that 44 people were now known to have died.
A video shared by ZBC on Tuesday showed several people appearing to be sitting on the upturned ferry, while at least four speedboats came to their aid and a helicopter circled overhead.
Maxwell Kanhema Page, who describes himself as a media practitioner and originally posted the video shared by ZBC, reshared a video on his Facebook page filmed from the shore, in which he had noted that the lake was “angry”.
He said: “A few moments later I get over 200 calls about [the ferry] sinking. A sad day indeed.”
Lake Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, stretching about 150 miles along Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia. It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people. The Kariba dam supplies at least a third of both countries’ electricity.
It is not uncommon for boats to overturn on the lake. In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.
On the Zimbabwean side, five drowned in a 2021 incident and three were feared dead in an October 2023 capsizing. The month before, a police boat overturned although no one died.
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report.

Fears grow for missing Israeli mother and daughter after they fail to board flight home

19:34:11 KST

Concern for missing Israelis Mali Yahalomi, 50, and her daughter Liel, 23, intensified Wednesday after the two failed to board their scheduled flight from Prague back to Israel, while overnight searches in Vienna produced no breakthrough.
The two have been missing since Friday, when they last contacted relatives from Vienna. Authorities are continuing to examine all possibilities, and fears for their safety are growing. The Shin Bet and Mossad are not currently involved in the investigation, but a senior Israeli police officer who also works with Europol has been dispatched to Vienna to assist the search.
Mali and Liel began their trip in Prague on August 4 and traveled to Vienna, where they sent their family a video on Friday, August 7, from the apartment where they were staying. The apartment was later found empty. The two are experienced travelers and normally remain in regular contact with relatives, making the sudden loss of communication highly unusual.
Phone-location data reviewed by police in Israel and Austria indicates that the two, who observe Shabbat, were last seen during Saturday in the area of a Vienna train station and a nearby public park. The information provides investigators with one of the few concrete leads since contact with them was lost.
Their relatives filed a missing-person report Sunday at the Modi’in police station, which transferred the case to the Israel Police foreign affairs unit and activated contacts with Austrian authorities. Family members said Mali and Liel had spoken with them Friday before Shabbat and appeared completely fine, but did not respond to messages after Shabbat ended.
“The situation obviously isn’t very good,” Mali’s brother Moshe said Wednesday morning. “We spoke with them for the last time on Friday, and they were completely fine. They said they were in an apartment in Vienna and that everything was okay. They didn’t share their plans with us beyond that.”
The two had also ordered a meal from the Chabad House in Vienna but never arrived to collect it.
“At the moment there is nothing new from the investigation,” Moshe said. “We are in contact with the consulates in Vienna and Prague and with the Modi’in police, and they will update us if there is anything new.”
An Israeli official said authorities and other organizations were making extensive efforts to locate the pair.
“The whole world is on its feet trying to find them,” the official said. “Various parties are involved. They can’t be found anywhere. It doesn’t smell good, but we hope they will be found safe and well.”
Despite the expanding search, local Austrian media has so far given the disappearance little attention beyond publication of the Israeli Embassy’s missing-person notice.
At the family’s request, the Israeli search and rescue company Magnus has joined efforts to locate the two. The family has also launched a crowdfunding campaign to help cover mounting search expenses, including local professional assistance, transportation, translation, logistics and other emergency costs.
“Mali and Liel are experienced in traveling abroad, know how to manage on their own and normally update the family group or remain in contact with their mother and grandmother,” the family wrote on the fundraising page. “The sudden and unusual loss of contact is deeply worrying.”
The family added that resources were needed to expand and accelerate searches in Vienna.
“Every hour matters,” they wrote.

Negative views of Poland’s justice system have grown under Tusk government, finds state pollster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:34:03 UTC
19:34:03 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The proportion of Poles who negatively assess their country’s justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law and ensure that courts function more effectively and independently.
New polling by state research agency CBOS found that, in June this year, 61% of Poles had a negative view of the functioning of the justice system, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017, when the former Law and Justice (PiS) government was in power.
Only 26% now positively assess the system, down from 28% in 2022 and 36% in 2017. The last time positive views were lower was in 2005 (22%).

— CBOS (@CBOS_Info) August 11, 2026
The findings come two and a half years after the current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative PiS administration.
One of Tusk’s main promises was to restore the rule of law after eight years in which PiS had implemented a series of contested judicial reforms that experts, European courts and many Polish judges had condemned as undermining the independence and functioning of the judiciary.
However, Tusk’s government has struggled to implement its promised changes. In many cases, its efforts have been blocked by PiS-aligned Presidents Andrzej Duda and Karol Nawrocki or other officials appointed under the former government.
But in other cases, such as with a pledge to separate the functions of justice minister and prosecutor general, which were fused by PiS in 2016, the current ruling coalition has simply not followed through on its promises.
In its latest polling, CBOS found that supporters of the current opposition are most dissatisfied with the functioning of the justice system: 72% of PiS voters have a negative view, as do 71% of those who support the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja).
However, even among voters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, a majority, 53%, have a negative opinion, with only 38% holding a positive one.
Interestingly, public attitudes towards judges themselves have hardly changed. Currently, 19% of Poles have a positive view towards them and 23% a negative one. That is similar to findings in 2017 (22% positive, 24% negative) and 2012 (19% positive, 23% negative).
More Poles (35%) think that the rule of law has got worse under Tusk's government than believe it has improved (24%).
A further 28% think there has been no change, finds a new poll https://t.co/KkiuY2vDSW
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2025
When asked to identify the greatest problems with the justice system, Poles instead often point to structural issues – that is, those that are under the control of politicians.
The most commonly identified problem (chosen by 38% of respondents, who could select up to three main problems) was “prolonged proceedings” in court cases. The second biggest issue was “politicisation of courts” (18%).
Only 4% said that “judges’ neglect of duty, incompetence and impunity” were among the biggest problems. However, 23% of respondents were unable to name a single major issue that the justice system faces.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025
CBOS’s findings echo a number of other polls. After the first year of Tusk’s government, a survey by SW Research for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 35% of Poles thought the rule-of-law situation had got worse, compared to only 24% who thought it had improved.
Another poll by the same agency for Onet, a news website, in January this year similarly found that 40% of Poles believe the justice system has not improved under the current government, while only 33% think it has got better.
In response to the latter poll, justice minister Waldemar Żurek admitted to Onet that there had been problems in addressing the rule of law. But he blamed the “hurdles [put] in our path” by Presidents Duda and Nawrocki.

In 2024, Duda refused to sign government bills overhauling the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which still contains judges illegitimately appointed under the former PiS administration. As a result, Tusk’s government refuses to recognise rulings issued by the TK.
In February this year, Duda’s successor, Nawrocki, vetoed a government bill intended to restore the legitimacy of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), the body responsible for nominating judges to positions on courts.
In 2017, the KRS was overhauled under PiS in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to multiple Polish and European court rulings. That in turn has led to doubts over the legal status of around 3,000 judges appointed by the KRS since 2017 and all the rulings issued by them.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in four new TK judges nominated by parliament this year, despite an order by the European Court of Human Rights that they be allowed to take up their positions.

Russian attacks kill 8, injure 57 across Ukraine over past day, as deadly strike hits oil tanker truck in Odesa Oblast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russian attacks kill 8, injure 57 across Ukraine over past day, as deadly strike hits oil tanker truck in Odesa Oblast
Russian attacks killed eight people and injured 57 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Aug. 12.
One of the attacks took place in Odesa Oblast on Aug. 11, when Russian forces struck a truck carrying oil. The flames spread quickly to a nearby passenger car, killing two people and injuring three others, regional Governor Oleh Kiper said.
Kiper did not specify what type of Russian weapon was used in the attack.
In addition, Russian forces attacked Ukraine overnight on Aug. 12 with an Iskander-M ballistic missile, an anti-radiation Kh-31P missile, Kh-35 guided air-launched missiles, and 138 Shahed-type drones, the Air Force said. The main areas targeted were Odesa and Sumy oblasts, according to the report.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 112 drones over northern, southern, and eastern Ukraine. Missile and drone strikes were recorded at 16 locations, while falling debris from downed targets was reported at two locations.
The Air Force did not specify how many Russian missiles were launched. Its morning report did not list any of the missiles as having been intercepted.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian forces targeted 33 settlements, including the regional center of Kherson, killing two people and injuring 14 others over the past day, the local military administration said.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks killed a 61-year-old man in the Sumy community and a 62-year-old man in the Velyka Pysarivka community. Four other civilians were injured in Russian attacks elsewhere in the region, according to the local military administration.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian forces killed one person in Druzhkivka, while 14 others were injured in Russian attacks on other settlements across the eastern region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured nine others over the past day, according to local authorities.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, eight people were injured in Russian attacks, including a 15-year-old boy, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In northern Chernihiv Oblast, two people were injured in Russian drone attacks over the past day, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, two people were injured in Russian attacks on the Nikopol district, which lies across the Dnipro River from Russian-occupied territory, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
In Kyiv Oblast, a 65-year-old man was injured in the Brovary district and hospitalized, local authorities said.

Kyiv • UNN
Japan's JAXA space agency successfully launched the H3 rocket, placing the Michibiki No. 7 satellite into orbit. This is the second successful launch after the failure in December, bringing Japan closer to a complete satellite system.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) successfully launched the H3 rocket on Tuesday and placed a positioning satellite into orbit, marking the second successful launch of Japan's flagship rocket after last December's failure, UNN reports, citing Kyodo.
Details
H3 rocket No. 9 lifted off from the Tanegashima Space Center on Tanegashima, a small island in southwestern Japan, early Tuesday, carrying the Michibiki No. 7 positioning satellite, which is part of the country's Quasi-Zenith Satellite System used to provide location information for smartphones and vehicle navigation.
The launch, initially scheduled for last Friday, was postponed to Monday because of a passing typhoon and then delayed by another day due to unfavorable weather conditions around the launch site.
Last December, the agency launched Michibiki No. 5 aboard an H3 rocket but failed to place the satellite into orbit, delaying the subsequent launch of positioning satellite No. 7, which had been scheduled for February.
Five Michibiki satellites currently provide positioning services. The government aims to have seven such satellites in orbit to ensure a full range of services without relying on any other countries.
The H3 became Japan's flagship rocket after its highly reliable H2A rockets, which served as the country's primary launch vehicles for more than two decades.
But so far, the H3's track record has been mixed. Following the failure of H3 rocket No. 8 in December, JAXA sought to correct the problem and successfully launched another H3 rocket in June, placing several miniature satellites into orbit.

How difficult is it to become a doctor or an engineer in India?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:33:23 UTC
19:33:23 KST

For a very long time, anyone considered particularly good at studies in India was almost automatically tipped to become a doctor or an engineer. 3 Idiots made a joke of that national fixation years ago, showing a world in which parents and professors seemed convinced they knew what success ought to look like.Alternative streams of education have slowly gained popularity since then. The race to become a doctor or engineer, however, has hardly become easier. As the pool of aspirants expands beyond the metros, competition for a coveted seat has only become harder. Many tuition centres, almost like factories, in Kota and other places train students rigorously to pass these coveted exams.The May 3 NEET-UG examination was cancelled after the paper-leak controversy and nearly 20 lakh candidates returned for a re-examination on June 21. The anger travelled from coaching rooms to Jantar Mantar and towards Parliament, propelled by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party. Dharmendra Pradhan resigned as education minister on July 25. The CBI chargesheet has since named 13 accused, including three subject experts associated with NTA, while CJP has demanded that the testing agency itself be replaced. Similar protests over exam leaks have now erupted in Jharkhand.The anger that erupted at Jantar Mantar after the leak is merely a reflection of the deeper anxiety over competition for quality jobs and the yearning for a stronger CV, which for many begins with studying at a hallowed institution. How difficult, then, is it to get into a top-tier engineering or medical college in India?
The IIT-NIT funnel
Engineering here means the route to the country's most sought-after public engineering institutions, particularly the IITs and NITs, not every engineering college.
The pathways are slightly different. JEE Main is the direct gateway to the 31 NITs participating in JoSAA 2026, while it also acts as the screening stage for candidates hoping to reach the IITs through JEE Advanced.NTA recorded 15,38,468 unique candidates appearing for JEE Main 2026. Of the 1,87,389 who registered for JEE Advanced, 1,79,694 appeared in both papers and 56,880 qualified. The JoSAA 2026 matrix provides 18,826 IIT seats.Put another way, the original Main candidate pool is roughly 82 times the number of IIT seats. Even after reaching JEE Advanced, there were 9.5 test-takers and almost exactly three qualifiers for every IIT place.
How competitive is the field
Not every JEE Main candidate is a serious IIT contender, so the 82-to-one comparison is largely academic. It is a measure of the scale of the field, not an individual's admission probability. Seats are allocated across categories and other reservation rules. But in both IITs and NITs, the fight is not only for a seat, but also for a preferred stream and college.Interest in admission wanes considerably as one goes down the value chain. That distinction becomes clearer when one looks at the rest of India's engineering system. The latest Rajya Sabha disclosure by the ministry states that BTech/BE enrolment in AICTE-approved institutions rose to 13.56 lakh in 2025-26. Yet adding up the state-wise vacancies in the same annexure produces 2,52,914 empty seats. In the same year, 67 AICTE-approved engineering and technology institutions applied for closure or were listed as closed. So India does not lack engineering seats. What it lacks are the seats students value most in IITs, top NITs and other highly sought-after institutions.
What government told in Parliament
The engineering race does not necessarily end with a BTech for all. For those aiming for an MTech from an IIT, NIT or another premier institution, GATE becomes another competitive gate.The numbers are substantial. In GATE 2026, 2,11,020 candidates appeared for the Computer Science and Information Technology paper, while 95,752 appeared for Electronics and Communication, 76,385 for Civil Engineering and 69,242 for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence.Those figures cannot simply be converted into applicants-per-MTech-seat ratios. Candidates can sit more than one GATE paper. For NITs, the pool is still broader. CCMT 2026 accepts valid GATE scores from 2024, 2025 and 2026. So candidates for these seats can effectively be competing with more than one year's GATE cohort. However, suffice to say, the odds are tough for aspirants.
Medicine has its own hierarchy
Medical education runs on the same preference for high-value seats. For the valid June 21 NEET re-examination, 22,79,743 candidates were registered, 19,99,895 appeared and 11,21,185 qualified. The cancellation itself affected the denominator, with 2,79,848 registered candidates not sitting the re-test.Against this pool, the NMC's July matrix lists 1,36,939 MBBS seats for 2026-27, excluding Institutes of National Importance such as AIIMS. The NEET test-taker pool is about 14.6 times the listed MBBS capacity, while the number of qualified candidates is about 8.2 times the capacity. These are broad national comparisons, not individual admission odds, since seats are divided across quotas, categories and state eligibility rules. But the headline number conceals another hierarchy.Of those 1,36,939 NMC-listed seats, 63,296 are in government colleges and 73,643 are private. Private colleges account for about 54% of the listed capacity. If we compare the NEET re-test pool only with NMC-listed government seats, the candidate pool is roughly 31.6 times the available government capacity.
Level of competition
Government seats are prized because of substantially greater affordability, the reputation of established institutions and, in many large public hospitals, the prospect of extensive clinical exposure. This year's expansion makes that distinction sharper. NMC approved 9,911 additional MBBS seats for 2026-27. Of these, 7,800 are private and only 2,111 government.
Skewed nature of growth of MBBA seats
Nearly four out of every five newly approved seats were added on the private side. So medicine and engineering are more alike than they look. In both, the real contest is increasingly over which seat, in which institution, and at what cost. There is, however, an important difference between the engineering and medical journeys.An engineer can enter another fierce competition through GATE for MTech, but postgraduate study remains an optional route for most. For doctors who want to specialise, postgraduate training is much closer to another necessary career gate.The latest completed NEET-PG examination makes the scale clear. More than 2.42 lakh candidates appeared for NEET-PG 2025, according to the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences. NEET-PG 2026 is yet to be held and is scheduled for August 30.And the postgraduate pool is much smaller than the undergraduate universe. The Centre said in July that India had 86,360 postgraduate medical seats in 2025-26. Earlier this year, it said 8,967 additional PG seats, including those in AIIMS and other Institutes of National Importance, had been approved for 2025-26. For some who pursue super-specialisation, there may still be another competitive gate beyond that.
Governments have tried to build capacity
Governments have tried to accommodate more students in quality institutions. Seven IITs have been established since 2014, while approved expansion at five newer IITs is intended to create capacity for another 6,500 students. In medicine, 157 government medical colleges have been approved under one central scheme, with 137 already functional. Separate government programmes have also expanded undergraduate and postgraduate capacity.But adding seats does not automatically solve the problem. The latest figures placed before Parliament show 15.35 lakh registered allopathic doctors and 7.52 lakh AYUSH practitioners and, assuming 80% availability in both groups, a government-estimated combined practitioner-population ratio of 1:778. Yet the existence of incentives for hard-to-serve areas underlines another problem. Doctors and specialists are not distributed evenly. So hierarchy exists beyond educational institutions too, which makes the work of policymakers even harder in a large country like India.
How other countries filter their best
In the US, 54,699 people applied to MD-granting medical schools in 2025 and 23,440 matriculated, but candidates generally apply after or during undergraduate study and typically take the MCAT. In England, medicine remains one of the most competitive university routes, with a sizeable socioeconomic gap in acceptance rates.France pushes much of the filter inside university, with two in five students entering its PASS or L.AS health routes in 2022 reaching medicine or another major health discipline within two years. China's Gaokao had 1.29 crore registrations in 2026, but admissions are distributed across provinces, universities and programmes rather than through a single NEET-style medicine pool. Russia uses another lever altogether, with targeted state-funded medical training linked to future employment and workforce.
Every country has tried different approaches based on the reality of the land. Whether a test like NEET is the best way forward is still being intensely debated. However, for policymakers, the only feasible solution seems to be building more institutions of comparable quality, ones students believe can offer strong education, credible employment prospects and a better quality of life. Simply multiplying seats is unlikely to be enough if aspirants continue to see only a small proportion of them as worth fighting for.

Human rights groups sue US government over Hague court sanctions

Human rights groups sue US government over Hague court sanctions
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Four US human rights organisations have sued the Trump administration over its sanctions against the International Criminal Court in The Hague, arguing the measures are unconstitutional and should be struck down.
The American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch and the Open Society Institute filed the complaint in New York on Tuesday.
It challenges the executive order signed by US president Donald Trump in February 2025, which authorised sanctions on court officials and on anyone assisting its investigations.
Washington has since used it against the court’s former chief prosecutor and two of his deputies, eight of its judges, a UN human rights expert and three Palestinian rights organisations.
The four organisations say the measures have forced them to drop work such as representing war crimes victims and making legal submissions to the court, in breach of their rights to free speech, association and religion under the US constitution.
They also argue the order exceeds the president’s powers and rests on a declared national emergency that has no basis in fact, describing it as a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice”.
Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch, said governments should step up to protect the court and those seeking justice before it.
The case follows Washington’s announcement in July of a campaign to dismantle the court, which the Netherlands hosts and has a duty as host state to protect.
Federal courts in New York and Maine ruled in 2025 that the order breached free speech protections, blocking enforcement against the claimants in those cases.

Kosovo echoes Ukraine: Why Zelenskyy's remarks in Serbia outraged Kosovans and Russia's role here
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:31:00 EEST
19:31:00 KST

Kosovo echoes Ukraine: Why Zelenskyy's remarks in Serbia outraged Kosovans and Russia's role here
The massive "Free Ukraine" banner on the wall of the Grand Hotel in the centre of Prishtina was the most visible sign of the heartfelt, sincere and unconditional support and sympathy Kosovo’s Albanian majority hold for Ukraine as it undergoes an annihilating assault from Russia that for them parallels what they suffered in the late 1990s at the hands of a still unrepentant and revanche-minded Serbia.
The banner’s demonstrative removal by the ambitious opposition mayor of Prishtina in a populist, kneejerk and parochially-centred rebuke to President Zelenskyy’s remarks in Belgrade on non-recognition of Kosovo – at a moment when Kosovo’s national governance is consumed in failed coalition negotiations and the prospect of a fourth general election within two years – has done both Kosovo and Ukraine a disservice.
Disgust over embracing Vučić
Disgust among Kosovans at the optics of President Zelenskyy’s embrace of Serbia’s Vučić – a henchman to Milošević’s genocidal campaign in 1998-1999 – and his apparent rejection of Kosovo impedes their understanding of the pragmatic, sometimes ugly calibrations – and occasional miscalculations – of a nation fighting a war for its survival.
Kosovo actually has a strong case to make to Ukraine for ultimate recognition and some striking affinities, but has so far failed to overcome its own provincialism sufficiently to make this heard,
notably against the cacophony of President Putin’s frequent, insistent analogising of Kosovo with Crimea and Donbas.
Over the past four years Kosovo has attempted to translate its natural empathy for Ukrainians into such assistance as its modest means allowed: joining in all the sanctions, a government-funded project to harbour Ukrainian journalists, contributing to the UK-based "Operation InterFlex" training of thousands of Ukrainian soldiers, several small packages of military assistance sent via the UK, welcoming hundreds of Ukrainian personnel to the international mine clearance training centre near Peja in western Kosovo.
So, being confronted with the optics of President Zelenskyy – a perceived hero – siding with Serbia has come as a visceral shock.
It stings.
Scrolling through Facebook in Kosovo reveals the heartbreak.
The pros and cons of removing the banner
Arbana Xharra, a journalist with 90,000 followers wrote, "Kosovo stood with Ukraine. This Hurts….. It is painful to see that solidarity met with political calculations that disregard our own history and suffering."
Even a page devoted to tourism could not hold back: "Not to get too political on Explore Kosovo, but sometimes it just hurts your heart."
Prishtina’s mayor Përparim Rama, of Kosovo’s third-placed party, the LDK, is at odds with the acting government of Albin Kurti’s Self-Determination Movement Vetëvendosje! (LVV) even as the embattled LDK party leadership has attempted coalition talks with LVV.
Previously a London-based architect, Rama increasingly appears to have ambitions on the national political stage and the prominent 80-square metre banner his municipality originally erected in 2022 has offered him an opportunity to grandstand.
Its performative removal, announced by Rama on Facebook, became part of a recent pattern of peremptory and personalised actions in which he has denounced and withdrawn Prishtina’s public space from projects that fell into his disfavour.
"No just cause and no policy can be built upon belittlement of Kosovo’s statehood and the sacrifice of its people" argued Rama in his Facebook announcement. While his own verbal tone was measured, it appears to have licenced bitter recrimination in the bubble of his supporters. Among the 800 comments plenty argue for Ukraine’s "cancellation",
that Ukrainians are no better than Serbs,
with some recalling how Ukrainian helicopter pilots were employed to attack the Albanian side in North Macedonia’s brief 2001 civil war.
Kosovo’s acting government was caught flat-footed by Rama’s "When Kosovo is not respected, the Capital, Prishtina, responds!"
Acting foreign minister Glauk Konjufca, a scholar of Hegel, put out a long-winded statement on X, expressing "regret" for Zelenskyy’s Belgrade words, arguing that Kosovo has consistently supported Ukraine and that its statehood has been legitimately birthed in international law.
Yet his wall on X cannot compete for attention with that of the Grand Hotel, his reluctance to burn bridges is outbid for attention by Rama’s populist act of arson.
Plenty of citizen disquiet about Rama’s grand gesture of rejection is also emerging on Facebook.
Arianit Koci, a lawyer with a large following, called it out as "amateurism"; "dissatisfaction is one thing, foreign policy is another"; this should not be "a municipal matter, but a political message that requires coordination with the government"; Kosovo should "be working to persuade Ukraine to change its position towards us, rather than taking down its flag whenever its president says something we don’t like.
After all, if we follow this logic, why did we put up the Ukrainian flag there several years ago? Ukraine didn’t recognise us then either."
Journalist Besnik Krasniqi called for the banner to be reinstated: "Kosovo supported Ukraine because it knows what war means. It knows what it means to be attacked, expelled, killed, and to have someone attempt to eradicate you as a people."
None of Kosovo’s support was offered "so that Ukraine would recognise us. And that should not change because of the position Zelenskyy reiterated today in Belgrade."
Fellow journalist Enver Robelli called out Zelenskyy’s statement for its "scandalous lack of respect for Kosovo," but was scathing about the mayor’s action. "… today’s populist stunt of removing the Ukrainian flag from a building in Prishtina does absolutely nothing to help Kosovo.
It merely shows how local politicians who are unable, and do not know how, to remove even Prishtina’s rubbish try instead to climb into the realms of high politics, scoring points by flexing their flabby muscles in the small-town bazaar of grand gossip. Before flags or other symbols are displayed in such prominent places in the city, there should be a public debate about it.
Because hysterical solidarity subsequently leads to hysterical actions like today’s."
Benefits for the Kremlin
For Ukraine Serbia simply weighs heavier than Kosovo, both in terms of potential support and threat. In its multi-vectoral dance Serbia both supplies Ukraine with significant armaments – deniably, through intermediaries – and engages deeply with Russia, refusing to apply sanctions.
During 2023 President Vučić made several statements to the effect that Serbia was withholding recognition of Crimean, DNR and LNR independence (and of their subsequent absorption into Russia) as a quid pro quo for Ukrainian non-recognition of Kosovo; "if Ukraine recognises the independence of Kosovo, it will lose everything in one day."
President Zelenskyy made no reference to Kosovo in his prepared statement.
The words extracted from him, like a tariff, in the final question from a Serbian journalist at the joint press conference with President Vučić, were a careful restatement of an existing position, precisely with Serbia’s position on Ukraine’s occupied territories in mind, as was made pretty clear in President Vučić’s closing remarks, praising Zelenskyy’s "accuracy".
The out and out loser in this transaction was of course Kosovo; ungraciously thrown under the bus.
With resulting Serbian tabloid headlines like "Prishtina on life support", it appears to have lent Vučić the elan to propose a next assault – reversing the course of the River Ibar to dry up Kosovo’s water supply.
But to what extent was the visit successful in prising Serbia away from Russia?
American analyst Ed Joseph argued that the visit sends a valuable message to regional leaders otherwise inclined to favour Putin that Ukraine is the winning side.
Inside Serbia however, the regime’s geopolitical balancing continues, through its unofficial outlets. At a home football match on 8 August Red Star Belgrade’s famously pro-Russian supporters, the Delije, long associated with Vučić, displayed a banner: "While you host a Nazi in Belgrade, Serbs are bleeding in crucified Kosovo!", Russian flags were waved, to chants of "Serbs and Russians, brothers forever!"
The very mirroring of Ukraine and Serbia’s "respect" for each other’s "territorial integrity" is instilled and framed by Russia, almost as a Pavlovian adverse conditioning of Ukraine to Kosovo through constant referencing of it, associating it with Ukrainian nightmares.
By allowing itself to be coerced into denial of Kosovo’s statehood, despite that country’s many parallels with Ukraine’s own experience,
Ukraine is paradoxically falling into the role of a Russian proxy in the Western Balkans,
furthering Russia’s project of sowing division and obstructing consolidation and giving oxygen to Serbia’s allied long game of waiting upon a geopolitical opportunity to reverse its territorial loss in Kosovo, for which the Banjska attack in September 2023 was an early signal.
Kosovo echoes Ukraine
In reality Kosovo only resembles Crimea in what has been done to each of them by aggressors – forced takeovers of parliament and mass expulsions of the core population: the Crimean Tatars by Stalin in 1944, the Kosovo Albanians by Milošević in 1999. Did Crimea ever have the status in the Soviet Union to nominate and provide the head of state?
Kosovo did, twice, as one of the seven constituent federal units of Yugoslavia. Its closer analogue is Ukraine itself.
Russia and Serbia each root and justify their own identities respectively in medieval Ukraine and Kosovo and thus leave neither in peace.
Both modern Ukraine and Kosovo emerged from decaying, splintering multinational socialist federations, having been dragged into these respective federations in the first place by violent conquest in the 1910s, by each federation’s dominant republic, which a century later still refuse to accept respectively Ukraine’s and Kosovo’s legitimacy and territorial integrity.
During their decades in the two federations Ukraine and Kosovo both suffered cultural and linguistic oppression.
Just as in the USSR Khruschev’s cultural thaw of the 1960s was essentially for Russians and did not extend to Ukrainian writers and artists, who continued to be repressed, Kosovo got very scant taste of Yugoslavia’s liberalism: from the 1980s a generation of Kosovo Albanian men was decimated by political imprisonment.
While Ukraine suffered the Executed Renaissance at the hands of Russia, Serbia liquidated Kosovan intellectuals: Jusuf Gervalla, Fehmi Agani, Bajram Kelmendi.
Eventually, perhaps after the war, Ukraine and Kosovo will be able to invest in sufficiently powerful binoculars to at last "see" one another properly.
Alex Anderson,
an analyst and former director of the International Crisis Group for Kosovo,
for European Pravda

Powerful cartel in Mexico sought to buy weapons overseas in exchange for fentanyl and meth, U.S. says
The U.S. Justice Department unsealed indictments on Tuesday against four members of one of Mexico's most powerful drug cartels accused of seeking to purchase arms and ammunition in exchange for drugs in the Czech Republic.
The four alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation cartel, known by its Spanish acronym CJNG, were arrested in the Czech Republic in June, Justice Department officials said.
Two of the defendants — Edgar Alejandro Lopez Velasco, 44, and Jose Miguel Alvarado Morales, 23 — have been extradited to the United States and made a court appearance in Tampa, Florida, on Monday, they said.
Extradition is pending for the other two accused — Noe Diaz Jimenez, 33, and Leobardo Gaxiola Lopez, 63, also known as "Bado," the officials said.
The four alleged CJNG members are charged with drug importation conspiracy, firearms trafficking and other offenses which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison.
Lopez Velasco and Diaz Jimenez negotiated the sale of weapons in the Czech Republic "to commit acts of violence against rival cartels, civilians, police forces, and military personnel in Mexico," the Justice Department said in a statement.
"These weapons included different kinds of European machineguns, rocket-propelled grenade launchers, mortar launchers, and accompanying ammunition and ordnance," it said.
"In exchange for the weapons, the defendants paid in the form of fentanyl and methamphetamine imported into the United States for distribution," it said.
The United States last week announced charges against several high-ranking members of CJNG and increased reward money for the capture of its leaders to more than $100 million, including $25 million for information leading to the capture of the cartel's alleged leader, Juan Carlos Gonzalez, or "Pelón." According to the State Department, Gonzalez was born in Santa Ana, California, on Sept. 12, 1984.
The State Department said the charges and reward money were aimed at "crippling the organization's leadership" while President Trump has ramped up pressure on Mexico and other Latin American nations to carry out his security agenda.
CJNG is among eight Mexican cartels designated as foreign terrorist organizations. The group was dealt a blow in February when leader Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, or "El Mencho," was killed by the Mexican military. The U.S. provided intelligence for the operation, which resulted in a burst in violence in the state of Jalisco.
Last month, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on 50 people and companies linked with the cartel, including González. The sanctions froze assets and blocked U.S. financial transactions with those cited.
In June, the U.S. Treasury announced a new bank alert targeting the cartel.

Heard about the ‘luteal uglies’? Women know more about our hormones than ever – and that’s beautiful | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:29:33 UTC
19:29:33 KST

Have you got the “luteal uglies”? I’m not trying to insult you, merely deploying the latest hormonal buzz phrase on social media, which refers to the phase in a woman’s cycle, two or so weeks between ovulation and menstruation, when she apparently feels at her lowest and most unattractive due to a drop in oestrogen levels.
Women’s hormones have become trending topics and, as someone who only found out what a “luteal phase” is when she Googled it, mid-fertility panic, in her late 20s, I am somewhat in awe of the expertise with which younger women discuss their menstrual cycles now. They’re just so incredibly literate.
Beyond being taught at school about periods and my mum explaining PMT, the impact of hormones on our emotional lives wasn’t discussed much when I was younger. In the “post-feminist” 1990s and early 2000s, female biology was seen as something to be suppressed and overcome, and the emphasis of most sex education was preventing teenage pregnancy. Being on the pill from 14 didn’t exactly put you in touch with the natural rhythms of your cycle, either, though of course it had other benefits (such as preventing the aforementioned teenage pregnancy).
You can understand the rationale, which was that female biology should never hold you back. Yet sometimes that felt like pretending your reproductive system didn’t really exist, or that you should simply push through the more difficult, painful aspects. “My period always comes as a surprise to me,” a friend said recently. She’s not the only one.
There were always girls who diligently marked the days in their diaries, but a large proportion of us barely kept track, unless of course your period arrived very late (prompting an urgent trip to the school nurse). By contrast, today’s young women have access to a plethora of period tracker apps and products, not to mention an avalanche of content pertaining to menstruation, ovulation, the luteal phase and how our hormones can impact everything from our psychological states to our body image to our sex lives. This also applies to postpartum and older women, with topics such as matrescence, perimenopause and menopause being discussed far more widely.
Despite the proliferation of psychobabble and therapy-speak, there’s also some good science. I can’t help but be impressed. Knowledge is, after all, power. I’m glad I was taught that biology doesn’t have to be destiny, but it shouldn’t have meant needing to play catch-up on educating myself about my own reproductive system. Knowing what’s going on in your body and having the language to describe it can have all sorts of psychological benefits. It’s comforting that the negative body image and the tiredness, bloating and other symptoms that come with the luteal phase can be fleeting. There’s a reason you feel this way, so maybe you don’t need Botox, you just need a rest.
And maybe, actually, you don’t want to have an affair, you’re just ovulating, which can increase your libido (or, to quote another friend, cause you to “go a bit feral”) and make you appear extra attractive to members of the opposite sex.
For me, it has been important to understand that a monthly desire to explode my life is probably a mild form of premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Knowing this not only helps me warn my loved ones in a “here be dragons” sort of way, but also prompts me to try to take better care of myself instead of deciding to get divorced and move to Crete to become a ceramicist. I don’t think my symptoms are serious enough to warrant treatment, but the increase in online discussion about these issues has helped equip many with the language needed to access diagnosis. Misinformation can be an issue, though, which is why the curriculum needs to catch up.
The fact is, hormones can shape our lives in profound ways. It’s something I explore in my fiction. That is not to say that we should always let them. We must, too, be vigilant. We have seen, especially in the US, how women’s cycles can be co-opted to forward patriarchal, authoritarian agendas, as in the period tracker data scandal, and Maga’s attempts to put women off taking birth control. I’m less worried about women’s willingness to adopt labels than I am about capitalism’s inevitable response to labels: a “fix”, whether that’s a pill that can “cure” the luteal uglies, an app that “tracks” your cycle and sells the data on, or something even more sinister.
Usually, when the mainstream media talks about this subject, it is almost always in a pro-natalist context of women needing better “fertility education” so that they don’t leave it too late to have babies, despite the fact that the biological clock is one of the few things we are very used to being lectured about. That’s why hearing reproductive education discussed in the context of aiding women’s self-understanding, wellbeing and mental health feels so radical.
The information itself isn’t new – I could have looked it up in a textbook – but the way of talking about it is. It’s emancipatory, in that it encourages women to know and take control of their bodies, but it’s also realistic about the reality of living in those bodies. Women of previous generations have also navigated that balance – they weren’t all sold on the notion of “burying the body” – but never so many, all at once. It’s basically a movement, and I am here for it.
- 
  Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist and the author of Female, Nude

Expert: European forests at the threshold of major changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:29:00 UTC
19:29:00 KST

Expert: European forests at the threshold of major changes
The loss of forest biomass in Europe has accelerated in recent years, with natural disturbances linked to climate change, particularly droughts and the damage they cause, playing an increasingly significant role, a new study found.
In a study recently published in Nature Geoscience, researchers analyzed the loss of aboveground biomass in European forests between 1985 and 2023 using satellite data. Biomass includes all wood, branches and leaves above ground. In essence, it is a natural carbon bank. Biomass can absorb carbon, helping to reduce global warming, while also supporting biodiversity. When biomass is destroyed, for example through decomposition or fire, the carbon is released back into the atmosphere.
Tiit Maran, who holds a doctorate in biology, told Vikerraadio that the study found European forests have lost 6.5 billion metric tons of biomass over nearly four decades. Although the lion's share, or 82 percent, can still be attributed to clear-cutting, researchers are particularly concerned about natural disturbances such as bark beetles, storms, droughts and wildfires. Biomass loss caused by natural disturbances has surged by nearly 50 percent since 2018.
The study suggests 2018 marked a turning point of sorts. From 2018 to 2022, Europe was hit by a historic drought that weakened trees and left them vulnerable to attacks by the European spruce bark beetle. Areas of Central Europe with dense, old forests were hit particularly hard, as damage to even small patches of forest can result in disproportionately large carbon losses.
"We have two major factors simultaneously affecting this extremely important ecosystem and that adds an entirely new dimension to the issue. In other words, we are no longer talking about forests only in terms of biodiversity or the economy. Increasingly, what matters is the overall state of our forests across Europe because that will affect how our climate develops. So we are on the threshold of very significant changes," Maran said.
The European Union's climate targets rely heavily on the assumption that forests absorb more carbon from the atmosphere than they release into it. When forests die, they shift from carbon sinks to carbon sources. The trend identified in the study runs counter to the EU's goal of increasing carbon sequestration by 2030. The study therefore calls into question the European Union's hopes of relying on forests as a dependable tool for mitigating climate change in the coming years.
According to Maran, the findings of this and several previous studies indicate that a different approach is needed toward the environment, and forests in this case, than in the past. "We cannot look at forests solely from an economic perspective as a resource base. All of this needs to be placed in a broader context. Forests are ultimately a determining factor in whether we can continue to live anything resembling a normal existence," he said.
Maran explained that forests do indeed help stabilize the climate through cloud formation and energy and water cycles. At the same time, he said, the changes have reached a point where their effects are beginning to affect the ecosystem itself. "We are starting to approach some kind of threshold. We are on the verge of very significant changes and these changes need to be taken very seriously," he said.
These changes, however, are global. It is therefore important to thoroughly reconsider how society and the economy function so they can adapt to new conditions because it is no longer possible to prevent all of the changes — some are already here.
"It's true that the weather is fairly cool here at the moment, but if we look at what is happening not very far to our west, the situation is very bleak. And when you also consider how the effects of climate change are steadily moving northward and eastward, they will inevitably reach us much more strongly at some point," Maran said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Sandra Saar
Source: "Vikerhommik"

Former Ukrainian Armed Forces psychiatrist suspected of laundering UAH 34.5 million through criminal means — case sent to court
Kyiv • UNN
The former chief psychiatrist of the Ukrainian Armed Forces is suspected of laundering more than UAH 34.5 million obtained through criminal means. His case has been referred to court, and he is in custody.
The Specialized Prosecutor's Office in the Field of Defense of the Office of the Prosecutor General has filed an indictment with the court against the former chief psychiatrist of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. He is suspected of laundering property obtained through criminal means totaling more than UAH 34.5 million, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
According to the investigation, during 2023–2024, the suspect carried out transactions involving funds whose origins investigators link to illegally acquired assets. These funds were used, in particular, to purchase vehicles and real estate, which were subsequently registered in the names of relatives, family members, and other persons.
The investigation established a significant discrepancy between the official incomes of the official and persons associated with him and the value of the acquired property. Financial analysis materials and an anti-corruption review also confirmed transactions used to conceal the origin of the funds and the actual ownership of the assets
In January 2025, the official was notified of suspicion of illicit enrichment and declaring inaccurate information. In February 2026, as part of separate criminal proceedings, he was notified of suspicion of laundering property obtained through criminal means. The accused is currently in custody.
After the completion of the pre-trial investigation, on August 6, 2026, the indictment was filed with the court under Parts 1 and 2 of Article 209 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The articles provide for punishment in the form of imprisonment for a term of 3 to 12 years, with deprivation of the right to hold certain positions or engage in certain activities for up to 2–3 years, and confiscation of property.
To remind you
The Kyiv Court of Appeal left the chief psychiatrist of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in custody, with bail set at UAH 24 million.

Iran refutes Trump’s claim to ‘control’ Hormuz: What’s the latest in talks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:27:22 UTC
19:27:22 KST

Iran refutes Trump’s claim to ‘control’ Hormuz: What’s the latest in talks?
Iran declares Hormuz closure until US meets its demands and changes its ‘behaviour’ as global energy prices tick higher.
Iran has refuted President Donald Trump’s claim that Washington has “total control” of the Strait of Hormuz, saying the critical waterway will remain closed until the United States accepts its demands and changes its “behaviour”.
According to the semi-official Tasnim news agency, Mohsen Rezaie, the newly appointed head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told China’s ambassador to Tehran, Cong Peiwu: “As long as America does not change its behaviour and does not accept Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran holds firm on Hormuz conditions as Pakistan’s Naqvi visits Tehran
- list 2 of 3US military fires on cargo vessel it said sought to break Iran blockade
- list 3 of 3War on Iran: Mojtaba Khamenei is in ‘perfect health’, Iran says
The Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas is shipped during peacetime, has emerged as a key flashpoint in the US-Israel war on Iran, with peace talks stalled until the question of its management is resolved. Iran closed the strait shortly after US-Israeli bombing of Iran began at the end of February.
It currently says it is only talking to Oman, whose territorial waters the strait also passes through, about the future management of the waterway.
Commercial shipping remains severely disrupted in the strait, with attacks on vessels continuing on Tuesday when US forces targeted a vessel they said was headed for an Iranian port, in the Gulf of Oman.
At the same time, six people were killed in a Houthi attack on a Saudi cargo vessel in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, according to Yemeni authorities, in what is being described as the first deaths from Houthi attacks on shipping since the US-Israel war on Iran began.
So, is the war entering another dangerous phase? And is there still a diplomatic route out?
What has Trump said about the Strait of Hormuz?
“We totally control the Strait of Hormuz. We have control over it; nobody else, only us,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Tuesday.
On the ground, however, the situation is more complicated. United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said shipping remained at reduced levels and attacks and “harassment activity” persisted in the Strait of Hormuz as Iran and the US both maintain blockades in and around it.
Iran, meanwhile, has made clear that it does not intend to reopen the waterway unless Washington meets its demands for the lifting of sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets and compensation for attacks, among other things.
Writing on X, Rezaei also demanded an end to the US’s naval blockade on Iranian ports as well as a region-wide ceasefire, including in Gaza and Lebanon.
What has happened in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb?
A US Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at a Panama-flagged cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman after the vessel allegedly attempted to violate the US blockade of Iranian ports, US Central Command (CENTCOM) reported. The strike disabled the ship’s steering gear.
The M/V Vela Nova had ignored warnings before a helicopter fired missiles into its engine room, disabling it, CENTCOM said. The US military did not report any casualties among the crew.
The war has now also spilt into another key maritime passageway in the region, the Bab al-Mandeb at the entrance to the Red Sea off Yemen and Saudi Arabia’s western coast, where the Iran-backed Houthis have been targeting Saudi shipping amid renewed fighting in Yemen. Saudi Arabia has announced a new maritime alliance in a bid to secure the waterway.
On Tuesday, six people were killed in a Houthi attack on a cargo vessel in the strait, Yemeni authorities claimed.
Four crew members on board the Egyptian-owned Tihamah were killed, along with two Yemeni rescuers who were responding to the attack. Ten others were injured. The Houthis have yet to directly comment on the attack.
Later in the day, Houthi-affiliated media reported that the ship was carrying Saudi military equipment.
Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb are both critical maritime chokepoints. Besides the one-fifth of global oil and natural gas trade through Hormuz, about 11 percent of global oil and 8 percent of liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade passes through Bab al-Mandeb.
The conflict has badly affected traffic through the waterways, sending oil prices spiralling.
The number of vessels tracked passing through the Strait of Hormuz fell to a one-week low on Tuesday.
Shipping data from Kpler, cited by the Reuters news agency, showed eight vessels transiting the strait, below the 10-day average of about 12 and the lowest daily tally since August 5. Before the war, about 130 ships passed through the strait daily.
Could open warfare begin again?
The latest attacks in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb strongly indicate that the conflict is not winding down.
Despite both appearing open to talks last week, the US and Iran have escalated their rhetoric in the past few days.
On Monday, US President Donald Trump said he would demand compensation from Iran for deaths and injuries linked to conflicts and attacks over several decades after Iran last week issued new demands for reparations for the US-Israel war.
However, US media have reported that the country may be running low on weapons, particularly air defence interceptors used in Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) air defence systems, which could pose a threat to US forces and its allies in the region.
Trump and other US officials have denied this.
Meanwhile, on Tuesday, an Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) adviser said it was developing the capability to conduct operations on “enemy soil”. Until now, Iran has been limited to carrying out strikes on US military assets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf countries and Jordan.
“We need to be able to move the operations to the enemy’s soil, whenever this is needed and ordered,” he said, according to Iranian state TV.
What’s the latest on Oman-Iran talks for Hormuz?
Last week, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said negotiations with Oman for future management of the Strait of Hormuz, with new shipping lanes, have made progress and are in their “final stages”.
Iran says it is not talking directly to the US about this – only Oman, with which it proposes sharing management of the strait.
On Tuesday, Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said he had heard positive messages from both Tehran and Muscat regarding the reopening of Hormuz.
What are the prospects for a broader US-Iran peace deal?
Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi travelled to Tehran on Tuesday to meet Iranian officials as part of efforts to persuade Tehran to resume negotiations with Washington under the interim Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) brokered by Islamabad and Qatar in June. This is due to expire next week.
The vague wording of the MoU, under which Iran had agreed to keep Hormuz open for at least 60 days, caused it to fall apart because of disagreements about who had control over the strait. Iran then fired on several ships taking a route through the channel that it had not approved.
The visit is Naqvi’s sixth trip to Iran as part of diplomatic efforts to end the US-Iran war.
On whether any future talks between the longtime foes will succeed, analyst Negar Mortazavi said the key question is whether the escalatory rhetoric from both sides is “opening negotiating positions or actual red lines”.
“If both sides are prepared to compromise, there is still a path towards ending the conflict and reopening the strait,” Mortazavi, senior fellow at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera.
“If they are not, Hormuz could remain restricted and the confrontation risks becoming another prolonged, open-ended conflict in the Middle East.”

No catch for the day: Pakistan's tuna trade caught in US-Iran crossfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:27:06 UTC
19:27:06 KST

- Pakistan's ship building industry has not received any new order over past 5 months
- Fishermen pin hopes on latest diplomatic efforts to end Strait of Hormuz standoff, US-Iran war
In Iranian waters, a strange trade is taking place — Pakistani fishermen exchange subsidized Iranian fuel for high-value tuna, a barter system now under threat from escalating US-Iran tensions.
Shah Zamin Khan is among thousands of Pakistani tuna traders whose lucrative business has been at a near standstill since February, when the war between the US, Israel and Iran began.
The recent targeting of Iranian seaports by Washington has made matters worse.
Iran's southern ports of Konarak, Pasabandar and Beris, which border Pakistan's southwestern Balochistan province and serve as key fish trade hubs, are among the sites targeted by US airstrikes in recent weeks.
"Our businesses were already affected by the war but the recent targeting of Iranian seaports have turned the region into a no-go area for us over the past one month," Khan told Anadolu.
Boat owners, according to Khan, have completely stopped sending their vessels to the Iranian ports for fear of US strikes.
In July, three fishermen were killed and 15 others injured in a US strike on a commercial fishing pier in the coastal city of Sirik in Iran's southern Hormozgan province.
Earlier in March, a 17-year-old Pakistani fisherman was killed after debris from an intercepted projectile struck his vessel in the Arabian Sea.
Tuna is a staple in Iranian kitchens, but it has little demand in Pakistan, leaving fishermen with few options for selling their catch.
"There is not even a single company in Pakistan to buy our tuna. Iran is the only option for us," said Hussain Baloch, another fisherman involved in tuna trade.
Speaking to Anadolu, he said that tuna fetches prices six to seven times higher in the Iranian market than in Pakistan.
Without access to the Iranian market, he went on to say, the entire tuna fishery would collapse, threatening both income and employment for thousands of fishermen.
 
Boat building industry also takes a toll
Since the start of the war, Pakistan has shut its border with Iran, disrupting both the inflow of fuel and the export of fish.
This double blow has added to the woes of fishing communities already suffering from the impacts of climate change and overfishing.
The escalating fuel prices have also brought Pakistan's boatbuilding industry to a standstill, with new orders declining by up to 90%.
The Karachi Fish Harbor – Pakistan's primary seafood hub – and other coastal areas are known for building a wide range of fishing vessels, not only for local fishermen but for neighboring Iran as well.
"We normally build 25 to 30 big cargo vessels for our Iranian clients, in addition to over 100 small and big boats for local fishermen annually. But over the last five months, we have not received any new order (from Iran)," said Haji Mohammad Wada, chairman of the Pakistan Boat Building Association.
"Currently, we are just finishing a few previously placed orders from Iranian clients," he said, while speaking to Anadolu.
The impact of the Middle East tensions has not been limited to foreign contracts, but has also taken a toll on local orders.
"There is a huge decline in local orders as well during the past few months because of rising fuel costs and a halt in fish trade with Iran," Wada said.
Mohammad Moazzam Khan, the technical advisor to WWF-Pakistan, said Pakistan’s tuna trade and boatbuilding industry heavily depend on orders from Iran, and if the Mideast conflict continues, it will permanently strip tens of thousands of Pakistanis of their livelihoods.
Speaking to Anadolu, he said Pakistan's boatbuilding industry produces fishing vessels, particularly large-sized gillnet boats for Iran, which operate in the high seas, including the Strait of Hormuz.
 
Fishermen pin hopes on ceasefire efforts
Fishermen, including Khan and Baloch, however, pin hopes on the ongoing diplomatic efforts aimed at bringing an end to hostilities and reaching a permanent ceasefire between the US and Iran.
Mediators from Pakistan and Qatar hope the two warring sides are close to reaching an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently hold talks to end the months-long conflict.
Hundreds of Pakistani fishing boats and trawlers have left the ports of Karachi, Jiwani and Gwadar over the past few days on a 40-day catch-and-sell journey, putting their faith in Allah.
"Insha'Allah (God willing), there will be good news by the time we end catching and proceed to the Iranian ports to sell that," said Khan, who is leaving in a few days to catch fish.

In the Russian city of Omsk, security forces have begun detaining men on the streets and taking them to military recruitment centers.
This was reported by the Omsk Civil Association publication, citing relatives of those detained.
One such incident occurred in Omsk on August 8, where a 31-year-old man was detained after drinking beer on the street.
He was taken to the Sirius 55 recruitment center. According to his relatives, he was subjected to psychological pressure there, after which he signed a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The man’s relatives contacted the prosecutor’s office, but were asked to provide additional documents and resubmit their request.
Formally, raids involving police and military personnel may be justified as efforts to identify individuals violating military registration requirements. However, those detained are also offered or pressured into signing contracts.
According to representatives of the Idite Lesom human rights project, it is becoming increasingly difficult for the Russian authorities to recruit volunteers for the war, prompting them to expand the practice of forced recruitment.
The methods include street detentions, visits by officials to people’s homes and workplaces, as well as recruiting debtors, people serving suspended sentences, and recently demobilized servicemen.
Such trends had been predicted earlier. Nearly a month ago, Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine reported that recruitment to the Russian army had slowed and that the shortfall in meeting the annual target for contract soldiers was growing.
According to economist Janis Kluge’s estimates, the total number of contracts signed this year is only slightly below last year’s figure.
At the same time, according to his data, the average amount spent by regions on signing bonuses has increased by approximately 30% compared to last year.
This suggests that recruiting volunteer contract soldiers has become increasingly difficult, which may be driving the expansion of other recruitment methods based on pressure and coercion.
Militarnyi has previously reported cases of men being forcibly detained on the streets in the city of Penza, Russia, for subsequent deployment to the war.

Taiwan and Thailand deepen smart agriculture ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:25:32 UTC
19:25:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taiwan and Thailand on Tuesday held an online meeting on spatial information and survey applications in farming, focusing on drones and artificial intelligence.
According to a Ministry of Agriculture press release, Department of International Affairs Director-General Fu Tzu-yu (傅子煜) and Thai Trade and Economic Office in Taipei representative Narong Boonsatheanwong co-chaired the event. Fu said that digital technologies are important production and governance tools that address food security and labor shortages.
Boonsatheanwong said smart agriculture is a key direction for bilateral cooperation. He added that Thailand plans to invite Taiwan to an exchange in September to discuss partnerships on tech-enabled monitoring, governance, and net-zero.
Boonsatheanwong then shared Thailand's geospatial information, digital twins simulation, and tree database, while Fu presented how Taiwan uses satellites, drones, and AI to maintain a nationwide farmland parcel map with a street-view system to verify farmland and crop conditions. Both sides then shared experiences with AI image recognition, geospatial data integration, and agricultural carbon sinks.
Geospatial information, or coordinates, uses latitude, longitude, and elevation to locate a person or object. Drones capture and relay visual data via satellites to determine the exact location.
An agricultural carbon sink or agroforestry is a system in which crops or trees absorb and remove more carbon dioxide from the air than they give out, promoting water and soil retention. Enterprises trade these outcomes as carbon credits to others looking to keep carbon emissions low to avoid fines.
A digital twin is the virtual counterpart of its physical object, process, or system. It gathers data from the physical world, which AI applies to the digital twin for simulation, helping with predictions and data-backed decision-making.
The agriculture ministry noted that both sides have collaborated on agricultural and fisheries initiatives since 2003. Both will continue to partner on test projects to identify practical applications that will improve domestic resilience and strengthen global competitiveness.

BEIJING, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- China's new-energy vehicle (NEV) sales in July 2026 accounted for more than 60 percent of the monthly new car sales for the first time, while the cumulative share for the first seven months of the year also surpassed 50 percent, industry data showed on Wednesday.
In July alone, NEV output and sales reached over 1.57 million and 1.56 million units, respectively, up 26.8 percent and 23.7 percent year on year, according to data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM).
Among the NEVs, pure electric vehicle output and sales both exceeded 1 million units in July, rising over 30 percent from a year earlier, the data revealed.
In the first seven months of 2026, NEV output and sales reached 9.01 million and 9 million units, respectively, both up nearly 10 percent year on year.
Overall auto output and sales in July stood at 2.57 million and 2.58 million units, respectively, edging down both month on month and year on year, a decline that CAAM Deputy Secretary-General Chen Shihua attributed to seasonal factors.
July is traditionally a slow season for auto sales, said Chen, who also noted that early demand release from the half-year sales push and persistent high temperatures, as well as typhoons and flooding in some regions, all weighed on market performance.
Vehicle exports maintained strong momentum in July, topping 1.04 million units for the second consecutive month, up 81.3 percent year on year. Notably, NEV exports of the month rose 1.5-fold to 553,000 units, making up over half of total vehicle exports for two straight months.
During the January-July period, vehicle exports totaled 6.14 million units, up 66.8 percent, including 2.91 million NEVs, a 1.2-fold increase. ■
