Ukraine’s drone strike shut Russia’s biggest LPG plant as fuel rationing returned in 16 regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:12:08 UTC
18:12:08 KST

A Ukrainian drone strike shut the plant that produces 40% of Russia’s liquefied petroleum gas on 10 August, and the country’s fuel crisis snapped back across at least 16 regions within days.
The shutdown of the Sibur ZapSibNefteKhim complex in Tobolsk, western Siberia, removes about six million metric tons of annual LPG capacity from a fuel system that was already under strain.
“This is money of his accomplices burning”: Russian partisans and Ukraine hit Siberian plant tied to Putin’s inner circle
Gasoline restrictions had begun easing across Russia at the end of July, when Ukrainian drones temporarily shifted to other targets. When the strikes resumed in early August, fuel rationing returned immediately, the independent Russian outlet 7×7 reported.
Three industry sources told Reuters on Tuesday that the complex stopped operations indefinitely “while the extent of the damage and its consequences are being assessed.”
No LPG volumes were offered from the Tobolsk delivery point on Russia’s commodity exchange—a point that earlier this year handled about 4,000 metric tons of propane-butane mix per day. Sibur declined to comment.
A strike on one unit stopped the entire plant
Tyumen Oblast Governor Aleksandr Moor confirmed a fire at an industrial site following a drone attack but did not identify the facility.
Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces Deep Strike units, working with the Russian insurgent movement Chornaya Iskra (Black Spark), claimed the strike. The plant sits more than 2,200 kilometers from the front line.
Militarnyi’s OSINT analysis identified the specific target as the complex’s central gas fractionation unit—the plant’s entry point, where raw hydrocarbons are separated into usable products before anything else in the production chain can run. About half of ZapSibNefteKhim’s output feeds Sibur’s own petrochemical complex in Tobolsk; the rest goes to market.
Sibur held contracts to supply feedstock to defense-industry enterprises, including the Kamenskiy Kombinat, which produces solid rocket fuel and motors for the Grad, Smerch, and Uragan rocket systems.
Sibur also supplied the Perm Gunpowder Plant, which makes charges for multiple-launch rocket systems, air-defense complexes, and cruise missile boosters, Militarnyi also reported. The Sverdlov Plant and Biysk Oleum Plant, both explosives manufacturers, were also Sibur clients.
Trending Now
Fuel rationing returned within days
Across at least 16 regions, the fuel restrictions that had briefly eased in July are back, 7×7 reported.
In Sochi—Russia’s most famous beach resort—Mayor Andrei Proshunin said on Telegram that fuel was available at only 38 of the city’s 58 gas stations. Deputy Mayor Vyacheslav Bauer told residents and tourists to use public transport or stop driving, the Moscow Times reported.
In Bashkortostan, authorities banned gasoline sales in canisters, leaving at least one resident unable to fuel his lawnmower—as he complained to regional head Radiy Khabirov during a televised address, a Bashkortostan outlet reported. Production at the Ufa petrochemical complex is unaffected by the drone strikes, Khabirov said.
Still, the shortage persists for a different reason: every time a drone-alert protocol is activated, fuel tankers halt en route to gas stations, regional official Elena Prochakovsky explained at a briefing reported by Prufy. Three districts remain in a fuel “red zone,” and 19 of 26 gas stations in Sterlitamak are operating.
Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov told residents not to expect improvement for one to two weeks, Lipetsk outlet Ploshchad reported. “If you can leave 10 liters unfilled, the person arriving on empty will thank you,” he said.
Russia’s fuel system was already breaking
The Tobolsk shutdown lands on an already fractured system. By mid-July, fuel rationing had spread to more than half of Russia’s regions. Ukraine’s drone campaign had struck Russian refineries 194 times in the first half of 2026 alone—eleven times the previous year’s pace—knocking nearly half the country’s refining capacity offline, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on 4 July.
Repair timelines keep slipping because sanctions block the spare parts Russian plants need. To plug the gap, Russia has banned gasoline exports, permitted lower-grade fuel, and begun importing gasoline from India and Morocco, refined from its own crude—shipping it 14,000 kilometers home because its refineries cannot meet domestic demand.
The Tobolsk shutdown removes more LPG output than any single strike of the war. Russia was already rationing fuel in more than half its regions before this strike.

Top 3 best bograch recipes that everyone can make successfully
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:10:55 EEST
18:10:55 KST

Top 3 best bograch recipes that everyone can make successfully
Kyiv • UNN
UNN offers three ways to prepare hearty Ukrainian bograch. The dish is made with meat, vegetables and spices, including beef, chicken, stewed meat, or veal with pork.
Bograch is a hearty Ukrainian dish with meat, vegetables, and spices that can be prepared in different ways. UNN offers the top 3 best ways to prepare this dish for the whole family.
Bograch with beef, chicken, and homemade oshipky
Ingredients:
Beef with a bone – 500 g;
Water – 3.5 l;
Chicken drumsticks – 700 g;
Potatoes – 4 large;
Carrot – 1 large;
Sweet red peppers – 2 large;
Fresh tomatoes – 400 g;
Onions – 2 medium;
Garlic – 8–10 cloves;
White and red beans – 1 cup;
Herbs (cilantro, parsley, green onions) – to taste;
Lard – 1 tsp;
Bay leaves – 4;
Smoked paprika – 2 tbsp;
Hot paprika – 1 tsp, optional;
Cumin – 1 tsp;
Coriander – 1 tsp;
Dried garlic – 2 tsp;
Salt – to taste.
For the oshipky:
Egg – 1;
Flour – 5 tbsp;
Salt – a pinch.
Preparation
1. Prepare the meat. Rinse the beef, cover it with cold water, and bring to a boil. Boil for 5 minutes, then drain the water. Rinse the meat, cover it with fresh water again, bring to a boil, add the bay leaves, and cook for approximately 2 hours over low heat.
2. Prepare the beans. Soak them overnight in advance, then boil until tender.
3. Prepare the sautéed vegetables. Melt the lard in a frying pan. Add the finely chopped onion and half of the garlic. Fry until golden brown.
4. Add the carrot and pepper. Cut the carrot into strips and add it to the onion. Fry for about 5 minutes. Then add the diced sweet pepper and continue cooking, stirring occasionally.
5. Season the vegetables. Add the coriander, cumin, half of the smoked paprika, and the dried garlic. Stir and continue frying.
6. Prepare the tomatoes. Pour boiling water over them for 3 minutes, then transfer them to cold water and remove the skins. Dice the tomatoes.
7. Add the tomatoes to the sautéed vegetables. Add them to the vegetables and simmer for several minutes.
8. Prepare the broth. Add the remaining smoked paprika, salt, and cooked beans to it.
9. Prepare the meat. Remove the beef and chicken drumsticks from the broth. Separate the meat from the bones and skin, dice it, and return it to the broth.
10. Add the potatoes. Dice them and place them in the broth. Cook for 5–7 minutes.
11. Add the vegetables. Transfer the prepared sautéed vegetables to the pot and stir. Cook everything together for approximately 10 minutes over low heat. If the bograch is too thick, add a little boiling water.
12. Prepare the oshipky. Mix the egg with a pinch of salt. Add the flour and knead the dough. 13. Shape it into a thin sausage, flatten it slightly, and cut it into small, thin pieces. Leave them for a while to dry slightly.
14. Add the oshipky. Place them in the bograch, stir, and cook for approximately 5 minutes.
15. Add the herbs. Sprinkle in the chopped cilantro, parsley, and green onions. Cook for another 5 minutes or so.
16. Let it rest. Cover the finished bograch with a lid and leave it for 30 minutes.
Bograch with canned stewed meat, vegetables, and tomato paste
Ingredients:
Canned stewed meat – 1 can;
Potatoes – 6 medium;
Onion – 1 large;
Carrot – 1 large;
Bell peppers – 2 medium;
Tomato paste – 1 package;
Smoked paprika – 1 tsp;
Red hot pepper – 1 tsp;
Dried garlic – 1 tsp;
Salt – 1 tbsp or to taste;
Vegetable oil – for frying;
Bay leaf – optional;
Water – 3 l.
Preparation
1. Prepare the vegetables. Cut the potatoes and carrot into large pieces. Dice the onion finely, and cut the bell pepper into strips.
2. Cook the potatoes and carrot. Bring the water to a boil, add the potatoes and carrot, and cook over medium heat.
3. Prepare the sautéed vegetables. Heat a frying pan with a small amount of vegetable oil. Add the onion and fry until softened.
4. Add the pepper. Add the sliced bell pepper to the onion and continue frying.
5. Add the tomato paste and spices. Place the tomato paste, smoked paprika, hot red pepper, and dried garlic in the frying pan. Stir and heat everything together.
6. Combine the ingredients. Transfer the prepared sautéed vegetables to the soup pot. Add the canned stewed meat and, if desired, the bay leaf.
7. Cook the soup until done. Bring it to a boil, then turn off the heat. Cover the pot with a lid and let the soup steep for 15–20 minutes.
8. Before serving, check the soup for salt and add more to taste if necessary. Serve hot.
Bograch at Home on the Stovetop
Ingredients for 7 liters;
Veal – 1 kg;
Pork – 1 kg;
Pork ribs – 500 g;
Smoked ribs – 300 g;
Hunting sausages – 300 g;
Lard – 4–5 tbsp, as needed;
Onions – 7;
Potatoes – 1 kg;
Tomatoes – 2;
Sweet pepper – 1;
Garlic – 1 head;
Carrots – 3;
Ground paprika – to taste;
Smoked paprika – to taste;
Bograch seasoning – to taste;
Ground black pepper – to taste;
Smoked crushed chili – to taste;
Salt – to taste;
Water – enough to completely cover the meat;
Fresh herbs – 1 bunch.
Preparation
1. Prepare the base. Melt the lard in a large pot or deep frying pan. Add the pork ribs and fry them.
2. Add the vegetables. Chop the onions and add them to the ribs. When they become soft, add the chopped carrots. If necessary, add a little more lard so that the vegetables and meat do not burn.
3. Add the paprika and tomatoes. Sprinkle in the ground paprika and stir. Then add the chopped tomatoes and stew everything together thoroughly.
4. Add the meat. Place the veal in the pot, followed by the pork. Fry for approximately 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
5 Pour in the water. Add enough water to completely cover the meat. Add the smoked ribs, hunting sausages, sweet pepper, and garlic.
6. Cook the bograch. Leave the dish to cook for approximately 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
7. Add the spices. Season the bograch with salt, ground black pepper, bograch seasoning, smoked paprika, and crushed smoked chili.
8. Add the potatoes. After another 30 minutes, add the chopped potatoes and cook until tender.
9. Finish cooking. Add the chopped herbs and cook the bograch for a few more minutes.

Concert activities at Patarei Sea Fortress to end after this summer

Concert activities at Patarei Sea Fortress to end after this summer
Organizers behind the concert and party program at Tallinn's Patarei Sea Fortress say the venue will host its final events in early September, after which they will end operations at the historic complex.
"On one hand, we want Tallinn to have places where people can listen to world‑class artists and enjoy summer evenings with friends. At the same time, we understand that others must be able to rest in their homes. Sound carries differently by the sea, and we have reached the conclusion that in this location, these two wishes can unfortunately no longer be combined," said Rainer Kala, head of the Patarei Sea Fortress program.
According to the organizers, their story reflects a broader challenge faced by many cultural and entertainment venues. "We do not want Tallinn's already modest nightlife to become even poorer. On the contrary, we believe the city needs places where people can gather, dance, listen to good music, and create shared memories. Therefore, we see this decision as a step forward and an opportunity to seek something new," Kala said.
Kala confirmed that they wish to continue operating at Patarei, but the format will clearly change. "In addition to changes in urban space, cultural organizers are affected by wider societal trends. People's — especially young people's — leisure habits have changed, and in Estonia the weather and weather forecasts play a major role, often leading to last‑minute decisions. When every event is organized with a real risk of financial loss, today's cultural event VAT system is not very motivating. We are not giving up, but we are looking for new ways to bring quality culture and entertainment to people," he explained.
According to the organizers, the full program will continue until the end of summer: German producer Claptone will perform, and at the beginning of September Nublu will close the concert season.
Preparations for opening the Museum of Communist Victims at Patarei also continue, with the museum expected to be completed by 2027.

====================================================================================================

"Easier to attack than defend" against drones: Swiss expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:09:42 UTC
18:09:42 KST

“Easier to attack than defend” against drones: Swiss expert
Following the discovery of a drone laden with explosives at Leipzig airport in Germany, Europe is asking itself how to protect infrastructure from increasingly sophisticated aerial threats.
Switzerland, a country at the forefront of drone research, is taking steps to address the issue, but according to expert Roland Siegwart, the gap between attack and defence remains a cause for concern.
“Generally speaking, unfortunately, it has to be said that carrying out attacks with drones is much easier than defending against them, especially in a civilian environment,” says the professor of autonomous systems at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich (ETH) in an interview with Swiss public broadcaster SRF.
More
Inside Geneva: How to cope with killer robots
“You can’t simply fire randomly into the air, because of the risk of collateral damage. This means that there are still no truly reliable systems for shooting down drones with a reasonable expenditure of resources,” he added.
The main difficulty lies in the very nature of the devices. “Firstly, drones are very small and therefore difficult to detect, whether by radar or cameras,” explains the specialist, who works with Armasuisse, the Federal Office for Armament. “Secondly, defence systems are typically designed for aeroplanes: in that case, one can afford to fire ammunition costing half a million francs a round.”
Various defensive options
“With drones, one cannot simply fire cannons at sparrows. Small systems are needed, and it is by no means easy to develop them.”
+ “We have a unique opportunity to regulate autonomous weapons”
Researchers are exploring alternative approaches. “There are various groups around the world working on this issue. We, too, are studying a system to reliably detect drones, combining radar, infrared cameras and optical cameras,” said Siegwart.
“Once detected, they could be brought down with nets, using other drones or, depending on the situation, possibly by firing at them.”
“Switzerland, relative to its size, is in a very good position,” Siegwart said. “I have been in contact with Armasuisse’s German and Austrian counterparts and would say that our colleagues at Armasuisse are much better informed, understand the subject far better and know how to collaborate with universities. We are therefore relatively well positioned.”
The country boasts a favourable ecosystem. “Switzerland is very strong in the drone sector, particularly when it comes to civilian applications in research. There are several start-ups specialising in drone defence.”
“We won’t have a definitive solution within the next five months. But hopefully, sensible, cost-effective and, at the same time, reliable systems will become available fairly quickly,” Siegwart said.

New packaging rules take effect across EU, further protecting consumers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:07:54 UTC
18:07:54 KST

Burak Bir
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
New rules under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) began applying across the EU on Wednesday, aiming to better protect consumers.
“The PPWR will further help tackle the environmental challenges caused by packaging and make Europe less dependent on imported fossil fuels from which plastic packaging is almost entirely made,” the European Commission said in a statement.
“The measures will also help strengthen the Single Market for packaging and facilitate cross-border businesses through common rules,” it added.
A key measure taking effect Thursday is a restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in food-contact packaging, meaning such packaging containing PFAS above strict limits can no longer be placed on the EU market.
According to the Commission, the measure is designed to reduce exposure to so-called “forever chemicals” — a group of highly persistent substances that can accumulate in the environment and the human body.
“The new Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation is an investment in Europe’s future: it will help reduce waste, increase recycling, make food-contact packaging safer for the consumers by limiting harmful substances such as PFAS, and reduce our dependence on virgin raw materials,” said Jessika Roswall, commissioner for Environment, Water Resilience and a Competitive Circular Economy.

Europe readies for total solar eclipse- So, what will happen in the once-in-a generation stellar spectacle?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:07:12 UTC
18:07:12 KST

Maximum totality will occur off Iceland’s west coast. By the time it reaches a small patch of Portugal and then Spain with its massive crowds, totality will have dwindled to a minute or so. The spectacle will end in the Mediterranean.
A spectacular solar eclipse wowed those lucky enough to be on Easter Island in the Pacific Ocean in October 2024, but now a different part of the world is preparing to witness the astronomical phenomenon.
This Wednesday (12 August 2026), the moon will pass perfectly between the sun and the Earth, casting its shadow across a narrow swathe of the planet with many parts of Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain, experiencing the total eclipse while millions of Europeans across western Europe will witness a visible partial eclipse.
It will take 1.5 hours for the umbra, or moon’s sun-blocking shadow, to race along the 8,260-kilometre course, most of it over an empty Atlantic.
But starting near the North Pole around Siberia in Russia, before tracking south, totality is expected to last up to 2 minutes and 18 seconds. Daytime darkness will descend across the Iberian Peninsula, plus slivers of Greenland and Iceland.
This rare sight is expected to attract crowds who want to experience darkness during the day, the sudden drop in temperature that comes with an eclipse, and animals and birds going quiet as they confuse the moment with nighttime.
In London, the historic Royal Observatory Greenwich will host a watch party from its terraces, live streaming the event—weather permitting—as the sun is obscured over the city's skyline.
Spain to experience total eclipse—the first time in over a century
In the UK, more than 90% of the sun will be covered by the moon for most parts.
"From here in the UK, we're going to actually be very fortunate. We are seeing a partial eclipse, but it is a very strong partial, between 90 and 95%, depending on where you are in the UK," explains Jake Foster, an astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
"It's going to be happening around sunset. It is the golden hour eclipse, so it's going to be low on the western horizon. If you want to see the full eclipse, you need to get into the path of totality. And to get into the path totality, you're going to need to go to places like Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain.
Those are the places where the moon's shadow will be at its darkest, and you'll get that absolute 100% coverage of the moon in front of the sun."
A new moon passing between the sun and Earth is known as an eclipse. Only on the rare occasions when the moon passes exactly between our planet and the sun may that occur. Although the sun is 400 times larger than the moon, they appear to be about the same size in the sky because of their 400-fold distance from one another.
It's this quirk of the solar system that allows the moon to almost completely block the light of the sun.
Where the moon casts a total shadow is known as the umbra. Where it only partially blocks the sun and gives viewers on Earth a partial eclipse, it's known as the penumbra.
It can be a long wait to see such an event: Spain’s last full solar eclipse—not counting the Canary Islands—occurred two days before the Titanic’s sinking in 1912.
Maximum totality will occur off Iceland’s west coast. And by the time it reaches a small patch of Portugal and then Spain with its massive crowds, totality will have dwindled to a minute or so. The spectacle will end in the Mediterranean.
"Well, in order to see a total solar eclipse from the very same location more than once, you could be waiting over 200 years for that to happen. Partial eclipses can be slightly more common. But again, if we're talking about just from one particular country or one particular region of a country, you might get lucky; you might have a few partial eclipses in a decade. However, they can be very rare depending on where you are," says Foster.
Solar eclipse glasses to see the eclipse
To watch the phenomenon, viewers need a simple but essential piece of kit: solar eclipse glasses.
Without these, staring directly at the sun—even if just a slither of light remains—could damage eyesight.
"The safest way to view the eclipse directly is with a pair of solar eclipse glasses. They have special lenses in them that block out 99.9999% of the sun's light, only then making it safe to view. You've got to make sure that they are ISO certified so that they've been through the rigorous safety standards testing. But as long as you know that they're safe to use, you can directly look up towards the sun when viewing the eclipse," says Foster.
While these events are very predictable, even hundreds of years into the future, they are still a source of excitement for the scientific community. But also millions of people across the world.
Across Europe, astronomy shops are seeing a last-minute rush for certified viewing equipment. At one specialist store in Paris, the French capital, customers queued for more than two hours to get their hands on eclipse glasses and binoculars.
"Two hours! Two hours for a pair of sunglasses," 27-year-old Simon Noé who works in video game research, said Monday. "But for me, the eclipse is kind of a big deal. I remember when I was a child, I thought, What, there won't be another eclipse before 2026? 2026 seemed so far away. So this is a bit about making my inner child happy," he added.
Two of ESA’s space telescopes will observe the eclipsed sun and its corona, or outer atmosphere.
Proba-3, the space agency’s artificial eclipse-making satellite duo, will be positioned poorly but will try to sneak in some before-and-after shots.
"Solar eclipses are still incredibly exciting, even if you've seen a few of them. It really is a bucket list event, and there's really no limit to the amount of times you can see a bucket list event," says Foster.

Nearly 80 French departments were placed under an orange heat alert for Wednesday, with temperatures forecast to reach 40C (104F).
France’s national weather service Meteo-France issued orange heat wave alerts for 78 departments for Wednesday, while the number is expected to rise to 80 on Thursday.
The ongoing heat wave is forecast to push temperatures to between 36C and 40C (97F-104F) across France.
Temperatures of up to 39C-40C (102F-104F) are expected in Saumur in the Maine-et-Loire department.

According to the government, nearly 70% of France is currently subject to water-use restrictions.
Meanwhile, 45 departments have been placed under orange alert due to a high risk of forest fires.

Lithuania’s opposition conservatives are seeking talks with staff at the country’s embassy in Washington as questions grow over the performance of Ambassador Gediminas Varvuolis, according to sources.

The initiative came from Žygimantas Pavilionis, deputy chairman of the parliamentary Committee on Foreign Affairs, and former Prime Minister Ingrida Šimonytė, with embassy employees helping distribute the message.
Varvuolis said he was unaware of any such invitations from politicians.

The ministry said it was assessing the allegations and would decide within five working days whether to launch a formal investigation.
Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the parliamentary Committee on Foreign Affairs, said the allegations should be assessed by the Foreign Ministry and its General Inspectorate rather than by lawmakers.
Pavilionis said the leaks to the media did not come from him, but acknowledged that he had been aware of staff grievances for about six months.
Varvuolis has served as Lithuania’s ambassador to the United States since August 1, 2025.
FM slams opposition for harming US ties
Lithuania’s Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys has criticised the conservative MPs’ initiative, saying it does damage to ties with the US.
“This is yet another instance of provocation and political intrigue by the conservatives, this time with harmful consequences for our foreign policy. Their desire to discredit and damage our relations with the US is shameful and knows no bounds,” Budrys Wednesday.
He argued that using embassy staff for political games was unacceptable and disrupted the work of both the diplomatic mission and the ministry.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has also commented on the controversy, urging opposition politicians to stop interfering in embassy work.
“It is vital for us to maintain our strategic partnership with the US. Internal perturbations and conflicts do not bring credit to us as a state, nor do they improve our relations. Therefore, I would suggest that while politicians should not ignore situations that may exist and should investigate them, they must not interfere in their escalation,” the prime minister told reporters Wednesday.

Parliament speaker calls for improvement of Marriage and Family Code in Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12

MINSK, 12 August (BelTA) - In Belarus, there is a growing need for comprehensive improvement of the Code on Marriage and Family, Chairman of the House of Representatives Igor Sergeyenko said at a seminar to discuss ways of improving legislation in the field of marriage and family relations hosted by the Loshitsa historical and cultural complex in Minsk, BelTA has learned.
According to Igor Sergeyenko, the venue for the seminar was chosen not by chance. It is a unique site in Minsk, which many Belarusians choose for wedding ceremonies. Last September, the renovated Loshitsa historical and cultural complex was visited by the head of state. “Aleksandr Lukashenko has repeatedly emphasized that a truly strong family is a continuation not only of someone’s name, but of the entire Belarusian people. A strong family with two or more children should become a way of life. As the president noted yesterday at a meeting with the Council of Ministers, motherhood and fatherhood should become a fashionable trend. The formula is simple: two parents, two children. Only this way can we be confident that future generations will continue, firmly holding sovereignty in their hands and living in peace,” he stressed.
Igor Sergeyenko noted that the Code on Marriage and Family does not directly impact the birth rate or the demographics, but it does create guarantees for the protection of the rights of every family member, making marriage and family more stable and attractive for having children. “The protection and strengthening of the institution of family and marriage, according to the Constitution of our country, is a priority of state policy, and its effective implementation is impossible without proper legal regulation. Several years ago, we adopted a law amending certain provisions of the Code on Marriage and Family. The amendments affected a wide range of issues and were targeted in nature, from the property interests of minors to the registration of civil status acts. But today, there is a growing need for comprehensive improvement of the Code, taking into account both the accumulated law enforcement practice and advancing technologies,” Igor Sergeyenko explained.
The House of Representatives has received the proposals for a range of amendments to the Code from the Supreme Court, the Justice Ministry, and the Minsk City Executive Committee, the Speaker noted. “These proposals are supported by the MPs as well. The Standing Committee on Health, Physical Culture, Family and Youth Policy is ready to work hand in hand with all these institutions to swiftly draw up a bill revising the Code on Marriage and Family,” he said. “I have no doubt that today’s meeting will allow us to tackle the most pressing issues, which will then find their way into the bill. After all, stable legislation in such a vital area is invaluable."

Illegal miners killed in South Africa dump site collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:05:49 UTC
18:05:49 KST

Illegal miners killed in South Africa dump site collapse
At least 14 suspected illegal miners have been killed and eight others injured after the walls of an excavation collapsed at a dumping site in South Africa’s North West province, the authorities have said.
The suspected ‘zama zamas’ – a local term for illegal miners – were digging for platinum-group metals at Nkaneng, near the mining city of Rustenburg, when walls of heaped earth gave way on Monday night, the South African Police Service (SAPS) said in a statement. Police said a company had been granted a permit to extract the metals at the site.
“[The] authorities are continuing to assess the situation amid concerns that an unknown number of illegal miners may still be trapped underground,” North West provincial police commissioner Lieutenant General Arthur Adams said.
According to the commissioner, most of the dead are believed to be Basotho nationals from neighboring Lesotho.
SAPS said three of the injured were arrested on suspicion of illegal mining after being discharged from hospital, while five remained under police guard as they received treatment.
The site lies in the heart of South Africa’s platinum belt, about 130 km northwest of Johannesburg.
Mikateko Mahlaule, chairman of the parliament’s Portfolio Committee on Mineral and Petroleum Resources, called the deaths a “painful reminder” of the hazards surrounding illegal mining and demanded stronger action against the industry. He also urged the authorities to expand lawful opportunities for small-scale and artisanal miners while enforcing health, safety, and environmental rules.
#sapsNW [NORTH WEST SAPS CONFIRMS 14 DEATHS OF ILLEGAL MINERS]
The Provincial Commissioner of the South African Police Service (#SAPS) in the North West, Lieutenant General Arthur Adams, has confirmed the deaths of 14 illegal miners at the Nkaneng dumping site in Bojanala… pic.twitter.com/jvAvzgxDiZ
Illegal miners in South Africa are commonly called zama zamas, a Zulu expression loosely translated as ‘chance takers’. Tens of thousands are believed to work in abandoned commercial mines or makeshift excavations, often without safety equipment and sometimes underground for weeks. The authorities have linked parts of the illicit industry to criminal syndicates, gang violence, undocumented migration and illegal firearms.
South Africa launched operation Vala Umgodi (Close the Hole) in December 2023 to target illegal mining networks. The campaign is led by SAPS, with 2,200 South African National Defense Force personnel deployed in March 2026 to support operations across five provinces, including North West. As of June 2025, police said the operation had led to more than 27,000 arrests.
The latest Nkaneng deaths follow several mass-casualty incidents linked to illicit mining. In 2023, at least 31 suspected illegal miners died in a methane explosion at a disused mine in Free State province. At least 87 miners also died during a months-long standoff at an abandoned gold mine near Stilfontein in late 2024 and early 2025.
Police restricted supplies to force the miners to surface, prompting fierce criticism of the authorities. A court-ordered operation eventually recovered 78 bodies and brought 246 survivors above ground.

AI generated
MOSCOW – Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Aug 12 that Russia will respond in kind if European countries start to seize Russian merchant vessels and the commander of Russia’s Pacific Fleet said his forces were ready to “inspect and detain” foreign vessels.
The comments, which Putin made as he oversaw navy drills in Russia’s far east, come as the EU intensifies pressure on Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, expanding sanctions against hundreds of vessels and detaining some ships and their crews for checks.
Some European governments have said they are exploring tougher maritime enforcement measures against ships suspected of sanctions evasion.
“We can see that the authorities of certain countries, in violation of international maritime law, are attempting to restrict the movement of our economic operators’ vessels... and have recently gone so far as to consider the possibility of seizing our vessels and selling off the property they have plundered from us,” said Putin.

Viktor Liina, commander of Russia’s Pacific Fleet, told Putin that what he described as hostile countries like Britain and France also transported goods on vessels flying flags of convenience which – if the EU and Britain’s own language was used – could also be described as a “shadow fleet”.
“Western states are actively using vessels flying the flags of third countries to transport cargo in their own interests. In essence, this constitutes their shadow fleet,” Liina told Putin.
“We have the capabilities to inspect and detain vessels belonging to unfriendly states and their shadow fleet; inter-agency coordination is in place, and we are ready to tackle these tasks.”
He said his fleet had carried out a detailed analysis of maritime traffic in the Asia-Pacific region and knew the routes, the cargo, and ownership of the vessels.
Putin also accused NATO of threatening behaviour in the Asia-Pacific region, and of creating tension in the Arctic.
“We can see that, unfortunately, the potential for conflict is growing here; NATO is making inroads here; new military-political blocs are being formed; and new weapons systems are being deployed here, or are planned for deployment, which also pose a threat to our country,” said Putin. REUTERS

LONDON — Prime Minister Andy Burnham will lead a meeting of the government's emergency committee Wednesday afternoon in response to ongoing heatwaves, droughts and wildfires across the U.K.
COBR (Cabinet Office Briefing Room) meetings are convened during a crisis or emergency — and come as the record-breaking conditions take a severe toll on U.K. infrastructure.

Advertisement
A Downing Street spokesperson said: “We know how challenging this summer is proving, particularly for firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units.
“We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies, support farming communities and safeguard the environment.”

The U.K. is grappling with wildfires including at the New Forest national park in south England. The National Fire Chiefs Council responded to 458 wildfires last month, its busiest month on record.
'Snail's pace'
The rival Green Party first demanded a COBR meeting weeks ago after a wildfire engulfed parts of Suffolk in eastern England. Green Leader Zack Polanski said Wednesday's meeting is “only a first step. This is a climate emergency which is leading to hundreds of deaths and stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit. What we urgently need is concrete action.”
Advertisement
Liberal Democrat Energy Spokesperson Pippa Heylings warned a COBR meeting alone “will not put out fires or protect our communities,” and said government is “moving at a snail’s pace.”
Prior to today's COBR, the U.K.'s National Drought Group and Severe Weather Resilience Network have held regular meetings, and the government has also vowed to work with water companies to build nine new reservoirs for the U.K. — which built its last reservoir back in 1992.
U.K. climate advisers have meanwhile spent much of the summer urging the country to up its game when it comes to adaptation for a warming world.
The Committee on Climate Change, a government advisory body, said in May that cooling to protect from heat, “increased flood preparedness, and improved water management are the highest priorities.”
“Deploying these adaptations at scale will help avoid loss of life – particularly amongst those most vulnerable to climate impacts – and unnecessary damage and disruption to people and to the economy,” it said.
The U.K. has been “built to a climate that no longer exists,” Swenja Surminski, a member of the Climate Change Committee Adaptation Committee, told MPs in June.

Germany’s best viewpoints from above: Scenic walks, mountain peaks and sky-high bridges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:04:07 UTC
18:04:07 KST

Some of Germany’s best places to take in the views are from above, including at the country’s highest mountain standing next to a statue of mythological hero Hercules.
An expansive country of bustling cities plus calmer forests, alpine summits and rivers, Germany offers plenty of ways to experience its landscapes.
But for a different perspective on the country: look up.
Some of the country’s best panoramic viewpoints are from the country’s treetop walks, viewing platforms and dramatic suspension bridges that put its forest canopies, river valleys and coastal cliffs at centre stage.
See the top of Germany from the Zugspitze on the Austria-Germany border
Germany’s highest mountain stands 2,962 metres tall and is home to the country’s last remaining glaciers: the Nördliche Schneeferner and the Höllentalferner.
Situated on the border between Germany and Austria, this mountain peak’s summit offers scenic views of 400 surrounding mountain peaks across Germany, Austria, Italy and Switzerland.
The Zugspitze is a hotspot for mountaineers, skiers, snowboarders and toboggan enthusiasts alike and is accessible via a choice of three cable cars, including an almost 100-year-old cogwheel train.
Views beside Hercules in Kassel
Europe’s largest hillside park, covering a total area of 560 hectares and at a height of 530 metres, is located in the city of Kassel.
Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe in Kassel is famed for its array of trees, plants and architectural waterwork attractions that date back to the 18th century, joining UNESCO’s World Heritage Site list in 2013.
For the best views of Kassel, visitors should stand beside the park’s 8.3-metre-high statue of Hercules. From there, views include Wilhelmshöhe Palace and Löwenburg Castle in the distance and, on a clear day, the Harz and Rhön Mountain ranges on the horizon.
Stand sky-high in Berlin
Got some extra time in Berlin? Add the Berlin Gasometer in the Schöneberg district to your itinerary for a different perspective on the German capital.
The former low-pressure gas tank, first established in 1913, has lived several lives, serving as an advertising space, event venue and television studio.
Rising to almost 80 metres into the sky, the structure houses a Sky Lounge with a roof terrace located at a height of around 66 metres above ground. For those with a head for heights, the elevated vantage point leaves the entire city at your feet, with sights including the Zoological Garden, the Reichstag government building and Victory Column on offer as far as the eye can see.
Walk along the treetops of Black Forest in Bad Wildbad
Bad Wildbad is home to a walkway that stretches 1,250 metres and leads to a 40-metre high observation tower that rewards visitors with unmissable panoramic views of the Black Forest mountain range and Enz Valley river.
The route winds over the course of one to two hours to get to the top, where visitors can see The Nature Park Schwarzwald Mitte/Nord – the country’s third largest nature park. On especially clear days, visitors might be lucky to even see as far as the Stuttgart TV Tower and the Swabian Jura mountain range.
Sights fit for a king on Rügen Island
Germany’s largest island, the Baltic Sea island Rügen, houses the “King’s Chair”.
Known locally as Königsstuhl, the 118-metre high King's Chair is the highest point of Rügen's famous chalk cliffs located within the Jasmund National Park.
From the top of the viewing platform, visitors are rewarded with a sweeping view of the endless blue Baltic Sea, coastal formations, white chalk cliffs and lush green beech tree forests.
See Saxony from Bastei Bridge in Lohmen
This 76.5-metre-long and 305-metre-high stone bridge rises above the Elbe River in Germany in the heart of Saxon Switzerland Park.
This historic bridge peaked local interest for its tourist potential as early as 1824 as a site of sandstone rock formations. Today, it leads visitors through the rocky ravine of the Mardertelle to the ruins of the 13th-century Neurathen medieval rock castle.
The monument is open to the public year-round, but for travellers keen to skip the crowds, it’s best to either arrive early in the morning or in the evening to catch the sunset.

Russian Aerospace Forces Day: What’s inside the arsenal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:03:32 UTC
18:03:32 KST

Russian Aerospace Forces Day: What’s inside the arsenal
The Russian Aerospace Forces (VKS) mark their anniversary on Wednesday. One of the youngest branches of the Russian military in its current form, the VKS were established 11 years ago.
While its aviation arm traces its lineage through the Soviet and Imperial Russian air forces, the modern VKS are a significantly broader and more complex branch of the military.
The formation of the VKS began in the late 1990s, when the Russian Air Force was merged with the country’s Anti-Aircraft Defense Forces, receiving aviation assets of the Russian Ground Forces a few years later. The VKS took its current form in 2015, when the Air Force was merged with the short-lived Aerospace Defense Forces, established in 2011.
The VKS, which currently have some 165,000 active duty personnel, has three distinctive sub-branches – the Air Force, the Anti-aircraft and Missile Defense troops, and the Space Forces.
The VKS oversee fighter, frontline, and long-range aviation, the aerial component of the Russian nuclear triad, anti-aircraft units, and assorted space-related assets. It also has dedicated mechanized infantry units under its direct command. Originally intended to guard rear installations, the VKS were ultimately expanded into two full-fledged regiments, often jokingly referred to as ‘Spacemarines.’
As the Russian Aerospace Forces mark their anniversary, RT looks at its arsenal.
Air superiority
The Sukhoi Su-30 and Su-35 jets are Russia’s key air superiority aircraft. The 4.5-generation fighter jets are heavily modernized successors of the Su-27, modern variants of which are still widely used by the military. The entire stock is expected to be modernized to the Su-35 standard by the end of the decade.
The aircraft are complemented by the fifth-generation Su-57 multirole fighter, which boasts both air superiority and long-range strike capabilities. In recent years, the military has received more planes of the type, with the current fleet estimated at some 35 mass-produced aircraft, as well as ten prototype jets. The Russian Air Force is expected to have at least 76 mass-produced Su-57 jets by late 2028.
Frontline aviation
The Su-34 fighter-bomber has become the backbone of Russia’s frontline aviation, seeing extensive use in the Ukraine conflict. The introduction of the Universal Correction and Guidance Modules (UMPK) winged upgrade kits, which are fitted onto old-school freefall bombs, has greatly expanded the capabilities of such planes, turning the munitions into high-precision weaponry and drastically increasing their range.
The aircraft, colloquially known as ‘Hell Duckling’ thanks to its distinctive cockpit shape, is slated to replace aging Su-24M planes. The aircraft, however, are still in active use within the Russian military and operate alongside their modern counterparts.
Close air support
The veteran Su-25 jet remains the key tool in Russia’s close air support inventory. The plane, however, has largely lost its prominence amid the Ukraine conflict, given the extremely dense anti-aircraft coverage on both sides, as well as the new threat posed by drones for low-altitude flying planes.
The frontline strike helicopter, by contrast, has shone during the ongoing conflict. Assorted long-range guided weaponry has allowed such aircraft as the Kamov Ka-52 and Mil Mi-28 to dominate the battlefield, striking moving armored and soft vehicles, as well as stationary targets with pinpoint accuracy, while remaining largely out of reach of short-range anti-aircraft systems.
The strike helicopters have also been extensively used in anti-aircraft roles, hunting down fixed-wing drones, which have been launched by Kiev’s forces en masse on an almost daily basis in recent months. The helicopters are able to intercept drones with air-to-air missiles, as well as onboard cannon armament.
Long arm
Russia maintains a fleet of different long-range aircraft dating back to the Cold War era, namely the Tupolev Tu-22M3, the Tu-160 jets, and the true veteran, the Tu-95 turboprop strategic bomber. All of the aircraft in this class have been deeply modernized and effectively share only airframes with the original Soviet-era planes. The strategic aircraft are part of the Russian nuclear triad and are capable of carrying missiles with thermonuclear warheads.
In recent years, the Russian long arm received a somewhat unconventional addition – the modernized MiG-31K jets. The high-altitude interceptors have been transformed into carriers of Kinzhal aeroballistic hypersonic missiles, seeing action in the Ukraine conflict to strike high-value targets.
Anti-aircraft defenses
The VKS are responsible for anti-aircraft and missile defense save for the shortest-range systems used directly by units subordinate to Russia’s ground forces. The inventory includes assorted systems filling different roles.
The S-300 and S-400 systems are the key elements in the medium-to-long range anti-aircraft defenses. The systems within the family, and the upcoming S-500 in particular, are believed to have capabilities to strike targets even in low Earth orbit, potentially serving as an anti-satellite weapon.
On the tactical level, the Pantsir-S system and its derivatives have emerged as one of the key tools in the Russian inventory. The system has proven to be highly efficient in the Ukraine conflict, providing cover to frontline troops and installations deep in the country’s territory alike.
Space troops
The space component of the VKS is, rather unsurprisingly, the most secretive sub-branch of the entire force. The Space Troops are responsible for launching military satellites, maintaining long-range communications, gathering electronic intelligence, and providing early warning for missile attacks.
It remains unclear whether the force actually has any strike capabilities in the domain, given that Moscow has long argued against the militarization of space. Recently, however, several unconfirmed Western media reports alleged that Russian military satellites approached other space vehicles and attempted to jam their communications.

ALBAWABA - In a new innovation in subduing civilians, ICE is spending millions on new gloves that give 'bee sting' electric shocks to ‘combative’ individuals.
ICE is planning to spend $20 million on what they have called “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for their agents by March of next year, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
The “distraction and de-escalation” devices are also known as G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter. ICE will not be the first to use these devices as they have been in service by some jails and police departments in the U.S. in recent years.
Civil rights activists are understandably alarmed at the new addition to ICE’s arsenal as they say that ICE agents already face criticism of unnecessary violence when subduing civilians, adding that giving them more weapons is not the right move.
The company responsible for the creation, Compliant Technologies, says the gloves will function as normal gloves until the agent presses a switch giving any suspects a painful shock, giving the agent the upper hand.
“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” according to the president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. “If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”
While Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union said:
“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

US Navy reclassifies nineteen submarines as missile boats
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:03:06 BST
18:03:06 KST

The United States Navy is reclassifying 19 planned Virginia-class submarines fitted with the Virginia Payload Module as guided missile submarines, changing their designation from SSN to SSGN, the service stated.
The change covers Blocks V and VI of the class. It is a designation change rather than a modification, and the boats remain part of the Virginia programme, but it formally separates them from the attack submarines that share the name.
The Virginia Payload Module is an additional hull section inserted into the boat, adding length and four large vertical launch tubes to the two already carried forward. Each tube holds seven Tomahawk cruise missiles, taking the total from 12 in earlier blocks to 40, roughly tripling the strike load a single submarine can carry.
The first of the type, SSGN 803, is estimated to deliver in the 2029 financial year, with deliveries running through to 2038.
Vice Admiral Rob Gaucher, director of submarine programs, said: “This reclassification is a clear acknowledgment of the increased lethality VPM brings to the undersea fight. These VPM-equipped SSGNs will ensure the Navy continues to dominate the undersea domain for decades to come. By integrating this additional payload capacity, we will have the ability to surge strike power to assure our allies, deter aggression, outmatch any adversary, and give our Fleet commanders an incredibly versatile, hard-hitting instrument of national power.”
Admiral Daryl Caudle, the Chief of Naval Operations, tied the announcement to the retirement of the boats the new designation effectively replaces.
He said: “This transition comes at an important moment as USS Georgia, one of the Navy’s four Ohio-class guided-missile submarines, begins the inactivation process after more than four decades of exceptional service. Georgia and her sister ships proved the enduring value of combining undersea stealth with unmatched clandestine strike capability. The next generation of Virginia-class SSGNs builds on that legacy with greater survivability, adaptability, and sustained combat power.”
The four Ohio-class SSGNs were converted from ballistic missile submarines in the 2000s after the arms control treaties then in force required a reduction in the number of boats carrying nuclear weapons. Rather than scrap them, the Navy stripped out the Trident tubes and refitted 22 of them for seven Tomahawks apiece, producing submarines able to carry 154 cruise missiles alongside accommodation for special forces. USS Florida fired more than 90 Tomahawks against Libyan air defences in 2011.
Those boats are now reaching the end of their hulls’ certified lives, and their retirement removes a large slice of the Navy’s undersea strike capacity at once. Nineteen Virginias at 40 missiles each restores the total, though spread across many more platforms.
Vice Admiral Rick Seif, commander of submarine forces, said: “The Submarine Force is defined by our ability to operate undetected and strike without warning. By integrating high-volume precision strike capabilities into these stealth platforms, these SSGNs serve as the ultimate enabler for Distributed Maritime Operations, giving our warfighters the overwhelming, flexible firepower required to win decisively in any theatre.”

Türkiye’s export, import unit value indices rise in June
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:01:51 UTC
18:01:51 KST

Türkiye’s overall export unit value index increased by 12.6 percent year-on-year in June, while the import unit value index rose by 12.9 percent, according to foreign trade indices data.
The export unit value index increased by 11.6 percent for manufactured goods, 5.9 percent for food, beverages and tobacco, 4.8 percent for crude materials, and 40.7 percent for fuels, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said on Aug. 12.
Meanwhile, the overall export volume index rose by 8.1 percent compared with June 2025.
On the import side, the overall import unit value index climbed 12.9 percent year-on-year in June. Import unit values decreased by 3 percent for food, beverages and tobacco, but increased by 39.3 percent for fuels, 9.1 percent for crude materials excluding fuels, and 6.6 percent for manufactured goods excluding food, beverages and tobacco.
The overall import volume index increased by 9 percent from a year earlier. Import volumes rose by 46.8 percent for food, beverages and tobacco, 25.9 percent for crude materials excluding fuels, and 13.9 percent for manufactured goods excluding food, beverages and tobacco. Fuel import volumes declined by 7.5 percent.
Seasonally and calendar-adjusted data showed that the export volume index fell 5.5 percent from May to June, while the adjusted import volume index increased by 8.3 percent month-on-month in June.
Türkiye’s terms of trade fell to 90.1 in June from 90.3 a year earlier, the data showed.

Introducing Count Binface, Britain's Political Satirist Who Is Standing Against Nigel Farage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Satirical candidates are a long-standing tradition in British politics. When former Prime Minister Keir Starmer delivered a victory speech after winning his north London seat in the 2024 General Election, he was flanked by someone in an Elmo costume and a man wearing a laboratory coat and a comically large hat. To the uninitiated, it may have seemed as though a major security breach had taken place. In reality, those were just some of the candidates Starmer had defeated.
But few, if any, novelty candidates have made as much of an impression as Count Binface. The self-described “intergalactic space warrior” wears a garbage can on his head and has become a regular name on election ballots across England over the past decade. He recently went up against Andy Burnham in the Makerfield by-election, and was among the first to congratulate Burnham on his victory, which cleared the now-Prime Minister’s pathway back to Westminster.
Now, Count Binface has landed himself firmly in the middle of the fraught Clacton by-election taking place Thursday, emerging as the main rival for Nigel Farage, leader of the right-wing populist Reform UK party and a long-time ally of President Donald Trump.
In July, amid mounting scrutiny over undisclosed gifts and donations, Farage resigned as the Member of Parliament (MP) for Clacton, a coastal town in the east of England, in order to trigger a by-election in which he could run.
"I've decided that the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions," he said, predicting a “people vs. the establishment by-election” would soon follow.
The main political parties in the U.K. said they would not be taking part in the by-election, which the Conservatives leader referred to as a "fake" election intended to distract people from the investigation into Farage's finances.
It remains to be seen if Farage’s gamble will pay off when voters head to the polls. A Survation poll conducted in July suggested 73% of Clacton adults may vote for Farage, with 20% of those remaining opting for Count Binface. Still, the British media is jubilantly anticipating a “showdown” between Farage and his garbage can-wearing adversary.
Ahead of the polls opening, TIME’s Richard Hall caught up with Count Binface. True to form, the comedian, whose real name is Jon Harvey, stayed in character throughout the conversation.
(This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity).
TIME: Our readers from all around the world may not be familiar with the peculiarities of British politics or your political platform. Can you introduce us to Count Binface, the candidate?
Count Binface: I am an intergalactic space warrior, leader of the Recyclons from planet Sigma IX, and a part-time democratic politician on Earth. My hobbies include invading star systems, dominating species, and watching the Lovejoy box set. That won't mean anything to most of your readers, but it should. It’s the greatest art your planet has produced. Well, that and the Sistine Chapel.
You have stood in a number of elections, sometimes in different forms. Can you tell us what drew you to this one in Clacton?
Clacton is where the election is. If I’d gone elsewhere, it would have been less effective. Dare I say it, we wouldn't be talking now.
You've stood in many elections, and lost them all. This time people appear to be taking you a bit more seriously. They think you may be able to improve on your previous personal best of 308 votes. Why do you think that is?
I have lost my previous seven elections on Earth, but only numerically. Let's look at my past opponents. Theresa May, remember her? Thought not. Boris Johnson, Rishi Sunak, they’re all on [the] scrapheap of history, something I know a lot about. And yet I am going stronger than ever. I'm playing the long game. Do I think I can beat 308 in Clacton? I wouldn't want to presume. Let's see what happens.
This time you're up against Nigel Farage, a man mired in a personal financing scandal. What does it tell us about British politics that people are considering voting for a garbage can over a real human?
Mr Farage's finances are a matter for him, but he has decided to make them a matter for the Clacton electorate, too. I'm not interested in ad hominem attacks on any of my 33 opponents. But do I think it's strategically odd to call a by-election while you're being investigated by a parliamentary committee, the result of which could also lead to a by-election? Yes I do. Is that a waste of time and money? You might think so. I couldn't possibly comment.
As for why they're choosing me, I offer the perfect blend of fully-costed policies, intergalactic drip, and as bizarre as it seems, I'll be the best local champion for the inhabitants of the area.
Your policies include a “windfall tax on cosy crime novels written by celebrities” and a referendum on whether Pluto should regain its planet status. How have the people of Clacton reacted to your manifesto, and to your campaign in general?
I've been very gratified by the response both on the ground and in cyberspace. In actual fact, the policies you mention aren't the biggest hits so far. Top of the pops is my pledge that 99 Flake ice creams [a British tradition for generations] should be price-capped at 99p. For a seaside town, this was a no-brainer.
Another one which has done well in polling is this: Bosses of privatised water companies take a dip in British rivers to see how they like it, because they're full of excrement and all sorts. Curiously, I didn't even put this one in my Clacton manifesto, but I stand by all my past commitments, so this is an active pledge.
If we wake up on the morning after this election and Count Binface has been defeated by Nigel Farage, what do you want people to have taken away from your campaign? And will you stick around for your opponent's victory speech?
I hope they take the policies, my broader points, a smile, and a rehabilitated respect for democracy. Yes, of course, all candidates should respect the winner's victory speech. I'm sure Nigel will stick around to listen.

Zambia's 2026 election: Key issues to watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:57:00 UTC
17:57:00 KST

Zambia's 2026 election: Key issues to watch
August 12, 2026
Zambia's general election on Thursday will be fought on economic recovery, governance reforms and a sweeping change to the country's parliamentary map.
Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND), is seeking a second term against 14 opponents.
His principal challenger is Brian Mundubile, a former ally of the late President Edgar Lungu, who has surged to the front of a fragmented opposition after being backed by a coalition of rival parties.
The Electoral Commission announced in April that 70 new constituencies would be added, raising the number of parliamentary seats from 156 to 226, creating smaller, more local voting districts. Up to 8.7 million voters are expected to take part in the elections, a majority of whom are women.
Economic issues dominate Zambia's election campaign
Economic issues dominate voters' concerns. Official data shows that over 70% of the population lives on less than three dollars a day, and many households survive on salaries between $60 and $100 (€52 and €87) a month while grocery prices keep rising.
"I would like the new government to increase our salaries. [Maize meal] is very expensive. Everything is expensive," said security guard Lucky Mutelo.
Rebecca, a market shopper, echoes the sentiment, noting that "the cost of living is still too high."
The government has been making significant gains on these issues.
Hichilema's government has secured a landmark debt restructuring agreement, restoring an International Monetary Fund program and supporting economic growth. Inflation fell to 6.5% in June this year.
The administration has also rolled out free education and an expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.
Nevertheless, a historic drought that crippled agriculture and forced severe hydro‑power load‑shedding has strained household finances.
Election demographics amid a fragmented electoral field
To become president, a candidate must secure 50% plus one of the total votes cast. If no contender reaches this threshold, the two highest‑scoring candidates will face off in a second round — a mechanism designed to ensure that the president enjoys a clear popular mandate.
There are 14 names on the ballot, so even small swings in support across the 10 provinces could determine whether the election goes to a second round.
Analysts say the election's outcome would hinge on urban centers such as Lusaka and the Copperbelt, where cost‑of‑living pressures are most acute, while rural provinces traditionally follow established party loyalties.
Rural voters in the Southern, Western and North‑Western provinces historically back the UPND, whereas the opposition targets the Northern, Luapula and Eastern provinces.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported that the high youth turnout that propelled the current president Hakainde Hichilema to a landslide victory in 2021 is expected to be a decisive factor again, especially in densely populated urban districts.
Nearly half of registered voters are aged between 18 and 35, making young people a potentially pivotal bloc, Institute for Security Studies researcher Zenge Simakoloyi told AFP.
Can women swing Zambia's election?
Gender representation is another prominent theme. In this election, there is one female presidential candidate and four female running mates.
Mwaka Nyirenda is one of a handful of women contesting for a parliamentary seat.
"Politics is still a man's world. People doubt you, underestimate you and try to intimidate you," she told DW, noting that the financial bias still favors male candidates.
Women comprise roughly 51% of Zambia's population but hold only about 15% of parliamentary seats, and fewer than 20% of political leadership positions.
Leah Diana Mitaba, publicity secretary of the Non‑Governmental Coordinating Council, warns that these figures "demonstrate that Zambia remains far from achieving the 50:50 gender representation envisaged in the Constitution, the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development, the African Union Agenda 2063 and the UN Sustainable Development Goals."
Girls Gone Political, a civil‑society group, campaigns for greater female participation. Its leader, Dorothy Mtanga, thinks more civic education is needed. "There's the need for sustained democratic civic education to ensure that more women are elected into office," she said.
Judicial independence called into question
This election also raises questions about the independence of Zambia's judiciary.
In 2024, President Hichilema suspended three Constitutional Court judges who ruled in favor of his rival, former President Edgar Lungu.
Lawyer Linda Kasonde argued that "judicial independence is the ability to adjudicate on any matter, without fear or favor, regardless of the stakes involved in the case." In practice, opposition lawyers think the executive is trying to interfere with justice delivery.
Kasonde identifies two recent concerns. First, an executive‑approved salary increase for judges that bypassed the constitutional emoluments commission.
"The government increased salaries for judicial officers in 2025 outside the proper procedure, raising questions about whether the process was independent," she told DW.
Second, the appointment of 16 new judges in early 2026, many of whom hail from the incumbent's strongholds.
"These appointments call into question whether any decisions that will be made regarding the elections will be done independently," lawyer Kasonde concluded.
Amnesty International says Zambian laws, including the Public Order Act and cybercrime legislation, have been weaponized to restrict dissent, opposition gatherings and freedom of expression. It also warns that the increasing use of criminal charges against government critics could have a chilling effect on political expression.
Chief Justice Mumba Malila recently reassured the public.
"The judiciary stands ready to discharge its constitutional responsibility, independently, professionally and within the strict timelines established by the law," he said. Critics, however, maintain that true independence requires full structural and financial autonomy from the executive.
Continuity or change in Zambia?
Zambia's status as one of the region's stable multi‑party democracies in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) means that this election will influence regional democratic norms.
The country's ability to host a peaceful transition or renewal of power is a barometer for neighboring states, especially after recent defeats of incumbents in Botswana and Malawi.
Polls will be open from 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Zambians will elect a president, National Assembly members, mayors, councilors, and council chairs.
This election holds the potential to either consolidate President Hichilema's reform agenda or usher in a new administration.

Wisconsin Democrats choose moderate Crowley for governor's race in US battleground state

2026-08-12

17:56:42 KST

Moderate Crowley beats democratic socialist Hong in Wisconsin governor's primary
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley on Wednesday eked out a stunningly narrow win against democratic socialist Francesca Hong in the Democratic party primary for the Wisconsin governor's race. Crowley's win by less than a percentage point comes as the party faces a divide between establishment candidates and an insurgent progressive movement ahead of the 2026 US midterm elections.
Moderate Democrat David Crowley won the Wisconsin primary for governor, defeating a democratic socialist who fell short of trying to deliver another win for progressives in a battleground state.
Crowley, who is vying to become Wisconsin’s first Black governor, pitched himself as the candidate best positioned to win in November against Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump.
Crowley narrowly defeated democratic socialist Francesca Hong, who was hoping to ride the wave of recent victories by progressive candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in neighbouring Michigan’s US Senate race last week.
Read moreLeftist El-Sayed narrowly wins high-profile Michigan Democratic Senate primary
His win was the movement’s first major success in a purple state. It also fed fears in the party’s leaders that such candidates, farther afield and often carrying political baggage of past stances such as defunding the police, would struggle to beat Republicans and imperil the party’s hopes of recapturing control of the US Senate and US House.
Crowley didn’t address supporters Tuesday night but was expected at a unity event later Wednesday.
“Now, David is focused on bringing people together, earning the support of Democrats, Republicans, Independents, and anyone who believes Wisconsin is at its best when we work together and deliver results," Crowley's campaign manager Garren Randolph said in a statement.
Hong’s loss in Wisconsin may have doused the momentum, but it’s far from snuffing it out. A democratic socialist coming close to victory in a battleground state sends a clear message: there’s unignorable angst among the party’s voters.
“We have built something that will change politics forever,” Hong told supporters as the outcome of the race hung in the balance late Tuesday. “The work we have done will be remembered forever. I know we don’t have the final results right now, but what I do know is we are ready to keep fighting.”
Her campaign manager Becky Cooper said after Hong conceded the race that she was “proud of the race we ran”.
“Our team campaigned clean, our souls are intact and we really made meaningful change for the progressive movement,” she said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Associated Press declared Crowley the winner once Hong’s concession removed the possibility of a recount in the exceptionally close race.
Hong could have requested a recount since Crowley’s margin of victory was less than 1 percentage point. But because it was wider than 0.25 points, Hong’s campaign would have had to pay for it.
Progressives had wanted to notch a clear win, but national progressive leaders, most notably Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and US Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, sat out the race and did not endorse.
The movement is not entirely aligned. Not all candidates are democratic socialists or have endorsements from Sanders, but they are often tilling similar voter anger with politics and the party: over military aid to Israel, the amount of money wielded in campaigns, the Trump administration’s immigration raids and the rising cost of daily life.
In New York City in the June primary elections, two democratic socialist candidates and a progressive came out on top, booting two Democratic incumbents from Congress in the process. All three were backed by the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, himself a democratic socialist who framed the upsets as a question of electing “better Democrats”.
Read moreZohran Mamdani takes office as first Muslim mayor of New York City
Democrats in Wisconsin are hoping to capitalise on low approval ratings for Trump in a state he won in 2016 and 2024 to retain control of the governor’s office and flip both chambers of the Legislature to earn full control of Wisconsin state government for the first time since 2010.
Both Hong and Crowley said in the waning days of the race that they expected Democrats to come together and unite to defeat Tiffany, a congressman from conservative, rural northern Wisconsin.
“Our ultimate goal is to make sure we don’t have a MAGA extremist occupying the governor’s office,” Crowley said Sunday.
Democrat David Zimmerman, a 79-year-old retired industrial engineer professor in Madison, voted for Crowley on Tuesday. He said Hong’s chance of beating Tiffany in November “worries me a lot”.
“I think she’s going to have trouble winning,” he said.
The photo finish, and possible recount, is just the latest twist in a chaotic primary that saw two major candidates drop out amid scandals. Crowley had also dropped out in early July, but he got back in 10 days later with Gov. Tony Evers’s endorsement.
Both of them crisscrossed the state in the final week, making the case that Crowley was the better matchup against Tiffany in a swing state known for close elections where independent, moderate voters often decide the outcome.
Hong, a single mother and former line cook, tapped into Democratic anger with the party’s mainstream and Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.
The 37-year-old known for sprinkling her comments with profanity and leaning into her edgy and sometimes humorous social media profile excited the liberal wing of the party. Hong called for free childcare and healthcare and a moratorium on artificial intelligence data centre construction. But she also wrestled with her past support for defunding the police, saying at the race’s only debate that she would not support cutting law enforcement funding.
She also drew criticism for past social media posts in which she called for cancelling Thanksgiving because “we should stop celebrating colonialism” and disparaged Valentine’s Day as “another day capitalism tells you how to show love”.
Hong has since downplayed the posts as her attempt at making jokes.
Evers’ decision not to seek a third term created an open race for governor that initially had seven Democrats file to run.
Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez appeared to be making a move to consolidate mainstream Democratic support in July, but she dropped out in the middle of the month amid a campaign finance scandal. That led Crowley, who had dropped out a week earlier and endorsed Rodriguez, to get back in the race, this time with Evers’s backing.
Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who was seen as an early front-runner after nearly beating Republican U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson in 2022, bowed out less than two weeks before the election amid questions about inappropriate behavior.
In one more twist, reporting the results of about 28,000 absentee ballots from Milwaukee was delayed until early Wednesday morning after a human error related to uploading the data, the city’s election leader said shortly before midnight on Tuesday.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Putin says Russia to ‘respond in kind’ to seizure of its vessels by EU countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:55:51 UTC
17:55:51 KST

Burc Eruygur
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that his country would “respond in kind” to the seizure of its merchant vessels by EU countries, defining such plans as “nothing more than piracy and robbery.”
 
"If this begins to be implemented in practice, we will be forced to respond in kind," Putin, attired in navy blue military gear, said while addressing servicemen of Russia's Pacific Fleet aboard the cruiser Varyag, the fleet's flagship vessel, in the country's Far Eastern region of Sakhalin.
 
Putin said Russia sees authorities in some EU countries attempting to restrict the movement of its merchant vessels “in violation of international maritime law.” He argued that these countries have even considered seizing them and selling the property, which he said, "they stole from us.”
 
“This, of course, is nothing less than piracy and robbery,” Putin went on to say, adding that Russia’s response would not necessarily occur in the waters where the seizures take place, but “wherever we deem necessary and appropriate, anywhere,” including in the Pacific.
 
Putin's remarks come amid increasing pressure from the EU on Russia's "shadow fleet," with the 27-member bloc expanding sanctions in this regard in recent months.
 
The Russian president arrived in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the Far Eastern island's administrative center, earlier Wednesday to participate in the final stage of a large-scale exercise conducted by the Pacific Fleet, which began on Aug. 4.
 
In his address to Russian servicemen, Putin said that exercises such as those taking place since earlier this month are necessary to maintain readiness and protect his country's interests and security in the Asia-Pacific region, where he accused NATO of trying to "infiltrate."
 
Arguing that the potential for conflict in this region is growing, Putin said tensions are also escalating in the Arctic region "around the use of the Northern Sea Route."
 
"Russia has always ... confirmed its readiness to cooperate in utilizing the advantages of the Northern Sea Route, within the framework of current maritime law," Putin said, expressing that plans to deploy new weapons systems in the Asia-Pacific region pose a threat to Russia.
 
He went on to accuse Japan of imposing sanctions on Russia that he said were "unprovoked" on Moscow's part.
 
The Russian president also said that Japan continued to have territorial claims against his country through the Kuril Islands and that Moscow had constructive relations with Tokyo on the issue during former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's administration.
 
"Now we see, unfortunately, changes in positions, which, I emphasize, were not provoked in any way on our part," he added.
 
Japan and Russia have an ongoing territorial dispute over the four southernmost Kuril islands, namely Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and the Habomai islets, which are controlled by Russia, but Japan identifies them as the Northern Territories.
 
The dispute has prevented the signing of a peace treaty between the two countries since World War II, and tensions have deepened in recent years amid Tokyo’s sanctions against Moscow over the Russia-Ukraine war.
