Estonian intimacy coordinator: Always ask if the nudity is necessary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:36:00 UTC
17:36:00 KST

Estonian intimacy coordinator: Always ask if the nudity is necessary
A new Estonian summer production brings intimacy front and center onstage. A professional intimacy coordinator explains how performers can safely handle vulnerable scenes.
"By intimacy, we mean all those moments where you're vulnerable," said Alice Aleksandridi, an intimacy coordinator who trained in the U.S. and France. That can include simulated sex, but also medical or hospital scenes, racism or scenes involving minors.
"Many professions emerge from situations where something went wrong and ask how to make sure it doesn't happen again," she explained, adding that intimacy coordination is one of them.
Aleksandridi works as a choreographer and liaison between performers and productions, helping actors feel safe while ensuring directors can safely achieve the intended scene and message. She said the profession combines her backgrounds in law and choreography.
The point of their work, she continued, is not to impose rules but find a way to stage difficult material safely. If an intimate scene is genuinely necessary, the next question is how to handle it appropriately.
"One of the basic questions an intimacy coordinator asks as a rule when reading a script is, 'Could this be done another way? Do we actually need this nudity to get the message across?'" she explained. "If the answer is yes, we move forward and figure out how to do it."
Intimate onstage
That question is relevant to "Moonlight" ("Kuuvalgel"), a Haapsalu summer production based on Terrence McNally's 1987 play "Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune." Kaia Skoblov and Karl-Markus Pihlakas play the two leads in a story about intimacy, trust and fear of letting another person get close.
Pihlakas said the material immediately appealed to the cast and director Helen Rekkor because of its focus on intimacy and closeness. The production also uses headphones to create an even more intimate experience for the audience.
Skoblov noted she would not have accepted the role if she had been uncomfortable performing intimate scenes.
"I read the material and felt this was a story worth telling, because these themes really spoke to me," she said.
Pihlakas said the production also reflects a broader change in how intimacy is viewed onstage.
"Society has gotten more open about these topics," he said, adding that the increased interest in seeing intimacy onstage and on screen is in some ways a reflection of that. "'We're freer and we want to see that [freedom] onstage too!'"
'You bring it with you on set'
While the two actors confirmed they were able to handle the intimate scenes themselves and did not need an intimacy coordinator for this production, Aleksandridi said the need for such a coordinator can arise even when performers and directors know each other well.
She recalled examples from her training where actors struggled with violent or intimate scenes due to various personal circumstances or experiences.
In one case, two actors had played a couple in several films already, and the male actor denied needing an intimacy coordinator because they had worked together for so long already.
"But he didn't know the female actor had been raped two weeks before filming began," the Estonian intimacy coordinator said.
"At the end of the day, an actor is first and foremost a person," she stressed. "Whatever's going on in your everyday life, you bring it with you on set."
--
Editor: Annika Remmel, Aili Vahtla

Laos continues drive to attract more investment
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:34:09 CST
17:34:09 KST

VIENTIANE, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Lao officials and business representatives have gathered for the country's first nationwide investment promotion and management conference, emphasizing investment's role in national development and the need for improved management to attract more investment.
The meeting, held in Lao capital Vientiane from Tuesday to Wednesday, was chaired by Lao Deputy Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith and attended by Lao Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone, ministers and deputy ministers, senior officials, and business representatives, the Vientiane Mai newspaper reported on Wednesday.
In his speech, Saleumxay said the Lao People's Revolutionary Party (LPRP) and government have recognized the important role of domestic and foreign investment in national development.
Since opening the country to private investment, the government has continuously revised investment laws and policies to respond to changing development needs and attract capital, expertise, and technology, he added.
From 1989 to the present, Laos has approved 5,394 domestic and foreign investment projects with a combined value of 65.5 billion U.S. dollars. The largest number of foreign investors have come from China, followed by Vietnam and Thailand.
During the first seven months of 2026, 34 investment projects, worth a total of 8.5 billion dollars, were approved, an increase of 68 percent year-on-year.
Addressing the conference, Prime Minister Sonexay called for a new approach to investment promotion and management to make the process faster, more timely, transparent, professional, and effective.
He emphasized the need to strengthen monitoring and management of both existing projects and newly approved projects, ensuring strict and consistent compliance with laws and regulations. He also called for stronger action to address irregularities in the investment sector, including stricter enforcement against violations and greater use of modern tools and cooperation across sectors.
The meeting called on relevant sectors to strengthen their roles in promoting private-sector investment to increase private investment in line with the 10th National Socio-Economic Development Plan (2026-2030). ■

Column: Why China's favorability is rising across the Global South
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:34:02 CST
17:34:02 KST

by Maya Majueran
The global perception landscape is changing. For decades, the United States occupied a dominant position in international public opinion. The latest Pew Research Center survey, however, points to a notable turning point: for the first time in more than two decades, China is viewed more favorably than the United States across a larger number of countries.
What explains China's growing appeal?
For many developing countries, China offers a practical development partnership centered on infrastructure, investment, industrialization, technology transfer and trade. Rather than prescribing a single pathway to modernization, it has generally emphasized allowing countries to pursue development in line with their national priorities.
One reason China's influence has grown is that its development model is highly visible. From Ethiopia's railways to Pakistan's power plants, Chinese-financed projects address everyday development challenges by improving transport, energy security and connectivity. Through the Belt and Road Initiative, China has mobilized nearly 1 trillion U.S. dollars in infrastructure investment, producing projects that citizens can see, use and associate with economic progress.
The distinction lies not only in the scale of investment but also in the evolving priorities of development cooperation. While many Western partners have increasingly emphasized economic security, strategic de-risking, private-sector mobilization and governance reform, China has combined large-scale investment in physical infrastructure with technology transfer, industrial cooperation and human capital development.
At the same time, China has actively promoted trade by expanding market access, including granting zero-tariff treatment to many least-developed countries, deepening currency-swap arrangements, and encouraging the use of local currencies in cross-border trade. Together, these measures seek to strengthen economic connectivity, reduce transaction costs and exchange-rate risks, and create new opportunities for developing countries to integrate into regional and global value chains.
This integrated approach has produced tangible improvements in productivity, connectivity and local capacity, reinforcing perceptions of China as a long-term development partner.
Equally important is the philosophy underpinning China's engagement. Beijing consistently emphasizes sovereignty, mutual respect and non-interference, maintaining that every country should determine its own political and development path. For many governments across the Global South, this approach is a partnership based on equality rather than political conditionality, allowing them greater policy space to pursue domestic development priorities.
Diplomatic style has also influenced perceptions. Through mechanisms such as the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation and regular engagement with Pacific Island countries, China has committed itself to equality and shared development. For many governments in the Global South, that sense of respect and recognition is not merely symbolic -- it contributes to long-term political trust.
Perhaps the most important nuance is this: the Global South is not becoming anti-American; it is becoming strategically pragmatic. Its foreign policy decisions are increasingly guided by national interests, economic opportunity, and development priorities rather than Cold War-style geopolitical alignment.
The Global South's primary ambition is neither ideological nor geopolitical -- it is developmental. Governments want to create jobs, eliminate poverty, modernize infrastructure, strengthen industrial capacity and improve the quality of life for their citizens. China's transformation over the past four decades, from lifting hundreds of millions of people out of poverty to becoming a global leader in infrastructure, manufacturing and technology, has demonstrated what sustained long-term planning can achieve. Consequently, many developing countries are looking to China not as a model to replicate wholesale, but as a development partner from which they can learn, cooperate and pursue shared prosperity while preserving their own policy autonomy.
This contrast is also reflected in broader policy priorities. At a time when many Western governments are increasingly emphasizing tariffs, export controls, technology restrictions, sanctions and economic security, China has continued to promote infrastructure investment, trade, industrial cooperation, technology partnerships, open-source AI initiatives and greater access to its domestic market. Whether one agrees with either approach or not, many developing countries evaluate partnerships primarily through the lens of economic development and tangible outcomes. That difference in emphasis is helping reshape global perceptions.
The world is changing, and the transition toward a more multipolar international order is becoming increasingly evident. The Global South is no longer a passive participant in world affairs. Its countries are exercising greater strategic autonomy, making decisions according to their own national interests, development priorities and the aspirations of their people. In China, developing countries have found a true friend and good partner.
Editor's note: Maya Majueran serves as the director of the Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka, an independent and pioneering organization with strong expertise in Belt and Road Initiative advice and support.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.

SINGAPORE, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's economy is on track to outperform earlier expectations in 2026, with major research houses raising their growth forecasts as the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom continues to fuel technology exports and manufacturing.
UOB Global Economics and Markets Research has raised its 2026 gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast to 5 percent, from 4.8 percent previously, citing continued AI-related tailwinds in the second half of the year. However, it expects momentum in the semiconductor and electronics sectors to moderate.
UOB expects GDP growth of 0.5 percent quarter-on-quarter on a seasonally adjusted basis in both the third and fourth quarters, translating into 4 percent year-on-year growth in the second half, compared with 6.1 percent in the first half.
DBS Group Research has also lifted Singapore's 2026 growth forecast to 5 percent from 4.3 percent, following stronger-than-expected first-half performance and expectations that the global AI boom will persist. The upgrade comes despite geopolitical risks and a moderation in the broader economic cycle due partly to high base effects.
Denise Cheok, head of Southeast Asia Economics at Moody's Analytics, said Singapore's economy had proved more resilient than expected, largely because of a surge in technology exports linked to the AI boom.
Beyond cutting-edge chips used in graphics processing units, she said demand for other electronic components produced in Singapore and elsewhere had also benefited from the broader increase in technology-related demand.
U.S. tariffs and the conflict in the Middle East could derail growth in the second half of the year, but given the current growth trajectory, this seems increasingly unlikely, she added.
Nomura Global Markets Research was more bullish, raising its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 5.7 percent, from 4.6 percent. It expects growth to remain strong at 5.3 percent in the second half, following 6.1 percent growth in the first half.
Nomura said the global technology uptrend and broadening AI-related demand should continue to support electronics manufacturing, alongside new capacity.
Trade-related services, financial services and construction are also expected to contribute to growth. Financial services could benefit from stronger credit growth, while construction should be supported by major projects and a resilient property market. ■

Feature: Diver injured in sea salvage turns into seasoned rescuer
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:33:40 CST
17:33:40 KST

HANGZHOU, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- The ache in Dong Jianhai's legs was a warning he had learned to trust. At 58, the resident of Zhoushan, a city consisting of islands off the coast of east China's Zhejiang Province, knew it meant a storm was coming.
The day before Typhoon Dolphin, the 13th typhoon of the year, made landfall in Zhejiang, Dong spent the whole afternoon preparing for it, checking anchor points for vessels seeking shelter and making sure each ship was securely fastened, just as he had done hundreds of times before.
For more than three decades, Dong has seen the sea in nearly every mood. He began his career as one of Zhejiang's first professional salvage divers after earning his national diving certificate in 1991. Young, strong and ambitious, he was eager to make a name for himself underwater. Then an accident changed the course of his life.
During a salvage operation in 1994, Dong suffered severe decompression sickness, a potentially fatal condition caused by rapid changes in pressure after diving. Two months of difficult treatment saved his life, but when he finally left the hospital, he could no longer walk as he once had.
For a diver whose life had been bound to the ocean, the injury seemed to mark the end of a career. But Dong's bond with the sea endured, taking a different form.
"People told me my diving days were over, and maybe they were right about my body," he said. "But no one could convince me that my journey was over. If I couldn't go down into the water anymore, I would find another way to keep my promise."
Dong began a new chapter by bringing together people with diving and salvage experience to form his own rescue team. Over time, the team became a familiar presence along the coast, responding to sunken vessels, maritime accidents and calls to recover those lost at sea.
He would arrive at rescue sites with a cane in hand, helping divers prepare their equipment, secure hoses and ropes, and watching closely as they disappeared beneath the surface. Though he could no longer descend into the depths himself, he knew the pressure, darkness, currents below -- and the razor-thin margin for error -- as well as anyone else.
When Dong could not be at the scene, he directed operations remotely. His cell phone stayed with him around the clock, and over the years his number became a trusted lifeline for people along the coast.
The calls came in for all kinds of emergencies: a vessel that needed salvaging, a missing diver, someone who had fallen into the water, a ship that had run aground, or people stranded on an island by a storm.
The team has also taken part in large-scale maritime operations. In one case, it participated in the salvage and subsequent repair of a 10,000-tonne cargo ship. In another, it was called to assist a 300,000-tonne Panama-registered oil tanker that had gone off course and run aground.
For Dong, the hardest calls were not always those that came in the middle of a rescue. Sometimes it was the quiet voice on the other end of the phone, telling him that another life had been lost at sea.
Such calls meant there was no longer a life to save. But Dong knew the mission was not necessarily over. For him, and for the families waiting on shore, there was still one final task: bringing their loved ones home.
Over the past 30 years, Dong has taken part in or directed the salvage of more than 120 sunken vessels, while his team has recovered more than 80 bodies.
The work is demanding and often dangerous, but Dong has never seen it as something to be carried out for a reward.
"When someone loses their life at sea, and you can bring them back to their family, that is not just a job," Dong said. "It is simply the right thing to do as a human being."
To Dong, it was all part of a promise he had made to the sea long ago -- one he could not easily let go of, even though he could not have known what it would eventually cost him.
That promise has taken different forms over the course of a life intertwined with the water: the boy who lost loved ones to the sea, the diver who ventured beneath the waves, the survivor of a near-fatal underwater accident, and the man who refused to give up helping others.
Typhoon Dolphin made landfall the following evening after Dong felt his leg ache. The seasoned rescuer was out before dawn, leaning on his cane as he moved between harbors, checking vessels and directing his crew while strong winds swept the coast.
For most people, a storm is a reason to stay ashore. For Dong, it is a reason to set out. Somewhere beyond the waves, someone may be waiting -- for rescue, for hope, or simply for a way home. ■

The sector's growth was supported by resilient domestic demand and stronger trade activity, the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) said in a statement.
Higher household spending and increased mobility during festive celebrations and the mid-year school holidays boosted activity in wholesale and retail trade, food and beverage, accommodation, and transportation and storage. The gains also benefited related consumer and tourism services.

Belarusian oversight agency: Road inspections are year-round, not seasonal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:33:00 UTC
17:33:00 KST

MINSK, 12 August (BelTA) - Control over the state of roads is neither seasonal nor sporadic in nature, Oleg Kundelev, deputy head of the directorate for monitoring of material production industries at the State Control Committee of Belarus, said in the latest episode of BelTA’s project The Nation Speaks.
According to him, monitoring of the situation is carried out constantly and virtually in real time. “Here I would even go further and say that these are probably not inspections as such, but rather the processing of information about negative aspects, shortcomings, and violations that we receive. Based on the analysis of this information, a decision is made on whether we need to launch a full-scale inspection or whether it is sufficient to make recommendations,” the expert explained.
He emphasized that auditors strive to act as efficiently as possible, without distracting the road organizations from their main work. If an identified shortcoming does not constitute an administrative offense, the situation is often resolved through dialogue with the head of the organization, who promptly takes measures to eliminate this shortcoming.
Oleg Kundelev cited statistics for the first half of 2026: the committee's bodies examined the activities of 13 road organizations, but full-scale inspections were conducted in only six cases. “We understand that an inspection is about recording a violation, identifying those responsible, and, as a rule, administrative liability. But often we identify not only violations, but also reserves for cost reduction,” he noted.
As an example of working with reserves, the speaker described a situation involving the analysis of design and estimate documentation prior to the start of work. Sometimes it is possible to identify excessive requirements or items that can be omitted without compromising quality. In such cases, recommendations are made, potential reserves are utilized, and shortcomings are eliminated without penalties or complex inspection procedures.
In addition, a number of systemic issues are brought up for discussion at the committee's board meetings. For instance, this year, the results of inspections of road organizations were discussed at meetings of the regional administrations in Minsk Oblast and Mogilev Oblast. Together with local authorities and representatives of road services, they drew up comprehensive solutions to address the identified problems and shortcomings.

David Crowley defeats Francesca Hong to win Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:32:37 UTC
17:32:37 KST

David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, won the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor after beating the Democratic socialist Francesca Hong.
Crowley pulled off a last-minute victory after re-entering the campaign and snagging an endorsement from Tony Evers, the outgoing governor.
With most votes counted, Crowley had 39.8% of the vote, ahead of Hong’s 39.4%, according to the Associated Press: a lead of just more than 3,000 votes. The race came down to the wire, with Hong and Crowley running close to each other as each batch of results came in.
Polls had shown Hong as a clear frontrunner during the campaign, but with large chunks of voters still undecided and an ever-changing field of candidates, polling was difficult. Polls in Michigan had similarly shown the progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed with a more sizeable lead than he ended up with in his victory in the Democratic primary for US Senate.
Hong, a chef and former restaurant owner from Madison, ran on a platform that included childcare for all, free school meals and a one-year moratorium on the construction of new datacenters, which differentiated her from her Democratic colleagues in the governor’s race.
Evers, a Democrat who has served as Wisconsin’s governor since 2019, did not seek re-election. He endorsed Crowley, who re-entered the race after leaving it earlier in the cycle.
Crowley’s pitch to voters in the waning weeks of the campaign was electability: he felt he was more poised to win against Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman and ardent Trump supporter who ran unopposed in the Republican primary. Tiffany voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost.
Crowley previously told the Guardian: “We knew that the stakes were too high for me to sit on the sideline, and that we need the best candidate, not just with executive leadership, but somebody who has a proven track record of getting things done. And that’s what voters want. They want someone they can trust. And that’s why we got back into this race.”
Hong’s previous statements had dragged her down in recent days, including past support for defunding the police and a tweet calling to cancel Thanksgiving, which she had since retracted. She had previously vowed to use her grassroots network built during the primary to aid whoever won.
Kelda Roys, a state senator, and Joel Brennan, who previously led the Wisconsin department of administration, rounded out the Democratic field.
There were entries and exits from the chaotic race in recent weeks. A previous top contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race after campaign finance irregularities, after which Crowley re-entered the race, with Evers’ backing. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July.
The Wisconsin governor’s race became the latest test of the progressive wing of the party’s durability with Democratic voters in the midwest, after Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan last week. Next door, Minnesota voters were also weighing a US Senate primary between a moderate and a progressive. Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won the Democratic primary for Senate over congresswoman Angie Craig. The midwest primaries came after a wave of wins of progressives and Democratic socialists in solidly blue parts of the country.
Democrats in Wisconsin are angling for a governing trifecta, trying to win back control of both chambers of the state assembly and keep the governor’s office so they can enact a full agenda.
The governor’s race is expected to draw massive money and attention – Wisconsin is a close state for most statewide elections, and its voters are known to swing in either direction depending on the candidate or platform.
Elsewhere in Wisconsin, voters in the western part of the state chose Rebecca Cooke, a blue dog Democrat, to advance and face the Republican Derrick Van Orden in the third congressional district, a key pickup opportunity for Democrats. Cooke previously ran for the seat in 2022 and 2024, coming close to Van Orden.
Emily Berge, a former Eau Claire city council president, ran against Cooke. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee endorsed Cooke, which angered some local Democrats who saw it as interfering in a primary. Berge’s momentum, amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, had other national groups spending to boost Cooke, who they believe is most poised to win the district.

Several drones hit Sudanese capital, northern cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12

17:31:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Wave of drones attack Sudan's capital and northern cities
Drones attacked the Sudanese capital and two northern cities at dawn on Wednesday, in what appeared to be a coordinated strike after months of calm in Khartoum.
Since April 2023, Sudan has been ravaged by war between the Sudanese military, led by its chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the UAE-backed paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, commanded by Burhan's former deputy Mohamed Hamdan Daglo.
The capital Khartoum, which was recaptured by the army last year leading to the return of 2.3 million people, has been targeted by drone strikes before but enjoyed relative calm for months.
An AFP correspondent in the city reported a drone attack at 5 am (0300 GMT) along with the sound of anti-aircraft missiles from the direction of the army's Wadi Seidna base, just north of the twin city of Omdurman.
Witnesses in the northern cities of Atbara and El-Damer—both also under army control—gave similar reports of hearing explosions and seeing drones in the sky.
There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Across the country, aid workers estimate more than 200,000 people have been killed in what the UN calls a "war of atrocities". The conflict has also caused the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.
Burhan and Daglo, allies until they fell out in a bitter power struggle, have spent most of the war in a relative stalemate, unwilling to hold negotiations while vying for a decisive battlefield advantage.
The RSF last year consolidated its hold on the vast western region of Darfur, and has since pushed to seize territory in the southern Kordofan region and along the southeastern Ethiopian border.
The army holds the country's centre, north and east, and last month clinched a victory in Kordofan by pushing the RSF off a key highway leading to the capital.
Daglo in the aftermath said he would "unleash" his fighters—already accused of war crimes including genocide—and his forces have since repeatedly threatened a large-scale retaliatory attack.

U.S. Army wants a robot truck that fires four different missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:31:49 UTC
17:31:49 KST

- The U.S. Army published a solicitation on August 11, 2026, seeking an autonomous vehicle able to carry and fire munitions up to 36,000 pounds (16,329 kg).
- Company submissions are due by noon Eastern time on September 1, 2026, with only U.S.-based, security-cleared firms eligible to compete.
The U.S. Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive Fires office, the branch responsible for developing the service’s next generation of missile and rocket systems, published a request on August 11 seeking companies capable of designing an autonomous vehicle that could reshape how American ground forces move and launch weapons on future battlefields.
The program is called the Common Autonomous Multidomain Launcher, or CAML, and its centerpiece is something the Army calls the Autonomous Mobility Platform, or AMP, an optionally crewed vehicle, meaning it can drive itself or carry a human operator, engineered to load, transport, fire, and reload munitions weighing up to 36,000 pounds (16,329 kilograms) without a soldier ever having to physically handle the weapon. That weight limit matters because it determines just how much destructive capability a single vehicle can carry into the field, and 36,000 pounds sits comfortably in the range needed to move some of the Army’s heaviest guided weapons.
What makes the AMP unusual isn’t just that it drives itself. It’s designed to load and unload its own cargo using something called a Load Handling System, essentially a robotic mechanism that lets the vehicle pick up and swap out standardized munition pallets on its own, the same way a forklift moves a shipping container but built directly into a combat vehicle operating in hostile territory. Those pallets, which the Army calls Unique Munition Pallets, come in four distinct configurations, and each one transforms the same base vehicle into a completely different weapon system.
One pallet carries the Tomahawk, the long-range cruise missile the Navy has used for decades to strike targets hundreds of miles away. Another carries PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors, the interceptor missiles used by the Patriot air defense system to shoot down incoming aircraft, drones, and ballistic missiles. A third houses AIM-9X missiles configured for the Indirect Fire Protection Capability system, a short-range air defense weapon built to counter the kind of drone and rocket attacks that have become common on modern battlefields. The fourth carries rocket pods for the Multiple Launch Rocket System family of munitions, the guided and unguided rockets the Army has relied on for decades of long-range ground bombardment.
That kind of flexibility represents a significant departure from how the Army currently fields its missile systems, where each weapon typically rides on its own dedicated vehicle built specifically for that munition. Under the CAML concept, a single AMP could theoretically be loaded with a Tomahawk pallet for a long-range strike mission one day and swapped out for a Patriot interceptor pallet defending against an incoming drone swarm the next, all without soldiers needing an entirely separate fleet of vehicles for each weapon type. The Army’s solicitation also calls for a Leader Vehicle Autonomy Kit, a modular system that can be installed on other vehicles, autonomous or not, to serve as a command node that synchronizes multiple AMP vehicles as they move in convoy, execute fire missions, or rapidly set up and break down firing positions, capabilities that matter enormously on a battlefield where staying in one place too long can mean getting hit by enemy fire.
The Army is pursuing this program under a legal authority known as Other Transaction Agreements, a contracting method that lets the Pentagon move faster than the traditional defense acquisition process by working directly with companies, including ones that have never held a full defense contract before, to build and test prototypes before committing to a full production program. The solicitation specifically invokes 10 U.S. Code Section 4022, the law that governs these prototype agreements, and notes the Army may eventually move to full-rate production without running a separate competition if the prototype phase goes well, a significant incentive for companies competing to land this initial contract.
The Army has also built a specific data ownership requirement into the program that could reshape how it buys weapons going forward. The solicitation requires companies to turn over full technical ownership of the system, including detailed engineering documents and interface specifications, to the government rather than keeping that information proprietary. Army officials describe this approach as eliminating vendor lock, the situation where a military branch becomes dependent on a single company because that company controls the only detailed technical knowledge of how a system works, a problem that has driven up costs and slowed modernization efforts across multiple Pentagon programs over the years. By owning the technical baseline outright, the Army says it will be able to distribute that information to other companies down the line, opening the door to competition on future upgrades or replacement parts rather than being locked into whichever single company builds the first prototype.
Companies interested in competing have a narrow window to respond. The Army is requiring initial submissions, capped at ten pages, by noon Eastern time on September 1, 2026, with only U.S.-based companies cleared to handle secret-level classified information and hardware eligible to participate. Those chosen to advance will move through additional rounds of in-person pitches and potential prototype demonstrations before the Army decides who ultimately builds the system, a process the solicitation indicates could stretch well into 2027 before any contract is finalized.

Wallabies prop Angus Bell is leading the tributes for dual rugby union international and former NRL star Brian Smith, who has died aged 59.
Smith, who played six Tests for Australia in 1987 and nine for Ireland after switching allegiance, had battled cancer.
Once described by former Wallabies coach Alan Jones as one of the world's most gifted players, Smith was most recently the Head of Sport at Scots College in Sydney, where Bell and many other Wallabies graduated from.
"He was coaching at the Scots school and coached a lot of us coming through the grades and I just wanted to say it's a really sad time," Bell said from Wallabies camp in Townsville on Wednesday.
"We're wishing the best for his wife and kids. He's an avid rugby person and helped a lot of individuals in the squad and in the Wallabies today, so just sending my condolences from both the Wallabies and myself."
Smith, who also played 43 games for Balmain and Eastern Suburbs from 1991 to 1994, coached Bell at GPS and NSW schoolboys' level when the emerging front-rower was only 16.
"Fair to say that I wouldn't have played as good or anywhere near as good without him," Bell said.
"Me, Jeremy Williams and Will Harris from the (Western) Force were really close with him and he was a great bloke, a great father and a great coach.
"So, yeah, very sad."
After playing schoolboys' rugby for Australia, Smith made his Wallabies debut under Jones in 1987, partnering Nick Farr-Jones in the halves and bagging 18 points from a try, five conversions and a penalty in a 65-18 win over South Korea.
After his playing career, Smith coached in Japan and England, where he was the national team's attack coach, and served as Australia's sevens coach.
"Brian had been very unwell in recent months and was battling an aggressive cancer," Scots College principal Dr Ian PM Lambert wrote to school colleagues.
"This is very sad news for our College community and I know it will come as a shock to many of you who knew and worked closely with him.
"Our immediate thoughts are with Brian's wife Lisa, his daughters Ruby and Santana, and his son Chilli."

The removal means iPhone users in Russia can no longer download or update Yandex Pay. The app allows users to store cards, make contactless payments and split purchases across Yandex’s suite of services.
In a statement, Yandex Pay assured customers that their money remained secure and that the app would continue to function for users who already had it installed.
“Most importantly, don’t delete the app,” Yandex Pay said, urging users to turn off automatic updates and use its web-based version within mobile browsers instead.
“We’re sad this happened too… We’ll figure something out with the app,” Yandex Pay said.
Apple has not publicly commented on the removal, though it has delisted apps linked to sanctioned Russian entities in recent months.
While Yandex Pay has not itself been targeted directly by Western sanctions, Yandex Bank was sanctioned by the United Kingdom in June.
Yandex Pay is still available for Android users on Google Play.

IDF identifies remains of soldier killed in Cyprus, buried as unknown in Haifa since 1948
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:30:44 UTC
17:30:44 KST

The IDF announced on Wednesday that after a lengthy investigation, the burial place of IDF soldier Shlomo Haimson, whose burial place had been unknown for almost 78 years, has been located.
Haimson was killed by guards at a detention camp in Cyprus during an escape attempt in September 1948.
He was initially buried in the Jewish cemetery in Margo, Cyprus.
In 1970, his remains, along with others buried there, most of whom were buried in Haifa as unknown persons.
Following an intensive investigation by the IDF's Missing Persons Branch and the Military Rabbinate, along with the Defense Ministry and Cypriot associations, it was determined that he is buried in the immigrant section of the Haifa cemetery. His family was informed last night that his burial place had been located.
Who was Shlomo Haimson?
Haimson was born in Romania in 1930, losing his father during the Holocaust. After World War II ended, he immigrated to Israel along with his mother and girlfriend aboard an immigrant ship.
The ship was captured by British soldiers, who deported its passengers to Cyprus, then a British Crown Colony.
While being held in a camp in Cyprus, Haimson joined an organization that operated under the Haganah and trained to become a soldier to fight for the Jewish state.
When the state was established in May 1948, his mother and girlfriend were released and immigrated to Israel, moving to the Negev. In September, he learned that his daughter Miriam had been born, and decided to escape the camp and immigrate to Israel to be with his family.
Along with eight others, he broke through the fences on the night of September 29-30, 1948. The nine, including Haimson, attempted to escape, but were discovered by guards who opened fire, killing Haimson.
The others were caught by the guards and returned to the camp.

How Hong Kong can unlock the real value of its Asean trade boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:30:05 UTC
17:30:05 KST

How Hong Kong can unlock the real value of its Asean trade boom
By providing high-value services that enable cross-border transactions and corporate expansion, the city can convert surging commerce into long-term economic returns
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has a role to play in Hong Kong’s plans for its economy. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu signalled as much when he touched on the city’s first five-year plan in his August 7 meeting with Asean Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn.
For businesses, however, the central question is not whether Hong Kong-Asean economic ties will continue to grow. They will. The harder question is who will capture the value that growth creates.
Asean has been Hong Kong’s second-largest trading partner since 2010. In 2025, merchandise trade reached HK$1.67 trillion (US$212.8 billion), accounting for 15.3 per cent of the city’s global goods trade, while Hong Kong’s direct investment stock in Asean exceeded HK$670 billion at the end of 2024.
These figures describe a mature economic relationship. They also conceal an uncomfortable truth: enormous trade volumes do not necessarily generate a large pool of profit.
Goods can be re-exported through Hong Kong while most of the value remains elsewhere. Re-exports generate legitimate business for ports, freight forwarders, insurers and banks. Yet if a shipment changes hands only on paper or through financing arrangements before moving on, Hong Kong captures just a thin slice of the transaction.
The larger margins accrue in the services surrounding the goods: trade finance, treasury management, insurance, intellectual property, legal contracts, arbitration, supply-chain data and regional headquarters. Hong Kong’s Asean opportunity therefore depends less on moving more containers than on attaching more high-value services to each transaction.

Russia is capable of producing up to 80 S8000 Banderol missiles per month, the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine reported this to Militarnyi in response to an inquiry.
The Banderol was designed and manufactured by Kronstadt JSC. The missile has a maximum speed of 620–650 km/h and a cruising speed of 520–560 km/h.
The missile is equipped with an OFBCh-150 high-explosive fragmentation warhead with a total weight of 114.3 kilograms. Of this, 49.5 kilograms is the explosive filling.
They have a relatively short range of about 500 km, which is why Russia frequently launches them from Crimea toward Odesa.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Russian enterprises operate in three shifts to maintain the stated production rates. At the same time, Russia uses Western-made components to manufacture ammunition.
According to the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), these components reach Russia through intermediaries, including companies linked to Russian oligarchs and enterprises in the Russian defense-industrial sector.
Thus, Russia’s defense industry retains the ability to scale up production of Banderols, despite sanctions and the need to source some components through complex supply chains.

Russia's hybrid attacks are increasingly moving from the information domain into the physical one, including on the territory of other countries. This incident makes sabotage on NATO member states' territory potentially more dangerous if suspicion of Russian involvement is confirmed.
Footage contradicts the warning-shot theory
The drone struck the wing near the fuel tanks, then bounced off the aircraft's surface and fell to the ground. The explosive device also ended up on the ground and did not detonate. Eclipse craze grips European countries - millions of people are preparing for the &quot;event of the century&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
11:28:31 EEST
17:28:31 KST

Eclipse craze grips European countries - millions of people are preparing for the "event of the century"
Kyiv • UNN
Millions of people in Spain and Iceland are preparing to watch a total solar eclipse. Authorities expect up to 6 million visitors in Spain and up to 80,000 in Iceland.
Millions of people across Spain and Iceland are preparing to see a total solar eclipse on Wednesday, packing protective glasses and heading to locations where they will be able to observe the rare astronomical event in its entirety, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
People's fascination with eclipses is well documented. Historically, the sudden darkening of the sky was often interpreted as an omen, a cosmic struggle, or a sign of divine power.
Modern sky-watchers seek to experience that same strange feeling when day briefly turns to twilight and some animals fall silent as the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun.
"I hope a wonderful generation of astrophysicists will emerge this evening," said Juan Cruz, Spain's Secretary of State for Science. "It is such a special moment," he noted.
According to Cruz, authorities expect up to 6 million visitors, mostly in rural areas along the eclipse's path in northern Spain and the Balearic Islands. In Spain, the eclipse will quickly be followed by sunset, making the event especially attractive.
As this year's eclipse coincides with one of the periods of highest wildfire risk, Spain has deployed a large-scale police operation and public safety campaign.
The government also sees this as an opportunity to showcase rarely visited regions and help address overtourism on the coast by redirecting crowds away from overcrowded beach resorts.
The Iberian Peninsula last saw a total solar eclipse in 1912. Another eclipse is expected to occur on August 2, 2027, followed by an annular eclipse in January 2028, completing the so-called "Iberian eclipse trio."
Hotel prices in Europe have surged ahead of the historic eclipse - FT11.08.26, 12:37 • 3236 views
In Iceland's capital, Reykjavik, eclipse glasses have been sold out for several days, as the Scandinavian country, with a population of approximately 400,000, expects to host up to 80,000 visitors.
The narrow path of totality will reach Iceland's westernmost coast at approximately 17:44 (20:44 Kyiv time), before the Moon's shadow heads eastward.
The total eclipse will last up to 2 minutes and 13 seconds in the far west, although periods of darkness will be shorter in most towns. Authorities have warned of heavy traffic and urged viewers to arrive early.
Singer Björk was scheduled to perform with a DJ at an eclipse-themed event south of Reykjavik.
The U.S. space agency NASA plans to launch a WB-57 high-altitude aircraft from Iceland to track the Moon's shadow, while NASA-funded teams will launch balloons to study how the sudden darkness and cooling affect the lower layers of the atmosphere.
In addition to casual observers, the event is also attracting "eclipse chasers," enthusiasts who travel across the world to be in the path of totality whenever an eclipse occurs.
Gordon Telepun, a retired plastic surgeon and amateur astronomer from the United States who has photographed six total eclipses, said he would watch this one from the island of Mallorca, as Spain meets all the requirements for those who want to observe eclipses.
"In August, the weather conditions here are quite acceptable, the duration of totality is decent at more than a minute and a half, and it is easy to get there," he said.

Romania Destroys Two Russian Drones Drifting Near Critical Black Sea Gas Project
Romanian army divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones drifting in the country's Black Sea exclusive economic zone near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project, Reuters reported on August 11.
A civilian vessel working near the platform first spotted the drones that Tuesday, according to the outlet. Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta noted that Ukraine had confirmed the systems were not its own.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"For the safety of the shipping lane and the works being carried out around the platform, the decision was made to carry out a controlled destruction by detonation," Miruta explained.
The minister added that Romania's defense ministry had "contacted Ukrainian partners, who confirmed that the systems do not belong to them."
The Neptun Deep project, jointly owned by OMV Petrom and state producer Romgaz, is due to begin output in 2027 and is expected to make Romania the European Union's largest gas producer, according to Reuters.
Romania, a NATO member, shares a 614-kilometer (382-mile) land border with Ukraine. It has repeatedly seen Russian drones breach its airspace during more than four years of Moscow's invasion, alongside mines drifting across key Black Sea trade and energy routes, the report noted.
The Gerbera is a low-cost drone of Russian design, typically fielded as a decoy and reconnaissance platform alongside heavier Shahed-type strike drones to overwhelm and confuse air defenses.
Cheaply built, largely from plywood and foam, the type carries a standard range of roughly 700 kilometers, though examples recovered abroad have been fitted with extra nose fuel tanks to stretch that endurance. Its low cost allows the drones to be launched in large numbers, forcing defenders to expend far costlier interceptors or, as in Romania, to neutralize the aircraft directly.
Only days before the Neptun Deep detonation, an unidentified explosive drone crossed from Romania into Bulgaria and detonated near the Trans-Balkan pipeline, a corridor now used to carry gas north toward Ukraine.
The August 8 blast struck about 100 meters inside Bulgarian territory, roughly a kilometer from a compressor station, yet its origin was never established.

British driver sets speed record in a hydrogen-powered car
Kyiv • UNN
64-year-old Andy Green accelerated a hydrogen-powered car to 654 km/h on the Bonneville Salt Flats. This is the highest speed for this type of vehicle.
64-year-old British driver Andy Green set a new speed record for hydrogen-powered cars. He accelerated the vehicle to 654 km/h. The BBC reports, as cited by UNN.
The British driver who was the first to break the sound barrier in a land vehicle has set a new speed record, this time in a hydrogen-powered vehicle
Andy Green is a 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot. He achieved the new result in a car with two hydrogen internal combustion engines. This took place on the Bonneville Salt Flats in the state of Utah. The man reached a speed of 406 miles per hour, or 654 km/h. The engines' combined braking power was 1,600 horsepower. The record was determined as the average speed over two runs.
This record is a tremendous achievement for a world-class team and outstanding technology
Thus, Green recorded the highest speed ever achieved by a hydrogen-powered car.
At the same time, according to the publication, Andy Green set another record in 1997. In the ThrustSSC jet-powered car, he drove across Nevada's Black Rock Desert at a speed of 763 miles per hour, or 1,228 km/h.
Green then became the first person to break the sound barrier on land. He remains the only person to have achieved this.

The Ministry of Defence says the programme sustains 2,500 skilled jobs across Scotland and the UK supply chain, along with 400 apprenticeships set up through partnerships with colleges in Fife and elsewhere in Scotland.
Delivery has slipped. The department now expects the first ship to be handed over by the end of the decade, and Babcock has set aside around £140 million against design changes and rework.
The Common Combat Vessel is the Royal Navy’s planned general purpose warship, intended to be built in numbers and offered for export. The MOD has not said which hull form it will use.
Mr Streeting said during his visit: “From the skilled workers and apprentices building the next generation of Royal Navy warships at Rosyth, to the service families who support our Armed Forces every day, Scotland sits at the heart of our national security.
“It is inspiring to see proud heritage combining with modern technology to make our country fit for the future. That also presents huge opportunities for jobs and reindustrialisation.”
Harry Holt, chief executive of Babcock International Group, said: “The defence industry makes a vital contribution to Scotland’s economy, sustaining thousands of skilled jobs and apprenticeships. Our workforce and operations at Rosyth are a clear demonstration of this, delivering sovereign capability, supporting economic growth, and contributing to UK reindustrialisation.
“We look forward to working with the Defence Secretary and the Ministry of Defence as they implement the Defence Investment Plan, further strengthening our sovereign and export capabilities and the defence of our nation.”

U.S. Army and Marines train together on a remote Pacific island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:23:24 UTC
17:23:24 KST

- U.S. and partner forces conducted Exercise Tenacious Archer 2026 in Airai, Palau, last month to train integrated air and missile defense.
- Echo Battery, 5th Battalion, 5th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, fired its final live-fire exercise using the Avenger air defense system before transitioning to new equipment.
Soldiers from Echo Battery, 5th Battalion, 5th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, wrapped up their final live-fire exercise using the Avenger air defense system last month during Exercise Tenacious Archer 2026, held in Airai, Palau, according to a report by Army Sgt. Martin Nalls of 8th Army. The multiday exercise brought together soldiers and Marines from multiple branches to practice defending against aerial threats across the Pacific, a region where the United States has steadily built up joint training as concerns grow over China’s expanding military reach.
Palau, a small island nation in the western Pacific with deep historical and defense ties to the United States dating back to World War II, sits along strategic sea lanes that connect the Philippines, Guam, and the broader Indo-Pacific theater American planners increasingly view as the most consequential region for future conflict. The exercise drew soldiers from artillery, military police, and sustainment units, working alongside Marines assigned to an aircraft wing, to run live-fire events and rehearse the planning and coordination needed to defend critical assets and friendly forces under conditions meant to mirror actual combat rather than a scripted training scenario.
Tenacious Archer exists specifically to force different branches and specialties that rarely operate together to figure out how to fight as one team, an increasingly urgent skill as the Pentagon leans harder into what it calls joint and combined operations, meaning missions where Army, Marine Corps, Navy, Air Force, and allied units all have to communicate and coordinate in real time rather than fighting in separate lanes. Beyond simply shooting at aerial targets, participants spent the exercise validating planning processes, testing communications networks, and rehearsing the command-and-control procedures, the systems and protocols that let commanders issue orders and receive updates across multiple units, that determine whether a joint force can actually respond fast enough when a real aerial threat appears.
For Echo Battery, the exercise carried extra weight because it marked the end of an era for the unit’s primary weapon system. The Avenger, formally designated the AN/TWQ-1, is a surface-to-air missile system typically mounted on a Humvee that has provided short-range air defense protection against low-flying aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and drones since it entered service in the late 1980s, making it older than most of the soldiers who currently operate it. The system carries Stinger missiles, a shoulder-launched infrared-guided weapon originally designed to shoot down aircraft, and has been repeatedly upgraded over the decades even as the Army has steadily worked to replace it with more modern platforms better suited to the drone-heavy threats that have come to define recent conflicts, including Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Army Capt. Eric Sandlin, Echo Battery’s commander, framed the exercise as both a farewell to a system that has served the unit well and a step toward whatever comes next.
“Tenacious Archer 2026 will be the final live-fire exercise for Echo Battery using the Avenger weapon system,” said Army Capt. Eric Sandlin, Echo Battery commander. “The Avenger has been a capable platform for our formation, and we’re now transitioning to new equipment that will further modernize our air defense capabilities and prepare us for future operational requirements.”
Sandlin did not specify which system will replace the Avenger in Echo Battery’s arsenal, and the Army’s broader modernization push offers several candidates without confirming which one applies here. The Army has spent the past several years fielding the M-SHORAD system, officially named SGT Stout after a Medal of Honor recipient, a Stryker-mounted platform that combines Stinger missiles, Hellfire missiles, and a 30mm cannon with its own radar to give crews faster response times and better protection than the decades-old Humvee-based Avenger can offer. Whether Echo Battery is transitioning specifically to SGT Stout, a newer variant, or an entirely different system remains unclear from Sandlin’s comments alone, leaving the exact shape of the unit’s future arsenal as an open question the Army has not yet answered publicly.
The exercise also gave Echo Battery something less tangible than new equipment: practice working with people it doesn’t normally train alongside.
“This was a unique experience for my battery,” Sandlin said. “Training with the Marine Corps, soldiers from other Army branches and our partners strengthened our ability to communicate, coordinate and accomplish the mission together.”
That kind of cross-branch familiarity matters more than it might seem from the outside, since real combat rarely respects the tidy organizational lines that separate one branch’s units from another’s, and confusion over communication procedures or command relationships in the middle of an actual attack can cost lives. Army Sgt. 1st Class Joshua Hogan, Echo Battery’s master gunner, the senior enlisted soldier responsible for training crews on weapon systems and ensuring live-fire safety, pointed to the practical, hands-on value of actually firing weapons rather than simulating the process.
“Live-fire exercises like Tenacious Archer give air defenders valuable hands-on experience by allowing soldiers to fire the Stinger missile and observe its performance in flight,” said Army Sgt. 1st Class Joshua Hogan, Echo Battery master gunner. “It’s also an opportunity to train alongside other military branches and partner forces, helping us better understand each other’s capabilities and improve how we operate together.”
Watching a missile actually fly and strike its target, rather than reading about the process in a manual or running through it on a simulator, builds a kind of confidence and muscle memory that no amount of classroom instruction can replicate, particularly for young soldiers who may never have seen the weapon system they train on actually work under field conditions. The integration of Army, Marine Corps, and partner nation forces throughout Tenacious Archer reinforced a lesson the Pentagon has repeated across multiple recent Pacific exercises, that interoperability, the ability of different forces to fight effectively together despite different equipment, procedures, and chains of command, has become as important to regional security as any single weapon system fielded by any single branch.

Landslide in Mumbai kills 6 as India is drenched by monsoon rains
MUMBAI, India (AP) — Heavy monsoon rains triggered a landslide in a densely populated neighborhood in India’s financial capital, Mumbai, early Wednesday, killing at least six people and injuring four others, authorities said.
The landslide struck before dawn when a section of hillside collapsed onto two or three homes in a tightly packed cluster of houses in Mumbai’s suburb of Ghatkopar, said Tanaji Kambli, a civic official.
Authorities immediately launched a rescue operation involving firefighters, police, the National Disaster Response Force and civic officials but efforts were hampered by narrow access lanes that prevented the use of heavy machinery, officials said.
Rescue teams pulled at least 10 people from the debris and rushed them to a government hospital. Six people, including two children and two teenagers, were declared dead on arrival, Tanaji said. Four others were hospitalized and were receiving treatment.
Ritu Tawde, the mayor of Mumbai, visited the area and announced monetary compensation for the families of the victims.
India’s weather department has forecast more active monsoon conditions across western India. Authorities have urged residents in flood- and landslide-prone areas to remain alert.
Mumbai, a city of more than 20 million people, receives some of its heaviest rainfall between June and September. Torrential downpours routinely inundate roads and railway lines, disrupt air and rail traffic. They trigger landslides and building collapses, particularly in crowded hillside settlements where houses are often built on unstable slopes.
Experts have long warned that rapid urbanization, construction on fragile hillsides and poor drainage have left Mumbai increasingly vulnerable to deadly monsoon-related disasters, with climate change adding to those risks, bringing heavier and more unpredictable rainfall.

Spain prepares for rare solar eclipse against backdrop of heat and wildfires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:23:02 UTC
17:23:02 KST

Eclipse excitement sweeps Spain as millions prepare to watch the skies
MEDINACELI, Spain (AP) — Spaniards rushed to buy specialized glasses to view a rare total solar eclipse Wednesday, as authorities warned people flocking to rural areas to avoid anything that could spark new wildfires.
Across a swath of northern and central Spain, millions of people will have some of mainland Europe’s best views of the celestial spectacle. A sliver of Greenland and Iceland, too, will witness the spectacle, when the sun, moon and Earth align, briefly bringing parts of the planet into darkness.
Totality — when the moon completely covers the sun’s light — is expected to last less than 2 1/2 minutes, reaching its maximum duration off Iceland’s west coast. By the time it gets to a small patch of Portugal and then in Spain just before sunset, totality will have dwindled to a minute or so. The spectacle will then end over the Mediterranean.
Against the backdrop of scorching summer temperatures and wildfires, Spanish officials have rolled out a large public safety campaign.
The eclipse could draw at least an additional half a million visitors, authorities say. Demand for hotel rooms along the path of totality, including in the northern cities of A Coruña, Bilbao and Santiago de Compostela, has soared.
In Medinaceli, a Roman-era hilltop town in northeast Spain, sky watchers secured grassy viewing points several hours early.
“It must be thrilling to see the darkness come suddenly and the image of the sun disappearing,” said Agatha Bak, a 40-year-old philosophy professor who left Madrid for the town at sunrise with a group of friends.
Rural areas prepare for an influx of visitors
Spain’s Interior Ministry said 350 official viewing sites have been set up across the sparsely populated interior, often referred to as “Empty Spain.” Authorities have limited or restricted access to another 123 sites because of environmental conditions or obstacles that could hinder an evacuation in the event of a wildfire.
Only weeks ago, the most destructive wildfire in Spanish history devoured 500 square kilometers (193 square miles) and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in Ávila, in central Spain. Several smaller wildfires remain active elsewhere in southern and central parts of the country.
More than 33,500 law enforcement officers will be deployed to observation areas and access points, the ministry said.
Spain is preparing to witness a total solar eclipse on Aug. 12, the first to cross the country’s mainland in more than a century. (AP Video: Iain Sullivan)
“High temperatures, the accumulated dryness of vegetation, and the intense pressure on natural areas due to projected travel necessitate extreme preventive measures,” Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said.
Much of Spain was on alert Wednesday as temperatures climbed above 35 Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) in many areas where the total eclipse will be observed.
Authorities’ top priority is to prevent even a single spark that could lead to a fire, as happened in Ávila in late July. They are urging visitors not to light fires, litter or park in areas with dry vegetation.
Eclipse glasses are going fast
Special eclipse glasses are essential for safe viewing, even if only a sliver of the sun remains visible.
“To look at the sun, you must always use proper protection, and the most suitable protection is eclipse glasses,” said Telmo Fernández Castro, director of the Madrid Planetarium. The glasses are made with special filters that block solar radiation that can damage the eyes.
For months, supermarkets, department stores, museums and planetariums across Spain have sold or distributed the glasses, with many pharmacies running out of stock ahead of Wednesday.
On Tuesday evening in downtown Madrid, a long line formed outside a photo shop where a sign read, “We carry eclipse glasses.”
One woman emerged triumphantly and reassured those waiting: “He has boxes and boxes of them!”
A ship circles waters near Greenland hoping to catch a glimpse
For sky watchers hoping to peek at the solar eclipse, spare a thought for Sverre Rudd.
Rudd, captain of the MS Spitsbergen, is circling the waters of Rypefjord in eastern Greenland trying to make sure he is perfectly positioned for his 126 passengers to view the spectacle. All day, people have been coming up to Rudd to ask if he has nailed the right spot — no clouds will do if they are to see it.
“I will do my best,’’ Rudd said. “I will pull out my superman powers.’’
The eclipse may be startling for the passengers, who have been experiencing 24 hours of daylight on a 17-day cruise in locations mostly north of the Arctic Circle.
Suddenly, for two minutes it will be dark.
Even so, the mood on the ice-strengthened polar ship is pure anticipation.
“Everyone is very enthusiastic,” Rudd said. “When we were down for breakfast earlier, it was almost like a little bit of a Christmas Eve feeling here.”
Hotel costs skyrocket in Spain and Iceland
Rooms in Reykjavík, Iceland’s capital, were averaging more than $1,000 for Wednesday night as Icelanders prepared for their first total solar eclipse since 1954 and the first visible from the capital since 1433.
Prices were roughly double 2025 rates, according to data group Lighthouse Intelligence. But tourists, many of whom made bookings years in advance at exorbitant prices, may be disappointed as cloudy skies are forecast across most of the island when the eclipse peaks.
Authorities expect up to 20,000 additional overseas visitors during an already busy peak tourist period. Iceland is home to fewer than 400,000 people.
The 70-room Hotel Keflavík in the Reykjanesbaer municipality was fully booked, with guests hoping to see around one minute and 45 seconds of totality.
“Eclipse time, of course, has been very demanding, and many people came to us early, like last year,” said hotel owner and manager Steinþór Jónsson.
Jónsson said he had seen nothing like it since 1986, the year the hotel opened and U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev held their summit in Reykjavík.
“When I opened the hotel, we had Reagan and Gorbachev meeting. It was very hectic here,” he said with a smile. “Besides Reagan and Gorbachev, the eclipse is the biggest.”
___
Associated Press journalists Danica Kirka and Brian Melley in London and James Brooks in Snæfellsnes, Iceland, contributed.

- IBRiS poll published in July finds 52.2% of Poles support continued military assistance to Kyiv
 
 More than two-thirds of Poles support a proposal by the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party to send Ukrainian men of military age who are not legally working in Poland back to Ukraine, according to a new poll for daily newspaper Rzeczpospolita.
The survey found that 67.2% of respondents supported sending the men back to Ukraine, while 23.4% opposed the proposal and the remainder were undecided.
The proposal concerns Ukrainian men aged 25 to 60 who are of military age but are not legally employed in Poland.
The findings are the latest indication of hardening attitudes in Poland toward some Ukrainian refugees more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Poland remains a major political and military supporter of Kyiv and hosts one of the largest Ukrainian refugee populations in the EU. But public and political debate has increasingly focused on whether Ukrainians living in Poland should work, pay taxes and have the same access to welfare benefits as Polish citizens.
Earlier this year, Poland backed discussions at the EU level on excluding Ukrainian men of military age from the bloc’s temporary protection mechanism. Deputy Interior Minister Maciej Duszczyk said in June that Warsaw supported such a move as EU governments considered changes to the system introduced after Russia’s February 2022 invasion.
Poland has also tightened some of the special provisions introduced for Ukrainian refugees after the invasion. Legislation signed by President Karol Nawrocki in February began phasing out the separate Ukrainian assistance regime while maintaining legal residence and temporary protection arrangements until March 2027.
The shift comes despite the significant presence of Ukrainians in the Polish labor market. Polish officials have previously stressed that hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians are legally employed and paying social security contributions in the country.
Attitudes toward continued support for Kyiv, however, remain mixed rather than uniformly hostile. A separate IBRiS poll for Rzeczpospolita published in July found that 52.2% of Poles still believed Poland should continue providing military assistance to Ukraine.

Ukrainians have had the rules for checking military registration documents abroad changed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
11:20:27 EEST
17:20:27 KST

Ukrainians have had the rules for checking military registration documents abroad changed
Kyiv • UNN
Men aged 18–60 no longer need to generate an e-military registration document 72 hours in advance; a valid document at the time of the visit is sufficient. Refusal is possible if the document is invalid or the data has not been updated.
The Government has updated the rules for verifying military registration documents of men aged 18 to 60 when receiving consular services abroad. This was reported by the Consular Service Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine, UNN writes.
The Law "On the Legal Regime of Martial Law" stipulates that, in order to receive consular services abroad, men aged 18–60 are required to present a valid military registration document to the consul for verification. In electronic form (e-MRD), it is generated through the Reserve+ mobile application
Previously, men aged 18–60 had to present an e-MRD generated no earlier than 72 hours before their visit to the consulate or embassy. Now it is sufficient to provide the consul with a document valid at the time of the visit to the diplomatic mission for verification.
A consular action may be refused if:
-  the verification confirmed that the e-MRD is invalid or that the data require updating; 
-  the applicant did not present a valid e-MRD; 
-  the presented e-MRD does not contain confirmation that the personal data are up to date. 
Exceptions (in which cases an e-MRD is not required):
-  issuance of an identity document for return to Ukraine;  
-  performance of consular actions concerning children of Ukrainian citizens whose other parent is a foreign national or a stateless person;  
-  performance of actions based on applications from Ukrainian citizens who are under arrest, detained, or deprived of their liberty abroad. 
If the data are unavailable or cannot be updated through Reserve+, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, together with the Ministry of Defense, will introduce the possibility of updating the data through consular registration. For this purpose, men will need to register for consular registration (if the person is not registered for consular purposes), or update their data at a diplomatic mission (if the person is already registered for consular purposes).
Citizens who cannot independently update their data through Reserve+ due to the absence of a tax identification number may personally contact the nearest Ukrainian embassy or consulate abroad to obtain one through the e-Consul system.

Russian President Vladimir Putin threatened on Aug. 12 to "respond in kind" if European countries seize Russian commercial vessels, calling such attempts "nothing more than piracy."
The statement comes as the West ramps up efforts to clamp down on Russia's shadow fleet, a group of aging and poorly insured tankers Moscow uses to circumvent sanctions and carry out hybrid operations.
"We see that the authorities of some countries, in violation of international maritime law, are attempting to restrict the movement of vessels belonging to our economic operators," Putin said while visiting exercises of Russia's Pacific Fleet.
"And recently, they even came up with the idea of seizing our ships and selling the property they stole from us," he said, adding that Moscow "will be forced to respond in kind" if such methods are put into practice.
In recent months, countries like Sweden, France, the U.K., and Belgium have intercepted vessels from Russia's shadow fleet, many of which were sailing under third-country flags and in violation of sanctions.
Swedish courts have since agreed to hand over Caffa, a shadow fleet vessel transporting grain looted from occupied Ukrainian territories, to Ukraine.
The U.S. also seized a Russian-flagged tanker in the Atlantic Ocean on Jan. 7 for the first time in recent history, even after Moscow had reportedly dispatched a submarine to protect it.
Western governments and watchdogs have warned that Russian shadow fleet vessels pose a risk not only to international security but also to the environment and marine life, as the aging tankers are more prone to oil spills.
