More than 4.4 million Ukrainians are under temporary protection in EU countries — Eurostat
Kyiv • UNN
As of the end of June, more than 4.4 million Ukrainians were under temporary protection in the EU, 24,000 more than in May. The largest numbers of such people are in Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic.
The number of beneficiaries of temporary protection in EU countries who left Ukraine as a result of russia's full-scale invasion exceeded 4.4 million people as of the end of June. This was reported by Eurostat, UNN writes.
Details
It is noted that compared with the end of May, the total number of people from Ukraine under temporary protection in the EU increased by 24,380 (+0.6%) and amounted to 4,407,675.
Among EU countries, Germany (1,286,230 people; 29.2% of the total), Poland (961,170; 21.8%), and the Czech Republic (390,810; 8.9%) received the largest numbers of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine.
Compared with the end of May, the number of people under temporary protection increased in 24 of the 27 EU countries. The largest absolute increases were observed in Italy (+4,115; +8.8%), the Czech Republic (+3,835; +1%), and Germany (+2,960; +0.2%). The three countries where decreases were recorded were Poland (-6,335; -0.7%), Belgium (-35; -0.04%), and Ireland (-15; -0.01%).
As of June 30, more than 98.5% of beneficiaries of temporary protection in the EU were Ukrainian citizens. Adult women accounted for 43.4% of the total, adult men for 27%, and minors for nearly a third (29.6%) of the total.

Singapore wins first ever Olympic gold in 2016 – SCMP archive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:30:06 UTC
15:30:06 KST

On This DaySingapore wins first ever Olympic gold in 2016 – SCMP archive
On this day 10 years ago, Joseph Schooling outswam Michael Phelps to bring Singapore its first Olympic gold medal
This article was first published on August 14, 2016.
Lion City celebrates first golden hero
by James Porteous
Singapore exploded into celebration as it feted a new sporting hero yesterday (August 13, 2016) after swimmer Joseph Schooling did the improbable – beat his one-time idol Michael Phelps – to win the Lion City’s first ever gold medal. Schooling completed a wire-to-wire victory to deny American Phelps a fourth successive title in the 100 metres butterfly, winning in an Olympic record of 50.39 seconds as Phelps, amazingly, dead-heated for silver with South Africa’s Chad le Clos and Laszlo Cseh of Hungary.
The 21-year-old Schooling also became an instant millionaire, collecting a cool S$1 million (HK$5.76 million) bonus as part of an incentive programme encouraging Singaporeans to excel in sport. The city state also offers a Foreign Sports Talent programme which grants promising foreign athletes citizenship.
“It’s been a hard road. I’ve done something that no one in our country had done before,” said Asian champion Schooling. “It’s been a tough road, I’m not going to lie. The first guy through the wall, it’s always bloody. I had to take that blow and I’m thankful and blessed that I have the ability to accomplish this.”
Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong led the adulation, saying in a Facebook post: “It is an incredible feat, to compete among the world’s best, stay focused, and emerge victorious.” Singapore had only four medals (two silvers and two bronzes) to show for its efforts since it joined the Olympic fold in 1948. The first – a silver – was won by weightlifter Tan Howe Liang at the Rome Games in 1960.
“I hope this opens a new door, opens more doors for sports in our country and hopefully I set a precedent for a lot more guys to come up,” Schooling said. Schooling first met Phelps by chance as a 13-year-old when the US Olympic swim team visited Singapore in 2008, and the American helped inspire the young Singaporean to move to the US for extensive training. Schooling is now based at the University of Texas.

At least 15 dead, dozens missing as ferry capsizes in Zimbabwe
Zimbabwe’s Civil Protection Unit says the ferry was carrying more than its capacity of 90 people when it capsized.
At least 15 people have been killed and 27 remain missing after an overloaded ferry capsized on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba, according to the country’s Civil Protection Unit.
The boat overturned on Tuesday after hitting strong waves, the agency said in a statement, adding that at least 77 people were rescued.
The boat provides transport between the northern town of Kariba and several islands and fishing camps and was carrying more than its capacity of 90 people when it capsized, the agency said.
While exact numbers of passengers and crew are yet to be announced, the agency said it could only confirm through registered ticket sales that there were 114 adult passengers on board, along with five crew members.
There could have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age who were on board and not accounted for, the agency added.
Zimbabwe’s national police service said rescue efforts were under way.
The state broadcaster ZBC published video of speedboats making their way to what appeared to be an overturned boat on the lake as a helicopter hovered overhead. An underwater team for search and rescue operations was deployed on the huge lake, it said.
Witness Maxton Kanhema told the AFP news agency that the vessel departed in bad weather, and that a wave may have hit the boat, causing its engines to switch off.
“When we were in the waters, then you could see a distress sign and then boats that were close by responded,” said Maxton Kanhema.
He said the Matusadona National Park provided a helicopter to help in the rescue effort alongside bigger boats and divers from the local area and the army.
“People were in distress… There were bodies in the water and it was a sad situation to witness. Those that could be rescued were rescued,” he added.
“However, due to the bad weather, the responses were a bit late,” he said. “Getting to the boat took time and unfortunately lives were lost.”
Lake Kariba lies on Zimbabwe’s border with Zambia, more than 300km (186 miles) northeast of the capital Harare. It is the world’s largest man-made lake by volume and was created in the late 1950s and early 1960s by building a dam wall to block the Zambezi River, resulting in a valley slowly filling with water to form a huge lake that is now more than 200km (124 miles) long and up to 40km (25 miles) wide in places.

Lauri Laats: Estonia cannot tax or borrow its way to prosperity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:29:00 UTC
15:29:00 KST

Lauri Laats: Estonia cannot tax or borrow its way to prosperity
Higher taxes, more debt and weak economic growth all at once begs the question whether Estonia's chosen policies are actually working, Lauri Laats writes.
The public finance debate (in Estonian — ed.) at Opinion Festival in Paide once again confirmed that the problem facing Estonia cannot be reduced to a simple question of whether taxes should be raised or spending cut. The question is much more fundamental: How can Estonia get its economy growing sustainably again while also putting a stop to the rapid increase in government debt?
Estonia cannot tax itself into prosperity, nor can we cut or borrow our way to prosperity. Estonia must grow its way to prosperity.
Banking tax working in Latvia and Lithuania
Estonia's economy contracted by a total of approximately 5.5 percent from the end of 2021 to the end of 2024. The economy returned to growth in 2025, but growth remained at around just 0.5 percent. This year, growth of approximately 2 percent or slightly more is forecast.
But GDP growth alone is not enough; the quality of that growth is what matters. Is Estonia's economy growing thanks to exports, productivity and private-sector investment, or because the government is spending more and consumption is increasing? The former creates long-term prosperity; the latter may give the economy a short-term boost but does not solve our structural problems.
The same applies to tax policy. We often hear that Estonia's tax burden is not high compared with the European Union average. There is some truth to this when looking at the overall tax burden: Estonia still remains below the EU average. But what matters is not only how much tax is collected, but also where it is collected from.
Estonia's tax system relies heavily on taxing consumption. Consumption taxes account for approximately 39 percent of total tax revenue in Estonia, compared with an EU average of about 27 percent. At the same time, capital taxes account for approximately 8.5 percent in Estonia, compared with an EU average of more than 20 percent. Estonia's tax system is therefore clearly tilted toward consumption.
Tax policy in recent years has tended to deepen this disparity. Just a few years ago, VAT was 20 percent; it has now risen to 24 percent. A motor vehicle tax has been introduced, while excise duties and other taxes have also been raised.
Higher consumption taxes affect everyone, but their impact is not the same for everyone. People on lower incomes spend a larger share of their income on food, housing, energy and other basic necessities. This is precisely why we have repeatedly proposed lowering VAT on staple foods. It is a matter of principle: Should the government finance its growing expenditures by increasingly taxing people's everyday shopping baskets? In my view, it should not.
That does not mean the solution is to impose higher taxes on businesses and investment. Estonia needs more private investment, not less, and any effort to rebalance the tax system must therefore distinguish between productive capital and sectors where profitability has become exceptionally high.
One option is to look to the financial sector. Latvia and Lithuania have imposed additional taxes on the banking sector. Estonia, too, needs to have an honest discussion about whether some government revenue could come from sectors that have enjoyed exceptionally high profitability in recent years. The goal should be to create a fairer tax structure that does less harm to economic growth.
Economy growing slowly, debt rapidly
An even bigger issue is the growth of government debt. In 2019, Estonia's general government debt stood at 8.6 percent of GDP. By 2025, it had risen to 24.1 percent, and according to current forecasts, we are on track to approach 40 percent by the end of the decade. Estonia's debt burden remains low by European standards and there is no reason to deny that. The main problem is the pace at which it is growing. If the economy grows slowly while debt grows rapidly, such a trajectory cannot continue indefinitely.
This points to one of the biggest contradictions in economic policy in recent years. More taxes are being collected from people and businesses, yet government debt is also rising. If the result is simultaneously higher taxes, more debt and weak economic growth, we have to ask whether the chosen policies are actually working.
We need to be honest when discussing the budget deficit. Defense accounts for a significant share of the increase in spending in the coming years. Estonia's defense spending is moving toward approximately 5 percent of GDP, and in the current security environment, I do not believe this is an area where we should make cuts to balance the budget.
That is precisely why the rest of the state budget needs to be managed better. Instead of across-the-board cuts, we need a review of the efficiency of government spending. Duplicative functions, rising administrative costs and programs and subsidies whose impact cannot be measured must be reviewed.
At the same time, we need to distinguish between current spending and investment. From an economic perspective, a euro spent on administration does not have the same value as a euro invested in infrastructure, energy security, research and development or digitalization. We need both a smaller deficit and a higher-quality state budget.
Where will economic growth come from next?
Estonia needs tax stability and investment certainty. Businesses need to know what the tax environment will look like not only next year, but also three or five years from now. Constant changes to the tax system increase uncertainty and delay investment.
We need competitive and predictable energy prices. For industry in particular, the price of energy can determine whether production takes place in Estonia or another country. Estonia must also become a more attractive place to invest. Additional investment incentives should be considered for new production facilities, automation and research and development.
We need less bureaucracy and faster permitting processes. If an investor has to wait years for a permit, the next investment may go to Lithuania, Poland or elsewhere instead of Estonia. Exports must once again become a central focus of Estonia's economic policy. A domestic market of 1.3 million people cannot on its own deliver the economic growth we need to raise living standards and fund defense, healthcare, education and social spending.
Goals for 2031
By 2031, Estonia should have reached a point where the budget deficit is significantly smaller than it is today and the growth of the debt burden has been brought under control. We should aim for a budget deficit of around 1 percent, but achieving that must be based on stronger economic growth, not on stifling the economy with new taxes. The faster the economy, investment and exports grow, the larger the government's revenue base will be.
Economic growth is one of the main prerequisites for sound public finances. When the economy and productivity grow, the tax base expands and the debt burden becomes easier to control. If the economy stagnates, every additional euro spent on defense, pensions, healthcare or education becomes increasingly difficult to finance.
We do not have to choose between sound public finances and a strong economy, because we need both. The experience of recent years should serve as sufficient warning that ever-higher taxes combined with ever-growing debt are not a sustainable economic model.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Belarus introduces new measures to boost power grid reliability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:27:00 UTC
15:27:00 KST

An archive photo
                    
                    MINSK, 12 August (BelTA) – Belarusian Prime Minister Aleksandr Turchin has signed a resolution to introduce additional measures to boost power grid reliability in the country, BelTA learned from the press service of the Belarusian government.
The document was adopted to implement Presidential Order No. 84 of 17 June 2026, “On improving power grid reliability.” The order establishes procedures for allocating land plots needed for widening and clearing rights-of-way along overhead power lines of 35 kV and above, aimed at preventing emergencies caused by falling trees.
The resolution provides for the approval of regulations on partial cost reimbursement for clearing woody vegetation, as well as regulations on the official write-off procedure for the cleared vegetation.
The costs of clearing woody vegetation will be covered by the value of the removed timber itself. However, in certain cases, this value may not fully offset the expenses due to the low quality of the vegetation or the inability to transport it for future use. Any remaining costs not covered by the value of the cleared trees and shrubs will be reimbursed to forestry enterprises by regional power utilities. Commission-based write-offs will be permitted if there are no access roads for logging equipment or if other circumstances prevent the removal of the cleared vegetation.
The adopted measures will accelerate the widening of overhead power line rights-of-way and boost the reliability of the power supply.
Statistics show that overhead power lines with widened rights-of-way experience nine times fewer emergency shutdowns on average compared to those with unwidened clearance zones.

Primary elections in 6 states determine nominees for US House, Senate, state gubernatorial races for midterms

Primary elections in six US states on Tuesday determined nominees for both Democrats and Republicans in Congressional, Senate and gubernatorial races leading up to the November midterm elections.
In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley defeated Francesca Hong 59.0% to 39.4% with 96% of precincts counted. Crowley will face US Rep. Tom Tiffany, who easily secured the Republican nomination with 95.3% of the vote and got the endorsement from President Donald Trump.
Tiffany’s run for governor created an open race for Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District, where Michael Alfonso handily won the Republican primary against his four opponents and received 48.8% of the vote with 97% of precincts reporting. Alfonso also received an endorsement from Trump and will face Fred Clark, who defeated Ginger Murray in the Democratic primary 37.3% to 31.8% with 95% of ballots counted.
In Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District, Rebecca Cooke won the Democratic nomination with 60% of the vote with 94% of ballots counted. Cooke will face Republican US Rep. Derrick Van Orden, who flipped the seat in 2022 and ran unopposed in his party's primary.
South Carolina held a special Republican primary to replace the late US Sen. Lindsey Graham on the November midterm ballot. Graham's sister, US Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to serve the remainder of his term, will head to a runoff with Ralph Norman, as the two remained standing at the top of the ballot with 10 candidates. Graham, whom Trump endorsed, finished with 32.7% of the vote to Norman's 24.6%, with 99% of precincts reporting.
US Sen. Amy Klobuchar easily won the Democratic nomination for Minnesota governor with 89.6% of the vote, with 96% of precincts reporting. Klobuchar will face state House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who beat Trump-endorsed MyPillow founder Mike Lindell 43.6% to 32.3% with 95% of ballots counted.
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan secured the Democratic nomination for Senate after Democratic US Sen. Tina Smith retired. Flanagan beat US Rep. Angie Craig by a margin of 59.0% to 39.4% with 97% of votes counted. Flanagan will face former television sports broadcaster Michel Tafoya, who won the Republican nomination with 52.1% of the vote with 95% of precincts counted.
In Connecticut, US Rep. John Larson will not get to seek a 15th term in Congress, as he was upset in the Democratic primary by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, who received 54.4% of the vote to Larson's 32.7%. Bronin will face Amy Chai, who ran uncontested for the Republican nomination.
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont is seeking a third term, having defeated state Rep. Josh Elliott 67.9% to 32.1% with 94% of precincts counted. Lamont will face Ryan Fazio, who ran unopposed for the Republican nomination.
In Alabama, Jerry Carl won the Republican Special Primary for the state's 1st Congressional District with 74.7% of the vote. Carl will face Democrat Clyde Jones, who ran uncontested.
In Alabama's 2nd Congressional District, Trump-endorsed state Rep. Rhett Marques beat his five opponents with 50.0% of the vote for the Republican nomination. Marques will face incumbent Democratic US Rep. Shomari Figures, who ran unopposed.
Ammie Akin defeated David Perry 73.4% to 26.6% in the Republican primary for the 7th Congressional District. Akin will face US Rep. Terri Sewell, who ran unopposed in the Democratic primary and is seeking a ninth term in the office.
In Vermont's 1st Congressional District, Gerald Malloy won the Republican nomination with 76.3% of the vote. Malloy will face incumbent US Rep. Becca Balint, who ran uncontested in the Democratic primary.
In Vermont's Democratic primary for governor, Amanda Janoo narrowly defeated Aly Richards 49.1% to 46.5% with 98% of precincts counted. Janoo will face incumbent Gov. Phil Scott, who has held the office since 2017 and ran unopposed in the Republican primary.

Estonia to adopt new EU transparency rules on AI and 'deepfakes'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:25:00 UTC
15:25:00 KST

Estonia to adopt new EU transparency rules on AI and 'deepfakes'
New European Union requirements intended to protect the public from manipulation involving artificial intelligence (AI) are to be rolled out in Estonia.
The regulations aim to help people identify when they are encountering AI-generated content or interacting with an AI system, and include measures to combat "deepfake" images. Fines of up to €15,000 may be issued in the case of violations.
The new EU Guidelines on transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems took effect this month and are aimed at harmonizing requirements across sectors and defining when users must be informed about AI use or content.
"It may not be obvious when AI presents itself in the name of a person, or in a human-like manner, without a clear indication. The user may mistakenly come to believe they are communicating with a real person, or the AI may be integrated into a service in a way that is not visible to the user," said Aivar Pau, strategic communications adviser for digital affairs at the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs.
In practice, the presence of AI may be "obvious" or self-evident in some cases: For example, when a user enters an environment that is clearly presented as an AI chatbot, or an AI character, or when the name and design of the design of the service clearly indicate AI is used. In these cases, separate labeling is not required under the new EU rules.
Pau noted that individuals must also be informed when they encounter AI systems capable of processing biometric data, identifying or inferring a person's emotions or intentions, or categorizing them by gender, age, appearance, ethnic origin, personal preferences or by other definitions.
The regulations are the first of their kind when it comes to cross-sector AI, Pau noted; previous regulations were sector- or field-specific.
The justice ministry said it takes a positive view of the transparency obligations, as they ensure individuals are informed and reduces the risk of manipulation.
As well as AI systems being required to indicate that the user is not interacting with a human being, specific labeling is also required for deepfakes: Content created or altered using AI and which could mistakenly be perceived as authentic.
Notification is also not required when the use of AI is permitted by law for the detection, prevention, investigation or prosecution of criminal offense, Pau noted, adding: "The condition here is that safeguards must be implemented to protect the rights and freedoms of third parties," Pau added, "except when people use these systems to report crimes."
Exceptions will also apply to edited texts – for instance readers do not have to be separately informed about the use of AI if this was used in preparing a published text, provided authors, editors or others responsible have reviewed that text. In such cases, a "natural person," meaning a legally defined person or persons, bears editorial responsibility for publishing the AI-generated content, the ministry said.
Any required AI information must also be provided in a format accessible to people with disabilities.
The government will only be able to formally delegate responsible authorities for the AI labeling, monitoring, supervision and penalties once the Riigikogu has transposed the EU regulations into domestic law.
To indicate the use of AI, the European Commission has developed three visual labels: A basic icon, a label for content generated entirely by AI and a label indicating part-use of AI. Under the new rules, these labels must remain attached to the text throughout the entire creative process. The labels are available on the European Commission's digital policy hub.
The new requirements apply both to providers of AI systems and to their users. Violations can result in fines of up to €15,000 or 3 percent of a company's total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year.
Previously, the labeling of deepfakes was only done on a voluntary basis per standards developed by the tech industry – standards not applied uniformly worldwide.

"Business is coming back, it's normalising," chief executive Sebastian Ebel said on an earnings call. "We have seen strong weeks."
"Business is coming back, it's normalising," chief executive Sebastian Ebel said. [Getty]

"The ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and elevated fuel prices continue to weigh on oil consumption," the Paris-based IEA said.

Russia has lost around 1,461,660 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 12.
The figure includes 1,260 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,259 tanks, 25,127 armored combat vehicles, 132,931 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,773 artillery systems, 2,022 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,561 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 456,339 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,203 unmanned ground systems, 34 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Fruit fusion: how will the market react to Chinese scientists’ lychee-longan creation?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:15:52 UTC
15:15:52 KST

Fruit fusion: how will the market react to Chinese scientists’ lychee-longan creation?
Described as tender and crisp, Cuimi delivers about double the yield compared with Shixia longan, say developers
The new variety, named “Cuimi”, was bred using the Shixia longan – a popular cultivar in Guangdong province – as its maternal parent and a lychee as its paternal parent, according to the research team. The hybrid fruit breaks long-standing reproductive barriers between plant genera.
It has been planted across Guangdong, Sichuan and Yunnan provinces in southern China, with its yield this year reaching several thousand jin, a Chinese unit equal to 500 grams or 17.6 ounces. Trial sales are scheduled for mid-September.
Speaking at an on-site demonstration hosted by South China Agricultural University (SCAU) in Guangzhou on August 9, Liu Chengming, a professor at the university’s College of Horticulture and the lead developer of the variety, told media that about 90 per cent of Cuimi’s genetic material comes from its mother. Consequently, its appearance and flavour lean closer to those of the longan.
Compared with the Shixia longan, Cuimi delivered about double the yield, was more cold resistant and ripened 15 to 20 days later, the researchers said.
According to Liu, these characteristics could help expand longan cultivation areas in China while extending the fruit’s commercial selling season.
“The creation of Cuimi is significant for its breakthrough in intergeneric hybridisation, long regarded as a major technical obstacle,” the state-run newspaper Science and Technology Daily said on Monday.

How to choose natural honey: simple ways to check
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:13:21 EEST
15:13:21 KST

How to choose natural honey: simple ways to check
Kyiv • UNN
Beekeeping technician Mykola Maliarchuk explained how to distinguish natural honey from a product with additives by its density, crystallization, and foam. He also explained the characteristics of acacia honey and the effect of additives on its consistency.
Natural honey can be partially checked before purchasing it. A technician and beekeeper, Mykola Maliarchuk, told UNN journalist in more detail how to distinguish a natural product from honey containing additives by its outward characteristics.
The beekeeper notes that the first feature to pay attention to is the honey’s density; natural honey is also distinguished by its tendency to crystallize quickly.
First and foremost, natural honey should gradually crystallize and thicken. Different varieties do this at different rates: for example, sunflower honey may thicken in approximately 10–12 days. To check the consistency of fresh honey, you can scoop it into a spoon, raise it to a height of about 30–40 centimeters, and pour it slowly: natural honey should run in a continuous thin stream rather than in drops
According to the beekeeper, this test is primarily suitable for fresh, still-liquid honey. However, if the product remains excessively runny or begins to drip when being poured, this may indicate a change in its consistency. According to Mykola Maliarchuk, one possible reason may be the addition of sugar syrup.
If it starts dripping, this means that sugar syrup may have been added. In that case, the honey no longer has the same viscosity. And if the honey is purchased already crystallized, it should have a completely thick consistency
Crystallized honey also has its own characteristics, and its firmness depends on the variety, the expert explains. He emphasizes that in high-quality, natural honey, the density should be present not only at the top but throughout the entire container. At the same time, different varieties may have different structures.
It all depends on the variety. There are softer types, for example, rapeseed and wildflower honey. Sunflower honey is firmer. From top to bottom, such a product should be thick and firm
Another feature that Mykola Maliarchuk advises paying attention to is the top layer of the honey. According to him, a light, thick foam may form near the lid of a natural product. However, the beekeeper himself advises against drawing conclusions based on just one characteristic.
A light layer resembling foam may form on the surface of the honey. It should be thick and dense. By the way, if the foam is specifically white, this also indicates that the honey is natural
The specialist separately explained that the graininess of honey does not necessarily mean that it contains sugar. In particular, buckwheat honey may have this structure after crystallization. It can be either fine-grained or coarse-grained.
Buckwheat honey after crystallization may have either a fine-grained or coarse-grained structure. Fine-grained honey resembles butter in consistency, while visible grains form in coarse-grained honey. This structure does not mean that sugar was added to the honey. It is a natural crystallization process of buckwheat honey, through which large crystals form in it
Speaking about honey varieties that can be purchased, Mykola Maliarchuk singled out pure acacia honey in particular.
Pure acacia honey is considered the best. To obtain precisely such a product, bees need to be specially transported to a honey-gathering site where acacia predominates. If acacia is mixed with wildflowers, it becomes spring honey, which contains nectar from acacia, meadow grasses, and other nectar-bearing plants
The beekeeper describes pure acacia honey as very light in color, with a slight greenish tint. According to him, this product can remain liquid for several months.
Fresh acacia honey has a very light, pale greenish tint. If you scoop it into a spoon, this color is clearly visible. Pure acacia honey can retain a liquid consistency for up to six months because it crystallizes much more slowly than many other honey varieties
At the same time, according to the expert, if acacia honey begins to thicken significantly sooner, this may indicate that it is not pure acacia honey. Its consistency may be affected by wildflowers, rapeseed, and other nectar-bearing plants. Therefore, when choosing honey, it is important to consider not only its appearance but also its variety.
If acacia honey is not pure, it may begin to thicken after approximately 10–14 days. This indicates that nectar from other honey plants, including wildflowers, rapeseed, and garden crops, has entered it along with the acacia nectar. These impurities affect the consistency of the honey and accelerate its crystallization

Number of Ukrainians with temporary protection in EU increases – infographics
As of 30 June, 4.41 million people in EU countries had been granted temporary protection under the mechanism established to provide refuge to Ukrainians following the start of the full-scale war.
Source: European Pravda, citing the EU's statistical office Eurostat
Details: In June, the number of Ukrainians with temporary protection in EU countries increased by 24,380, up 0.6% compared with May.
The largest increases in temporary protection beneficiaries in June were recorded in Italy (more than 4,100 people), Czechia (over 3,800) and Germany (almost 3,000).
Nonetheless, the largest decreases in the number of people with temporary protection status were recorded in Poland (more than 6,300), Belgium (35) and Ireland (15).
Germany hosts the largest number of Ukrainians under temporary protection at more than 1.28 million, accounting for 29.2% of the EU total. Poland follows, hosting more than 960,000 people (21.8%), while Czechia has more than 390,000 (8.9%).
Relative to the population of the host countries, the highest concentrations of Ukrainians were recorded in Czechia, Slovakia and Cyprus.
Ukrainian citizens remain by far the largest group among temporary protection beneficiaries, accounting for 98.5% of the total. Women account for 43.4%, adult men for 27%, and minors for 29.6%.
Background:
- In late July, the European Union extended temporary protection for Ukrainians until 4 March 2028, introducing a new provision under which newly arrived Ukrainian citizens liable for military service will be eligible for the status only if there are no issues with their military registration documents.
- Czech authorities reported that last year, for the first time, more Ukrainian men than women were granted temporary protection in the country.

Ultra-Orthodox protesters opposed to military conscription are expected to block roads Wednesday after the arrest of a yeshiva student suspected of draft evasion, the first such detention in roughly three weeks.
The demonstrations are expected to begin around 4 p.m. in the Bnei Brak area. Previous protests of this kind have frequently targeted Route 4 or Jabotinsky Street, though additional protest sites are also possible.
According to Shas lawmaker Moshe Abutbul, the student had been summoned to the Lahav 433 police unit to give testimony in connection with a fraud investigation.
Abutbul claimed that once the testimony was completed, a police officer escorted the student to the parking lot and then transferred him to military police.
“This is crossing a red line and a serious violation of the police commissioner’s commitment to the ultra-Orthodox public,” Abutbul said. “This is not how trust is built. This is how it is destroyed.”
In a letter to National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Abutbul argued that police instructions may not have been sufficiently clarified to officers in the field.
“There is an immediate need for clear procedures allowing ultra-Orthodox young men to file complaints at police stations without being arrested,” he wrote.
“Continuing to operate in this way could severely damage public trust in the police and cause citizens to avoid turning to them when needed, something that could cost lives.”
The arrest comes against the backdrop of the ongoing political and legal battle over military service for ultra-Orthodox men.
The governing coalition had advanced legislation intended to shield draft evaders from arrest until the elections, but the High Court of Justice suspended the measure with an interim order.
In practice, however, arrests of ultra-Orthodox draft evaders inside Israel have remained rare.
The IDF has not been given the operational tools needed to carry out widespread arrests, police generally do not assist military authorities in such operations, and attempts to detain draft evaders in ultra-Orthodox neighborhoods have repeatedly drawn large crowds that confront military police.
As a result, even as the dispute over Haredi conscription has intensified, relatively few suspected ultra-Orthodox draft evaders have been arrested inside the country.

Australia approves new rules benefiting gig delivery workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:05:00 UTC
15:05:00 KST

Australia approves new rules benefiting gig delivery workers
August 12, 2026
Food and grocery delivery workers in Australia will be paid at least A$31.30 (€19.15, $22.11) an hour and be given accident insurance on the job under new rules approved by Australia's industrial relations tribunal.
The hourly rate, set out in an order issued by the Fair Work Commission (FWC) on Tuesday, is above Australia's minimum wage of A$26.44.
The FWC's order, which could serve as a precedent for other countries, has been hailed by the Transport Workers Union (TWU) as "a landmark moment for the Australian gig economy." The union called the new rules a "world-leading set of standards."
What rights and protects did the FWC give gig delivery drivers?
The minimum hourly rate will be paid for "engaged" time, i.e. the time between taking on a delivery job and completing the commission.
The order, which takes effect on August 17, also requires companies to provide a "reasonable minimum level of cover" for personal accident insurance on the job, without specifying exactly how much.
The workers will, however, still be responsible for maintaining third-party insurance for the vehicles used for deliveries.
Unions and workers in Australia have long sought reforms benefiting gig workers.
They have previously not been covered by many of the protections given to other employees, being classified as "independent contractors."
The new rules are expected to affect some 250,000 workers.
UN moves to protect gig workers
The FWC's order comes after the United Nations' International Labour Organization (ILO) in June adopted a new global treaty for decent working conditions in the gig economy.
The standards laid down in the treaty, the first global treaty of its kind, still need ratification by governments.
In Australia, the parliament passed legislation in 2023 and 2024 under the center-left Labor government that granted gig workers more negotiating rights over minimum pay and working conditions.
Those laws gave the FWC the power to set rules for pay and insurance.

15:04:54 KST

Civil Defence crews in Gaza began recovering the bodies of 13 Palestinians on Tuesday from beneath the rubble of a multi-storey home destroyed by an Israeli strike during the early days of the war.
The operation is being carried out in coordination with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) at the home of the Gharbiya family in the Al Katiba area west of Gaza City.
Civil Defence spokesperson Mahmoud Basal told Anadolu that a large number of Palestinians were killed in the strike. Some bodies were recovered at the time, while 13 remain beneath the rubble.
The victims include women, children and the elderly, he said.
Basal warned that severe shortages of heavy machinery, equipment, fuel and protective gear continue to hamper efforts to recover thousands of Palestinians believed to remain beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza.
“If we remain in this situation, we are talking about many years” to complete the recovery operations, he said, adding that adequate equipment and resources could reduce the process to a matter of months.
Basal said Civil Defence crews are working with extremely limited resources and at times “with their bare hands,” without adequate protective equipment while handling bodies, human remains and debris.
He said crews continue their work without salaries, bonuses or compensation and called on the international community, international organisations and human rights groups to provide the heavy machinery and logistical support needed to continue recovery operations.
Tuesday’s operation is part of the second phase of a Civil Defence project launched on July 19 to recover Palestinians buried beneath buildings destroyed during the Israeli war.
The 800-hour phase covers 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and northern and central Gaza, where 1,072 bodies are believed to remain beneath the rubble, according to Basal.
During the first phase, launched in November 2025, crews recovered 333 bodies and human remains from 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Limited resources prevented them from reaching around 226 others.
Gaza’s Government Media Office said in October 2025 that around 9,500 Palestinians had been reported missing since the start of the Israeli war, including those believed to remain beneath the rubble and others whose fate remains unknown.
The Israeli army continues to target Palestinians in several areas of Gaza despite an Israel-Hamas ceasefire that went into effect on October 10 2025. The ceasefire violations have killed at least 1,258 Palestinians and injured 4,139 others, according to Gaza’s health ministry. 
Since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, Israel has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000. The war has also caused widespread destruction, affecting 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure.

The 22-year-old Bulgarian finished third with a jump of 8.26 metres, achieved on his sixth and final attempt, with a headwind of 1.7 metres per second. Saraboyukov also recorded four other jumps beyond the eight-metre mark.

FT learned details of the US request to Ukraine regarding strikes on tankers
Kyiv • UNN
US Vice President J.D. Vance asked Ukraine to stop striking tankers using a Russian port.
Ukraine "halted an intensive campaign of drone strikes against oil tankers using the critically important Black Sea port after a request from US Vice President J.D. Vance" late last month, the Financial Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
"Washington was concerned that Ukraine would further destabilize oil markets and harm American companies by attacking tankers carrying oil delivered via pipelines from Kazakhstan to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal at the Russian port of Novorossiysk," the publication writes.
"Vance asked President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop the attacks during a phone call on July 31," Ukrainian officials and other people familiar with the matter said.
"Since then, Ukraine has not struck tankers near the CPC terminal," according to officials and an analysis of open-source information conducted by the FT.
According to officials, "it agreed not to attack CPC infrastructure or non-Russian vessels unless those vessels are under Ukrainian sanctions and are carrying Russian oil or other Russian cargoes."
"We listen very carefully to our American partners," a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv had created the relevant "mechanisms" in response to the US request. The CPC was a "regular part of discussions with the governments of the United States and Kazakhstan," the source said.
American energy giants Chevron and ExxonMobil own stakes in the CPC, which is Kazakhstan's main oil export route, as well as in the western Kazakh oil fields it serves. Chevron owns 50% of Tengiz, the country's largest oil field, while Exxon owns 25%.
A US official confirmed that "the administration warned Ukraine to stop attacks on non-Russian vessels in the Black Sea, as well as on CPC infrastructure."
"The administration views the CPC as a vital channel for supplying energy of Kazakh origin to European markets, serving as an alternative to Russian energy supplies," the official said.
"The United States has "confirmed" Kyiv's commitment to refrain from attacks on CPC infrastructure and non-Russian vessels headed to the pipeline terminal in Novorossiysk, provided that they are not subject to Ukrainian sanctions," the official added.
Vance's office, Zelenskyy's office and Kazakhstan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The CPC, Chevron and Exxon declined to comment.
"A person familiar with Ukraine's position said that Kyiv agreed to the Trump administration's request because it sought a US license to produce Patriot interceptor missiles. It also hopes to purchase several hundred of them by winter, when Russia is expected to intensify its air attacks on critical infrastructure," the publication said.
Vance's request is not the first time American officials have attempted to restrain Ukraine from striking American business interests in Russia, the publication notes.

Justice chancellor on presidency: My only criterion is maintaining an independent image
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:01:00 UTC
15:01:00 KST

Justice chancellor on presidency: My only criterion is maintaining an independent image
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise said she would be prepared to run for president if she receives broad support across the Riigikogu, while stressing that she is not actively seeking the office and intends to maintain her political impartiality.
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise told ERR in an interview she would be prepared to run for president if she receives sufficiently broad support from Riigikogu members, but stressed that she is not actively seeking the office and must remain politically impartial.
Madise said she has not put herself forward as a candidate, asked anyone to nominate her or reached any agreements with political parties. However, if enough MPs see her as an impartial and experienced candidate capable of serving as head of state, she believes accepting their nomination would be the responsible course.
"If members of the Riigikogu ask for my consent to be nominated as a presidential candidate, I will treat that proposal with great respect and accept it," Madise said.
She declined to specify a numerical threshold for sufficient support. Under Estonian law, 21 Riigikogu members are required to nominate a presidential candidate, but Madise indicated that simply securing the minimum number would not necessarily demonstrate the broad-based support she is seeking.
"It is not a question of the number of votes," she said. "My only criterion is that I maintain an image of impartiality, because I am, in substance and in practice, impartial."
Madise said a nomination should demonstrate that MPs across political lines are prepared to accept her as an impartial figure rather than the candidate of a particular party or political camp. She would not, however, require support from every party or dictate how MPs should vote.
Madise also said she could meet with parliamentary groups before becoming an official candidate if MPs begin collecting signatures in support of her nomination and such meetings can take place without compromising her impartiality. She stressed that she could not make promises to parties or enter into political agreements.
Asked whether she would resign as chancellor of justice to campaign for the presidency, Madise ruled out doing so. She said there was no substantive or formal reason for her to step down and noted that the Constitution provides for a serving chancellor of justice's term to end if they are elected president and take the oath of office.
"I am not seeking to leave my current office for another position," Madise said. "I have not put myself forward as a candidate, I have not asked anyone to nominate me, nor have I given my consent to be nominated."
Madise also rejected the idea of viewing Tallinn University of Technology Rector Tiit Land, whose name has also emerged in connection with the presidential election, as a rival.
"Since I have not put myself forward as a candidate and am not fighting to win the office, I do not look at it that way at all," she said.
Madise emphasized that she is familiar with the demands of the presidency and does not regard it as an attractive position to be pursued for its own sake.
"Doing the job well is just as difficult as serving as chancellor of justice," she said. "It is, above all, a very demanding way to serve the country."

Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent – and the consequences are deadly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:00:22 UTC
15:00:22 KST

Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?
The climate crisis is hitting Europe hard in 2026, warming twice as fast as any other continent – and the consequences are deadly
The whole world is getting hotter as carbon pollution from fossil fuel burning traps ever more heat, but Europe is heating up twice as fast as other continents. The consequences are increasingly deadly, with tens of thousands of heatwave deaths so far this summer.
Why is Europe most affected by global heating?
Land requires less heat than the vast and deep oceans to warm up, so all continents are warming more quickly than the seas. But Europe is particularly vulnerable for four reasons: changed weather patterns, its closeness to the Arctic, less snow and less air pollution.
As a result, Europe is now 2.5C hotter than before the mass burning of fossil fuels, almost double the global average 1.4C rise. Temperatures in Europe have risen by 0.56C a decade since the mid-1990s, compared with 0.42C in North America, 0.36C in Africa and 0.27C in South America.
How have Europe’s weather patterns changed?
Shifts in how the atmosphere circulates over Europe have led to more frequent and more intense summer heatwaves. This includes the worst ever heatwave, in June 2026, in which a vast area of hot air was trapped under a stationary “heat dome”.
Scientists are still investigating the role of global heating in causing changes in atmospheric circulation, but a link seems increasingly likely.
Dr Samantha Burgess, from the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, said: “We see statistically significant changes in surface pressure patterns and other measures of circulation when we look at trends over the last 40 or more years, and on this timescale they are more likely associated with climate change than natural variability.”
The association may be the result of a changing jet stream, a fast high-level wind that has a powerful influence on Europe’s weather and is itself affected by rising temperatures.
Why is the Arctic important?
The Arctic is the fastest warming region on the planet, despite having no land. This is because the white polar ice cap, which normally reflects the vast majority of sunlight back into space, is melting away fast. As a result, the darker ocean exposed by the melting absorbs much more heat, which then melts more ice, forming a vicious circle. With a significant proportion of Europe relatively close to the Arctic, temperatures are therefore rising faster.
What about snow cover?
Most of Europe had snowfall in winter in the past. Like the Arctic sea ice, this snow reflected sunlight and kept the continent cooler. But the climate crisis is shrinking snow-covered areas.
In March 2025, Europe’s blanket of snow was about 1.3m km2 below the 1991-2020 average, a 31% drop. That lost area is roughly the area of France, Italy, Germany, Switzerland and Austria combined. It was the third lowest snow cover since records began in 1983.
Why does reduced air pollution affect temperatures?
Air pollution kills millions of people globally every year and so Europe’s record of cutting toxic air levels in recent decades is unequivocally a good thing. However, cleaner air is also unmasking the impact of the rise in carbon dioxide pollution in the atmosphere.
Air pollution particles can reflect the sun’s rays, directly or by seeding the formation of clouds, meaning the heat does not reach the ground. Fewer particles means less reflection and more heat that is trapped by greenhouse gases. Lower pollution might even be connected to the increase in blocking weather patterns.
How important is each of the four factors above?
The short answer is that scientists don’t yet know, but they aim to have an estimate next year.
Burgess said: “What we can say is that the importance of each factor must vary with season, with proximity to the Arctic important in autumn and winter, and circulation changes since the late 1970s of greater statistical significance in summer.”
The drop in air pollution is most marked in winter because of declining coal heating in homes, and snow cover is a winter issue. Winter warming in Europe in recent decades has been strongest in the north, while summer warming has been strongest in the south-east.
What are the consequences?
The rapid heating is leading to ever more deaths and more intense wildfires and droughts. Storms, intense rainfall and floods are also being supercharged by the extra heat in the climate system. All deeply affect lives and livelihoods across the continent and will continue to worsen until emissions reach net zero. Rapid cuts in CO2 pollution and the rollout of measures to protect citizens are urgently needed.
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, said in late July: “The awful costs of this climate crisis – both human and economic – are now reaching national emergency levels. What needs to be done is clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people.”
The Guardian’s climate forum 2026: On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts, including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman, for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book tickets here or at guardian.live

Paid police paternity leave to double after fathers reported being ‘ostracised’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:00:22 UTC
15:00:22 KST

Paid paternity leave for police in England and Wales is to double, after the Guardian revealed last year that officers were “mocked and ostracised” for taking time off to spend with their babies.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has increased the amount of paid parental and adoption leave for officers from one week to two across all forces, with fathers’ leave upped to be in line with mothers’.
Before the change, only a quarter of forces offered two weeks’ full pay, with others offering one week on full pay and the second week on statutory pay. This resulted in only 40% of officers in the latter group taking the second week’s leave, compared with 88% of those in the first group. Civilian staff in the Metropolitan police were entitled to three weeks’ paternity leave at full pay.
The policing minister Sarah Jones said: “Police officers work tirelessly to protect the public, so it is right that new fathers are better supported to spend time with their families. By expanding police paternity leave, we are recognising the importance of family life.”
The government is now coming under increased pressure to improve paternity leave across the public sector, which campaigners argue offers poor and patchy leave for fathers. The win for police officers has galvanised a campaign for better paternity leave for military fathers, with the Conservative peer Joanna Penn tabling an amendment to the armed forces bill that would triple paternity leave to six weeks for serving personnel.
The government-led tri-forces survey last year found that nearly 30% of families in the armed forces were separated for more than three months in the last year. A survey of 450 serving parents by the campaign group The Dad Shift found that more than 95% agreed the current paternity offer was not enough.
“We ask so much of our military families,” said Penn. “The least we can do is give new fathers the chance to properly support their partners and bond with their babies.”
Campaigners, backed by MPs on the women and equalities select committee, are pushing for a change to give fathers six weeks of paternity leave at 90% of pay. The UK’s statutory paternity leave of two weeks, paid at £184.03 a week, is one of the worst in Europe. Recent research found one in three UK fathers took no paternity leave after the birth of their child. An 18-month government review of the UK’s parental leave system is expected to report in December.
Joel Brady, a police inspector who was part of the campaign, said the policy change would give thousands of fathers in the police more “precious time” with their babies. “This is a massively positive step and great news for policing fathers who want to be there for their partners and involved in their children’s lives,” he said. “I’m optimistic that the government will now listen to dads and increase the amount of leave available to all of us.”
More than 20 organisations – including a new group of Labour MPs that has been lobbying ministers to improve rights for fathers – have written to Andy Burnham urging him to commit to the men and boys’ agenda, which gathered pace under Keir Starmer.
In November, the government launched the first men’s health strategy for England, and Starmer assigned the then deputy prime minister, David Lammy, to lead work across the government to improve outcomes for men and boys. Writing to the new prime minister, the group said: “Taken together, these developments represent something more significant than a series of individual policies. They represent the beginning of a new consensus: one that rejects the false choice between supporting men and supporting women.”
George Gabriel, a co-founder of The Dad Shift, said: “Times are changing. This is the most active generation of dads there’s ever been and momentum is clearly building across the public sector for better paternity leave.
“If Andy Burnham wants to prove his is a cost of living government then, as their review of parental leave concludes later this year, we hope they’ll get alongside working families at one of the moments that matters the most.”

====================================================================================================

Nigel Farage looks trapped and rattled - now the nationalist tide can be turned | Rafael Behr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:00:22 UTC
15:00:22 KST

Nigel Farage can be confident of victory against a man posing as an ennobled space traveller with a dustbin on his head. At least, in Clacton he can.
The refusal of major parties to contest this week’s byelection sets the bar low. But even if the competition were more serious than Count Binface, the Reform UK leader would be the favourite to win on his chosen turf. He picked the constituency as his safest shot for a parliamentary seat in the 2024 general election for a reason. Now he is betting that the stench of scandal around his personal and party finances, pungent in Westminster, won’t sicken his fans on the Essex coast.
He’s probably right, which is why Labour and the Conservatives sensibly denied him the spectacle he craved – a “people versus the establishment” prize fight. The plan was to put the question of his failure to declare a £5m donation to the electoral court of Clacton. It would be settled not by adjudication of the parliamentary standards authority but with a knockout blow from the fist of Furious Farage.
Unfortunately for the crypto-billionaires’ champion, the investigation hasn’t disappeared and could resume if he wins his pantomime bout with a bin.
If a subsequent decision goes against him, a second byelection could follow. That twist could easily be written into Farage’s script as further proof that the system was rigged against him; that the acclamation of his innocence by his loyal Essex jury was not sufficient and they must vindicate him again, louder.
The shape of the argument is textbook populism. A candidate’s virtue is measured by the volume of clamour he can summon from a crowd. Institutions of established democracy are valued only as ladders aiding his ascent. If they hold him accountable in any way, they are dismissed as tools of the elite that conspires against the will of the people.
It is a sign of vulnerability that Farage’s definition of “the people” has shrunk to whatever portion of Clacton constituents turns out for him on Thursday. When his cause was Brexit, he could wield a national referendum mandate to denigrate dissent. When opinion polls and council ballots showed Reform on course to win a general election, the party leader had a putative prime ministerial swagger in his step. He has slipped.
For now, Reform strategists are not too anxious about losing their headline lead to Labour. Second place, after a period of unusually hostile media coverage, while a new Downing Street regime enjoys a (probably brief) honeymoon is not a calamitous position. It could be proof of resilience as much as weakness. More worrying for Farage are his tanking personal ratings and evidence from recent Greater Manchester byelections (two for parliamentary seats; one for the mayoralty vacated by Andy Burnham) that aversion to Reform is coalescing into an effective tactical bloc vote.
That sentiment is resolute. Farage has been a prominent British public figure for two decades. People who see his multiple, rebranded parties as one metastatic malignancy in the body politic are not open to persuasion that he can be something more benign. He used to curate his brand with feinted moderation. That is harder now that Reform faces competition from Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party in the far-right zone where hostility to immigrants dispenses with non-racist euphemism.
Lowe is more anchor of a social media channel than leader of a party. He harvests clicks in the field of digital paranoia, irrigated by extreme content on Elon Musk’s X platform, where it is axiomatic that “indigenous” Europeans face systematic replacement in their homelands by dark-skinned aliens.
Restore took almost 9% of the vote in the first round of the Manchester mayoral byelection, ahead of the Tories and Liberal Democrats. Lowe, elected to parliament in 2024 as a Reform MP, has offered to form an alliance with his old party, but with conditions attached, including the insistence that Tory defectors be barred from any future role in government.
A less-rattled Farage would heap derision on his former comrade. He might even have exploited the schism to confect a new boundary between “mainstream” and “far” right. He could highlight tonal differences between his and Lowe’s politics and apply them as camouflage of respectability.
That he doesn’t suggests lack of confidence in the loyalty of Reform’s hardcore vote. More disturbingly, it implies openness to the idea that, where immigration is concerned, British politics is not yet maxed-out at the furthest limits of rightward expansion.
The shift is stark enough already. Parliament has passed a new act tightening border control or limiting migrants’ rights every year since 2022. Such assiduous attention to the issue has done nothing to satisfy demands for harsher measures. Nor has it refuted the absurd suggestion that mainstream politics and media, constrained by timorous liberalism, refuse to address a question that has, in reality, dominated the agenda for a generation.
The legislative ratchet is also a rhetorical dial, turning public debate more shrill. The language of invasion, once the metaphorical preserve of extremists, has been normalised. Gangs of masked marauders who go on racist rampages through UK towns are cast as protesters manifesting legitimate concerns. The articulation of their grievance in terms that make foreignness synonymous with parasitic consumption of benefits, criminality and sexual predation goes unchallenged.
Meanwhile, net migration has fallen dramatically from its peak earlier this decade. Instead of welcoming the turning tide, the anti-immigrant right has shifted its focus from resisting new arrivals to undermining the status of legally settled communities, denying their entitlement to public services, blocking paths to naturalisation and building a case for mass deportations. This used to be the stuff of skinhead rallies and crank byelection candidates who lost their deposits. Now resistance depends on the guy with the bin on his head. Or at least, in Clacton it does.
Elsewhere the picture is less bleak. Farage retreated to his coastal haven for an electoral comfort break, getting relief from scrutiny in a place where he can still enjoy unchallenged status as the man of the people. But his people are fewer than they were and never as many as he claims. If he has hit the ceiling of his national support and feels part of his base wobbling beneath him, he will try to consolidate by further radicalisation. That will then give more urgency to the anti-Reform voter coalition.
He is trapped. But only if other parties refuse to follow him a single step further down the road to ethno-nationalism, where immigration policy degenerates into sinister fantasies of demographic engineering, and instead push back.
It isn’t a hard choice. There are many more people in Britain who like to live happily alongside their neighbours, regardless of skin colour and country of origin, than want to burn them out of their homes. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to draw a line between rigorous migration control and racist demagoguery.
There were good reasons for major parties to sit out this Thursday’s byelection. But from Friday onwards, the task of fighting Farage can’t be delegated to a man with a bin on his head. Not even in Clacton.
- 
  Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

====================================================================================================

‘It’s been a revelation’: how heat pumps can cool your home in a heatwave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:00:21 UTC
15:00:21 KST

“If it is 35C outdoors, I can get the temperature down to 21C,” says Andrew Ingram of the sanctuary that his living room has provided this summer.
“On the nights I’ve slept in there, you have to put your thick pyjamas on,” jokes Ingram, who lives in Maidenhead, Berkshire, with his wife, Sue.
“When I post on Facebook about it, people say: ‘That’s air conditioning’ and I say: ‘No, it’s the heat pump.’ It’s just working the other way around.”
Rather than generating heat from burning fuel, a heat pump transfers heat energy from one place to another. However, despite the name, heat pumps can be used for cooling, too.
The energy is released through an “emitter” such as a radiator or underfloor heating. The Ingrams have an air source heat pump. It extracts heat from the air outside and uses it to warm the radiators of their three-bedroom house (this is called an air-to-water system).
In 2023, when the Ingrams ripped out their gas boiler, the firm suggested they consider whether they wanted to cool any rooms.
“We thought about it because the sitting room gets really hot, and that’s the room we spend time in,” Ingram says.
“It’s been a revelation. We bought it on the basis that there might be a heatwave, and it’s been an absolute lifeline this year.
“You know those times when you are really feeling exhausted and want to sit somewhere cool. We turn it right down and then let the temperature drift back up again.”
The couple have radiators throughout but the living room also has another “emitter” – called a fan coil unit. This is an appliance that blows air over hot or cold pipes. The whole new home energy system cost roughly £18,600, with the cooling aspect accounting for £1,700 of that.
“If you’re pumping cool water around a property, it’s a bit like putting cool beer in a glass on a warm day,” says Ingram of what is potentially one of the pitfalls of cooling this way.
“You get loads of condensation, so you either have to wrap pipes in quite sophisticated trunking or do what we did, which is have them outside.
“We used the cooling a bit in 2024, and, guess what, in 2025 even more – and in 2026 we’ve been a rather popular place for people to visit.”
The government’s boiler upgrade scheme offers grants of £7,500 to assist homeowners in England and Wales with the cost of installing an air-to-water or ground-to-water system (a heat pump that extracts heat from the ground through buried pipes).
Households not connected to the gas grid qualify for an additional £1,500 in support, increasing the grant to £9,000.
If you live in Scotland, you may be able to get an interest-free loan or a grant to make your home more energy efficient.
To qualify for funding, the heat pump must be certified through the Microgeneration Certification Scheme, which certifies installers.
Previously heat pumps that also cooled required planning permission, as the permitted development rights rules (legal permissions that allow certain home improvements without a planning application) stated they had to be solely for heating. The PDR has now been updated to allow cooling.
To date, Britons have mostly installed air-to-water systems, and of the UK’s 358,000 heat pumps, approximately 323,000 are this type, according to MCS data.
This could be about to change because the government is to offer £2,500 grants for air conditioning units that can heat and cool. The air-to-air heat pumps move heat using wall-mounted fans and cost about £4,500 to fit in a flat or small house. (Air-to-water heat pumps typically cost in the region of £12,000.)
The run of heatwaves has thrown the spotlight on “heat-trap homes”. A recent report by the Climate Change Committee said that hotter heatwaves could lead to 92% of existing homes overheating by 2050 and they may require air conditioning, as passive measures such as drawing curtains and opening windows are unlikely to be enough.
A recent study conducted in the Energy House 2.0 – a £16m climate-controlled chamber at the University of Salford – found that using a heat pump for cooling can “significantly reduce overheating” in modern homes.
Two new modern houses have been built inside the weather simulation facility so that scientists can test how “real” homes perform under extreme conditions.
The Salford scientists paired a heat pump with fan coils in one of the houses. When the lab weather was 32C, the rooms stayed comfortable – between 19C and 24.9C. With the heat pump running around the clock, the cost was £2.50-£3 a day.
Prof Lubo Jankovic, the scientist leading the research, says the results “demonstrate that reversible heat pumps can play an important role in protecting future homes against overheating”.
But Jankovic says the challenge of designing systems with both heating and cooling in mind “needs to be addressed before cooling this way becomes mainstream”.
With the October price cap predicted to exceed £1,700 a year for a typical dual fuel bill, the big question for many is: will a heat pump save me money?
A recent poll by the consumer group Which? revealed growing consumer interest in heat pumps, but also that they were a “high-stakes gamble” owing to their unfamiliarity, high upfront costs and uncertain impact on bills.
One way to get a better understanding is to look round a home with one and quiz the owner. The charity Nesta runs the “visit a heat pump” scheme, which offers tours of more than 1,200 homes, including the Ingrams’.
When it comes to bills, the Energy Saving Trust says the biggest saving comes in homes that switch to a dedicated heat pump energy tariff and add other green technologies such as solar panels.
The tariff is vital because heat pumps run on electricity, which is generally more expensive per unit than gas. On a standard tariff, this can lead to substantial energy bills, negating some of the efficiency benefits.
Heat pump users moving on to a time-of-use tariff can save about £330 a year compared with sitting on a flat-rate tariff, the trust says. This rises to about £800 with extras such as solar, although these add to the upfront costs.
The Ingrams have solar panels and a home battery to help keep their bills down. “There’s lots of juice in the batteries from the solar,” Ingram says. “The batteries charge up overnight if they’re not full, but they have been recently. So if you want to run the pump, it is running on free or very cheap electricity.”
