Katendrecht: Rotterdam’s sailors’ quarter reinvented as cultural hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

Why go now?
A thin peninsula just south of Rotterdam’s centre, Katendrecht was once at the heart of the world’s busiest port, home to continental Europe’s first Chinatown and a lively sailors’ quarter. Its later reputation as a red light district has been shrugged off – part of the city’s wider reinvention in the aftermath of extensive second world war bombing.
Still Europe’s largest port, Rotterdam’s maritime history is very much evident today, with the former headquarters of the Holland-America Line now a hotel just a short hop across the Rijnhaven Bridge. The 2012 opening of this pedestrian and bicycle bridge finally connected cut-off Katendrecht to Wilhelminapier, which was a jumping off point for transatlantic migration, and is today a major cruise terminal, with more than 100 ships departing every year.
The opening of the Fenix museum of migration last year and the reopening of the Nederlands Fotomuseum in a new location here in February have accelerated Katendrecht’s rise in status, following on from the entrepreneurs and creatives who have introduced craft breweries, food halls and design boutiques in recent years.
Former warehouses have been transformed – into the aforementioned museums among other venues – and a lively cultural and arts scene has grown as the neighbourhood has seen new residents rediscover the formerly downtrodden area.
With more big construction projects under way, Katendrecht will be transformed further over the next five years, with apartments, shops, a five-star hotel, an urban beach and, notably, the Rotterdam Centre for Dance, Danshuis, on the horizon.
Where to eat and drink
Deliplein is the place to begin – the tree-lined square lies at the heart of the old sailors’ quarter and houses more than 20 restaurants and bars. Originally home to the first Chinese restaurant in the Netherlands, Delistraat is buzzing from morning to night.
Start at Jordy’s Bakery, where flaky pastries, vegan muffins, sourdough sandwiches and speciality coffees will fuel you for the morning. Across the road in the Fenix atrium, O: Anatolian Café is run by the Michelin-starred chef Maksut Aşkar; on the menu are all-day Turkish breakfasts, meze platters, sandwiches and salads at extremely reasonable prices.
Kaapse Brouwers in the Fenix Food Factory is where the post-work crowd heads. Sit on the terrace, admire the waterfront view and explore its range of more than 20 craft beers on tap – from Belgian blonds and New England IPAs to pilsners and sours. And back on Delistraat, Café de Ouwehoer is a classic old-style pub with a nod to the area’s past – and a huge range of whiskeys to boot.
A few doors down, finish your evening at the small but perfectly formed fine-dining establishment De Matroos en Het Meisje (The Sailor and the Girl), which offers a changing daily menu. With the option of choosing from four to six courses, dependent on season and produce, dishes could be charred carrot, cured Japanese fish, creme fraiche and onion, or chicken breast with mushroom beurre blanc, blackberries and crisped rice.
Cultural experiences
Fenix is the obvious first stop. Funded by the philanthropic foundation Droom en Daad (Dream and Do), the museum of immigration opened last May in a renovated historic warehouse and finally gave Katendrecht a real focal point for visitors.
Formerly part of the world’s largest warehouse for cargo transfer, the museum reflects the fact that millions of migrants arrived at and departed from the port in search of a new life. At its heart is the Tornado, a spectacular mirrored spiral staircase, which offers 360-degree views across the neighbourhood, docks and the city. It symbolises the central theme, with architect Ma Yansong describing it as “a metaphor for the journeys of migrants”.
The industrial space is used sparingly to display photography, art and sculpture that communicate the experience of immigration, movement and displacement of peoples. It’s humbling and moving. The exhibition All Directions features more than 100 artists, with stories of the war in Kyiv and refugee camps in Tunisia, Jordan and Lebanon, as well as a lifesize New York bus made from fabric.
The Family of Migrants exhibition showcases more than 200 photos from around the world, depicting the story of migration from the late 19th century to the present day. And the Suitcase Labyrinth has about 2,000 donated cases, dating from 1898 to today, with 30 audio stories detailing the unique past of some of them.
Farther down the waterfront, the newly opened Nederlands Fotomuseum is also in a renovated warehouse – formerly used to store coffee from Brazil – and is topped with a modern anodised aluminium structure. Inside, the exposed brick, rough-edged concrete and steel girders offer a striking contrast to the impressive photography on display.
The original museum opened in 2003, and the collection now comprises more than six million negatives, transparencies, prints, photo albums and other archival matter – visitors are encouraged to look in the depots and studios. Every week, thousands of images are digitised and made available online, while old and damaged photography is conserved and restored.
On the first floor, the Gallery of Honour of Dutch Photography showcases 99 distinguished photographs, selected by a group of experts, spanning 1842 to the digital era. And as you go up the central staircase, which leads all the way to the rooftop restaurant, a mosaic of projected images merely hints at the breadth and depth of photography in storage.
Where to shop
In the Bay House development, close to the Nederlands Fotomuseum, there are a number of designer fashion and vintage furniture stores. Selected With Love has “upcycled” clothing, Caesar sells designer menswear, while The Gallery by Collectors Network is a space for numerous independent dealers selling vintage design pieces – Vintage Hoarder, for example, has 1980s Belgian floor lamps, a 1970s French slate table and 1960s Italian dining chairs.
The museum shops offer the best range of unique purchases. Fenix has items created in collaboration with artists and designers as well as chocolates from Rotterdam, slippers from Greece and tea from small family-run plantations in China.
Don’t miss
Verhalenhuis Belvédère is perhaps the best place to get a sense of where Katendrecht has come from. Dating from 1894, the building was originally a cafe then a jazz club – saved from demolition, it became a cultural centre, community hub and exhibition space in 2009.
As part of its cultural programmes, community meals and storytelling events, Belvédère collects and shares the stories of Rotterdam residents, from the first Cape Verdean migrants to Jewish families and Chinese seafarers.
Where to stay
Of Hotel New York’s 72 rooms, the suites in the former offices of the Holland-America Line’s directors, overlooking the Nieuwe Maas river, and the two tower rooms are the ones to book. Rooms from €110.
On the western tip of Katendrecht, the former cruise ship SS Rotterdam is permanently moored and is now a 254-room hotel that retains much of its original styling, with wood panelling throughout, and the public spaces – bars, restaurants, theatre – are like stepping back in time. Tours are available. Rooms from €73. The five-star Eurostars hotel is expected to open in the autumn, next door to the Nederlands Fotomuseum and right by the Rijnhaven metro station, which connects easily to Rotterdam Centraal train station.
The trip was hosted by the Netherlands Board of Tourism & Conventions

Gallery: Touch, memory at the core of Finnish-Estonian duo's Tallinn show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:59:00 UTC
14:59:00 KST

Gallery: Touch, memory at the core of Finnish-Estonian duo's Tallinn show
A new exhibition at Tallinn's Foku Gallery brings together Finland's Hilla Kurki and Estonia's Taavi Rekkaro to explore memory, history, touch and how we relate to images.
In their new joint show, "Something That Should Be Felt," the artists examine how people relate to images and how memories shape experiences of closeness and presence. Their work moves beyond traditional two-dimensional images toward more spatial forms.
Kurki's "Clay Diaries" series draws on her family history as she seeks new ways to relate to tradition and heritage. Her photographs depict people alongside plants and other living beings that are reborn each season seemingly unchanged.
By inviting a range of fellow artists to visit her great-grandparents' house, she creates a living archive through shared moments where friendship can become the main outcome of the work, not just its subject.
'How can we be sure these moments really happened?'
Rekkaro presents photographs and objects that rethink photography as something to be touched, and where closeness becomes part of the experience.
The images capture fleeting moments, inner uncertainties and attempts to understand oneself and one's relationships with others, while the gallery wall features a melting moment composed of works dating back to 2023, inviting viewers to slow down and build their own narratives instead of telling a single, fixed story.
Exploring the connections between memory, body and self-perception, the artist asks: "How can we be sure that we were truly there, that these moments really happened?"
"Something That Should Be Felt" will remain open at Foku Gallery through September 26.

Colombia: Rescuers search for survivors after 7.6 magnitude earthquake kills 216 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:58:55 UTC
14:58:55 KST

As rescuers search through the rubble for survivors, volunteers join to help clear the wreckage. People brought water and food to the victimes and lined up in front of blood donation centres.
Colombian rescuers pulled a 32-year-old woman alive from the rubble of a collapsed building Tuesday, sparking cheers and applause as exhausted crews raced to find more survivors from the country's strongest earthquake in a century.
Daniela Largo was carried from the wreckage wrapped in a blue blanket as rescuers embraced her and relatives shouted out with joy.
Soldiers, firefighters and volunteers continued to scour collapsed buildings across western Colombia after Monday's 7.4-magnitude quake.
Authorities revised the death toll down to 216 after local officials in Cali corrected earlier figures.
"We were losing hope and then we received a call," said her mother Sandra Milena Perez in Pereira.
Perez said a local resident heard cries for help beneath the rubble and joined neighbors in removing debris before professional rescuers arrived.
"Thanks to him, today we're happy," she said. "At home, her 12-year-old son is waiting for her."
A spark of solidarity
In Pereira and in Cali, emergency crews used cranes, dogs, and heavy machinery to search ruined buildings while volunteers formed human chains to clear debris by hand, hoping to reach people still trapped beneath collapsed structures.
As darkness fell, families prepared to sleep in parks as aftershocks rattled damaged neighborhoods where entire blocks had been reduced to rubble.
The quake overwhelmed parts of the health system, turning the rescue effort into one of Colombia's largest disaster responses in years.
"The house came down on top of us. I wasn't able to get out," said Beatriz Arcos, who was trapped with her husband and mother beneath their collapsed condominium.
"It took about an hour to get us out," Arcos said. She was hospitalized after a concrete block fell on her back. Her husband and mother were also injured.
In Cali, residents armed with picks, shovels and their bare hands joined firefighters in digging through collapsed buildings.
Rescuers stopped every few minutes to call into the rubble and listen for any response.
"We're doing this with our hands, with gloves," said volunteer Pablo Cesar Ruiz. "It's sad to see time slipping away."
In Pereira, army units and sniffer dogs combed through twisted concrete and exposed steel.
Desperate search
For many families, the desperate search was becoming a vigil.
"My aunt lived there. She's under the rubble," said Jorge Gonzalez, standing beside a collapsed building in Pereira. "I arrived yesterday and I haven't left, and until they find her body I don't intend to leave here."
While some families waited for news of missing relatives, others were grappling with the loss of homes, possessions and livelihoods.
"We lost everything," said Stella Galvis, fighting back tears after escaping the collapse of her home. "We survived by a miracle, since I managed to get my little boy out and my partner managed to get out too."
From the air, neighborhoods in Cali appeared flattened, with piles of grey rubble replacing entire blocks of homes and apartment buildings. Nearby, cars lay crushed beneath fallen walls and concrete slabs.
Many survivors spent the night outdoors, either because their homes were damaged or because they feared aftershocks.
One park in Pereira was transformed into a makeshift shelter with tents and mattresses.
"We lost everything, but we're alive," said 23-year-old John Tabasco, who was camped there with his wife and seven-month-old son.
"We've never had to do this before, to depend on someone else to help us. It's amazing how life can change."
Destroyed homes
Others struggled to come to terms with losing homes built over decades.
"You buy a little house with so much effort, spending 40, 50 years struggling to get yourself that house, you finally get it and in just a few days it all goes down the drain," said 79-year-old Jaime Alzate.
In Cali, part of the Hospital Universitario del Valle collapsed during the quake, forcing doctors to move patients into a parking lot and treat some in the open air.
Yet amid the destruction, many Colombians mobilized to help. Thousands brought water, food and supplies to affected neighborhoods, while long lines formed outside blood donation centers.
"It's about wanting to help your community, your city and your country," said blood donor Ferney Cabrera.
President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a state of emergency and promised rent subsidies for affected families Tuesday during a visit to Pereira.
The United States announced $15.5 million (€13.4 million) in emergency aid, while messages of support and offers of assistance arrived from around the world.
As aftershocks continued to rattle damaged cities, rescue crews pressed on through the ruins, hoping more voices, taps or whistles might still emerge.

Trump and the plane change: Everything was decided by the Secret Service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:58:33 UTC
14:58:33 KST

The Washington Post reported on the 10th of August that US President Donald Trump changed planes before taking off from a NATO summit in Turkey in July, writes Politico.
Trump denied on the 11th of August that he was involved in planning the dramatic and secret plane change when he left the NATO summit in early July. It is reported that most of the passengers who remained on the first plane did not realize that Trump had left and gone to another plane. The US president told reporters that the action depends solely on the Secret Service, and he himself is just following what the service tells him to do.
The covert operation, first reported by the Washington Post, involved Trump discreetly leaving Air Force One and being transported by airport shuttle to a smaller military plane that initially flew him to London. The transfer took place after Trump boarded a regular U.S. government plane in front of the media. The reporters and many of the administration officials on board were unaware that they were serving as decoys.
At the time, Trump insisted he would fly Air Force One, not the Boeing 747-800 donated by Qatar (which he had flown in to Ankara), “for old times’ sake.” The media report later suggested that the Secret Service had learned of the potential threat from Iran and had decided to switch Trump’s planes. The flight out of Ankara came just a day after the U.S. resumed strikes on Iran after the truce collapsed. After checking in to the UK, Trump boarded Air Force One again and officially disembarked.
The Washington Post has not been able to determine how the planes were switched upon arrival.
Trump did not elaborate on the security threat that prompted the plane switch, and told reporters that he did not ask unnecessary questions.
The White House Correspondents’ Association said on the 11th of August that it had raised concerns with the administration about how the ruse had affected journalists’ ability to report on the president’s movements and also posed risks to their safety. Trump, meanwhile, said that the plane he was on was certainly more at risk because the enemy would have targeted it.
The initial decision to switch the Qatari-donated plane for Air Force One raised questions about the safety of the newer plane. The Trump administration subpoenaed The New York Times journalists for discussions regarding the publication’s safety, but withdrew its demands after the publication went to court.

'We're not asking for an easy life': The three key issues at the heart of Australia's 'polycrisis'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:58:17 UTC
14:58:17 KST

IN BRIEF
- Experts say housing insecurity and climate fears are compounding young Australians' uncertainty about their future.
- Young people's belief they can create change improved after the 2025 federal election, a recent report found.
For 24-year-old Sophie Blach, the future feels increasingly difficult to plan.
Working full-time hours in retail and hospitality while undertaking her degree, she said she has been forced to return to her Brisbane family home while she tries to save a deposit to eventually buy a property.
But rising everyday costs mean saving is difficult, leaving her feeling as though the traditional path into adulthood is becoming increasingly out of reach.
"I feel like I'm doing everything you're told you're supposed to do. I'm working, I'm studying, I'm saving when I can," she told SBS News.
"But I wouldn't say my goals feel in reach."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Young Australians are struggling to plan for the future
Sophie's experience reflects a broader trend identified in a new five-year analysis of the Australian Youth Barometer.
The Monash Centre for Youth Policy and Education Practice has tracked more than 2,700 Australians aged 18 to 24 since 2021, examining their experiences across work, education, housing, wellbeing, relationships and civic participation.
Its latest report describes young Australians as living through a "polycrisis" of overlapping economic, social, environmental and political pressures that compound one another.
Affordable housing was the biggest issue young people flagged as needing urgent action, rising from 60 per cent in 2022 to 82 per cent in 2025.
Also recognised as needing urgent action was employment opportunities, which rose from 48 in 2022 to 64 per cent in 2025. Climate change was identified as an issue needing urgent action by 44 per cent in 2025, falling from 47 per cent in 2022.
Monash University professor Lucas Walsh, the report's lead author, says the significance of the findings is in how those issues connect.
"These are all embedded within the idea of a polycrisis, which involves overlapping independent events in crisis that intersect and amplify each other," he told SBS News.
Walsh said the study started tracking young Australians at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, providing a five-year window into how their lives and priorities have changed as the country moved through and beyond it.
He describes the pandemic as a "flash of light into more persistent problems" which exposed pressures that were already disproportionately affecting young people.
For Sophie, housing uncertainty isn't isolated from the rest of her life.
Housing and financial pressure are compounding
"I don't necessarily expect to own a house tomorrow, but I would like to feel like it's something I could realistically work towards. It can be discouraging to feel like the goalposts for how much I need to have saved, how much I need to be earning or even spending to get a home keeps changing," she said.
Wendy Stone, a professor of housing and social policy at Swinburne University, told SBS News that secure housing provides the foundation that young people need to establish independence, work, study and relationships.
But she said Australia's housing system is increasingly failing to provide that security, which can affect whether young people can sustain employment or education and even their ability to plan ahead.
"The affordability problem compounds other parts of our system's structural challenges for young people," stone said.
"One of the things that we do know is that the earlier you can get into a secure housing situation, the more likely you are to be able to pursue your education, your employment and your relationships in a way that is sustainable."
Stone said governments need to treat secure, affordable housing as an investment in young people, rather than relying on increased housing supply alone.
She points to targeted housing subsidies for young people undertaking study or training, alongside stronger protections and incentives for long-term renting.
The pressures are also being felt in young people's mental health, with the Barometer finding 99 per cent of the young Australians surveyed reported at least one feeling of anxiety or pessimism in 2025.
Meanwhile, the proportion who sought and received mental-health support fell from 31 per cent in 2021 to 23 per cent in 2025.
Professor of psychiatry Ian Hickie said much of the distress being experienced by young people is connected to practical pressures in their everyday lives.
"A lot of distress is being expressed by young people at the moment has to do with these broader sets of issues that are confronting them on a daily basis," he said.
He said solutions need to be practical measures, from reducing transport costs and providing rental assistance to improving access to health and other essential services.
Climate change adding another layer
Sydney University research fellow Scarlett Smout said young people can feel particularly powerless because they have been "failed by generations preceding them" and now feel they have inherited a problem they have little individual power to solve.
She told SBS News that effective solutions need to create connection and agency, including better access to nature, public transport and community spaces, while making clear that responsibility cannot rest on individuals alone.
"Seeing the government address climate change as a matter of inter-generational inequality but also inter-generational fairness … would hopefully provide some assurance to young people that this matter is being taken seriously and not just the can being kicked down the road."
For Sophie, her concerns can feel inseparable.
"I don't think we're asking for an easy life. We just want to believe that if we work hard, we'll have some control over what happens next," she said.
"In my parents' generation it was more simple, so I didn't think I would be making all these sacrifices and doing all the right things and still not have any reprieve or certainty over what my future will look like. It's demotivating."
Walsh urged governments to respond to these overlapping issues by breaking down siloed policy approaches and, crucially, giving young people a meaningful role in shaping the policies that affect them.
Bleak but not hopeless
The Barometer also found that young people's belief that change is possible improved following the 2025 federal election.
But for Sophie, that hope remains conditional.
"I recognise the privilege we have here in Australia and I do believe there are ways to fix the problems people in my generation are concerned about," she said.
"I try to stay optimistic; it would just help if there was a bit more to be hopeful about, or if it felt like my generation's concerns were actually being prioritised or even considered."

North Korea fires ballistic missile ahead of US-South drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:56:06 UTC
14:56:06 KST

North Korea fired a ballistic missile off its east coast towards Japan early on Aug. 12, Seoul's military said, days before the planned start of massive U.S.-South Korea joint drills.
The 11-day exercises due to begin on Monday are a regular fixture of the summer calendar, designed to steel the United States and South Korea for defence against the nuclear-armed North.
Pyongyang calls them rehearsals for an invasion and has staged missile launches before and after them in the past.
"Our military detected at around 6:00 am (2100 GMT on Tuesday) a ballistic missile launched by North Korea from the Wonsan area towards the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a message to reporters.
The missile flew more than 700 kilometres (435 miles) over the body of water — also known as the Sea of Japan — it said, adding that Seoul and Washington were analysing its specifications.
Japan's defence ministry also described the object as a suspected ballistic missile, adding that it was thought to have "already fallen", without providing further details.
"North Korea has never simply let a South Korea-U.S. joint military exercise pass without a response," Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
"This is a message that Pyongyang is closely watching the upcoming drills and could stage a provocation if it deems one necessary."
Japan's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi called Wednesday's launch a "threat to peace and security in our region" and said Tokyo had "lodged a strong protest" with North Korea through diplomatic channels in Beijing.
North Korea has recently been hurling criticism at Japan, a former regional colonial power, over what Pyongyang describes as its remilitarisation.
Japan has long held a pacifist stance, but has been increasing military spending, ramping up defence pacts and deploying missile launchers to its outer islands.
Koizumi said last week that Japan needed to boost its military with a "sense of urgency and crisis".
Pyongyang lambasted Japan's "transformation into a war state", and shortly afterwards fired a short-range ballistic missile off its eastern coast, according to Seoul's military.
South Korea's national security office convened an emergency meeting on Wednesday, where participants called recent launches "provocative acts" and demanded Pyongyang "immediately halt them".
North Korea has been playing a more active role in international conflict, notably backing Russia in its invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine accused Russia on Tuesday of launching North Korean missiles in an attack that killed 10 and wounded dozens.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also warned — without providing evidence — that Moscow has been receiving more ballistic projectiles and troops from Pyongyang.
Experts say North Korea has received financial and military benefits from Moscow in return for its support.
Its troops have also gained crucial experience on modern battlefields.
The U.S.-South Korea "Ulchi Freedom Shield" drills due on Monday will include 18,000 South Korean troops and counterparts from the U.S. contingent of 28,500 in the country.
A spokesman said they will prepare soldiers for a potential fight against North Korean troops battle-hardened from deployment in Europe.
North Korean soldiers have "taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea," said Colonel Ryan Donald, spokesman for the U.S. and South Korean Combined Forces Command, on Monday.
"Our training accounts for that threat," he told reporters.

UK extreme heat prompts Cobra emergency meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:55:32 UTC
14:55:32 KST

Andy Burnham will chair an emergency Cobra meeting in response to the extreme heat, which has caused wildfires and plunged many parts of Britain into drought.
The prime minister will meet ministers, officials and agencies as high temperatures continue across the UK, with 33C forecast on Wednesday and up to 38C on Thursday.
A No 10 spokesperson said the government understood that firefighters, farmers and NHS staff were all facing challenges connected to the weather.
It will be the second Cobra meeting this year on heatwaves, after one took place amid high temperatures in June. It comes as parts of the country face their fifth heatwave this summer and the number of days reaching 30C in any year in the UK hits a new record at 35 days so far, beating the 34 days set in 1995, according to the Met Office.
The climate breakdown has been linked to the increasing frequency of wildfires, burning larger areas, across many parts of the world. The “fire wave” under way in the UK is the most widespread on record, with the combination of wet winters and prolonged heatwaves exacerbating the risk.
Speaking before the Cobra meeting, Burnham raised the idea of a possible ban on disposable barbecues, which are a known fire risk. “There is obviously a significant problem of wildfires in the south,” Burnham said during a visit to a community centre in Stevenage. “Many of them have been created by disposable barbecues.”
He continued: “I do believe we need to get the message out loud and clear. People should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time.
“I don’t know yet what the remedy is, but I do want to leave the meeting today with a loud and clear message that we do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires.”
Some Labour MPs will be keen to see more ambitious ideas emerge from the meeting, amid concern that the UK is lagging when it comes to immediate policies to adapt to a changing climate. “Adaptation has always been the poor relation in government,” one MP said. “Look how much better we are at getting energy projects off the ground than reservoirs.”
A No 10 spokesperson said: “The prime minister will chair a meeting of COBR – the government emergency committee – this afternoon on the UK’s ongoing response to extreme heat, wildfires and drought.
“We know how challenging this summer is proving, particularly for firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units. We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment.”
Ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the Department of Health and Social Care, the Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government and the Cabinet Office were expected to attend along with representatives from the Met Office, the Environment Agency and the UK Health Security Agency.
Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green party, said calling the emergency meeting was “only a first step”. He said: “This is a climate emergency which is leading to hundreds of deaths and stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit. What we urgently need is concrete action.
“That must include taxing fossil fuel giants to pay for firefighting helicopters, a cool space in every community, and a maximum working temperature. The prime minister must also commit to no new oil and gas extraction in the North Sea. We cannot negotiate with the science.”
Rare amber “extreme heat” warnings have been issued for London and parts of the south-east, East Midlands, east of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire from 9am to midnight on Thursday.
The government urged the public to pay attention to UK Health Security Agency heat alerts and advised people to drink plenty of fluids and check in on family, friends and neighbours who may be at high risk.
The Met Office chief forecaster Chris Bulmer said: “While the peak heat will be more short-lived than recent heatwaves, temperatures widely into the mid-30sC on Thursday bring the potential for impacts for some, which is why a Met Office warning has been issued.”
On Tuesday, Steve Wright, the general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union (FBU), warned the country faced an “unprecedented summer of dangerous and volatile wildfires”. The National Fire Chiefs Council said firefighters had responded to more than 950 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August alone, while July was the busiest month on record for wildfires with more than 450 incidents.
Nearly three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought, as a record dry July and very dry start to August have combined with high temperatures to put pressure on water resources.
The FBU said that in many parts of the country, firefighters did not have the latest equipment to deal with these “flash droughts”. “They do not have the new modern personal protective equipment, the lightweight fire kit that we wear, the right helmets, lightweight helmets, breathable uniforms to make sure they’re better protected, their health is protected when they’re out dealing with these incidents for hours and hours on end,” Wright told Times Radio.

Hong Kong authorities charge woman who allegedly kept 136 dogs without licences
Agriculture, Conservation and Fisheries Department issues court summons to suspect after conducting raid on Yuen Long shelter
Hong Kong authorities have charged a woman on suspicion of keeping 136 dogs without valid licences at a shelter previously investigated for alleged animal cruelty, the South China Morning Post has learned.
“During the operation, a total of 136 dogs were suspected of being kept without valid licences,” a spokesman said.
Authorities have issued a court summons to the woman, with the case expected to be mentioned in Tuen Mun Court on September 2.
The woman will be prosecuted under the Rabies Ordinance, which mandates that an owner or handler must have a licence for any dog over five months old, to be renewed every three years.
Anyone convicted of keeping an unlicensed dog faces a maximum fine of HK$10,000 (US$1,270).
A source said the suspect and the dog shelter had previously been investigated for alleged animal cruelty.

Chinese automaker Chery buys Nissan plant in Africa as EV production shifts to new markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:53:02 UTC
14:53:02 KST

Chinese automaker Chery buys Nissan plant in Africa as EV production shifts to new markets
NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Chinese automakers are increasingly shifting from exporting vehicles to building them in Africa, betting that rapid urbanization, a growing middle class and supportive government policies will make the continent one of the industry’s last major growth markets.
It’s part of a strategy for coping with slowing demand at home and rising trade barriers in Europe and North America. Analysts say the shift could reshape Africa’s automotive industry by creating jobs, developing local supply chains and accelerating adoption of electric vehicles, although weak infrastructure and policy uncertainty remain significant obstacles.
In July, Chery, China’s largest auto exporter, acquired Nissan’s former Rosslyn plant near Pretoria, South Africa, where it plans to make plug-in hybrids, battery-electric vehicles and models under its Jetour brand.
The move reflects a broader strategy by Chinese automakers to manufacture closer to African consumers rather than rely solely on imports, though the trend is just getting started.
Beijing Automotive Group (BAIC) has an automotive manufacturing and assembly facility in Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth), South Africa, and China’s Great Wall Motor has some localized assembly and component distribution capacity.
“Africa has become known as the next frontier for the automotive market,” said Hiten Parmar, executive director of The Electric Mission, a South African nonprofit promoting sustainable mobility.
Transition to EVs is accelerating in Africa
Analysts say South Africa, Morocco, Kenya, Ethiopia and Ghana are among the countries best positioned to attract Chinese EV investment because of their industrial capacity, supportive policies or growing electricity infrastructure. Morocco also benefits from proximity to European export markets, while Zimbabwe’s large lithium reserves could support battery supply chains.
Local manufacturing could eventually lower vehicle prices by avoiding import duties while stimulating investment in charging infrastructure, component manufacturing and battery production. Africa’s first large-scale battery gigafactory is already planned in Morocco.
Rapid urbanization, rising incomes and the relative affordability of Chinese brands are enabling Chinese automakers to capture markets historically dominated by European, Japanese and American giants.
“Whilst African consumers have been thriving on used cars, the affordability of Asian brands is providing a wider accessibility reach for new vehicles,” Parmar said.
Nick Hedley, an energy transition research analyst at Zero Carbon Analytics, said Africa’s fast-growing population and expanding middle class create a natural market for affordable electric vehicles while helping governments reduce dependence on imported fuel.
“Africa is also a net importer of refined fuels, which drains foreign reserves and weighs on local currencies and budgets,” Hedley said. “Switching to local electric cars for transportation is in African countries’ national interest.”
“As electric vehicles become more cost-competitive, their uptake will accelerate across Africa, and Chinese automakers will benefit,” Hedley said.
The shift is also being driven by changing economics inside China.
Tombo Banda, managing director of CrossBoundary Group, a renewable energy consultancy, said Chinese factories are producing more vehicle s than the domestic market can absorb while exports face mounting barriers.
“Onshoring production on the continent is a sound long-term investment,” Banda said, noting that local manufacturing helps companies navigate tariffs while positioning themselves closer to fast-growing markets.
Governments are aligning transport policies for energy security
A Green Minerals Strategy adopted by the African Union aims to increase domestic processing of critical minerals. That would make more usable raw materials available locally.
Ethiopia has banned imports of fossil fuel-powered vehicles and is encouraging local production by mandating lower import duties on EVs assembled domestically.
South Africa has taken a different approach, using production incentives like customs duty rebates, production-linked credits, direct cash investments, and tax breaks to encourage investment in electric- and hydrogen fueled-vehicle manufacturing.
“This is becoming a notable change in approach from Asian brands, from pure imports, to considerations of assembly and manufacturing,” Parmar said.
Africa is increasingly positioned to become more than just a destination for imported vehicles.
“If Chinese manufacturers want access to these markets, they need to add value locally rather than simply sell into them,” Banda said. “That is what will move Africa from a sales market to a genuine manufacturing base.”
South Africa has a head start
South Africa already has manufacturing capacity, skilled workers and established export markets, Banda said. Purchasing facilities such as the Rosslyn plant can enable automakers to retool existing factories rather than build new ones from scratch.
“Companies can pivot, or enter partnerships, far faster than anyone starting from scratch,” she said.
But she cautioned that converting factories designed for internal combustion engines is complex and requires long-term certainty on taxes, tariffs and industrial policy.
Stable policies are essential, since sudden changes in taxes or regulations can undermine investor confidence. Reliable infrastructure is also vital.
“Without clean, reliable, affordable electricity, forget about operating EVs. Without sufficient, well-located charging, forget about functional EVs,” Banda said.

Shares are mostly higher in Asia, with Kospi up 4%, while oil prices gain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:53:01 UTC
14:53:01 KST

Wall Street flirts with a record after AI stocks jump and worries about inflation ease a bit
NEW YORK (AP) — Wall Street is flirting with a record Wednesday after several AI stocks reported better growth for the spring than analysts expected, while a report showed inflation across the United States was slightly less bad last month.
The S&P 500 added 0.3% and was on track for its first gain since setting its all-time high on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 65 points, or 0.1%, as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.6% higher.
Stocks in the artificial-intelligence technology business helped lead the way after strong profit reports bolstered hopes they can continue to deliver big-enough growth to justify the huge gains their prices have made.
Super Micro Computer, which sells servers and other equipment, jumped 13.7% after reporting earnings per share for the latest quarter that were 84% higher than analysts expected. It also gave forecasts for upcoming profit and revenue that topped analysts’ expectations.
CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, leaped 20.3% after reporting better revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, along with a milder loss. CEO Michael Intrator said demand is accelerating from customers as big businesses adopt AI.
CoreWeave gives its customers access to AI chips from Nvidia, and Nvidia climbed 2% to act as the single strongest forces lifting the S&P 500.
It’s a return to strength for AI stocks, which have been veering on a roller-coaster ride for months. After surging to records, AI stocks came under pressure on worries that they shot too high. Investors wanted to see big spenders on AI prove that their investments are yielding better profits to make them worth it. That in turn could lead to continued demand for chips and other building blocks of AI data centers.
Wall Street also got some broad support from easing yields in the bond market. Treasury yields fell after a report showed that U.S. consumers paid prices for gasoline, groceries and other costs of living last month that were 3.4% higher than a year earlier.
That’s higher than anyone would like, but it’s not as bad as the 3.5% inflation rate of June.
The deceleration could give the Federal Reserve more leeway to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but it would do so by making it more expensive for U.S. households and companies to borrow and forcing a slowdown in the economy. Higher interest rates also would undercut prices for stocks and other investments.
The Fed’s members have been notably split about whether they should have already begun hiking interest rates. But Wednesday’s update on inflation pushed traders to pull back on bets the Fed will hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in September.
Traders are betting on just a 36% chance of it, down from the coin flip’s chance seen the day before, according to data from CME Group.
That helped pull the yield on the 10-year Treasury down to 4.65% from 4.70% late Tuesday. It, though, still remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran, which sent oil prices and worries about inflation spiking.
Oil prices edged lower on Wednesday, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.5% to $88.48.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia.
South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.7% for one of the world’s bigger gains. It’s been at the center of the jarring swings for AI stocks because it’s dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

Chinese meteorological satellites track Typhoon Dolphin in coordinated observation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:52:13 CST
14:52:13 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- China's Fengyun meteorological satellites, developed by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology (SAST), have been deployed in coordinated multi-satellite observations to track Typhoon Dolphin, providing critical data support for the country's meteorological authorities.
The Fengyun-4C and Fengyun-4B satellites operated in tandem to continuously monitor the typhoon's evolution from its formation over the open ocean to its approach toward China's coast.
Positioned at 133 degrees east longitude, Fengyun-4C is currently the world's most powerful single geostationary satellite for comprehensive atmospheric sounding. Facing the typhoon-prone waters of the northwestern Pacific, it offers wide-coverage, high-frequency and continuous observation capabilities, according to the SAST.
Equipped with advanced payloads, including a multi-channel scanning imaging radiometer and a lightning mapping imager, this satellite captured real-time information on cloud structures, severe convection activities and lightning variations, enabling timely detection of key signatures during the typhoon's rapid intensification phases.
As the typhoon edged closer to China's coastal areas, Fengyun-4B, positioned at 105 degrees east longitude, adopted a more favorable viewing angle to focus on offshore waters, conducting high-frequency, high-resolution monitoring at one-minute intervals and 250-meter resolution for the typhoon, the associated mesoscale and smaller weather systems, the SAST noted.
Fengyun-3 low-orbit meteorological satellites have also been mobilized, leveraging their multi-orbit and multi-payload synergies to probe the typhoon's internal structure from different angles and at different times.
Equipped with microwave imagers, microwave temperature and humidity sounders, and precipitation measurement radars, these satellites can penetrate cloud and rain layers to retrieve data on internal temperature and humidity profiles, moisture distribution and precipitation dynamics, enabling a comprehensive characterization of the typhoon from its outer bands to its inner core, the SAST revealed. ■

China's major river-to-sea canal begins vessel trials ahead of opening
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:51:58 CST
14:51:58 KST

A trial vessel drives into a navigation lock on the Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, on Aug. 12, 2026. Pinglu Canal started vessel trials on Wednesday, marking a key step toward the planned opening of this major Chinese waterway in September. The tests will assess navigation under both normal and adverse conditions and examine whether the canal's waterways, locks, anchorages, service areas and navigation facilities are ready for operation. Designed to accommodate vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the 134.2-km Pinglu Canal is China's first major river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949. Stretching from the Pingtang River in Guangxi's Hengzhou City to the Beibu Gulf in the South China Sea, the canal is the backbone of the country's New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, which has evolved into a strategic route linking China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. (Xinhua/Zhou Hua)
NANNING, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Pinglu Canal started vessel trials on Wednesday, marking a key step toward the planned opening of this major Chinese waterway in September.
The trials began when an unloaded 5,000-tonne vessel departed from the Xinfu service area along the canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.
Four vessels representing the main types expected to use this canal will take part in the trials, namely loaded and unloaded 5,000-tonne ships as well as loaded 3,000-tonne and 1,000-tonne vessels.
The tests will assess navigation under both normal and adverse conditions and examine whether the canal's waterways, locks, anchorages, service areas and navigation facilities are ready for operation.
The vessels will travel through major sections of the canal and carry out tests including passing through locks, meeting and overtaking other vessels, making turns, docking under tidal conditions and navigating at night.
Additional tests are planned under potentially hazardous conditions, such as reservoir discharges, flooding from tributaries and combinations of strong winds and high tides.
The test vessels are equipped with BeiDou positioning systems, drones and sensors to collect data on their routes, movements, water currents and safe distances between ships.
Designed to accommodate vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the 134.2-km Pinglu Canal is China's first major river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949.
Experts believe that it is likely to shorten transport time, lower logistics costs and strengthen connectivity between China's western inland regions and Southeast Asia.
Stretching from the Pingtang River in Guangxi's Hengzhou City to the Beibu Gulf in the South China Sea, the canal is the backbone of the country's New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, which has evolved into a strategic route linking China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets.
The corridor's rail service handled a record 1.425 million 20-foot equivalent units of cargo in 2025, up 47.6 percent year on year. As of early July 2026, its network reached 593 ports in 128 countries and regions. ■

HANOI, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam aims to train or update the basic AI skills for at least 10 million workers by 2030 under a national program on AI human resources development, local daily Nhan Dan reported Wednesday.
The program, approved by Deputy Prime Minister Le Tien Chau on Tuesday, aims to develop a workforce to meet the demand of strategic technology sectors and strengthen national technological self-reliance.
It targets the training and upskilling of 10,000 highly qualified and specialized AI professionals, including at least 1,500 experts capable of researching and mastering core technologies and leading key AI tasks.
To achieve these targets, the program sets out several groups of tasks focusing on improving institutions, developing AI experts, expanding AI education and reskilling, linking training with businesses and the labour market, and developing infrastructure, data and practical training environments.
By 2035, Vietnam aims to rank among the leading countries in the region in AI human resources development capacity, said the report. ■

TOKYO, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Typhoon Chan-hom moved westward and was downgraded to a tropical depression Wednesday after making landfall in the eastern Japanese prefecture of Ibaraki the night before, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said.
While Chan-hom was significantly weakened over the Sea of Japan, the weather agency warned of potential flooding in lowland areas and overflowing rivers on Wednesday in the Tohoku region in the northeast and the Kanto-Koshin region, including Tokyo, due to its lingering influence.
The year's 15th typhoon, traveling in an unusual direction from east to west, was the first typhoon to make landfall in Ibaraki Prefecture, northeast of Tokyo, since records began in 1951, the JMA said.
Seven people sustained minor injuries -- two in Iwate Prefecture, northeastern Japan, as well as four in Ibaraki Prefecture and one in Tochigi Prefecture, both near Tokyo, Jiji Press reported Wednesday, citing the Fire and Disaster Management Agency.
Weather officials forecast up to 150 millimeters of rain in Tohoku, the central region of Tokai and the Kinki region in the west in the 24 hours through 6 a.m. local time Thursday, as well as up to 120 mm in Kanto-Koshin. ■

Officers and soldiers stand in formation at a military port in Sanya, south China's Hainan Province, Aug. 12, 2026. SANYA, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- The 49th escort fleet of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy on Wednesday morning departed from a military port in Sanya, south China's Hainan Province, bound for the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia to carry out escort missions in the region.
The fleet consists of the guided-missile destroyer Kunming, the guided-missile frigate Yueyang and the comprehensive supply ship Luomahu, with dozens of special operations personnel and two helicopters on board.
The deployment marks the Kunming's first escort mission.
The fleet will take over duties from the 48th escort fleet, which set sail in October last year.
In line with relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions, China has maintained a regular naval escort presence in the Gulf of Aden and Somali waters since 2008 to safeguard the security of international shipping routes, escort Chinese and foreign vessels, and rescue, protect or assist ships in distress. ■

Feature: From Amman to Beijing: Young sinologist builds a literary bridge between Arab and Chinese cultures
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:51:21 CST
14:51:21 KST

Manal Al-Khammash gets an interview with Xinhua at her home in Amman, Jordan, July 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Xin Mengchen)
AMMAN, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- In a quiet neighborhood north of the Jordanian capital, Amman, Manal Al-Khammash sits with unwavering concentration before a Guzheng, a Chinese traditional musical instrument, carefully plucking its strings and practicing one note after another.
Nearby is a collection of books, some of them Chinese classics and contemporary works, offering a glimpse into a passion that has shaped much of her life: China and its culture.
"I started learning Chinese when I was 17. Now I am approaching 30, and I am still immersed in the language and culture with the same passion," Al-Khammash said.
If given the choice again, she said, she would choose China again without hesitation.
Her fascination with China began in childhood, when she watched kung fu films starring Chinese actor Jackie Chan. The films ignited her curiosity about a distant country in the Far East and prompted her to wonder about its language and people.
"Chinese pronunciation is so different from Arabic. How are these characters pronounced?" she recalled.
That curiosity eventually grew into a plan to study Chinese in high school and, later, to a firm determination to make the language her major at university.
Learning Chinese was far from easy at the beginning.
"Both the grammar and pronunciation were difficult," Al-Khammash said. But with patient guidance from her Chinese teachers, who carefully corrected her and followed her progress, together with her own persistent practice, she gradually mastered the pronunciation.
As her proficiency improved, she began to discover the joy behind the struggle.
"I gradually started to feel the pleasure of learning and the sense of achievement that came with it," she said.
After graduating from the University of Jordan with a bachelor's degree, Al-Khammash realized that her knowledge of the language and understanding of China still needed to be deepened. With strong support from her family, she moved to Beijing in 2019 to pursue postgraduate studies at Beijing Language and Culture University.
As her mastery of Chinese grew, she began translating Chinese television dramas into Arabic. Seeing Arab viewers understand and connect with Chinese stories through her translations brought her immense satisfaction and encouraged her to venture into literary translation, which, she soon discovered, demanded even more patience and effort. Yet for Al-Khammash, passion made the challenge worthwhile.
Among her favorite works is Cold Nights, a novel by renowned Chinese writer Ba Jin. Although the story is set in China, Al-Khammash found in it emotions that transcend borders -- the warmth of family relationships and the emotional struggles experienced by its characters.
That sense of shared culture inspired her to bring the novel to Arabic-speaking readers. Her Arabic translation was published in 2024.
During the translation process, Al-Khammash gave every character in the book Arabic names that she felt suited their personalities. She also included a detailed table at the end of the book explaining the original names of people and places, as well as distinct cultural terms appearing in the novel.
Her goal was not simply to translate words, she said, but to open a window through which Arab readers could gain a deeper and more accurate understanding of Chinese culture.
"When I see Arab readers interacting with these Chinese stories through my translation -- crying, laughing and being moved by the characters -- I feel an indescribable sense of pride and achievement," she said with a smile.
Today, Al-Khammash is pursuing a PhD in contemporary Chinese literature at Sichuan University in southwest China. She spends most of the year in China and returns to Jordan mainly during academic breaks.
Her home on the northern outskirts of Amman reflects the life she has built between the two cultures. Chinese musical instruments, traditional tea sets, and other Chinese cultural artifacts are displayed throughout the house.
Whenever friends visit and express curiosity about them, she eagerly introduces them to Chinese tea culture, preparing tea in accordance with traditional customs.
There is a difference between tea traditions in the two countries, she noted. In China, tea is often prepared using traditional brewing methods, whereas in Jordan, it is commonly boiled. Yet behind the different techniques lies a shared value: hospitality.
The deeper Al-Khammash delves into Chinese culture, the more similarities she discovers between Chinese and Jordanian societies -- from filial respect for parents to reverence for teachers and elders and the willingness to help others.
"Many aspects of Chinese culture are similar to those found in Jordan and other Arab countries," she said.
For her, these cultural parallels have become a source of motivation to continue studying Chinese and researching its culture.
In November 2025, Chinese President Xi Jinping replied to a letter from young sinologists, encouraging them to serve as messengers to promote mutual understanding between Chinese and foreign civilizations.
Al-Khammash was among the young scholars who co-authored the letter.
"His response strengthened my determination to deepen my research on China and tell its story in the best possible way," she said.
In May 2026, she took another step toward advancing that mission by participating in a special China-Arab States session of the 2026 International Youth Poetry Festival.
At the Great Wall of China, beneath the red walls of the Forbidden City and at the Guangdong Literary Museum, she drew on her knowledge of both the Chinese language and culture to help young poets from China and the Arab world communicate and connect.
For Al-Khammash, these encounters offered a firsthand glimpse of how exchanges between the two ancient civilizations can transcend geography and time.
"I am therefore willing to be a cultural bridge connecting the Chinese and Arab cultures and to promote greater understanding between the two civilizations," she said.
Looking ahead to life after completing her doctorate, Al-Khammash has a clear vision: "I hope to work with Chinese people in the future, continue translating more Chinese literary works, and introduce more Arabs to the real and beautiful China," she said. ■

Bill proposes licensing rules, fee cap for foreign booking platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:51:10 UTC
14:51:10 KST

Foreign-based online accommodation platforms would need a permit from the Culture and Tourism Ministry and face a 17 percent ceiling on fees under a bill submitted to parliament by lawmakers from the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP).
The permit would cost 5 million Turkish Liras, remain valid for two years and could not be transferred.
The fee would be raised annually in line with the official revaluation rate, while the president could double it or reduce it by half.
Platforms seeking a permit would have to be registered as digital services taxpayers, have no outstanding tax debts, maintain a contact address in Türkiye and appoint at least one representative in the country.
The representative would handle requests from judicial and administrative authorities, respond to applications and oversee compliance with the proposed rules.
Under the bill, platforms could directly handle bookings for accommodation businesses certified by the ministry and homes licensed for tourism rentals, as well as online airline ticket sales.
Services reserved for travel agencies would have to be offered through licensed agencies, while vehicle rentals would need to be arranged through businesses authorized by the Trade Ministry.
Turkish law would apply to disputes arising from activities covered by the permit, with Turkish courts holding exclusive jurisdiction.
The total amount collected by a platform on a covered sale, regardless of how it is described, could not exceed 17 percent of the sale price excluding value-added tax.
Platforms would also have to verify and display the certificate numbers of accommodation businesses and licensed rental homes.
They could not prevent service providers from offering the same services through other channels at the same or different prices, force them to join promotional campaigns or penalize them in rankings for filing complaints with public authorities or courts.
Exceeding the 17 percent ceiling or collecting an undisclosed charge could result in a fine equal to 10 times the improperly collected amount.
Violations involving rankings, alternative sales channels or compulsory campaigns would carry a fine of 500,000 liras, with repeated breaches potentially leading to the cancellation of the permit.
Platforms operating without a permit, or after a permit had expired or been revoked, could have access to their services blocked, subject to judicial review.
The bill would also require the platforms to pay a tourism contribution of 0.075 percent, calculated on the basis used for the digital services tax.
Platforms already operating in Türkiye would have three months after the legislation took effect to apply for a permit.

Palestinian students, staff take Columbia University to court over discrimination accusations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:48:26 UTC
14:48:26 KST

A group of current and former Palestinian students and staff have sued Columbia University in New York, accusing discriminatory treatment of the university's Palestinian community since late 2023, according to a court filing.
The lawsuit accuses Columbia of failing to protect Palestinian students and staff from harassment while subjecting them to what it describes as "unfair and biased disciplinary hearings."
Columbia has previously denied discriminatory treatment and condemned hate. Local media reported that the university declined to comment on the pending litigation. It did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Pro-Palestinian protests
Protests erupted at Columbia and universities across the United States after Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
Demonstrators called for an end to US support for Israel and demanded that universities divest from companies they said supported Israel.
In May 2025, Columbia suspended more than 65 students over a pro-Palestinian demonstration that shut down the university's main library.
The protest came as Columbia was negotiating with US President Donald Trump's administration, which had cut federal funding to the university after accusing it of failing to adequately address anti-Semitism during pro-Palestinian demonstrations.
Protesters, including some Jewish groups, have argued that opposition to Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and its occupation of Palestinian territories is not inherently anti-Semitic.
Columbia agreed in July last year to pay more than $200 million to the US government to resolve federal investigations and restore most of its federal funding.
Free speech groups have criticised the university's crackdown on protests, during which students faced arrests, suspensions, expulsions and, in some cases, the revocation of degrees.

General Staff: almost a third of the battles took place in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions
Kyiv • UNN
Over the past day, there were 237 combat engagements on the front, most of them in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions. The enemy launched 2 missile and 80 air strikes and deployed 11,155 kamikaze drones.
237 battles took place at the front over the past day, with the largest number—almost one-third—on the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported in its morning briefing on August 12, UNN writes.
A total of 237 combat engagements were recorded over the past day
Yesterday, the enemy launched two missile strikes using 13 missiles and carried out 80 airstrikes, during which it dropped 284 guided aerial bombs. In addition, the invaders deployed 11,155 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,422 attacks on populated areas and the positions of our troops, 28 of them using multiple-launch rocket systems.
The enemy shelled the populated areas of Korenok, Sopych, Bachivsk, Neskuchne, Rohizne, Tovstodubove, Bezzalivka, Vyntorivka, Hirky, Yastrubshchyna and Topolia in Sumy region. Sumy, Hurko-Ozhynka and Pustohorod came under airstrikes.
Over the past day, the aviation, missile forces and artillery of the Defense Forces struck three command posts, one area where enemy personnel were concentrated, one artillery system and four unmanned aerial vehicle command posts.
Situation by axis
On the North Slobozhanskyi and Kursk axes, our defenders stopped seven enemy assaults over the past day. At the same time, the aggressor carried out 71 attacks on the positions of our troops and populated areas, including one using a multiple-launch rocket system.
On the South Slobozhanskyi axis, Ukrainian units repelled 13 enemy attacks. The invaders attempted to advance near the populated areas of Lyman and Starytsia and toward the populated areas of Khatnie, Kolodiazne, Okhrimivka and Vodiane.
On the Kupiansk axis, the enemy carried out 15 offensive actions near Zahryzove and Kurylivka and toward Radkivka and Petropavlivka.
Attempts to penetrate our defenses were repelled on the Lyman axis, where the occupiers attacked seven times near the populated areas of Karpivka, Serednie, Zarichne and Dibrova.
On the Sloviansk axis, the enemy carried out 18 assault actions near the populated areas of Riznykivka, Zakitne, Kryva Luka and Kalenyky and toward Rai-Oleksandrivka and Ozerne.
On the Kramatorsk axis, the Russian invaders carried out one offensive action toward Yurkivka.
Thirty-four attacks were recorded on the Kostiantynivka axis. The invaders conducted assault operations near the populated areas of Kostiantynivka, Ivanopillia and Illinivka and toward the populated areas of Dovha Balka, Stepanivka, Toretske, Novyi Donbas and Kucheriv Yar.
The enemy carried out 37 attacks on the Pokrovsk axis. The occupiers attempted to advance near the populated areas of Nove Shakhove, Myrne, Dorozhnie, Novooleksandrivka, Hryshyne, Kotlyne, Udachne and Novomykolaivka and toward the populated areas of Shevchenko, Myrne, Vasylivka, Serhiivka and Novopavlivka.
On the Oleksandrivka axis, the invaders carried out one attack toward Ternove.
On the Huliaipole axis, the occupiers attacked the positions of our defenders six times. The enemy attempted to advance toward the populated areas of Vozdvyzhivka, Charivne, Kosivtseve, Staroukrainka, Tsvitkove and Huliaipolske.
On the Orikhiv axis, our defenders stopped two attempts by the enemy to advance toward Prymorske and near Luhivske.
On the Dnipro axis, the enemy did not conduct any assault operations over the past day.
No signs of the formation of enemy offensive groups were detected on the Volyn and Polissia axes.

A pair of Democratic primaries in Minnesota on Tuesday were among a string of high-profile battles between progressive and moderate candidates, where Israel and the pro-Israel lobby serve as key wedge issues.
The state’s highest-profile race was the US Senate primary between Rep. Angie Craig, who has been endorsed by the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC, and Lieutenant Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who said she would reject AIPAC’s money and accuses Israel of committing genocide.
The race, and the candidates’ sparring over AIPAC, comes as the lobby and Israel under the leadership of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have become increasingly unpopular among Democratic voters. Israel is also an issue in the Democratic gubernatorial primary in neighboring Wisconsin taking place on Tuesday.
Flanagan has referred to Craig as “AIPAC’s candidate” in the Senate race, which prompted Craig to distance herself from the group’s spending during a TV debate in June.
“AIPAC has not contributed at all, the PAC, to my Senate campaign,” said Craig, whose wife, Cheryl Greene, is Jewish. “Not one penny.”
Flanagan countered that, while AIPAC itself has not donated to Craig’s campaign, it has held fundraisers for the four-term congresswoman. AIPAC did not respond to a request for comment.

Too many holes! Why badgers are digging up Britain’s lovingly maintained golf courses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:04:38 UTC
23:04:38 KST

Name: Badgers.
Age: European badgers live for five to eight years in the wild. They have been in the UK, where this story is set, for half to three-quarters of a million years.
Appearance: Black and white mustelid anarcho-syndicalists.
Hardly. Badgers are quite posh, aren’t they? Well, perhaps. But everyone has their breaking point, and now I must inform you that badgers have become embroiled in an aggressive form of anti-capitalist class warfare.
What turned them? The cost of living? The rise of the billionaire class? Close, but no. It was the drought.
How so? This has been a historically hot summer in the UK. England and Wales endured the driest July since records began (1836). All the grass is brown and dead. There are wildfires everywhere and 26 million people are living with a hosepipe ban.
It’s awful. Yes, especially for the badgers. Most of their food lives underground, and it’s much harder to get to it when the earth has been baked dry by the sun.
So what’s the solution? That’s easy: turn over a few golf courses.
Are they really into clubhouse sandwiches? Not when there are nice wet lawns to tear up.
Why do golf courses have wet lawns during a drought? The Water Use (Temporary Bans) Order 2010 permits exemptions for watering sports turf. That means that while you are carefully sharing your bathwater, your local golf course is hosing its lush greens.
Yes, but the badgers. Oh, right. Well, if you’re a badger and you need to dig up some worms, and all the ground is hard except for golf courses, where do you think you’re going to get your worms?
From golf courses? That’s right! Jim Croxton, chief executive of the British and International Golf Greenkeepers Association, says: “Badgers generally dig turf to find food and August is the beginning of the period when chafer grubs are generally present.”
Is it a widespread problem? Golf courses from Suffolk to Staffordshire to Worcestershire have reported greens being torn up by badgers, according to the Telegraph.
This sounds like a victimless crime. You would think so, but the golf courses are very upset about it.
How upset? A video of one ripped-up course posted to Facebook prompted the furious comment: “They’re a f*ckin pest, I’ve had countless ornamental lawns wrecked by these f*ckers.”
Quite right. Will nobody think of the ornamental lawns? Exactly. It’s clear that there needs to be an urgent change to the law.
To what? Well, it obviously isn’t fair that golf courses are exempt from the hosepipe ban in a time of national crisis.
But then the badgers would have nowhere to eat, and they would die. No they wouldn’t. Badgers are enterprising creatures. They’d find a way.
Do say: “The badgers have absolutely massacred hole nine.”
Don’t say: “Four legs good, golf clubs bad.”

Foreign ministry condemns Colombia’s recognition of Israeli sovereignty over Golan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:47:48 UTC
14:47:48 KST

Türkiye has condemned Colombia’s recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights, saying the decision violates international law and carries no legal weight.
“We strongly condemn the statement made by Colombia aimed at legitimizing Israel’s occupation of the Golan Heights, which constitute an integral part of Syria,” the Foreign Ministry said in a written statement.
The ministry said such unilateral moves amounted to a “grave violation” of international law, citing U.N. Security Council Resolution 497.
Adopted in 1981, the resolution declared Israel’s decision to impose its laws, jurisdiction and administration on the occupied Syrian Golan “null and void and without international legal effect.”
Ankara also renewed its call for the international community to press Israel to end its occupation in southern Syria, including the Golan Heights, and what the ministry described as attacks on Syria’s sovereignty and stability.
“Türkiye will continue to support the preservation of Syria’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, as well as the establishment of lasting peace and stability in the country,” it said.
Colombia announced on Aug. 10 that it recognized Israeli sovereignty over the territory.
Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria in 1967 and extended its laws to the area in 1981.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:47:15 UTC
14:47:15 KST

Germany is considering giving its intelligence services new powers to launch preemptive cyberattacks against Russian drone manufacturers, amid growing concerns over sabotage, espionage, and drone threats, a senior lawmaker said.
Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the Bundestag’s Parliamentary Control Committee, said Germany’s intelligence agencies need to move beyond simply gathering information and be able to disrupt threats before they reach German territory.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We really have to enable our services to paralyze and turn off the attack drone in Russia or the factory that manufactures it, before it is directed against the German airport or against the safety of life and limb of people in Germany,” Henrichmann said in an interview with WELT TV on Tuesday.
“The best drone is the one that never rises and can threaten Germany,” he added.
Henrichmann said the reform should give Germany’s intelligence agencies the operational capabilities needed to get ahead of the threat, including potentially disrupting hostile cyber operations.
He also argued that Germany needs to pool its intelligence and cyber capabilities more effectively as threats from Russia increase.
Additionally, cyberattacks, sabotage, and espionage or unauthorized drone overflights are “now part of a reality for which we must be better prepared,” Henrichmann told the Rheinische Post.
Romania Destroys 2 Russian-Made Drones Near Major Black Sea Gas Project
The German government is expected to discuss reforms to the laws governing the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution on Wednesday.
Henrichmann said the reform should bring Germany’s intelligence services to a level of capability already considered standard among European partners.
The proposal has won support from some opposition lawmakers. Green Party security expert Konstantin von Notz called the reform long overdue but said stronger parliamentary oversight was also needed.
Civil liberties groups, however, have warned that the changes could dramatically expand the powers of German intelligence agencies.
The Society for Civil Rights said the draft could allow expanded use of state trojans, AI-powered analysis, access to private surveillance cameras and “hackbacks,” potentially with insufficient legal safeguards.
Kai Dittmann of the group called for the draft law to be fundamentally revised, arguing that parts of it could violate Germany’s constitution.

New Zealand PM fends off leadership challenge months before vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:47:08 UTC
14:47:08 KST

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said he had the "full support" of his ruling National Party on Wednesday after surviving a leadership challenge called with less than three months until a general election.
Luxon has led New Zealand since 2023 but has been unable to reverse his party's slide in the polls, with a series of gaffes, divisions within his ruling coalition, and rising living costs and unemployment denting his popularity.
He called an emergency meeting on Tuesday after media reported growing speculation that his leadership was no longer tenable.
Following hours of closed-door talks with party grandees, Luxon said he had secured their backing.
"There was a confidence vote in my leadership this morning at our caucus meeting, and I have the full support of our caucus," he told journalists.
"Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election," he said.
"We're going back to work, and we're moving on."
The leadership challenge was brought by New Zealand's Defence Minister Chris Penk, who has since been fired, Luxon said in a statement.
Wednesday's was the second challenge to Luxon's leadership this year.
In April, Luxon made it through a vote after reports National members were displeased with the party polling under 30 percent.
Luxon was flanked by two rumoured leadership contenders as he faced journalists — ministers Chris Bishop and Erica Stanford.
Immigration Minister Stanford had appeared to have growing support to take on the leadership and would not pledge her backing to prime minister in recent days.
And ex-tobacco lobbyist Bishop has long been said to have interest in the top job, but told reporters on Tuesday he backed Luxon.
Leaving the caucus meeting, members said they were "united" and "100 percent behind the prime minister", but as in April they would not say if Luxon had unanimous support.
Troubled premiership
The former Air New Zealand boss led the centre-right party to election victory three years ago vowing to tame inflation and bring down interest rates.
The millionaire touted himself as a master negotiator from previous business experience.
But it took over six weeks for him to broker a three-way coalition government with populist New Zealand First and libertarian ACT, a marriage of convenience he has struggled to manage throughout his premiership.
His political savvy became a long-running concern with a series of gaffes and miscommunications.
Luxon also drew ire with an attack on small-business owners, a key part of his base, saying they had a "parent-child mentality" towards the government.
And his inability to rein in coalition partners hurt his popularity.
Foreign minister and New Zealand First leader Winston Peters sparked an international incident last month when he told a Chinese-born lawmaker during a parliamentary debate to "go back to your own country".
Beijing complained about the comments and while Luxon condemned them as racist he did not sanction his coalition partner.
Peters dismissed the leadership vote on Wednesday as "much ado about nothing".
Polling has suggested some of Luxon's most senior ministers could be turfed out of parliament when New Zealanders vote on November 7.
