15 dead, 27 missing as ferry capsizes in Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:38:00 UTC
14:38:00 KST

At least 44 people drowned when an overcrowded ferry capsized on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba, police said Wednesday, updating the toll a day after the disaster.
A witness said soon after the government ferry sank in rough weather Tuesday that bodies could be seen in the water as rescuers tried to reach the vessel, reported the Agence France-Presse (AFP).
It was carrying 114 adult passengers, five crew members and an unspecified number of children when it went down, the civil protection unit (CPU) said.
The Rural Infrastructure Development Agency (RIDA) vessel – which ferries people between the northern town of Kariba and several islands and fishing villages – had the capacity for 90 people, it said.
The unit said initially that 77 people were rescued and 15 bodies retrieved.
The Zimbabwe Republic Police updated the toll later Wednesday, saying on X: "The ZRP informs the public that the death toll in the Kariba RIDA boat accident is now 44."
It is one of the worst recorded passenger boat disasters on the lake, which is on the border with Zambia and more than 300 kilometers (185 miles) northeast of the capital, Harare.
It is the world's largest man-made lake by volume.
Two funeral parlors were engaged to collect the bodies, the CPU said, as the search continued for any unaccounted people.
The witness, Maxton Kanhema, told AFP that the boat left in the morning in bad weather and may have been hit by a wave, causing its engines to switch off.
"When we were in the waters, then you could see a distress sign and then boats that were close by responded," Kanhema, who was on a small boat which attended the scene Tuesday afternoon, said.
A national park provided a helicopter to help in the rescue effort alongside bigger boats and divers from the local area and the army, he said.
"People were in distress ... there were bodies in the water and it was a sad situation to witness. Those that could be rescued were rescued," he said.
A specialized aquatic rescue unit was airlifted to the area to aid in the search, the CPU said.
It said the 77 people who had been rescued were taken to Long Island in the middle of the lake.

Ancient wrestler’s tomb discovered in Aspendos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:36:37 UTC
14:36:37 KST

The tomb was discovered in the East Necropolis, which has been identified for the first time within the ancient city. (DHA Photo)
A 2,400-year-old cist tomb believed to have belonged to a wrestler has been uncovered during excavations at the ancient city of Aspendos, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has said.
The tomb was discovered in the East Necropolis, which has been identified for the first time within the ancient city. The tomb dates to between the last quarter of the fifth century B.C. and the fourth century B.C.
Ersoy said the findings from the tomb indicate that the person buried there may have been involved in sports and could have been a wrestler from Aspendos.
The minister also shared information about the discovery on his NSosyal account.
“We have made a very important discovery during the excavations we are carrying out at the ancient city of Aspendos, shedding light on the city’s history in the classical period,” Ersoy said.
“We have uncovered a cist tomb dating to between the last quarter of the fifth century B.C. and the fourth century B.C. in the East Necropolis, whose existence has been identified for the first time within the city.”
He said Aspendos coins found in the tomb, featuring depictions of wrestlers, along with other finds, indicate that the person buried there was involved in sports and may even have been a wrestler from Aspendos.
“I sincerely congratulate our General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums, our excavation team and all the scientists who contributed to this valuable discovery,” Ersoy said.
“We will continue to complete the missing pages of our history with every new find from Aspendos and to preserve our cultural heritage through scientific studies and pass it on to future generations.”
The ministry said the findings provide important information about life in Aspendos during the classical period, burial traditions and the city’s social structure.
The discoveries are also expected to enrich knowledge of Aspendos’ classical period, which has so far been known to a limited extent through archaeological evidence, and contribute to new scientific studies that will shed light on the history of the ancient city.

The tours take place on the Kızılırmak around the historic Asma Bridge, known locally as the ‘swinging bridge,’ one of the district’s landmarks.
Visitors to Central Anatolian province of Nevşehir’s historic Cappadocia region are adding a touch of Venetian charm to their travels, taking peaceful gondola rides along the Kızılırmak River in Avanos district.
The gondola tours offer an alternative to activities such as horseback and all-terrain vehicle rides among Cappadocia’s fairy chimneys and hot air balloon flights over the UNESCO World Heritage-listed region, attracting visitors who prefer to experience the area surrounded by greenery.
The tours take place on the Kızılırmak, which runs between the two sides of Avanos, around the historic Asma Bridge, known locally as the “swinging bridge,” one of the district’s landmarks.
Gondolas carrying groups of up to six people glide along the calm waters of the river, offering visitors a different perspective of Avanos.
Ali Sarıyürek, a representative of the tour company, told state-run Anadolu Agency that the gondolas had become part of Avanos’ tourism identity, which is closely associated with the Kızılırmak River.
Sarıyürek said the views during the tours offered visitors glimpses reminiscent of Venice, Italy, known for its canals and gondolas.
“We have 10 gondolas and two jet boats. The tours are organized for groups of six, although we can also arrange tours for two or four people upon special request. Visitors are particularly impressed by the fairy chimneys in the region. They take balloon tours and when they come to the Avanos side, they also join gondola tours here, which is like the Venice of the region,” he said.
He said the 15-minute tours take visitors under the Asma Bridge and to other points along the river.x
“We do our best to provide a service that leaves our guests satisfied. The Kızılırmak, Türkiye’s longest river, flows calmly through this region. Its presence adds a distinct beauty to Avanos, which is why visitors come here and leave very satisfied. Visitors to the district also tour pottery workshops,” Sarıyürek said.
He added that the gondola tour costs 300 Turkish Liras per person.
Necdet Endar, who joined the tour, said he was visiting Cappadocia’s tourism destinations with his family.
“We can call this place Türkiye’s Venice. You feel refreshed. I learned about this tour when we came here. The children loved it and want to ride again,” he said.
Another visitor, Mehmet Aras, said the gondolas added color to the scenery.
“It is a different pleasure, a great beauty. I think it is one of the beauties that completes Cappadocia’s magnificent, magical landscape. At the same time, we felt a Venice atmosphere. I recommend that everyone visit and see Cappadocia and definitely join the gondola tour in Avanos, which resembles Venice,” he said.
The gondolas gliding along the river also provide colorful scenes for visitors taking photographs and videos.

New initiative to map history and dialects of Turkish language
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:35:46 UTC
14:35:46 KST

Researchers will clarify the structure of root words by linking them to elements with similar structures that have undergone the same development.
The Turkish Language Association (TDK) is preparing a series of projects aimed at documenting the roots, historical development and regional diversity of the Turkish language, including an etymological dictionary, a comprehensive dialect atlas and a Turkish language museum in Ankara.
According to the TDK’s 2026 Institutional Financial Status and Expectations Report, the association will compile an Etymological Dictionary of the Turkish Language to protect and enrich Turkish and promote its proper use.
The project will examine the origins of words by tracing them back to their forms in the earliest available sources, the changes they have undergone throughout history and, where applicable, their forms in languages with which they have been in contact.
Researchers will seek to clarify the structure of root words by establishing links with elements of similar structure that have undergone the same developments.
A total of 100 scientists from different fields of expertise and working under different job descriptions will take part in the project.
Another major initiative is the “Atlas of Turkish Dialects in Türkiye Project.” The project aims to collect data based on approximately 200 phonetic, morphological, syntactic and vocabulary criteria across the entire geographical area of Turkish spoken in Türkiye.
The data will then be entered into computer mapping programs to identify isoglosses and produce an atlas of the dialects of Turkish spoken in Türkiye.
The dialects of Turkish spoken in Türkiye constitute the largest group within the Turkic language family in terms of speakers.
The TDK also plans to transform its former building on Atatürk Boulevard in Ankara into a Turkish 
Museum.
The museum will introduce visitors to the historical periods of the Turkish language and contemporary Turkic languages and dialects through documents, examples, maps and slides.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:35:36 UTC

Photographers worked from dawn to document endangered species and build a visual archive.
Van, home to Türkiye’s rich biodiversity, has once again become a destination for nature and photography enthusiasts. Butterfly researchers and nature photographers who traveled from different parts of Türkiye covered nearly 2,000 kilometers to document and photograph rare butterfly species found in the region.
Nurtured by rich flora and unique microclimates, the Van Lake Basin serves as a thriving sanctuary for many of Türkiye’s butterfly species.
Despite rugged terrain, nature enthusiasts and lepidopterists spent days conducting fieldwork and searching for vibrant butterflies. Meanwhile, photographers equipped with specialized gear worked from dawn to document endangered species and build a visual archive to boost the city’s nature tourism.
After traveling long distances, photographers were thrilled by Van’s pristine environment and abundant butterfly population and emphasized the urgent need to protect and promote the basin’s extraordinary biodiversity globally.
The photographs and observation data collected are expected to be included in exhibitions and nature conservation projects in the coming period.
Nihat Kaymaz, who traveled from Siirt, said he came to Van with friends to observe and photograph valuable butterfly species.
“I came from Siirt to Van. We do butterfly watching. There are very valuable butterflies here at the moment. We came with our friends just to photograph them. Three of my friends came from Istanbul. We are currently in the Güzeldere area,” Kaymaz said.
He said they were searching for the Hazar Piri Reis and Iranian Fire butterflies in the Güzeldere area.
“The Van basin is a very important place for butterfly watching. Its habitat, flora and fauna make it a wonderful place for butterfly watching. Every year, my friends come to Van from different provinces of Türkiye to photograph these butterflies. I accompany them. I both photograph butterflies and guide them,” he said.
Kadir Özakkü, who came from Istanbul with his friends, said Van and neighboring Hakkari are particularly rich in butterfly diversity.
“We had been to Van before. This time, we climbed to the summit in the Güzeldere area to look for the Hazar Piri Reis. It was very windy. But we photographed and recorded other species, including several types of false witches and the mountain false witch,” Özakkü said.
He added that they were also looking for the Iranian Fire butterfly but had not been able to find it despite its previous records in the area.
“Last year’s records were our basis for coming here. But we did not come across it. We will try our luck again tomorrow, both for the Hazar Piri Reis and the Iranian Fire,” he said.
Özakkü also drew attention to pollution in the area.
“There is so much diversity here and nature is wonderful. But we see waste along the roads, especially plastic bottles thrown from vehicles. We need to be very careful about this. Even if we are walking, we should put the waste in our pockets and take it with us. We need to protect such wonderful nature as if it were our own eyes,” he said.
He noted that people from Europe had visited the region last year specifically to photograph the Iranian Fire butterfly.
“They came all the way from Europe just to photograph the Iranian Fire. But we could not find it this year. We will see. Hopefully, there is tomorrow and the day after. We will not leave before finding it,” Özakkü said.
Fuat Gülseren, who also traveled from Istanbul to photograph butterflies, said they wanted to observe and document the species found in Van.
“We want to take butterfly photographs and make observations in Van. Van is one of our cities that is extremely important in terms of butterfly diversity and abundance. Van’s nature is beautiful. There are still many places that have remained untouched,” Gülseren said.
He said the region is home to endemic and rare species, including the Roz’s large blue and the Iranian Fire butterfly.
“We want to see these beauties resulting from Van’s natural environment. We put our work and responsibilities aside and came here. We want to observe nature. The heat and weather conditions do not really make things difficult for us. What makes us happy is being together in nature. This is a passion,” Gülseren said.
“We want to photograph Van’s valuable butterflies. We also invite nature lovers like us to Van,” he added.

====================================================================================================

Seven hidden lakes reveal Uludağ’s geological legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:34:56 UTC
14:34:56 KST

A breathtaking view of one of Uludağ Mountain’s seven hidden glacial lakes, glimmering high in the alpine heights of Bursa.
High above the northwestern Turkish city of Bursa, seven alpine lakes scattered across the summit of Uludağ preserve traces of geological processes that unfolded over millions of years.
Known as the Lakes Region, the area sits near the summit of Uludağ, a mountain that rises to over 2,500 meters and is one of Türkiye’s best-known destinations for winter sports and nature.
The seven lakes, Aynalı, Karagöl, Buzlu, Kilimli, Heybeli, Kovukdere and Cayırlıdere, were shaped by glaciers and are fed by surface and groundwater.
Their rocky basins and surrounding formations offer a glimpse into the mountain’s geological evolution, while the lakes themselves have become destinations for hikers, mountaineers and nature enthusiasts.
President of the Southern Marmara Branch of the Chamber of Geological Engineers Mehmet Yıldız said the lakes should be regarded as part of Türkiye’s geological heritage.
“These are natural formations that have the characteristics of geoheritage. They form over millions of years,” Yıldız said.
He said the concept of geoheritage, natural formations that provide evidence of Earth’s geological history, has yet to become fully established in Türkiye.
Understanding such formations is important for studying how the Earth has evolved over time and guiding future geological research, Yıldız said.
The Chamber of Geological Engineers conducted fieldwork in the Lakes Region in 2023 together with members of the Association for the Protection of Geological Heritage, known as JEMİRKO, as part of efforts to secure geoheritage status for the area.
Despite its rugged landscape, Uludağ is not a volcanic mountain, Yıldız said.
The mountain was formed through tectonic activity and magmatism, rather than volcanic eruptions. As a result, the lakes at its summit are not crater lakes.
Instead, they were formed by glaciers that eroded the underlying geological formations. Moraine deposits, accumulations of rock and sediment left behind by glaciers, helped create natural basins where surface and groundwater could collect.
Water levels in the lakes have risen this year compared with recent years, the expert said, attributing the increase to heavy snowfall over the winter and spring rainfall.

Türkiye plans interagency push on critical minerals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:34:29 UTC
14:34:29 KST

Türkiye plans to establish two interagency bodies to coordinate policy on critical minerals and raw materials, with the aim of increasing domestic production and reducing supply risks for defense, energy and high-technology industries.
Officials told daily Milliyet that the council will operate under the leadership of the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry and bring together institutions, including ETİ Maden, the General Directorate of Mineral Research and Exploration (MTA), the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TÜBİTAK), the Industry and Technology Ministry, the Trade Ministry, the Defense Ministry and the Presidency of Defense Industries (SSB).
It would assess the strategic importance of minerals for key industries, potential supply-chain disruptions and the environmental and social effects of extraction and processing.
The board would also coordinate steps to increase domestic output for sectors including defense, electronics and energy production.
A separate Critical Raw Materials Board is also planned.
It would develop strategies to secure inputs needed by industry and technological transformation, including processed materials, agricultural inputs and recycled materials.
Minerals are considered critical when supply difficulties or sharp price increases could disrupt industrial production.
Lithium, cobalt, nickel and graphite are used in electric vehicle batteries and energy-storage systems, while rare earth elements are needed for electronics and magnets. Copper, boron, tungsten and antimony are used in advanced manufacturing, aerospace and chemicals.
Türkiye’s Critical and Strategic Minerals Report assessed 37 minerals. Lithium, silver, titanium, iron, manganese, zinc, copper and aluminum, each with a criticality score of 16 or above, were placed in the highest-priority category.
Beryllium, fluorite, chromium, boron, platinum, magnesite, feldspar, kaolin, trona and bentonite, which scored below 10, were classified as potentially critical. The report separately identified 26 strategic minerals based on defense industry requirements.

Why have several nations raised red flags over Indian farm exports?
As Japan turns back mangoes, China blocks rice and European inspectors flag spices, India’s growers ask what stands between their harvest and the world market.
New Delhi, India – The vapour heat treatment (VHT) facility in Rehmanpur village of Lucknow, the capital of the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh – used to sterilise fruit and vegetables – was preparing for the busiest time of the year when Japanese quarantine inspectors turned up in March.
Export documents had been cleared, shipping schedules finalised, and growers in the western states of Maharashtra and Gujarat reserved their best Alphonso and Kesar mangoes for export to Japan, one of Asia’s premium markets.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4‘It all depends on the crop’: Gulf crisis hits South Asia farmers
- list 2 of 4US wants to sell GM soya and corn to India, farmers wary
- list 3 of 4How India’s ban on some rice exports is ricocheting around the world
- list 4 of 4The legendary flavoured ground salt from India: Pisyu loon
Everything appeared set for the season to begin when production ground to a halt. Japanese inspectors reviewing the fumigation, disinfection and certification procedures raised concerns about the whole process, prompting Japan to suspend imports of the fruits.
However, on March 31, the plant protection authorities in Yokohama sent a formal letter, saying all Indian mango shipments bearing inspection certificates issued on or after March 25 would be barred until inspectors could confirm that operational standards had improved.
It was the first major disruption in India-Japan mango trade in nearly two decades. In 1986, imports of the fruit were barred over fruit fly concerns. Restrictions were lifted in 2006 after the country built VHT infrastructure, strengthened pest surveillance and agreed to annual inspections.
Japan ‘gave us credibility’
The 2026 halt now affects six approved varieties of mango – Alphonso, Kesar, Langra, Banganapalli, Chausa and Mallika – covering the peak export window of April through to June.
Japan imported roughly $1.54m worth of fresh and processed mango products from India between 2025 and 2026. It might appear to be a modest sum, but the Japanese market holds huge significance for the rest of the global trade. Japan pays premium prices for mangoes and the country’s approval signals quality to the rest of the world.
The suspension came at an already challenging time for mango farmers in India. Sustained heatwaves through the Konkan belt had destroyed much of Maharashtra’s Alphonso crop. Geopolitical disruptions in West Asia had pushed freight costs higher, and exporters who had spent years establishing relations with the Japanese suddenly faced cancelled contracts and inventories rotting in storage.
Vikram Shah, a Mumbai-based exporter who shipped about 2.5 tonnes of mangoes to Japan in 2025, highlighted the importance of its market.
“Japan was never our biggest market in terms of quantity, but it was the one that gave us credibility,” Shah told Al Jazeera. “We spent six years building trust with buyers there. I travelled to Osaka twice, sat with importers, visited their cold storage facilities and learned exactly what they expected from us. Relationships like that take years to build and can disappear in a single season.”
Rajesh Patil, an Alphonso grower in Ratnagiri, Maharashtra, said his family had cultivated mangoes on a three-acre (1.2-hectare) orchard along the Konkan coast for two generations. The Japanese market, he said, consistently delivered far higher returns than domestic auctions, leading him to invest heavily in meeting Japan’s stringent import standards.
“We upgraded the orchard because Japan rewarded quality,” Patil said. “I spent nearly ₹80,000 [$840] on grading and handling equipment, attended pest-management training sessions, and changed the way we harvest and pack fruit,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The Japanese market paid almost twice what I could earn locally. When you make those investments, you expect the system supporting exports to be as reliable as the fruit you grow.”
China objects to rice
On April 17, China revoked the import licences of three Indian rice exporters after the General Administration of Customs rejected their consignments, claiming traces of genetically modified organisms (GMO).
The exporters disputed the finding, pointing out that their shipments received GMO-free certification before their departure and that the Indian government also said all domestic paddy and rice fields are free of genetic modification.
Rice makes up more than 20 percent of India’s agricultural exports, with a record-breaking $12.5bn of it shipped in the last financial year (2025-26). The three suspended exporters now face an uncertain path back into China, rattling their community.
Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), under India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, notified the companies and, on June 8, published a list of laboratories approved for GMO tests on China-bound shipments.
SK Singh, an agricultural scientist in New Delhi, told Al Jazeera the dispute exposed weaknesses in India’s testing system.
“Our labs built expertise in pesticide residue and aflatoxin testing because that’s what most markets wanted,” he said. “China’s demand for GMO verification calls for a different scale of capacity.”
The exporters’ certificates came from accredited labs even if the certification network remains uneven, he added.
Only a handful of facilities, concentrated in New Delhi and Hyderabad in the southeastern state of Telangana, run the required protein analysis, forcing exporters in northern Punjab and Haryana states to ship samples hundreds of kilometres away.
Fragmented supply chain
There were other warning signs before the crisis hit mangoes and rice.
Hong Kong suspended several Indian spice products over pesticide residues, and testing found quality deviations in nearly 12 percent of the samples. The European Union also raised the inspection frequency on Indian cumin to 30 percent in January 2025, following 312 spice alerts on its rapid alert system in 2024.
Ananya Bose, a food safety scientist in Kochi in the southern state of Kerala, traced the problem to a fragmented supply chain.
“A farmer sells to an aggregator, who sells to a trader, who supplies a processor. Somewhere in that chain, the record of what was sprayed disappears,” she said. “The trail is detailed until the first sale, then it effectively ends.”
Bose has pushed for mandatory digital pesticide records, since regulators abroad expect traceability from field to shipment, a standard many states still treat as optional.
These setbacks may read as isolated incidents, but they expose a gap between India’s agricultural strength and the traceability, food safety and certification standards that Japan, the EU, the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada now demand. Those standards are tightened by consumer pressure for transparency, climate-driven pest concerns, food-security strategy and the COVID pandemic.
At the same time, competitors have moved faster, with Thailand building a nationwide traceability programme, Vietnam investing in farmers’ training, and Brazil and Chile pouring money into cold-chain systems.
India’s progress has lagged with just 207 registered pack houses, 72 percent of them concentrated in Maharashtra. Moreover, scarce cold storage facilities and logistical costs eat up roughly 15 percent of export value, almost double that of advanced nations. Small farmers owning less than 2 hectares (5 acres) of land make up more than 86 percent of India’s cultivators, making standardisation difficult at scale.
“India built its strategy around producing more, while premium markets reward proving quality along the way,” agricultural economist Anil Gupta told Al Jazeera.
Gupta pointed to some real gains: recognised laboratories grew from 22 to 89 over the past decade, and approved export certificates climbed from roughly 61,000 to more than 170,000.
“The progress is measurable, but so is the scale of the challenge,” he said. “These improvements mark a beginning, well short of the finish line.”
Ujjwal Kumar Ghosh, a senior official in the government’s Department of Commerce, has called for tighter controls on antibiotic residues, pesticides and aflatoxins in spices, tea, fruits and vegetables. He said funds have been set aside to upgrade laboratories, though without a timeline.
“The government is strengthening the system from testing to inspection and traceability. We are tightening controls on antibiotic and pesticide residues and aflatoxins, expanding laboratory capacity, introducing risk-based inspections and using digital systems and rapid screening to identify problems faster. The objective is to help exporters meet stricter global food-safety standards while protecting India’s access to international markets,” said Ghosh.
India still holds just 2.4 percent of global agri-exports despite ranking as the world’s second-largest agricultural producer, with processed exports stuck near 17 percent, against 25 percent in the US and 50 percent in China.
And growers are facing the fallout.
Gujarat’s Kesar mango farmers lost their strongest Japanese buyer. A basmati rice farmer in Haryana’s Karnal said local prices had already dropped 8 percent. And a turmeric processor in Kerala’s Erode said residue testing cost him 15,000 rupees ($157) last quarter, almost 10 percent of his profit.
Agriculture still employs about 42 percent of India’s workforce while producing less than a fifth of the national output.
“This is about far more than a few rejected shipments,” Gupta said. “The countries that succeed will consistently meet the standards global buyers demand.”
Indian farmers have long proven they can grow for the world. The task now is building systems that convince the world to keep buying.

Heavy rain continued to lash the Chinese capital Beijing on Wednesday, forcing authorities to shut tourist attractions, suspend bus services and construction work and evacuate residents from high-risk areas, state media reported.
The city closed over 300 tourist and camping sites and suspended operations at more than 4,100 rural homestays.
Some 250 bus routes were halted, while trains on 10 subway lines were ordered to run at reduced speeds. All sightseeing boat services were also suspended, Xinhua News Agency reported.
Residents in mountainous villages, low-lying areas and other places at risk of flooding and geological disasters were evacuated, authorities said.
More than 5,000 elderly people were also evacuated from care facilities.
Beijing recorded an average of 23.5 millimetres of rain from Tuesday noon to Wednesday morning.
All 3,357 construction sites across the city were also ordered to suspend work as authorities stepped up flood-control measures, with reservoirs releasing water in advance to create additional storage capacity.
Renewing its orange alert for torrential rain on Wednesday, the National Meteorological Centre forecast heavy rain across a broad swath of the country through Thursday morning.

U.S. President Donald Trump said that the secret flight from Turkey using an Air Force One decoy aircraft was organized by the Secret Service and the military. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were aboard the decoy aircraft.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday evening that his secret flight from Turkey last month, during which a decoy Air Force One aircraft carrying passengers was used, was arranged by the Secret Service and the U.S. military, UNN reports, citing ABC News.
Details
"It depends solely on the Secret Service. I just follow their instructions," Trump told reporters on the runway at Joint Base Andrews after a trip to Ohio.
"So I defer to the Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to fly on a different flight, a different aircraft. Same security. But they wanted me to do it, so I did it. I do what they say," Trump said about the plan to secretly transfer from Air Force One to another aircraft.
Sources familiar with the situation told ABC News that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were aboard the president's decoy aircraft.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was on another aircraft flying alongside the president, sources said.
All three administration officials knew that Trump had secretly transferred from the old presidential aircraft to a military aircraft because of a threat, sources said.
When asked Tuesday evening whether he knew about a specific threat at the time, Trump brushed off the question.
"I guess there was a threat. I didn't particularly ask about it. I get threatened a lot," Trump said.
When asked about the security of the Air Force One decoy aircraft, Trump said that he had faced greater risk on the other aircraft.
"I think the aircraft I was actually flying on was at greater risk," Trump said. "I think it was at greater risk because, I think, that was the aircraft they most likely would have chosen," he said.
Trump had publicly said that he would fly on the old Air Force One rather than the new Air Force One aircraft gifted by Qatar because he was sending it to a base in the United Kingdom so that military personnel could inspect it.
ABC News reported at the time that Trump had been advised not to fly on that aircraft because of security concerns amid the escalating conflict with Iran.
Aboard the Air Force One aircraft on which Trump was believed to be flying, journalists were told that the windows had to remain closed throughout the entire flight, and that this was a Secret Service directive. According to the Post, the Air Force One transponder was turned off despite the president not being aboard.
In a statement to ABC News regarding the Post's report, the White House said: "As the president recently stated, America has many enemies who are targeting him, and we are using every means at our disposal to counter these threats."

More than 1.3 million people in Gaza, or over half the population, have access to less than six liters of water per person a day, the United Nations said on Aug. 11.
The figure is well below the emergency standard of 15 liters, U.N. deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq told reporters at the organization’s headquarters in New York.
Haq said most of Gaza’s population lacked adequate water, sanitation and hygiene services. Much of the limited water available for household use must be delivered by tanker, while more than 900,000 people are exposed to accumulated garbage in residential areas, he added.
He also reported continued Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank. On Aug. 9, settlers set up a checkpoint in the Nablus governorate that cut several Palestinian families, including children, off from essential services such as emergency health care, Haq said.
The World Health Organization recorded 37 attacks on health care in the West Bank in July, well above the monthly average of 10 recorded at the beginning of the year, according to figures cited by Haq.
Reiterating the U.N.’s support for a two-state solution, Haq said Israelis and Palestinians had no alternative but to find a way to live in peace.

'You want it darker?' The ideal total solar eclipse playlist is here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:29:13 UTC
14:29:13 KST

Mainland Europe experiences its full solar eclipse in two decades tonight. The Euronews Culture team picks the 10 songs you need to listen to when darkness falls...
The moon is due to pass directly between the Earth and the sun this evening, leaving millions of mainland Europeans experiencing the first full solar eclipse in two decades.
Considering the next total solar eclipse is not due to occur until 2081 for France, 2090 for the UK and not until the next century for Germany (Spain, on the other hand, get to see one next year), it's worth getting it just right.
We're of the opinion that everybody needs the perfect soundtrack for a celestial event of this magnitude, so to here are our handpicked eclipse (and eclipse-adjacent) songs to accompany you through the sunlight block – in chronological listening order for maximum effect.
Len - 'Steal My Sunshine'
This 90s song by one-hit-wonder Canadian alt-rock band Len was initially released on the soundtrack to the 1999 crime comedy film Go, and became an instant summer hit. Not hard to hear why, as it’s a sun-kissed tune about not plunging anyone into depression by stealing their happiness. Yes, it sounds like an outdated 90s throwback; sure, it’s twee; and granted, good taste dictates that it should only be played at pool parties. But you try resisting that sugary sweet chorus... This should open your eclipse playlist before the great concealing, before things get a bit more ominous... DM
Bill Withers - 'Ain't No Sunshine'
I know, I know, I know, I know that Bill Withers' 'Ain't No Sunshine' is the perfect addition to any total solar eclipse playlist. Inspired by the 1962 film Days of Wine and Roses, Withers penned the soulful masterpiece while working at a toilet seat factory, aged 31. When the song went gold, the record company awarded the singer with a golden toilet seat, marking the start of his new career. The song has since been covered by the likes of Paul McCartney, Tom Jones and Prince, but we can all agree that Wither’s rendition remains unmatched. TF
Bonnie Tyler - 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart'
We sadly lost Bonnie this year, and what better way to honour her musical legacy than by playing her biggest hit? As you “turn around” to look at the sun being obscured by the moon, there’s nothing more appropriate to listen to than her 1983 ballad ‘Total Eclipse of the Heart’. It was written by the late Jim Steinman, a composer with a flair for the theatrical (his other hits include Meat Loaf's ‘I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)’ and Celine Dion's ‘It’s All Coming Back to Me Now’). Whether or not the solar event mirrors your own internal torment, we can surely all agree that belting “forever’s gonna start tonight” will add a sense of cinematic drama to the event. AB
Max Richter - 'On The Nature Of Daylight'
Arguably one of the most famous compositions from neo-classical artist Max Richter, this song off his 2004 album ‘The Blue Notebooks’ (Euronews Culture's top pick for the Best European Albums of the 21st Century) was originally conceived as a response to the Iraq War. Since then, it has been used in countless films and TV shows, from Shutter Island to Hamnet, via Jiro Dreams of Sushi, The Handmaid's Tale and The Last of Us. Granted, it may now have become an overplayed shortcut to punish your tear ducts, but listen to it during the eclipse, and you'll hopefully be reminded of how beautiful, poignant and powerfully cathartic it remains. DM
Soundgarden - 'Black Hole Sun'
From a stellar 80s power ballad to a 90s grunge anthem... Widely recognised as Soundgarden’s signature track, this was arguably Chris Cornell’s shining moment of glory (if you don’t count his often-undervalued work in the supergroup Audioslave). It came out mid-1994, when the world was still under the shock of Kurt Cobain’s death, and it’s the ideal dark anthem to listen to while you’re luxuriating in darkness, appreciating the contradictory beauty of both the eclipse and this song about concealed darkness in humanity. DM
Pink Floyd - 'Eclipse'
If you're not enjoying this playlist, there's a case to be made for just listening to the entirety of Pink Floyd's 'The Dark Side of the Moon' prior to, during and following the eclipse. But if you're sticking with us and our somewhat protracted curation, we suggest you choose the aptly titled 'Eclipse'. The album's closing track ends with the lyrics "All that is now / And all that is gone / And that's to come / And everything under the sun is in tune / But the sun is eclipsed by the moon". Perfection. DM
Leonard Cohen – 'You Want It Darker'
This year's total eclipse will pass over the Arctic, Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain. The rest of Europe will get a partial eclipse – a little more than 90%. So, why not be greedy and pick this cut from Leonard Cohen's final studio album? “You want it darker / We kill the flame." Prepare for shivers. DM
David Bowie – 'Blackstar'
While we're luxuriating in darkness (and appreciating two back-to-back tracks from artists we lost ten years ago), listen to David Bowie's title track from his final LP, 'Blackstar'. Released two days before his death, this song is tailor-made for the celestial event. And it wouldn't be a true eclipse playlist without the Starman, would it? DM
Bruce Springsteen - 'Dancing In The Dark'
Let's get a little less dour, shall we? Bruce Springsteen’s classic 1984 tune should prepare you to see the sun once more. Written about the pressures of fame and trying to force creativity, Springsteen told the BBC: “All I could do was write another song about not wanting to write another song". In the years since, it’s become a beloved anthem that always starts a fire in your belly. And how often is it that you actually get to dance in true darkness?! AB
The Beatles - 'Here Comes The Sun'
As the moon begins to move away and the sun reemerges, what better way to celebrate the return of the light than with The Beatles’ timeless classic 'Here Comes the Sun'? Written by George Harrison in early 1969 from the country house of Eric Clapton, the heartwarming song reflects the temporary respite he was experiencing from the band’s Apple Corps business affairs. As one of the standouts from the Fab Four's legendary 'Abbey Road' album, the song earned Harrison his songwriting flowers, previously reserved for Lennon and McCartney. It’s the perfect way to end your eclipse. TF
Enjoy full blackout and remember to put on special eclipse glasses. And headphones.

Russia appoints former CJI DY Chandrachud as arbitrator in Ukraine's Oschadbank case
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 12, 2026, 13:02 IST
Comments

File photo: Former CJI Justice DY Chandrachud (Picture credit: PTI)
Former chief justice of India D Y Chandrachud has been appointed by Russia as its arbitrator in an investment treaty dispute filed by Ukrainian state-owned bank Oschadbank, according to a report by Global Arbitration Review, as cited by Bar and Bench.The dispute is being heard by a three-member arbitral tribunal under the 1998 bilateral investment treaty between Ukraine and Russia.Costa Rican arbitrator and former trade minister Dyalá Jiménez will serve as the tribunal's president after being jointly selected by both parties.Greek arbitrator and National University of Singapore professor Stavros Brekoulakis was appointed by Oschadbank, while Justice Chandrachud was appointed by Russia.
Dispute concerns Oschadbank assets in four Ukrainian regions
Oschadbank's claim concerns assets and operations in Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia that the Ukrainian state-owned bank says it lost following Russian military actions in Ukraine, particularly after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.The claim is understood to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. According to Bar and Bench, Oschadbank initiated the arbitration after serving Russia with a notice of dispute in July 2025, which allegedly went unanswered.
The proceedings have been initiated under the 1998 Agreement between the Government of the Russian Federation and the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine on the Encouragement and Mutual Protection of Investments.The dispute is separate from an earlier Oschadbank arbitration concerning its operations and assets in Crimea following Russia's 2014 annexation of the peninsula.In that earlier case, a tribunal constituted under the Permanent Court of Arbitration found Russia liable for unlawful expropriation and awarded Oschadbank approximately $1.1 billion in damages, along with interest and arbitration costs.Russia had declined to participate in those proceedings, but the tribunal proceeded under the applicable arbitration rules.
Chandrachud had earlier declined Russia's approaches
Justice Chandrachud had previously declined approaches from Russia to serve as its arbitrator in treaty disputes involving German energy company Wintershall Dea and Ukrainian state energy company Ukrenergo.He had also been designated by the Permanent Court of Arbitration as the appointing authority in the Wintershall proceedings. He later stepped down from that role after disclosing the communications from Russia.His appointment as Russia's arbitrator in the Oschadbank case therefore marks a change from his earlier decision not to accept Russia's approaches in those proceedings.
Three-member tribunal to hear the case
Jiménez, who was jointly selected by Oschadbank and Russia, will preside over the tribunal. Brekoulakis was appointed by Oschadbank, while Justice Chandrachud was appointed by Russia.Oschadbank is represented by Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan partners Epaminontas Triantafilou and Alex Gerbi, along with Asters partners Oleksiy Didkovskiy, Andrii Pozhidayev and Oksana Legka.Russia is represented by Pinna Goldberg partner Andrea Pinna, counsel Pratyush Panjwani and senior associate Dimitrios Papageorgiou.The case comes against the broader backdrop of investment disputes arising from Russia's military actions in Ukraine and the resulting loss of Ukrainian businesses and assets in territories under Russian control.
Russia-Ukraine war sees fresh escalation as Zelenskyy flags North Korean support
Meanwhile, the Russia-Ukraine war continued to escalate, with at least 10 civilians killed in Russian missile, drone and glide-bomb attacks across Ukraine on Tuesday, according to Ukrainian officials.President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces used North Korean-supplied ballistic missiles in a strike on Zaporizhzhia that killed seven steel plant workers and injured 21 others.
Zelenskyy also said North Korea was preparing to deploy additional troops to Russia.Russia, meanwhile, said it intercepted nearly 400 Ukrainian drones, while Ukraine reported strikes on a Russian oil refinery in Orsk and a Ukrainian drone attack in Tatarstan that killed at least 12 people and injured 39 others.The UN also said more than 16,000 Ukrainian civilians detained by Russia remain deprived of their liberty, with reports of continuing torture and ill-treatment.

Indonesia: Passengers rescued after Bali ferry catches fire
August 12, 2026
Indonesian authorities rescued 172 people from a burning ferry on Wednesday near the tourist island of Bali.
At least one person, a 19-year-old woman, was killed in the incident, officials said.
The fire broke out on the Padang Bai-Lembar ferry route connecting Bali and Lombok and is also used by tourists travelling between the two popular destinations.
It is the second major ferry fire in Indonesia this month.
What Indonesian authorities said about the ferry fire
Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office, had initially told Metro TV that all passengers had been deboarded from the burning ferry.
"We have approached the ship and confirmed that all passengers are no longer on board," he said. "We visually see no passengers on the ship."
Later, Hariyadi told reporters that a woman had been declared dead.
The ferry was estimated to be carrying 114 passengers and 17 crew members, Hariyadi had said referring to the passenger manifest data released by Padang Bai's port authority.
However, the final tally of passengers and crew was significantly above the 131 people estimated.
What else do we know about the fire and rescue efforts?
Fire broke out on board the Putri Yasmin Ferry at about 4:15 a.m. (1045 GMT) while it was en route from Padang Bai port in Bali to Lembar port on the adjacent island of Lombok, according to the search office in Mataram.
The agency received an emergency report nearly half an hour later and then deployed rescue vessels and personnel.
Survivor Kiky Okta Pradika, 25, told reporters in Lembar he had grabbed a life jacket before jumping overboard with several other passengers."There were a few hours before there was any help," he said.
The burning ferry was in the midst of rough seas with waves as high as 4 meters (13 feet), Hariyadi said, adding that conditions had complicated rescue efforts.
A ferry in the vicinity had evacuated 30 passengers and brought them to Bali. A search and rescue vessel was on its way to Lembar port with 59 of the rescued passengers. A naval vessel picked up another 17 passengers.
Two of the rescued passengers were Australian tourists.
Marine safety in Indonesia
Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia where ferries are a common mode of transport.
Last week, five people died in a ferry fire off the coast of Java Island. Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Seayar Island. The rescue operation had been closed after four bodies were recovered, but 14 were officially still missing.
And in July last year, a ferry sank while travelling between Java and Bali, killing nearly 20 people.

Fire at polystyrene manufacturing plant in Rivne region extinguished: what about air pollution
Kyiv • UNN
A plant producing polystyrene and dry mixes caught fire in the village of Varkovychi. The fire was extinguished, there were no casualties, but elevated concentrations of nitrogen dioxide and soot were recorded in the air.
In the Rivne region, rescuers extinguished a large-scale fire at an enterprise, the regional office of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reported on the evening of August 11, UNN writes.
Details
Rescuers received a report of a fire in a warehouse building in the village of Varkovychi, Dubno district, on August 11 at 12:32.
"Upon arriving at the scene, the rescuers saw that the fire had engulfed the warehouse premises. Dry grass was also burning in the open area next to the warehouse," the statement said.
As indicated, the fire was contained at 15:04 and completely extinguished at 17:49.
There were no fatalities or injuries.
Seventeen pieces of specialized equipment and 48 rescuers were involved in extinguishing the fire.
The cause of the fire and the amount of damage caused are currently being established.
As reported by the Varkovychi village territorial community on Facebook, the enterprise that burned is engaged in the production of plastic (foam/polystyrene) boards and sheets and dry construction mixtures, and advised residents to close their windows.
The Rivne Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention reported that, as of 8 p.m. on August 11, the latest laboratory tests in the village of Varkovychi recorded exceedances of the maximum permissible concentrations: nitrogen dioxide — 1.4 times; soot — nearly 3 times.
In the village of Molodizhne, exceedances were also recorded: nitrogen dioxide — 1.1 times; soot — 2 times. No exceedances were detected for the other indicators tested — sulfur dioxide, formaldehyde, and phenol.

More moving and less screens — Finland's school year starts with active plans for kids
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:17:53 EEST
14:17:53 KST

Children will return to classrooms across Finland on Wednesday, with schools opening again after the long summer break in cities such as Helsinki, Lahti, Jyväskylä, Joensuu, Oulu and Rovaniemi.
Kids in the cities of Espoo and Vantaa get one more day of summer holiday, as they return tomorrow, while schools in Tampere have been back in business since last week.
The new school year also brings many changes, with education authorities keen to tighten the ban on mobile phones introduced last year, while a new initiative called 'Finland on the Move' aims to promote a physically active lifestyle for all children.
Terhi Nissinen of the Finnish National Agency for Education told Yle that the changes will be visible in the lives of every primary school student.
"Lesson planning will emphasise activity, and there will be less sitting time," Nissinen explained.
This also means that during breaks between classes, teacher-led games and pursuits as well as "välkkäri" (peer mentoring) activities will be increased.
The Finnish term "Välkkäri" — derived from the word "välitunti", meaning break or recess — refers to a peer mentoring or buddy system in Finnish schools where older students help, play with or look after their younger peers during breaktimes.
"Hopefully this [the promotion of a more active lifestyle] will also be reflected in every student's journey to school, that they travel by physical means," Nissinen added, referring to kids walking or biking to school.
"School shopping" takes on racist tone
As the school year starts again, recent changes to student catchment area boundaries in the east of Helsinki have reignited a debate around so-called "school shopping".
The term refers to the practice of parents trying to get their children into non-local schools that they see as more desirable.
In practice, the boundary changes in the east of Helsinki means that some children from the Herttoniemi and Myllypuro areas would in future go to the Itäkeskus Primary School — but many parents have strongly opposed the proposed changes.
According to Annette Ukkola of the Finnish Education Evaluation Centre (FINECC), schools in areas where there are perceived to be many foreign-language speaking students tend to be considered less desirable.
"Yes, it can certainly look like racism if [schools] are avoided specifically on the basis that there are many S2 students," Ukkola said.
S2 refers to suomi toisena kielenä (Finnish as a second language), a specialised school subject and alternative curriculum for students whose native language is not Finnish, Swedish, or Sámi.
Ukkola added that there is a growing perception in Finland that a child must attend a reputable primary school and upper secondary school if they are to have any chance of securing a spot at university, but this idea is mistaken.
She noted that there are many different routes to university or higher education in general in Finland, and there is no obligation for children to progress in school at exactly the same pace as the majority.

Analysts said the introduction of North Korean missiles into Russia’s long-range arsenal would complicate Ukraine’s air-defense planning, noting that the weapons differ in flight profile and guidance behavior from Russian-made systems, forcing Kyiv to adapt intercept tactics and sensor coverage to counter a more varied threat set.
Analysts said the use of North Korean missiles would likely force Ukraine to expand its intercept tactics across multiple layers of its air-defense network, noting that the differing speeds and trajectories of Pyongyang-supplied weapons complicate shooter-to-target pairing and increase the strain on already limited interceptor stocks.
They added that Russia’s reliance on foreign munitions could allow Moscow to sustain high-tempo air assaults even as its domestic production struggles to keep pace, giving the Kremlin additional flexibility in timing and sequencing long-range attacks against Ukrainian cities.
Ukrainian officials said the attack demonstrated that Russia was broadening its missile inventory in ways designed to exploit gaps in Ukraine’s defenses, arguing that the arrival of North Korean systems made rapid Western resupply even more critical.
They warned that without accelerated deliveries of long-range interceptors, Ukraine would face increasing difficulty countering mixed-origin missile packages, particularly those combining Russian ballistic missiles with Pyongyang-supplied systems launched in coordinated waves.
The Kremlin, in its initial reaction, denied that North Korean weapons were used in the assault and claimed that reports from Kyiv were “fabricated,” repeating Moscow’s standard line that Russia relies solely on domestically produced munitions.

10th Baltic Film Days bring the best of new Latvian and Lithuanian cinema
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:16:00 UTC
14:16:00 KST

10th Baltic Film Days bring the best of new Latvian and Lithuanian cinema
The Baltic Film Days will take place from August 25–26, bringing recent major Latvian and Lithuanian films to the screen at Tallinn's Sõprus Cinema.
The program will feature a selection of Latvian and Lithuanian feature films from the past year, as well as a documentary and a program of short films. Selected screenings will be followed by meetings with the filmmakers, offering audiences an opportunity to discuss the films' themes in greater depth and hear the filmmakers share their knowledge and experience.
The event will also take place simultaneously in Latvia and Lithuania, celebrating the cultural distinctiveness of the Baltic states and marking the anniversary of the Baltic Way.
"The Visitor"
Director: Vytautas Katkus
As summer comes to an end in Šventoji, the Lithuanian seaside town draws its last warm breath. Danielius, a new father, leaves his family life in Norway behind and returns to Lithuania to sell his late parents' apartment. He reconnects with childhood friends, their relatives and new residents. He wanders alone through the forest, settling into quiet routines, candid conversations and playful games in nearly deserted places where few words are spoken. Everything here has changed.
It feels as though director Vytautas Katkus merely glanced at the screenplay before setting it aside and improvising. Shooting on 16 mm film, he captures poetic moments with friends, most of whom are not actors. "The Visitor" drifts along in the irreversible flow of time and undoubtedly deserves to be seen more than once.
"Flesh, Blood, Even a Heart"
Director: Alise Zariņa
When you think positively, the universe responds. This gentle, feel-good coming-of-age dramedy for 30-somethings follows Liv, a passionate woman struggling with body insecurities. She carries her past lightly and never judges others. She loves water flowers and has a soft spot for poodles, despite never having owned a dog. Once, Liv dreamed of being a Barbie and still hopes her loving, somewhat old-fashioned husband finds her irresistible, even if their kisses are few and far between.
Everything changes when Liv receives a sudden call: her estranged father is in a coma and undergoing intensive therapy. Her awkward, cynical mother remains stuck in the past with rigid rules and sees the stroke as a random attempt to escape. Liv wants to speak to her father, but each visit leaves her lost in the maze-like corridors of the brutalist hospital.
"Dog of God"
Directors: Raitis Abele, Lauris Ābele
It seems our southern neighbors have really hit their stride when it comes to animation. While their "Flow" captivated mass audiences and even the American Academy, the Ābele brothers' nightmarish offering is aimed primarily at genre fans and anyone with a taste for more perverse humor that pushes the boundaries of good taste. And there is plenty of it here — a great deal, in fact!
The film is set in the village of Zaube in Livonia in the late 17th century where everyone seems to be gripped by an inexplicable delirium, awaiting the arrival of evil. A witch trial culminates in the testimony of an old man branded a werewolf who claims he travels to hell to battle the devil and his witches in order to ensure a good harvest. But this bodes well for no one.
"Renovation"
Director: Gabriele Urbonaite
Translator Ilona and tour guide Matas plan to move in together after two years as a couple. They move into a new apartment just as renovations begin on the building. The constant drilling and hammering soon become exhausting.
Ilona's sharp-tongued mother visits to voice her disappointment over her daughter's unfulfilled potential, comparing her with former classmate Laura who has earned a doctorate and is now engaged. Ilona could have made many different choices. She resents Matas reminding her that she will soon turn 30 and dodges any talk of marriage.
One sunny day, Oleg, a Ukrainian construction worker, unexpectedly enters Ilona's life via the neighboring apartment's balcony and changes it profoundly. A painter before the war, Oleg knows the work of Lithuania's most famous artist and composer, Čiurlionis. Hoping to impress him, Ilona pretends to be a poet. Their encounters become more frequent and the air fills with unspoken attraction. Oleg tells Ilona that if she truly loves Matas, she should talk to him.
"A Goodnight Kiss"
Director: Giedrė Žickytė
Following her widely acclaimed film "The Jump," Giedrė Žickytė returns with her most heartfelt documentary to date. It is impossible to remain indifferent to the story of Irena Veisaitė. She was a writer, human rights activist and one of Lithuania's most perceptive and wise women who warned of the wars that continue to shape our world today.
A Holocaust survivor, Irena lost her parents and found refuge with a Christian family during the Soviet occupation of Lithuania. She died in 2020 while the film was in pre-production. Her death prompted Žickytė to seek new ways to bring to life Irena's moving memories of her two mothers, her lifelong friendship with Estonian composer Arvo Pärt and her guiding principle: to live without revenge or hatred.
Exploring Irena's story through archival footage, photographs and old interviews inspired Žickytė to uncover previously untold stories of Jewish Vilnius, once known as the Jerusalem of the North.
"Red Code Blue"
Director: Oskars Rupenheits
This independently produced crime drama authentically transports viewers back to the dangerous, frantic and uncertain 1990s. Riga is consumed by lawlessness and chaos, marked by high-stakes chases, intense interrogations and shootouts between rival gangs, reckless punks, corrupt agents and ruthless cops. In this harsh world, honesty and loyalty are punished without hesitation.
Young and idealistic investigator Romans Skulte struggles from his very first shift to find his footing in the brutal, cold labyrinth of newly independent Latvia. Drug traffickers and violent gangsters rule the desolate streets under the covert protection of high-ranking officials. Those who show initiative pay a heavy price. Young cadets quickly learn that trust is a liability, even among close friends, as traitors and informants lurk at every turn.
Cunning Georgian smugglers are deeply entrenched in a frightened society, while an aggressive Armenian mafia fearlessly stakes its claim. This slow-burn police thriller is packed with nerve-wracking heists, betrayals, extortions, bribes and relentless pursuits. All characters are fictional, though inspired by real-life investigations. In his debut lead role, Raitis Sturmanis brings to mind a young Charlie Sheen.

Craig was among the minority of House Democrats who voted against that effort, maintaining her support for U.S. military assistance to Israel.
Flanagan also repeatedly highlighted Craig’s past endorsements from AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and sought to cast the race as a fight against the influence of wealthy donors and outside groups.
She emphasized during the campaign that she did not accept “AIPAC money.”
AIPAC, however, did not endorse Craig in the Senate primary and did not directly spend money on her behalf in the race.
Craig’s past support from the organization nevertheless became a political liability among progressive voters, reflecting the widening divide inside the Democratic Party over Israel.
“I love that she doesn’t take any corporate money, she doesn’t take any money from AIPAC,” Flanagan supporter Andrea Ropella said. “The things that she says, she believes in and she stands for.”
The race was also shaped heavily by immigration policy and the Trump administration’s enforcement campaign in Minnesota.
Flanagan attacked Craig for voting for the Laken Riley Act, a Trump-backed immigration measure passed early in the president’s second term. Craig later repudiated her support after federal immigration officers shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.
The killings, both captured on camera, fueled a backlash against Trump’s immigration policies and became a major issue in the closing stages of the primary.
Gov. Tim Walz declined to endorse either Democrat, although his wife, Gwen Walz, endorsed Craig late last month, a move viewed as a notable break with Flanagan, who has served as Walz’s running mate and governing partner for two terms.
On the Republican side, Tafoya emerged from a crowded field despite Trump declining to endorse a Senate candidate. She had support from the national GOP and defeated rivals including Marine veteran and former Navy SEAL Adam Schwarze and conservative commentator Royce White.
Republicans also held a closely watched gubernatorial primary in which state House Speaker Lisa Demuth defeated Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and longtime Trump ally.
Trump had endorsed Lindell and wrote on social media Tuesday that he “deserves a BIG WIN.”
Lindell has been one of the most persistent promoters of false claims that Trump’s 2020 election defeat was fraudulent. Some Minnesota Republicans had openly questioned whether his polarizing profile would make him unelectable in a general election.
Demuth will face Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who defeated six opponents to secure her party’s gubernatorial nomination.
Republicans have not won a statewide race in Minnesota since 2006, but they hope a major public-funds fraud scandal will give them an opening this year.
At least 65 people have been convicted in overlapping food-fraud cases stemming from investigations launched during the Biden administration. One former nonprofit leader was sentenced in May to 42 years in prison in connection with a $250 million fraud scheme.
Trump has cited the scandals in defending a sweeping immigration crackdown in Minnesota, which he initially said would focus on the state’s large Somali community.
For Democrats, however, Flanagan’s victory is likely to draw broader attention because of what it signals about the party’s internal battle over Israel.
Her win follows other recent successes by progressive candidates willing to sharply challenge longstanding Democratic support for the Jewish state, while candidates identified with the party establishment and the pro-Israel camp face growing pressure from primary voters.

Hong Kong was once again gripped by extreme heat on Wednesday as temperatures reached 37.5 degrees Celsius (99.5 Fahrenheit) in parts of the city, prompting calls for a district-level index to better protect outdoor workers.

Solar eclipse followed by meteor shower: Portugal prepares to watch two rare events
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:05:53 UTC
14:05:53 KST

In some parts of the country, the Moon will completely cover the Sun, plunging onlookers into a sci-fi-like scene.
In Portugal today, the national team are not playing, the prime minister is not addressing the country, there are no COVID-19 press conferences, but the country will still stop at the same time to look at the same thing: the total eclipse of the Sun.
Around 19.30, in the Bragança region, the total eclipse of the Sun will occur, meaning day will turn into night as the Sun is covered by the Moon. As well as getting darker, ambient noise drops, the temperature changes and many more shadows are cast.
This will be an astronomical spectacle nobody will want to miss, not least because it is highly unusual and the last total eclipse visible from mainland Portugal took place in 1912.
But the eclipse will not be the only phenomenon to amaze this evening. From 21:30 on Wednesday, about an hour after the eclipse ends in mainland Portugal, there will also be a meteor shower. These meteors, known as the Perseids, leave a trail of light as they pass through the atmosphere.
This is an annual meteor shower, usually active from mid-July until the end of August. The peak generally occurs around 12 and 13 August.
As the Moon will be practically new, the sky will be very dark and conditions will be especially favourable for observing the phenomenon. However, for the best possible viewing experience, experts recommend finding a dark place with an unobstructed horizon.
Activity is expected to increase between midnight and 02:00, but the most favourable period to try to spot the highest number of meteors will be between 02:00 and 05:00 in the early hours of the 13th, when the Perseus constellation, the point from which the meteors appear to radiate, rises higher in the sky.
The best places to watch the phenomenon are Dark Sky Alqueva in the Alentejo, the world’s first certified dark-sky territory; in the North, the Montesinho and Bragança area in Trás-os-Montes; in the Serra da Estrela, Peneda-Gerês or any high, inland area away from settlements.
For an even more exciting experience, a few tricks also help, and it is essential to avoid looking at screens for 20 to 30 minutes beforehand so that your eyes adapt to the darkness and can focus on the meteor shower.
What is a solar eclipse?
The astronomical phenomenon known as an eclipse occurs when one celestial body blocks the light from another. In the case of a solar eclipse, the Moon completely or partially covers the light of the Sun, producing what is known as the "diamond ring", which lasts only a few seconds.
Where can I see the eclipse?
The eclipse will be visible across the country but it will not look the same in all regions. The total eclipse, which corresponds to 100%, will be visible only in the Montesinho Natural Park, in Bragança.
The deep partial eclipse, with between 92% and 99% coverage, can be observed throughout mainland Portugal.
On the islands, the Azores and Madeira, the percentage is much lower, between 74% and 77%.
It is advisable to watch the moment from a wide-open space, so buildings don't block your view.
What time does the eclipse happen in Portugal?
The eclipse will begin at around 18:33 and end at around 20:23, lasting roughly two hours. Its maximum will be reached close to 19:30. The total eclipse phase lasts just 25 seconds.
Can I watch the eclipse without glasses?
No. You must never look directly at the Sun during the phenomenon. There is only one safe way to see the eclipse: using proper eclipse viewing glasses. The phenomenon must not be watched with sunglasses, through telescopes or with the naked eye, as it can cause eye damage. Direct sunlight does not cause immediate pain, but it can burn the retina, leading to later consequences such as permanent loss of vision.
In Portugal, ZEISS launched a campaign offering free eclipse glasses across the country. All you had to do was go to an optician in the Club de Visão network, after registering in advance. However, the initiative was limited to existing stock and it is no longer possible to obtain them free of charge.
You can buy eclipse glasses, but the optics community has set out some key features to check that you are purchasing the right model. The glasses must have ISO 12312-2 or ISO 12312-2:2015 certification for solar observation, as well as the CE marking printed on the frame. They must also ensure the blocking of UV, IR and intense visible light. They should be prefabricated and ready to use, with no assembly required.
You can buy the glasses in pharmacies, some supermarkets and online shops such as Astroshop, Telescopiomania, ESTUDIOPT, Aff Camera Store or Sol & Salvo, which sell these glasses for prices ranging from 2.90 to 3.25 euros per unit. These shops also offer packs for families or groups of friends.
Protect your phone as well as your eyes
Your smartphone can also be easily damaged by taking photos of the eclipse. A smartphone's optics work, in a way, like a magnifying glass: they concentrate the light entering through the lens onto a tiny surface, the camera sensor. Pointing that lens at the Sun for several minutes with no protection can overheat the camera module and permanently burn the photodiodes that make up the sensor, leaving blotches or dead pixels that cannot be recovered. It can also trigger the phone's thermal protection, shutting it down abruptly.
There is no need to splash out on an expensive accessory. An affordable option is to cut a lens from a pair of certified eclipse glasses and tape it over your phone's camera, covering the whole lens with no gaps where light can leak in.
Are there places where I can watch together with other people?
Yes, there are lots of events taking place across Portugal. Some no longer accept participants, as they required prior registration. Even so, here are some of these initiatives, from north to south of the country, where you can still try to take part free of charge:
- Faro and Albufeira
Promoted by the Centro Ciência Viva do Algarve, there will be guided sessions for observing the partial solar eclipse in Faro and Albufeira. In Faro, the event will take place in the Parque Ribeirinho from 18:30. Admission is free and the minimum age for participants is 12.
In Albufeira, it will be held in the parish of Paderne, at the parish castle. The event is free and will continue into the night with observation of a Perseid meteor shower.
- Tavira
- "Solar Eclipse and Night-time Observation of Celestial Bodies"
Organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Tavira in partnership with Tavira municipality, it will take place in Praça da República. Admission is free and the minimum age is 3.
"During the activity, there will be a brief explanation of how solar eclipses form and discussions will be held on the importance of scientific research and observing the sky," the organisers say.
- "Solar Eclipse at Praia do Arraial" and "Solar Eclipse at Praia do Barril"
Both events are organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Tavira and are free of charge. They start at 18:30, but it is advisable to arrive a little earlier. At Praia do Arraial, the minimum age to take part is 5. At Praia do Barril, it is 3.
- Oeiras The partial solar eclipse will also be visible from Santo Amaro beach in Oeiras. Here, the phenomenon is expected to reach around 95%. The event is organised by the local authority, which has prepared a festive afternoon from 16:00, combining a summer party atmosphere with observation of the phenomenon.
As well as a DJ set, a large screen will be installed to show the eclipse live, allowing everyone to follow it without risk to their eyesight. The session will be accompanied by explanations of what is being seen.
- Enxara do Bispo (Mafra)
"When the sky darkens: Understanding the Solar Eclipse and how to observe it safely" is one of the initiatives taking place in the late afternoon of the 12th. It is organised by the Associação Astronómica Horizonte Estelar, with the meeting point set for the churchyard at 17:00. The event lasts 3 hours and 30 minutes. Before the eclipse, there will be a theoretical introduction to the phenomenon and, during it, explanations will be given to participants. The minimum age to take part is 6.
- Porto
"Solar Eclipse 2026 at Time Out Market Porto" is organised by the market, which invites everyone to gather in the outdoor square, with a privileged view of the Clérigos Tower. The event starts at 18:00 and runs for 3 hours.
The organisers say that "to mark the occasion, a themed cocktail called 'Eclipse' has been created. With the purchase of this cocktail, a pair of solar viewing glasses will be offered, while stocks last."
- Vila do Conde
Organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Vila do Conde, the eclipse can be observed in a group from the seafront, in front of the Farol restaurant. Admission is free and the event starts at 16:00. The recommended minimum age to observe the phenomenon is 6.
There are also private initiatives organised by groups of friends on social media pages. Check whether anything is being organised in your area.

Anxious dogs and silent birds: What happens to animals during a total solar eclipse?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:02:16 UTC
14:02:16 KST

Today's rare solar eclipse is thrilling for humans, but animals will face something they can't prepare for: sudden confusing darkness in the middle of the day.
Once day seemingly and unexpectedly turns to night, many animals will likely feel confused, disorientated or stressed - thankfully, for just a few minutes.
Animals, both wild and domesticated, rely on important environmental cues - like light and temperature - to help them navigate their daily lives. As light fades and temperatures drop, these cues suddenly change.
Scientists who have studied animal behaviour during eclipses have a fairly clear picture of what tends to happen - even if not every animal reacts the same way.
How different species react to eclipses
People observing a total solar eclipse often notice the sudden silence. Birds that sing throughout the day frequently stop the moment darkness falls, as though evening has arrived hours early. Nocturnal animals, such as owls, can do the opposite and become active, behaving as though dusk has begun.
Many - from zoo mammals to bees and other insects - interpret the sudden darkness as nightfall. Elephants have been seen heading straight for their night-time dens, treating the eclipse as their usual lock-up signal. Others show clearer signs of stress: gorillas have charged the glass of their enclosures, while giraffes have paced and swayed.
House pets may be worried too. Dogs and cats often pace, whine or hide during totality - a response some researchers compare to how pets react to fireworks or thunderstorms.
Normality returns within minutes
Total darkness itself is brief - lasting only a few minutes. As sunlight returns, the animal behaviour reverts just as suddenly.
Birds often burst into song, reportedly singing even louder than they would at a normal dawn. Within a short time, most animals settle back into their ordinary daytime routines, as if nothing unusual had happened at all.
