Gagauzia head transferred to prison with conditions degrading to human dignity — lawyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
03:24:37 UTC
12:24:37 KST

CHISINAU, August 12. /TASS/. The head of the Gagauzia autonomy, Evgenia Gutsul, has been transferred to a women's prison with worse conditions of detention, her lawyer, Sergiu Moraru, told TASS.
"The state is obliged to provide conditions that do not degrade human dignity. And the conditions there are very poor. First of all, the tap water is of very poor quality, it is dreadful to look at. It often happens that there is no water at all for two or three days. And this is in such heat. It is impossible to wash properly, to use the toilet, to maintain basic personal hygiene. There are also other peculiarities of this prison," the lawyer said.
The reference is to the only women's prison in Moldova, No. 7, located near the village of Rusca in the Hincesti District. According to the lawyer, the politician is isolated from other inmates and is held in a solitary cell. Chisinau Prison No. 13, where Gutsul spent just over a year, is known in human rights reports for its inhumane conditions. However, the prison near the village of Rusca is even worse, Moraru said.
"There are grounds for Gutsul to remain in Prison No. 13. We filed a corresponding motion so that I could participate in investigative actions in another criminal case. But they did not want to - they somehow specially arranged for Gutsul to be sent to the prison in the village of Rusca. Probably knowing that the conditions there are even worse than in Prison No. 13," the lawyer said.
Last August, a Moldovan court sentenced Gutsul to seven years in prison on charges related to irregularities in funding her political party. Gutsul has denied the charges, and her legal team has filed an appeal, which remains pending. Relations between Gutsul and Moldova’s leadership soured further in 2023 after her electoral victory in Gagauzia and her public statements advocating for stronger ties with Russia, as well as her criticism of Chisinau’s confrontational policies toward Moscow.

Reds rally late, beat the White Sox 5-4 in the 10th to spoil pope hat giveaway night
CHICAGO (AP) — Elly De La Cruz drove in automatic runner Matt McLain with a sacrifice fly in the top of the 10th inning as the Cincinnati Reds snapped a three-game skid with a 5-4 comeback win over the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday night.
The Reds rallied from three runs down in the eighth inning after White Sox starter Sean Burke allowed only one run on three hits in seven innings.
Sean Newcomb (1-3) took the loss. Brock Burke (5-4) picked up the win and Emilio Pagan recorded his 14th save with a perfect 10th.
Bryan Hudson gave up an RBI single to De La Cruz in the eighth and Tyler Stephenson drove in two runs with a basesloaded single off Grant Taylor to tie the score.
The White Sox drew 38,113, their ninth sellout, for a unique giveaway: team-branded papal-style hats in honor of Pope Leo XIV, a lifelong White Sox fan who attended Game 1 of the 2005 World Series as Father Robert Prevost. Sister Mary Jo Sobieck threw out the first pitch.
Brenton Doyle hit Nick Lodolo’s first pitch 415 feet to deep center, his fourth career leadoff home run and the sixth for the White Sox this season. Edgar Quero and Miguel Vargas also hit solo home runs for the White Sox.
Burke scattered three hits over seven innings, allowing one run on Eugenio Suarez’s third homer in four games, his 17th. Burke, who has allowed two or fewer runs in eight of his last nine starts, struck out eight Tuesday, walking none.
Muneteka Murakami extended his on-base streak to 26 games with a double in the eighth.
Lodolo was activated off the injured list (blister) to make his first start since July 11. He gave up four runs on five hits in four innings.

Mostly dry weather in Ukraine today, temperatures up to +33°C
Ukrinform

Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) will push ahead with talks on extending stock market trading hours by releasing a discussion paper, even as it faces brokers’ concerns over a longer trading time and cancellation of the trading lunch break, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter.

If the discussion paper gained supportive feedback, HKEX would later issue a public consultation paper to propose new trading hours for the cash market, said one source, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.

====================================================================================================

Dobronsky carries experience from abroad Israel can use, but only if he comes home - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
03:19:31 UTC
12:19:31 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s first handpicked addition to Likud’s Knesset slate is Oren Dobronsky, an Israeli-born technology entrepreneur who has spent much of the past two decades in the United States. Dobronsky co-founded Hotbar, became a Silicon Valley investor, and built the California restaurant chain Oren’s Hummus. His public professional profile lists Palo Alto as his location.
Likud announced this week that Dobronsky would be Netanyahu’s first reserved candidate and said he would lead the party’s work on artificial intelligence across the economy, education, medicine, and other fields. Walla subsequently reported that Netanyahu had promised him a ministerial portfolio dealing with AI if the prime minister forms the next government.
Within hours of the announcement, a recent social media post in which Dobronsky sharply attacked US President Donald Trump was circulated widely. Dobronsky apologized, saying he had lost his temper and regretted the post.
The appointment also comes in the middle of a heated national argument over Israelis who live abroad and plan to return to vote in the October 27 election. The Fly&Vote initiative says tens of thousands of Israelis overseas have registered and hopes eventually to help bring as many as 70,000 to Israel for Election Day.
Dobronsky may have a great deal to contribute. Israel needs serious people in public life who understand technology, entrepreneurship, investment, and the global competition over artificial intelligence. His record in the technology sector gives him experience that could prove valuable in government.
Netanyahu’s choice nevertheless raises a basic question that deserves a clear answer before Election Day: Is Dobronsky coming home?
This should not be read as criticism of Israelis who spend periods of their lives abroad. Israelis leave for work, study, family, professional opportunities, and many other legitimate reasons. Many remain deeply connected to the country, contribute to Israeli society from overseas, and eventually return. Israel benefits from those ties.
Israelis abroad should be encouraged to remain engaged with Jewish state
In many cases, time abroad allows Israelis to gain experience, expertise, and connections that ultimately strengthen the country. We should encourage those Israelis to remain engaged with Israel and, when they choose, to bring that experience home.
The issue here is much narrower. What level of commitment and physical presence should Israelis expect from someone seeking to represent them in the Knesset and potentially serve as a cabinet minister?
Publicly available profiles have placed Dobronsky and his family in Palo Alto for years. Israelis living abroad retain a legitimate stake in the country and have made enormous contributions to it, especially since October 7. Serving in the Knesset carries a different level of responsibility. Members make decisions about war, taxation, education, health, military service, and countless other matters whose consequences are felt every day by the people living here.
Israeli law makes the distinction relevant. An Israeli citizen who meets the legal requirements can run for the Knesset without a general residency requirement. Ministers, however, must be Israeli citizens and residents of Israel. If Dobronsky is being prepared for an AI ministry, voters deserve to know where he intends to base his life and when.
The question matters even more because Netanyahu is exercising considerable control over the Likud list. Likud members are preparing to vote in primaries while a number of reserved positions will bypass the party electorate.
Every reserved slot therefore carries a higher burden of explanation. Why this person? What public mission does the candidate bring? Has the candidate been properly vetted? What commitment is being made to voters?
The questions surrounding Dobronsky's selection
The Trump episode adds to those questions. Dobronsky has every right to criticize an American president. Israeli public officials must be able to disagree with Washington when Israel’s interests require it. His rapid apology immediately after entering politics does, however, raise questions about how carefully the party examined its first personal selection beforehand.
Israel should welcome talented Israelis who return from abroad to serve. Dobronsky could bring valuable experience from Silicon Valley into Israeli public life.
If that is what he intends to do, he should say so plainly.
A Knesset seat is a public trust. Likud voters, and the country as a whole, deserve to know that those asking to exercise that trust intend to live among the people they represent.

ABIDJAN, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Cote d'Ivoire aims to become a leading African hub for land tenure security to drive sustainable development and social cohesion, Ivorian Minister of Agriculture, Rural Development and Food Production Bruno Nabagne Kone said Tuesday.
Kone made the remarks when announcing the inaugural Abidjan Land Tenure Days scheduled for Oct. 5-7. The event is expected to bring together representatives from public administrations and the land and private sectors, technical and financial partners, and experts from 14 countries.
The event aims to position Cote d'Ivoire as a key platform for land-related issues in Africa, facilitating the exchange of experiences to promote better land management, according to Kone.
He stressed that land tenure security is an essential lever for productive investment, job creation, and sustainable development.
Kone noted that Cote d'Ivoire now has about 23 million hectares of rural land requiring tenure security, with 8,631 villages remaining undemarcated, roughly 1.5 million land certificates yet to be issued, and an equal number of agricultural contracts yet to be formalized.
The minister called for accelerated reforms through appropriate financing, faster digitalization, the conversion of land certificates into land titles, and more equitable access to land for women and youth.
Cote d'Ivoire established a legal framework governing rural land in 1998. It recognizes customary land rights and formalizes them through the issuance of land certificates. ■

A new era for Australia's gig workers? The changes coming for delivery drivers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
03:09:45 UTC
12:09:45 KST

IN BRIEF
- On-demand food delivery drivers in Australia will be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 per hour in Australia.
- The changes will take effect from 17 August and have been praised by the Transport Workers' Union.
The Fair Work Commission has issued a new minimum standards order for gig workers, including on-demand food, beverage and grocery delivery drivers.
The standards, released on Tuesday, stipulate that on-demand delivery workers must be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 or up to $32 per hour, depending on the type of vehicle used. The order also specifies that delivery platforms must insure workers for on-the-job injuries.
The Transport Workers' Union (TWU), which represents Australian gig workers, said these changes have been years in the making. The TWU initially applied for the minimum standards order in 2024, alongside food delivery platforms Uber Eats and DoorDash.
In a joint statement provided to SBS News, TWU national secretary Michael Kaine described the new standards as "world-leading".
"The world is looking on as gig workers in Australia win new rights and protections that will change their lives, after years of campaigning for a better industry," Kaine said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth also believes the order is a "big step" in providing more robust worker protections.
She said it means "food and delivery workers don't have to trade off flexibility for fairer protections".
The new standards are set to start on Monday 17 August.
Who is covered by the order?
The TWU said "hundreds of thousands" of delivery workers in Australia will be impacted by the new orders.
They specifically apply to employee-like workers who are engaged through digital on-demand delivery platforms — such as Uber Eats and DoorDash — and mainly deliver consumables (food, beverages or liquor) or supermarket groceries.
These workers will be entitled to a guaranteed minimum hourly rate for their "engaged time" between accepting an order and completing the delivery. This is also called an "earnings floor".
People operating bicycles or e-bikes will be paid $31.30 an hour. For motorbikes, this increases to $31.80 per hour, and workers driving cars will earn $32 per hour.
According to the interim order, platforms will calculate a worker's total earnings over a period of up to 21 days. If a worker "has been paid less than the earnings floor in an earnings period, the digital labour platform operator will pay a top-up amount to ... make up the difference", it said.
Right to unpaid time away
The standards also aim to provide a clearer dispute resolution process and workers the right to (unpaid) time away. Key provisions include:
- Platforms will establish a feedback forum to enable workers to raise questions or concerns about their work.
- If an issue is unable to be resolved between the worker and delivery platform, drivers can refer the dispute to the Fair Work Commission.
- Delivery drivers can choose to take "time away" from work without pay.
- Time away is at the discretion of workers.
Maggie Lloyd, DoorDash's head of public policy for the Asia-Pacific, Central Asia and the Middle East, described these changes as a "defining moment" for Australia's on-demand economy.
"These new standards prove that strong worker protections and the flexibility that delivery workers value can go hand in hand," Lloyd said in a statement.
Insurance changes
Under the standards, delivery drivers will be responsible for taking out and maintaining compulsory third-party insurance for any vehicles used to provide services. They must also inform their insurer that the vehicle will be used for delivery driving.
Delivery platforms must, at their own expense, take out and maintain a personal accident insurance policy to cover employee-like workers.
Previously, not all workers received these protections because they were considered independent contractors.
In 2023, Uber warned the government that reforms to the gig economy would lead to "catastrophic" job losses. That same year, DoorDash also claimed that food delivery prices could more than triple under a worst-case scenario analysis.
Both companies have since walked back these comments and engaged with the TWU on the new standards.
Ed Kitchen, managing director of Uber Eats in Australia and New Zealand, said he is "proud" to have worked on the industry-first framework.
"This is a great moment for gig workers who play such a critical role in Australia's economy and in the lives of millions of Aussies who rely on food delivery every day."

Six killed in Houthi attack on Bab al-Mandeb ship, Yemen’s government says
The deaths on board the Egyptian-owned Tihamah mark first shipping deaths linked to Houthis since the US-Israel war on Iran began.
Cargo ship in flames after Houthi attack in Bab al-Mandeb strait
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has accused the Houthi rebel group of killing at least six people and wounding 10 others in a double-tap strike on a cargo vessel in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The attack on the Egyptian-owned Tihamah on Tuesday marks the first shipping deaths linked to the Iran-aligned Houthis since the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28.

Yemen’s Transport Ministry said three Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian national were killed after the Houthis fired three ballistic missiles at the commercial ship, sparking a fire and causing “significant damage” to the vessel.
Yemen’s coastguard said in a separate statement that the Houthis fired another missile at the ship as rescue personnel were evacuating the dead and wounded.
“The attack struck the site of the rescue operation and resulted in deaths and injuries among the forces participating in the response operation,” the coastguard said.
At least two troops were killed in the second strike.
Ten people were wounded in total, including seven crew members, it added.
Houthi-Saudi truce unravels
Yemen’s Foreign Ministry condemned the attack and called on the international community “to move from condemnation to effective and decisive action” against the Houthis.
There was no official comment from the Houthis.
But the Houthi-run news agency Saba reported that the group had attacked a Saudi ship carrying military equipment in Bab al-Mandeb. It did not name the ship, and there was no immediate Saudi response to the report.
In a separate incident on Tuesday, the US military said it fired on a ship attempting to break its blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf of Oman. The US Central Command said a Navy helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged Vela Nova cargo vessel, but did not say if any crew members were wounded.
The escalation in Yemen follows the collapse of a years-long truce in the country’s civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.
The breakdown of the United Nations-backed 2022 truce followed a Saudi air strike on the runway of Sanaa airport on July 13, preventing the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a high-ranking Houthi delegation.
The Houthis then attacked the Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia and announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. They have also attacked Saudi vessels as well as oil facilities in the kingdom, adding further disruption to the global economy.
The Saudi-led coalition, in turn, has struck Houthi-controlled Hodeidah and Kamaran, Yemen’s largest island in the Red Sea.
The Houthis have also launched attacks on government-held areas in Yemen, including the port city of al-Makha (Mocha) on the Red Sea and the central city of Marib, killing dozens of troops and civilians.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government on Tuesday said the Houthis launched 10 missiles and four drones during a series of further attacks on sites on the country’s western coast.
The Houthis said they had launched ballistic missile and drone attacks “targeting Saudi military buildups, weapons depots and command posts” in al-Makha and the central Marib province.
The UN has called for restraint, saying the renewed hostilities risk “drawing the country into a broader regional confrontation, with devastating consequences for its people”.

Mr Singh's profile has now been removed from the party's website. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has distanced himself from Mr Singh's views and said One Nation is "one of the gayest parties in Australia".
A failed One Nation candidate in WA has described gay people as having a mental illness in an offensive new video posted on social media.
The comments were made by Parminder Singh, who was the number three on One Nation WA's Legislative Council ticket at the 2025 election, in a clip posted by Perth comedian and content creator Jasky Singh, better known as "Mr Sikkant".
In the bizarre post, Mr Singh said gay parades "advertise" being gay to young people, and claimed women who tried relationships with women did not "go back" to men.
Asked if he thought people were born gay, he said no.
"No, no, it's a mental illness," he said.

"Such statements are inaccurate, harmful and inconsistent with decades of medical, psychological and community understanding that sexuality and gender diversity are a part of human diversity.

"That is not a good sign, is it? To be pulled off the website," he told the ABC's Afternoon Briefing.

When asked if he was referring to gay animals, he responded: "Yeah."
"I think we're one of the gayest parties in Australia,"
In the video, when Mr Singh was asked how gay people parading affected him personally, he said it was an "advertisement" to young people.

Despite the comments, Mr Singh insisted he did not "care" nor have a problem with gay people.
"I don't care. But not advertise and not legalise their marriages."
Same-sex marriage was legalised in Australia in 2017.
Candidate claims people not born gay
Mr Singh said animals were smarter than humans because they were "not gay" and claimed people were on Earth to create the "next generation".
"Have you seen the male animal with the male animal? Female animal with the female animal?" he said.
"So we are worse than the animals. Animal don't think much but they are better thinker than us."

"Almost two-thirds of the nearly 80 per cent of Australians who participated in the 2017 postal survey voted in support of marriage equality.
"We think that speaks far more to what mainstream Australian attitudes are than the outdated and deeply offensive opinions of some outspoken individuals.
"People can listen to these candidates and make up their own minds as to whether they present a coherent view that is in line with modern Australian values."

"He's now said a bunch of patriotic Australians and his Party's supporters are mentally ill, including his party's national director."
One Nation national director James Ashby is a gay man.
"Mr Singh is clearly a bit of a snowflake who doesn't like seeing other Australians happily living their lives," Mr Wilson said.
"And also doesn't believe in free speech nor bringing our country together."

====================================================================================================

The Domino Fear: Why a 2% Party Threatened Putin’s Endless War in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
03:07:13 UTC
12:07:13 KST

Russia’s Yabloko party was never likely to threaten Vladimir Putin at the ballot box.
But it had the potential to become something more dangerous: a place where Russians with very different reasons for wanting the war to end could suddenly find one another.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
For more than four years, Putin’s state has worked to make opposition to the invasion politically invisible. Anti-war politicians have been jailed, excluded from elections or driven abroad. Independent media have been dismantled or forced into exile. Public opposition to the war can bring criminal prosecution.
Anti-war is not pro-Ukraine
There is a crucial distinction between opposing the war and supporting Ukraine.
Yabloko’s blueprint for ending the war has drawn fierce criticism from Kyiv. Its founder, Grigory Yavlinsky, advocates an immediate, unconditional ceasefire that would freeze the current front line, leaving roughly one-fifth of sovereign Ukrainian territory under Russian occupation.
Yabloko does not represent Ukraine’s interests, nor is Yavlinsky broadly embraced by Russia’s anti-Putin opposition.
But Yabloko had the potential to unite a constituency much broader than its traditional liberal base: soldiers’ relatives, draft-age men frightened of another mobilization, citizens exhausted by casualties, people angered by economic deterioration and Russians who simply no longer see a reason for the war to continue.
Ukraine Repels 185 Combat Clashes on Tuesday
Yabloko could have become the institutional container into which those separate forms of discontent flowed.
The Belarus lesson and the domino effect
The Kremlin appears to have absorbed one of the central lessons of Belarus’s 2020 uprising.
Aleksandr Lukashenko allowed Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya onto the presidential ballot and publicly dismissed her as no serious threat. He failed to see that in a closed system, a candidate the regime dismissed as harmless can quickly become a proxy for a mass movement.
The Kremlin appears unwilling to run that experiment inside Russia.
The immediate reaction to Yabloko’s disqualification showed why.
The 2% party that drew a crowd
Critics have long ridiculed the party for its roughly 2% level of support, yet hundreds of supporters gathered outside the Supreme Court during the hearing, many of them young, some carrying apples in reference to the party’s name.
In today’s Russia, showing up outside a courthouse to support an anti-war political party is not a cost-free gesture. Protesters know the state possesses extensive surveillance and facial-recognition capabilities and has repeatedly used them against political dissent.
In 2019, the exclusion of opposition candidates from Moscow city elections brought thousands into the streets and produced one of Russia’s largest sustained protest movements in years.
In 2021, Alexei Navalny’s arrest triggered demonstrations across dozens of Russian cities.
The Kremlin knows how to suppress a crowd once it forms.
What it cannot know is what will trigger it.
Allowing Yabloko several more weeks to campaign nationally as the only registered anti-war alternative would have tested something the authorities evidently preferred not to test.
Endless war as the foundational ideology
This pre-election purge exposes a deeper truth about the evolution of Putinism.
For years, the Kremlin’s propaganda machine has worked relentlessly to convince Russians that the invasion of Ukraine was not a choice but a necessity – that war was forced on Russia, that there was no alternative, and that refusing to fight would have meant accepting national defeat.
Yabloko was offering an alternative vision of Russia’s future – one that does not have to be organized around endless war.
The hypocrisy of Putin’s election demands
There is a profound irony in Yabloko’s forced disappearance.
Vladimir Putin has repeatedly attacked Ukraine’s democratic legitimacy, weaponizing the fact that Kyiv has not held presidential and parliamentary elections while under martial law.
Ukraine cannot hold national elections while martial law is in force.
Moscow demands elections from a country it is actively bombarding while eliminating the only registered option for its own citizens to vote against that very war.
Yabloko’s removal demonstrates what the Kremlin itself appears to mean when it lectures others about elections.
This is Putin’s vision of an election: there can be ballot boxes, party logos and official results – voting is permitted, provided it has already been decided what you are allowed to choose.

Furor over Albanese's melons joke could force Japan into drama it wanted to avoid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
03:04:19 UTC
12:04:19 KST

analysis
Furore over Albanese's melons joke forces Japan into drama it wanted to avoid
Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has commented on several issues in the past 48 hours: a rocket launch, solar power, recovery efforts following a recent earthquake.
She has not mentioned melons. Or Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
For a month the Japanese government has studiously remained quiet on the "joke" Albanese made about the crown melons Takaichi gifted him during her visit to the country in May.
And for a month it barely registered in the country.
Japan had hoped its silence would help kill the issue. It underestimated Australia's media and political cycles, with the latest round of controversy over Albanese's podcast appearance finally pushing the story into Japanese news and social media.
As Albanese faced a grilling in parliament on Tuesday about his references to Takaichi's two "smuggled" melons — comments made while gesturing in front of his chest — people in Japan were enjoying a day off in the sun.
The public holiday leads into Obon, an annual Buddhist custom where the country slows down as people visit family and take time off.
The prime minister has continued working — something she has become synonymous with — taking to social media to make some statements, but her office hasn't held any formal press conferences.
Instead, it was Tokyo's ambassador in Canberra who ended up breaking the Japanese government's silence on the political furore in Australia.
"We have been informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported," Japan's ambassador to Australia Kazuhiro Suzuki told the ABC in a statement.
"In any case, the dinner hosted by Prime Minister Albanese during the prime minister's visit to Australia this May was held in a very relaxed atmosphere.
"We believe it helped build a personal trust relationship between the two leaders."
Why Japan stayed silent
Japan is enjoying its growing relationship with Australia, particularly its tightening defence ties.
Presenting a solid front with Australia is beneficial at a time when Tokyo is taking a strong stance against China, trying to maintain its position with an erratic US administration, and position itself as a defender of the rules-based order in the region.
In a leaked diplomatic memo from last month, reported in The Australian newspaper this week, Japanese diplomats are said to have told Australia they believed there was no "ill intention" in Albanese's comments and it would take "no action" to "allow the Australian media to move on".
That has not happened.
If the cable was passed onto the press in the hope of dimming the story by showcasing Japan's lack of offence, it has had the opposite effect.
The Coalition has now referred the leak to the Australian Federal Police, pushing the issue into new territory, and putting a comment from Japan on record — something it had wanted to avoid.
But it was a former Japanese ambassador to Australia who pushed the story back into the spotlight.
Yamagami Shingo's opinion piece in The Australian at the start of the week suggested the comments could damage the relationship between the two countries.
It is not the first time he has criticised the government's approach to Japan. Late last year he penned a piece saying Australia should have done more to publicly defend Prime Minister Takaichi against attacks from China.
Loading...
Behind the scenes, Japanese officials were at pains to distance their government from those comments.
Yamagami enjoyed a good relationship with the Coalition government during his time in the role, and a less-than-good relationship with the then Labor opposition.
That is worth noting, as his commentary on the melons saga provided the ammunition for a fresh deluge in Question Time, so long after the initial faux pas.
But it doesn't mean the criticism was unwarranted.
Joking about a Japanese gift is always ill-advised
Gift giving is a serious business in Japan. In stores there are rows and rows of perfectly packaged boxes of chocolates, rice cakes, fruit — called "omiyage", they are presents to be shared with friends and colleagues.
Gifts are regular, well thought out and carry significant weight.
Insulting a Japanese gift is a baffling diplomatic misstep.
Loading
Albanese brought up the melons in response to a question about "the most crap gift" he's received overseas. And that is aside from the sexual innuendo in relation to Japan's first female prime minister.
Loading...
Labor ministers have stood behind Albanese and denied this, saying his comments and gestures have been misrepresented.
The problem is potentially being compounded with the fact a month later, Takaichi's office may be forced to directly respond.
The media and political press conferences are far more controlled in Japan than in Australia, but the melon comments have now been reported in local news outlets and are starting to be criticised on social media. When the chief cabinet secretary next steps up he may field a question on the issue. Japan is expected to try to downplay it.
But the Obon season may give the Japanese government cover. It could be days before a press conference is held, by which time the melons issue may have been superseded in the headlines.
Like Albanese, Takaichi is currently facing a drop in the polls and has many other issues she would prefer to focus on: economic issues, cost of living, immigration debates, a possible cabinet reshuffle — and the fact North Korea has fired two ballistic missiles toward Japan in the space of a few days.
If she was a man, she likely would be able to.
The initial lack of coverage of the melon comments in Japan, both in the media and online, perhaps also reflects that while Australia's relationship with Japan is growing, it isn't on the same level as some other countries, such as the United States.
This episode won't have helped in swinging that dial.

US primaries deliver mixed wins as November races take shape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:59:50 UTC
11:59:50 KST

The latest round of US primary contests has delivered mixed results as progressive candidates made gains alongside establishment figures and Trump-backed contenders, sharpening several key races ahead of November midterms.
Results were still being counted early on Wednesday following Tuesday's primaries in Connecticut, Minnesota, Vermont and Wisconsin, as well as a special Senate contest in South Carolina.
One of the biggest surprises came in Connecticut, where former Hartford mayor Luke Bronin held a commanding lead over veteran Democratic Representative John Larson in the state's 1st Congressional District.
Bronin had about 54 percent of the vote, compared with 34 percent for Larson, according to preliminary results.
Larson has represented the district for nearly three decades.
Elsewhere in Connecticut, Democratic Governor Ned Lamont comfortably advanced with about 67 percent of the vote and is set to face Republican Ryan Fazio in November.
Minnesota also produced several closely watched contests.
Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar dominated her party's gubernatorial primary with nearly 89 percent of the vote as she seeks to succeed Governor Tim Walz, who stepped aside.
On the Republican side, Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth led with about 45 percent, ahead of MyPillow founder Mike Lindell on 32 percent and Kendall Qualls on about 21 percent.
The race for Minnesota's open Senate seat exposed a divide within the Democratic Party.
Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan led Representative Angie Craig by about 57 percent to 42 percent in a contest closely watched as a test of the party's progressive and moderate wings.
Former television journalist Michele Tafoya led the Republican Senate primary with about 56 percent.
Wisconsin races take shape
In neighbouring Wisconsin, Trump-backed Representative Tom Tiffany cruised towards the Republican nomination for governor, taking about 96 percent of the vote against Andy Manske.
The Democratic contest was considerably tighter.
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, backed by outgoing Governor Tony Evers, held a narrow lead over progressive state Representative Francesca Hong, with roughly 41 percent to Hong's 37 percent.
Other candidates, including Kelda Roys, trailed as counting continued.
Vermont race remains tight
Vermont's Democratic gubernatorial primary was also too close for a decisive early call, with Amanda Janoo holding a narrow advantage over Aly Richards, about 49 percent to 46 percent.
The eventual nominee is expected to face Republican Governor Phil Scott in November.
In South Carolina, the special Republican Senate primary triggered by the death of longtime Senator Lindsey Graham was headed for a runoff.
Darline Graham, the late senator's sister and interim replacement, and Representative Ralph Norman advanced from the Republican field after neither secured enough support to win outright.
Graham had received the endorsement of President Donald Trump.
The eventual Republican nominee will face Democrat Annie Andrews in November.
Some races remained uncalled or provisional early Wednesday, so exact final certified percentages could shift slightly.
Earlier primaries deliver progressive win
The latest contests follow another round of primaries on August 4 that produced one of the most significant progressive victories of the election cycle.
In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Representative Haley Stevens for the Democratic Senate nomination, winning by roughly one percentage point.
He will face Republican Mike Rogers in November in a race for the open seat.
Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson easily secured the Democratic nomination for governor, while Republican Representative John James emerged from his party's primary.
In Kansas, Republican Senator Roger Marshall comfortably won renomination with about 80 percent of the vote.
Taken together, the August contests have offered mixed signals about the direction of the two major parties.
Progressive Democrats have recorded a major victory in Michigan and strong showings in Connecticut and Wisconsin, while prominent establishment candidates including Lamont and Klobuchar have remained dominant elsewhere.
Trump-backed Republicans have also continued to perform strongly in several contests, including Tiffany's overwhelming Wisconsin victory.
The results are beginning to sharpen the November election map, with open governorships in Minnesota and Wisconsin, Senate contests in Michigan and Minnesota, and competitive congressional races among those likely to draw national attention.

No Cabinet officials joined Trump in the truck, according to the newspaper.
After a day of social media memes portraying Trump as hiding out in the catering truck, the image-conscious president, who often promotes memes of himself as a bold and courageous leader, said he was following the direction of the Secret Service, the agency that protects the president.
"Well, it's only up to Secret Service. I just follow what they'd like to do, so I go by Secret Service and the military," Trump said.
"I guess there was a threat out there. I didn't really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats," Trump said.
The White House said at the time that the president was flying aboard Air Force One from Turkey to Britain. But moments after Trump boarded the plane, he left it in secret via the catering truck and boarded another aircraft for the flight to Britain, the Post said on Monday, quoting unnamed sources.
Trump had taken a newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit but unexpectedly announced he would use an older Air Force One when departing the country, a move that prompted questions about the newer plane's security.
The trip to NATO was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Turkey. REUTERS

Yemen’s Houthi group claimed Tuesday that missile and drone strikes targeting military sites in Marib in central Yemen and the coastal city of Mokha left dozens of people killed or injured.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched a large number of ballistic missiles and drones at military deployments, weapons depots and command centers in Mokha and the Tadawin military camp in Marib governorate.

Earlier Tuesday, Yemen’s National Resistance Forces, which are aligned with the internationally recognized government, said the Houthis had launched 10 missiles and four drones at sites along the country’s western coast since the morning.
The forces said their air defenses responded to the attacks and shot down an explosive-laden drone.
Yemen has been under a relative lull in fighting since April 2022 following nearly 12 years of war between government forces backed by a Saudi-led coalition and the Iran-backed Houthi group, which seized the capital, Sanaa, and large parts of the country in 2014.
Since late 2023 following the start of Israel’s war on Gaza, the Houthis have increasingly become involved in regional hostilities, launching attacks on Israel and commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Recent renewed fighting has raised fears of a return to full-scale conflict in Yemen.

Court blocks US postal service from implementing Trump admin's restrictions on mail-in voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:53:23 UTC
11:53:23 KST

A federal judge in the US has blocked the country’s Postal Service (USPS) from implementing provisions of President Donald Trump's executive order aimed at tightening rules for mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections.
Judge Indira Talwani of the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts issued a new injunction barring USPS from implementing the challenged provisions nationwide, according to an order issued Tuesday in the case brought by the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts and other plaintiffs.
The order directed, among other measures, the USPS to establish requirements for mail-in and absentee ballots, including refusing to transmit ballots that do not comply with new requirements or are not associated with voters appearing on lists provided to the Postal Service.
Talwani had previously blocked key provisions of the order in June in 23 states and Washington, DC.
The latest order extends the injunction nationwide.
The Supreme Court is currently weighing requests from the Trump administration to lift Talwani's earlier injunction against the same executive order.
'Citizenship Verification'
Several voting rights groups had urged Talwani to go further and prevent USPS from implementing anywhere in the nation a proposed rule requiring states to provide lists of voters and adopt new balloting procedures before the mail agency would make deliveries.
If states did not comply, USPS would have refused to deliver the ballots. The plaintiffs had contended USPS would have no legal basis for such a refusal.
Trump signed Executive Order 14399 titled "Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections" on March 31.
The legal dispute comes ahead of the November midterm elections, when voters will determine control of the US House of Representatives and Senate.

A guide to this week’s election in Zambia, a southern African country rich in critical minerals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:53:02 UTC
11:53:02 KST

A guide to this week’s election in Zambia, a southern African country rich in critical minerals
LUSAKA, Zambia (AP) — Zambia holds an election Thursday to decide if President Hakainde Hichilema will get a second five-year term as reward for his economic recovery plan in the southern African nation that’s one of the world’s top copper producers but was recently mired in a debt crisis.
Zambia defaulted on sovereign debt repayments to China and other nations in 2020 in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, drawing attention to the unsustainable burdens faced by some developing countries.
Hichilema was elected a year later, and Zambia has restructured more than $12 billion in debts to other countries and private creditors under his leadership while reining in inflation and stabilizing the currency.
His long-term economic plan involves a pledge to more than triple Zambia’s copper output to 3 million metric tons a year by 2031 — a staggering rise that could put Zambia ahead of the United States and China in terms of global producers of the in-demand critical mineral.
Opposition leader likely Hichilema’s strongest challenger
Hichilema won a presidential election in 2021, having lost in five votes before that stretching back to 2006. The 64-year-old is a former financial services executive but also has a background in farming and is one of the nation’s biggest cattle ranchers.
He is a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church and has led the United Party for National Development since 2006.
In a field that includes 13 other presidential candidates, analysts say Hichilema’s strongest challenger will likely be Brian Mundubile, the leader of an opposition grouping called the Tonse Alliance.
The 55-year-old Mundubile, who is a law graduate, was not considered a major political figure in Zambia but emerged in January as the leader of Tonse after it was embroiled in internal wrangles.
The big issues
While inflation has dropped and the value of Zambia’s currency, the Kwacha, has improved under Hichilema, ordinary Zambians bemoan high food and energy costs. Some critics say the macroeconomic stability hasn’t benefited most people in the landlocked country of some 22 million.
“You expect a minimum of three years to be able to drive an economic agenda and turn around a country,” Zambian economist Trevor Hambayi said. “That has passed and they’ve had five years. But these effects have not yet trickled down to the Zambian people.”
Hichilema promised this week while campaigning to build more schools, health facilities and roads, and to create more jobs. “We love you so much and this is why we are working round the clock to lower the cost of living,” he said.
Another criticism of Hichilema is that he has squeezed dissent in a country where elections have been largely peaceful.
On Tuesday, the Tonse Alliance accused Hichilema’s government of being behind a law enforcement agency raid on its offices that saw vehicles, communication equipment and other items seized. The alliance alleged it was politically motivated to disrupt its campaigning.
Why a dead president’s body is relevant
Zambia gained independence from Britain in 1960 and was a one-party state from 1973 to 1991. Since then, several parties and political alliances have won and lost power.
Hichilema’s rivalry with his predecessor, the late former President Edgar Lungu, was especially bitter and continued even after Lungu’s death last year. When Lungu was president, then-opposition leader Hichilema was imprisoned for four months in 2017 on charges of treason after Lungu alleged Hichilema’s motorcade didn’t gave way to his on a road.
Lungu claimed he was effectively put under house arrest during Hichilema’s first term and had to sneak out of the country to seek medical care in South Africa.
Lungu died in South Africa in June 2025, prompting a macabre yearlong battle between Hichilema’s government and Lungu’s family over where the body should be buried. The government insisted it be repatriated for a state funeral, while the family said one of Lungu’s last wishes was that he not have a state funeral presided over by Hichilema.
The dispute, which fascinated Zambians, went to South Africa’s Supreme Court of Appeal. It ruled in favor of the family, though burial plans have still not been announced.
Interest from China and the US
China is the top foreign investor in Zambia, especially for its copper and cobalt — critical minerals that are used in electronics, electric vehicles and other new technologies.
Those minerals have also drawn interest from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, though Zambia has accused the U.S. of tying critical minerals access to a proposed $2 billion health deal between the countries — allegations the U.S. rejected.
How the election works
Voters in the one-day election on Thursday will also choose lawmakers in Parliament and local government councilors. Around 8 million people are registered to vote.
Zambia’s presidential election works on the 50% plus one system where a candidate has to get an outright majority to win. That raises the possibility of a second round of voting if no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote first time around.

North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the sea amid preparations for U.S.–South Korean exercises
Kyiv • UNN
On August 12, North Korea launched a ballistic missile from the Wonsan area, marking the second test in a week. The launch took place amid preparations for joint U.S.–South Korean exercises.
North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the sea on the morning of August 12, conducting its second missile test in less than a week. South Korean military officials reported this, NBC News said, citing the Associated Press, reports UNN.
Details
The launch was detected at around 6:00 a.m. from the Wonsan area on North Korea’s east coast. The South Korean military has increased surveillance and is sharing information about the launch with the United States and Japan.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense also reported the launch of a ballistic missile. According to its data, the weapon did not reach Japan’s exclusive economic zone, indicating that it fell farther from the Japanese coast.
North Korea responded to military exercises
The launch took place two days after the United States and South Korea announced that they would hold annual large-scale military exercises. The Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises will begin on August 17 and last 11 days.
According to the South Korean military, about 18,000 South Korean service members will take part in them. Pyongyang traditionally regards joint exercises by Washington and Seoul as preparations for a possible invasion, while the United States and South Korea call them defensive.
North Korea conducted its previous launch on August 6. At that time, South Korea, the United States, and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile. It was North Korea’s first test of ballistic weapons since late June.

Darline Graham advances to runoff, vows to carry on brother Lindsey’s fight in US Senate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:41:40 UTC
11:41:40 KST

Sen. Darline Graham Nordone thanked US President Donald Trump and invoked the memory of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, as she addressed supporters on Tuesday night after advancing to the runoff in South Carolina’s Republican Senate primary.
Speaking exactly one month after her brother’s death, Graham described the past several weeks as “absolutely brutal,” as she simultaneously mourned Lindsey Graham, assumed his seat in the US Senate, and launched her first campaign for elected office.
“I want to thank President Trump,” Graham told supporters. “His steadfast support and his complete and total endorsement means so much to me. He knows that I will stand with him and fight for his agenda, just like Lindsey did.”
Graham said she hoped Trump would travel to South Carolina to campaign for her during the two weeks leading up to the runoff, though she said no such appearance had yet been confirmed.
“I’m hopeful that President Trump will come down, but we’ll see,” she told reporters.
Her remarks came shortly after Trump himself praised Graham and said she had called him to thank him for his endorsement.
Graham spoke about her childhood
Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother’s Senate seat following his death, sought Tuesday night to portray herself simultaneously as the guardian of Lindsey Graham’s legacy and as a political outsider with an identity of her own.
“I’m a conservative Republican. I’m not a career politician,” she said. “I know how families are struggling to make ends meet because I’ve been there too.”
‘I never expected it would happen under these circumstances’
Graham repeatedly returned to the story of her childhood with her brother, recalling that the two grew up in a room behind the bar and liquor store operated by their parents.
“That’s where we learned a strong work ethic and the value of $1,” she said. “From a young age, our parents taught us that you’re not given anything in life, and no one owes you anything. If you want something, you work for it.”
Before entering the Senate, Graham said she spent seven years leading a South Carolina agency that assists blind and visually impaired residents in finding employment and becoming more independent.
“I never expected that career of service would lead me to the United States Senate,” she said. “I certainly never expected it would happen under these circumstances.”
Graham touted what she described as an unusually productive first three weeks in Washington, saying she had already helped pass a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill that was particularly important to her brother.
She also highlighted her role as the deciding vote to confirm Trump’s attorney general nominee, Todd Blanche.
“Some politicians never get a major piece of their legislation passed, so I’ve already accomplished more in a few weeks than many do in decades,” Graham said.
Graham described herself as ‘fighter’
Graham laid out a strongly conservative platform, pledging support for Trump’s immigration agenda, voter identification requirements, abortion restrictions, and Second Amendment rights.
“Joe Biden let 12 million illegal immigrants into this country,” she said. “President Trump and I are going to walk them right back out.”
She also declared that “boys have no place in girls’ sports, especially not in the locker room,” and joked about criticism of her lack of political experience.
“I’ve been accused of not being a politician,” she said. “Guilty as charged.”
Graham said she would spend virtually every day of the coming runoff campaign traveling throughout South Carolina and meeting voters.
“This seat belongs to the people of South Carolina, and I will work hard to earn your vote,” she said.
Asked about facing Rep. Ralph Norman in a debate, Graham said she had not previously heard about the proposed Monday event but was prepared to participate.
“I’ll be willing to debate him. Yes,” she said.
‘I have buried my precious brother – and I’m still standing’
One month after Lindsey Graham's death, his sister is 'still standing'
The most personal moment of the night came when Graham was asked how she had handled the whirlwind month since her brother’s death.
“Today is the 11th. My brother passed one month ago today, so none of this has been comfortable for me,” she said. “But like I said, I’m a fighter.”
“I have buried my precious brother. I have taken on the role of a United States senator, and I have had this brutal campaign schedule. And I’m still standing. If that doesn’t tell you I’m a strong person and a fighter, nothing will.”
Graham acknowledged that the demands of the Senate and the campaign had left her with little opportunity to fully grieve.
“I have not had a whole lot of time to process it,” she said. “I’ve had my moments. They typically come early in the morning, before my day gets started, and late at night when I go to bed.”
Asked what she believed Lindsey Graham would say to her if the two could speak privately at that moment, she paused on the memory of her brother.
“I think a lot about what I would say to him and what he would say,” Graham said. “Right now, I think he would be very proud.”

Russia may have funded attempt to help influencer wanted by Benin flee South Africa — Bloomberg
According to Ukrinform, Bloomberg stated this in an article.
In court documents related to the extradition case brought by Benin in South Africa, prosecutors allege that there is an unexpected connection between Seba, a native of France and former leader of a black nationalist movement in that country, and François van der Merwe, who heads the South African white nationalist movement Bittereinders. According to prosecutors, both men have links to Russia.
Seba, whose real name is Stellio Gilles Robert Capo Chichi, was arrested in Pretoria together with his son and van der Merwe on April 13 as they were preparing to illegally leave South Africa by crossing the Limpopo River into Zimbabwe, prosecutors said.
According to the publication, police officers posed as employees of a private security company hired by van der Merwe to help Seba leave the country. More than 300,000 South African rand (over $18,000) were seized during the arrest.
Documents from South Africa's Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation state that the country's financial authorities were asked to help trace "the funds that Mr. van der Merwe had received allegedly from the Russians to assist with the safe escorting and transfer of Mr. Capo Chichi from South Africa to Zimbabwe."
Russia has provided support to military juntas in West Africa and has been linked to information campaigns across the continent aimed at undermining support for the West. Seba has been accused of assisting these efforts, including by spreading pro-Russian and anti-French content online.
According to documents submitted during hearings on applications by Seba and van der Merwe for release on bail, Seba was allegedly supposed to travel to Zimbabwe and then to Europe to carry out terrorist attacks there and in the United Kingdom. The documents also stated that "the person is trained by the Russians and is extremely dangerous." Both men remain in custody.
Benin issued an international arrest warrant for Seba after he expressed support on social media for potential rebels. In addition, the blogger and influencer has been charged in Benin with money laundering and terrorism.
Seba was a prominent anti-French activist in West Africa. In 2024, he was stripped of his French citizenship for allegedly inciting violence against the state.
In 2022, the U.S. State Department accused the Russian private military company Wagner of using Seba to spread pro-Russian narratives.
The Bittereinders movement also has links to Russia. Last year, van der Merwe attended a meeting of far-right organizations, including Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD), in St. Petersburg.
As Ukrinform reported, Andrii Cherniak, a representative of the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense (HUR), said that Russia is conducting information operations in at least 22 African countries, reaching millions of people.

Iran holds firm on Hormuz conditions as Pakistan’s Naqvi visits Tehran
Iran’s top security official says the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen unless the US meets its conditions.
Iran has held firm on its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as Pakistan’s interior minister, Mohsin Naqvi, visited Tehran, and the United States and Yemen’s Houthis launched attacks on shipping in the Gulf of Oman and the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The developments on Tuesday came as the US-Israel war on Iran showed no sign of ending, despite repeated claims from US President Donald Trump that a deal was close.

Mohsen Rezaei, the newly appointed head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told China’s ambassador to Tehran that Washington must end its military campaign and release Iranian funds held abroad for a full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
“As long as the US does not change its behaviour and accept Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened,” Rezaei told Cong Peiwu, according to Iranian media.
Writing on X later, he insisted on an end to the US’s naval blockade on Iranian ports as well as a region-wide ceasefire, including in Gaza and Lebanon.
“IRAN’s message is clear,” he wrote. “The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until the U.S. ends the war and blockade, releases Iran’s frozen assets, and agrees to a region-wide ceasefire, including in Lebanon and Gaza.
“Until all conditions are met, the Strait will remain closed.”
There was no immediate comment from Washington.
Pakistan mediates
Trump has swung between threats of escalation and assurances of an imminent peace deal throughout the conflict.
In an interview broadcast late on Monday, he suggested that the uncertainty could last for a while, saying he might just “bop along” and let Tehran fail economically, or “hit” them “really, really hard”.
“I’m sort of negotiating,” Trump told Real America’s Voice. “They’re very devious negotiators.”
In Tehran, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Pakistan’s interior minister, with the two sides discussing closer political, economic, trade, cultural and security ties, according to the Iranian presidency.
Naqvi’s visit comes as Islamabad mediates efforts to end the ongoing conflict.
Earlier, Qatar – another mediator in the conflict – said talks between Iran and Oman on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz had reached an advanced stage.
“We have heard positive statements from both capitals in the recent couple of days,” said Majed al-Ansari, spokesman for the Qatari Foreign Ministry. “Our main priority here is the reopening of the strait, maintaining the ceasefire and making sure that we are able to push forward towards the negotiation.”
Iran, meanwhile, said any agreement between it and Oman on routes in the Strait of Hormuz will have no impact on the reopening of the waterway.
Alan Eyre, a former senior US diplomat, said Iran is keeping the strait closed to increase pressure on the US.
“Even though they’ve [Iran] worked out a deal with Oman in terms of where ships would go entering and exiting the strait, they don’t want to to activate and implement that yet because they want to increase the pain on the United States who in their mind has attacked them twice in the last two years,” he told Al Jazeera.
“What they’re trying to do is reestablish strategic deterrence to prevent future attacks,” he added.

It said the ship had ignored repeated warnings to stop violating the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The killings on board the Egyptian-owned Tihamah would be the first by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi strikes on shipping since the war on Iran began in late February.
The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that the group had attacked a Saudi ship carrying military equipment in Bab al-Mandeb. It did not name the ship, and there was no immediate Saudi response to the report.
Thousands of people have been killed since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28. Iran has also struck US assets and infrastructure in Oman, Jordan, Kuwait, Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
In Iran, at least 3,527 people have been killed, while more than 27,00 have been wounded. At least 18 Americans have also died.
The conflict has also widened to Lebanon, where Iran-backed Hezbollah has launched attacks on Israel, and Israeli forces have carried out near-daily strikes.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry says Israel’s latest military escalation there, which began on March 2, has killed more than 4,300 people and injured more than 12,000. In Israel, at least 60 people have been killed in Iranian and Hezbollah attacks.

Drone strike rocks Zawiya power station in Libya, igniting fire

Tarek Chouiref
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
A drone targeted a power station in Libya’s western city of Zawiya early Wednesday, sparking a fire at the facility, local media reported.
 
Footage carried by Libyan outlets showed flames rising from the power station following the reported strike.
 
The attack follows a series of drone strikes on key infrastructure in Zawiya, around 40 kilometers (25 miles) west of Tripoli.
 
Libya’s General Electricity Company said the South Zawiya transformation station was targeted, causing it to burn completely and go out of service, cutting electricity to wide areas.
 
The recent attacks and security instability in Zawiya have directly damaged electricity facilities, transmission lines and grid equipment, while also affecting maintenance work at the 1,300-megawatt Zawiya power plant, the company said.
 
The US company had already withdrawn its technical teams from the plant in June due to security conditions, delaying major maintenance work and leaving more than 700 megawatts of the plant’s capacity unavailable to the national grid, it added.
 
All work has halted at the plant and teams have been evacuated until safe working conditions are restored, the company said.
 
The company warned that continued attacks on electricity infrastructure could threaten the stability of the national grid and lead to wider disruptions, including partial or general blackouts.
 
No group has claimed responsibility.
 
- Series of attacks
 
On Tuesday, Libya’s National Oil Corporation (NOC) said the Zawiya Oil Refinery had been targeted for the fifth time since Sunday.
 
The state-run company said an explosive-laden drone struck the roof of a diesel tank, piercing it and triggering a fire that emergency teams later brought under control.
 
Another drone had targeted a separate diesel tank at the refinery earlier Tuesday, also causing a fire. No casualties were reported in either attack.
 
The corporation said refinery operations had resumed following the earlier strikes and that fuel supplies and reserves remained unaffected.
 
Last week, clashes between armed groups in Zawiya spread to the nearby city of Surman, leaving people dead and injured and resulting in a prison break.
 
Libya remains divided between the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh and a rival administration appointed by the House of Representatives and headed by Osama Hammad in Benghazi.
 
The UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) has sought to resolve political disputes that have delayed long-awaited national elections, which Libyans hope will help end years of political division and armed conflict following the 2011 overthrow of longtime ruler Moammar Gadhafi.

"We are hearing that Hamas is deliberately pressuring you to approach the Yellow Line, while completely disregarding the danger to your lives," COGAT said. "Do not allow Hamas to push you into reckless actions that put your lives at risk and once again turn you into victims of its irresponsible actions."
In July, Haaretz reported Israel had constructed a land barrier that extends hundreds of meters beyond the official line.
In 2025, Haaretz reported the Yellow Line is not always clearly marked on the ground, and anyone who approaches the forbidden area is shot immediately, even when they are children. Gazans claim the Israeli-controlled area, marked by the so-called Yellow Line, changes without warning, moving west.

Iran, U.S. not discussing cease-fire extension, senior Iranian official says
There were no discussions between Iran and the United States to extend their cease-fire because, from Tehran's perspective, the deal had no start date and therefore had nothing to extend, a senior Iranian source told Reuters on Wednesday.
The source's comments came after Turkey's Anadolu news agency, citing Pakistani government sources, reported on Wednesday that Tehran and Washington had agreed to extend a 60-day cease-fire under their interim deal signed in June.
The deal declared an "immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts", but quickly unravelled, with U.S. President Donald Trump saying it was "over" on July 7 and Iran's foreign ministry declaring it "suspended" a week later.
"There is no talk of an extension because, from Iran's perspective, there is no period that began and therefore nothing to extend. The United States violated the interim agreement 48 hours after it was reached and withdrew from it a few days later," the source told Reuters.
In the agreement, the 60-day period refers to an extendable time frame within which Iran and the United States were expected to reach a final deal limiting Tehran's nuclear programme and lifting U.S. sanctions.
A series of requirements, such as a cease-fire in Lebanon, free navigation in the Gulf and waivers for Iran to sell its oil, were viewed as necessary before entering the further negotiation period.
"One of the issues that is being discussed via mediators is the U.S. returning to the interim agreement and defining a time frame for implementing the commitments. There has been absolutely no progress on this issue," the source added.
Israeli strike damages school in southern Lebanon as town officials seek intervention, local media says
Israeli forces struck a school building overnight into Wednesday in the southern Lebanese village of Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, Lebanon's official National News Agency reported.
The village council appealed to Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam to intervene to halt the destruction of buildings in the area.
Speaking to the Qatar-based Al Araby TV, a Lebanese Armed Forces source said the Israeli military destroyed the town hall, a clinic, a kindergarten and several homes.
In a statement, the council said the buildings destroyed were civilian infrastructure or private homes and had not been used for military purposes.
Israeli man charged over alleged role in smashing Haaretz, Channel 12 News doors
A 44-year-old Ramat Gan man has been charged with allegedly smashing the entrance doors of Haaretz in July, prosecutors said Wednesday.
Avraham Hadi was indicted on suspicion of carrying out a series of attacks targeting Israeli media outlets and public institutions last month, including smashing the entrance doors of Channel 12 News with a brick, spray-painting a threatening message near the headquarters of Channel 13 and vandalizing the Justice Ministry building.
The indictment charges Hadi with extortion by threats, making threats, malicious damage, defacement of property and obstruction of justice. Prosecutors requested that he be held in custody until the end of the legal proceedings.

The perfect storm that turbocharged Venezuela's twin quakes

The perfect storm that turbocharged Venezuela's twin quakes
- Venezuela's twin earthquakes caused massive damage due to loose soils, poor construction, and outdated regulations, killing over 6,300 people and collapsing many buildings.
- Many buildings, including social housing, were poorly built or reinforced, worsening the destruction and trapping residents under rubble.
- Survivors face stress and delayed government aid, with promises of housing only by 2026, fueling public frustration and anxiety.
AI generated
CARCAS – A dangerous cocktail of tectonic positioning, loose earth and shoddy construction contributed to the unprecedented damage caused by Venezuela’s twin earthquakes, experts say.
Jennire Garcia’s home in the coastal Catia La Mar neighbourhood was rendered unliveable by the tremors in late June, which devastated the state of La Guaira.
The 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes killed over 6,300 people and sent 190 buildings crashing down, while 856 more sustained damage.
Garcia and her family are now living in tents next to the ruins, and the 42-year-old says she is “sick with stress all day long.”
This was the same site as deadly mudslides that killed thousands of people in 1999.
The region’s “unconsolidated” soils, where construction requires specific geotechnical studies, added to the severity of the damage, according to engineer Feliciano De Santis.
“These soils generally tend to be loose soils” and caused the ground to move with even greater intensity, said De Santis, who is president of the Venezuelan Geologists Society.
Garcia’s residential complex, which was declared uninhabitable, was built after the landslide.
Deep cracks run through its yellow walls, several balconies have dislodged from the building and some high-rises have crumbled altogether.
‘So anxious’
Rescuers across the quake zone have not abandoned the search for victims under the rubble, and are working through the debris of buildings up to 12 stories high.
The last adjustment made to earthquake regulations for buildings was in 2019, and before that, in 1967 when a horrific 6.6 magnitude tremor struck the country.
A closer look at La Guaira’s infrastructure reveals significant construction flaws, said Japanese engineer Kit Miyamoto, who is touring the state with support from Washington.
For instance, large quantities of steel “seems like it’s really good,” he told AFP.
“But once you get down to look at how actually the rebar (steel reinforcement) is connected to the foundation, it’s not much,” the engineer added.
In the early 2010s, the government of late leader Hugo Chavez built 43 flagship social housing high-rise buildings.
The quakes flattened 16 of them, crushing hundreds of residents underneath.
A recent investigation by Armando.info revealed that “contracts awarded at discretion to companies whose experience was unknown” fueled the damage.
In Caracas’ worst-hit neighbourhood Chacao, 68 people died while three buildings collapsed and dozens more are uninhabitable.
Most of these buildings were constructed before the 1967 earthquake, Venezuela’s Engineering Order said.
“Some had been reinforced,” said organisation representative and engineer Felix Ojeda, adding that rubble samples taken on site can provide clues about the state of the infrastructure.
“The obvious next step,” said Miyamoto, “is to take down the buildings,” adding that retrofitting and strengthening buildings was also important to do as much as possible.
Public fury about the government’s slow response to the quakes is widespread.
Interim leader Delcy Rodriguez – who effectively governs under Washington’s thumb since her predecessor Nicolas Maduro’s ouster – has promised to deliver around 4,000 housing units in 2026.
Back in Catia La Mar, Garcia pines for her former home.
“It makes me sad because I see it there every day. I think about the comforts I had and that I can’t have here,” she said.
“We are so anxious,” she said, “waiting for an answer, and we don’t have one.” AFP

Unknown Publisher

02:19:18 UTC

New Zealand’s prime minister Christopher Luxon has survived a second leadership showdown in four months, just 87 days out from the country’s general election.
Talking to media after a three-hour meeting of his MPs in Wellington on Wednesday, the embattled leader said he had the full support of his party.
“There was a confidence vote in my leadership this morning at our caucus meeting, and I have the full support of our caucus,” Luxon said. “Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election.”
As he spoke, Luxon was flanked by his deputy Nicola Willis, the National party president, Sylvia Wood, and, in what was likely a deliberate move to show unity, three senior politicians who had been tipped as top contenders to take his place: Chris Bishop, Erica Stanford and Mark Mitchell.
Luxon said National’s plan for the country was positive and the choice for voters was “crystal clear”.
After less than one minute speaking, Luxon thanked the media and said his team was “going back to work”. He took no questions from reporters.
Luxon may have emerged triumphant for a second time in four months, but his victory is likely to leave scars.
For the prime minister, whose popularity among the public has failed to reach the lofty heights of his predecessors, the perceived lack of confidence within his own caucus could further rattle his reputation.
While the party, which positions itself as the best option for a “strong stable government”, has sparked doubt over its ability to deliver on that message, with its display of disunity.
Rumours of a leadership coup against Luxon began swirling on Monday. By Tuesday speculation had reached fever pitch, compelling Luxon to call his MPs to Wellington for an urgent meeting, where a vote of confidence was expected to take place.
Luxon, who survived a leadership confidence vote in April, has seen support for National remain weak in opinion polls due to sluggish economic growth, and his personal popularity has declined after a series of missteps.
National’s support has weakened as the economy struggles, with unemployment at an 11-year high and inflation above the central bank target of 1% to 3%. While recent polling suggests the coalition would scrape back into power, Luxon’s personal popularity has remained consistently low throughout his term.
A 1News / Verian poll released on Wednesday showed his popularity had dropped further, to 17%, though he still remained the more popular leader, above Labour’s Chris Hipkins on 15%.
The leadership challenge comes off the back of a rocky week for Luxon, who came under fire for a series of gaffes, including having to apologise to small business leaders after telling them they held a “negative view” about operating in a tough economy and had a “parent-child mentality” with the government.
He then made a surprise captain’s call on talkback radio pledging to put the country’s electoral system, MMP, to a referendum if voted back in. That announcement caught his party off guard and he again found himself apologising to his members.
Luxon drew criticism from opposition politicians for using the New Zealand Defence Force aircraft to travel to Auckland after a National party fundraiser, and faced backlash for expressing confidence in the foreign minister, Winston Peters, who told a Chinese-born Green MP to “go back to your own country”.
Posting to social media after the prime minister’s announcement, the Labour leader, Chris Hipkins, said National had spent the day fighting over jobs.
“The National party is deeply divided. And the instability this week has shown exactly why nothing is getting better for hard working Kiwis,” he said.
Green party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said as the party “tussle about who should be in the top job, they continue to show their focus is on anything other than what matters to the people of this country.”
Ben Thomas, a political commentator, said removing a sitting prime minister requires a high threshold to be met, and in this case, it was “better the devil you know”. He added that polling for National and Luxon had marginally improved. “It’s not exactly a new dawn, but it is a glimpse of sunlight.”
The political commentator and author Dr Claire Robinson said something had clearly gone wrong inside the party, to warrant an urgent confidence vote.
“But they’ve clearly made a risk assessment: is it better to stick with what people know rather than pick an untested leader?”
Luxon would now need to prove he is capable of avoiding further missteps, she said.
“If he doesn’t actually do the work on himself, then there’s just going to be more and more moments like this.”

The National Meteorological Center renewed its orange alert for torrential rain on Wednesday, forecasting heavy rain across a broad swath of the country through Thursday morning, including Henan, Shandong and Hubei.
China has a four-tier emergency response system, with Level I being the most severe response. It also has a four-tier, color-coded weather warning system, with red representing the most severe warning, followed by orange, yellow and blue. ■
