Kabir Adeniyi
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Industrial action by aviation unions in Nigeria disrupted domestic flight operations Tuesday in the commercial capital Lagos and the capital Abuja, leaving hundreds of passengers stranded at airports.
It was led by the National Union of Air Transport Employees (NUATE), the Air Transport Services Senior Staff Association of Nigeria (ATSSSAN) and the National Association of Aircraft Pilots and Engineers (NAAPE), with support from the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) and the Trade Union Congress (TUC).
The unions are protesting what they describe as anti-union practices by domestic airlines and the failure to remit a 5% Ticket Sales Charge (TSC) collected from passengers and owed to aviation agencies.
The action particularly disrupted the operations of Nigeria’s largest airline, Air Peace, after union members picketed its facilities at Murtala Muhammed Airport in Lagos and Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja.
Air Peace said the industrial action resulted in the barricading of entrances to its departure terminals, preventing scheduled flights from leaving Lagos and Abuja.
“The ongoing industrial action has resulted in the barricading of the entrances to our departure terminals at Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal 1 (Alpha and Zulu Terminals) and Terminal 2 in Lagos, as well as the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport Terminal in Abuja,” the airline said in a statement.
It added that the disruption had “significantly affected” passengers travelling across its network and apologized to those stranded.
“Air Peace sincerely apologizes to all affected and stranded passengers for the disruption and inconvenience caused by circumstances beyond the airline’s control,” it said.
United Nigeria Airlines also suspended its flight operations, citing concerns over passenger and crew safety amid the industrial action.
“We regret to inform our valued passengers that we have temporarily suspended our flight operations due to the ongoing industrial action embarked upon by labor unions against domestic airlines,” it said.
“This decision was taken to protect the safety of our passengers and crew, which remains our priority at all times.”
The unions had earlier issued a three-day strike notice to airlines they accused of obstructing workers from joining unions and withholding the 5% TSC.
They said the remittance of the charge was necessary to enable aviation agencies to meet their financial obligations and implement negotiated conditions of service for workers.
The Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) said it was aware of the industrial action and its impact on passengers and other stakeholders.
The disruption comes during a period of heightened tension between aviation unions and domestic airlines over workers’ unionization and financial obligations to aviation agencies.
The unions have demanded that airline workers be allowed to join unions of their choice without intimidation, victimization or discrimination, while also calling for the immediate remittance of outstanding TSC revenues.
The action caused frustration among passengers at affected airports, with travelers facing uncertainty over their scheduled flights and alternative travel arrangements.

UNESCO: 2.4 million girls barred from school in Afghanistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:49:00 UTC
07:49:00 KST

UNESCO: 2.4 million girls barred from school in Afghanistan
August 12, 2026
Around 2.4 million girls in Afghanistan have been denied access to secondary education since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, UNESCO said Tuesday.
The figure has risen by about 200,000 since last year and could reach nearly four million by 2030 if the ban remains in place.
"Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are formally banned from secondary and higher education," Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO’s program coordinator for education in emergencies, said.
"Five years is not a temporary interruption in a child’s education. It is clearly almost an entire secondary school cycle."
Why are Afghan girls banned from secondary schools and universities?
The Taliban seized power on August 15, 2021, as US and NATO forces withdrew after two decades of war.
They initially assured the international community that women would be allowed to continue studying.
But secondary schools were closed to girls in March 2022. Women were barred from universities in December that year.
The Taliban described both measures as temporary, but they remain in force.
The authorities say they respect women's rights in line with their interpretation of Islamic law and Afghan culture. They have also insisted the issue is a domestic matter.
Restrictions extend beyond education. Women face limits on employment and movement and have been barred from public parks, gyms and beauty salons.
The UN has described the broader system of restrictions as “gender apartheid.” Russia is the only country to formally recognize the Taliban administration.
What has happened to girls' education since the Taliban takeover?
UNESCO says the restrictions have reversed two decades of progress.
Girls had very limited access to schooling in 2001. By 2021, nearly one million were enrolled in secondary education.
"Afghanistan had made really major progress in expanding girls’ access to education," Jaberian said. "But unfortunately, much of that progress now has been completely reversed."
UNESCO has called for the immediate and unconditional restoration of girls' and women's right to secondary and higher education.
The agency continues to support community-based education as well as literacy and skills programs, often held in community spaces or facilitators' homes.
How is the Taliban ban affecting Afghanistan's economy?
UNESCO estimates that excluding women from secondary and higher education could push around 600,000 women out of the workforce by 2066.
The restrictions could also cause cumulative income losses of 9.6 billion US dollars and increase the risk of early marriage.
The ban is also worsening a shortage of female teachers. UNESCO expects Afghanistan to face a deficit of more than 11,000 qualified female teachers by 2030.
"Many teachers have left the country and those who were in the system are banned from continuing teaching," Jaberian said.
She added that restrictions on women teaching boys had left some pupils with unqualified male teachers or no teachers at all.
How severe is Afghanistan's wider education crisis?
Afghanistan's education system is facing problems far beyond the ban on girls.
More than two million primary school children are already out of school for other reasons. More than 90% of 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text, while the national literacy rate stands at 37%.
Many schools are overcrowded and poorly equipped. Nearly half lack water, sanitation or heating.
The system is also under pressure from people returning to Afghanistan.
Three million people returned in 2025 alone, either voluntarily or forcibly. More than seven million have returned or been forced back since 2023.
Natural disasters have added to the crisis. Earthquakes, floods and other disasters have forced around 1,000 schools to close since 2021, UNESCO said.
Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

PBS Chief Paula Kerger on the Aftermath of Federal Funding Cuts—and What People Get Wrong About Public Media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:44:45 UTC
07:44:45 KST

Paula Kerger is navigating arguably the most challenging period of her 20-year tenure at the helm of the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS), which has more than 330 member stations. Last spring, President Donald Trump signed an executive order calling for all federal funding to PBS and NPR to be blocked, accusing the organizations of bias. Soon after, the Department of Education notified the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB) that it was terminating the 2020-2025 Ready To Learn grant for educational content, affecting PBS as well as dozens of public television and radio stations. PBS and NPR sued, and in March this year a federal judge ruled that the executive order barring the federal funding violated the First Amendment.
But the organization must still grapple with a funding shortfall created by a Congressional vote to rescind around $1.1 billion in advance appropriated federal funding for PBS and NPR, and an entirely new landscape for public media. The CPB, which was created in 1967 as a nonpartisan nonprofit to direct federal appropriations to public television and radio stations, announced in January that it would officially dissolve. PBS has since reduced its budget by 21% and cut 15% of positions, or around 100 jobs.
It’s not the first time PBS has faced such a threat, Kerger says, pointing to Newt Gingrich's “Contract with America” platform in 1994. But his idea was a “three-year glide path to zero,” she says. By contrast, the latest move gave stations just three months to find alternative funding, since they were already expecting the appropriated funds for 2026 and 2027, she says.
Since the rescission, Kerger has been touring the U.S. and speaking with affected communities. “The light bulb went off,” she says of the public’s reaction. “It's like, ‘Oh, Viewers Like You. That means us.’” Since the July 2025 rescission, PBS has seen more than a million new memberships. Philanthropy and commercial partnerships are helping. And Kerger hopes to get “some level of government funding back,” particularly to support rural communities and infrastructure, she says.
Kerger says she is most concerned about the future of content for children. “The kids' media landscape right now is really scary. A lot of kids are on YouTube, and there is some good stuff on YouTube, but kids get caught in the algorithm and they end up in places they shouldn't. Not all of it is by educators—our stuff all is, and it's rigorously tested,” she says. PBS is also working on games and content for “the significant number of kids that are not in formal pre-K, and whose family may not have access to as much technology or broadband.”
TIME spoke with Kerger on July 15 about the aftermath of the funding pullback, what people get wrong about PBS, and what gives her hope about the future for the organization.
This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.
You've talked before about how some people don't understand what PBS is. What do people get wrong about PBS?
Media in most countries started out as government-based, and then commercial media came second, and we were the other way around here. So commercial media was actually a growing industry, and it was the first woman FCC commissioner—a woman by the name of Frieda Hennock—who was looking at what she was anticipating as something that was going to have an enormous impact on society, but that was all rooted in commercialism in the marketplace. She worried there would be limitations, that there would be things that would be in the public interest that [the] commercial marketplace wasn't going to take up, and so she lobbied to have spectrum put aside for both TV and radio, and that's how we began.
Flash forward to Lyndon Johnson. He was particularly taken with what the BBC was able to do in terms of bringing great culture and history to the public, and he thought that our country should have that. He recognized that this loose confederation of individual stations that were mostly doing local or educational stuff wasn't exactly it, and that with some support you could create something that was more akin to the BBC, and that's when he signed the Public Broadcasting Act. Part of that was to create a network [that] could pull all these individual stations together. The second part of it was to ensure that there was federal funding available for communities that would perhaps be challenged to have their own stations. And so our funding always looked like that up until we lost the money last year. The largest percentage of most of the money went to stations, not to PBS and NPR. I think that was a confusion with some members of Congress. I'm not sure they knew exactly what they were voting on.
Those that were in smaller communities would get a larger proportion of their budget from the federal government. In Alaska, there actually is no other media except public radio and public television stations. Almost half of their budget comes from the federal government. So, it sort of played out exactly as LBJ anticipated. Our stations are all locally owned, locally operated, locally governed. I don't tell anyone what to do, but everyone pays dues to PBS. We take that money, we raise some other money, leverage some additional money. We work with producers. We pull together a full schedule that we distribute. The whole broadcast infrastructure is all managed by PBS. The digital infrastructure that was built— apps, PBS.org that a lot of stations plug into—all built by PBS. Stations’ positions on cable and on places like YouTube TV, negotiated by PBS. The work that we do in schools, which is all distributed via broadband—free, all done by PBS. Stations then contribute their content, so that it is still very much bottom up, but the glue that pulls it all together is PBS.
Can you talk me through where things stand today with the funding pullback?
So last year was quite a year, and we're still navigating through quite a few things. It started out with the FCC saying, "We think you're running commercials.” We actually are not. What we are running is sponsorship credits. We actually had worked with the FCC to define what is appropriate for public media, and we've worked closely with every Administration. Then we had the executive order that was going to make it illegal for any federal money to come to PBS and NPR. We won that suit. And the government [missed] the deadline to appeal, so it stands.
And then, of course there was the rescission. The executive order took out a program that we have managed for 30 years, which has funded our kids' content: Ready To Learn. For many years, the Department of Education would fund programming out of PBS that was all built around what the Education Department's priorities were, whether that's literacy or math skills or executive function or, in the last round—which had been re-upped under the first Trump Administration—workforce preparedness. Now, you can decide what that means for preschool, but we interpreted it as giving kids a really good start on the basics, before they entered school, as a way of just helping to make sure that we were jump-starting them in their school career that would lead to a professional career. After the executive order, that money was gone.
Then in June we lost the House vote, and this money had been advance appropriated for 2026 and 2027…I worked with the Public Media Company and within a very short period of time, we were able to raise bridge funds. That helped stabilize smaller stations that I think, some of them, would have gone dark very quickly.
PBS have been working pretty deliberately to make sure that the public is aware that the funding is gone. In the time since the rescission, we’ve picked up more than a million new members, and most of those are people that didn't just write a check, but they agreed to give every month, so they've really signed up to be part of this. It has not solved all of our problems, but we're in at least a stable position right now.
What I've been really focused on is our business model moving forward. Obviously, I would really love to get some level of government funding back, and I would argue [that’s] infrastructure money. If we could get that back, that would make an enormous difference. In addition to being a broadcaster, we're also the backup system for the emergency alert for this country because we operate broadcast, so we can reach everywhere. It's not just the messages to the public, but it's also using our spectrum to get information to first responders. It's a stable platform. Data and so forth can be pushed out via broadcast very effectively and very efficiently.
The philanthropy is going to continue to be significant. We continue to look for production partners. We are streaming content on Amazon. So, some business revenue, some philanthropic investment, and the hope of trying to get at least some [funding] from the government. I think if we can get all those pieces aligned, we'll be in really strong shape.
Can you give an indication of the proportions of those different funding streams?
So historically, half of our money came from our stations, and a lot of that was contributed money. So I would say probably moving forward, I would assume that half of our money would continue to be contributed money, if we can manage this properly. Of the government money, it was 15% in aggregate. Whether some piece of that would come back, I can't even begin to quantify what that would mean. The rest of it would be some combination of increased foundation grants, as well as the contributed money. So a quarter of earned revenue, a quarter of high net worth and then foundation grants and individual giving. Individual giving is what's kept us anchored in communities. It's also what makes this so powerful, because everyone feels that they own it.
On the philanthropy side of things, how are you thinking about who you want to take funding from? You've said before that you don't really want billionaires.
There were a lot of people that said, “Don't you have a billionaire that could solve your problems?” If people want to make more generous contributions, that’s great. We have some big needs. I just think that this idea that someone is going to sail in and save you is not good, and it's particularly not good for media. Even if someone has the very best of intentions, there's always going to be that doubt of, is someone really directing, or does someone have a thumb on the scale, or so forth.
There are some people that really did step up this last year. I'm out talking to a lot of them, particularly around specific genres, and particularly around kids, right now. Kids have been impacted on so many different levels in the last couple of years, whether it's access to health care, there's so many children that have food insecurity now, and daycare circumstance—particularly high quality pre-K—has deteriorated, not improved. You just see that kids have borne the brunt of so much. We've got the history going all the way back to Fred Rogers and Sesame Street—we reach all those children. Our stations live in communities across the country. There are a lot of philanthropists that are looking at this, and these are areas that they care deeply about. So I'm hoping to continue to make that good case.
The current administration has turned its attention to some foundations as well. Is that a consideration when you're thinking about which foundations you will accept funding from?
I'll tell you what I pay attention to. One is, obviously, we have a firewall between our editorial and the contributed money, and that's really important. What I do pay attention to is not whether I'll take money from this foundation or that foundation for political reasons. What I do pay attention to is that we have a mix of donors that represent a range of interests, perspectives, geography, and so forth. I think there was a fallacy in the arguments around us and our funding that somehow we were left-leaning, or that we were funded by left-leaning organizations. Look at Ken Burns' recent series on the American Revolution. If you look at those funders, particularly the larger ones, you see people across the political spectrum. That's how it should be. We want all people engaged and involved. We're a public media service for the country, and we need to reflect the country in that way.
I think the combination of doing that with the larger contributions, as well as lots and lots of small contributions, that's really always been the bedrock of public broadcasting. Every year, I think 23 years in a row, we have fielded a study that ranks us most trusted of public institutions. YouGov has been doing a similar survey in the last years. Same thing. I think we're number two after the Weather Channel. I think part of it is that if you anchor your support in a lot of grassroots philanthropy, people have to trust you, and so we take all of this really super seriously.
And I would say that in the funding discussions in the last year, and actually on an ongoing basis, occasionally someone says—and believe me, I get these calls—”What, are you just catering to the Administration?” or “You're too hard on the Administration.” A lot of times I'll get those calls around the same broadcast, which is a little weird. People say, “Well I think you're biased” and it's like, OK, we do take this really seriously, can you give me an example? And oftentimes they can't.
Are these the sorts of conversations that you're having with members of Congress? What is it that they are expressing they're most concerned about?
Some, I think, were surprised when we were defunded that it actually affected their local station. Ironically, a lot of the legislators spend time at the stations. That's where a lot of them end up doing town halls and debates, and they come in for various community events. I went and visited a couple of the senators that had voted against us and some of them said, well it was really the advance appropriation we were trying to get rid of and we'll look at the regular appropriations process, and it's still a dance. There was a little movement this year in looking at the infrastructure money that I'm talking about, at least reopening the program that existed where that funding had flowed before. That's a really important first step. Government funds infrastructure—it makes sense to me.
What would it take to get that through?
Getting enough people to vote from both sides of the aisle. I don't know [that], out of this budget process, we’ll be successful, but we're going to just keep plugging away at it because I think as people are setting priorities, the important thing is to get on that list. One of the things, both helpful and not, is in this last year, for the most part, people haven't seen enormous change. Unless we get some help, I think it'll become apparent in this next year we’ll likely lose a few stations, and I think that will also get people's attention, particularly if it happens to be in your legislative district.
This isn’t the first time that PBS has faced these sorts of challenges, but to your mind, why do you think PBS has become a target in this moment?
Well, I think media in general has been a target. I frankly think that's part of why so many people have also stepped up. I think a lot of people are very concerned about the impact of what they're seeing and how it's affecting different media organizations. It's a challenging time for media anyway because of the changes in how people are consuming content, and so we have been very much involved over a number of years, in really looking at how do we meet people where they are. YouTube has been a great partner of ours, and they helped us get all of our stations on YouTube TV, and that's opened up other possibilities on other platforms. So it's been a complicated time to navigate through. People's patterns have shifted a lot.
Who are your audiences, in terms of demographics?
Depends on what you're watching. We have a very big audience under 5. We have a very large audience across demographics on digital. For example, the Frontline broadcast audience is well over 60. The YouTube audience is under 35 [and] is also global.
I'd say the one commonality for a PBS viewer is that [it’s] people that are curious about the world, just want to learn more. I've been talking a lot over this last year as we've rolled into the 250th [anniversary of the U.S.]. I've always been struck by what I view as our key values of our country. The pursuit of happiness. What does that mean? I think what it means is lifelong learning. It's this idea that anyone would have the opportunity to achieve their potential, and that's who we are, and so I think that for our viewers, that very much captures who watches.
Where would you like to see PBS over the next 10 or 15 years?
I feel like we have had a role in the life of people and families and communities across this country, and I am deeply committed to making sure that we continue to meet the needs of people that clearly will evolve over the next 10, 15 years. I think how we connect to people will continue to change. I think the power of a story well told is extraordinary, and so, however that story [is told], I want to make sure that we're there to do that. I think our place in local communities is pretty profound.
But I think for us to thrive, we also have to make sure that we're continuing to bring in new voices and new perspectives. Our focus is around making sure that we're educating and engaging and inspiring. I really hope that as we look forward over the next 10 to 15 years, that it will continue to also be a through line. We want to embrace that whole idea of pursuit of happiness and really ensure that people see possibility. And if we do that and we do it well, then I'll be really proud of what we've accomplished at PBS.

EU has no idea who will pay for €90 bn Ukraine loan – MEP
The EU is pumping €90 billion ($105 billion) into Ukraine without knowing how the burden of the interest-free loan will be distributed among member states, German MEP Fabio De Masi told the Berliner Zeitung, warning that the money will enrich “corrupt oligarchs” in Ukraine.
Member states gave the green light to the scheme in April, with Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia securing exemptions.
On Monday, German MEP Fabio De Masi, who co-chairs the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance party, told the Berliner Zeitung that the “European Commission apparently doesn’t even know the extent to which EU member states will have to guarantee the Ukraine loan.”
He cited the commission’s response to his inquiry, which said that a “breakdown [of the financial burden] by member state” could not be provided.
De Masi said the funds, which are being backed by joint EU borrowing on the capital market, would end up enriching “corrupt oligarchs” in Ukraine.
“One wonders how the German government and parliament could have waved through this bottomless pit of debt without a thorough assessment of the consequences,” he added, as quoted by the daily.
Since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, the EU has given more than €216 billion to Kiev. Germany has spent over €43.3 billion, while earmarking an additional €57.6 billion in military aid for the coming years, thus emerging as Ukraine’s top backer within the bloc.
In late June, the European Commission began disbursing the first €3.2 billion tranche as part of the scheme, under which Ukraine is due to receive €30 billion in budgetary aid and €60 billion for its military needs in 2026 and 2027. The installment was soon followed by another 3.9 billion earmarked for drone procurement.
European Council head Antonio Costa previously said Ukraine would only need to pay back the money after it receives reparations from Russia following the conclusion of the conflict. Moscow has dismissed the notion as “detached from reality.”
Commenting on the EU loan scheme, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused the bloc of “digging into the pockets of its own taxpayers” to prolong the conflict.
In an article for Politico Europe in June which the Brussels-based media outlet eventually rejected, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov argued that EU leaders view the Kiev regime as a battering ram against Russia, with no regard for the lives of ordinary Ukrainians.

GM reaches up to $4.5 billion parts deal designed to avoid supply chain troubles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:42:10 UTC
07:42:10 KST

DETROIT — General Motors has reached a unique, multibillion-dollar parts deal as it aims to preserve cash and prevent supply chain disruptions like ones that have hit the global automotive industry this decade.
In a public filing Tuesday, GM said the up to $4.5 billion purchasing facility includes a company called Procura Auto Parts that specializes in sourcing rare or critical parts. It will receive funding through a bank syndicate led by JPMorgan Chase and Banco Santander to prepay select suppliers on behalf of GM.
In return, GM will issue formal promises called irrevocable payment undertakings, or IPUs, to pay back the company after it uses the parts in production, no later than July 31, 2029. The deal allows GM to keep inventory costs off its books, while better securing future supply.
GM pays interest, plus an agreed-upon premium on what's used, as well as a customary annual fee on the unused portion during that year, according to the filing. For accounting purposes, the prepayments show up as an asset and each purchase is booked as unsecured debt, and the cash flows are shown as if GM paid suppliers directly, the filing said.
These payments are excluded from adjusted automotive free cash flow until GM actually buys the inventory. The company typically books the capital within 90 days of purchase.
GM declined to disclose what parts the company may be targeting. Problematic parts for the automotive industry have included semiconductor chips, including dynamic random access memory, rare earths and wire harnesses.
The deal follows years of global automotive supply chain issues and comes after GM and other automakers reevaluated their sourcing or parts following U.S. tariffs and a push to move away from Chinese companies.
GM established the deal with Procura and the banks on Friday, according to the filing.

Trump administration ends Medicaid, CHIP funding for child gender transitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:38:49 UTC
07:38:49 KST

Rabia İclal Turan
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced Tuesday that it is ending federal Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) funding for gender transition procedures for children and youth.
The final rule, implemented through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), ends federal funding for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgical operations for children, which HHS describes as "experimental and life-altering sex-rejecting procedures that carry serious long-term health risks."
"Today, we are ending federal taxpayer funding for sex-rejecting procedures on children," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said, citing "serious risks" and "irreversible harm."
CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said children "deserve our protection, not experimental interventions."
"By cutting off federal funds for these sex-rejecting procedures, we’re following the science, saving taxpayer dollars, and, most importantly, protecting children from potentially irreversible harm so they can truly flourish," Oz added.
Mental health coverage is unaffected, and children currently on hormone therapy will retain funding for up to six months. The rule takes effect Oct. 13.
President Donald Trump said he directed the move, writing on his Truth Social platform that the administration would not "pay for our innocent children to undergo these barbaric surgeries and practices, which result in unthinkable and irreversible harm to their young bodies."
"Thanks to our strong position and pressure on this issue over the past year and a half, dozens of U.S. hospitals have already ended this so-called ‘gender-affirming care,’ and we expect many more to follow," he added.
He linked the announcement to the midterm elections, saying: "Please remember this when you are casting your vote in the Midterm Elections in November."

Iran announced plans to create a ballistic missile with a range of up to 15,000 km, which could reach U.S. territory. It is noted that this would require a complex technological step, possibly involving the use of North Korean technologies.
Iran has announced plans to create a ballistic missile with a range of up to 15,000 km, which could potentially reach U.S. territory. Defense Express reports this, citing a statement by Abd al-Nabi Musavi Fard, a representative of Iran’s Supreme Leader, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the Iranian leadership representative made the statement during Friday prayers. Currently, Iran’s longest-range ballistic missile is considered to be the Khorramshahr, with a claimed range of up to 4,000 km.
Defense Express notes that transitioning from medium-range missiles to an intercontinental system with a range of 15,000 km would be a difficult technological step. To strike Washington and New York from Iranian territory, a range of at least approximately 10,000 km would be required.
Possible role of North Korea
Defense Express suggests that Iran may attempt to use North Korea’s existing missile technologies. The publication recalls that the Khorramshahr was developed on the basis of the North Korean Hwasong-10, which, in turn, originated from the Soviet R-27 ballistic missile.
North Korea already has several intercontinental ballistic missiles with a claimed range of approximately 15,000 km or more. In particular, the Hwasong-18’s range is estimated at approximately 15,000 km, while the Hwasong-19 is claimed to have a range of more than 17,000 km. The Hwasong-17’s range is estimated at approximately 15,000 km.
Defense Express suggests that Iran may obtain some of the necessary technologies through cooperation with North Korea. At the same time, the publication does not rule out the direct transfer of missile technologies by Russia, although this is currently an assumption rather than a confirmed fact.

Budget Instability Puts Golden Dome at Risk, Guetlein Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:26:27 UTC
07:26:27 KST

HUNTSVILLE, Ala.—The four-star general in charge of the Pentagon’s Golden Dome program warned that uncertainty around the Pentagon’s $350 billion reconciliation request could slow progress on the homeland missile defense effort, a top priority for President Donald Trump.
To date, the Pentagon’s strategy for funding the $185 billion program has been to bypass the annual budget process and rely instead on a separate funding maneuver called reconciliation, which isn’t subject to standard appropriations rules and can be passed by a simple majority in both chambers of Congress.
That approach allowed the program to hit the ground running last year after Trump signed an executive order announcing the initiative, according to Golden Dome Director Gen. Michael Guetlein. As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed in 2025, Golden Dome received $25 billion—90 percent of which it has since obligated, Guetlein told an audience Aug. 11 at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium here.
This year, the Pentagon requested $17 billion for the effort as part of a proposed $350 billion reconciliation package and just $400 million in the normal “base” budget for fiscal 2027. This time around, though, there appears to be little political will to pass another spending bill via reconciliation, leaving Golden Dome without a clear path for near-term funding.
“We’ve got to figure out as a nation a different way of funding Golden Dome, at least for ‘27,” Guetlein said. “Both sides of the aisle, as well as the House and the Senate, are working through the math about how do you do this in ‘27. I will tell you that if they don’t figure it out, there is no Golden Dome because there is no funding.”
For now, the reconciliation process is stalled in Congress. The House approved a slimmed down $60 billion version of the White House’s proposal in July. It’s possible some Pentagon priorities initially included in reconciliation could be funded through a separate $67 billion Iran war supplemental, though that proposal is also in limbo.
Meanwhile, the prospects of passing a standard appropriations bill by the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30 have also dimmed. The House and Senate have passed separate versions of a continuing resolution that would provide stopgap funding to avoid a government shutdown. Guetlein noted that the continuing resolution—which freezes funding at the prior year’s levels—doesn’t provide relief for Golden Dome.
“A CR doesn’t help me under Golden Dome because I don’t have a top line to fall back to to get that percentage of the continuing resolution,” he said.
Speaking with reporters after his speech, Guetlein said the department is discussing contingency plans should reconciliation fail. One option is for the military services to take over funding some elements of the Golden Dome architecture. He pointed to the Space Force as an example, which has already invested heavily in Golden Dome-enabling capabilities like the Space Data Network and space-based missile warning and tracking satellites.
“Several of the space capabilities that we are investing in are also being invested in by the Space Force,” he said. “So, if Golden Dome is not able to continue to invest in those type of capabilities, then the Space Force could decide at that time to continue the investments.”
He added: “Because we have diversified execution of a lot of these capabilities, and a lot of these capabilities are already requested by combatant commands, there are some alternatives that we can pursue. We have not made any decisions on any pathway.”
Guetlein said he’s hopeful the department and Congress will find a way to fund the program in ‘27 given the urgency around bolstering U.S. defenses against missile threats and the capabilities he says the team has already proven.
During his speech, Guetlein highlighted recent milestones, which include breaking ground on the Golden Dome’s first operational site at Joint Expeditionary Base Fort Story, Va., and a major test event it conducted in June at White Sands Missile Range, N.M. Of note, Guetlein told reporters the Pentagon’s independent Director of Operational Test & Evaluation did not oversee the test; instead a “separate entity” is charged with leading validation efforts in close coordination with DOT&E.
Guetlein also reported progress on one of Golden Dome’s more ambitious technical lifts—demonstrating the integration of space-based interceptors to defeat missile threats at various phases of flight. The Space Force is leading a prize competition among 12 companies to incrementally showcase SBI capabilities with the goal of an initial capability by 2028.
Contractors have completed the first of those increments, dubbed Gate One, which focused on solidifying a design and conducting component-level testing. Guetlein said it appears all of the providers will move to Gate Two, where they will build a prototype. Those that progress to Gate Three must prove the capability works in space and then the Gate Four providers must show their interceptors can be integrated with the broader Golden Dome architecture.
“We have not put in any operational requests for production capabilities until after they prove through the prize-based competition that those capabilities are effective, but more importantly, that they’re scalable and affordable,” he said. “At that point, we will then make a decision if we are going to move into production or not.”

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Aug 12, 2026
Hormuz to stay closed unless US meets Iran’s conditions
The Strait of Hormuz will remain closed as long as the US does not change its behaviour and accept Iran’s conditions to end the war, the newly appointed secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said on Aug 11.

“As long as America does not change its behaviour and does not accept Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened,” Mohsen Rezaei, a close ally of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, was quoted by semi-official Tasnim news agency as saying.
“America must end the war, pay Iran’s frozen assets, the war must end throughout the region, including in Lebanon and Gaza,” he said.
Air India pilot tests positive for marijuana after mid-air plunge
The captain of an Air India aircraft that suddenly dropped about 90m on a flight last week tested positive for marijuana in a second test, according to people familiar with the matter.
On Aug 9, the Indian government said the pilot in command of AI2379, which flew from Phuket to Delhi, would undergo a second round of drug screening to confirm whether he was under the influence of a psychoactive substance when the aircraft suddenly lost altitude.
The incident, which occurred on Aug 4 and is being probed by India’s Aircraft Accidents Investigation Bureau, left several passengers and cabin crew members injured.
Quake death toll tops 250, amid race to find survivors
Rescue crews on Aug 11 dug through mountains of rubble in western Colombia, shouting for quiet so they could listen for survivors still trapped under the buildings that collapsed in a powerful earthquake estimated to have killed at least 250 people.
The 7.4-magnitude quake, the most devastating to strike Colombia this century, tore through its coffee-growing heartland early on Aug 10, leaving apartment blocks, homes, schools and health centers cracked, leaning or flattened.
Separate reports from affected cities put the death toll at 254 on the morning of Aug 11, with 101 people killed in Pereira, deep in coffee country, and 95 in Cali, the country’s third-biggest city.

Judge again bars Trump administration from implementing order that sought to limit mail voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:23:01 UTC
07:23:01 KST

Judge again bars Trump administration from implementing order that sought to limit mail voting
BOSTON (AP) — A federal judge on Tuesday ruled against President Donald Trump’s executive order that sought to create a federal voter list and directly involve the U.S. Postal Service in election operations in a way that would limit mail voting.
U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani had already halted the order Trump signed in March, his second one attempting to set national election rules. On June 25, she sided with Democratic state attorneys general in granting summary judgment, preventing the core parts of Trump’s order from taking effect.
Tuesday’s ruling creates another legal hurdle for the Trump administration to overcome should it get the initial injunction lifted by the U.S. Supreme Court.
“That it is now less than 90 days before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections underscores the critical need for an injunction to prevent Defendants from changing election rules on the eve of the election,” she wrote.
The Trump administration in late July requested that the Supreme Court halt lower court decisions that have blocked the sweeping changes in nearly half the country.
In the latest lawsuit, Talwani, who was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama, sided with the League of Women Voters and other voting rights groups.
Her ruling granting a preliminary injunction barred the Postal Service from taking any steps to implement the order for this year’s midterm elections. She said the administration has so far declined to defend the constitutionality of the executive order.
“The executive branch has no authority to regulate elections,” she wrote.
In response to the ruling, the White House noted that Trump has called for Congress to pass a stalled bill to restructure American elections,
“The entire Trump Administration will continue lawfully enacting the agenda President Trump was elected to enact — which includes the safety and security of American elections,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. “This campaign pledge from the President is why millions of Americans sent him back to the White House.”
Voting rights groups hailed the decision.
“This ruling is a victory for voters and for the Constitution,” Marcia Johnson of the League of Women Voters said in a statement. “Neither the president nor the U.S. Postal Service has the authority to rewrite election rules.”
Plaintiffs argued in two lawsuits, both filed in federal court in Boston, that the Republican president’s order should be found unconstitutional because the states and Congress, not the president, have the power to set election rules. The League of Women Voters also argued that Trump lacked the authority to issue his order and the U.S. Postal Service and other defendants lack the authority to carry it out.
Trump’s Republican administration, in its motions to dismiss the lawsuits, argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing to bring their claims. They also argued that the motions are premature and that plaintiffs lack the legal basis to bring their claim based on the Administrative Procedure Act, which governs how federal agencies develop and issue regulations.
Stephen Pezzi, a lawyer for the Trump administration, said the harms the plaintiffs referenced were subjective, because much can change with the voting list before it is made final. He also said no one would be prosecuted for violating the order.
Trump’s executive order, the second one aimed at elections during his second term, comes as he continues to suggest that there is widespread voting by noncitizens. Along with his executive orders, Trump is pushing legislation in the Republican-controlled Congress to create a proof-of-citizenship mandate. The SAVE America Act has passed the House but has stalled in the Senate.
States already have detailed processes aimed at keeping their voter rolls accurate, and voting by noncitizens has been shown to be rare. It also is a felony that can be punishable by deportation.
Trump issued the order in March after a bill he supported to overhaul voting stalled in Congress. The order would have had the federal government create a list of eligible voters and then directed the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to those on the list. Election officials argued that it was ripe for abuse and could cause chaos, and the postal union has objected to the idea of mail carriers policing ballots.
The Postal Service had published a proposed rule required by Trump’s executive order in the Federal Register, but it was put on hold by Talwani’s first ruling.
In a separate lawsuit filed against the executive order, a federal judge in Washington in May agreed with the Trump administration that it was too early to block the order because it had yet to be implemented. That lawsuit was brought by Democratic and civil rights groups. In July, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia upheld the May ruling by U.S. District Court Judge Carl J. Nichols that said an injunction against the order was premature.
Other rulings have gone against the Trump administration’s first executive order on elections, signed just months after he took office in his second term. That order would have required people to show documents proving their citizenship when registering to vote, among other changes.
Since his 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, Trump has groundlessly claimed mail voting is rife with fraud and has launched a federal investigation into that year’s vote, even though repeated audits and investigations, including ones run by Republicans, found it was free of widespread fraud. Trump also has said he wants to “take over” election administration in Democratic areas.
___
Riccardi reported from Denver.

Medicaid says it will stop paying for some gender-affirming care for transgender minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:23:01 UTC
07:23:01 KST

Medicaid says it will stop paying for some gender-affirming care for transgender minors
President Donald Trump’s administration said that Medicaid will stop paying for gender-affirming surgeries and hormone treatments for transgender minors and the state Children’s Health Insurance Program won’t pay for the treatments for those under 19.
The announcement is the latest in a series of policies from the administration aimed at transgender people that began the day Trump returned to office last year.
The policy is to take effect Oct. 13.
It is not clear how much taxpayer funding is going to cover gender-affirming treatments for transgender youth now. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services did not respond to questions about the policy on Tuesday.
At least 27 states have already banned gender-affirming care for those under 18. Even in states that haven’t, many major hospitals have stopped providing some of the treatments. And gender-affirming surgeries for minors are rare. Puberty blockers and hormone treatments are more common.
The policy calls for Medicaid and CHIP to continue to pay for mental health treatment for transgender minors but phase out coverage of hormone treatments that are used both to block puberty and to produce sex-related physical changes for those already receiving them as of April 2027.
Trump said in a social media post Tuesday that he directed Dr. Mehmet Oz, the CMS administrator, to make the change.
“We are not going to pay for our innocent children to undergo these barbaric surgeries and practices, which result in unthinkable and irreversible harm to their young bodies,” Trump said in his post.
Advocates for LGBTQ+ young people look at it differently.
GLBTQ Legal Advocates and Defenders legal director Josh Rovenger said the rule “is putting up barriers between parents and their ability to make the best medical decisions for their children” and would face a legal challenge.
“The Trump administration is terrorizing trans youth and their families with these kinds of actions, and it has to stop,” Human Right Campaign President Kelley Robinson said in a statement.
HRC is already suing the administration for efforts to bar gender-affirming care coverage under federal employee benefit plans.
The American Medical Association and most other major medical organizations support access to gender-affirming care, though the American Society of Plastic Surgeons said earlier this year that it found “insufficient evidence” that the benefits of chest, genital and facial surgeries on minors experiencing gender dysphoria — or the unease a person may have because their assigned gender and gender identity don’t match — outweigh the risks.
The administration has already announced it would cut off Medicaid and Medicare funding for hospitals that provide gender-affirming care for minors, along with barring transgender athletes from sports competitions for girls and women and blocking people from being able to choose male, female or X to designate their sex on passports.
It also released a report last year urging therapy only for transgender youth and not broader gender-affirming health care.
Most of the changes have faced legal challenges. The U.S. Supreme Court let the administration’s passport policy stand and allowed states to enforce the sports bans. A lower court ruled against the administration’s declaration that called the treatments unsafe and ineffective. A challenge over the policy targeting hospitals is still pending.

Fuel shortages now reported across 16 Russian regions
Fuel shortages and restrictions at petrol stations, which have resurfaced following new Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, are now affecting at least 16 regions of Russia.
Source: The Moscow Times, an independent Amsterdam-based news outlet; Russian media outlets
Details: On 10 August alone, restrictions on petrol sales, which had begun to ease in July amid the "diversion" of Ukrainian drones towards Wildberries warehouses, were extended to three more federal constituents.
For example, in the Achinsk district in Krasnoyarsk Krai, home to more than 110,000 people, 13 of 47 petrol stations are not operating, according to the district's deputy head, Natalia Grigorieva. She said only 16 filling stations have several types of petrol available. Local authorities also reported shortages of 294 tonnes of diesel and 16.6 tonnes of AI-92 petrol for agricultural producers.
In Bashkortostan, where drones have attacked one of the country's largest petrochemical complexes in Ufa several times this month, petrol stations have temporarily banned the sale of petrol in jerry cans and other containers. Residents have complained to Radiy Khabirov, the head of the republic, saying the restrictions prevent them from refuelling lawnmowers. The regional Ministry of Industry and Energy confirmed the restriction and asked residents to be understanding.
The authorities also said three districts in Bashkortostan – Baltachevsky, Iglino and Ilishevsky – are in the "red zone" for fuel shortages, while seven out of 26 petrol stations in Sterlitamak are not operating. The Saratov Oblast Duma (parliament) has also acknowledged that the fuel shortage is continuing.
Read also: Oil superpower queues up for petrol from India. Will it help Russia?
Stanislav Denisenko, a lawmaker from the LDPR (Liberal Democratic Party of Russia), said some petrol stations in the region have designated separate pumps for emergency services, but private car owners – "people close to the authorities" – have also started using them. Vladimir Yesipov, a member of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), said he was unable to refuel at a Lukoil station because it had run out of petrol.
Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov also described the situation with petrol in the oblast as difficult. "I won't sugar-coat the bitter pill: we should not expect any serious improvement over the next week or two," he said. He also asked residents for "mutual assistance" and urged them to "reduce their travel" where possible.
The Sochi administration issued a similar recommendation, urging residents and visitors to use public transport instead of private cars. According to local authorities, petrol is available at only two-thirds of the city's filling stations.
Since the beginning of August, reports of fuel sales restrictions at petrol stations have been recorded in Krasnodar and Primorsky Krais, as well as in Kaluga, Rostov, Tambov, Tula, Saratov, Penza, Voronezh, Ryazan, Ulyanovsk and Smolensk oblasts of Russia.
Previously:
- In June, fuel shortages emerged in most Russian regions amid regular Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries.
- On 23 June, at least 15 Russian regions introduced restrictions on fuel sales amid a fuel crisis caused by shortages of petrol and diesel.
- In late June, Russian leader Vladimir Putin acknowledged for the first time that the country was experiencing problems with motor fuel following Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and fuel depots.
Background:
- Traders shipped almost 30,000 tonnes of refined fuel to Russia from South Korea in late July.
- The Russian government previously extended its ban on petrol exports until 31 January 2027 and on diesel exports until 31 August 2026.
- Russia recently began importing petrol from Africa, bringing in around 30,000 tonnes of A-92 petrol by sea from Morocco.

Besides, govt has decided to fix the retirement age of chairperson of tribunals at 70, with members to retire at 67, unless they complete their five-year terms
NEW DELHI: Tribunal Reforms Bill, piloted by govt in Parliament, is seen as a move that reinforces the constitutional position in appointments: ensuring primacy of the judiciary in deciding top positions. At the same time, it seeks to maintain a three-tier architecture between the tribunal, the secretariat and the administrative ministry with clear roles mapped out for each.In the bill — passed by RS Tuesday and LS Monday — govt has sought to ensure the independence of National Tribunals Commission (NTC) that will supervise the appointment, functioning, discipline and administrative needs of tribunals. To be headed by a retired judge of the Supreme Court or chief justice of a high court, the proposed NTC will have two judicial members drawn from among retired HC judges apart from two technical members. The chairperson and judicial members will be appointed by govt in consultation with the CJI.The commission, through its search and selection committee, has been tasked to streamline selection of chairpersons and members of tribunals. Unlike the current system, where a panel of names is sent, the committee will recommend a single name for each vacancy, along with a waiting list. Strict timelines have been proposed for recommending names to govt and for the Centre to approve them.
It addresses a constant complaint that ministries have in appointments getting delayed.Besides, govt has decided to fix the retirement age of chairperson of tribunals at 70 years, with members to retire at 67, unless they complete their five-year terms.The commission will be assisted by a secretariat with the administrative ministry having no role in either advertising for the post or scrutinising the candidates. The ministry concerned will merely forward inputs to the secretariat on the candidate and Intelligence Bureau will provide its reports. Officials argued that this will end any possible conflict of interest that the ministry concerned will have as a litigant.

Trump secretly changed planes in Turkey due to a threat from Iran
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. President Donald Trump secretly switched to a C-32A military aircraft while departing Turkey because of a credible threat of assassination by Iran. The old Air Force One was used as a decoy, and the journalists on board were unaware of the switch.
U.S. President Donald Trump secretly switched from the old Air Force One to a C-32A military aircraft while departing Turkey after the NATO summit due to a real threat of assassination by Iran. Reuters reports this, citing The Washington Post and The New York Times, writes UNN.
Details
The White House initially said that Trump would leave Turkey aboard the old Air Force One. However, after the president boarded the aircraft in front of cameras in Ankara, he was discreetly transported to another plane in an airport catering truck.
The old Air Force One was effectively being used as a decoy at that time. Journalists and some White House staff members remained on board, believing that the president was flying with them. They were advised to keep the curtains in the press cabin closed.
Secret operation due to threat to Trump
According to The Washington Post, the decision to secretly change aircraft was made because of a real threat to Trump. After the switch, the C-32A transported the president to the United Kingdom.
Trump arrived in Turkey on a recently refurbished aircraft donated by Qatar. It was the aircraft's first international trip after the modernization, which sparked discussions about its cost and security.
A similar security measure had been used before. In 2000, President Bill Clinton used an unmarked aircraft during a trip to Pakistan, while his Air Force One served as a decoy.

Roundup: Heatwave tightens grip on Europe, straining transport, power and agriculture
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:06:59 CST
07:06:59 KST

ROME, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- A persistent heatwave is tightening its grip on large parts of Europe in August, compounding drought conditions and disrupting river transport, power generation and agriculture in parts of the continent.
Western Europe recorded its hottest June-July period on record, and the trend has continued into August, with some countries experiencing their fourth heatwave since May, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said Tuesday, citing figures from the Copernicus Climate Change Service.
In Italy, temperatures are expected to exceed 37 degrees Celsius across much of the country this week and reach 39 to 40 degrees in some inland areas, around 7 degrees above the mid-August average, Italian news agency ANSA reported Tuesday, citing meteorologists.
Belgium's Royal Meteorological Institute has also issued a yellow heat warning, with temperatures forecast to rise sharply from Wednesday and reach around 35 degrees Celsius inland by Friday.
In Central Europe and the Balkans, numerous station and all-time temperature records were broken in countries including Austria, Hungary and Slovakia during the first week of August, according to the WMO.
The WMO warned that extreme heat, exceptionally low soil moisture and drought are having a devastating impact on ecosystems, agriculture, river levels, transport and energy, while increasing the risk of fires.
In Bosnia and Herzegovina, water levels in several rivers have fallen significantly. The Sava River basin authority warned that without substantial rainfall in the next 10 to 15 days, water levels could approach record lows.
Germany's Rhine, one of Europe's most important industrial waterways, has also fallen to historically low levels. At Kaub, a key gauge for inland shipping, the water level has dropped below the previous record low set in 2018. The shallow water is forcing cargo vessels to reduce their loads, requiring more ships to carry the same volume of goods and driving up freight costs.
High temperatures have further strained power systems, as low water levels affect the cooling of power-generating facilities while demand for air conditioning and refrigeration rises.
In Poland, grid operator Polskie Sieci Elektroenergetyczne invoked emergency measures on Thursday to ensure electricity supplies amid the heatwave, the English-language news outlet Notes from Poland reported.
It was the second activation in three days and the third this summer, the outlet said. Low water levels in the Vistula River, Poland's longest river, also forced state-controlled energy company Enea to reduce operations at two coal-fired plants, taking around 1.1 GW of generation capacity offline.
Agriculture is facing mounting pressure as well.
In Belgium, public broadcaster VRT NWS reported that heat stress was reducing yields and producing smaller open-field vegetables, including broccoli, cauliflower and leeks. Greenhouse tomatoes were ripening faster, while strawberries were also becoming smaller.
Persistent drought has forced some Belgian growers to irrigate their crops daily, compared with once or twice a week under normal conditions, according to VRT NWS.
Italy's wine industry is facing similar pressures. Hot and dry weather has brought forward grape harvesting in several regions, with picking already underway unusually early in parts of the country.
Marco Caprai, a wine producer in Italy's central Umbria region, told ANSA that prolonged drought and high temperatures could leave regional grape output 5 to 10 percent below average this year. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Neighbors with tusks -- how Kenyans learn to live alongside elephants
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:06:56 CST
07:06:56 KST

Elephants are pictured at Sheldrick Wildlife Trust's Nairobi Nursery in Nairobi, Kenya, on Aug. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Jianfei)
By Xinhua writers Zheng Mengyu, Xie Jianfei
NAIROBI, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- In August, wildlife migration across East Africa reaches one of its busiest periods, drawing visitors from around the world to Kenya's vast savannas.
Across Amboseli, Maasai Mara and Tsavo, safari vehicles set out in search of lions, rhinos and cheetahs, while many visitors hope for an encounter with the world's largest land animal -- the African elephant.
Safari has also become increasingly popular among young Chinese travelers, with phrases such as "saving up for a trip to Kenya" and "go on safari at least once in a lifetime" frequently appearing on Chinese social media.
But beyond the safari routes lies a more complicated relationship between people and elephants.
Ahead of World Elephant Day on Aug. 12, a visit to communities surrounding Kenya's Amboseli National Park shows that for local residents, elephants are not simply animals to be photographed. They are neighbors sharing the same landscape.
For Maasai communities, encounters with elephants can sometimes come at a cost. Elephants may enter farms, trample crops, disturb livestock and, in some cases, injure people.
"Our work is not to drive elephants away, but to make sure both people and elephants are safe," said Purity Lakara, a female Maasai ranger.
When elephants are reported near villages or farmland, rangers rush to the scene, advise residents to keep their distance and use non-lethal methods to guide the animals away.
Conservation, however, is not only about protecting wildlife. It also needs to bring tangible benefits to the people living alongside it.
Some conservation programs in the area have helped communities improve access to water and other basic services, while encouraging local residents to take part in wildlife monitoring, early warning and protection.
"Years ago, most Maasai people did not like elephants," said Maasai resident Daniel Mulandi.
Mulandi showed a visitor photographs of elephants on his phone. Earlier this year, he spent the final night with Craig, one of Amboseli's famous "super tuskers," who died of natural causes at the age of 54.
For Mulandi, elephants have gradually changed from a source of conflict into part of the community's natural heritage.
That change has taken place against a long history of elephant poaching.
During the 1970s and 1980s, African elephants suffered a severe poaching crisis driven by demand for ivory. Their numbers fell sharply across the continent. In 1989, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora imposed an international ban on commercial ivory trade.
A decade on, the picture is mixed. Poaching has eased from its peak, and some savanna elephant populations in southern Africa have stabilized or begun a slow recovery. But the latest IUCN assessment, released in November 2025, still lists the African forest elephant as critically endangered, with habitat fragmentation from mining, roads and large-scale agriculture emerging as a growing threat alongside the ivory trade.
In recent years, stronger anti-poaching measures, habitat protection, international cooperation and greater community participation have helped improve elephant conservation in parts of Africa. Yet habitat loss, human-elephant conflict and illegal killing remain long-term challenges.
In Nairobi, the consequences of these challenges can be seen at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust's Nairobi Nursery, where orphaned elephants are cared for after losing their mothers to poaching, human-wildlife conflict, drought and other causes.
The young elephants are fed milk, cared for by keepers and gradually taught the skills they need to survive in the wild. The purpose is not to keep them in captivity, but to give them a second chance to return to nature.
"Ecosystems need elephants, and elephants are also important to building resilience to climate change," said Evan Mwavua Mkala, programs manager at the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW).
According to Mkala, Kenya's elephant population has increased from about 16,000 in 1990 to around 42,000 today, reflecting the combined impact of stronger laws and enforcement and community-centered conservation.
The idea that wildlife protection should involve people as well as animals can also be seen thousands of kilometers away in southwest China.
In 2020 and 2021, a herd of Asian elephants traveled more than 1,300 kilometers northward from their traditional habitat in Yunnan Province. As the elephants passed through populated areas, authorities used monitoring and early-warning systems and managed human activity along their route to keep residents and elephants at a safe distance.
The herd eventually turned south and returned toward suitable habitat.
The journey attracted global attention, but also offered a practical lesson: protecting wildlife is not always about keeping people and animals completely apart. It can also mean finding ways for them to share the same landscape safely.
As elephant populations recover in some parts of Africa, human-elephant conflict, habitat protection, community livelihoods and tourism will remain closely connected.
Conservation ultimately comes down to a practical question: how can people and wildlife continue to share the same home?
For elephants, it means a landscape where they can move freely and grow old without the threat of guns, traps or poisoned arrows.
For people, it means being able to live, farm and raise livestock in safety.
Between the two lies the long, practical work of conservation -- not keeping people and wildlife apart at all costs, but finding ways for both to remain part of the same home. ■

Water shortages in occupied Palestinian territory threaten public health: UN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:06:42 CST
07:06:42 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- Most of the population across the occupied Palestinian territory lacks sufficient access to water, sanitation and hygiene, UN humanitarians said Tuesday.
More than 1.3 million people -- more than half of the population -- have access to less than 6 liters of water per person per day for drinking and cooking, said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
According to humanitarian standards, the minimum amount of water needed in an emergency is 15 liters per day, which includes water for drinking, washing and cooking, said OCHA.
The office said that another 700,000 people have access to less than 9 liters of domestic water per person per day, which compromises their ability to maintain hygiene, clean their homes, and meet their children's needs.
Three in every four people rely on collecting water from trucks. Humanitarian partners took water to more than 2,500 water collection points every day and over 100 displacement sites across Gaza last month, said OCHA.
"People face overcrowding at water collection points and lack enough containers to transport water back to their homes -- a task that is often left to children," OCHA said. "Only half of all households have access to basic sanitation, or private facilities that prevent contact with human waste. The other half rely on shared, inadequate or unsafe options, which increase health risks."
The office added that humanitarian partners collect about 80 percent of all primary solid waste generated across the strip. Yet more than 900,000 people report being exposed to garbage that accumulates in residential areas.
OCHA said that consistent funding, additional permits to import spare parts, and renewed access to landfills in access-restricted areas remain essential. ■

Ships ran aground near a harbor of the Rhine in Tolkamer, Zevenaar municipality of the Netherlands, Aug. 11, 2026. According to the Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, the Rhine's discharge at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands from Germany, fell below 615 cubic meters per second on Aug. 11, 2026, marking the lowest level ever recorded amid the persistent drought. (Xinhua/Shao Haijun)
THE HAGUE, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Netherlands is facing a prolonged drought, with measures to retain and distribute freshwater coming under increasing pressure, the Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management said Tuesday.
In its weekly Drought Monitor, the ministry described the situation as "highly exceptional." The Rhine's discharge at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands from Germany, has fallen to 615 cubic meters per second, the lowest level ever recorded there.
Flows in the Meuse, a major river running through France and Belgium before entering the Netherlands, are also low, while groundwater levels across most of the country range from low to extremely low, the ministry said.
Low river flows could persist into December, while warm weather and little significant rainfall are forecast for the coming week, according to the bulletin.
The nationwide precipitation deficit is expected to reach around 300 mm, comparable to levels seen during the severe drought of 2018, the bulletin said, adding that in some regions, the deficit has already exceeded 400 mm.
The prolonged drought is taking an increasing toll on agriculture and ecosystems, with crop and environmental damage worsening in some regions. Water quality has also deteriorated, with blue-green algae and fish deaths reported in some areas, said the bulletin.
The ministry said drinking water supplies remain secure, although rising salinity levels are causing growing concern and are being closely monitored at several drinking-water intake points.
Last month, the Dutch government raised the country's water status from an "imminent water shortage" to an "actual water shortage" as persistent drought and high temperatures continued to strain water resources.
Authorities have introduced measures to conserve freshwater and maintain water levels, including restricting lock operations in several areas to reduce water use. ■

====================================================================================================

News Analysis: Saudi Arabia-Türkiye-Pakistan joint defense agreement reflects shifting Mideast security dynamics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
06:06:29 CST
07:06:29 KST

ISTANBUL, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- The recently signed Makkah Joint Defense Agreement among Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan underscores a significant shift in Middle East security dynamics, analysts say, as regional powers seek greater autonomy over their security arrangements.
The deal, signed Friday in the Saudi city of Makkah, stipulates that any armed attack against one of the three countries will be considered an attack against them all.
Following the signing ceremony, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stated the pact was based on "collective deterrence" and the right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. In an interview with local media, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described the mutual defense clause, a key provision of the agreement, as "technically identical" to NATO's Article 5 on collective defense.
Beyond the wording of the agreement itself, analysts see the pact as a sign of a broader reassessment of the security architecture in the Middle East, particularly the role of the United States.
Baris Doster, an international relations professor at Türkiye's Marmara University, emphasized that the move is a direct response to a shifting regional order.
"The diplomatic convergence among Ankara, Riyadh and Islamabad accelerated with recent developments involving the United States, Israel and Iran," Doster told Xinhua. "Needs change, and consequently, alliances change. This new pact must primarily be evaluated in the context of these changing regional power dynamics."
The regional conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran, analysts say, has further exposed vulnerabilities in the existing security paradigm.
Following the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, nearly all Gulf states with military ties to the United States found themselves drawn into the conflict.
Canan Tercan, a scholar at Istanbul Aydin University, said the conflict demonstrated that the United States could not fully protect the Middle East.
"Yes, there are U.S. bases here, but how much did they protect? It is a massive question mark. Regional countries had to overcome this vulnerability with new partnerships. We can essentially summarize this as one of the main reasons for the Makkah agreement," she told Xinhua.
Against this backdrop, the agreement underscores a growing emphasis on strategic autonomy among regional countries. While Erdogan has stressed that the agreement "does not target any country," emphasizing deterrence rather than confrontation, viewed from within the Middle East, it also represents an effort by regional actors to recalibrate the regional balance of power.
According to Doster, regional balancing is the core driver behind the agreement. "This agreement was primarily established to balance Iran's regional weight and influence," he believed.
The recent escalation in tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi group has also tested Riyadh's rapprochement with Iran, which supports the Houthis.
While the agreement's political implications for the region should not be underestimated, analysts say its prospects for effective implementation remain uncertain, with a number of procedural hurdles still to be addressed.
In recent days, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for multiple attacks on Saudi Arabia, one of the agreement's signatories. Yet the other parties to the agreement have refrained from directly intervening, suggesting, as Tercan noted, that its collective-defense provision does not automatically trigger a military response to every incident.
The provision does not mean automatic military responses to minor incidents, Tercan said, adding that Turkish military participation would strictly require parliamentary authorization rather than immediate deployment.
Beyond legislative procedures, experts stress the need to preserve the alliance's strategic autonomy.
Abdullah Agar, a Turkish security expert, warned against external manipulation. He cautioned that the three signatories must maintain their strategic autonomy and avoid being drawn into costly conflicts driven by great-power interests.
Bao Chengzhang, an associate professor at the Middle East Studies Institute of Shanghai International Studies University in China, noted that the agreement could face several challenges in its future implementation, including differences in the three countries' respective security priorities, pressure from the United States and the impact of developments in the regional conflict, among others. ■

Defence experts say PLA carrier fleet is expected to complement land-based forces and extend reach into the western Pacific and beyond
Yet behind the high-profile ship launches, experts say quieter changes in pilot recruitment, command structures and fleet integration point to a carrier doctrine distinct from the American model.
“The biggest misconception among Western analysts is the tendency to evaluate the [Chinese navy] through the doctrinal mirror of the US Navy,” said Brendan Mulvaney, director of the China Aerospace Studies Institute.

China’s carrier force is evolving under strategic conditions unlike those that shaped the American naval doctrine of using carriers to project power thousands of kilometres from home.
