12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
By Mucahithan Avcioglu
ISTANBUL (AA) - US stocks opened higher Wednesday after consumer inflation for July was in line with expectations.
The Dow Jones industrial average edged up 0.01% to 53,797.47 at the opening bell.
The S&P 500 rose 0.48% to 7,765.46, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.89% to 26,680.46.
The US Consumer Price Index increased 0.1% month-on-month and 3.4% annually in July, matching market estimates.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.2% on a monthly basis and 2.5% from a year earlier, also in line with forecasts.
Expectations that the US Federal Reserve could raise interest rates next month weakened slightly following the release of the figures.
Analysts said the inflation data, coupled with last week’s report showing weaker employment growth in July, reinforced expectations that the Fed could keep its policy rate unchanged at its September meeting.
Another consumer inflation report is due before the meeting; however, investors will closely monitor producer inflation data scheduled for Thursday.
Technology shares led the advance as corporate earnings indicated continued demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Shares of cloud-computing company CoreWeave surged more than 20% after its second-quarter revenue nearly doubled from a year earlier.
Super Micro Computer climbed more than 10% after the server maker reported financial results that exceeded market expectations.
Investors also continued to monitor geopolitical developments in the Middle East, particularly their effect on energy prices and the inflation outlook.

Researchers, advocates rail against government’s efforts to end workforce data collection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:53:02 UTC
06:53:02 KST

Researchers, advocates rail against government’s efforts to end workforce data collection
Civil rights groups and researchers at a public hearing Tuesday called on a federal agency to continue its annual collection of workplace demographic data, arguing that a proposal to end the practice will undermine efforts to fight discrimination.
Twenty-two speakers testified at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s hearing, which lasted more than two hours. Most opposed the proposal to toss a 60-year-old requirement for tens of thousands of private sector employers to submit annual workforce demographic reports to the EEOC, which is responsible for enforcing anti-discrimination laws.
Six speakers, however, spoke out in favor of the proposal, siding with the Trump administration’s stance that reporting such data is burdensome and encourages companies to adopt discriminatory practices to diversify their workforces.
The proposal, currently subject to a 30-day public commentary period ending Aug. 24, is a key step in President Donald Trump’s efforts to overhaul the country’s civil rights enforcement, particularly stamping out diversity and inclusion practices.
Since 1966, the EEOC has required companies with at least 100 employees, or federal contractors with at least 50 workers, to submit a report each year called an EEO-1 that breaks down gender and racial representation across different roles, from executives to laborers and service workers.
The Republican-led EEOC voted 2-1 last month to stop collecting that data, arguing that the reporting requirement may encourage employers to engage in discriminatory tactics.
Civil rights groups argued the data has been a crucial tool for uncovering systemic discrimination in the workplace and tracking the progress of women and minorities since the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
“By weakening EEOC enforcement, these changes will harm all workers, but particularly Black workers and other workers of color who continue to face racial discrimination more frequently,” said Amalea Smirniotopoulos, senior policy counsel at the civil rights group Legal Defense Fund.
Researchers said EEO-1 data has been crucial to their work.
Donald Tomaskovic-Devey, co-director of the University of Massachusetts Amherst’s Center for Employment Equity, said he has relied on EEO-1 data for dozens of research articles and two books. He said his research has found that while workplace discrimination has declined since 1964, progress has most recently stalled.
Without EEO-1 metrics, “our society will be flying blind into the future,” he said.
Rachel Lee, president and general counsel of Stand with Asian Americans, said the data has been critical for demonstrating that many Asian Americans rarely reach the highest ranks of many companies, despite comprising a large portion of professional roles.
“The EEO-1 report is the only federal instrument that exposes what we call the bamboo ceiling,” Lee said.
Several conservative advocates, however, criticized the EEO-1 data as outdated and conducive to stereotyping and discrimination.
“It is inconsistent with equal opportunity law, potentially unconstitutional, unnecessary to enforce anti-discrimination laws, and imposes substantial burdens on both employers and the EEOC that are not outweighed by its marginal benefits,” said Rachel Morrison, fellow at the conservative Ethics and Public Policy Center and a former EEOC attorney.
Morrison pointed out that since the EEOC investigates some forms of discrimination not captured in the EEO-1 data, such as religion and pregnancy-related discrimination, the data “is not actually necessary for EEOC to enforce Title VII or fulfill its mission.”
However, two prominent employer groups said there is little evidence that companies have used EEO-1 data to engage in racial quotas or other discriminatory employment practices, as the EEOC under the leadership of its current conservative chair Andrea Lucas argues.
“Regarding the possible misuse of EEO-1 data, we cannot square that with the experience of our members, and I might add with my personal experience,” said David Fortney of the Institute for Workplace Equality, a nonprofit employer association whose members include many of the biggest U.S. companies.
Fortney, a former chief legal officer of the Labor Department under President George H.W. Bush, said many employers instead use EEO-1 data to detect and prevent discriminatory practices. He said the EEOC has not identified any instance of an employer using EEO-1 data for discriminatory purposes.
“Presumably after six decades, if the agency had specific instances, it would have called those out,” Fortney said.
Michael Eastman, of the Center for Workplace Compliance, described examples of how its member companies have used the EEO-1 data to uncover hiring and promotion practices that excluded certain groups.
One large company, he said, found data showed that an employee referral program at a manufacturing facility consistently produced a narrow applicant pool and “a homogenous hiring pattern at the facility.”
Another company, he said, found an “unusual pattern” in its promotion decisions that suggested that managers had misunderstood internal policies to mean race and gender could be considered in promotions.
“These examples reflect what many large employers are trying to do when they use demographic data for compliance purposes,” said Eastman.

Aaron Rodgers is leaning into his final year, except when it comes to playing in the preseason
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:53:02 UTC
06:53:02 KST

Aaron Rodgers is leaning into his final year, except when it comes to playing in the preseason
LATROBE, Pa. (AP) — There was a time when the preseason felt like the Super Bowl to Aaron Rodgers.
Now is not that time.
While the Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback is trying to soak in every moment of what he says will be his 22nd and final NFL training camp, he doesn’t sound like someone who thinks he needs to be on the field when the Steelers host Green Bay in their exhibition opener on Thursday night.
“It’s not real football,” Rodgers said.
At least, not “real” compared to what things will look like when the games start to count in September. Most defenses are vanilla. Most offenses too. The four-time MVP understands August is still a valuable time of year, just not for someone who has been in the league nearly as long as some of his teammates — backup quarterbacks Drew Allar (22) and Will Howard (24) — have been alive.
“I think preseason football is good to see guys with pads on, under the lights, how they react to the nerves,” he said.
Nerves that Rodgers once had himself. He remembers running onto the field as a rookie with Green Bay in 2005 and trying desperately to keep his breathing under control. He failed as much as he succeeded.
Back then, the goal was to make sure he could hear the play coming through the headset so he could repeat it with conviction in the huddle. And that was the easy part.
The challenge was then walking to the line of scrimmage and “trying to remember what else is going on in the play and who’s got what.”
Those jitters eventually subsided. It took a while, but they’re long since gone. It’s why he feels the Steelers will be better served with Rodgers watching from the sideline with a headset on while Howard — who didn’t take a live snap last year after getting hurt early in camp — and Allar do the majority of the work.
Rodgers described the first game as traditionally “hectic,” one of many reasons his preference is to be in sweatpants offering perspective.
“I like to be the voice of reason, tell the occasional dad joke or one-liner,” he said. “Just help everybody settle in a little bit.”
Mike McCarthy, in his first season coaching his hometown team, played a little coy about whether he’ll ask Rodgers to see a little game action, though McCarthy might have tipped his hand a bit when he said he’d divide the offense into three groups.
One group will handle the first couple of series. The second will play until halftime, with the third taking over for the final two quarters.
The math is pretty easy. Pittsburgh currently has four quarterbacks — Rodgers, Howard, Allar and Mason Rudolph — on the roster. Only one of them has operated a McCarthy offense in a game, and it’s the one who will turn 43 in December.
“Frankly, the most important part is the health of the team,” McCarthy said. “That drives these decisions. That’s where you tend to maybe pull back and maybe not play the veteran or the older guys in those situations. You just lean on their experience.”
McCarthy is well-versed in what Rodgers can do. Howard and Allar remain very much works in progress and could have the opportunity to be a long-term part of Pittsburgh’s future. They’ll take their first real steps in that direction on Thursday, and Rodgers wants to help make sure those steps are more assured than tentative.
“Quarterback, just like all things, can be overcomplicated to make it seem more difficult than it might be sometimes,” he said. “It’s not easy, but you can simplify things, and that’s what I’m trying to help with.”
Rodgers’ most recent preseason snaps came three years ago during the first of his brief two-season stint with the New York Jets. He was “open” to doing it last summer in Pittsburgh, though former head coach Mike Tomlin opted to hold him out. The decision looked like the right one when Rodgers threw for four touchdowns in a Week 1 win over his old team.
Rodgers was still finding his way back then. Now, he’s far more familiar with the personnel around him and his reunion with McCarthy means he’s ending his career in the same system where he began it a generation ago.
It’s why he believes the real growth during camp comes on the practice field. He likes what he’s seen so far, which is part of why he’s just fine letting others get chased around by opponents during the waning days of summer.
“I think we’re right where I’d like to be,” he said. “I think we’re ahead of where we were last year. I think you’re seeing guys take some steps and then play with confidence.”

High school football player in Arkansas practices with a venomous snake in his helmet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

High school football player in Arkansas practices with a venomous snake in his helmet
MAUMELLE, Ark. (AP) — A high school football player in Arkansas had every right to be rattled after finding a venomous snake inside his helmet during practice.
The Maumelle High student felt unusual movement inside his headgear following warmups last week and brought his helmet to an assistant coach for inspection. A slithering 2-foot cottonmouth was discovered behind some padding.
The pit viper was so reluctant to exit the helmet that police officers had to pour water into it to force the snake out and into a bag. Animal services technicians arrived a few minutes later, identified the snake as a deadly cottonmouth and took it to a wooded area far from the school.
Cottonmouths are the second-most venomous snakes found in Arkansas.
Animal services director Chris Davis said the player wore the helmet for nearly an hour and was fortunate he wasn’t bitten.
“It was unreal,” Davis said. “You had to kind of be there and take pictures to say this was real.”
The player grabbed a different helmet and continued practice. But the situation caused the head coach to reiterate to his team that players should examine their equipment carefully before using it, checking for insects — or maybe something larger and more dangerous.

North Korea launches a suspected ballistic missile, Japan’s says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:53:02 UTC
06:53:02 KST

North Korea launches another missile toward sea ahead of US-South Korean military drills
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea on Wednesday performed its second ballistic missile test in less than a week, its neighbors said, a likely protest of the upcoming South Korea-U.S. military drills that North Korea views as an invasion rehearsal.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said a ballistic missile fired from the North’s eastern coastal Wonsan area around 6 a.m. flew more than 700 kilometers (435 miles). The Japanese Defense Ministry also detected the launch, saying the weapon landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, between the Korean Peninsula and Japan.
The launches, within days of each other, were seen as part of North Korea’s extended run of weapons tests as the country has refused to return to talks with the U.S. and South Korea for years. Experts say North Korea often uses its rivals’ military training as a pretext to boost its own testing activities.
South Korea’s military said it remains ready to repel any provocation by Pyongyang in cooperation with the United States. South Korea’s national security council called North Korean ballistic missile launches “acts of provocation” and urged the North to halt them immediately.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters that Japan strongly protested the North Korean launch through their embassies in Beijing. “It’s a serious problem that affects the safety of the Japanese people,” he said.
The latest launch came two days after South Korea and the United States announced they will kick off their annual large-scale military drills on Aug. 17 to beef up readiness against North Korean threats.
North Korea has previously responded to the Ulchi Freedom Shield training and other major South Korea-U.S. military exercises with provocative weapons tests and harsh rhetoric. The U.S. and South Korea have repeatedly said their training is defensive in nature.
After last year’s Ulchi Freedom Shield training exercises began, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said the drills showed the U.S. and South Korea’s “will to ignite a war” and claimed they have grown more provocative than before, which has prompted North Korea to respond with “proactive and overwhelming” countermeasures.
On Aug. 6, South Korea, the U.S. and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile from North Korea in what was the North’s first ballistic weapons testing activity since late June. North Korea didn’t confirm the reported launch, though it usually releases details of weapons tests a day later.
Multiple U.N. Security Council resolutions ban North Korea from launching ballistic missiles. But North Korea has ramped up ballistic and other weapons testing activities to expand its nuclear and missile arsenals since Kim’s high-stakes diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump fell apart in 2019. Experts say Kim likely hopes to use his enlarged arsenals to wrest concessions from the U.S., such as relaxing international economic sanctions on the North.
In recent years, Kim has boosted his diplomatic footprint by strengthening cooperation with Russia by supplying troops and ammunition to support its war against Ukraine. He’s also recently taken steps to bolster ties with China, the country’s traditional ally and economic pipeline. Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the North Korean capital Pyongyang in June for the first time in seven years.

Video captures rescue of river tubing group stranded for 3 days, living off bark and flowers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Video captures rescue of river tubing group stranded for 3 days, living off bark and flowers
Pushing through dense, shoulder-high brush near a river in west Michigan, a trooper yells out: “Make some noise!”
A boy’s scream can be heard in the distance on body camera footage showing how rescue teams last week found two women and a 9-year-old boy who had been stranded for three days after their river tubing trip went wrong.
“We’re coming, guys,” says Cameron Wright, a conservation officer from Newaygo County, his breath heard in ragged gasps.
The team picks up their pace, pushing through sharp switchgrass and stinging nettle, the footage released by the Michigan Department of Natural Resources shows. A few moments later, they find Sarah Vida, 28, and her son Kayden Kovalcik, 9, along with Jazmin Hock, 28; wearing just their swimming suits.
Hock’s legs are almost entirely covered in deep, red cuts from scrapes after trudging through the brush. They have a broken phone and a single water bottle with only a few sips left.
“You’re talking about vegetation that’s higher than your eyes and switchgrass that cuts you when you touch it and stinging nettles that makes your skin set on fire,” Anna Cullen, a conservation officer from Muskegon County who helped with the rescue, said Tuesday.
The trio had been on a tubing trip on the Muskegon River in the small community of Twin Lake on Tuesday when they’d hit logs and their tubes popped, according to officials. They were reported missing after one of the women hadn’t shown up to her dentist appointment.
“I was just in disbelief at finding them because we were just running out of ideas and places to search and it was nothing short of a miracle that we ended up finding them the way we did,” Wright said.
For days, teams had scoured the river and rugged terrain.
The group was found Friday about 7 miles (11.27 kilometers) from where they entered the river, according to Wright. The rescuers had tracked them from a tube next to the river, following footprints, broken twigs and bent grass.
In the video, Kayden explains that they’ve been eating bark and flowers, while Hock says they had to drink river water.
They’d been tubing down the river and kept hitting log jams, Hock explains.
“The last one that we ran into just popped everything,” she says.
They started walking and soon realized they were going in circles, she says.
Members of the rescue crew handed over their own shirts to protect them from the bugs swarming their cuts and put medical gloves on some of their hands and feet. Wright inflated his life vest for Hock to sit on. As she answered the rescue team’s questions, her legs, lined with scratches, shook.
“There was not even an inch of their exposed skin that was not just covered in cuts and bug bites and mud and scrapes where they were just physically not able to go any further,” Wright said, explaining that he still had cuts on his arms from the search.
Cullen said the women later explained that when they saw the rescuers, they thought they were hallucinating.
The two women couldn’t walk, so the rescuers put them in Stokes baskets, a type of stretcher, to get them out of the brush, while Wright carried the boy on his back. They were taken to the hospital and treated for infections, dehydration and rashes, according to Lt. Pat Agema, a spokesperson for the Michigan State Police. As of Tuesday, they were all back home, he said.
Wright said the entire hike out, Kayden was telling him about everything he was going to eat and drink.
“He’s just telling me about all of the root beer he’s going to drink and the slushies and the pizza and doughnuts he’s going to eat,” said Wright.
He adds: “You would have no idea that he had just spent 72 hours in the woods from how happy he was.”

3 states are set to hold executions on the same day, a first in the US since 2010
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:53:02 UTC
06:53:02 KST

3 states are set to hold executions on the same day, a first in the US since 2010
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (AP) — Tennessee, Alabama and Oklahoma plan to execute inmates Thursday in what would be the first time in nearly 16 years that three people are put to death on the same day in the United States.
The executions come as a small number of states, including the three with scheduled lethal injections Thursday, drive execution numbers in the United States.
“You look at the country as a whole, you’ve just got this little pocket of five or six states that are using the death penalty, executing people, and a small number of states that are still imposing new death sentences,” said Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Maher said it is highly unusual to have three executions on one day, although it is largely a scheduling coincidence.
Eleven states executed a total of 47 people in 2025, the highest number since 2009. Florida accounted for most of the surge with 19 executions. Alabama, South Carolina and Texas each carried out five. Tennessee carried out three. Oklahoma, Mississippi, Arizona and Indiana each carried out two. Louisiana and Missouri each carried out one execution.
The 19 executions so far in 2026 have occurred in four states. Florida, which again leads the country, executed two inmates on the same day in July.
The last time three executions were held on the same day was Jan. 7, 2010, when Louisiana, Ohio and Texas put inmates to death. Three executions were scheduled on the same day in 2018, but only one went forward after a Texas man was granted a reprieve and prison officials in Alabama had problems with the IV line.
Tennessee will attempt another lethal injection after IV problems
Tennessee plans to execute Anthony Darrell Hines three months after the attempted lethal injection of another inmate was called off because of problems inserting an IV. The aborted execution put a spotlight on issues states have sometimes had in establishing IV lines during lethal injections.
“All eyes really are on Tennessee at this moment because of the problem that happened,” Maher said.
During the attempted execution of Tony Carruthers in May, the IV team established a primary line right away but then worked for more than an hour trying to insert a required backup line. The execution was ultimately called off and Carruthers was given a one-year reprieve.
Hines, 66, has seized on the problems with the previous execution, saying his health issues — including two strokes that left him partially paralyzed — increase the risk of difficulties at his execution. He has unsuccessfully asked the governor and courts to intervene, claiming the doctor who oversaw that execution was unqualified and is likely to botch his execution, as well.
Gov. Bill Lee has declined to take any action on Hines’ requests, and last week the Tennessee Supreme Court ruled against a stay of his execution. The state has declined to say whether the same doctor will preside over the upcoming execution, but the court noted that Hines had not proved that doctor was unqualified.
Hines was convicted of stabbing Catherine Jean Jenkins to death in 1985 while the 54-year-old was working as a motel maid in Kingston Springs. He was sentenced to death in 1986, won an appeal for a new sentencing hearing, and was again sentenced to death in 1989.
Alabama inmate asks to be put to death for killing girl
Alabama is scheduled to execute Jeremy Williams, 42, by lethal injection for the 2021 rape and murder of a 5-year-old Georgia girl.
Williams, who pleaded guilty to killing Kamarie Holland, has asked for his death sentence to be carried out.
Prosecutors said Williams raped and strangled Holland after offering her mother $2,500 for the child to perform oral sex on him. Williams filmed his attack on the girl and kept her body to continue to abuse, prosecutors said.
In 2022, Williams also was charged with the 2005 death of his infant daughter in Alaska.
“This man left a trail of destruction of children,” Russell County District Attorney Richard Chancey said.
About 10% of executed inmates are so-called volunteers who drop appeals, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, but most of those have been on death row longer. The time between Williams’ 2024 conviction and his scheduled lethal injection is unusually brief, Maher said.
It will be Alabama’s first execution of the year if it goes forward. A nitrogen gas execution was halted in June after a federal judge ruled the method unconstitutional.
Oklahoma inmate says he doesn’t want clemency
Oklahoma is scheduled to execute Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez, 70, for the 2003 murder of his girlfriend.
If the lethal injection goes forward, he will be the third person executed in Oklahoma this year.
Prosecutors said Olimpia Fisher, 43, had been making plans to leave Cuesta-Rodriguez when he shot her in one eye and then waited about eight minutes as she screamed for help before firing the fatal shot into her other eye.
Oklahoma’s Pardon and Parole Board voted 3-1 last month against recommending clemency for Cuesta-Rodriguez. Cuesta-Rodriguez’s attorneys had asked the board to recommend he serve life in prison without parole, saying he had a difficult childhood and suffered from brain damage, post-traumatic stress disorder and major depression with psychotic episodes.
But Cuesta-Rodriguez told the board that he did not want clemency. He said he wanted Fisher’s two daughters to know that he regretted what happened.
“I can’t have been in my right mind to have done something so horrific,” he said through a Spanish-language translator. “I have not been able to find any sense in all this.”
___
Stengle contributed to this report from Dallas. Loller contributed to this report from Nashville.

ICE plans to give officers gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:53:02 UTC
06:53:02 KST

AP Exclusive: ICE plans to give officers gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers may soon be outfitted with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks intended to gain compliance from combative individuals.
ICE plans to spend up to $20 million to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.
The devices are known as the G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky. They have been used in recent years by some jails and police departments.
DHS said Tuesday that it was working on a response to an Associated Press inquiry and offered no immediate comment. Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, wrote in an email, “Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject.”
The notice said the solicitation for a no-bid contract could be published as early as Friday.
Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone’s skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.
“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. “If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”
Peters said he believed ICE’s planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.
“For smaller officers or weaker officers or older officers, I think it has a great advantage” because it can produce faster takedowns and shorten confrontations, he said.
The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting “verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.
Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, said the public should have no confidence that ICE officers will use the devices appropriately. She questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement and noted those getting shocked might have no advance warning.
“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”
Supporters say the devices are generally used in specific jail and transport situations, rather than broadly to patrol on the streets. They have been used to subdue violent suspects who are refusing to get into squad cars and inmates who are harming themselves and threatening officers, according to Compliant Technologies.
Peters said he expected the devices to be misused by a small number of employees, as with other policing technologies, but he said they are unlikely to cause injuries. He said it would be important for ICE to have robust policies and training in place.
To use the device, officers must complete a course and be recertified every two years, the manufacturer says.

Trump’s Air Force One deception faces scrutiny over ‘decoy’ passengers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:46:34 UTC
06:46:34 KST

Democrats called on Tuesday for a congressional briefing over a stunning charade in which Donald Trump was secretly spirited to a different plane than the one the public and press believed he was travelling on. Critics now question why reporters and the public had been deliberately misled.
When US intelligence allegedly found a credible threat that Iran plotted to kill him last month, Trump left Air Force One in a catering truck, an episode first reported by the Washington Post and also by the New York Times. While the president was reportedly snuck out the side door of the plane, more than a hundred aides, officials and reporters were kept onboard to fly towards Britain, without being told there was a threat to their lives.
“It appears that the idea was we can reduce the danger to President Trump by offering up 100 or so people to be killed by the Iranians in his place,” said Steven Cash, executive director of the Steady State and a former CIA intelligence officer and senior adviser to the Department of Homeland Security’s intelligence branch.
Trump confirmed on Tuesday that he secretly switched planes, but said the plane he ultimately flew on was still more vulnerable than Air Force One. “I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk,” Trump told reporters. “I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for.”
“Well, it’s only up to Secret Service. I just follow what they’d like to do, so I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trump added.
Richard Blumenthal, a Democratic senator for Connecticut, called the operation “unprecedented and surreal” and “downright scary” on CNN. “There has to be a congressional briefing because it involves not just the safety of the president.
“I want to know what precautions were taken to make sure that all of the passengers on that Air Force One, which was judged too dangerous for the president to fly on, what precautions were taken to keep the staff and reporters on that plane safe?”
The White House had publicly said the president would fly to Britain onboard Air Force One – albeit an older version instead of the new Qatari-gifted aircraft. In reality, Trump boarded the presidential jet in full view of television cameras before being spirited away minutes later and transferred to an air force C-32A.
The deception was sufficiently elaborate that journalists travelling with the president – and some White House staff – believed Trump remained onboard Air Force One. Reporters were instructed to keep the shades over their windows closed during the flight.
The C-32A carrying Trump flew to RAF Mildenhall in Britain, arriving at about 10.20pm. The older Air Force One and the travelling press pool arrived minutes later. Photographers subsequently captured Trump descending from the presidential aircraft, apparently after he had been secretly reunited with it.
Trump then greeted troops at the base before boarding the newly refurbished Boeing 747 donated by Qatar and flying on to Washington.
Ned Price, a former deputy to the US ambassador to the UN, said he did not begrudge any White House taking extraordinary measures to protect the president but the current administration had perpetuated an “outright lie” for weeks and turned reporters into “unwitting conspirators”.
Price, an ex-special assistant to President Barack Obama on the national security council, added: “There was a way to do this where they didn’t need to lie. They could have enlisted the travelling press pool, who would have very willingly, I am certain, not reported on certain security arrangements.
“Once all was said and done and the president was safely in the UK or back at Andrews air force base, they could have said, ‘This is what we did and this is why we did it,’” Price added. “But they feel no compunction to the truth. They feel no loyalty to the truth. Instead it’s just an effort over the past month to lie and to mislead.”
Journalists also raised concerns. Jake Tapper, an anchor on CNN, tweeted: “Obviously the life of the president is paramount, and previous White Houses have used deception to protect the president’s life. But no officials I’ve spoken to have ever before heard of using an AF1 full of WH staff and journalists as a decoy during an imminent threat.”
And Jose Zamora, Commitee to Protect Journalists’ regional director for the Americas, said the administration had a responsibility to ensure reporters weren’t exposed to unnecessary danger. “Reporters should be informed of credible security threats so they can make informed decisions about their safety,” he said. “Transparency should be the norm for any administration, particularly when safety is at stake.”
The revelation sheds new light on an abrupt decision that had already raised questions about the security of the Qatari aircraft. Trump had flown the newly refurbished jet to the Nato summit – its first international journey – but unexpectedly announced that he would instead use the older Air Force One on the first leg of his return journey.
At the time, Trump said the new aircraft was being flown to Mildenhall so US troops stationed there could inspect it. The New York Times and CBS News subsequently reported that intelligence officials had raised concerns about a possible attack on Trump or his aircraft amid the escalating conflict with Iran.
During the summit, the US military was conducting major strikes against Iran, adding to fears of Iranian retaliation. The new account suggests that the threat was taken more seriously than previously understood.
Not everyone is convinced the threat justified what happened next. “From the Iranian perspective, pulling off an attempted targeting of presidential aircraft at this depth would be extremely implausible; it would require close-in clandestine operators with man-portable anti-air systems,” said Ankit Panda, the Stanton senior fellow in the nuclear policy program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Panda said it was not clear there had been a specific, credible threat within Turkey itself, though presidential security routinely plans around “known unknowns”.
“Iran doesn’t have surface-to-air missiles that could target an aircraft taking off from Ankara,” said Dr Jeffrey Lewis, a distinguished fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute. Iran could in theory strike a plane on the runway with a ballistic missile, he said, “but that seems very unlikely”. His guess: US officials were worried about “a terrorist-like attack using a man-portable air defense system,” such as a Chinese-made QW-12 or FN-16, or a North Korean version of the Russian Igla.
James Jeffrey, a former US ambassador to Turkey and deputy national security adviser under George W Bush who is now a distinguished fellow at the pro-Israel Washington Institute, said the secrecy around moving Trump to another aircraft pointed to serious intelligence behind the threat.
“This is very unusual, and indicates that they had very good intelligence of a threat, and that they did not trust the aircraft that he was in,” said Jeffrey, who has extensive experience traveling onboard Air Force One.
Jeffrey said he believed the intelligence may have come from Israel, which has extensive intelligence capabilities focused on Iran. While Israeli officials sometimes seek to “not only inform but influence” US policy, he said they would not risk fabricating a threat involving the president’s safety.
“They wouldn’t play with something as serious as the president’s safety,” Jeffrey said, adding that any such warning would prompt the US government to verify the intelligence, gather more information about the threat and follow up on it.”
Trump himself appeared to hint at the security concerns when reporters questioned him about why they had been ordered to keep their window shades closed. “You’re probably on a dangerous flight,” he said. “But if I go, you go. Right?”
Asked later whether there had been a credible Iranian threat against Air Force One, Trump said: “Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list before you.”
The operation has nevertheless prompted questions about the decision to deceive the press corps and the public, particularly after the White House continued to maintain the cover story.

Trump White House asked Justice Dept to explore new Reflecting Pool charges, sources say
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump’s White House has asked the Justice Department to examine potential new charges related to alleged vandalism at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool despite the department’s decision to drop prior cases, according to two people familiar with the matter.
The discussions followed Trump’s fury at Jeanine Pirro, the top federal prosecutor in Washington, for moving to dismiss cases against former US Olympic canoeist David Hearn and others accused of damaging the pool following Trump-ordered renovations.
Pirro’s office dropped the case against Hearn after concluding that widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool, a landmark on Washington’s National Mall, was the result of flawed contracting work rather than intentional destruction, as Trump has repeatedly alleged.
The discussions, which were first reported by the Wall Street Journal, are an indication that the Trump administration could seek to revive those cases and are another example of the White House intervening in criminal investigations, in a sharp break from decades-long Justice Department practice.
Lawyers for Hearn said new charges would “add another bizarre turn to a sad chapter in the DOJ’s history and further harass an innocent man”.
The White House referred questions to the Justice Department, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A local Washington, D.C., judge has dismissed the case against Hearn and is set to decide in the coming weeks whether to give prosecutors the opportunity to seek new charges or permanently end the prosecution.
The most recent conversations involved the Criminal Division at Justice Department headquarters, which typically manages complex cases on corporate fraud, international gangs and other issues, rather than Pirro’s office, whose remit includes local criminal cases in Washington, according to the two people familiar with the matter.
One of the people said the talks were aimed at exploring whether there was a basis to bring a misdemeanour case.
The conversations are preliminary and no final decision has been made.
Hearn was indicted last month on a felony destruction of property charge after Pirro initially alleged he forcibly pulled on and damaged the lining on the bottom of the Reflecting Pool while cycling in the area. 
Hearn pleaded not guilty and denied wrongdoing.
Less than a month later, prosecutors reversed course, telling a judge that newly disclosed documents showed that a botched renovation, not vandalism, damaged the pool.
Trump raged at Pirro’s decision to drop the case and urged her to revisit it. 
He has continued to blame issues with the US$14.7 million project on vandals, despite acknowledging in a social media post on Aug 9 that there was no proof of sabotage. REUTERS

Boltinhouse won the title in June and was preparing to represent North Carolina at the 75th annual Miss USA pageant in Miami later this month.
Organizers said in a statement that the decision to remove Boltinhouse “was not made lightly”. The first runner-up, Myla Hadley, has been named Miss North Carolina USA 2026.
“It followed a thorough review of recently surfaced information and was based on the totality of the circumstances and our responsibility to preserve the integrity of the Miss North Carolina USA title and the values of our organization.”
Thom Brodeur, president and CEO of Miss USA, said that the brand “does not tolerate racism, homophobia, transphobia, nor language that strips any person of their dignity – whoever they are”.
Mincey said in an Instagram video on Monday that his firm had evidence his client, who is Mormon, was “targeted because of her Christian faith and her conservative political views”, Mincey said.
Mincey said his firm had obtained recorded statements of pageant officials acknowledging there was no “legitimate or legal basis” for the decision to strip Boltinhouse, who would have been the third Latina and first Honduran woman to represent North Carolina at Miss USA, of her state title.
Mincey, who did not lay out specific allegations of religious or racial bias, called Boltinhouse the “very best of the American dream” and pointed to her background as a daughter of immigrants who grew up in rural North Carolina and how, as a pageant newcomer, she won four of five awards at the June Miss North Carolina USA.
Boltinhouse told the Carolina Journal: “I believe I was stripped of my title because of my political stance and my belief system as a conservative Christian woman.
“I’m proud of my faith, I’m proud of my standards, I’m a proud conservative woman, but Christian woman, a God-fearing woman,” she said.
“Every teenager has made a mistake; every person has made a mistake,” she added. “I’m here to talk about the woman I am today, things may have happened a decade ago, but I am the hardworking woman who stood up there and won Miss North Carolina USA fair and square.”
Boltinhouse claimed pageant organizers had not offered her a clear reason for being dethroned: “Honestly, I don’t know; I wasn’t really given anything.”
A Blaize Productions, license holder for Miss North Carolina USA, told The News & Observer that the reasons “were clearly shared and expressed” to Boltinhouse.
Mincey said Boltinhouse had “earned the respect and admiration of millions who support her. And one thing is for certain: Brittany Boltinhouse will not be canceled.”

One Ukrainian soldier to 26 Russian occupiers: Military officer reports losses on Huliaipole front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:34:00 UTC
06:34:00 KST

One Ukrainian soldier to 26 Russian occupiers: Military officer reports losses on Huliaipole front
Dmytro Perun Filatov, commander of the First Separate Assault Regiment named after Dmytro Kotsyubailo, said this in an exclusive interview with Ukrainian Radio.
"At present, this section of the front is under control. The enemy’s attempts to conduct further offensive operations have been reduced to zero. The enemy does not stop attempting daily assaults, but has had no success. We have built an effective system of countermeasures. We are actively advancing despite the fact that the enemy is trying to attack intensively in this area.
"The main challenges we expect from the enemy are increased mobilization after the completion of the electoral process in Russia. It is likely to be carried out covertly in Russia. However, we do not rule out broader mobilization. We will not be able to compensate for this through increased mobilization ourselves, since the enemy has greater manpower resources. Therefore, we are trying to find methods of countering this and conducting the war through asymmetric actions," he emphasized.
Filatov also said that the casualty ratio on this section of the front is one Ukrainian soldier to 26 Russian occupiers.
"Our ratio has reached 1 (Ukrainian soldier) to 26 (Russian occupiers). In general, during combat operations, the average ratio of losses between attacking and defending units is 1 defender to 3 attackers or 1 defender to 4 attackers. In our case, we are finding methods that result in significantly higher Russian losses.
"We pay great attention to protecting our equipment and artillery, which puts significant pressure on the enemy. Our assault operations are not as rapid as they are traditionally understood to be. We are looking for ways to reach operational space so that a single offensive operation could advance 30–40 kilometers in depth. This is difficult, and not all of our units have such a ratio," said the commander of the First Separate Assault Regiment named after Dmytro Kotsyubailo, Dmytro Perun Filatov.
According to Ukrinform, the total combat losses of Russian forces since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, through August 11, 2026, amount to approximately 1,460,400 personnel, including 1,190 over the past day.

‘We’ve seen this somewhere in history before, haven’t we?’ Inside Russia’s plan to resettle 114,000 of its people in occupied Ukraine.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:30:46 UTC
06:30:46 KST

‘We’ve seen this somewhere in history before, haven’t we?’ Inside Russia’s plan to resettle 114,000 of its people in occupied Ukraine.
Over the next 20 years, Russian authorities plan to resettle nearly 114,000 Russians in the occupied Ukrainian territories. Despite the grim circumstances, some people really are moving there. The independent journalists’ cooperative Bereg took Melitopol as its example — a city in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region that Russian troops entered as early as February 25, 2022 — to understand what kind of people move from Russia to the seized regions, and what occupation means for Ukrainians. Bereg talked with Russians who have resettled there, with lifelong Melitopol residents, and with the Ukrainian nonviolent resistance movement Zla Mavka (“Angry Mavka”). Meduza is translating the story in full.
‘I thought, “God, my business is closed.” I didn’t yet know what they would do to my family’
Lyudmila Plachkova, 34, was born and raised in Melitopol. She left for Bulgaria because of the occupation. Officers of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) abducted her parents, Tatyana and Oleg.
We’re a family of entrepreneurs. In Melitopol, we lived through good times and bad. The city was alive and growing, and we grew with it — new businesses, public gardens, parks, and fairs kept appearing. The COVID years were hard on business, but we all helped one another.
In 2013, my parents rented a space and opened their own business: a café. My mom had worked as a cook and had always dreamed of a restaurant of her own. The café became her baby. We had no real capital, so we took out loans.
It was hard at first. I worked there as a waitress, and my dad did all the physical work himself. My mom’s friends, cooks themselves, took jobs in the kitchen. Eventually it all grew into a fairly successful venture — a large banquet hall, where you’re constantly dealing with guests. My mom was very outgoing, and everyone in town knew her. A lot of people came to the café partly because of her. They’d all say, “We want to see Tanya.” I think the café became popular because of how open she was.
My parents were always like two lovebirds, together all the time. In 2023, the business turned 10. That was part of why my mom didn’t want to leave [the occupied territory] while she still could. She’d grown too attached to it.
When they started bombing us [on February 24, 2022], I froze and didn’t know what to do. Then [Russian] troops took up positions outside Melitopol, waiting for the order to move in, since Ukrainian forces were still in the city.
My dad said there would be a mop-up phase, but I didn’t know what that meant or what they’d do to us. As a young woman, I was terrified, especially given the news from Bucha and the stories about Kadyrov’s men. At that point, we [Lyudmila, her husband, and several relatives and friends — Bereg’s note] moved in with my parents. We huddled together and waited. My parents lived near a school, and when things got really frightening, we’d go to the bomb shelter there. Somehow it was all easier to bear when we were together.
Then Mariupol happened, and people started fleeing that city. We helped where we could, gathering supplies and food for them. In March and April 2022, pro-Ukrainian rallies were held in Melitopol, and I went out to them.
Looting had started in the city, and it mattered to me to show that decent people lived there. We [the protesters] said we didn’t want Russia here, and at first the soldiers even told us they might leave soon. Later, once Russian flags started going up around the city, I realized nothing good would come of it.
Melitopol changed. Business owners and young people left. I remember my dad saying at one point, “We’re back in the 1990s.” Makeshift markets sprang up (half the entrepreneurs had gone), and a lot of people of “eastern nationalities” arrived. The streets filled with strangers. It’s a small city — a lot of faces used to be familiar. Moscow plates, Krasnodar plates… You’d walk around and realize this wasn’t your city anymore.
I had little direct contact with the occupiers before I left. I just watched our city fill up with people who’d never lived in it. It frightened me: strangers had arrived and started imposing new rules on me. Before I left [the occupied territory], I was afraid even to go outside.
Leaving was frightening too — there was no telling what to expect at filtration. Vasylivka was still open then, the only crossing into Ukraine. I was afraid to go through it after hearing terrifying stories about people being taken to a basement. And you had to travel under shelling. I didn’t risk it. Vasylivka was later closed, and we left through Crimea, Russia, and Turkey.
In Crimea, [FSB officers] questioned us. The filtration drags on, and you don’t know whether your husband will come out of it at all. You drive across Russia not knowing whether you’ll make it… In the end, surprisingly, my husband got through.
My husband had a clothing store; I had a decor studio. We had to close it all and leave. At the time, I thought, “God, my business is closed.” I didn’t yet know what they would do to my family.
Overnight into September 26, 2023, FSB officers broke into my parents’ apartment. I had already left by then. I later learned from my mom’s cellmates that she’d been beaten on the head with a mop.
My grandmother was home too. They locked her in a room and told her, “Don’t try anything.” After my parents were taken away, two FSB officers stayed behind to search the apartment. She sat locked in that room from 11 p.m. to 11 a.m., without food or water.
I think my mom and dad were taken because they refused to recognize Russian rule. They believed the occupation would end — my mom especially.
Shortly before the abduction, a post about my mom appeared on the Telegram channel Zhduny. It said she was pro-Ukrainian. That was the first warning sign.
My mom was sure they wouldn’t touch her — she wasn’t doing anything, just living her life. Besides, my grandmother had just come through surgery, and my parents couldn’t leave her alone. In our last conversation, my mom said that if nothing changed, they’d leave in November. She held out hope to the very end that the occupation would be pushed back. My mom was always a huge optimist.
Everything I know about what happened to my parents afterward, I learned from my mom’s cellmates. My parents were taken to a basement room in Melitopol, in the building the FSB now occupies. They were tortured in captivity. My dad was beaten, and my mom was made to watch. As I understand it, that’s how they tried to force a confession out of her.
From September 26 until her birthday on October 2, my mom was held in that basement room. As far as I understand, it had no windows and no doors, and they kept her there without food. She was then moved to a women’s cell. There was no water, no shower, and no toilet, and the temperature was around 10 degrees Celsius (50 degrees Fahrenheit). Many of the women were still in the summer clothes they were taken in. Guards would starve my mom, then give her scraps and tell her, “Be glad for the leftovers.” They made her learn the anthems of Russia and of the self-proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics.
On February 8, 2024, my mom was brought to a hospital in Melitopol already in critical condition. She was in a coma, with no clothes on and bedsores on her body. Where she’d been before that is unknown — possibly another hospital. She was put in the infectious disease ward after being diagnosed with the flu. She wasn’t breathing on her own; she arrived already on a ventilator.
I think her condition [the coma — Bereg’s note] came from the blows to the head [during torture at interrogations] and the lack of timely medical care.
Her cellmates later told me my mom started feeling ill back in December. When she asked for help, she was told, “You’re not at a resort.” She was vomiting, couldn’t eat, and couldn’t even drink. She kept getting worse, and toward the end she just lay there. The women said they once begged the guards for a piece of bread, cut it into small pieces, and dried them for her, but she couldn’t even eat those.
By late December, my mom had stopped coming to. There was no help. She wasn’t brought up from the basement until early January, when she began foaming at the mouth.
An FSB investigator let my grandmother visit my mom in the hospital for 10 minutes at a time, under strict supervision. They even mounted cameras over her, [although she was] in a coma. The investigator said that once she recovered, she’d be tried for espionage. I don’t know whether he really believed she could recover…
My mom died on May 23, 2024. I couldn’t say goodbye — investigators made it clear to the family that if I came, they’d do the same to me. All of it broke my grandmother. She lost her daughter.
Very little is known about my dad. For a time he was held on the other side of a wall from my mom, and she heard him being tortured with electric shocks. Where he was taken after that is unknown. My mom’s cellmates said she believed to the end that he’d been released and was home. She looked for him, and managed to write him notes. Some of the guards — mostly Kadyrov’s men — told her he’d been let go. We don’t know where he is.
There’s hope that he’s all right… As far as that’s possible. He may be held incommunicado. There are a great many such people, held for years. People say there are penal colonies in the occupied territories where they’re kept for years on end, unable to say anything about themselves.
I’m sending inquiries to detention facilities and to the FSB. The Investigative Committee has opened a case to find my dad. Investigators there don’t say he’s in their custody. They often reply that we should wait — that we may learn something once he’s charged with something.
One time when we went to the local Investigative Committee, officials told us, “Well, you understand where he is [the FSB — Bereg’s note]. There’s nothing we can do.” They also said something like, “Today we’re here, and tomorrow we could be where your parents [ended up].” But these were all unofficial conversations.
Officially, they write that they know nothing and are searching. The FSB says, “We have no information on him; no one detained him.” Every detention facility says he isn’t there — though there are plenty of cases where people are being held and their relatives told otherwise.
I personally know of six cases of abduction, torture, or arbitrary deportation of civilians in Melitopol alone. Many of us have people close to us in captivity, held without charge and with no way to communicate. Some have gone missing. Others have been convicted — and they’re people we know. And we’re ordinary people.
What's known about the abduction and torture of Melitopol residents by Russian security forces
In October 2023, the independent Russian outlet iStories detailed the system of abductions, torture, and terror in Russian-occupied Melitopol.
Journalists described the abduction by Russian troops of school principals and teachers who, as of fall 2023, were still teaching to Ukrainian standards, along with residents suspected of partisan activity.
Maksym Ivanov, a 29-year-old landscape designer from Melitopol, was abducted while putting up flyers for Ukrainian Independence Day, the outlet reported. His ribs were broken during questioning at a police station, and he was then driven — with a bag over his head — to “the garages under the bridge,” where he was beaten with rebar and given electric shocks.
The mother of 24-year-old Melitopol resident Leonid Popov told iStories that Russian troops abducted and tortured her son three times. He had been diagnosed with schizophrenia earlier, and his health became critical in captivity. Three months after his abduction, Popov weighed 40 kilograms (88 pounds) at a height of 195 centimeters (6 feet 5 inches). The FSB later charged Popov with espionage; he faces up to 20 years in prison.
They’re simply destroying people and covering it up. I still can’t fully understand why they do it. I could understand it if this were about a pool of prisoners for military exchanges, but they’re taking civilians — not by the dozens, by the thousands. They charge them with nothing and don’t exchange them. Why? What kind of terrorism is this?
A classmate of my husband’s is now being held somewhere in Siberia, without charge and with no way to contact his family. He was taken in 2022.
After what happened to my parents, [people still in Melitopol] are afraid to talk to me. It can be dangerous — they’re hunting for “traitors” there.
Russian passports were introduced for everyone. If you don’t get one, you’re called in for a talk; an acquaintance of mine was deported over it. My parents never had Russian passports.
If the occupation ends, I’ll go back. Though that’s hard to imagine right now, because everything there is steeped in memories of my parents. I can’t look at photographs from there. It hurts too much. I’m 34 now, but my life stopped in 2023. The two people closest to me were taken from me, and I don’t understand how to go on living.
The Russians did what they set out to do. They frightened everyone and showed what they’re capable of. They broke me. They broke my family. My dad is being held somewhere, unable to say anything about himself, and I can’t find him or help him. That’s a particular kind of torture, when you can’t do anything. But I keep fighting. I’ve switched on my mom’s optimism, and I’m still looking for my dad. I believe he’s alive.
‘I never managed to get used to this lack of civilization’
Darya, 30, moved to Melitopol from Izhevsk but went back home a year later.
We moved at the start of 2025, when my youngest child was two months old. After nearly a year, we went back — we didn’t like it.
I’m probably not giving away any great secret if I say that plenty of people are moving to the “new territories.” The main reason is simple: military personnel qualify for their pensions faster there, because a day of service counts as two or three days. And pay overall is a bit higher than outside [the “new territories”].
My husband was in the military, and we moved so he could qualify for his pension sooner. I didn’t really have doubts about it. The idea came up fairly spontaneously and was settled in a single night: my husband suggested it, and I didn’t say no.
We have two children, our own apartment in Izhevsk, and my parents nearby. So when my husband brought me to Melitopol, to a house in the Semenivka neighborhood where everything was old and in terrible shape, of course I cried.
It was very hard for me to adjust. Then I started looking for an apartment in Melitopol itself and ran into catastrophic prices. Insane ones.
Melitopol wasn’t badly damaged [during Russia’s military offensive]. It’s just that all the buildings are old; there’s no new construction in the city. To rent a two-room apartment, you need 60,000 [rubles] up front, and landlords may ask for a deposit on top.
Because Avito wasn’t operating [in Melitopol] at the time, you had to look through Telegram channels, go to real estate agents, or find listings from owners. I ended up finding an apartment for 30,000 rubles, which counts as cheap there. It hadn’t been renovated — everything was Soviet-era — but you could live in it. In Izhevsk, for that same 30,000 rubles, I was renting out my own two-room apartment, perfectly renovated.
What surprised me was that no store in the city had reasonable prices. Selection was limited, and grocery prices were catastrophic — multiply [Izhevsk prices] by three. And a lot of the food was expired. The markets were very popular.
It also surprised me that there were practically no banks, and you had to pay cash for everything. Readjusting to the old way was hard. It felt like I’d gone back to the 1990s, to a complete absence of civilization.
The power went out fairly often, whenever there were incoming strikes. You get used to them, and in the end they’re not that frightening. But at those moments you can’t go to a store unless it has a generator. A beauty salon without a generator won’t take you either. Banks close. And no electricity means no water.
To see a doctor, you need a compulsory medical insurance policy, but a new one issued under the Russian system, because the insurer there is Russian.
I ran into one big problem: there isn’t enough medical staff. There simply are no doctors. My child is a year old, and we can’t see all the doctors [required for a checkup at that age]. There are no cardiologists at all, for instance — the nearest are in Crimea or Rostov. Traveling to another city just for a checkup… And I needed to see a neurologist myself; the earliest appointment was two months out. All in all, I wasn’t thrilled.
The locals treated me pretty well. We had good relations with people, and thankfully there were no misunderstandings. I didn’t ask about what had happened in the city before. It’s tactless. It’s not right. I’m for neutrality, after all.
In the end we decided to leave. The trouble with doctors wore us down, and besides, my husband had become a [military] retiree. And I never managed to get used to this lack of civilization.
‘Occupation means living in constant fear of searches, detentions, and denunciations’
An activist with the Ukrainian movement Zla Mavka, familiar with the situation in Melitopol.
For us, occupation isn’t a change of government — it’s living in constant fear. People are afraid to speak and afraid to move around. They lose their jobs, their homes, and contact with their families, as though their lives are being taken apart piece by piece. The most painful part is the sense that you can be stripped of everything you spent years building.
The occupation has changed almost every area of life. Above all, people have lost their sense of security. You live in constant fear of searches, detentions, denunciations, and persecution for no reason at all. Simply to keep everyone afraid.
People have lost their jobs and their access to decent medicines, reliable communications, banking services, and a working legal system. Prices have risen, goods are often in short supply, or the goods are there but of terrible quality (that goes for everything, textiles and food alike). Many go months without income; others survive on odd jobs or help from relatives.
Enormous pressure is applied through [the forced issuance of Russian] passports, and through education, medicine, and work. People were effectively made to take Russian documents, move their children into the Russian education system, and work under Russian rules. For many, the choice wasn’t between “good” and “bad” but between survival and even bigger problems.
Some residents were forced to leave, abandoning apartments, houses, businesses, and belongings.
The occupiers have built a system that forces owners to re-register their property under Russian law. If someone has left, can’t return, or refuses on principle to go through these procedures, the property is declared “ownerless.” It can then be handed to someone else or registered as state property of the occupation administration.
If someone hasn’t been seen at their home for a long time and the occupation administration notices, officials leave a warning that the documents need to be updated. A month or two later, they come back with paperwork putting the property on the administration’s books — a peculiar sort of privatization.
For people leaving because of the war, it means risking their only home. Many can’t come back just to handle paperwork because that could mean checks, filtration, or persecution.
Formally, this is presented as putting the registries in order, but for many Ukrainians it’s a mechanism that legalizes the confiscation of any property. It isn’t only the loss of money as such; it’s also a way to pressure people into either accepting Russian rules and resigning themselves, or facing the risk of losing what they own.
It’s especially cynical, because a person can lose a home for the very reason that war and occupation drove them out.
To me, this looks like a deliberate policy of pushing Ukrainians out and replacing the population. In effect, they’re simply driving Ukrainians out and settling the cities with their own citizens. We’ve seen this somewhere in history before, haven’t we?
Large-scale propaganda has become a problem of its own. The occupation authorities construct a picture of normal life, but it doesn’t reflect reality. It’s especially painful to watch Russians move into Melitopol — most of them gangsters and thieves of one kind or another. And they’re untouchable by local law enforcement.
‘Military vehicles drive around, but otherwise I forget where I am’
Ruslan, 34, came from Rostov-on-Don on a work assignment lasting several months.
I’m a surveyor, working on the construction of a gas distribution station. I came to Melitopol in early February and will be here until around winter, going home every couple of months.
Housing is a bit hard to find, but easier with a real estate agent. Everything here is priced in rubles. Prices vary: you can find a one- or two-room apartment for 30,000 [rubles a month], or pay 45,000. And the apartments are identical — as far as I can see, the price depends on whether the owners have the paperwork.
I need a lease and an extract from the state property register so the rent will be reimbursed [at work], but not everyone is willing to provide those documents. Plus, most places are rented by the day — apparently a lot of people come for short stays.
I had a hard time forming a first impression. I’d been driving a long time and was simply glad to have made it. When I drove in, it felt like an ordinary Russian city: small, quiet, clean.
The only difficulties on the ground were finding an apartment and repairing my car, which started breaking down while I was here. The repairs went fine in the end.
From what I noticed, the power went out about four times in two months. I wouldn’t say it was a problem for me. In some neighborhoods it may be worse than where I am. But I could have missed outages at night or while I was at work. The water [in my rental] was shut off once.
I’ve seen a couple of destroyed houses. Nothing else caught my eye. What makes Melitopol different from the life I’m used to is probably the curfew, from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m., plus stores and some businesses closing early. Sometimes you hear “pops” [drone strikes and air defense fire — Bereg’s note], and military vehicles drive around. And there are checkpoints on the way out of town. Otherwise I forget where I am. I live in Rostov, which gets hit often too, so I don’t see a big difference.
There’s a curfew here, and people observe it. Without a pass, you can be jailed for 24 hours and fined. Even alcohol is sold only until 8 p.m.
The people who come to the city are usually [military personnel and] civil servants. Or just people who decided to take a spot that had opened up. Many come from Krasnodar, Volgograd, and Rostov.
I think you need a Russian passport to live here.
I haven’t noticed problems with the locals, and blending in is possible. Not everyone can tell I’m not from here.
‘Sometimes you hear drones and explosions, but otherwise everything’s calm’
Timur (name changed), 29, came from Uzbekistan to earn money.
I came to Melitopol in February from Uzbekistan; back home I do decorative plastering. Before that I lived in Nizhny Novgorod, working as an electrician from August 2025 until January 1. I heard about the job in Melitopol from an acquaintance.
They’re planning to open a hospital here, and the developer, the Russian company Profstroy, brought in workers from Uzbekistan: electricians, plumbers, and concrete workers.
As an electrician, I was promised a steady salary of 110,000 rubles a month and a day off every two weeks. Shifts run 11 hours, nine on Sundays. They say the paperwork is dragging on because of the influx of migrant workers. On the job it’s all bearable — nobody leans on you or pushes you.
A lot of the people I work with are from Central Asia — probably 90%. Usually from Uzbekistan, but there are Tajiks too. Russians and Turks work here as well, mostly in management and as security guards.
It’s an ordinary old provincial city, a little dirty. There are sometimes problems with water, but everything comes back quickly. Same with electricity.
Sometimes you hear drones and explosions, but otherwise everything’s calm. Nobody hides from the drones — everyone’s used to them, I guess. I see them about once a day. There are more at night, but I’m usually asleep and don’t notice. They fly around, and that’s that.
At the construction site, the electricity and water get shut off for an hour or two, then come back on. They have generators.
The internet works very poorly here; even the “whitelisted” sites load slowly. You can’t always spend time on VK or RuTube the way you’d want.
Prices in Melitopol are a little higher than in Nizhny Novgorod. Housing is hard to find here, as in other Russian cities, and especially for Uzbek citizens. In that respect, I don’t see any difference from Nizhny Novgorod.
And then there’s the red tape. You have to carry all sorts of documents, so that if you’re detained, you can prove to the police that you’re here legally.
As for the Ukrainians, I don’t know anything about that.

How India’s government can be a good parent to its young people
While recent protests were triggered by irregularities in the national medical entrance exam, the quality of education more broadly warrants attention
Outraged over the leaking of the medical school entrance exam question paper, protesters, led by a group calling itself the Cockroach Janata Party, demanded accountability and reforms. At least 20 young people had taken their own lives after a retest for the medical entrance exam was announced, underlining how such exams have become life-or-death affairs, providing many young people with a rare chance of economic security in India’s hypercompetitive job market.
In both India and China, education is often a key pathway to social mobility. In social systems with perceived inequalities, fair admissions to elite higher education institutions are a safety valve for social discontent. Undermining that valve led to predictable social consequences in India.
In the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) tests for 15-year-olds in mathematics, science and reading, Singapore and East Asian economies have consistently ranked at the top. East Asian economic successes have been built on human capital development.
In the 2022 Pisa test results, Singapore, which has often been the top performer, led the world again. In 2018, when China’s regions of Shanghai, Beijing, Zhejiang and Jiangsu were assessed, they narrowly beat Singapore.

2026-08-11
21:30:01 UTC
06:30:01 KST

The war in Ukraine is already in its fifth year; Israel has been through two rounds of fighting with Iran within a year, and China continues to put pressure on the countries around it.
The result: another record quarter for Elbit Systems.
The manufacturer of Hermes drones, munitions, and intelligence systems reported a 16% increase in sales in the second quarter of the year to $2.3 billion, putting it on track for annual sales of $9 billion. Net profit rose even more sharply, jumping 40% to $173.6 million.
The company's order backlog reached an all-time high of $32 billion, compared with $23.8 billion a year earlier, a 33% increase.
Sales to the Defense Ministry continued to grow in the latest quarter, reaching 37% of the company's activity, driven by munitions, drones, and intelligence systems.
Increased sales of radio and command-and-control systems in Europe drive profits
Sales of C4I and cyber systems rose by about 11%, mainly due to increased sales of radio and command-and-control systems in Europe. Intelligence and electronic warfare sales increased by about 22%, primarily due to higher sales of land- and airborne high-power laser systems, electronic warfare systems, and naval systems in the Asia-Pacific region.
Land systems sales rose by about 32%, thanks to sales of munitions and ammunition in Israel. Drone sales, by contrast, fell by about 8%, mainly due to an unfavorable one-time project mix and a decline in sales of training systems and simulators in Europe, which was partly offset by increased sales of unmanned aerial vehicles in Israel.
Earnings per share stood at $3.61, compared with $2.69 in the corresponding quarter last year.
"Most of the new orders are from abroad, which indicates the demand and interest in our products. We presented the airborne laser for fighter jets and combat helicopters, which will help, among other things, deal with swarm attacks by UAVs and drones, and there is great interest in them,” Bezhalel "Butzi" Machlis, president and CEO of Elbit Systems, told Walla.
“At the same time, we are continuing to increase deliveries of the high-power laser to the Defense Ministry and Rafael. Hundreds of our engineers are employed on this."
Elbit container reportedly held up at a port due to boycotting
When questioned about a recent report indicating an Elbit container had been held up at a port as part of a boycott of Israel, Machlis said the incident was being investigated.
“Containers are sometimes delayed for all kinds of reasons. We have no problems in the supply chain. Since the days of the coronavirus pandemic, we have invested in building up inventories of raw materials and diversifying suppliers."
Machlis also noted that the Defense Ministry has yet to settle its debt with the company.
“Fortunately, Elbit is a strong company and benefits from payments from abroad that allow us to continue supplying the IDF and move up delivery schedules. I am confident that the debt will be paid, and we are in dialogue with the Defense and Finance ministries about it," he said.
