How does the man behind Russia’s most soothing cartoon dog end up with an 18+ horror hit? Leonid Shmelkov’s ‘Restlessness’ strands two travelers in a roadside hotel they can’t escape.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:44:02 UTC
04:44:02 KST

How does the man behind Russia’s most soothing cartoon dog end up with an 18+ horror hit? Leonid Shmelkov’s ‘Restlessness’ strands two travelers in a roadside hotel they can’t escape.
Nepokoy (“Restlessness”), a feature-length art-house animation for adults, is now playing in Russian theaters. That in itself is news: 18+ animation is a real rarity not only in Russia but worldwide. Nepokoy has already become a phenomenon: it’s the highest-grossing Russian animated film for adults, the living legend Yuri Norstein has praised it, and its heroine has been turned into a Dymkovo toy, a traditional Russian painted-clay folk figurine. Nepokoy’s director, Leonid Shmelkov, is known online for his viral animated clips about a dog named Andrei and the dog’s friends. The feature looks nothing like them: it’s a surreal story about travelers stranded in a mysterious hotel run by the eccentric Madam. The critic Anton Khitrov explains how to read this puzzle of a film — and why it became a hit.
Warning: This review contains spoilers. If you want to avoid them, read up to the next yellow banner, then come back once you’ve seen the film.
Had A24 released Nepokoy, movie buffs worldwide would already be snapping up the studio’s merchandise — tiger-print infinity scarves, pink bunny keychains. Slow-paced, unsettling, and not fully comprehensible on first viewing, the film is bound — despite all those qualities — to build a fan base. A Russian one, though, not yet an international one.
Leonid Shmelkov — who won Russia’s Nika Award and Berlin’s Crystal Bear for his short film Moy lichny los (“My Personal Moose”) — spent three and a half years making Nepokoy and showed it at several festivals in 2025, including the Moscow International Film Festival and the Big Cartoon Festival. The film has only now reached theaters; online, it will be available on Okko.
For all its originality, Nepokoy produces a sense of déjà vu at every turn, and each new review of it arrives with its own catalog of spotted references. Shmelkov himself cites Groundhog Day, the films of David Lynch, and Julio Cortázar’s story “House Taken Over” — a classic of magical realism about a brother and sister who live alone in their family’s city mansion but meekly abandon it as unnamed entities take over one room after another. There are far more sources than that, conscious and unconscious alike, from mythology and folklore to 19th- and 20th-century prose and contemporary cinema. Animation is in the mix too: the most obvious analog is Hayao Miyazaki’s Spirited Away. But in Shmelkov’s hands, everything is much darker.
The story opens with two travelers — the imperturbable Yasha and the perpetually drowsy Bernard — driving across Russia one hot summer in a car whose pink color is no accident. They turn off the road for the night at a roadside hotel called the Rose, lost among the fields. Its owner, a certain “Madam” — cheerful, talkative, and somehow a little too pushy — takes a distinct interest in Yasha.
By the next day, the travelers realize that they can’t leave the Rose and that something is off about the hotel itself. The longer they stay, the more marvels they find. One guest can teleport. Another turns into a little pyramid. A third is a tiger, though he walks on two legs. Little by little, the Rose’s residents start disappearing, and strange creatures overrun the surrounding fields — all of it set to the unbearably disquieting music of Sergei Kuryokhin, performed by Alexei Aigi’s ensemble 4’33”.
The new film has little in common with Shmelkov’s therapeutic reels about Andrei, though his followers will still find familiar touches — his characteristic gentle voice, for instance, which he lends to several characters, including the leads, Yasha and Madam. Much closer to Nepokoy is another of his works, the 2021 short Komnata s vidom na more (“A Room with a Sea View”), which is also available online. Visually it’s sparer than the feature — black-and-white with occasional flecks of red and green — but the character designs already hint at the future cast of Nepokoy. And the plot is all but identical.
The idea for the short seems to grow entirely out of observations of the frustration that sets in on vacation: you travel for the experience and find only boredom when you arrive. A traveler named Herbert checks into a rented room whose sea view is nominal at best — really just a narrow strip between buildings — and spends his hours moping in front of the television. Before long he meets a mysterious florist from the shop across the street, and she takes over his thoughts completely. Like Madam, she rules an enchanted kingdom of her own — a kingdom of plants — but in looks she is closer to Rita, another of the hotel’s residents: the same silence, the same wide eyes.
Still, Shmelkov has never worked in a visual language as complex and varied as the one in Nepokoy.
Nepokoy gives us a convincing portrait of the Russian backwoods, full of living detail: the road overgrown with gray weeds, the air swarming with flies — leave a car in the yard overnight and by morning you’ll find a couple of apples on the hood. In some scenes, the balance of stylization and realism is no less exact than the celebrated Studio Ghibli’s: a flock of sheep drawn as a single creature, many-headed and flowing, or the painstaking animation of food, from a meager hotel breakfast to a fantastical pomegranate that might have been borrowed from Sergei Parajanov.
The effect is all the more startling when the lifelike image suddenly gives way to a schematic, deliberately primitive one, as in the Andrei cartoons. Or, on the contrary, to detailed, intricate surrealist images, such as the imagined “eternal tiger” coiled into a ring like an ouroboros. Nepokoy has both ordinary-looking people and humanoid pink bunnies — frankly cartoonish creatures, a cross between the putti of Old Master paintings and the Hattifatteners from Tove Jansson’s books. They apparently embody Yasha’s unconscious — since they anticipate desires he doesn’t yet know he has.
The bunnies are the only characters the animators didn’t draw from life. For everyone else, they used rotoscoping, a retro technique, an old analog of today’s motion capture. It works like this: a live actor plays the character and is filmed; an artist then traces the movements, adjusting the proportions as needed (the textbook example is Walt Disney’s Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs). The characters in Nepokoy have cartoon faces and human everything else, so the facial expressions come out exaggerated while the body language is startlingly natural. The dancing is especially expressive; the choreography in Nepokoy, incidentally, is quite idiosyncratic — like something out of an experimental dance piece.
Spoilers start here!
Nepokoy’s plot and visual style are in fine harmony: the animation here is realism plus stylization, and the script is everyday life plus archetypes. Madam, for instance, is drawn, acted, and voiced in a way that lets you picture her at the register of your nearest supermarket. But is she human? Hardly. More likely she’s good at pretending.
A goddess or sorceress who keeps a mortal man as her lover by force is an ancient image with a rich history. Readers of Homer — and viewers of Christopher Nolan — will inevitably think of the nymph Calypso, who kept Odysseus from going home for seven years. Then there’s the legend of the German knight Tannhäuser, who spent those same seven years in the cave of the goddess Holda — Venus, in Richard Wagner’s opera. The most obvious Russian counterpart is Pavel Bazhov’s “The Stone Flower”: the Mistress of the Copper Mountain may not make Danila the Craftsman her husband, but everything else matches.
In all these stories, the hero is either across the sea or underground — in short, in the land of the dead. And since the world of the dead is an inverted world, it’s no surprise that a woman rules it, with patriarchal logic being what it is. To some extent, all these stories are about male fear of women in general and of women with power in particular. Nepokoy is no exception: in Shmelkov’s film, that fear takes the form of Madam — mocking, loud, demanding, with a short “masculine” haircut.
If the hero in all such stories is symbolically held in the land of the dead, does that make the Rose the afterlife? Not quite: the clue is in the title. The Russian word nepokoy — literally the absence of pokoy, rest — is bound up with unquiet souls, the ones stuck between life and death. That is the oldest horror story there is, familiar to just about every culture. So the Rose appears to mark the border between two worlds, like Baba Yaga’s hut in Russian folktales (another of the film’s many sources). Madam, with her big nose, even looks like her. The Rose’s eccentric guests die off one by one because they are, in fact, already dead: at some point they’re simply let through. And you can pass, it seems, only by understanding something about yourself.
Yasha, at any rate, understands a great deal before he’s allowed to leave the hotel. He meets his own fear, for instance, at the very start of the film, when he spots his pursuers from the car window: mysterious runners. There’s a whole crowd of them, and they’re something like zombies — vicious, frenzied, nearly indistinguishable from one another apart from the numbers on their shirts.
In time it becomes clear that the runners, it seems, are a projection straight out of Yasha’s head: this is how he sees human society. Tellingly, he admits that he loves cars and hates buses — implying, of course, that in a car he picks his own fellow passengers. Only after living at the Rose does Yasha realize that he, too, is one of the runners in some sense.
Seconds before the closing credits, the audience learns for the first time what year — roughly — Yasha and Bernard arrived at the Rose. Shmelkov conceived Nepokoy quite some time ago, in 2019, but he must have settled on the final shot much later — and if he didn’t, one can only marvel at his foresight. A hint will do in a review: if the Rose really is a refuge for unquiet souls, it won’t be short of guests.
Fantastical as it is, Nepokoy conveys the present condition of many of its viewers more precisely than a social media feed does. Shmelkov’s film answers not only Nolan’s The Odyssey but another international box-office hit, Kane Parsons’s Backrooms.
The internet legend behind that film popularized the term “liminal space.” Online, it’s taken to mean an empty, sinister room, preferably windowless. In the humanities, “liminal” simply means transitional, in-between. The Rose fits that definition perfectly. Millions of people are living in liminal space today: between freedom and prison, between normalcy and catastrophe, and, in the end, between their own country and someone else’s.
One more thing. For all the differences between Nepokoy and the Andrei reels, the secret of their relevance is one and the same: Shmelkov is not only a tremendous animator but a brilliant voice actor.
There is no weighty philosophical dialogue in his feature, only ordinary speech — as though you were eavesdropping on a conversation aboard a commuter train. There’s nothing mystical in Madam’s voice, and Yasha talks like a man who’s never surprised by anything, or who is surprised but doesn’t let it show. Sure, a tiger in the hotel, unusual. Sure, the old man turned into a little pyramid, terrific, thanks for showing us, but we really do have to go. The Rose’s other residents are even harder to faze. Yesterday’s paranormal is today’s normal: adaptation is the most natural human quality there is. Nepokoy may be a surrealist film, but in a way it’s realist, with no prefix attached.

The airport problem passengers rarely see — until their flight is delayed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:41:15 UTC
04:41:15 KST

IN BRIEF
- Australia's air traffic control workforce is in the spotlight amid days of flight delays and a near collision at Sydney Airport.
- Experts say the job is highly specialised and requires years of experience to ensure public safety is not compromised.
On Tuesday, many Australians arrived at the airport with their plane waiting on the tarmac and clear skies overhead — only to discover their flight had been delayed.
Around 200 flights moving through Melbourne and Perth Airports were forecast to experience delays, according to a daily plan issued by Airservices Australia.
In Sydney, 138 flights were expected to be impacted by ground delays of around 43 minutes, in part due to strong winds, the government-owned air traffic management organisation said.
Rob Sharp, CEO of Airservices Australia, acknowledged that flight delays and disruptions can cause "very high frustration levels" for passengers, airlines and airport partners alike.
Behind the scenes, delays are often used to ensure public safety is not compromised during what Sharp described as a "challenging period" for air traffic controllers.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We do this through effectively putting space between aircraft. But it does come at a cost, and that cost is delays," Sharp said during a press conference on Monday.
His comments follow significant delays to flights on Friday and Saturday last week. On Sunday, two passenger jets also narrowly avoided a ground collision at Sydney Airport, with the incident now under investigation.
It's left industry leaders and aviation experts questioning whether Australia's air traffic control workforce can keep up with aviation demands.
Who's in control?
Uğur Turhan is a senior lecturer in aviation at the University of New South Wales in Canberra. He said controllers are responsible for air traffic safety and efficiency, both on the ground and in the air.
"You cannot put somebody as a high-performing air-traffic controller in one day or one year ... generally, we think that five years' experience is a really good level to perform at high levels in complex traffic situations," Turhan told SBS News.
There are three types of controllers — tower controllers, terminal controllers and en route controllers — responsible for various stages of flights including take-off, landing and airspace movement.
While training programs vary, typically air traffic controllers train for 12 months before undergoing additional on-the-job training.
Australian air services manage more than 51 million square kilometres of airspace, equivalent to approximately 11 per cent of the world's airspace. This area is managed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, Airservices Australia said.
Federal Transport Minister Catherine King believes the work of air traffic controllers is a "really stressful and difficult job".
"If you've been in an air traffic control tower, you've seen the number of flights they are managing, the complexities in how quickly they have to think. It's a really specialised job."
She held emergency meetings in Canberra on Monday following recent flight disruptions. King described her discussion with Sharp from Airservices Australia as "constructive" and said she felt "confident" the organisation was doing "everything they can to get on top of this".
Staff shortages
National disruptions due to air traffic control have fallen by 86 per cent over the past financial year, according to Airservices Australia. Ground delays caused by air services also reduced by 13 per cent.
The air traffic industry has recorded an uptick in staffing, with a record 109 new controllers employed last year. Sharp told the ABC's 7.30 on Monday there were now more than 1,070 air traffic controllers in Australia.
There are an additional 15 people in training, expected to join the workforce by the end of 2027, King said in a press conference on Monday. Experienced air traffic controllers have also been hired from overseas to work in Australia.
Sharp said the sector has traditionally relied on high staff overtime, which he does not believe is a "sustainable model" as Australian airports expand. He said new rostering systems are likely to ease staff burdens from September this year.
Turhan acknowledged the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the aviation industry too.
"Globally, we had COVID-19. We lost some manpower capability in aviation, not just for air traffic controllers. As I said, it is not easy to put someone, with a high performance level in [the job in] just one year; it takes time."
Between October 2021 and December 2022, more than 180 air traffic controllers accepted voluntary redundancies, according to online information published by the Brisbane Flight Path Community Alliance.
Turhan believes Sydney Airport is a particularly challenging environment for new air traffic controllers. It requires workers to train for two years, plus an additional two years to embed into the system, according to Sharp from Airservices Australia.
"It has a really complex layout ... and also it is operated by different domestic and international terminals," Turhan said.
"In Sydney Airport ... you cannot operate your flights during the night. So, during that limited time you should perform all traffic in a short time and traffic levels are not homogeneously distributed to the time. So, we have peak traffic."
A global issue?
Air traffic control is a highly competitive field which can offer high pay. The base salary for an initial trainee air traffic controller begins at $60,000, which increases to more than $171,000 for a Level 5 controller. Workers at a Level 10 classification can earn over $243,000, and supervisors more than $286,000.
Angus Mitchell, the chief commissioner of the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, said it's also considered a specialised profession.
"Airports are incredibly busy. You've got planes taking off, planes landing, planes being manoeuvred across crossing runways, across taxiways. It is a complex environment, but it needs to also be incredibly robust," Mitchell told SBS News.
"Even at low speeds, there can be very significant outcomes if planes come into contact with each other."
This complexity has fuelled a global shortage in air traffic controllers.
In July 2025, United States transportation secretary Sean Duffy told Congress it would cost US$31.5 billion ($44.6 billion) to fully modernise the country's air traffic control system. That same year, the Federal Aviation Administration told US media it was facing a shortage of around 3,000 air traffic controllers.
In July 2026, Singapore announced new air traffic controller recruits would receive a sign-on bonus of SGD$20,000 (approximately $22,100), as Changi Airport is expanded.
Parts of Europe, including Athens Airport in Greece, have experienced flight delays amidst seasonal summer travel peaks.
However, Turhan cautioned against comparing Australia's situation directly with Europe.
"In Australia, we have really broad and wide airspace. We have a few big airports but they are busy, and they're handling different kinds of traffic levels."
He is optimistic that discussions about Australia's air traffic control sector could eventually lead to reduced workloads, improved working conditions and fatigue management.

I used ice every day at work to chase a dopamine hit. After 10 years, the charade had to stop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:40:55 KST

What do extreme sports, doomscrolling, addiction, Parkinson's disease, and ADHD all have in common? Dopamine. This crucial neurotransmitter helps facilitate reward, motivation, memory and movement within the body, but are its effects always beneficial? Watch Insight episode Chasing Dopamine on SBS On Demand.
Content warning: This article references drug use and addiction.
When I was 18 years old at a party, someone offered me ice (crystal meth), and I said yes as I was fresh out of a breakup and wanted to escape reality.
Before I knew it, 10 years had passed, and I no longer recognised the woman that stood in front of the mirror.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
There were a few factors that went into me making that decision that night.
I didn't really know who I was and placed all my worth in what other people thought about me. And I actively avoided rejection or confrontation, which meant I had no boundaries and never said no. I also had a high appetite for risk, because I thought it would make me look cool and be liked.
For the next 10 years, I would smoke amphetamines every single day — chasing dopamine and trying to regulate my emotions in an unhealthy way.
Dopamine is a neurotransmitter in the brain that contributes to our motivation, reward systems, and habit development. Dopamine is not itself addictive, but the associated substances, behaviours or activities that cause the brain to release dopamine can be.
I liken smoking ice to the dopamine centre of your brain lighting up like a Christmas tree. Your dopamine receptors are the lights, and it takes so much power to light the tree. But you need more and more of the drug to reach the feeling of your first high, to power the lights. And with regular drug use over time, the dopamine receptors start to die off, and your brain needs more drugs to feel the same high.
I experienced a full spectrum in that decade: The hard times would send me further into my addiction, and I'd try escape the reality I had created for myself.
The good times would make me believe I didn't need to change — that I could manage it all. I would still go to work, look after my health in other ways, study at university, pay my rent and maintained my relationships with family.
But all the while, I would sneak off into the toilets to smoke a pipe — just to feel normal.
Keeping something like that hidden for long periods of time is exhausting because you can never keep up the charade. Eventually, the walls start to crumble around you.
The cycle of being able to keep it all together was getting shorter and shorter.
Things would be going "well" but then something would happen, and there would be a crash; I'd become dysfunctional with periods of couch surfing, hotel hopping, unemployment and being in unhealthy relationships.
And then I would seem to get it together again and then be highly functioning again.
Until I wasn't.
A fateful decision
One day, eight years into my addiction, I found myself sitting in my unregistered car, with no phone, no money, no job and no licence, feeling desperate.
It was in this moment I realised how I could make money quickly and get myself some power back.
I went to my dealer's house and asked to sell drugs for them. It was a poor decision that would change my life forever, for better and for worse.
And the newfound agency I felt as a drug dealer soon landed me in custody several times for supply of a dangerous drug, and my longest stint behind bars was 10 months.
The first time I was in a cell was terrifying. They strip searched me and took my shoes, which meant I was barefoot on the cold concrete.
They handed me a blanket that made me itch just by looking at it, and my bed: three small square mats, which slid apart during the night and exposed my body to the cold concrete.
As I lay in the cell with my itchy blanket, I thought about how I had reached this point in my life. I also thought of nothing and slept.
You would think this would be the time I would try and get myself together — to finally be rid of the drugs.
But for me, being incarcerated only pushed me further into that life, because now I was a criminal with no hope for the bright future I once believed I was going to have.
Chasing sobriety
I had tried many times to stop using drugs before, but it never stuck.
The stints would usually last one or two months. I would move from the Gold Coast back home to Moreton Bay, Queensland, to be with my mum and dad, convinced that I was only using because of the people I hung with.
I needed to understand why I sought out that world if I was ever going to get a handle on my addiction.
Coming off ice looks different for everyone.
For me, I would just sleep and eat for weeks on end. When my body had finally detoxed the drugs, what was left was a shell of a human — devoid of life.
I felt empty, like someone had turned down the volume for colour in my world — like my capacity to enjoy anything had died.
It was a feeling I had become scared to face, and so I stopped trying to get sober and continued using.
Establishing a new path forward
It wasn't until 2018, when I was in custody for the last time that things really started to change.
When you're sitting in a cell that's two by four metres for 22 hours a day with nothing to do, you soon realise that you must look inwards and work on yourself to not land back in custody.
So, I met with an incredible therapist weekly who taught me all the thing I needed to understand so I could stop masking my head noise with drugs. This included my behaviour patterns and understanding how I showed up in the world.
I also attended a narcotics support group and learnt that your brain has pathways for behaviour. In my case, when I learned new pathways (as in new ways to handle certain emotions) my brain stops telling me that I need to use drugs.
It's an oversimplified explanation — but all I needed to hold onto to break free of that life.
These days, my life looks worlds away from the girl sneaking to the work toilets to smoke drugs.
I had heard that your dopamine receptors die when you use ice, so I went through a time where I didn't think I'd feel happy again.
But slowly and surely, all the feelings a healthy brain lets you experience returned. Learning to emotionally regulate and sit with emotions joy, sadness, excitement, and pain has kept me from going back to drugs.
And despite everything that happened to me in that decade, I hadn't cried once. Being able to cry again was an experience I'll never forget.
These days, my life looks worlds away from the girl sneaking to the work toilets to smoke drugs.
I have built an entirely new life that doesn't require me to run from anything or occupy myself with anything or replace the drug use with anything. I worked through it and addressed the reasons why I was using drugs. I just replaced it with life and living life.
I'm a mum, a wife, a criminologist, and a whole person who experiences a whole life.
I also founded an advocacy organisation supporting women to break their cycles of incarceration, which is my main work. Going back into women's prisons and helping them is now a much healthier dopamine hit for me.
My joy now also comes from hearing my kids laugh, soaking up the sunshine with friends at lunch, or watching the beautiful colours of a sunset.

The White House chief said that he had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin before the American was released.
"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis. We appreciate this decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place," Trump said.
He also said that he had personally spoken with Gilman.
"I just spoke with him, and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!" the U.S. president wrote.
Trump also added that Gilman had been reunited with his mother, Nancy, who is flying back with him from Russia.
Gilman was detained by Russian authorities in 2022. He was initially sentenced to three and a half years in prison for assaulting a police officer after he was removed from a train for disorderly conduct. He was later repeatedly convicted of assaulting prison staff, and his total prison sentence was increased to 10 years.
Before his release, the 32-year-old American was being held in the psychiatric department of a civilian hospital. According to his lawyer, Gilman's condition had been deteriorating.

Release

Requests for pardon
- On August 6, Reuters quoted a US official as saying that the Washington administration had asked Russia to release Gilman.

Health problems
- On July 6, Gilman’s lawyer Irina Brazhnikova told TASS that his trials had been suspended due to him being hospitalized for treatment.
- She said the situation would move forward after treatment.
- Records from the Central District Court of Voronezh also stated that Gilman had a mental disorder or other serious illness that precluded him from standing trial.
The Gilman case
- Gilman was detained in 2022 at the Voronezh railway station after being involved in a drunken brawl on the Sukhum-Moscow train.

- The court sentenced him to 4.5 years in a general regime penal colony, and in 2023 his sentence was reduced by one year.

- Despite the attempt to attack a pre-trial detention center employee, the next day he was transferred to a correctional colony. Gilman again attacked an employee of the Federal Penitentiary Service.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, Aug. 11, that Russian intelligence documents confirm the Kremlin is preparing a massive wave of mobilization for this fall, timed to follow staged parliamentary elections.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Everything is confirmed by internal Russian documents,” Zelensky said.
“They are preparing it for the fall,” he continued – right after the State Duma’s parliamentary elections – which are widely believed to be rigged.
Staged vote with no real opposition
“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s plan is not particularly complicated,” Zelensky said.
He continued: “He wants to create the impression that Russians supposedly support the war – every party still permitted to run is, one way or another, against peace.”
His remarks come as Russia prepares for elections, which are scheduled for Sept. 18-20.
Putin’s United Russia party is currently facing no credible opposition after Russia’s Supreme Court barred Yabloko, the only liberal, anti-war party, from participating.
The court ruled in favor of a lawsuit filed by the nationalist Rodina party on Monday, Aug. 10 – a decision that drew protests from hundreds of Russian citizens outside the courthouse during the hearing.
Germany Grants Ukraine’s State Emergency Service Nearly €6M in Robotic Firefighting Package
Zelensky said the vote itself is part of the mobilization strategy.
According to Andriy Kovalenko, head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, Russia is preparing to falsify voting in the occupied territories of Ukraine as well, including in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s administration has instructed occupation authorities to report turnout of more than 65% to 70% and at least 70% support for the ruling United Russia party, Kovalenko said.
Hundreds of thousands to be mobilized
“After the so-called elections, he [Putin] plans an additional rapid mobilization of several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, plus just as many more next year,” Zelensky said.
According to him, “this will be on top of the recruitment they [Russia] are trying to carry out through contract enlistment.”
The warning aligns with concerns Ukrainian authorities have voiced throughout recent months.
Russia has declared only one official mobilization during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in September 2022, a move that triggered nationwide protests, prompting thousands of Russian citizens to flee the country.
As public fatigue grows and Russia’s economy continues to strain under war spending, a second, direct mobilization would carry heightened political risks for Putin.
Instead, Russia has increasingly relied on fraudulent recruitment schemes to draw in foreign fighters, particularly from third countries such as Colombia, Peru, and Bolivia – all with promises of well-paid civilian jobs, such as construction work or factory labor.
Additionally, Zelensky said that Russia can no longer sustain its war without North Korean support, which has become one of Russia’s most critical wartime partners, supplying troops, weapons,and manpower in exchange for financial and technological support. He warned on July 29 that Russia is preparing to receive 30,000 additional North Korean troops and more ballistic missile launchers.
Moscow signed a defense pact with Pyongyang on June 19, 2024, with both countries officially recognizing North Korean troop deployments in April 2025.
Ukraine vows countermeasures
According to Zelensky, Ukraine is preparing to respond directly. “We are preparing our own active steps to maximally complicate Russia’s implementation of such plans,” Zelensky said, adding that he has assigned specific tasks to Ukraine’s intelligence agencies and special services.
However, he did not disclose further details on what those measures would involve.
A broader pattern of Russia’s suppression
The move against Yabloko fits into Russia’s broader pattern of systematically suppressing progressive and liberal voices it associates with Western values.
Moscow has similarly promoted residency programs for foreigners who explicitly reject Western values and progressive social norms by issuing a “traditional values” visa scheme, framing itself as a refuge for those “under pressure” in liberal democracies.
Russia also continues to target its openly anti-war nationals, even those who remain in exile.
Yabloko’s removal from the upcoming elections, therefore, does not come as a surprise.

Meta and TikTok fail to halt thousands of social media addiction lawsuits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:23:20 UTC
04:23:20 KST

Meta and TikTok fail to halt thousands of social media addiction lawsuits
Thousands of lawsuits accusing major social media companies of fueling addiction and harming young users can move forward in the US after a federal appeals court rejected an attempt to halt the litigation.
The San Francisco-based Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed appeals by Meta and TikTok on Monday against earlier rulings that allowed more than 3,000 federal cases to proceed.
The companies sought to challenge the cases under Section 230, a US law that protects online platforms from some claims involving content posted by users.
The appeals court ruled that they could not use the law to stop the cases from moving forward at this stage, saying Section 230 “merely provides a defense to liability – not immunity from suit.” The ruling does not determine whether Meta, TikTok, and other companies are responsible for the alleged harms.
The lawsuits target Meta, Google, TikTok, Snap, and other companies and have been brought by individuals, school districts, US states, and local authorities. They accuse the platforms of using features designed to keep children and teenagers engaged, allegedly contributing to addiction, depression, anxiety, and other problems.
The court also rejected Meta’s bid to delay a separate case brought by 29 US state attorneys general. Jury selection is due to begin Wednesday, with the states accusing the company of improperly collecting children’s data, using features designed to keep young users engaged, and misleading consumers about the safety of its platforms. Meta denies the allegations.
The decision follows another setback for the industry in March, when a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google negligent in the first social media addiction case to reach a verdict. It awarded $6 million to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child. Both companies denied wrongdoing and have challenged the verdict.
The legal battles come as governments around the world tighten rules on children’s access to social media amid concerns over addictive features, harmful content, and weak age checks.
Last December, Australia became the first country to require major social media platforms to prevent people under 16 from holding accounts. Indonesia and Malaysia have since introduced restrictions for under-16s, and Britain has announced its own ban for next year. France has restricted access for children under 15, and the measure is due to take effect in September pending a constitutional review.

MLB-worst Angels fire pitching coach Mike Maddux, 2 assistants in staff shakeup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:23:02 UTC
04:23:02 KST

MLB-worst Angels fire pitching coach Mike Maddux, 2 assistants in staff shake-up
ANAHEIM, Calif. (AP) — The Los Angeles Angels fired pitching coach Mike Maddux and two of his assistants on Tuesday after interim general manager John Mozeliak determined the team wasn’t making sufficient use of the technology and analytics available to its pitchers.
Mozeliak also fired bullpen coach Dom Chiti and assistant pitching coach Darryl Scott in a shake-up of first-year manager Kurt Suzuki’s staff with just 43 games remaining for the Angels, who have the majors’ worst record at 45-74.
While Mozeliak said that “no one thing just stood out” in his decision to fire Maddux, he prominently cited his desire for the Angels to “use all the different tools that you see a lot of pitchers use today.”
“I think there was becoming some level of frustration with the inconsistency of that, and so ultimately that’s when we started thinking about, ‘Do we need to make a change?’” Mozeliak said. ”I do feel like we have a lot of great resources that we could be taking (greater) advantage of.”
The dismissals were the latest shake-up in a tumultuous year for the Angels, who fired general manager Perry Minasian in late June. Los Angeles is headed toward its 11th consecutive losing season and 12th straight non-playoff season, both the longest active droughts in the majors, under much-criticized owner Arte Moreno.
Mozeliak, the longtime St. Louis Cardinals general manager, agreed to take over baseball operations for Moreno on a temporary basis after Minasian’s firing, and he has endeavored to modernize the Halos’ long-struggling organization.
Mozeliak said the Angels have technology and information on par with the rest of the majors, and he’s confident it is being used properly by Suzuki’s offensive staff — but the pitching operation needed an urgent overhaul.
“There’s so many more resources out there that really every team in baseball is utilizing, so (we’re) just making sure that the Angels are up to speed with that and leveraging this,” Mozeliak said. “I know our research and development team upstairs, they’re providing a lot of useful things that I think we can be taking advantage of. And then moving forward ... what can we do to make this a state-of-the-art place for player growth? What you don’t want to do is have players outsourcing those types of things. You want it to be the internal model, and hopefully we can accomplish that.”
Maddux, who turns 65 later this month, didn’t last one full season with the Angels after leaving the Texas Rangers last winter. The former major leaguer is widely respected in the game after 24 seasons as a pitching coach, and he played a significant role in the Rangers’ success during their 2023 World Series title.
But in Anaheim, Maddux presided over a staff that has posted the majors’ seventh-worst ERA at 4.51 and an MLB-high 508 walks.
Angels left-hander Reid Detmers, whose 1.10 WHIP is the 14th-best in the majors, said “everybody is surprised” by the firings.
“I mean, if we have it, might as well use it, right?,” said Detmers, who evaluates his biomechanics in every bullpen session and consults with his personal coaches during the season. “I’m not saying we didn’t use it all the time, but there’s definitely times where we could have used it. In my eyes, it’s only going to make you better.”
Tim Leveque was appointed Los Angeles’ interim pitching coach, and Michael Wuertz will be the club’s interim bullpen coach. Leveque was the pitching coach at the Angels’ Double-A Rocket City affiliate after working in the Cardinals organization during Mozeliak’s tenure.
“He’s a smart guy who really understands where the game is at, and I think he’ll be a good resource for (Suzuki),” Mozeliak said of Leveque.
Suzuki is on a one-year contract in his first major league managerial job. Mozeliak said he won’t make any additional changes before the end of the season in seven weeks.
“I appreciated everything that they did,” Suzuki said of the fired coaches. “They worked hard. They prepared. At the end of the day, Mo and I felt like the path moving forward in these last 43 games ... we felt like this was the best way.”
Chiti was in his first season as the bullpen coach after rejoining the Angels organization in late 2023. Scott also was in his first season with the Angels after several years with the Colorado Rockies.

Federal report says firefighting tactics at Maine lumber mill explosion aided the blast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:23:01 UTC
04:23:01 KST

Federal report says firefighting tactics at Maine lumber mill explosion aided the blast
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Firefighters who responded to a fire at a Maine lumber mill used tactics that inadvertently contributed to a massive explosion that killed three people, according to a report from federal investigators.
The fire companies tried to extinguish the May 15 fire inside a silo at the Robbins Lumber mill in rural Searsmont, Maine, by injecting it with water — unaware of warnings from the manufacturer that doing so would be dangerous.
The silo then blasted skyward like a rocket as flames and a shock wave from the explosion hurled workers and firefighters away.
The firefighters didn’t know, the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health wrote this month, that the silo was oxygen-limiting, a type of sealed structure that can become pressurized with combustible gases during a fire.
That kind of buildup is a known hazard in oxygen-limited silos, and both the manufacturer and fire safety organizations put out firefighting guidance warning against putting water or foam into such chambers.
“The document warns against spraying water or foam into the oxygen-limiting silo as it will force air in and may create a potentially explosive mixture,” the report states. “The application of water into the silo in this incident likely entrained oxygen into the silo headspace, stirred up dust within the contents, and caused it to become suspended in an explosive concentration.”
The report recommends that fire departments make sure firefighters choose appropriate tactics for silo fires and never direct water or foam into oxygen-limiting silos. It also states that more training is needed for fire departments about the hazards associated with different types of silos.
The blast also injured at least 13 people and the toppling of the silo engulfed the surrounding area in fire, investigators have said. The explosion took place in the small town about 95 miles (150 kilometers) northeast of Portland and triggered a response of 299 firefighters from 46 departments across a four-county area. It took them hours to contain the fire.
Representatives for Searsmont Fire & Rescue did not return phone calls seeking comment Tuesday. The department’s assistant fire chief, Wayne Woodbury, 76, died from injuries suffered in the explosion. Andrew Cross, 27, of the Morrill Volunteer Fire Department, also died. Alden Robbins, the co-owner of the mill, died from injuries weeks later.
Robbins Lumber representatives said on the company’s website that “no report can fully capture the heartbreak experienced by our community, nor can it lessen the tremendous loss suffered by so many.” The company is working with industry experts to rebuild its facilities, the statement said.
“Our objective is not simply to meet current industry standards, but to exceed them. We are committed to learning from this event and to doing everything we can to help prevent anything like this from happening again,” the statement said.
The National Fire Protection Association declined to comment on the report beyond saying it encourages firefighters to participate in the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health’s work to improve safety investigations. The Maine Department of Public Safety also declined to comment.
Officials with the town of Searsmont said in a statement that a final investigation into the explosion is still ongoing.
“As investigations move forward, we should allow the facts to guide any conclusions. It is neither fair nor constructive to rush to judgment or to diminish the dedication of the firefighters who responded or the company that suffered such a devastating loss,” the statement said.
The Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office said in late May that rapid ignition of particulate material resulted in the silo explosion, which caused it to lift from its concrete base and release large amounts of sawdust and other materials. It said the fire and explosion were accidental.
The mill is a part of the historic lumber and wood products industry in Maine. The company has said it is a high tech lumber manufacturer that has been in existence since the 19th century.

Scientist explains late chestnut flowering in Brest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:23:00 UTC
04:23:00 KST

BREST, 11 August (BelTA) - Residents of Brest have spotted flowering chestnut trees in the city and took to social media. The reason for this anomalous phenomenon was explained by Viktor Demyanchik, head of the Laboratory for Ecosystem Optimization at the Polesie Agrarian-Ecological Institute of the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus, BelTA has learned.
“The chestnut tree is closely tied to the seasonal dynamics of the climate. Winter for it is a period of complete dormancy, spring is the beginning of awakening, sap flow, and vegetation. But this year, at the time when the trees should have entered the active phase of flowering and leaf unfolding, we had a drought. And the trees blocked all the biochemical processes typical for a normal spring due to increased aridity,” the scientist noted.
He explained that the dry and hot spring had blocked the normal course of vegetation processes. Some of the buds entered a state of suspended animation. “Only after the normal climatic phase was restored did they wake up belatedly and begin to bloom. This late flowering of these trees is connected to that,” Viktor Demyanchik noted.
He suggested that other trees might also bloom for the same reason. This could primarily affect apple trees, black plum trees, and bird cherry trees. Such an anomalous phenomenon is possible under certain conditions. “For example, for chestnut trees in a modern city, the conditions are far from the best: lots of asphalt and concrete. Heat comes not only from the sky but is also reflected from the ground. This does not happen in the natural environment,” the scientist emphasized.
He added that the climatic fluctuation has also had a negative impact on the animal world, which may go unnoticed by humans.

And the trees blocked all the biochemical processes typical for a normal spring due to increased aridity,” the scientist noted.
He explained that the dry and hot spring had blocked the normal course of vegetation processes. Some of the buds entered a state of suspended animation. “Only after the normal climatic phase was restored did they wake up belatedly and begin to bloom. This late flowering of these trees is connected to that,” Viktor Demyanchik noted.
He suggested that other trees might also bloom for the same reason. This could primarily affect apple trees, black plum trees, and bird cherry trees. Such an anomalous phenomenon is possible under certain conditions. “For example, for chestnut trees in a modern city, the conditions are far from the best: lots of asphalt and concrete. Heat comes not only from the sky but is also reflected from the ground. This does not happen in the natural environment,” the scientist emphasized.
He added that the climatic fluctuation has also had a negative impact on the animal world, which may go unnoticed by humans.

Syrian officials hail death sentences against Assad regime figures as victory for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:21:52 UTC
04:21:52 KST

- Officials say verdicts mark  step toward accountability and transitional justice
Syrian officials on Tuesday welcomed death sentences handed down against several senior figures of the ousted Bashar al-Assad regime, describing the verdicts as reflecting the will of the Syrian people, a victory for justice and a rejection of impunity.
Earlier Tuesday, the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus sentenced Brig. Gen. Atef Najib, the former head of the Political Security branch in the southern province of Daraa, to death.
It also handed down death sentences in absentia to Bashar al-Assad, the deposed regime leader and Najib’s cousin; Maher al-Assad, his brother and former commander of the Fourth Division; and six other former security and military officials who remain at large.
The court found them guilty of “crimes against humanity,” intentional killing, torture and arbitrary detention.
‘Just punishment’
Commenting on the verdicts, Interior Minister Anas Khattab said: “Today, justice has prevailed for the victims of crimes and violations committed against Syrians,” according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
“Congratulations to the Syrian people on the issuance of the first death sentences against the perpetrators of these crimes, in a historic step toward redressing victims and holding those responsible accountable,” Khattab said.
“We will continue pursuing everyone involved in these crimes until they receive their just punishment,” he added.
Information Minister Khaled Zaarour said the death sentences against the “leaders of the former regime” represent “another victory for Syrians and a definitive confirmation that there will be no impunity,” according to SANA.
He said transitional justice and national efforts are “the real guarantee of the rights of the victims of the Syrian revolution and the cornerstone for closing the era of authoritarianism and building a new Syria.”
Awqaf Minister Mohammad Abu al-Khair Shukri said the verdicts represent “a new step toward consolidating the rule of law and justice, providing redress to victims and restoring rights to their owners,” according to SANA.
‘Independent judiciary’
Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais said the verdicts against “criminals of the former regime” followed a series of judicial proceedings and were issued “in the name of the Syrian people,” Syrian Alikhbariah TV reported.
Al-Wais said Syrians had decided to build their new state on “justice, citizenship and the rule of law.” He called on citizens to trust state institutions and the national process launched after the fall of the former regime and seek their rights through the relevant institutions.
He said the verdicts were issued in accordance with Syrian penal law and international humanitarian law as part of efforts to provide redress to victims and prevent impunity.
He also stressed that “the Syrian judiciary is independent,” adding that the Justice Ministry and the Supreme Judicial Council were responsible for removing obstacles and ensuring the judiciary had the resources it needed.
Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said the death sentence represents “an important milestone on the path to justice and accountability for those responsible for crimes and violations against the Syrian people.”
He said transitional justice would continue to hold accountable anyone whose hands were “stained with the blood of Syrians,” regardless of position or rank, to establish a state based on law and justice.
SANA also quoted Syrian Bar Association head Mohammad Ali al-Tawil as saying the ruling was “a historic landmark” in the country’s judicial history and a legal culmination of the patience of mothers of those killed and wounded, as well as a tribute to victims of years of oppression and suffering affecting millions of Syrians.
“There will be no position or authority in the new Syria above the voice of law and justice,” al-Tawil said, adding that the judiciary is moving toward a more sustainable process of healing the country’s wounds.
‘Deterrent punishment’
Hama Governor Abdul Rahman al-Suhyan said: “Today, justice has spoken,” adding that Hama, “the province that knew the meaning of injustice and deprivation,” affirmed that justice is the foundation for building a new Syria, according to SANA.
Tartous Governor Ahmad al-Shami described the death sentence against “war criminals” as “a deterrent punishment for what they committed against humanity, restoring dignity to every victim and providing solace to the mothers of the missing,” according to SANA.
The ruling demonstrated that “justice, however long it takes, will come, and that the truth does not die no matter how much falsehood conspires against it,” he added.
Celebrations in Daraa
Later, SANA reported that residents of Daraa gathered in the courtyard of the Omari Mosque in the Daraa al-Balad neighborhood to celebrate the death sentence against Najib and other former regime figures.
Participants held signs reading, among other slogans: “Truth has prevailed and falsehood has perished,” “Daraa, birthplace of the revolution, has prevailed again,” and “The blood of the martyrs will not be lost.”
The Omari Mosque was the site of a deadly crackdown by former regime forces during the early days of the Syrian revolution, when troops stormed the mosque and killed and wounded dozens of worshippers.
The public prosecution and the prosecution authority had called for the maximum punishment, death, against Najib and the other defendants who remain at large, including Bashar and Maher al-Assad.
The case centers on Najib’s role in suppressing protests in Daraa, where the Syrian uprising began on March 18, 2011, after several children were arrested and tortured for writing anti-regime slogans on walls.
Najib was also linked to the storming of the Omari Mosque and the humiliation of local residents. The US and EU placed him on their sanctions lists in April and May 2011, respectively.
The trial, whose first hearings began on April 26, represents a major step in Syria’s transitional justice process following the capture of Damascus by Syrian opposition factions on Dec. 8, 2024, ending 61 years of Baath Party rule, including 53 years under the Assad family.

Countries in the Americas have offered humanitarian assistance and rescue support on Tuesday to Colombia following a magnitude 7.4 earthquake that killed at least 234 people and injured thousands.
President Nayib Bukele said Tuesday that El Salvador will send two cargo planes with 100 tons of humanitarian aid after Bogota requested supplies rather than foreign rescue personnel.
“Colombia has requested humanitarian aid only in the form of supplies to assist families affected by the earthquake,” Bukele wrote on US social media platform X.
He said the first plane would depart late Tuesday and the second Wednesday. The aid had been prepared according to needs communicated by Colombian authorities, he added.
Mexico is also preparing humanitarian assistance, said President Claudia Sheinbaum. The package, known as the “Cali” deployment, includes more than 8,000 food packages, 13,000 basic-needs baskets and 4 tons of medicine.
The US Embassy in Bogota said the Trump administration had activated a Disaster Assistance Response Team, which was expected to arrive Tuesday to support emergency operations and response coordination.
Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa offered to deploy a search-and-rescue team with 47 rescuers, specialized dogs and equipment capable of operating independently for seven days.
“We put our USAR team at your disposal,” said Noboa, referring to the Urban Search and Rescue team. “We are ready to mobilize when you require it.”
Argentina also offered assistance, with the Foreign Ministry in direct contact with Colombian authorities, while Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori expressed solidarity with Colombia and said Peru was ready to help.
Venezuela offered to send specialized rescue teams and humanitarian aid, while Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said his country was available to provide whatever assistance Colombia needs.
Colombian first lady Ana Lucia Pineda said humanitarian collection points had been established in Pereira, where authorities urgently need nonperishable food, medicines, clothing, mattresses, pillows and bedding.
The quake struck western Colombia Monday, causing widespread damage in cities including Cali, Pereira and Quibdo. Rescue operations are underway as authorities search for survivors and assess the extent of the damage.

Israel and Venezuela have agreed to resume consular ties and establish an official coordination channel after 17 years without diplomatic relations, according to Agencia AJN.
The agreement was reached following talks between Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Venezuelan Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia, according to the media outlet.
The two sides agreed to establish a coordination mechanism to provide consular services to citizens of both countries.
The development comes amid efforts to address the needs of Venezuela’s Jewish community.
Plasencia met Sunday in Caracas with Isaac Cohen, chief rabbi of the Israelite Association of Venezuela, who delivered a letter addressed to Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez that urged the restoration of diplomatic and consular relations with Israel.
The request aimed to address the needs of Venezuela’s Jewish community, according to statements on the Venezuelan Foreign Ministry’s social media accounts.
“Venezuela has historically welcomed an important Jewish community with open arms,” said Plasencia, praising its contributions to the country’s development.
The move restores a limited official channel between Caracas and Tel Aviv but does not amount to a full restoration of diplomatic relations, which were severed in 2009.
Venezuela under then-President Hugo Chavez broke diplomatic relations with Israel in January 2009, amid Israel’s military offensive in the Gaza Strip. Chavez had been a vocal critic of Israel and maintained close ties with countries opposed to Israeli policies in the Middle East.
Relations remained severed under Chavez’s successor, Nicolas Maduro, who has also maintained close ties with Iran and repeatedly criticized Israel’s policies toward the Palestinians.
Israel assisted Venezuela following a June 24 earthquake, with a delegation sent in June helping tens of thousands of Venezuelans return to their homes, according to Agencia AJN.
The two countries agreed to continue cooperating on emergency response and recovery efforts following the quake.
Plasencia also expressed gratitude to the Israeli government and people for their assistance following the “double earthquake” that struck Venezuela on June 24.

Putin Demands Private Business Fund Russian Science as War Drains Federal Budget
Unknown

04:14:18 KST

- Category
- World
Putin Demands Private Business Fund Russian Science as War Drains Federal Budget
Russian leader Vladimir Putin is urging private domestic companies to finance scientific development as state funding declines amid heavy defense spending.
One out of every three federal rubles is currently directed toward Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as reported by The Moscow Times on August 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to data from the Institute for Statistical Studies and Economics of Knowledge at the Higher School of Economics (ISSEK HSE), the federal budget allocated 792.1 billion rubles ($8.7 billion) to civilian science last year.
This accounted for only 2.5% of total government expenditure, making it 22 times smaller than the 17.8 trillion rubles ($195.8 billion) spent combined on the military and security forces.
Speaking at a meeting of the Council for Science and Education in Novosibirsk, Putin stated that commercial enterprises must directly commission technological developments.
"We need to set up the work in such a way that domestic business and enterprises act as direct customers of breakthrough scientific solutions and technologies. Taking clear obligations to create successful, competitive products based on them," Putin said.
He added, "To achieve practical, truly breakthrough results, maximum concentration of efforts of all participants in Russia's scientific and technological development is needed."
Although nominal federal funding for research grew by 11% over the past year, real expenditure adjusted for inflation dropped 14% below pre-war levels. Compared to 2013, real scientific funding has fallen by 25%. Spending as a share of gross domestic product reached 15-year lows, dropping to 0.35% of GDP in 2024 and 0.37% in 2025.
Initiative programs for technological leadership announced by Putin were left without funding following a federal budget deficit that reached 5.6 trillion rubles ($61.6 billion) where the gap expanded.
The primary space exploration initiative received no funding despite an original allocation plan of 10 billion rubles ($110 million). Funding for the automated production and robotics program was reduced by 75%, while funding for chemical development, new materials, and transport mobility projects was cut by 40%.
During the first nine months of 2025, Russia spent $146.4 billion from its budget on military expenditures—four times more than in 2021—which accounted for 39% of total government spending.
Meanwhile, the federal budget deficit grew to $69.8 billion in 2025, prompting the Kremlin to cover its widening fiscal gap by requiring state-controlled banks to purchase $87 billion in federal loan bonds backed by Central Bank liquidity.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

In Novosibirsk, fuel prices remained unchanged leading up to the official visit, marking a clear departure from the patterns observed during earlier presidential trips.

As a result, Putin called on commercial enterprises to act as direct customers and fund breakthrough technological solutions themselves.

US company stokes Greenland tensions by unloading drilling gear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:11:01 UTC
04:11:01 KST

US company stokes Greenland tensions by unloading drilling gear
- A US energy company unloaded drilling equipment in Greenland without authorisation, causing tensions amid fears of US territorial ambitions.
- Greenland's government issued a strong warning, emphasising all future activities need prior approval and noting environmental and social concerns.
- Local residents protested the project, which faces delays due to missing impact studies and harsh Arctic conditions, despite potential large oil reserves.
AI generated
COPENHAGEN - A US energy exploration company has sparked an outcry by unloading drilling equipment without authorisation on the east coast of Greenland, the autonomous Danish territory coveted by US President Donald Trump.
Texas-based Greenland Energy - which insists it has no connection to the US president’s territorial ambitions - maintains that it was merely taking a preliminary step towards exploration activities when it unloaded the gear in July in Nunap Qeqqa, also known as Jameson Land.
Greenland Energy did not respond to an AFP request for comment, but it told Danish media in July that it believed that authorisation to unload and store its equipment, which was located in another part of Greenland, was only required within the oil exploration licence area.
“It was a mistake on our part, a mistake that will not be repeated,” its managing director, Roderick McIllree, told Danish public broadcaster DR in late July.
The equipment is currently stored in a hangar at Nerlerit Inaat Airport, near the village of Ittoqqortoormiit, the closest settlement to the licence area.
The company has received a “strong warning” from the Greenland government, which in a statement in July added “that all future logistical arrangements must be notified to and approved by the mineral resources authority before they are carried out”.
Greenland Energy’s chairman, Larry Swets, has been described as being close to Trump.
And at a time when the US president still wishes to control the vast Arctic island, the prospect of a US energy company potentially carrying out exploration activities is making people uneasy.
“There is this vague sense of a connection to Trump,” Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told AFP.
‘Anxiety’
“This creates anxiety and tensions, all the more so because with Trump you can expect anything,” he added.
“With this unauthorised unloading of equipment, the company has really not improved its chances with the Greenland authorities,” said Anne Merrild, a professor at Aalborg University and Arctic specialist.
In 2021, the Greenlandic government, which manages the island’s natural resources, declared a moratorium on the exploration and extraction of oil across the Arctic territory, which has been profoundly disrupted by climate change.
But the exploration licences under which Greenland Energy operates were issued earlier, in 2015 and 2018, and therefore remain valid.
“One of the conditions for keeping the licence is to actively explore the area,” Pram Gad pointed out, while noting that “the company is under pressure”, as it is not active currently.
Activities are subject to specific permits, and Greenland Energy still hopes to obtain full approval to begin drilling soon in order to determine the quality of potential deposits.
There is a need to double down on preparations and equipment on land that is inherently hostile due to the harsh Arctic conditions.
“We continue to be encouraged by the progress being made toward the remaining approvals required for drilling,” Greenland Energy said in a letter to shareholders.
Greenland’s government is less optimistic.
“Given the current situation, I do not consider it realistic that the company can drill in the autumn,” Greenland Foreign Minister Mute Egede, who is responsible for natural resources, told the territory’s broadcaster, KNR.
Global tensions
The environmental and social impact studies required to approve the project have not yet been submitted, the Greenland government has noted.
“The few inhabitants of the region depend on the surrounding nature: they are hunters, fishers,” Merrild explained.
“Drilling causes a lot of disturbance, and increased human activity would have an impact on wildlife.”
In Ittoqqortoormiit, more than a hundred people – out of the 325 inhabitants of the village – demonstrated in mid-July against the project, according to KNR.
The geological survey of Denmark and Greenland (GEUS) estimates that the region could contain the equivalent of 2.35 billion barrels of oil, a considerable volume for a single oil project, but limited when compared with reserves around the globe.
“In the company’s logic, given current geopolitical tensions, the project sends a signal; it’s a way of saying ‘we have access to resources elsewhere’,” Merrild stressed. AFP

New Security Operation “VILKATIS” Began in Latvia’s Eastern Border Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:09:38 UTC
04:09:38 KST

Following the initiative of Prime Minister of Latvia Andris Kulbergs and an assessment of the situation by the defence and interior ministries, a decision has been made to launch Operation “VILKATIS” to ensure the security of Latvia’s eastern border. The operation is coordinated by the Crisis Management Centre of the State Chancellery, while its implementation primarily involves agencies under the Ministry of the Interior (the State Border Guard and the State Police) and the National Armed Forces.
The Ministry of Defence will ensure the continued involvement of the National Armed Forces in support of the State Border Guard by increasing personnel and material resources, including the use of new technologies such as unmanned aerial vehicles (drones), helicopters, and aircraft.
The State Border Guard, State Police, Military Intelligence and Security Service, State Security Service, and National Armed Forces will ensure the exchange of operational information regarding attempts at illegal border crossings and the persons involved, including possible involvement in organizing illegal migration.
As part of the operation, modern technologies will be used more intensively for the detection and detention of illegal migrants, as well as for the protection of Latvia’s entire eastern border. Unmanned aerial systems will be deployed more extensively in border areas to improve the early detection of illegal migrants and facilitate their detention if the border has been crossed unlawfully.
To address more effectively hybrid threats against Latvia and strengthen border-control capabilities, on 11 August 2026 the Cabinet of Ministers will decide on the establishment of a special working group with specific tasks. This will enhance the effectiveness of measures to prevent border violations and ensure coordinated and harmonized action with Lithuania, Estonia, Poland, and other countries in the region.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs will ensure cooperation and coordination with Lithuania, Estonia, and Poland regarding the prevention of illegal border crossings and secondary migration flows at the diplomatic level.
The Ministry of Justice will assess whether the sanctions provided for in the Criminal Law for organizing illegal border crossings, facilitating unlawful residence in Latvia, and fraudulently facilitating the acquisition of legal residence rights are sufficient.
Illegal migration is an instrument of hybrid warfare and a deliberate provocation against Latvia as one of the states forming the external border of the European Union and NATO. The instrumentalization of migration by Russia and Belarus as a form of hybrid threat has led to a disproportionately high and growing number of illegal border-crossing incidents. Limiting illegal migration is a shared responsibility of all relevant institutions.
A special border-security regime has been declared until 31 December 2026 in Ludza Municipality, Krāslava Municipality, Augšdaugava Municipality, the state city of Daugavpils, and Kaunata Parish in Rēzekne Municipality.

Coalition pushes VIP gambling crackdown in talks with Labor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:00:53 UTC
04:00:53 KST

Limited gambling changes on the table in Coalition, Labor talks
In short:
Labor and the Coalition have held a second round of "constructive" talks on the federal government's proposal to restrict gambling advertising, making a major party deal likely.
Negotiations have focused on VIP inducements, protections for self-excluded gamblers and online advertising rules, while there are also calls for an independent review.
What's next?
The federal government is hoping to get its gambling legislation through the Senate in the next fortnight, meaning the Coalition party room would have to sign off on a final deal within days.
The Coalition is seeking a targeted crackdown on VIP gambling inducements offered to high rollers and a simplified option to curb ads on streaming services amid ongoing "constructive" gambling bill talks with the federal government.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met early Tuesday evening for a second time in as many days to hash out details of an expected agreement to amend Labor’s proposed gambling ad restrictions.
Major changes such as an "opt-in" system for online advertising or a total ban on so-called gambling inducements are not on the table from either side, with Mr Albanese having previously indicated he would not entertain a wholesale rewrite of the draft legislation.
Instead, the asks put forward by Mr Taylor and Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson have focused on stronger protections for children and vulnerable people from exposure to advertising or predatory industry tactics.
With a modest deal seeming increasingly likely, gambling harm reduction advocates within the Coalition are calling for the bill to include an automatic independent review of the measures in the future.
It is hoped this would eventually expose what they believe are flaws in the legislation and create the case for further changes in the next term of government.
Labor is seeking to pass the legislation through the Senate by the end of the fortnight, which Mr Taylor is understood to be open to though is not in a rush this week as he has committed to take a final proposal back to the full Coalition party room for sign off.
Coalition asks for focus on high-end inducements
Rather than a broader crackdown on so-called gambling inducements, such as bonus bet offers, the Coalition has instead asked Labor for amendments focused on vulnerable and high-spending gamblers.
This included creating some type of cooling period preventing gambling companies from sending any inducements to Australians immediately after they remove themselves from the government’s self-exclusion register Betstop.
Loading...
The Opposition has also suggested targeting VIP offers extended to high rollers, such as access to exclusive events, game day tickets or large bonus-bet offers.
More common inducements pushed out to the average customer, such as deposit or bonus bet deals in the $25 range, are not the focus of the Coalition’s negotiations with Labor.
This is in part due to a view that the Liberals and Nationals must remain the parties of "personal responsibility" where individuals are expected to make their own decisions.
Coalition wants to give streamers option to comply with TV ad laws
The Coalition has also proposed a workaround for concerns among what has been dubbed a "triple lock" requiring all online platforms to restrict gambling ads to logged-in users who are aged over 18, while also giving every adult user a simple way to "opt out".
Harm advocates are unhappy with this proposal, because if a streaming service, social media or other online platform has a triple lock in place, they can show as many gambling ads as they want to over-aged, logged in viewers who have not opted out.
Streamers have also expressed concerns about the complexity of the proposed system.
The Coalition has therefore suggested streamers be given the option of either enforcing a triple lock or adopting the far more restrictive advertising rules for TV.
Under the bill, gambling ads are limited to three per hour between 6am and 8:30pm and banned during live sport broadcasts within those hours.
Liberal MP Simon Kennedy used a speech in parliament on Tuesday to attack the "two glaring problems" with Labor’s bill, which he said "did nothing" on inducements and allowed “unlimited advertising online” for adults who had not opted out.
"There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more," he said.
Inducements up for negotiation in ‘unusual’ leader talks
Coalition sources acknowledged it was "unusual" for Mr Taylor and Mr Albanese to meet twice to discuss legislative issues, attributing it to the prime minister's interest in being involved in negotiations.
Both leaders were on annual leave last week when a two-day Senate inquiry heard shocking evidence about the efforts VIP account managers at gambling companies went to strengthen relationships with high-rolling clients.
Allegations of offers to provide access to illicit drugs dominated media coverage of the hearings, but advocates also warned of harmful legal examples of so-called gambling inducements.
This included things like big spending gamblers being offered travel, accommodation and access to exclusive events linked to race days or football games.
Advocates also warned about the targeting of gamblers with inducements such as bonus bets, which the wagering sector described as “promotions”.
Last month Labor members unanimously voted to adopt a pledge to tackle these inducements into the party's 2026 national policy platform.
More than three years ago the You Win Some, You Lose More report into online wagering harms, which was authored by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, recommended a total ban on all inducements.
Multiple Labor backbench MPs have gone public with their push for the party to address inducements since the government’s draft bill did not deal with the issue.
MP Alicia Payne said today she looked forward to seeing changes.
"I understand that there are negotiations on amendments that are happening at the moment and look forward to what that will deliver," Ms Payne said.
Industry expects 'unscrupulous' VIP account manager crackdown
Sources in the wagering industry said one of the issues discussed between the Coalition and Labor was a crackdown on the "payment" of VIP account managers offering gambling promotions.
At the Senate hearing last week, ACT independent Senator David Pocock was visibly shocked by evidence account managers at some wagering companies were paid on commission based on customers’ losses.
A wagering source said they believed Labor's bill could be amended to stop "unscrupulous" account managers being paid in this way.
This would not impact every company however, as the ABC reported last year that Sportsbet and Tabcorp no longer pay commissions to VIP account managers.
Any deal between Mr Taylor and Mr Albanese would still have to be signed off by the Coalition party room, which meets weekly when parliament is sitting.
Five backbenchers using the regular meeting on Tuesday to push for tougher reforms, while four cautioned against over-regulation.
Greens communications spokeswoman Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said Labor always intended to make a deal with the Coalition on the gambling reforms, to get away with doing the "bare minimum" on the issue.
Loading
Senator Hanson-Young said she met yesterday with Communications Minister Anika Wells, who indicated the government was willing to amend the bill to limit inducements.
"Last week, we were told the government wouldn't move at all and now they're saying they're prepared to move. The question is how far?" she said.
"The government has always intended to put this piece of legislation through with the opposition because they want to do the bare minimum.
"I have no faith that Angus Taylor is up to the job of negotiating the best outcome for people here."
