Police in Spain bust network accused of trafficking migrant girls
- Spanish police dismantled a criminal network recruiting unaccompanied migrant girls from Gran Canaria and moving them to mainland Spain and France for sexual exploitation.
- The network used false identity and travel documents to exploit vulnerable girls and arranged their journeys, aiming to transfer them off the islands.
- Five people were arrested, two victims rescued, and concerns remain over the safety of many unaccompanied minors stranded in Ceuta after a mass border crossing from Morocco.
AI generated
MADRID - Spanish police said on Aug 11 they had dismantled a criminal ring accused of recruiting unaccompanied migrant girls from care centres on Gran Canaria, in Spain’s Canary Islands, and moving them to mainland Spain and France, where some were sexually exploited.
The operation comes as migration debates have returned to the forefront across Europe after a mass border crossing from Morocco into Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta in July left hundreds of unaccompanied minors stranded in the city.
The Guardia Civil said the investigation began after a migrant girl who had been under the care of authorities in Gran Canaria returned to Spain from France and told investigators she had been recruited with the promise of a job.
Investigators subsequently identified several similar cases involving girls who left care centres without their personal documents and were later linked to flights to mainland Spain, the Guardia Civil said in a statement.
The network allegedly exploited the girls’ vulnerability, offering to help them leave the Canary Islands while providing false identity or travel documents and arranging their journeys by air and land.
“All with the aim of facilitating their departure from the islands and subsequently transferring them to mainland Spain and France, where some of them are alleged to have been subjected to sexual exploitation,” the statement said.
The Guardia Civil said it rescued two victims and prevented four other minors from leaving the islands.
Five people were arrested, including one minor, following five searches across Gran Canaria.
Some 72,000 migrants breached Ceuta’s border in an unprecedented and deadly rush on July 30-31, with 70,000 having since returned to Morocco, according to Spanish government figures.
Spain’s Youth and Children Minister Sira Rego said Friday that 1,342 unaccompanied migrant minors had been registered in Ceuta following the mass influx from Morocco.
Aid groups have warned that the minors, many of whom are sleeping rough on the streets of Ceuta, are at risk of abuse and exploitation. AFP

Trump says NYC pied-à-terre tax 'must be stopped,' eyes federal block

President Donald Trump on Tuesday decried New York City's pied-à-terre tax and said he is exploring whether the federal government "has any legal right to avert this disaster, before it is too late."
The tax on nonprimary residences of wealthy owners "doesn't work in America, and must be stopped, NOW!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump's vow to seek federal intervention against the tax, which was pushed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and passed by the New York State legislature in late May, came one day after a Staten Island judge temporarily blocked the new policy.
New York City government quickly filed a motion to seek an appeal of that order, placing the judge's order on hold.
Mamdani's office did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Trump's threat to challenge the pied-à-terre tax. Asked about the ongoing lawsuit, the mayor's office referred CNBC to Mamdani's assurance at a Monday press conference that "we look forward to vigorously defend our city's position in court."
"We are confident in our position," Mamdani said. "And that is a confidence coming from both the legality of the City's actions as well as the importance of a surcharge on secondary homes worth more than $5 million, a surcharge that will help fund safer streets, that will help fund stronger schools, and it will help fund the city that New Yorkers deserve."
Trump, in his Tuesday morning post, called the tax a "dangerous political 'experiment' in New York will destroy what was once a great City and State."
Trump added that it's hard for him as president "to sit back and watch it happen, especially to a place I once loved."
Trump is a native New Yorker who lived in a penthouse in Manhattan's Trump Tower, but moved his primary residence to his Mar-a-Lago golf club in Florida in 2019. It is unclear whether Trump or his immediate family would be subject to the NYC tax.
Trump also asserted that the levy on second homes is spurring thousands of people to flee to more tax-friendly regions, canceling out any revenue that the policy might bring in.
The claim echoes other warnings that have followed the election of Mamdani, a democratic socialist who has vowed to make the city's richest pay more.
Citadel CEO Ken Griffin, for instance, threatened to move his business to Miami after Mamdani unveiled the pied-à-terre tax in a video that featured Griffin's ultraluxury Manhattan penthouse.
Griffin also suggested Citadel was reconsidering moving ahead with a pricey redevelopment of a Park Avenue building. Vornado CEO Steven Roth, however, said in a recent earnings call that Griffin was not abandoning his plans for the NYC building.
Some have shrugged off concerns that hiking taxes on the wealthy in New York, which already has among the nation's highest income tax rates, will push people out of the state. While some studies show New York's share of millionaires has declined in recent years, others dispute the idea that the rich flee high state taxes.
The pied-à-terre tax backed by Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul would raise taxes on second properties valued at $1 million or more, with more valuable residences facing higher rates.
Mamdani, who announced the policy on Tax Day, said it is expected to raise $500 million in revenue, though NYC Comptroller Mark Levine said weeks later that that estimate could fall to between $340 million and $380 million.
Last week, three NYC residents filed a lawsuit in New York Supreme Court challenging the city's distribution of a list showing the names, addresses and property values of hundreds of thousands of NYC homeowners. The suit also targets written notices the city mailed, informing 17,000 people on that list that they may be subject to the new tax.
The suit alleges that those actions "arbitrarily and capriciously foisted onto New York City residents the burden of proving they are not subject" to the tax, instead of the city first determining which properties are included.
On Monday, Judge Wayne Ozzi temporarily blocked the city from "taking any further action" in connection with the list or the mailed notices.
Hours later, an attorney for Mamdani said in a court filing that the city intends to file a motion for permission to appeal the ruling.
Doing so triggers an "automatic stay" of all proceedings to enforce Ozzi's order for the time being, the lawyer wrote.

Romania destroys drones drifting near major offshore gas project in the Black Sea
BUCHAREST, Aug 11 - Romanian army divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones drifting in the country's Black Sea exclusive economic zone near the offshore gas project Neptun Deep, Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Tuesday.
The NATO state shares a 614-km (382-mile) land border with Ukraine and has seen Russian drones repeatedly breach its airspace over the last four years, as well as mines floating in the Black Sea across key trade and energy routes.
In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace over three consecutive days after dozens of such incursions in the more than four years of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
On Tuesday, a civilian vessel working near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project spotted the drones, Miruta said. The minister did not specify the origin of the drones, but said Ukraine had confirmed they did not belong to its forces.
"For the safety of the shipping lane and the works being carried out around the platform, the decision was made to carry out a controlled destruction by detonation," Miruta said.
"The defence ministry contacted Ukrainian partners, who confirmed that the systems do not belong to them."
NATO states Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey, which share the Black Sea with Georgia, Russia and Ukraine, have neutralised more than 150 mines drifting across crucial trade lanes.
In July, the three states agreed to expand a joint task force that clears mines floating in the Black Sea to include missions to protect critical infrastructure.
All three countries have gas exploration or production projects in the Black Sea. Romania's Neptun Deep, jointly owned by OMV Petrom and state gas producer Romgaz, is due to come onstream in 2027 and make Romania the European Union's largest gas producer. REUTERS

Democrats clash again in Minnesota and Wisconsin primaries as big midterm races take shape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:05:12 UTC
03:05:12 KST

Progressives and moderates will face off again in Tuesday's Democratic primary elections in Wisconsin and Minnesota as the party decides whether to lurch further to the left or chart toward the middle after crushing losses to Republicans in 2024.
Populist progressives in recent months have capitalized on economic anger to defeat establishment Democratic candidates across the country, setting off a potentially seismic political shift within the party. Last week in Michigan, progressive former health official Abdul El-Sayed defeated the more moderate Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens in a primary to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich. — the latest stunning upset for longtime party power brokers who backed Stevens.
The progressive swell will be tested again on Tuesday as candidates in the mold of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., vie for gubernatorial and Senate nominations in Wisconsin and Minnesota against establishment-backed moderates.
Wisconsin
In Wisconsin, Francesca Hong is running to be the state's next governor and is the clear polling favorite heading into Election Day. Hong, who leads the field by double digits in recent polls, is endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America's Milwaukee chapter and is a staunch progressive. Some prominent Democrats such as Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., have endorsed Hong.
Some of Hong's past comments, including calling for the cancellation of Thanksgiving and abolishing the police, have garnered scrutiny in recent days. Hong has since distanced herself from both statements.
She is facing a field that includes the more moderate Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who is endorsed by retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Crowley had previously dropped out of the race, but reentered and scored Evers' endorsements as some Democrats fear Hong is too progressive to win the general election in the purple state.
Hong's platform includes offering universal childcare, creating publicly owned grocery stores, establishing a public option healthcare plan and launching a public bank. She has also called for raising taxes on the wealthy in Wisconsin to pay for more services.
The winner of the Democratic contest will likely face Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., in the general election. Tiffany, who has served in the House since 2020, represents northern Wisconsin. He is a member of the ultra-conservative House Freedom Caucus.
Tiffany is proposing freezing property taxes, rolling back other tax increases and increasing energy production.
Republicans have seized on the surge of progressives in the Democratic Party, branding the party's left flank as "communists." None of the high-profile Democrats in key primaries this year support communist policies.
Minnesota
In Minnesota, progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and moderate Democratic Rep. Angie Craig are in a tight race for the nomination to succeed the retiring Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn.
Flanagan, who is the No. 2 official in the state behind retiring Gov. Tim Walz, is running a progressive campaign and has been endorsed by Smith and top lawmakers on the left such as Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. She has also nabbed the endorsement of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party — the official state Democratic Party — but unlike Hong, is not backed by the Twin Cities DSA chapter.
She's pushing for a universal healthcare plan known as Medicare for All, wants to dismantle Immigration and Customs Enforcement and seeks to halt offensive weapons sales to Israel.
Support for Israel has become a flashpoint for Democrats in primary contests as many on the left recoil from the Jewish state's conduct during the war in Gaza that was launched in response to Hamas' attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Flanagan has called Israel's actions a "genocide."
Flanagan, however, has caught some flak for her proximity to Walz and the cascading social services fraud scandal that prompted the 2024 vice presidential candidate to abandon his reelection bid. Flanagan has expressed regret that the administration did not act faster, but has defended the governor's response and subsequent crackdown on fraud.
President Donald Trump and his Republican allies earlier this year seized on the fraud claims, some of which are years old, to launch an immigration crackdown and pause some Medicaid funding in Minnesota.
Craig, in a debate with Flanagan, said "Republicans are going to have a field day with you" over her connection to the fraud scandal.
Craig, meanwhile, is a moderate who flipped a Republican-held seat in 2018. She leapfrogged to the top minority slot on the House Agriculture Committee in this Congress, defeating several more senior candidates to secure the spot.
She contends that her ability to win a purple district makes her the best candidate against a Republican in what's expected to be a tight election. Craig has scored endorsements from House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.
While Craig does not support Medicare for All, she has introduced a bill to create a government-run healthcare plan known as a public option or Medicare for all who want it. Craig also supports the traditional U.S.-Israel relationship, voting against an amendment last month that sought to strip U.S. aid to Israel while expressing her dissatisfaction with current Israeli leadership.
Craig has been criticized, however, for being the only Minnesota Democrat to vote for the Laken Riley Act. That bill required ICE to detain undocumented immigrants who are arrested or face charges or who have been convicted of burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer or any crime that results in death or serious bodily injury.
Immigration enforcement is a key issue in Minnesota after federal agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens in the state during the immigration crackdown earlier this year.
Craig has since backtracked on her support of that bill, saying she regrets it in an op-ed in the Minnesota Star Tribune and calling it "the wrong decision" in a debate with Flanagan last month.
Flanagan has pounced on Craig for the vote.
"Voting three days into the second Trump administration for Donald Trump's immigration bill that allowed him to terrorize our communities, the loss of life, the economic impact, the trauma, it's horrific," Flanagan said of Craig's vote during the debate.
Tuesday's Democratic winner is expected to face Republican Michele Tafoya in the general election. Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster, is leading by a wide margin in public polls.
Minnesota will also host a governor's primary on Tuesday, which will likely determine who Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., will face in the general election. The Republican field includes MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell and Minnesota House member Lisa Demuth.

“Faster than originally planned”: Russia wants 292 Starlink-rival satellites by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:04:47 UTC
03:04:47 KST

Russia is deploying Rassvet satellites, its answer to Starlink, faster than originally planned, Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Chief of Ukraine's Defense Intelligence (GUR), told RBC-Ukraine.
Moscow aims to expand the network to 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and 924 by 2035, he said. Existing satellites can already provide intermittent connections as they pass over Ukraine.
Rassvet could give Moscow an independent alternative to Starlink, which Ukrainian forces rely on for battlefield communications and drone operations. Russian forces also used unauthorized Starlink terminals until Ukraine and SpaceX blocked access. Rassvet’s coverage remains intermittent but could eventually support strike drones, prompting Kyiv to consider countermeasures.
Why Russia wants its own Starlink
Ukrainian forces rely heavily on Starlink for frontline communications, drone operations, and command and control.
Russian forces also relied heavily on unverified terminals until Ukraine and SpaceX blocked them on 5 February. The shutdown disrupted Russian communications and assaults across multiple parts of the front. On 10 August 2026, the SBU said it had dismantled two schemes that registered terminals in Ukraine for transfer to Russian forces.
Rassvet could reduce Russia’s dependence on SpaceX and illicit supply networks. Ukrainian experts have warned that a mature network could also relay data to Russian strike drones.
32 satellites up, 260 to go by 2027
Bureau 1440, the Russian satellite developer behind Rassvet, began testing the network with three satellites in 2023. Three larger prototypes followed in 2024 to test upgraded equipment, including satellite-based 5G technology and laser links between spacecraft.
Russia launched its first batch of 16 serial Rassvet satellites on 23 March 2026 after manufacturing problems delayed the mission. A second group of 16 followed in July, Militarnyi reported.
In May 2026, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to the President of Ukraine, said each Rassvet satellite then in orbit passed over Ukraine roughly once daily, providing six to 10 minutes of connectivity. He estimated that continuous coverage would require 200–250 satellites.

The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:04:47 UTC
03:04:47 KST

The wildfire that began on protected heathland in the New Forest in Hampshire on Sunday was reported to be under control on Tuesday. But with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or higher in parts of England on Thursday, the risk of further outbreaks remains high. Firefighters responded to 185 wildfires in the first 10 days of August. In coastal Suffolk, conservationists and locals are counting the cost of the blaze that devastated Dunwich Heath. Its vegetation and rare bird populations are expected to take decades to recover.
Although the immediate cause of many wildfires is litter, the risks are elevated by heat and drought, and repeated warnings from climate scientists do not necessarily lessen the shock and distress caused. As people and governments across Europe assess this summer’s damage, experts including the UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, hope that the fires will focus minds on the urgent necessity of cutting emissions – as well as investing in emergency planning. Europe is currently heating up faster than any other continent, due in part to proximity to the melting Arctic.
The global, existential nature of the climate crisis makes it an awkward fit with Andy Burnham’s current focus on “everyday fixes”. But if he does not find more to say about the summer’s disasters, he is in danger of being left behind. The National Trust has already surpassed its £500,000 fundraising target to restore Dunwich Heath. Conservationists and farmers are publicly debating the best ways to prevent fires. The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) is pushing for 5,000 additional firefighters across the UK, along with new equipment.
In March, the then fire safety minister, Samantha Dixon, said that the fire and rescue service had suffered from “decades of drift and inertia”. Her speech also confirmed that a new College of Fire and Rescue would oversee professional standards, as recommended by the Grenfell inquiry. But three weeks ago Ms Dixon was sacked. If the government wants to avoid an impression that drift and inertia are ongoing, they need to provide an update, along with a response to repeated calls from the fire service inspectorate for new enforcement powers. MPs on the home affairs committee threw their weight behind this idea two years ago.
The fire and rescue service is popular with the public. Even highly critical sections of the Grenfell inquiry report did not significantly undermine confidence in it. This summer’s events seem likely to reaffirm this positive regard, and rightly so: public servants who do dangerous, difficult jobs, when many other people are on holiday, deserve to be appreciated. But scrutiny of the service is also important. An inquiry by the home affairs select committee, which was summarised in a letter to the home secretary in 2024, contained strong criticism of its culture and leadership.
Such concerns deserve a fuller response than they have so far received from ministers. So do the FBU’s call for investment to cope with rising risks, and proposals for a temporary ban on disposable barbecues. Ill-informed and ideological attempts to blame rewilding should also be addressed by ministers. Working groups on how to reduce wildfire risks must produce plans. The latest report from the government’s Climate Change Committee found that existing adaptation plans are not fit for purpose. This summer’s extraordinary heat, drought and wildfires should be a spur to action on both the fire service and the wider climate crisis.

Russia’s Central Bank approves Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT for exchange trading — with limits for retail investors
Russia’s Central Bank has added Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether (USDT) to its list of cryptocurrencies approved for trading on exchanges, the regulator said in a statement.
Nonqualified investors will have access only to the most liquid cryptocurrencies, with an annual cap of 300,000 rubles’ worth of those assets per intermediary — a broker, a crypto exchanger, or an asset manager.
Qualified investors, by contrast, will be able to buy any cryptocurrency traded on the exchanges without restriction.
Before making a trade, all investors must pass a test and review the risks of crypto investing.
In July, the State Duma passed a law legalizing the circulation of cryptocurrency in Russia. It set rules for using cryptocurrencies and capped the size of nonqualified investors’ portfolios. At the time, the Central Bank clarified that only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and the stablecoin USDT met the criteria for exchange trading.

The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:04:02 UTC
03:04:02 KST

As the huge societal ramifications of artificial intelligence have become clear, some of the tech industry’s most senior figures have taken to writing thinkpieces on what comes next. The latest to do so is Mark Zuckerberg, who this week published 6,500 words making the case for a laissez-faire approach to AI development. Worrying too much about regulation, Meta’s CEO unsurprisingly opines, could lead to the United States falling behind in the race to own the future.
Mr Zuckerberg’s plea for maximum autonomy is, of course, self-serving. Much of his essay – which airily envisions “invention superpowers” for every entrepreneur and “an abundance of jobs in the future” – reads like unadulterated tech-utopianism. But the lobbying at least has the merit of being out there in the open. As midterm elections loom in the US, darker arts are also being used to counter popular concern about what AI will mean for a host of topics, from the labour market to child safety, the environment and cybersecurity.
Replicating a strategy deployed by cryptocurrency backers in the 2024 election cycle, Silicon Valley is pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Super Pacs – groups unaffiliated to political parties or campaigns – to ensure that voices sympathetic to its deregulatory AI agenda get elected. OpenAI’s co-founder and president, Greg Brockman, and Palantir’s co-founder, Jo Lonsdale, have given large sums to Leading the Future, an organisation dedicated to “identifying, maintaining, and growing pro-AI candidates”. Vast amounts are being spent to try to tilt the balance in individual contests, sometimes through disingenuous means.
Earlier this summer, Leading the Future spent $6m on ads attacking Alex Bores, a New York state assemblyman and pioneer of AI regulation at state level. Rather than focus on his AI campaigning, the ads attacked Mr Bores’s progressive credentials, alleging that he had carried out tech work in the past for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which he denies. Running for Congress in a Democratic stronghold, he lost a tight primary race after battling what was in essence a smear campaign.
Countervailing forces are emerging. Guardrails Alliance, a union-backed Super Pac, is attempting to combat Leading the Future’s influence, while a bipartisan groundswell of opposition to datacentres is generating serious electoral clout. But as tech companies and their billionaire owners seek to shape and above all limit the scope of AI regulation, their influence is distorting debate in a political culture where the power of money already holds far too much sway.
In his essay, Mr Zuckerberg urges that AI’s democratising potential be protected from those who believe “a small set of experts … should decide what is best for humanity”. He appears to miss the irony that an unelected tech oligarchy, to which he belongs, is already performing that function by default. Its pressure has been instrumental in persuading Donald Trump to cancel the signing of an executive order which would have given the government the right to review new AI models. Its wealth is now being used to attack and undermine dissenting voices in the public square.
If a democratic debate about the benefits and dangers of AI is to take place, such presumption must be fiercely resisted in the US and elsewhere. The semi-covert manipulation of political discussion is no way to map out an inclusive future in challenging times.

MINSK, 11 August (BelTA) – Uzbekistan’s Samarkand Region intends to increase purchases of Belarusian beef and other meat products, the press service of the Belarusian Ministry of Agriculture and Food told BelTA.
Belarusian First Deputy Agriculture and Food Minister Vitaly Kulak met with a delegation from Samarkand Region led by its Hokim (Governor) Adiz Boboyev. The parties discussed the current state and prospects for bilateral trade and economic cooperation in the agricultural and industrial sector. 
“An analysis of the structure of Belarusian exports to Uzbekistan in 2026 shows that meat and meat products account for 63.8% of total supplies. There has been steady growth in almost all categories: meat products increased by 18.6%, dairy products doubled, while sugar and chocolate supplies rose fivefold and live animal supplies more than doubled. Imports from Uzbekistan have also shown positive dynamics: fruit and berries grew by 12.3%, vegetables and melons by 2.9%, and water and alcoholic beverages by 5.2%,” the ministry said. 
Vitaly Kulak reaffirmed Belarus’ readiness to ensure stable supplies to the Uzbek market of poultry, beef, butter, skimmed and whole milk powder, baby food, and sugar, as well as to continue work on setting up Belarusian agricultural enterprises in Uzbekistan. Adiz Boboyev positively assessed the dynamics of mutual trade and expressed his intention to discuss current issues and draw up a clear roadmap for future cooperation. 
The delegation from Samarkand Region, one of Uzbekistan’s largest agricultural regions, expressed interest in developing breeding livestock farming and proposed arranging annual supplies of Belarusian pedigree cattle, as well as increasing purchases of Belarusian beef and other meat products.
 
 
The Uzbek side expressed interest in investment cooperation with Belarusian businesses. It reaffirmed its readiness to create all necessary conditions for implementing joint projects and provide comprehensive support to Belarusian partners.

Brazil’s Supreme Court to weigh cases that could weaken Amazon protections
Brazil’s Supreme Court is set to hear several cases that could reshape protections for the Amazon rainforest, after a mostly conservative Congress overrode several of leftist Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s environmental vetoes.
The court will take up the cases on Wednesday, as lawmakers and environmental groups remain divided over how Brazil should balance economic development with environmental protections.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Under Lula, Amazon deforestation falls to lowest level in a decade
- list 2 of 3US to impose new 25 percent tariffs on some Brazilian imports
- list 3 of 3Brazil’s Lula launches fourth-term bid, focuses on national sovereignty
Deforestation in the Amazon has fallen to its lowest level in a decade during the first half of 2026. The cases put some of Brazil’s most consequential environmental fights before the country’s top court.
Indigenous land rights
On Friday, Brazil’s Supreme Court began reviewing final motions seeking clarification of a 2025 ruling that rejected the “time limit” thesis. The legal theory, backed by Brazil’s agribusiness lobby, restricts Indigenous land claims to territories occupied or under legal dispute when Brazil’s 1988 Constitution took effect.
The agribusiness caucus argues that a cutoff date would provide legal certainty for landowners. Indigenous groups say it ignores decades of forced displacement and violence that pushed communities from their ancestral lands. Indigenous communities across the Amazon, including the isolated and uncontacted Kawahiva people, could be affected by the ruling.
The justices are considering motions that seek clarification of the court’s ruling, addressing questions about compensation and possible deadlines for completing Indigenous land demarcations.
The soya farming moratorium
On Wednesday, the court will consider a legal fight over the future of Brazil’s soya moratorium, an agreement that barred major traders from buying soya grown on land deforested in the Amazon after 2008.
The agreement has been credited with helping curb deforestation, even as Brazil became an agricultural powerhouse. But states that are major soya producers passed laws in January revoking tax incentives for participating companies, prompting the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oil Industries (ABIOVE) to withdraw from the moratorium.
Brazil is the world’s largest producer and leading exporter of soya beans. The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change has defended the soya moratorium, saying it helped reduce Amazon deforestation even as Brazil expanded production.
Environmental licensing
The court will also consider on Wednesday a challenge to a new environmental licensing law that took effect in February.
The law fast-tracks approval for projects including mines, highways and industrial plants, prompting environmental groups to warn that it could weaken safeguards in one of the world’s most important ecosystems.
Suely Araujo of the Climate Observatory said the law is already having tangible consequences in the Amazon, citing the paving of a controversial highway and plans to dredge the Tapajos River without adequate prior environmental review.

FSSAI tightens pan masala packaging norms; bans plastic, foil and synthetic laminates

FSSAI tightens pan masala packaging norms; bans plastic, foil and synthetic laminates
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 11, 2026, 23:29 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Pan masala may now only be packaged in paper, paperboard, cellulose, or other naturally derived materials (Photo: Agencies).
NEW DELHI: India's food safety regulator has barred the use of plastic and plastic-laminated packaging for pan masala, under an amendment aimed at tightening existing packaging norms, according to a press release.The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has specified that pan masala may now only be packaged in paper, paperboard, cellulose, or other naturally derived materials. Such materials must be entirely free of plastic, including polyethene, polypropylene, polyester, polyvinyl chloride (PVC), and other synthetic polymers, copolymers or laminates, as well as aluminium foil or metallised layers, the release said. Tin and glass containers continue to be permitted, it added.The press release further stated that packaging will also need to conform to clauses (f) and (i) of sub-rule 1 of rule 4 of the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, framed under the Environment Protection Act, 1986.The amendment has been incorporated as a new entry in Schedule IV of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018, which lists suggested packaging materials. It has been placed right after the existing entries at Serial Number 10, the release said.
Notified as the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Amendment Regulations, 2026, the amendment will come into force from the date of its publication in the Official Gazette, according to the release.The regulations were issued by FSSAI in exercise of powers conferred under clause (k) of sub-section (2) of Section 92 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and with prior approval of the Central Government, the release said.

The Promise We Made to Americans with Disabilities Is Under Attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:58:28 UTC
02:58:28 KST

In the past, Americans with disabilities were sent off to large, isolating, state-run institutions as a matter of course. In overcrowded, understaffed facilities, residents were too often neglected and stripped of privacy, autonomy, or any meaningful connection to their communities. When these conditions were brought to light, they sparked national outrage. That reckoning helped galvanize the deinstitutionalization movement, a decades-long push to create services that support people with disabilities in their homes and communities.
Decades of advocacy to “deinstitutionalize” have fortunately transformed quality of life for people with disabilities, but it wasn’t until just 27 years ago that the Supreme Court's 1999 decision in Olmstead v. Lois Curtis made it so disabled Americans could rest easy knowing forced segregation wasn’t inevitable.
For much of our history, few options existed between mass institutionalization in expensive and confining facilities on one end of the spectrum, and fully independent living absent any supports on the other end of the spectrum. The legal precedent rooted in Olmstead, plus the proliferation of once-nonexistent community-based services, changed that.
Now, however, the foundation that underpins our nation’s wide spectrum of community-based services is crumbling.
Olmstead affirmed that the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) grants people with disabilities the right to live, work, and participate in their communities with the supports they need. That’s why we found it especially egregious that the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) released a legal memo last month coinciding with the decision’s anniversary, calling into question the established right of people with disabilities to receive services in the most integrated setting possible. The memo doesn’t change the law, but it seeks to erode decades of settled civil rights protections.
The DOJ memo follows a range of other actions by the Trump Administration, including significant cuts to federal Medicaid spending set to go into effect next year and the withholding of hundreds of millions of dollars of funding for community-based services in the name of protecting program integrity. In July 2026, the administration paused more than one billion dollars in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, citing fraud but offering little specificity to support their claim. Taken together, these moves seem to falsely imply that home- and community-based services (HCBS) are wasteful, rather than essential.
The Trump Administration has repeatedly questioned the value of HCBS by suggesting that Medicaid is paying professionals to carry out responsibilities families should simply provide themselves. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy told lawmakers that the waivers pay family members “for picking up the groceries, for driving somebody to a doctor’s appointment,” insisting that these family members are “getting paid to do things that they used to do [...] for free.” Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz has echoed that message, describing personal care services as helping “Medicaid patients do something that our families would normally do for us, like carrying groceries.”
Statements such as these have real-world implications and could serve to justify gutting these HCBS services—potentially forcing people with disabilities back into large public institutions, while pushing family caregivers and direct support professionals out of their respective workforces and into poverty.
The debate over how we invest in Medicaid cannot be separated from the debate over civil rights for people with disabilities. Olmstead’s promise of community living is only meaningful if people have access to the services that make community living viable. For millions, Medicaid is a lifeline. It funds the direct support professional who helps someone get dressed each morning. It funds the job coach who helps build skills needed to succeed in the workforce. It funds transportation to medical appointments, support to navigate public transportation, and countless other activities that enable people to participate fully in community life.
These activities are neither optional nor negotiable—they’re the foundation of the inclusion that this country promised through the ADA.
The notion that families should provide care without additional support is unrealistic and shortsighted, especially for families of people with highly complex medical or behavioral needs. Direct support professionals are trained to implement individualized care plans with a person-centered approach, respond to behavioral crises, administer medications, and more.
Moreover, this thinking also ignores reality. For instance, many disabled adults’ parents are elderly or deceased. Many of their spouses work full time, sometimes in multiple jobs to meet their families’ financial needs. Many of their siblings are in the same boat but may live hundreds of miles away. Some have no family to fall back on at all.
Suggesting that people don’t have the right to community-based support while insisting families provide needed care for free risks undoing more than a quarter-century of civil rights progress made possible by Olmstead. Furthermore, dismantling the spectrum of community-based services is expected to have negative down-the-line ramifications. We anticipate that more families will languish on states’ waiting lists for longer, more providers will reduce services or go out of business altogether, more professionals will leave the workforce to fill caregiving gaps, and more people with disabilities will be left with no other choice but expensive, isolating institutions.
All of this threatens to devastate families and local economies. If protecting taxpayers is truly the goal, community-based services shouldn’t be slashed—they should be upheld as the gold standard, especially given the dramatic cost savings they make possible. Supporting someone with an intellectual or developmental disability through home- and community-based services costs about $70,500 per year, versus more than $395,000 annually in a public institution.
While the DOJ’s memo and the administration’s other actions don’t overturn Olmstead, they do place another crack in the fragile foundation on which community living for millions of Americans is built. As we wrote last summer on the 35th anniversary of the ADA, we must reaffirm, not reinterpret or undo, the rights Olmstead upheld.

Here Comes the Sun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:58:00 UTC
02:58:00 KST

The Atlanta Hotel was an ordinary place – a respectable setting for a meeting.
Col. Yevhen Konovalets had some doubts about the man he was meeting, but went anyway. His commitment to Ukraine outweighed concerns for personal safety. He would not turn away from any opportunity to help his embattled nation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
May 23, 1938 was a Monday – a bright spring day in Rotterdam. Just before lunch, Konovalets took a seat in the café at a table near a window overlooking the street. He was 46. He asked for a sherry. The younger man who joined him – 30 years old – ordered a beer. They spoke for only a few minutes. Before leaving, the visitor gave him a gift: a box of chocolates. Konovalets liked chocolate.
Within minutes, Konovalets lay dead – assassinated by an NKVD agent acting on Stalin’s orders. The bomb hidden in those bonbons was meant not only to kill a man, but to decapitate the Ukrainian nationalist movement. Yet the Soviets failed. Col. Konovalets’ name endured.
I first learned about him when I was a young boy. A large photograph of him adorned Kingston’s Ukrainian hall on Bagot Street, a place where our community gathered to remember its history and heroes. I spied that very same image again and again in Ukrainian cultural centers across North America and Western Europe. For most of my early years, I did not fully understand who he was or why he might be worthy of such honor.
Germany Grants Ukraine’s State Emergency Service Nearly €6M in Robotic Firefighting Package
For my parents, like many who devoted their lives to the cause of Ukrainian independence, Konovalets represented a generation who refused to accept that Ukraine’s struggle for independence was over. He believed Ukraine would one day be free. So did they. They were proven right.
Now, almost nine decades after his murder, I am sitting in the Atlanta Hotel café, a sherry to hand. Not far from here, Col. Konovalets’ remains were exhumed at Crooswijk Cemetery – the latest step in his long odyssey to Ukraine, where he will be laid to rest at a military burial ground outside Kyiv. I will not accompany him. I chose instead to remain here, where his life was ended.
As an honor guard accompanies him across Europe, a rare solar eclipse will be visible over much of the continent – the Moon passing partly across the face of the Sun, dimming its light without ever fully extinguishing it. It is a strange coincidence, mirroring the story of Ukraine itself. For more than a century, that nation’s flame has been dimmed time and again – through conquest, famine, terror, occupation, and war – yet it has never gone out. Millions endured decades when freedom seemed beyond reach, and remembering became an act of resistance.
Following the revolutionary years of 1917-21, after Ukrainian statehood was extinguished, many believed this cause forlorn. Its leaders were scattered across the diaspora – imprisoned, hunted, and often killed. But Konovalets refused to accept defeat. Through the Ukrainian Military Organization, and later as the first leader of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, he continued the struggle in exile.
Moscow feared what Konovalets represented. His assassination was part of a wider campaign to suppress Ukrainian resistance. He would not be the only prey. Even after the collapse of the USSR, efforts to silence Ukrainian leaders continued – including the poisoning of President Viktor Yushchenko in 2004. President Volodymyr Zelensky remains a target, as Russia wages a genocidal war against the Ukrainian nation.
The parallel between the colonel’s time and ours is difficult to ignore. That is why bringing him home matters. This is about more than comrades-in-arms honoring a fallen soldier. His return restores a connection across generations – between those who took up arms then and those who fight now, despite overwhelming odds, against those who would deny Ukraine its right to exist.
In Rotterdam, as I think of a brave leader torn away from Ukraine, and of an ideal that could not be liquidated, I also remember what his widow, Olha, said as she grieved by his grave:
“This is for Ukraine...”
Four simple words. They echoed for she foresaw how her husband’s tomb was only temporary – hallowed ground where he would wait until his people came to carry him back to the soil of a free Ukraine. That day has come.
Ukraine’s son has gone home. His limbo is over.
And that is for Ukraine.

Lockheed Martin also announced the establishment of a dedicated product center to support Strigo, a move that is intended to advance the new solution system’s concept-to-delivery model.
The Strigo Product Center, which was created less than two years before its announcement, houses operations for developing and producing new RF sensor and missile technologies, in addition to serving as a storefront for the system.
Lockheed Martin aims to turn 'what if' into 'what's next'

According to Lockheed Martin, the product center has already been used to support the innovation of defense technologies from the initial design stage, through testing, and to operational capability in a matter of months.
The product center’s rapid pace of development and the adaptable nature of the Strigo system are intended to help the US and its allies counter emerging threats and maintain an advantage on the battlefield.
Lockheed Martin noted that technologies developed at the Strigo Product Center informed aspects of the development of the Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) Increment 2 seeker package.
Lockheed Martin stated that thus far, it has committed $250 million to the Strigo Product Center to fund innovation and development.

During the interview, the discussion turned toward the October 7 massacre and the subsequent demonstrations showing solidarity with the Hamas-led attack in New York.
Remnick asked Romer whether she would have participated in the protest held in Times Square, noting that it took place just one day after the attacks, and asked her directly: “One day after the slaughter of 1,200 people and the taking of over 200 hostages, you would have come and rallied behind Hamas?” Romer responded by saying that she “probably would have” attended the demonstration.
Romer defended her perspective by adding, “I think that October 7 was largely inevitable. When Remnick pushed back by noting, “Well, sure it is, you said you’re supporting it,” Romer replied, “I’m saying that I think it was inevitable. I think that you cannot put people in a cage and expect them not to revolt.”

We’ve seen this far too often.”
The organization emphasized that Romer’s refusal to denounce Hamas meant shielding a US-designated foreign terrorist organization responsible for the deadliest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, whose charter explicitly calls for the destruction of Israel, noting that she had previously urged followers to “read on,” to learn “why we do not, in fact, condemn Hamas.”
Continuing its breakdown of the interview, the ADL added, “She also called the Hamas-led October 7 massacre a mere ‘revolt’ and ‘largely inevitable.’ There is no justification for rape, kidnapping, torture, and slaughter.”
Addressing Romer’s remarks on LGBT rights and regional policy, the ADL pushed back against her attempt to contextualize the terror group’s record, stating: “Let’s be very clear: Hamas does not persecute LGBTQ+ people because of a conflict. It does so because persecution of LGBTQ+ people is a core part of its ideology, whether it fits the DSA and Romer’s narrative or not.”

Regarding Romer’s stance on a one-state solution, the ADL criticized her unfamiliarity with historical efforts, writing: “The co-chair of an organization constantly calling for a ‘free Palestine’ and who claims Palestinian people are ‘in a cage,’ does not know the basic diplomatic history of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and yet, she thinks she’s a legitimate commentator.”
The organization also argued that the DSA’s vision for a single-state outcome leaves no room for Jews’ self-determination in their ancestral homeland.
Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the ADL, concluded the response by writing on X, “When people and groups tell you who they are, believe them.”
The ADL noted that the DSA, which has over 120,000 members and more than 250 elected officials across the United States, is no longer on the fringes of society and possesses the ability to influence mainstream political discourse and policy.

"We are currently awaiting a meeting with the business community or a working session where we will hear what types of warehouses businesses need, since we have wet warehouses, dry warehouses, cold storage facilities, and grain elevators…," she said.

Earlier, in a comment to Interfax-Ukraine, CEO of the Bureau of Investment Programs Oleksandr Bondarenko said that distributors of imported goods may be interested in preferential leases of state-owned warehouses; but for food retailers, such an offer may not be economically viable.
"We all know the condition of the state's assets, as well as those held by ARMA and the State Property Fund. The equipment is outdated, and the facilities themselves are in poor condition-most are typically classified as "D' [the lowest quality]. Of the 190,000 square meters, at best half will be suitable for retrofitting, and about 500,000 square meters of logistics facilities were destroyed this year. So, in the most optimistic scenario, the government"s offer covers one-fifth of the need. "But the key point is that warehouses and logistics terminals are needed where the consumers are," the CEO of the Investment Programs Bureau said.

As Lake Maggiore runs low, Switzerland steps in as Italy faces growing water shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:54:19 UTC
02:54:19 KST

Lake Maggiore is suffering from drought and Switzerland is increasing releases from Lake Lugano. Water is also scarce in Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto and the Marche: this is Italy's new emergency.
Switzerland is opening the taps on Lake Lugano to help prop up Lake Maggiore. It is an emergency solution that, more than any set of figures, shows how sensitive the water situation in northern Italy has become: more water will be released from the Ceresio towards Ponte Tresa, with the aim of supporting the level of Lake Maggiore and, above all, guaranteeing supplies for the rice fields on the plain.
The discharge will rise from the current 3 to 8 cubic metres per second. The two lakes are connected and a significant share of the extra water will flow into Lake Maggiore.
The measure was discussed within the Italian-Swiss Bilateral Consultation Body on the regulation of Lake Maggiore's levels and the management of water resources in its basin, convened urgently by the Ministry of the Environment on the basis of data from the Po River Basin Authority. The Italian delegation, made up of representatives of the ministry and the Lombardy and Piedmont regional authorities, accepted the Swiss proposal, which could be implemented as early as today.
Switzerland's help and the 'short blanket' problem
The decision taken by Canton Ticino is temporary and will be reassessed in the coming days, but its significance goes well beyond this one-off intervention. The underlying problem is that the available water is no longer sufficient to meet all needs at the same time.
On the one hand are the rice paddies of Piedmont and Lombardy, which at this stage of the season need large volumes of water. On the other are the water supply networks, rivers, lakes and ecosystems, all having to cope with ever lower flows.
It is the classic "short blanket" situation: if you increase the provision for one sector, you have to check what is left for the others. And when the overall resource shrinks, even a seemingly technical decision on how to regulate a lake becomes a strategic issue.
The case of Lake Maggiore is particularly telling. Back in July, the Po River Basin Authority was already warning that the lake was close to its minimum operating level, while agriculture in Piedmont was among the sectors under greatest strain.
The problem is not confined to irrigation water for farmland. In several parts of Italy, scarcity has also started to affect drinking water supplies.
Lake Maggiore, who is in charge?
Lake Maggiore is a transboundary basin, shared between Italy and Switzerland, but its regulation is not by joint management in the strict sense. The lake level is controlled by the Miorina dam at Sesto Calende, on Italian territory, and day-to-day management is entrusted to the Ticino Consortium.
Italy and Switzerland nevertheless discuss and coordinate decisions within the Italian-Swiss Bilateral Body, because changes in the lake's level have consequences on both sides of the border.
The picture is even more complex because the Lake Lugano, also shared between the two countries, is linked to Lake Maggiore via the River Tresa: it is through this system that Switzerland is now providing support, by temporarily increasing flows from 3 to 8 cubic metres per second. So Lake Maggiore is regulated in Italy, but managing the water resource cannot be done without coordination with Switzerland.
Water tankers fill supply gaps
In Piedmont the situation is especially sensitive. By mid-July, the regional authorities reported that around 100 municipalities had already adopted ordinances to curb water use, above all in mountain areas and more isolated hamlets. In around 50 municipalities, with a combined population of 25,000, water tankers were already being used to top up reservoirs serving the water supply networks.
Figures from Arpa Piemonte painted an equally worrying picture: surface water resources were 37 per cent below the seasonal average, while in the first ten days of July many gauging stations were showing deficits of more than 40 per cent. At Isola Sant'Antonio, the Po had an average flow of just 62 cubic metres per second, 75 per cent below its historical reference value.
The heat has made matters worse. June 2026 in Piedmont was marked by temperatures far above the average, with a regional anomaly of about +3.5 °C. Higher temperatures increased evapotranspiration, causing soil and vegetation to lose water more quickly.
The crisis spreads across the Po basin
Piedmont, however, is not an isolated case. The problem affects a far wider area.
At the end of July, the permanent observatory on water use in the Po River District raised its assessment of water stress from "medium" to "high". Flows in the Po had progressively fallen to values below those typical of low-water conditions, and the drought index was indicating severe conditions across most monitored sections, with an "extreme" situation recorded at Cremona.
As early as 21 July, the Basin Authority was reporting problems not only for agriculture but also for water destined for households. In Lombardy, 50 municipalities were struggling, 17 of them supplied by tankers; in the Marche region there were 32. Critical situations were also reported in Veneto and Piedmont.
The picture also includes the Po Delta, where reduced river flows increase the risk of saltwater intrusion from the sea. When the river carries less freshwater, saltwater can push further inland, putting ecosystems, farming activities and water supply installations under strain.
Rice fields, drinking water, rivers: who comes first?
This is where the real issue emerges. The emergency is not just about "how much water there is", but how to distribute it when there is not enough.
Agriculture needs irrigation precisely during the hottest phases of the year. The rice fields of Piedmont and Lombardy are among the most exposed sectors, and Piedmont is one of the areas where the region has most clearly flagged the risk of crop losses linked to limited water availability.
But that same water is needed for water supply networks, to maintain minimum flows in rivers, for ecosystems, for certain industrial uses and, in some areas, for energy production.
Hence the growing need for increasingly sophisticated interventions and agreements between regions and countries. The release from Lake Lugano towards Lake Maggiore is a concrete example: a resource available in one basin is temporarily used to support another water system in difficulty.
And in the South the problem has not gone away
The water crisis, however, is not confined to the North. Conditions vary from region to region and not all of Italy faces the same situation at the same time, but vulnerability remains high, especially in Mediterranean areas and in regions that depend heavily on reservoirs.
ISPRA monitors the severity of water stress in the various Italian districts and defines the "high" scenario as a situation in which, despite preventive measures, the resource may not be sufficient to avoid damage to the system.
It is a snapshot that helps explain why water is becoming one of the most sensitive issues in land management: it is no longer enough to wait for rain. Reservoirs are needed, along with more efficient networks, reduced losses in water supply systems, reuse of treated wastewater, less wasteful irrigation systems and planning that takes account of increasingly variable water availability.

Electric scooter rentals banned in Chernivtsi
Kyiv • UNN
On August 10, the Chernivtsi City Council terminated its memorandums with Bolt, Vevi, and Jet.ua following complaints about parking and traffic violations. The companies have 14 days to remove the scooters; otherwise, they will be forcibly relocated.
The Chernivtsi City Council decided to terminate cooperation memorandums with electric scooter rental operators due to residents’ complaints. This became known from a live broadcast of the council session. 22 deputies voted in favor of the decision, reports UNN.
Details
Electric scooters can no longer be rented in Chernivtsi. The city council adopted the decision to terminate the memorandums during its session on August 10. The operators concerned are Bolt, Vevi, and Jet.ua. 22 deputies voted in favor of the decision.
The companies were given 14 days to completely remove the electric scooters, charging stations, and other equipment from the city.
The main reason for the decision was the numerous complaints from Chernivtsi residents. People complained about the chaotic parking of electric scooters. In addition, regular violations of road safety rules by riders were recorded in the city.
If the companies fail to comply with the requirement within the specified 14-day period, then the vehicles will be forcibly moved to a temporary storage facility.
Reminder
Electric scooters are officially recognized as vehicles, so riders must comply with the traffic rules. In the event of accidents involving children, their parents will be held responsible.

Chiefs WR Rashee Rice: 30 days in a Texas jail a ‘learning experience’ after probation violation
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. (AP) — Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice called the 30 days he spent in a Texas jail over the summer a “learning experience” and a “reality check,” one that he got through by rehabbing from knee surgery and watching plenty of comedian Kevin Hart on TV to keep his spirits up.
The 26-year-old Rice was booked into a Dallas County jail on May 19 for violating the terms of his probation, which stemmed from his role in a car crash that left multiple people injured on a Texas highway. He’d had surgery about a week before the sentence to clean up debris in his right knee, which had been causing inflammation throughout much of last season.
Rice was released in June, and he resumed his rehab work alongside Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes — who was rehabbing after his own surgery to repair torn knee ligaments — at their training facility in Kansas City leading into the start of training camp.
“It was tough. It was mentally tough,” Rice said of the jail stint Tuesday, the first time the wide receiver has spoken publicly about his offseason. “They gave me ways to communicate with my teammates as well as my athletic trainer. Besides the hard times in there, just tried to keep positive — as much Kevin Hart as I could to laugh, and communicating with my teammates on the outside.”
Rice has been brilliant for Kansas City when he’s been available, catching 156 passes for 1,797 yards and 14 touchdowns, and helping the Chiefs win the Super Bowl after the 2023 season. But he also missed games to a suspension following the car crash, and several injuries have kept him off the field, resulting in just 28 games played over his first three seasons in the league.
The upcoming season is without question his most important yet.
Not only does Rice has much to prove to a growing chorus of doubters, he’s also entering the final year of his rookie contract. If he wants to land a lucrative, long-term deal in Kansas City or elsewhere, Rice has to not only prove that he can stay on the field but also show that he can consistently be productive for an offense that desperately needs him to be.
“I mean, it’s motivating,” Rice said of impending free agency. “Honestly, just being back on the field with my brothers right now is motivating. That’s in the future. And I’m just focusing on what’s happening right now, and that’s getting better for the team.”
The Chiefs are coming off a 6-11 season in which Mahomes hurt his knee, several others went down with injuries, and what was once one of the NFL’s premier offenses looked like a shadow of itself — even before all those players were sidelined.
Chiefs general manager Brett Veach spent most of his draft capital upgrading the defense, though, including both of his first-round picks, and the biggest move to help the offense was to sign Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III to be their lead running back.
Otherwise, the Chiefs are banking on Rice and fellow wide receivers Xavier Worthy and Tyquan Thornton to take big steps forward in their development, all while hoping that 36-year-old tight end Travis Kelce can still be a reliable and effective pass-catcher.
“We’re going to do some amazing things,” Rice predicted, “not only because we’re great receivers but we have a great coaching staff around us, and a great quarterback and foundation in general.”
Mahomes has certainly looked like his normal self in camp, moving around on his reconstructed knee as if nothing ever happened. That bodes well for Rice, the passing game and the Chiefs in general as they prepare for the upcoming season.
“He was my motivation every morning,” Rice said.
Rice was asked whether he had anything to say to fans who felt let down by his off-the-field problems, or to young players who might be looking up to him. He went back to Mahomes and the teammates that have been with him through thick and thin.
“Find someone that you can lean on. Find someone you can talk to,” Rice said, “and basically don’t be scared to vocalize yourself, or say exactly what’s on your mind, because someone is going through the same thing. There’s too many people in the world for there not to be someone going through the same thing.”
Notes: The Chiefs are signing DE Emmanuel Ogbah, who appeared in 10 games for them during the 2019 season. The veteran spent last season with Jacksonville. “It was disappointing the year we had him. I thought he was coming on and he got hurt, and we didn’t have him at the end of the year,” Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo said. “If he’s part of our group, I’ll be excited.”

Candlelight vigil in Islamabad honors 10 climbers killed on Broad Peak
ISLAMABAD (AP) — Mountaineers, diplomats and members of civil society gathered in Pakistan’s capital Tuesday evening for a candlelight vigil honoring 10 climbers killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak, as rescuers described an arduous mission to bring their fellow climbers down from one of the world’s highest mountains.
Rain fell as mourners lit candles and prayed for the dead, shielding the flickering flames from the downpour as they gathered on the open lawns of a sports complex in Islamabad to remember the climbers who never returned from the mountain.
The vigil came days after search teams ended an operation that recovered the remains of eight climbers. Two bodies have not yet been recovered.
Among the dead was renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja. Nepal lost six climbers in the July 30 disaster, when a massive avalanche struck an international expedition.
Nepal’s ambassador to Pakistan, Rita Dhital, joined the vigil and paid tribute to the climbers as candles were lit in their memory. She recalled meeting Purja at her Islamabad home before the expedition and said he would often tell her, “Giving up is not in my blood.”
She thanked Pakistani climbers and rescuers who went onto the mountain in dangerous weather to search for the missing climbers and recover their bodies. Dhital particularly praised renowned Pakistani mountaineer Sirbaz Khan, who led the recovery team, as well as the Alpine Club of Pakistan, the military and government officials involved in the operation.
The bodies of all six Nepalese climbers have been returned to their families, she said.
Khan told The Associated Press that he and his team had set out hoping they would find the missing climbers alive. “I had hoped that I would hug them after finding them alive,” he said. Instead, the rescuers found climbers buried beneath the avalanche. Khan said the team used shovels to dig through the snow and pull out the bodies one by one.
Seeing fellow mountaineers dead on the mountain was difficult, he said, but the rescuers composed themselves and began the equally difficult task of bringing the bodies down, using ropes and makeshift stretchers. Khan said he remained deeply saddened by the deaths but took some solace in knowing that families who had waited desperately for news were able to receive the remains of their loved ones.
Irfan Arshad Khan, president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan and no relation to the rescuer, said the remains of seven climbers, including all six from Nepal, had been repatriated. He said bad weather repeatedly prevented helicopters from reaching the accident site, forcing rescuers to continue much of the search and recovery operation on foot. Eight bodies were eventually brought to a location from where they could be airlifted, he said.
“We have gathered here today to commemorate the passing of our great comrades,” Khan told those attending the vigil. He said the days following the avalanche tested not only the endurance of those searching the mountain but also the courage of rescuers who continued on foot when helicopters could not reach them.
The international expedition included climbers from Nepal, Oman, Pakistan, China, Britain and the United States.
Broad Peak, which rises 8,051 meters (26,414 feet) above sea level in the Karakoram range, is the world’s 12th-highest mountain and lies near K2, the world’s second-highest peak.
Mountaineering accidents are common in northern Pakistan, home to some of the world’s highest mountains.

Movie Review: ‘The Rivals of Amziah King’ is a Southern fried flick with too many ingredients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

Movie Review: ‘The Rivals of Amziah King’ is a Southern fried flick with too many ingredients
It turns out that the honey business isn’t as sweet as it sounds: In the new movie “The Rivals of Amziah King,” beekeepers steal from each other, poison rivals’ insects and rip folk off. “It’s not full of kind people,” the title character warns.
“The Rivals of Amziah King” isn’t as sweet as it thinks it is, either. Instead of picking a single variety to explore, the movie is a maddening mishmash of genres — blending Quentin Tarantino’s sudden brutality, a coming-of-age tale, a heist flick, a revenge fantasy and a sweet, music-filled country hoedown.
Matthew McConaughey returns to the big screen playing the title character in what can only be called Matthew-McConaughey-turned-up-to-11 mode, pure Cheshire Cat smile, rascally wink and buttery, Southern gentlemanly charm. Suspenders and scruff on, cowboy boots snug, McConaughey is the one who makes everyone’s life instantly better just by showing up.
Written by Andrew Patterson and James Montague and directed by Patterson, “The Rivals of Amziah King” follows McConaughey’s honey-producing King as he negotiates his patch of rural Oklahoma until he inexplicably leaves the movie at the hour mark and hands it off to Angelina LookingGlass, making her film debut.
We meet King ordering chicken fried steak sandwiches and cherry Cokes as he plays the banjo in a quartet of musicians at a beloved food joint. That gets interrupted when authorities need his knowledge to find out who abandoned $250,000 worth of honey barrels on the road and King starts to investigate. Then someone gets a chunk of their skull — including ponytail — ripped off in an industrial accident and that takes over. Settle in, the whiplash is just beginning.
King soon connects with his former foster daughter — that’s LookingGlass, fierce and preternaturally grounded — who he gets to mansplain in the local ways, like what to eat at the potluck (“There’s a story in every dish”), life lessons (“Patience is better than being smart”) and beekeeping (“Every queen is a survivor”). Bees here, if you didn’t already get from the clunky writing, represent community, sharing and caring.
Cinematographer M.I. Littin-Menz’s camera techniques never settle down in this movie, like a puppy forever pulling on its leash. Early sequences employ frozen shots irritatingly dropped into the mix and later we have furious close-ups, quick cuts, quirky flashbacks, ethereal river sequences and lingering poetic images of close-up bees like from a documentary, a kinetic approach that seems not to have much faith in the actual story keeping viewers’ interest alive. Music supervisor Winslow Bright swamps many scenes with loud choirs, loud banjo and loud strings.
Maybe that’s because as soon as you’ve settled down for one genre, it gets hijacked by the next. Warm and extended moments of communal song — the great T Bone Burnett had a hand in some of the outstanding Americana tunes like “Quill” with McConaughey exuberant, and “Johnny Come Outside” — are undercut by seeing kids smash their heads on school bus roofs or a cool Western-like tracking of a honey-stealing local rascal that is marred by his horrific, boiling-to-death murder. There are so many montages of honey production that viewers may qualify for a beekeeping certificate.
Great turns are produced by Kurt Russell as a lethal local kingpin who schmoozes his way past the law, and Jake Horowitz, a former Marine who knows how to plan a theft with military precision, mostly shirtless. One brazen theft here is of “O Brother, Where Art Thou?” and, however you liked that movie, you realize now how hard it was to actually pull off.
Patterson likes to remind viewers of his Oklahoma bona fides, but much of the overlong movie was shot in Alabama. And that hints at what’s wrong with “The Rivals of Amziah King” — it just doesn’t feel authentic, either in place or in story. Forget honey, it sort of leaves a vinegary taste behind.
“The Rivals of Amziah King,” a Black Bear release that hits theaters Friday, is rated R by the Motion Picture Association for “language and some grisly images.” Running time: 130 minutes. Two stars out of four.
___
This review has been updated to correct that the former Marine is played by Jake Horowitz, not Owen Teague.
