FACT FOCUS: Trump makes false claims as he signs order urging revisions around childhood vaccines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

FACT FOCUS: Trump makes false claims as he signs order urging revisions around childhood vaccines
While issuing an executive order on Monday aimed at getting states to revise childhood vaccine recommendations, President Donald Trump and others in his administration repeated several false claims about those vaccines, as well as their relationship to autism.
The order recommends separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate single-disease shots and administering childhood vaccines at separate appointments whenever possible.
But many public health experts expressed concern about the recommendations, saying that spacing out the shots could increase the risk that children would become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit. They noted that childhood vaccines and how they should be given have been rigorously studied around the world for decades, and continue to prove to be safe and effective at protecting children.
Here’s a closer look at the facts.
___
TRUMP: “In many cases, we were requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children.”
THE FACTS: That’s misleading. In 2025, the government’s childhood vaccination schedule recommended routine protection against 18 diseases. How many separate injections that added up to between birth and age 18 varied. It depended on things like the brand used, the availability of combination shots and the child’s starting age. But unless you counted once-a-year flu vaccines (which some kids can get as a nasal spray) or COVID-19 shots, the number of injections was closer to three dozen.
Those shots have been proven to protect children from preventable and sometimes devastating diseases. Even so, vaccines were never “required,” as families could opt out. States do require children to get certain vaccines before enrolling in school, but the state lists of school shots were narrower than the federal vaccine schedule, and many states offer different types of exemptions.
The Trump administration in January cut the national vaccine recommendations to injections against 11 diseases, with additional vaccines now separately categorized for at-risk children or as available through “shared decision-making” with a doctor. This drops the total number of injections to about 23 if children receive only the recommended-for-all vaccinations on the administration’s new schedule.
___
TRUMP: “You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they are quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal but just very effective.”
THE FACTS: This is false. Doctors say, and years of real-world evidence prove, that the current combination MMR vaccine is both safe and effective at protecting children from illness. Common side effects are mild and include a sore arm from the shot, fever, mild rash and temporary pain and stiffness in the joints. Doctors point out that separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella are not available in the United States.
“I’m concerned about an unintended consequence of people under vaccinating because of fear that giving a single dose of the MMR is going to put their child at risk when there’s no evidence to suggest that’s the case,” said Dr. Aaron Milstone, pediatric director of infection prevention at Johns Hopkins Health System and a fellow with the American Academy of Pediatrics. “There are many, many, many years of scientific data highlighting the safety of vaccines in children.”
___
TRUMP: “Large amounts of vaccine, large amounts of like vats of vaccine are currently pumped into your child’s body.”
THE FACTS: This is false. Dr. Molly O’Shea, a Michigan pediatrician, said amounts vary slightly by vaccine, but doctors give less than 0.5 milliliters per vaccine -- usually 0.1 to 0.3 milliliters per vaccine. By comparison, a teaspoon is about 5 milliliters.
“It’s a teeny amount,” she said. “So there are no vats.”
Trump also said during the executive order signing: “I’ve seen proof of it. Where they have a vaccination that looks like the size of a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body.” A typical plastic bottle of soda contains 500 milliliters, or about 2,500 times more than a typical vaccine.
___
TRUMP: “There’s nothing that we lose with this. The worst thing that would happen would be nothing happens. We’re not going to lose anything.”
THE FACTS: Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit. Doctors say, and real world evidence proves, that vaccinations save millions of lives.
“Vaccines are among the most thoroughly studied, effective tools we have to protect children from serious vaccine-preventable diseases,” said Dr. Willie Underwood, president of the American Medical Association. “Altering a proven vaccination schedule without credible evidence risks weakening public confidence and putting children’s health at risk.”
Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said that “delaying or skipping shots is risky, especially as measles continues to spread and children go back to school.”
Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, but rates are now climbing as vaccination rates decline. The number of cases this year has already surpassed the record-breaking tally for all of 2025, which was the worst year for measles in more than three decades.
___
HEALTH SECRETARY ROBERT F. KENNEDY JR.: “In 1970, the biggest epidemiological study at that time in history was performed. And the university scientists from across this country looked at all the 8-year-olds in Wisconsin, about 900,000 children, and they were looking for autism. And they knew what autism looked like. And they came back with an incidental rate of .8 per 10,000. So less than one in 10,000. The rate according to CDC today in this country is one in every 31 children.”
THE FACTS: It’s true that in the 20th century, only 1 in 10,000 children were diagnosed with autism —- the diagnosis was rare and given only to kids with severe problems communicating or socializing and those with unusual, repetitive behaviors. But the term became shorthand for a group of milder, related conditions known as ″autism spectrum disorders,” and the number of kids labeled as having some form of autism began to balloon.
Health officials have largely attributed growing autism numbers to better recognition of cases, through wide screening and better diagnosis. In April 2025, the CDC said the diagnosis rate was 1 in 31 children.
During the executive order signing, Kennedy and Trump suggested that childhood vaccines may play a role in causing autism. But studies by the CDC and others have ruled that out. A fraudulent single study that claimed a link between the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine was later retracted by the journal that published it.
There are no blood or biologic tests for autism; it is diagnosed by making judgments about a child’s behavior. Research has looked at a variety of other possible explanations, including genetics, the age of the father, the weight of the mother and chemicals in the environment.
“No environmental factor has been better-studied as a potential cause of autism than vaccines,” said Dr. Alycia Halladay, chief science officer at the Autism Science Foundation. “That includes vaccine ingredients as well as the body’s response to the vaccines. All this research has determined that there is no link between autism and vaccines. This is consistent across multiple studies, repeated in different countries around the world, including those mentioned in today’s press conference.”
Last year, Kennedy promised to conduct exhaustive studies to identify any environmental factors that may cause the developmental disorder. He said on Monday that his department will deliver research findings “as soon as they are ready.”
___
AP Medical Writer Lauran Neergaard contributed to this report.

Britain’s Andy Green sets another speed record, this time for fastest run in a hydrogen-powered car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

Britain’s Andy Green sets another speed record, this time in a hydrogen-powered car
WENDOVER, Utah (AP) — The only person to break the sound barrier in a car earned another world record Tuesday in a show of force for hydrogen power.
British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph (653.908 kph) in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, setting the record for that vehicle category, according to the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.
The 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot rocketed across the crystalline crust at Utah’s famous Bonneville Salt Flats in a 32-foot (9.75-meter) car engineered by British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The engines, adapted from those used in the company’s heavy machinery, mix pressurized hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create bursts of power.
“It’s magic to be able to showcase this technology and to showcase how good the engineering is on the best racing surface in the world, Bonneville Salt Flats,” Green told The Associated Press after the run.
To be clear, Tuesday’s feat didn’t come close to approaching the overall land-speed record, which Green set with jet power in 1997. That year, he climbed into the Thrust SSC, a black needle sandwiched between two cartoonishly large jet engines, and hit 763.035 mph (1,227.985 kph), breaking the sound barrier and achieving a feat no one has come close to matching. His runs in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert produced sonic booms that shook the nearby town of Gerlach.
In 2006, Green also set the land-speed record for a diesel-powered car — 350.092 mph (563.4 kph) — at the Bonneville Salt Flats. He returned there Tuesday with the goal of beating that mark using hydrogen power, which he has called the “fuel of the future.”
In targeting his diesel speed, Green easily topped the previous hydrogen combustion world record of 185.5 mph (298.5 kph). He had a 10-mile (16-kilometer) straightaway to build speed. A few dozen JCB staff members and reporters watched from a distance through cameras and binoculars.
Green said the cockpit of the car he used on Tuesday was “probably a little hotter” than in the jet-powered vehicle from 1997, with temperatures routinely above 122 degrees Fahrenheit (50 degrees Celsius).
“But I have been training four months for that, both training in the gym and actually just getting used to it with hot baths,” he said.
A remnant of a prehistoric lake bed, the Bonneville Salt Flats are about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Salt Lake City and sit atop a shallow aquifer that cools the tires. The low-friction surface and dry desert air are conducive to speed and have beckoned drivers since the first race there in 1914.
“It looks like snow, and it behaves a bit like packed snow — it is surprisingly slippery,” Green said.
Green was no stranger to speed when he took his first racing job. He had been flying supersonic military jets when he spotted a 1994 British newspaper ad seeking a high-speed driver to break the sound barrier.
Green did not approach supersonic speeds on Tuesday, but JCB engineers hope his feat with hydrogen power will shake up the clean-energy industry.
The company’s chairman has argued that hydrogen can better handle the demands of heavy industries than electric power.
Hydrogen is only as clean as its source, and the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels. JCB signed a deal to buy green hydrogen, which is created using renewable energy but makes up a tiny fraction of global hydrogen production.
The concept and development of such technology has been around for decades, but has had a resurgence over the past several years, said Greg Keoleian, a professor of sustainable systems at the University of Michigan and co-director of the school’s MI Hydrogen initiative.
Many major automakers have already developed hydrogen internal combustion engines or hydrogen fuel cell technology, but the higher cost of hydrogen production compared with gas and diesel is a barrier to wider usage, Keoleian said.
“It represents an important energy carrier for decarbonizing areas of the economy,” he said. “As far as its deployment, it’s influenced heavily by the cost.”
An emerging focus, he said, is extracting hydrogen from natural deposits instead of separating it from water, a prospect that could significantly reduce costs.
___
Associated Press reporter Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed reporting.

Lebanon Issues New Charges Against Former Central Bank Chief Riad Salame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:52:00 UTC
02:52:00 KST

Reported by
A Lebanese judge has issued new charges against former central bank governor Riad Salame and a former commercial banker over allegations of financial crimes, including embezzlement, money laundering, bribery, and illicit enrichment, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.
On Monday, Judge Raja Hamouche filed proceedings against 76-year-old Salame and Samir Hanna, 88, the former head of Bank Audi, one of Lebanon's largest banks. The allegations include the creation of shell companies, misappropriating funds belonging to the Central Bank, and the fraudulent use of those funds to purchase shares and bonds in commercial banks. He also charged them with illicit enrichment, money laundering, and bribery.
The Public Prosecutor of Appeal requested an arrest warrant against Salame. Media have reported that he is currently under medical supervision at a hospital in Beirut. He has repeatedly denied all charges against him. His lawyer has not responded to OCCRP’s request for comment.
Hanna, 88, has reportedly already paid a $1 million bail and is not in custody. He could not be reached for comment.
The development marks the second indictment against Salame in Lebanon this year and the third in total.
Lebanese prosecutors took their first formal legal action against Riad Salame in February 2023, charging him with money laundering and embezzlement after years of international scrutiny. Months later, in July 2023, Salame stepped down as governor of Banque du Liban, ending a three-decade tenure at the central bank.
In September 2024, Lebanese authorities arrested Salame in Beirut over his alleged role in a $44.8 million embezzlement scheme involving central bank commissions. He was released on bail in 2025 and placed under a strict travel ban as court proceedings continue.
In January 2026, prosecutors indicted him alongside two legal advisers on charges of embezzlement, forgery, and illicit enrichment for their roles in the embezzlement of $44 million.
European authorities allege that Salame siphoned more than $300 million from the central bank using a front company owned by his brother, which charged exorbitant commissions on commercial bank transactions.
Investigations across Switzerland, France, Germany, and Luxembourg also allege that hundreds of millions of dollars in stolen public funds were funneled into luxury real estate and bank accounts across Europe. Salame has denied those accusations too.
Concurrent with the latest judicial proceedings, Lebanon’s central bank launched legal action in July against additional targets alleged to have played a role in the country’s 2019 financial meltdown. The action followed a complaint initiated by current central bank governor Karim Soueid in January targeting Salame and Hanna, who reportedly stepped down from Bank Audi's board that same month.
The financial authority is also suing Lebanon’s BankMed, alongside several executives and a major investor, according to local media. The claim was confirmed to OCCRP's Lebanese partner, Daraj, by a person familiar with the process. BankMed did not respond to a request for comment.
Under the new leadership Banque du Liban is attempting to recoup funds lost during the 2019 economic collapse, which resulted from a systemic banking failure.
Lebanon had pegged its currency to the U.S. dollar, and to maintain the fixed exchange rate and fund government spending, the central bank lured commercial banks into depositing customer dollars at exceptionally high interest rates. When new dollar inflows dried up, the system collapsed, wiping out the life savings of millions of people. The World Bank ranked the collapse as one of the world's worst economic crises since the mid-19th century.
Badih Moukarzel, the central bank’s lead counsel in the cases, told Daraj that the bank is determined to pursue the matters, calling them key to restoring confidence in the financial system.
“Those who committed financial crimes have to be investigated, and if they are found guilty, they must be tried. I don't see how we can rebuild trust without doing this,” Moukarzel said. He described the financial collapse as a shared responsibility between the state, the central bank, and commercial banks, categorically rejecting out-of-court settlements. “The banks have to pay back. Money has to be returned; we are talking billions of dollars.”

Drivers stopped on a nearby blocked street waited about as long, according to the Telegram channel Govorit NeMoskva (Not Moscow Speaking).

Ahead of Putin’s visit, workers hastily repaved roads in Novosibirsk’s city center, laid new sod, and repaired sidewalks and building facades, local residents said.

Fast and fearless: Baltic defence startups innovate to counter Russian threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:48:28 UTC
02:48:28 KST

Fast and fearless: Baltic defence startups innovate to counter Russian threat
As the nature of Russia’s war in Ukraine evolves, Baltic startups are seeking new ways to respond to the hybrid threat from Russia, hoping rapid innovation can have a deterrent effect on Moscow.
One of the lessons of the war in Ukraine is that military technology evolves very rapidly, with the world's first-ever drone war making it harder for conventional armies to make gains on the battlefield.
But they may also herald a new dystopian future, where ordinary civilians become targets of flying objects manned by faraway operators.
Entrepreneurs in Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have taken note.
The Baltic region is already home to several companies that are well known internationally, such as Bolt, Skype and Vinted. Since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, the startup scene has focused on developing defence technologies.
The resulting innovations may be a low-cost and scalable solution to deterring Russian aggression, experts told FRANCE 24.
Faced with technological shifts on the battlefield in Ukraine, “startups tend to be able to equally rapidly develop technologies themselves”, said Tony Lawrence, research fellow at the International Centre for Defence and Security.
“It’s about providing niche solutions that bigger defence primes don’t traditionally have the ability to deal with,” he added.
The startups focus on autonomy – combining AI with hardware, drones and edge computing to operate in environments where GPS or communications have been jammed – as well as domains like software, cybersecurity and electronic warfare.
The Baltic states are quite conscious of their strategic weaknesses in the face of the Russian threat and aware that Moscow has been waging a hybrid war against them for years.
Read moreDrones, sabotage, surveillance: Moscow’s hybrid warfare takes to the high seas
“The whole rearmament process that the Baltic States and NATO in general are going through at the moment is dealing with the potential of a Russian attack on one of the NATO member states, including one of the Baltic states,” said Lawrence.
But the hybrid threat is more of an immediate worry, added Lawrence.
Read moreRussian secret services target Latvia as Ukraine's drone offensive worries the Kremlin
Innovations to counter Moscow
The Baltic states face frequent disinformation and propaganda from Russia. "After Soviet occupation, many people in the region still understand Russian. As a result, it is easier for Russian propaganda to spread its lies,” said Darius Antanaitis, a defence analyst from Lithuania.
One of the most promising AI startups to counter the propaganda is Repsense in Vilnius, according to Antanaitis. “It has developed tools capable of identifying the original sources of propaganda, tracing its dissemination, measuring its impact, and more.”
The company “helps uncover the truth and prevent propaganda from spreading in the future, or perhaps even neutralize it before it spreads”, he said.
Another startup with potential is DefSecIntel based in Tallinn, said Lawrence. The company, which provides surveillance for borders and critical infrastructure protection, helps conceptualize “the hybrid environment and being able to respond to it”.
Faced with a potential US disengagement from its security obligations over the European continent, the Baltic states have massively invested in their defence systems. Lithuania directs more than 5% of its GDP on defence in 2026, the highest share among NATO allies.
Read morePoland prepares to stand its ground with massive new civil defence programme
Yet “not as much money as you would imagine” is trickling down to the startups, said Lawrence. “The three [Baltic] states are spending a lot on defence in GDP terms; but in cash terms, it doesn’t amount to a huge amount. They also have other priorities in terms of conventional armaments, long-range weapons and artillery.”
For startups to be self-sustaining, they must be in the export business, Lawrence explained. “That said, Estonia is encouraging its defence companies more than it did, perhaps, three or four years ago, with various grant schemes that can assist the companies for the domestic market but also for export markets.”
Defence innovation also works in the Baltic states because of the nurturing startup culture that exists there.
A deterrent effect
“The three Baltic states all started from scratch in basically everything when they became independent in the early '90s,” Lawrence said. “That included, particularly in Estonia, e-governance and a digital state. You didn’t have a legacy that it had to maintain. It was starting from scratch. This kind of innovative spirit as to how you might run a state started back then and that kind of culture has been retained.”
Defence also has strong public consensus in the Baltic countries.
“Everybody thinks it’s important and everybody is ready to do their part. Part of that might be finding venture capital to fund startup companies who can make a difference in defence,” he said.
And it is hoped that this sort of rapid innovation will have its own deterrent effect.
Estonia wants Russia to think twice, knowing that it cannot just bring its "war-tested defence technology and use it against Estonia, and expect that Estonia will not have the ability to innovate ... and find countermeasures to what [Russia is] bringing to the game”.

Russia’s Odesa strikes halve Ukraine’s grain export forecast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:47:53 UTC
02:47:53 KST

Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry has cut its forecast for agricultural exports in 2026–2027 by 54% as Russian attacks disrupt shipping through Odesa’s ports, Bloomberg reported.
The ministry now expects 29.6 million tons of agricultural exports, down from 64.4 million. Its wheat export forecast fell by 53%, from 17.6 million tons to 8.3 million tons.
Ukraine grows far more grain than it consumes, exporting 65%–70% of its agricultural output. Bloomberg said the sector generated more than half of Ukraine’s export revenue last year. But Russia’s summer attacks have stalled the sea corridor as the harvest arrives, driving some wheat prices below production costs. Land and river routes cannot match the Black Sea shipping capacity, while sales through neighboring EU states remain politically contested. That leaves farmers with less money for the next sowing and further reduces Ukraine’s export income.
Ukraine has about 59 million tons of grain storage. That storage could be full by early November, leaving the country 11 million tons short of space by the end of fall 2026.
Wheat sells below cost as the silos fill up
Ukraine’s export bottleneck is already hitting its farmers. Port prices fell by another 12-15% in one week, while some farmers sold wheat below production cost. When ships stop, traders either stop buying or pass the higher cost of alternative routes on to producers. That leaves farmers with less cash for fall sowing.
To ease the pressure, the government has approved subsidized loans for agricultural producers. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would expand storage. Ukraine's Agriculture Ministry has also asked the European Commission for €220 million to help cover interest for small and medium-sized farms.
Ukraine and Moldova are discussing a rail route to Romania’s Constanța port. According to the report, grain was already being redirected through Romania, Slovakia, and Hungary, but these routes cannot replace Odesa’s capacity.
Now the ports and the ships are Russia's targets
The export bottleneck is only part of the problem. Russia’s bombardment also threatens the ports, civilian ships, and crews needed to keep the corridor operating.
The port of Odesa normally handles about 90% of Ukraine’s grain shipments. Russia intensified attacks on terminals and civilian ships in July 2026 as the harvest reached the coast.
On 19 July, three Russian missiles struck the foreign-flagged Golden Leo as it left Odesa carrying corn, killing 10 people, including a Ukrainian sea pilot. Three days later, no vessel passed through the corridor.
Alternative routes offer little relief, as record-low Danube levels were restricting river traffic. Poland continues to bar Ukrainian grain from its domestic market. Those constraints leave more of the harvest inside Ukraine and farmers with less money to plant the next crop.

How viable are Burnham’s plans to free up prison space?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:47:19 UTC
02:47:19 KST

Andy Burnham said on Monday he was “increasingly confident” that PC Andrew Harper’s killers would not be freed in the new year.
Determined to ensure that Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter, serve their full sentences, he has asked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to examine three options for increasing prison capacity.
The options outlined by Burnham are speeding up the deportation of foreign offenders, releasing female prisoners from jail and reviewing indefinite sentences given to “lower-risk” prisoners.
How feasible are they?
Accelerating the deportation of foreign prisoners
There were 10,134 foreign nationals held in prisons across England and Wales at the end of June 2026, according to the most recent Ministry of Justice figures.
Removing them from the UK would therefore be a major political coup for Burnham.
But there are several major obstacles.
Going back to Tony Blair, governments have pledged to clear jails of foreign prisoners, but all have failed.
Andrew Neilson, the director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the government would struggle to achieve any immediate relief for the overcrowding crisis by seeking to deport foreign prisoners.
He said: “Reciprocal agreements will have to be drawn up with many of the countries involved and they take time to draw up, and so it does not provide immediate relief to the capacity crisis.”
Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said: “Releasing foreign offenders is difficult because many of them don’t want to go, and quite often they are undocumented. If they have come over on small boats, you do not necessarily know where you might be able to deport them to.
“Many victims will want to see that justice has been served. If someone has been physically attacked or raped by someone from a foreign country which is corrupt, it may well be difficult to guarantee that their attacker’s sentence will be served.”
Emptying women’s prisons and filling them with men
This is an option that has been examined and re-examined by successive governments.
Ministry of Justice officials have been seriously examining schemes to divert female offenders out of jail for more than a year.
Burnham could adopt approaches pioneered by the Greater Manchester authority to steer women away from prison for lower-level offences. These reduced the number being jailed in the region by 55% in eight years.
Turning the biggest women’s prison – HMP Bronzefield in Ashford, Surrey – into a men’s jail would free up more than 500 spaces.
Neilson said: “There should be scope to reduce the number of women in custody, but it is difficult to assess whether Burnham’s plans would work without more detail.”
Wheatley said there would be difficulties in quickly converting women’s prisons so they could hold men.
He said: “Many women’s prisons would not meet the security measures needed for male prisoners.
“For example, some of the prisoner accommodation at HMP Styal is essentially a set of houses within a secure perimeter. The security standards would not meet the requirements needed for men.
“HMP Bronzefield is a newer, secure prison that could be used for men, but it needs to hold women so that women can be brought to London courts.”
Releasing ‘lower-risk’ offenders serving IPP sentences
Imprisonment for public protection sentences were introduced in 2005 for dangerous offenders whose crimes did not warrant a life sentence. They allowed offenders to be detained for a potentially unlimited period until they could prove that they were no longer a threat to the public. If released back into the community on licence, they could be returned to custody.
Although IPP sentences were abolished in 2012, the change was not retrospective, and more than 2,200 people remain in prison despite having served many years beyond their minimum tariff.
Neilson said: “Around 70% of IPP prisoners are in category C or D prisons so the system does not see them as a great risk.
“But identifying them and then putting in place the structures to be able to help people who have been in jail for many years would not be a quick fix.
“People do recognise that people who have been in prison for many, many years will require proper support. It will not free up space immediately.”

Ebola: Over 2,000 dead in DR Congo as virus gathers pace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:46:00 UTC
02:46:00 KST

Ebola: Over 2,000 dead in DR Congo as virus gathers pace
August 11, 2026
Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) said on Tuesday that an outbreak of a particularly virulent strain of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus currently raging in the east and northeast of the country has killed more than 2,000 people since the first case was confirmed.
In all, more than 4,380 infections have been recorded.
The current outbreak is the 17th ever recorded in the DRC, with Sania Nishtar of the Gavi global vaccine alliance warning it could become "the largest outbreak ever."
Until now, the worst outbreak recorded in the DRC was the one that took place from 2018 to 2020 when some 3,500 infections led to 2,300 deaths.
The pace of death is gathering momentum this time around, with the virus spreading faster and exhibiting a higher mortality rate than the 2014-2016 West African outbreak — the worst outbreak on record, which logged 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current DRC outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities say the first transmissions likely took place in February of earlier still.
The 1,000-death mark was not reached until nine weeks in, now — in just three-weeks' time — that figure has doubled again.
The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is 45.9% compared to 39.6% in the 2014-2016 West African outbreak.
'We haven't reached the peak yet,' says DRC health minister
Though there are vaccines against some strains of the Ebola virus, there are currently none approved for the rare Bundibugyo strain that is spreading across the DRC faster than health authorities can trace it.
Moreover, health authorities face massive logistics challenges due to the volatile security situation in the country, where bad roads and rebel violence coupled with lack of healthcare worker pay and mass strikes make it increasingly difficult to keep tabs on the illness.
"We haven't reached the peak yet," said Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba in an interview shared by the ministry on X. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added.
Ebola, which is transmitted through physical contact with bodily fluids, causing a hemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past half century.
Authorities in the DRC have placed restrictions on public gatherings as well as closing the airport in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak. Still, fighting and disease have forced the displacement of masses of people in the DRC, Rwanda and South Sudan.
On Monday, the World Health Organization's (WHO) regional director told reporters that authorities are "chasing the virus… the virus is ahead of us."
What's the latest on bids to treat or vaccinate this Ebola strain?
Clinical trials for two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July and on Friday the WHO recommended undertaking a full-scale human trial of the Ervebo vaccine.
Although Ervebo has proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola, its efficacy in fighting the Bundibugyo strain is unproven. WHO officials are hopeful that it can offer some protection against the DRC strain.
Vaccine alliance Gavi says it has made some 500,000 doses of Ervebo in its stockpiles available for the trial.
Virologists say the new Bundibugyo strain appears to have been transmitted from animals to humans and has changed from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012.
Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries published findings in the journal Nature Medicine on Monday, suggesting the outbreak began with an animal-to-human transmission event and was then spread between people.
Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities are looking into the possibility that the pathogen may have mutated.
Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa CDC, last week warned that fewer and fewer new cases could be traced back to contacts of existing confirmed patients, with researchers falling well below the WHO's targets of tracking 95% of potential contacts to contain the spread.

Crimean Tatar activist Leniie Umerova similarly recounted being cycled through seven separate detention facilities in what she described as “a carousel of repression,” according to the agency.
Oleg Gushin, representing Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, stated that Kyiv has identified more than 300 detention sites in Russia and occupied Ukrainian territories. While over 9,000 Ukrainians have been returned in prisoner exchanges, thousands remain held incommunicado. Moscow rejected the allegations during the meeting, with Russian Deputy UN Representative Maria Zabolotskaya dismissing the claims as a “disinformation campaign” and alleging that Russian prisoners in Ukraine faced physical and moral abuse, Reuters reported.
While UN monitors also documented instances of ill-treatment against Russian and third-country prisoners held by Ukraine, Fuentes Julio emphasized that those cases occurred on a “fundamentally different scale,” primarily limited to the initial stages of captivity.
In response to the findings, Ukrainian Chargé d’Affaires Volodymyr Pavlichenko urged the international community to increase pressure on Moscow to ensure accountability and secure the release of remaining captives, according to the publication.
These documented abuses extend beyond Ukrainian nationals to foreign captives as well, highlighted by the critical condition of former US Marine Robert Gilman. Imprisoned in Russia since 2022, the 32-year-old was reportedly subjected to torture and injected with mind-altering drugs before being transferred to a civilian psychiatric unit in a “dissociative stupor,” where he now relies on tube feeding.
With Russian authorities barring both US consular officials and Gilman’s mother from visiting him in the hospital, the White House and US State Department have urgently demanded his immediate release for emergency medical treatment in the United States.

Ex-Marine released and returning to US from Russian prison
August 11, 2026
Russia on Tuesday released Robert Gilman, a former US Marine who had spent more than four years in prison on disputed charges, according to a group advocating for him and US officials.
US President Donald Trump and the State Department both said the release was on "humanitarian grounds" and that it was not part of an exchange or prisoner swap with Russia.
Who is Robert Gilman?
The 32-year-old former service member had been working as a teacher in Russia when he was first detained in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer after being ejected from a train for causing a disturbance.
He was later accused of other violent offenses while incarcerated and was given a longer jail sentences, ultimately reaching a total of roughly 10 years.
Advocacy group Global Reach had warned of Gilman's deteriorating health condition in detention. His mother was in Russia trying to secure his release as the news developed.
What did Trump and the State Department say about the release?
Trump posted about the release on his Truth Social platform, also including what appeared to be a photo of a sedentary Gilman, his mother and others on a plane, holding an American flag.
"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote. "We appreciated the decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place."
He said that Gilman and others would land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington later on Tuesday to be welcomed back to the US.
The State Department, meanwhile, issued a statement attributed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"We thank Russia for working with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to release Mr. Gilman and allowing him to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States," Rubio said. "While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard."
The statement lauded Trump's efforts to free US-Americans from foreign detention during his second term and concluded that Trump "will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home."
Gilman's sister credits Trump, Democrat senator with her brother's release
Gilman's sister Lexie Hudson said in a statement from advocacy group Global Reach that Trump hearing about the case and taking action was the "reason that Robert is alive today."
She also thanked Democrat Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey "for leading our advocacy efforts in Congress."
"The Russians treated my brother so badly," Hudson said. "They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both an American and a Marine. What did they get out of this? Why did they do this to such a wonderful person?"
According to Global Reach's chief strategy officer Eric Lebson, Gilman had been in a "dissociative stupor" for 47 days, attributing this to abuse he suffered in prison.
He had been moved to a civilian hospital prior to his release, and would soon be medically and psychologically assessed and treated at a US military hospital, Lebson said.
Gilman's mother had traveled to Russia amid the reports of her son's deteriorating health to try to see him.
"It is a tragedy that it took Robert's near-death condition for his case to receive the attention that it required for his release to be negotiated," Massachusetts Senator Markey said in the statement from Global Reach. "Throughout his detention, Robert was subjected to physical torture, forced medication, and provocations by Russian authorities. There is no doubt that his treatment by Russian authorities is the reason Robert is in this precarious state today."
Gilman was arrested in January 2022, a few weeks before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. His prosecution proceeded as relations between Putin's Russia and NATO members deteriorated markedly.

US jury in Luigi Mangione murder trial to remain anonymous
The closely watched state trial over the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson is set to begin next month.
The jury in Luigi Mangione’s upcoming murder trial over the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson will remain anonymous, a New York State judge has ruled, as one of the most closely watched criminal cases in the United States moves towards trial.
New York state Justice Gregory Carro announced the decision at a hearing on Tuesday, ahead of jury selection, which is expected to begin on September 8.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4‘Terrorism’ charge on Mangione dismissed in health insurance exec’s killing
- list 2 of 4Luigi Mangione appears in court as lawyers seek to bar evidence at trial
- list 3 of 4US judge rules Luigi Mangione won’t face death penalty in CEO killing case
- list 4 of 4Luigi Mangione to use psychiatric defence in healthcare CEO murder case
Carro did not explain why the jurors’ identities would be withheld from the public. Anonymous juries are relatively unusual in US criminal trials, but judges sometimes use them in high-profile cases when there are concerns that jurors could face harassment or intimidation.
The judge also ordered that an overflow courtroom be made available to journalists and members of the public if the main courtroom reaches capacity, underscoring the intense interest surrounding the case.
Mangione, 28, has pleaded not guilty to murder, weapons and forgery charges over the December 2024 killing of Thompson, who was shot outside a hotel in Midtown Manhattan as he headed to an investor conference.
While the killing was condemned by public officials, it tapped into deep frustration in the US over rising healthcare costs and the practices of private health insurers. Footage of the shooting quickly spread online, while the five-day manhunt that followed sparked a national media frenzy. Mangione was eventually arrested in Pennsylvania.
Police have said the words “delay”, “deny” and “depose” were written on ammunition connected to the shooting, echoing a phrase used by critics to describe the tactics used by insurance companies to avoid paying claims.
Prosecutors say their case includes hundreds of hours of surveillance footage, fingerprints, DNA, a mobile phone and a gun they say matches the ballistics from Thompson’s killing.
They also plan to use a notebook allegedly belonging to Mangione. Carro ruled last month that both the gun, a 3D-printed pistol, and notebook could be admitted at trial. Prosecutors say the notebook contains writings about targeting a health insurance executive and rebelling against what it calls the “deadly, greed fueled health insurance cartel”.
Mangione’s lawyers have so far revealed little about how they plan to counter the prosecution’s case and have not conceded that he was the shooter.
His legal team briefly indicated in June that it could pursue an “extreme emotional disturbance” defence, which under New York law could have required the jury to convict him of manslaughter, carrying up to 25 years in prison, rather than murder, which can carry a life sentence, if the jury accepted it.
But the defence abruptly withdrew that plan a day later. Attorney Karen Friedman Agnifilo told Carro that Mangione was withdrawing the notice “at this time”.
Mangione is separately facing federal charges stemming from Thompson’s killing.
Federal murder and weapons charges against him were thrown out last January on legal grounds, eliminating the possibility of the death penalty. But he still faces federal stalking charges that could result in life in prison if he is convicted.
Mangione’s federal trial is scheduled to begin in January.

Arab states reject Colombia's recognition of Golan as 'Israeli'
Unknown

2026-08-11

Breadcrumb
Syria, Arab states reject Colombia's recognition of 'Israeli sovereignty' over occupied Golan
Colombia's decision to recognise Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights has triggered condemnation across the Middle East, with Arab governments accusing Bogota of legitimising Israel's decades-long occupation and defying international law.
The move makes Colombia only the second UN member state, after the United States, to recognise Israel's claim to Syrian territory it seized by force in 1967 and later unilaterally annexed in a move rejected by the international community.
Syria, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the recognition on Tuesday, stressing that a declaration by Bogota cannot alter the Golan Heights' status as occupied Syrian territory.
The decision represents a dramatic reversal in Colombian foreign policy just days after President Abelardo de la Espriella took office, and is among the clearest signs yet of his government's rapid rapprochement with Israel.
His predecessor, Gustavo Petro, severed diplomatic relations with Israel in 2024 over its war on Gaza and backed South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
De la Espriella has instead moved swiftly to rebuild relations with Israel, with the Golan recognition placing Colombia alongside Washington and against the longstanding international consensus on the occupied territory.
Colombia's foreign ministry sought to justify the decision by citing instability in the Middle East and the Golan's alleged strategic importance to Israel's "security", adding that Israel had a "right to protect itself" from supposed external threats.
But Israel's security claims do not alter the territory's status under international law.
Israel captured most of the Syrian Golan Heights during the 1967 war and imposed its laws, jurisdiction and administration on the territory in 1981. The UN Security Council responded unanimously with Resolution 497, declaring Israel's move "null and void and without international legal effect".
Damascus condemned Colombia's decision "in the strongest terms", highlighting that it was a flagrant violation of the UN Charter and international law.
Syria's foreign ministry stressed that the Golan remained "occupied Syrian territory and an inseparable part" of the country, saying Bogota's recognition could neither legitimise Israel's occupation nor change the territory's legal status.
Saudi Arabia also called on Colombia to reverse the decision, warning that it entrenched "the logic of imposing a fait accompli" and undermined efforts towards regional peace.
Riyadh said Israel's attempts to change the legal status of occupied Syrian territory created no rights and conferred no legitimacy on its control.
Qatar accused the move of helping Israel disregard UN resolutions governing the occupied Golan, stressing that recognition by individual governments could not change the fact that the territory remained occupied Arab land.
Doha also warned that unilateral recognition of Israeli sovereignty would pose a "major obstacle" to peace and reiterated its demand for Israel to withdraw from occupied Arab territories.
Jordan described the Golan as an inseparable part of Syrian territory and coupled its condemnation with criticism of Israel's continuing attacks and incursions inside Syria.
Egypt similarly rejected Colombia's decision as contrary to international law and an infringement on Syria's established territorial rights.
For decades, virtually the entire international community refused to recognise Israel's annexation of the Golan.
That consensus was first breached in 2019 when US President Donald Trump recognised Israeli sovereignty over the territory, overturning decades of American policy and making Washington the only country to recognise Israel's claim.

Is the EU’s African migrant hubs plan dead on arrival?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:33:10 UTC
02:33:10 KST

Is the EU’s African migrant hubs plan dead on arrival?
The leader of the center-right European People’s Party has called on the EU to set up migrant return hubs in Africa to enable swift deportations. However, similar schemes have failed before.
In an editorial for Germany’s Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Monday, Weber argued that the recent migrant invasion of Ceuta was enabled by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’ pro-immigration policies. Enforcement of EU migration law, the senior Brussels power-player argued, can no longer be left up to individual member states.
“Just as a village policeman has no chance against organized crime, no single member state will defeat the internationally operating people smuggling mafia alone,” he wrote. “Only a united Europe can put an end to their activities.”
The EU, he continued, should set up migrant hubs in Africa, where illegal immigrants and failed asylum seekers could be sent once ordered to leave the bloc’s member states. Governments in Africa could be enticed with “offers of strong trade relations, economic cooperation, and [pathways to] legal migration,” he suggested.
Weber is not a fringe MEP. The EPP is the largest umbrella party in the European Parliament, and counts European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and Parliament President Roberta Metsola among its members.
The EPP’s stance on immigration has never been considered ‘hardline’, and the group’s manifesto once described housing refugees as the EU’s “responsibility.” However, with right-wing parties surging in popularity across the bloc – 27% of sitting MEPs now belong to the so-called ‘far right’ – the group has finally hardened its positions. Yet even if the EU elite now has the political will to deport migrants to Africa, Weber’s scheme faces some significant obstacles – from other EU institutions.
Are migrant return hubs legal?
Until recently, the EU’s common rules on deportation were set out in the 2008 Return Directive, with enforcement left up to individual member states. The directive explicitly banned ‘return hubs’ in third countries, specifying that migrants could only be sent back to their home countries or countries they had transited on their way to the EU – with these countries’ consent.
This directive was overruled in June with the passage of the Return Regulation. The regulation allows for the establishment of return hubs and the detention of illegal immigrants pending removal, and forces individual member states to recognize deportation orders issued in other states.
We’ve just concluded the final negotiations on the Return Regulation - and we have a deal.
We now have longer detention, real entry bans, and return hubs in third countries.
The era of deportations has begun.
If you try to enter Europe illegally — you will never make Europe… pic.twitter.com/tncWDVt6Wu
Could migrants cheat the system?
However, while the regulation allows for the use of return hubs, their use will be optional. “It should be noted that the establishment of return hubs under the regulation is not mandatory and that it will be up to individual member states to determine whether they will seek to establish such an arrangement with a third country,” Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan said during a parliamentary debate on the issue in July.
As such, the EU’s returns policy will likely remain fragmented. Even if a member state negotiates a return hub arrangement with a third country, as Italy de-facto did with its establishment of processing centers in Albania in 2024, a migrant would be able to evade capture and deportation by entering the EU via a country with more lax immigration policies, such as Ireland or Spain.
This fragmentation is clearly a source of frustration for Weber, who argued that the EU’s external border control agency, Frontex, should be given the power to enforce the bloc’s migration laws where individual states fail.
“Independent, unannounced checks at Europe's border crossings to verify compliance with EU border protection law must become standard practice,” he wrote. “And it's also clear: if national authorities are unwilling to protect our borders, then Frontex must be given command authority. European laws must be upheld, if necessary, by the European border protection service. “
“At the next regular European Council meeting, we therefore need a binding implementation plan – with clear responsibilities, fixed deadlines, and verifiable targets.”
What do EU courts say about deportation?
If Weber gets his way and the EU’s 27 members synchronize their deportation policies, one major obstacle remains: the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). This Strasbourg-based court is tasked with interpreting the European Convention on Human Rights, which explicitly states that “no one may be removed, expelled or extradited to a state where there is a serious risk that he or she would be subjected to the death penalty, torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.”
In 2018, the court ruled that member states may not deport migrants to a third country where they would be at risk of deportation to a fourth country that may be unsafe, a practice known as “refoulement.” The 2018 case involved two Bangladeshi migrants who had entered Hungary via Serbia. The ECHR ruled that Hungary had broken the law by deporting the migrants back to Serbia, as the Hungarian authorities could not adequately prove that Serbia would not send them somewhere else afterwards.
Under Weber’s proposed system, the EU would still have to prove that migrants sent to African hubs would be “guaranteed access to reception facilities adapted to their specific vulnerabilities,” and would not be at risk of refoulement, a tall order in some of the states floated as potential hub locations: Ghana, Senegal, and Uganda. The EU does not consider these countries “safe,” meaning any effort to transfer migrants there could instantly be stricken down by the ECHR.
Have migrant return hubs been tried before?
As mentioned above, Italy signed a bilateral agreement with Albania in 2023, and two Italian-run detention centers opened on Albanian soil the following year. However, these were offshore processing centers rather than return hubs, and were intended as temporary facilities where adult males intercepted in international waters en route to Italy would have their asylum claims processed. Single adult males made up 74% of migrants arriving on Italian shores at the time.
The legality of the centers was immediately challenged in Italian courts, and at the Court of Justice of the European Union. Out of just 24 migrants transferred to the centers since October 2024, all have since been taken to Italy after Italian judges refused to validate their detention.
The UK also tried to offshore its migrant problem with the Rwanda scheme, set up in 2022. Under this plan, certain illegal immigrants would be sent to Rwanda to have their asylum claims processed. If successful, the migrants would be granted asylum in Rwanda, rather than the UK.
However, the UK Supreme Court declared the scheme unlawful in 2023, ruling that Rwanda could wrongfully reject claims and transfer migrants to unsafe countries. The ruling explicitly cited ECHR guidance on the subject. Although the UK is no longer a member of the EU, it is still a party to the European Convention on Human Rights.
Britain’s Conservative government challenged this ruling, signing an agreement with Rwanda in which the latter vowed to bring its asylum system up to British standards. Ultimately, the scheme was ended when Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer took power in 2024. The UK paid the Rwandan government £290 million ($391 million) in total before the scheme was scrapped, and not a single deportation flight departed for Rwanda.
Has anyone asked the Africans?
In addition to overcoming its own courts, and opposition from recalcitrant member states, the EU faces another problem in implementing a migrant return plan: how to secure African support. Rwanda agreed to the British plan only after London offered generous bribes: £370 million in development aid, another £120 million once 300 people had been relocated, and £150,000 for each migrant housed for five years. Weber, at least publicly, has only offered trade incentives and “economic cooperation.”
EU officials have not commented on negotiations with officials in Africa, although the idea of placing return hubs on the continent has been opposed by the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, the African Union, and officials in individual African nations.
Speaking to AFP in April, a European diplomat said that some African leaders have expressed contempt at the idea of being treated as a “geographical dump area” for people rejected by the EU.

"I'm sort of negotiating," Trump told Real America's Voice in a phone interview released late on Monday. "They're very devious negotiators."
Since the conflict began in late February, Trump has repeatedly oscillated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.
Pakistan said on Tuesday the US and Iran were close to "some sort" of deal, and Qatar said talks on managing the Strait of Hormuz were at an advanced stage, despite reports of new attacks on shipping in regional waters.
‘I'm their banker’

"Economically, they are a mess. They can't borrow money. We control their money, what they had, which is a lot. They had a lot, and we have total control of it. I'm their banker," he said, referring to frozen Iranian assets.
Another option would be to "Hit them really, really hard," Trump said.
Trump also shrugged off concerns of low munitions, saying the US was "building them like crazy" and cast blame on his predecessor, former US President Joe Biden.
Media reported last week that the US Army has used up much of its stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles during the war, raising concerns about the military's readiness for future conflicts.
"We're fine with munitions... But the reason it would be lower, and we're building them like crazy, but the reason it's low is because he (Biden) gave $300 billion worth to Ukraine," Trump said.

Konovalets’ remains to undergo series of scientific examinations upon return to Ukraine — Vereshchuk
She made these remarks in Rotterdam in comments to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Today’s event is extremely important, especially now that Ukraine is once again fighting for its independence. This is not merely the return of Yevhen Konovalets’ remains to his homeland. It is the restoration of our historical memory and the reestablishment of historical justice,” Vereshchuk said.
She also noted that upon their return to Ukraine, Konovalets’ remains will undergo a comprehensive series of modern scientific examinations.
“We want to utilize all the scientific knowledge and technology at our disposal to document history as thoroughly as possible. CT scans, MRIs, and other necessary procedures will be performed. Experts, historians, and anthropologists will be involved, and everything necessary will be done to leave our descendants with the most accurate evidence possible,” Vereshchuk noted.
The deputy head of the Office of the President of Ukraine emphasized that this is the first time such procedures have been carried out in Ukraine, and that the government plans to apply this approach to other prominent Ukrainians as well.
“This applies not only to Yevhen Konovalets. We have plans to repatriate other prominent Ukrainians: military figures, writers, and cultural figures. We want to establish a systematic approach to preserving our historical heritage,” she stated.
Following the completion of the scientific procedures, religious services will be held by the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. Vereshchuk noted that Konovalets was a Greek Catholic and came from a family with a centuries-old tradition of priestly service: “He had Greek Catholic priests on both his father’s and mother’s sides. It was the Church in Galicia that combined spirituality, education, and national consciousness. That is why his return holds such profound significance for the UGCC.”
Vereshchuk emphasized that the Ukrainian military had been eagerly awaiting Konovalets’ return.
“We’ve already mentioned today the military units named in honor of Yevhen Konovalets. His ideas regarding the creation of a Ukrainian army, discipline, responsibility, and strategic thinking continue to live on today in the Armed Forces of Ukraine,” she noted.
Following the church services, a state ceremony for Konovalets’ reburial will take place.
“The reburial will be attended by the President of Ukraine, the government, parliament, and military officials. This will be the highest form of state honor for a man who dedicated his life to the struggle for Ukraine’s freedom,” the official emphasized.
The exact date of the ceremony is not being announced for security reasons; however, according to Vereshchuk, it will take place in the near future, and a memorial site in honor of Yevhen Konovalets will remain at the “Crooswijk” cemetery in Rotterdam.
“I would like to thank Andrii Kostin, Ukraine’s ambassador to the Netherlands, and his team. They have already carried out the necessary work with the Dutch authorities. The burial site will remain in Ukraine, and a commemorative plaque will be installed there,” she said, noting that the memorial will serve as a place of remembrance for the Ukrainian community in the Netherlands and for official delegations visiting Rotterdam.
“We want the community to be able to continue coming here to honor the memory of Yevhen Konovalets. This will be part of a broader state project to commemorate outstanding Ukrainians abroad,” Vereshchuk added.
As reported by Ukrinform, the remains of Colonel Yevhen Konovalets were exhumed at the “Crooswijk” cemetery in Rotterdam.

Russia’s jam-resistant drones run on a Chinese modem no one has sanctioned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:30:38 UTC
02:30:38 KST

The radio that makes Russia's strike drones resistant to Ukrainian jamming is a Chinese-made part sold openly, and the company that makes it has escaped the sanctions hitting the rest of the drone supply chain, the OSINT group Frontelligence Insight found. The part, a mesh radio modem, has been pulled from downed Russian drones even as Western and Ukrainian sanctions expanded to cover the engines, navigation, motors, cameras, and chips around it.
Russia's war on Ukraine now runs on drones built largely from Chinese parts—a flow China keeps open to Moscow while restricting the same goods to Kyiv.
The part that isn't on any list
The modem is the XK-F358 mesh radio made by Shenzhen Xingkai Technology Co., Ltd. of Guangdong. It sells openly online. The company's Made-in-China storefront lists it at $8,100 to $9,000 apiece, and Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov previously put the price near $7,000.
Ukraine and its partners have sanctioned Chinese suppliers of drone engines, navigation receivers, motors, cameras, and chips—one Ukrainian round aimed explicitly at parts for drones built to bypass electronic warfare—but not the radios.
Ukraine finds uranium in six more Russian drones. Their radiation readings ran up to 80 times background
Recovered from downed drones, and hard to jam
Ukraine's Defense Intelligence photographed an XK-F358 recovered from a downed Geran-5, and Beskrestnov photographed another taken from a Gerbera, Militarnyi reported on 19 January 2026.
The modem uses COFDM modulation and a mesh design in which each unit relays traffic for the rest, so packets reroute automatically when a node drops.
The same modem also turns up under a second name—HX-50, in a more industrial variant—and its use is no experiment: it spread onto Russia's Shahed-136/Geran-2 strike drones from July 2025 and reached serial integration by early September.
The network keeps working after losing roughly 80% of its nodes and can link drones across more than 100 kilometers, or up to 600 in relay chains, according to Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian defense adviser who has examined the recovered units. That is why conventional jamming struggles against it: an attacker has to suppress every node at once rather than break a single link.
What sanctions cover, and what they skip
Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) has sanctioned Chinese makers of navigation receivers, motors, cameras, and chips. The US Treasury designated Xiamen Limbach and Redlepus in October 2024, the EU added Shenzhen Minghuaxin in June 2026. No maker of radio or data-link modems appears among them.
None of the four sanctions regimes that have pursued Russia's Chinese drone suppliers—the US, EU, UK, and Ukraine—lists Shenzhen Xingkai, a direct check of each register by Euromaidan Press confirms.
US sanctions 13 Iran-Belarus-China entities supplying Iran’s IRGC. That’s three of four “Axis of Upheaval” states
The gap cuts both ways. Ukrainian battalion commanders and industry sources put the share of parts in a standard Ukrainian FPV drone—batteries, motor magnets, fiber-optic cable—at up to 65% Chinese-made, and Ukraine buys from Shenzhen too.
Cutting one supplier, then the next
Tatarigami, who founded Frontelligence Insight, argues the fix is to extend controls beyond individual firms to the entire chain—down to the optical fiber, the reels it ships on, and the machines that make it. Fiber-optic drones already make up about 60% of Russian FPVs in key sectors, Euromaidan Press reports. The record on firm-by-firm designation is discouraging: after Washington hit Xiamen Limbach, Beijing Xichao took over the engine shipments, Reuters found, and Kupol's Garpiya order climbed from 2,000 drones in 2024 to more than 6,000 this year. But among all component categories in a Geran drone, the one that enables jam-resistant control is the only one absent from the registers.
“They hit what was in parking lot”: Russian drone operator adapted strike on Ukraine’s largest online retailer’s warehouse in real time
What controls can reach, and what they can't
Xingkai also markets the modem for civilian work—mining, firefighting, maritime. And as the Xichao case shows, cutting off one company rarely halts the flow.
China's foreign ministry claims it knew nothing of the parts exports, says it controls dual-use goods under its own law, and rejects sanctions it calls baseless.
The harder problem is that the same civilian electronics feeding Russia also stock Ukraine's drone lines, so any workable control has to reach named military buyers without severing the dual-use trade Kyiv still needs. And sanctions may not decide this contest at all: Ukraine is already testing electronic-warfare methods built to break the very mesh networks these radios create.

Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:30:14 UTC
02:30:14 KST

It was last year that Martin Lewis, the money-saving guru, advised the government to find “100 small things that piss people off” and set about sorting them out.
That approach has been adopted almost immediately by Andy Burnham since entering office, as he began his programme of “everyday fixes” to tackle problems that can be dealt with through minor policy tweaks.
Labour strategists say the philosophy behind this is to show that Burnham notices the frustrations of people’s lives, and that he will be decisive about improving these issues.
This started with scrapping VAT on electricity bills and capping bus fares. His latest policy assault is on garish signs on the high street and everything from excessive vape and betting shops to subscriptions that auto-renew without warning.
It is applying to politics the “broken window” theory of crime that suggests clamping down on small-scale antisocial behaviour such as littering can help discourage more serious crime.
As much as anything, Burnham’s moves against rip-off Britain should be a warning to companies that the government is paying attention to their behaviour towards voters, as he mulls over how far to go with a programme of increasing public control over essential services.
The intention is a long way from Keir Starmer’s promise to be a government that treads more lightly on people’s lives, as the new prime minister has taken a bet that voters want leaders who are active about everyday frustrations as well as embarking on major structural reform.
Burnham’s instinct to show the public that he is prepared to act on their behalf is a sound one, according to Peter Kellner, the pollster and former chair of YouGov, who has written recently about the difficulty of winning round “ungrateful voters”.
“Probably the best any government can do in the short run – short of some educational programme about where our taxes go – is gain the perception that they as politicians are on the voters’ sides. This is the key to the Burnham bounce. Plainly the amounts of money involved on bus fares and VAT and so on are small in the great order of things.
“But they are part of a story about where Burnham stands in relation to the responsibility of the government to look after people. How long this lasts I don’t know because we have yet to see what’s in the budget. And if at the end of the day they announce tax rises, then that changes. But if I were his communications adviser, this is what I would have advised him to do.”
He said Tony Blair and Margaret Thatcher successfully told the stories of their premierships in their first five to six years, and that Burnham needs to do something similar in terms of building a narrative. “What we have yet to see is Burnham joining the dots of what he’s done so far. And it’s got to be something clearer than Starmer saying life is difficult and we are doing the best we can and we want to make Britain fairer and more prosperous,” Kellner says.
However, there is also a risk for Burnham that hailing small changes as achievements will veer into the dreaded territory of consumer gimmicks that American strategist David Axelrod warned against.
The former Obama adviser, who was drafted in to help Ed Miliband’s 2015 campaign, memorably branded Labour’s approach on the cost of living in that election as: “Vote Labour and win a microwave”. In other words, it was a consumer retail offer of short-term bargains without an overarching big and inspiring message to pull it all together.
Another cautionary tale can be found in the fate of the Joe Biden and Kamala Harris administration. Together they targeted price gouging and unfair consumer practices. But while the overall economy began to improve under Biden, voters never give the US government credit for small changes like holding down medicine bills and expanded child tax credits because they were unhappy about the lasting effects of food and housing costs inflation that had an effect globally.
It will be a test for Burnham how far he can reap the rewards of dealing with consumer frustrations at a time when he has little room for bigger giveaways to help with the cost of living while the economy is barely growing.
Burnham must also guard against a third possible peril: the potential for mockery if the issues seem too inconsequential for a prime minister to be bothering with – in the vein of John Major’s “cones hotline” for people to report nuisance roadworks.
The new prime minister, however, seems aware of these pitfalls. He is openly flagging the policies as small wins – while promising bigger structural change to take place in the longer term on social care and public ownership of utilities.
Labour was also ready to paint Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, as out of touch when she tried to ridicule the cost of living policies by saying: “Is that it? The problems go way beyond bus fares and VAT on bills.”
Polling so far seems to suggest that voters are tentatively impressed and moving back towards Labour at a time when both Reform UK and the Greens are sliding. However, the latest data from Ipsos Mori says seven in 10 remain dissatisfied with the way the government is running the country. While they make think Burnham is outperforming the other parties and a substantial number feel he is on their side compared with other leaders, voters are still going to take some convincing that the new prime minister really will be able to change their lives for the better.

Russia Releases Ex-US Marine Robert Gilman After 4 Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:30:00 UTC
02:30:00 KST

Russia released former US Marine Robert Gilman from captivity on Tuesday, Aug. 11, freeing him from detention “for humanitarian reasons.”
Gilman was found in extremely poor health, with Massachusetts Senator Edward Markey describing him as “essentially catatonic.” He was also battling a “severe case of pneumonia.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Gilman was flown on a US plane to Washington, DC, according to BBC News, citing Kirill Dmitriev, special envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor – a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat,” Markey said in his official statement.
Four-year ordeal in Russian custody
Gilman, originally from Massachusetts, was 28 when Russian authorities arrested him for allegedly kicking a police officer while intoxicated aboard a train to Voronezh.
He was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in prison, and his sentence was extended to 10 years in 2024 after Russian state media accused him of assaulting prison staff – a claim his family and advocacy groups have rejected.
His father, Vladimir Gilman, has also denied the allegations.
In 2024, he wrote an opinion piece explaining that his son became ill during the incident and accidentally kicked the officer, who was not injured and later dropped the complaint.
“Throughout his detention, Robert was subjected to physical torture, forced medication, and provocations by Russian authorities,” Markey said.
Russian Strikes Hit Kramatorsk Church, Sloviansk Market, 4 Injured
“There is no doubt that his treatment by Russian authorities is the reason Robert is in this precarious state today,” he continued.
According to his family, Gilman was forcefully injected with mind-altering substances that eventually led to his current deteriorating mental state.
Health crisis prompted urgent calls for release
By late June, Gilman had been transferred from a prison hospital in the Voronezh region to the psychiatric ward of a civilian emergency hospital roughly 550 kilometers (about 342 miles) from Moscow, according to RBC-Ukraine.
Advocacy group Global Reach and the Foley Foundation had warned on Aug. 7 that Gilman was near death, unable to communicate, and being fed through a tube, prompting the White House and State Department to press Moscow for his release on medical grounds.
Family credits Trump for Gilman’s return
According to Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer of the advocacy group Global Reach, Gilman’s family was denied access to visit him, despite Russian court orders allowing access.
“I am more afraid for my brother than I have been since this horrible nightmare started,” Gilman’s sister, Lexie Hudson, said in her earlier statement.
“There is no other reason that Robert is alive today, other than that [US] President [Donald] Trump heard about the case and took action,” she said on Tuesday, according to BBC News.
Case had strained already tense relations
Gilman was reportedly one of at least 10 Americans known to be held in Russian custody.
His deteriorating condition had added to already strained US-Russia relations, burdened by the war in Ukraine and the Middle East conflict, as well as other diplomatic disputes. A source familiar with the matter told Reuters that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised Gilman’s case with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during their meeting in Manila on July 23. The source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said it was unclear how Lavrov responded.
“I urge the Trump administration to use Robert’s case as motivation to continue to advocate for the release of others wrongfully detained in Russia and around the world,” Markey said, wishing Gilman a recovery “from this nightmare.”
