US vaccination executive order: making sense of it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

Making sense of Trump's executive order on US vaccinations
August 11, 2026
US President Donald Trump signed another executive order on Monday, August 10, 2026: "Delivering gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for Americans."
The order reduces the current recommendation of 18 vaccines for children down to 11, which puts it almost in line with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations.
As DW reported in May 2025, there are vaccines against 30 infectious diseases. The World Health Organization recommends that every child get vaccinated against 12 of those:
- Tuberculosis
- Hepatitis B
- Polio
- Diphtheria
- Tetanus
- Pertussis (whooping cough)
- Haemophilus influenza type B
- Pneumococcal disease
- Rotavirus
- Measles
- Rubella
- Human papillomavirus
This is the WHO making recommendations for all nations — both rich and poor.
Many poor countries face challenges around access to vaccines at prices they can afford and distributing them safely to people living in remote areas.
Rich countries, on the other hand, can afford and therefore usually offer more vaccinations than the WHO's base level of 12. But not all of them do.
Germany, for example, recommends 14 vaccinations for children in their first two years after birth.
Germany no longer recommends the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis (TB), which is on the WHO list. It does recommend vaccination against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which is not on the WHO list.
This just goes to show that there are variations around the world. It's not just the US. These variations often depend on which diseases are considered by local health experts to be an ongoing threat to any given community.
Taking the example of TB in Germany: In 1998, the country's Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) decided the risk of TB infections was low, and herd immunity was deemed high enough at 50-80%. Therefore the STIKO stopped recommending the vaccine.
What does Trump's new childhood vaccine recommendation say?
Trump wants to create three distinct categories for vaccination.
The first category includes immunizations recommended for all children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b (meningitis), pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella (smallpox).
That removes vaccination against hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza and RSV from this baseline category that were on the recommended list until now.
These illnesses however can still affect newborns. As we reported in 2022, cases of RSV have risen in the US and Europe. Babies who don't receive the vaccine would remain unprotected against the illness.
By contrast, Germany recommends vaccination for RSV, rotavirus and hepatitis B in a child's first six months.
Trump's executive order also recommends that the combined MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella — which is a global standard — be split into individual jabs, spaced over time.
This appears to be a reflection on long-held rhetoric from the Trump administration suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine causes autism. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says there is no published evidence to suggest there is any benefit in single jabs.
In fact, its advice on the MMR vaccine states that "the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) agree that MMR vaccine is not responsible for recent increases in the number of children with autism."
But Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long suggested vaccines are dangerous in general.
Kennedy also thinks that the common painkiller Tylenol causes autism when taken during pregnancy. It is the only painkiller allowed during pregnancy in the US. And as we reported in September 2025, no high-quality scientific evidence substantiated their claim.
Trump's second category would include immunizations for high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue.
The third would include vaccines to be given "based on shared clinical decision-making" — so, doctor and patient or parent of a patient would have to agree. These include: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19.
The effect of political — rather than scientific — rhetoric on vaccines
While there's no direct recommendation to ban any vaccine, the second Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to destabilize public consensus over vaccination.
That can cause confusion in the community and rising rates of infection. For example, in July 2026, DW reported how "amnesia" about measles and how dangerous it is had led to a rise in measles infections in the US. People had missed opportunities to get vaccinated because infection rates had been low, but then they rose again.
This is not just the case in North America. Germany has also seen measles infections rise, with experts citing anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Allowing bird flu to spread
Kennedy however takes his hands-off rhetoric to farming communities, too. In March 2025, DW reported how the health secretary suggested bird flu should be allowed to spread through bird populations, even in places where it had already infected cattle.
Kennedy said it would enable researchers to develop "super" chickens. But instead, more than 150 million birds got infected. Bird flu virus was detected in raw milk. And there were bird-to-human infections as well.
On Monday, when Trump's executive order was released, the AAP's Andrew Racine said it was "not based on 'gold-standard science.' There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance."
Edited by: Carla Bleiker

Trump's second category would include immunizations for high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue.
The third would include vaccines to be given "based on shared clinical decision-making" — so, doctor and patient or parent of a patient would have to agree. These include: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19.
The effect of political — rather than scientific — rhetoric on vaccines
While there's no direct recommendation to ban any vaccine, the second Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to destabilize public consensus over vaccination.
That can cause confusion in the community and rising rates of infection. For example, in July 2026, DW reported how "amnesia" about measles and how dangerous it is had led to a rise in measles infections in the US. People had missed opportunities to get vaccinated because infection rates had been low, but then they rose again.
This is not just the case in North America. Germany has also seen measles infections rise, with experts citing anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Allowing bird flu to spread
Kennedy however takes his hands-off rhetoric to farming communities, too. In March 2025, DW reported how the health secretary suggested bird flu should be allowed to spread through bird populations, even in places where it had already infected cattle.
Kennedy said it would enable researchers to develop "super" chickens. But instead, more than 150 million birds got infected. Bird flu virus was detected in raw milk. And there were bird-to-human infections as well.
On Monday, when Trump's executive order was released, the AAP's Andrew Racine said it was "not based on 'gold-standard science.' There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance."
Edited by: Carla Bleiker

The World Curling Board has extended the suspension of adult Russian athletes from international competitions until the end of 2026, taking into account IOC recommendations. The Russian Curling Federation is challenging this decision at the CAS.
The World Curling Federation Council (World Curling) has decided to extend the suspension of adult Russian athletes from international competitions through the end of 2026, UNN reports, citing the NOC.
Details
In making its decision, World Curling took into account the latest recommendations of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the positions of national federations that are World Curling members, as well as those of the organizers of international competitions scheduled for 2026.
Following its consideration, the World Curling Council concluded that the return of adult Russian athletes to international competitions would currently create significant risks to the integrity of competitions. The federation emphasized its responsibility to hold tournaments in a safe and fair environment for all participants.
The suspension of Russian adult athletes from international curling competitions has been in effect since 2022. At the same time, in January 2026, World Curling allowed Russian and Belarusian juniors to return to international competitions. This decision did not apply to adult national teams, whose suspension remained in effect.
The federation separately reported that the Russian Curling Federation is challenging its suspension at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). A decision in the case is expected in the near future.
The NOC emphasized that World Curling's decision represents a consistent and responsible position of the international federation. As long as Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine continues, maintaining restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes in international competitions remains an important demonstration of the principled position of the international sports community and its solidarity with Ukraine.

Evergrande wins HK$6b debt-recovery case after court rejects ‘fabricated’ claims
Debt stemmed from March 2021, when Evergrande subsidiary State Hero reached agreement to lend HK$5 billion to Yingjia International
A Hong Kong court has ruled in favour of embattled conglomerate Evergrande in a debt-recovery case, allowing it to recoup about HK$6 billion (US$764.7 million) from a third party after a judge found the borrower’s arguments against enforcement of the loan were “fabricated”.
In a High Court judgment handed down on Friday and seen by the South China Morning Post, Judge Linda Chan dismissed an injunction application filed by Yingjia International Properties to restrain offshore entity State Hero Holdings from presenting a winding-up petition against it.
The court also rejected Yingjia’s separate bid for an interim injunction to block State Hero from filing the winding‑up petition pending a possible appeal.
State Hero is an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of China Evergrande Group, which is now controlled by court-appointed liquidators.
It served a statutory demand on February 13 this year on Yingjia International requiring the repayment of HK$5.97 billion in loan principal and accrued interest.
The court heard that the debt stemmed from March 2021, when State Hero reached an agreement in Hong Kong to lend HK$5 billion to Yingjia International, repayable in a single tranche within two years to avoid interest. Failure to repay by the deadline would trigger annual interest at 4 per cent.

US primaries in Minnesota and Wisconsin offer fresh test of Democrats' progressive surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:00:19 UTC
00:00:19 KST

Democratic voters across several US states are heading to the polls in another test of whether the party's progressives or leftists can extend a run of primary victories into races that could help decide control of Congress in November midterms.
The most consequential contest on Tuesday is in Minnesota, where progressive Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan faces congresswoman Angie Craig for the Democratic nomination to replace retiring Senator Tina Smith.
Flanagan has the backing of Smith and prominent left-wing senators including Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, while Craig is supported by Democrats who argue her record winning competitive elections makes her the safer choice for the general election.
"Special interests think they can buy this Senate seat. They've spent $20 million to do it," Flanagan posted on X ahead of polls opening.
"But I have seen what Minnesotans can do when we organize together. So when it comes down to the many or the money, I'm betting on us."
Their clash mirrors a wider argument inside the party over how aggressively to move left as Democrats try to regain Congress.
Immigration enforcement has become particularly charged in Minnesota after the state emerged as a focal point of government’s crackdown.
Flanagan has attacked Craig over her support for the Laken Riley Act, a Republican-backed immigration measure, while Craig has emphasised electability and later expressed regret over her vote.
The elections follow Abdul El-Sayed's narrow victory last week over democratic establishment-backed Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, which energised progressives but also exposed how unreliable polling can be in low-turnout contests.
Wisconsin race
Wisconsin provides another major test of the left, though in a gubernatorial rather than congressional race.
Democratic socialist Francesca Hong is widely seen as the frontrunner for the party's nomination for governor, despite unease among establishment Democrats and even some leftists over whether she can win a closely divided state in November.
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley has become the principal moderate alternative, while Sanders and leftist star congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — usually eager to boost insurgents — have notably stayed out of the race.
Hong's candidacy has nevertheless become a symbol of the same leftward pressure that has already toppled established Democrats in New York, Colorado and Michigan.
Republicans have eagerly seized on those victories, with Trump increasingly portraying November's elections as a choice between Republican "common sense" and what he calls socialist or communist extremism.
South Carolina seat
Republicans, meanwhile, have their own test of party loyalty in South Carolina.
Senator Darline Graham, appointed after the death of her brother Lindsey Graham, is seeking the Republican nomination for a full term with Trump's endorsement.
She faces a crowded field including congressmen Ralph Norman and Russell Fry and former governor Mark Sanford, with a runoff later this month considered likely if no candidate reaches 50 percent.
Trump held a telephone rally for Graham on Monday, calling her the "perfect person" to carry on her brother's legacy, but rivals have attacked her lack of political experience and argued that she inherited her position rather than earned it.
"Look, the United States Senate is no place for on-the-job training," Fry said last during a primary debate last week. "I didn't inherit a record. I earned it."
The South Carolina seat is safely Republican, limiting its importance for control of Congress.
The left vs. centre theme is also on display in Democratic primaries in multiple states voting on Tuesday, with other significant race in places like Alabama.
Voters in four of Alabama's seven congressional districts will select US House nominees under a new map that eliminates one of the state's two majority-Black districts currently represented by Democrats.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine's Health Ministry plan to regulate private MRI, CT centers threatens patient access – experts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:00:12 EEST
00:00:12 KST

The Health Ministry's initiative to ban private MRI and CT centers operating on the premises of municipal hospitals in Ukraine from receiving payments directly from patients threatens patients' access to diagnostic imaging, participants in a press conference held at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Tuesday said.
"Modern diagnostic imaging is much more than simply having a CT or MRI machine at a medical facility. Over many years, private diagnostic centers have built strong teams of radiologists. They invest not only in purchasing and maintaining equipment, but also in physician training, developing specialized protocols, consultations in complex cases and quality control. Not every hospital has enough specialists or the necessary clinical experience to perform the full range of complex examinations," said Anna Kravets, medical director of Apparatus Medicine LLC.
She said that "for patients, it is not enough simply to find an available scanner."
"Public and private medicine should not be pitted against each other. They have different capabilities and different tasks that should complement each other. The state's task is to establish uniform, transparent rules. We support the Health Ministry's effort to prevent double payments; at the same time, this issue can be resolved through electronic record-keeping, clear information for patients, a distinction between free and paid services, and monitoring of every examination," she said.
For his part, Oleksandr Haidabas, director general of Expert Medical Diagnostic Center, said that the bill presented by the Health Ministry "harms both patients and businesses."
"During four years of war, we have not stopped developing our network, upgrading equipment and expanding. Over four years, we have invested UAH 203 million, including UAH 60 million in the reconstruction of premises. The premises we leased were neglected; they had stood in disrepair for decades. After we reconstructed them, they became modern buildings with all engineering systems, providing services to people. All our centers are located on property owned by local communities; when the lease term expires, this property remains with the community," he said.
Haidabas noted that private diagnostic imaging centers provide a backup for medical facilities in the event of breakdowns of state-owned or municipal equipment and make it possible to provide medical services without interruption.
"We are also against charging patients twice. Therefore, we need to put things in order and develop a transparent mechanism that prevents corruption. If we are told to conclude a contract only with the hospital where we are located, this could lead to corruption, because the chief physician would decide whether to refer patients to us or not, and whether to transfer funds to us for services provided or not," he said.
Haidabas believes that "a quota could be developed, direct contracts could be concluded with diagnostic centers, tariffs of the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU) for diagnostic imaging could be introduced, and quotas could be allocated according to these transparent tariffs and the center's capacity. In this way, the Health Ministry would reduce the waiting list and people would not have to wait in line for months."
"If we scare away investors, no investor will come here tomorrow. Both patients and the state stand to lose from the proposed bill," he said.
Responding to a question from Interfax-Ukraine, Haidabas said that the bill proposed by the Health Ministry provides for no compensation to private diagnostic imaging centers if they are prohibited from operating on the premises of state-owned and municipal medical facilities.
For her part, Anna Kulyk, executive director of the Association of Private Medical Institutions of Ukraine (APMI), said that the Health Ministry explains its legislative initiative by "the need to 'protect' patients from double payments and strengthen control over referrals," while the wording of the bill could effectively block any lawful ways of paying for diagnostic services, from voluntary health insurance and employers' corporate programs to assistance from charitable foundations, international organizations or clinical trial sponsors.
"Many facilities do not have their own MRI or CT machines, and private centers have for years provided communities with the necessary diagnostic services. Restrictions on their operations could lead to longer waiting lists, which already reach several months, as well as loss of access to examinations and deterioration in the quality of medical care," the APMI director said.
Kulyk said that the model proposed by the Health Ministry "makes the hospital administration the sole purchaser of private diagnostic services, effectively depriving patients of the right to choose."
"Without additional funding, there is a risk that public facilities will not be able to provide the full range of examinations. The Health Ministry acknowledges a shortage of modern equipment in public hospitals, but at the same time proposes a model that could effectively dismantle the private diagnostic segment that helps compensate for this shortage," she said.
According to APMI calculations, purchasing one MRI machine and one CT scanner for a hospital costs at least UAH 75 million-107 million, while including the cost of premises reconstruction and servicing, the amount exceeds UAH 100 million.
"If replacing private infrastructure requires even 100 hospitals, this would mean at least UAH 10 billion in additional capital expenditures. The bill goes beyond combating double payments and creates a direct risk that private diagnostic centers operating in hospitals will cease to operate," Kulyk said.
She said that, as an alternative, APMI proposes "monitoring specific examinations and their sources of financing instead of imposing a blanket ban on lawful activities."
"Real control over public equipment, transparent waiting lists, accounting for every examination and accountability for hospital management for inefficient use of equipment must be ensured. The Health Ministry has not provided sufficient analytical data on the scale of double payments, the number of confirmed violations, or a causal link between the presence of a private center and the utilization of public equipment," the APMI director said.
For his part, Viktor Serdiuk, president of the All-Ukrainian Council for Patient Rights and Safety, said that "patients should not lose the right to choose a provider, the time of their examination and a lawful method of payment."
"The bill could increase waiting lists and restrict access to diagnostic services, particularly for military personnel, veterans, people with limited mobility and socially vulnerable patients. The Health Ministry needs to revise the draft so that it can actually stop patients from being charged twice, rather than creating new barriers to access to diagnostics. First and foremost, it should prohibit only duplicate payment for a specific service that has already been paid for by the NHSU, preserve insurance, charitable and private sources of financing without restricting lawful paid examinations, and introduce liability for established violations," he said.
As reported, in July the Health Ministry proposed amendments to Article 18 of the Fundamentals of Ukrainian Legislation on Health Care to prohibit private institutions leasing space in state-owned or municipal hospitals from charging patients directly for diagnostic imaging services. The ministry explained the initiative as part of efforts to combat the practice of forcing patients to pay for medical services that have already been paid for by the state under the Medical Guarantees Program (MGP).
According to the Health Ministry, 235 CT scanners worth more than UAH 3.36 billion have been supplied to Ukrainian medical facilities since 2020. Currently, Ukraine has a higher number of CT scanners per 1 million population than some European countries. At the same time, EU countries have a significantly higher number of examinations per scanner per day.
There are currently 749 CT scanners registered at Ukrainian medical facilities, including 496 used at facilities providing free medical care under the MGP. A total of 396 CT scanners operate at municipal medical facilities, another 58 CT scanners are in use at private facilities and 42 at state-owned facilities.

China’s hypersonic weapons can be guided by the stars if GPS fails: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:00:06 UTC
00:00:06 KST

China’s hypersonic weapons can be guided by the stars if GPS fails: report
Guangdong researchers build prototype star sensor after developing a way to accurately predict how starlight bends at extreme speeds
Hypersonic weapons are difficult to intercept, making them a key strategic asset in global competition, but they generally require navigation systems that are highly autonomous and precise.
Before the age of electronic instruments, sailors used tools like sextants to observe the sky and steer by the North Star.
Modern electronic systems can do something similar. By tracking the natural, predictable movements of stars, they can calculate a vehicle’s position and motion in space. This method is known as celestial navigation.
Unlike inertial systems that rely on ground stations or satellites, celestial navigation is completely self-contained and immune to external electromagnetic interference.

Feature: German city groans as water level of Rhine drops
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:59:57 CST
23:59:57 KST

FRANKFURT, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- River cruises have long been popular among tourists who can make a quick visit to towns along the river. Cities like Kaub, home to a famous castle right in the middle of the Rhine River called Pfalzgrafenstein, thrive on booming tourism business.
"Cruise passengers enjoy visiting our castles and tasting local delicacies," Bernd Vogt, mayor of the city Kaub, told Xinhua on Monday.
The 68-year-old who has been living in Kaub since his birth is concerned that fewer tourists are showing up in Kaub this year because the section of the river where Kaub is located has become barely navigable due to low water levels.
The long spell of dry weather is bringing down the water levels of Rhine River as extreme heat waves hit Europe this year. "I am 68 years old now, and I have never seen the river this low here before. I have never experienced temperatures of around 40 degrees (Celsius) here before."
The water level reading at the Kaub gauge stood at just 15 centimeters on Monday, breaking the previous record low set in 2018.
The measured water level does not represent the actual depth of the Rhine but the height of the river's surface relative to a fixed local reference point. It serves as the basis for determining the permissible cargo load for ships and is a crucial benchmark for assessing shipping capacity along the entire route.
On Monday, cargo ships and tourist vessels were almost entirely absent from the river, with only the ferry connecting the two shores still operating. However, even the ferry service was suspended starting from 8:00 p.m. local time.
As the waterway is blocked and local railway lines are undergoing renovation, visitors can only reach Kaub by bus or car, Vogt explained.
"We could see the number of ships on the Rhine decreasing daily, and now there are almost none. It's so hot, and with the railway renovation, far fewer tourists are coming to Kaub," a staff member at a biergarten in Kaub told Xinhua.
The closure of the iconic Pfalzgrafenstein Castle as a result of low water levels has dealt another blow to Kaub's tourism industry.
The low water levels are also driving up logistics costs along the Rhine River, which carries about 80 percent of Germany's inland waterway freight. Reduced shipping efficiency and capacity are impacting the delivery of raw materials and the shipment of industrial products for numerous chemical, steel, refining and energy companies along the river.
In a bid to alleviate the transport pressure caused by the low water levels, several federal states, including Lower Saxony, Rhineland-Palatinate, and North Rhine-Westphalia, have announced that they would temporarily relax Sunday and public holiday driving bans for trucks, encouraging businesses to shift some cargo originally transported by water to road transport.
What worries people like Vogt is that things could get worse before they improve.
The German Federal Institute of Hydrology has forecast that the water level at Kaub is very likely to drop below the 10-centimeter mark within the week, raising fears that the Rhine waterway could be effectively divided into two sections.
"If water levels fall any further, fewer and fewer vessels will be able to pass through this area. However, there are no official closures in place," said Fabian Spiess, deputy managing director of the Federal Association of German Inland Navigation (BDB), in a written interview with Xinhua.
If very few ships are operating in this area, the de facto result is that Rhine shipping is restricted to two separate sections: between the western North Sea ports and Koblenz in the north, and from Mainz southward in the south, Spiess elaborated.
"We are all hoping for rain now. But for the time being, there is no sign that the Rhine will rise again or that more activity will return to the river," Vogt said. ■

Russian grain exports risk dropping to a decade low in August due to shipping bottlenecks in southern ports caused by escalating attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, industry analysts warned Tuesday.
Agricultural consultancy SovEcon projects Russia will export between 3 million and 3.4 million metric tons of wheat this month — well below the five-year August average of 5 million tons and potentially marking the lowest August total since the 2016–17 agricultural season.
Independent consultancy ProZerno, meanwhile, forecasts that overall grain exports will fall to nearly 2.5 million metric tons amid severe congestion across the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. The five-year August average for grain exports is 5.7 million tons.
Russia, the world’s largest wheat exporter, and Ukraine, also a major agricultural exporter, have been attacking each other’s agricultural export facilities and commercial vessels in the Black Sea area in recent weeks, driving wheat prices higher on global markets.
The export logjam has left Russia’s domestic market oversupplied, driving local prices down by as much as 450 rubles ($5.46) per ton over the past week as farmers struggle to ship harvests abroad.
Despite foreign buyers backing away due to soaring shipping costs, Russia’s Agriculture Ministry announced it would raise the wheat export tax for the period between Aug. 12 and Aug. 18. The ministry noted that nationwide grain production has surpassed 72 million metric tons so far, including more than 60 million tons of wheat.
Meanwhile, the Institute for Agricultural Market Studies lowered its forecast for Russia’s overall 2026 grain harvest from 140 million to 138.5 million metric tons, while reducing its estimate for total export capacity in the 2026–27 season from 61.5 million to 60 million tons.
Russia’s main grain exporters union warned earlier this month that Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian ships and ports could shut down grain exports via the Black Sea in the near future, pushing up prices and causing hunger in Africa and the Middle East.

====================================================================================================

What is the FBI doing in Algiers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:58:15 UTC
23:58:15 KST

Breadcrumb
What is the FBI doing in Algiers?
A seemingly unassuming post on X by the U.S. Embassy in Algiers announced last month that an FBI law-enforcement attaché sub-office had opened.
Several Algerian media outlets reported the announcement. Some tried to explain what the office would do; others asked why the FBI was returning to Algiers now. However, to my surprise, the wider debate remained limited, as did the details of this new sub-office.
That said, this is likely because Algerian journalists have little freedom to interrogate decisions involving national security, foreign intelligence and sensitive diplomatic arrangements.
Old partners
It is important to point out that this isn’t the first time that the FBI has set up base in Algiers. The United States already had a full legal attaché office in Algeria following 9/11. Around 2010, when Algeria was considered safer and wealthier, it was moved to Tunisia, where Washington had a vested interest post-revolution.
The Tunisian authorities were also seeking support from several Western countries as they attempted to reform their judicial and security institutions, according to analyst Akram Kharief.
Nevertheless, the return of the FBI in Algeria is likely due to the efforts led by Ali Badaoui, who was appointed Director General of National Security in 2024. Soon after he started his role, the US was one of his major foreign engagements. He travelled there to meet with then head of the FBI’s New York Field Office, James Smith, to discuss transnational organised crime, law-enforcement cooperation and new operational methods.
This seems to fit into Badoui’s interest in extending practical police cooperation with foreign partners, including with Britain’s Home Office and National Crime Agency, Slovenia’s national police and Italy’s police leadership. The relationships cover biometric identification, criminal data exchange, forensic work, cybercrime, organised crime, and irregular migration.
What could Algeria gain?
In reality, criminal networks no longer respect national borders. Cybercrime, cryptocurrency fraud, terrorism financing, trafficking and money laundering frequently involve people, accounts and evidence spread across several countries.
A permanent FBI liaison officer could therefore make it easier for Algerian investigators to request information held in the US, trace suspicious financial transactions or coordinate cases involving American companies and digital platforms. The sub-office would be another liaison channel with the Algerian police, gendarmerie and ministry of justice.
Algerian authorities could also be seeking to benefit from the FBI’s specialist training and technical expertise.
Additionally, there may be a financial dimension to recent developments. Washington is possibly seeking to improve the international transparency of Algeria’s banking system. This would make sense given just last year Badoui was involved in the agreement signed between Algeria’s Directorate General of National Security (DGSN) and the Financial Intelligence Processing Unit over the exchange of information on money laundering, terrorist financing, and the financing of weapons proliferation.
Furthermore, when the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) decided to remove Algeria from its list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring, it was a highly mediatised event for the North African country.
The FBI sub-office was announced almost exactly one month later.
Whilst the timing does not prove that the two developments were part of the same agreement, it does suggest that financial crimes are likely to feature prominently in the new relationship.
Transparency?
Whilst partnerships related to policing and intelligence sharing may be increasingly common across borders, this does not remove the need for scrutiny.
There are several urgent questions that must be answered by Algerian authorities. Namely, what precise agreement governs the FBI’s activities in Algeria? Which Algerian institutions negotiated it? What information can be exchanged? Who authorises the release of citizens’ personal or financial data? Can information supplied to the FBI be passed to other American agencies or to a third country?
There is also the matter of parliamentary involvement in the FBI’s presence.
Not every form of diplomatic or police cooperation requires a parliamentary vote. Nevertheless, elected representatives should at least be able to establish the legal basis of a permanent foreign law-enforcement presence, the limits placed on it and the safeguards protecting Algerian citizens.
National security cannot be used to exclude the public and parliament from every discussion.
Ultimately, whilst the immediate reasons for the new FBI office may be operational rather than geopolitical, technical cooperation does not take place outside politics.
Even a limited American security presence fosters closer institutional relationships, regular exchanges and greater familiarity among officials on both sides.
This does lead us to question whether Algeria is therefore abandoning its traditional foreign policy or veering towards the Washington camp.
On the other hand, Algeria may simply be widening its diplomatic options and working with Washington where cooperation serves its interests. Nonetheless, Algerian authorities need to explain exactly what the country has agreed to, and who will ensure that the limits of the arrangement are respected.
Indeed, the FBI’s return is perhaps just a case of business as usual in diplomatic terms, but this does not make parliamentary scrutiny or public accountability any less necessary.

Israel ex-general says Gaza must remain in ruins for generations

2026-08-11

Breadcrumb
Israeli ex-general calls for Gaza to remain in ruins 'for generations'
A retired Israeli general who has repeatedly advocated making Gaza uninhabitable has called on Israel to prevent the territory from being rebuilt and instead leave it in ruins "for generations", as US-led efforts to bring the war to an end face growing resistance in Israel.
Maj-Gen (ret) Giora Eiland, a former head of Israel's National Security Council, condemned the Trump-backed Board of Peace's proposal to end the war as "very pro-Hamas" and urged the Israeli government to refuse to withdraw its forces from Gaza.
"Israel has no interest in Gaza being rebuilt. It is better for us if it remains destroyed for generations," Eiland said in a radio interview on Sunday.
"The greater the despair in Gaza, the greater the destruction, and the longer Gaza remains a monument to what they did on 7 October, the better."
His comments come as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejects the Board's 15-point plan and refuses to end attacks on Gaza or withdraw Israeli troops, which now occupy around 70% of the enclave.
The Board has belatedly called on Israel to comply with the ceasefire and withdraw to the Yellow Line, steps Hamas has set as conditions before it surrenders its weapons.
The Palestinian group's pledge to disarm has triggered a backlash among Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners, who fear that an agreement ending the war would kill off their ambitions to annex the territory.
Israel has largely ignored the October ceasefire agreement, continuing near-daily attacks on Gaza, expanding its occupation and maintaining heavy restrictions on aid shipments.
A history of genocidal statements
Eiland's latest remarks echo statements he made during the earliest weeks of the war, when he repeatedly argued that making life impossible for Gaza's civilian population should form part of Israel's military strategy.
He was among the most frequently quoted Israeli figures in South Africa's genocide case at the International Court of Justice, which cited statements by Israeli officials as evidence of alleged genocidal intent.
"Gaza will become an area where people cannot live," Eiland said in a radio interview on 12 October 2023, days after the war began, as he called for a "terrible, unbearable situation" to be imposed on the territory.
"Israel has no choice but to make Gaza a place that is temporarily, or permanently, impossible to live in," he later wrote in Yedioth Ahronoth.
The following month, Eiland went further, suggesting that the spread of "severe epidemics" could accelerate Gaza's collapse.
He also advocated the forced transfer of Palestinians from the territory, writing in the British pro-Israel journal Fathom that "the people should be told that they have two choices; to stay and to starve, or to leave".
Eiland has similarly erased the distinction between Palestinian civilians and combatants, describing "the entire Gaza population" as enemies of Israel.
Those ideas would later form the basis of a more formal proposal.
In 2024, Eiland was the lead author of the so-called "General's Plan", which proposed ordering civilians out of northern Gaza and treating those who remained as combatants.
The plan was ultimately not formally adopted, but its premise closely reflected the strategy Eiland had publicly advocated since the opening weeks of the war - applying overwhelming pressure on Gaza's civilians to force a the ingenuous population out.

76 draft workers charged with corruption since start of full-scale war; 2,500 illegal exemptions uncovered, police chief says
Seventy-six draft office workers have been charged in connection with 428 criminal cases involving the illegal evasion of military service investigated since Russia's full-scale invasion, acting National Police Chief Maksym Tsutskiridze said on Aug. 11.
Nationwide, the police has investigated the possible illegal exemption of nearly 2,500 military-eligible men, and annulled around 6,500 unlawful rulings by military medical commissions, Tsutskiridze said in comments to Ukrinform.
The cases involve illegal assistance with draft evasion, falsified medical certificates, and schemes to help men illegally cross the border despite being barred from leaving Ukraine under martial law.
Of those cases, 105 have been sent to court, while the rest remain under investigation, Tsutskiridze said.
Forced mobilization remains one of the greatest sources of social and political tension in Ukraine, as the military's need for the replenishment and rotation of combat units clashes with a reluctance to serve among much of the eligible male population not already in the armed forces' ranks.
While exemption letters are offered legally to those working in state structures, other essential roles or the defense industry, military-aged men looking to illegally avoid service have other options, including bribes paid for fake medical documents, removal from the register, or to leave Ukraine.
According to Tsutskiridze, police are concentrating resources on the areas of greatest risk — mobilization itself, deferment documents, and medical commission decisions — with an emphasis on thorough documentation, identifying all participants in a given scheme, and building files that will hold up in court, rather than simply increasing the number of cases opened.
The police chief added that the law "must apply equally" to conscripts and to officials responsible for mobilization or medical board rulings, and that no position, rank or resources should shield anyone from accountability.
At the same time, he stressed that accountability must be individualized and evidence-based, warning against letting the exposure of specific abuses turn into a blanket campaign against all draft officers or the annulment of legitimate rulings of medical commissions.
Law enforcement reportedly searched the offices of Ukraine's draft authorities and military medical commissions in Mukachevo, Zakarpattia Oblast, on Aug. 6 as part of an investigation into more than 1,000 alleged cases of men being illegally removed from the military register, Ukrainian media reported.

Total solar eclipse 2026: Where, when and how to watch on Wednesday?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:56:06 UTC
23:56:06 KST

Solar eclipse August 12: What time is it and where can you see it?
Millions will see the sun disappear as the eclipse sweeps from the Arctic to Europe, bringing two minutes of totality.
Today, millions of people across Europe will get the chance to experience their first total solar eclipse in 27 years.
Starting at 15:34 GMT, the brightness of the daylight hours will gradually be interrupted as the moon begins to block the sun, eventually turning day into sudden night for about two minutes along the path of totality.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Vietnam’s VinSpace announces deal with SpaceX to launch first satellite
- list 2 of 3Photos: ‘Blood moon’ rises during total lunar eclipse
- list 3 of 3Solar eclipse tracker: What time will it hit your location on August 12?
So which countries will see it? How do solar eclipses occur? Where and how can you watch it safely? In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera unpacks everything you need to know.
What time is the solar eclipse?
The time of the eclipse depends on where you are because the moon’s shadow will move across Earth’s surface from the Arctic towards Europe.
Here is how today’s eclipse will unfold:
- 15:34 GMT: The partial eclipse begins at the first location on Earth.
- 16:58 GMT: The total solar eclipse begins at the first location.
- 17:46 GMT: The eclipse reaches its maximum with totality lasting about two minutes and 18 seconds near the centre of its path.
- About 17:48 GMT: The eclipse reaches its maximum in Reykjavik, Iceland.
- About 18:27 GMT: Totality reaches Spain.
- 18:34 GMT: The total eclipse phase ends globally.
- 19:58 GMT: The partial eclipse ends at the last location on Earth.
Which countries will see the eclipse?
The path of totality, which is when the moon orbits in front of the sun and blocks its entire surface facing Earth, will cross northern Russia, Greenland and Iceland before sweeping across Spain and a small part of Portugal, bringing almost total darkness to about 15 million people.
A partial eclipse will be visible across much of Western Europe, parts of Northwest Africa, most of Canada and part of the northern United States. Overall, about 980 million people, nearly one in eight worldwide, might see the sun at least partly covered depending on weather conditions.
Will the eclipse be visible in Europe?
Most of Europe should see a partial eclipse in the evening around sunset.
In Paris, roughly 92 percent of the sun will be covered, in London 91 percent and in Berlin 85 percent.
For most European cities farther east, the sun will set before the eclipse reaches its maximum point, meaning the deepest part of the eclipse will never appear in the sky.
Will the eclipse be visible in the US and Canada?
Yes, but only as a partial eclipse.
In Canada, the northeastern city of St John’s, Newfoundland, will see about 53 percent coverage, dropping to 18 percent in Montreal and 8 percent in Toronto.
In the US, parts of Alaska will see the deepest eclipse in the country with about 37 percent of the sun covered in Fairbanks and 28 percent in Anchorage. Coverage will be much lower elsewhere in the US at about 24 percent in Bangor, Maine, 9 percent in New York and just 3 percent in Detroit, Michigan.
How long will the total solar eclipse last?
At the time of maximum eclipse, totality will last about two minutes and 18 seconds.
The duration will vary depending on the exact location.
In northern and eastern Spain, which will have prime viewing opportunities, the cities of Leon, Valladolid, Zaragoza, Teruel and Valencia are all located inside the path of totality.
Totality will begin at roughly 18:27 GMT in western Spain (8:27pm local time) and last for up to 110 seconds, depending on the exact location.
Madrid and Barcelona fall just outside this band, but observers there will still experience more than 99 percent solar coverage.
What happens during a solar eclipse?
A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes between Earth and the sun, temporarily blocking some or all of the sun’s light.
During a total solar eclipse, the moon completely covers the sun for those within the path of totality, briefly darkening the sky and revealing the sun’s outer atmosphere, known as the corona.
How to watch a solar eclipse safely
While eclipses are a spectacle to watch, looking directly at the sun can cause severe eye injury. For most of the eclipse, proper eye protection is essential. Here are some tips for what you should and shouldn’t do.
Do:
- Wear certified eclipse glasses or use a safe handheld solar viewer.
- Check glasses for scratches, tears or damage before using them. Supervise children using eclipse glasses.
- During a total eclipse, remove eye protection only when the moon completely covers the sun.
- Put it back on as soon as the sun begins to reappear.
Don’t:
- Use ordinary sunglasses, regardless of how dark they are. They do not provide enough protection during totality.
- Look at the sun through a camera, binoculars or telescope without a specialised solar filter.
- Use eclipse glasses with unfiltered cameras, binoculars or telescopes. Concentrated sunlight can burn through the filter and seriously damage your eyes.
Can you look at a solar eclipse without glasses?
There is only one exception: During the brief period of totality when the moon completely blocks the sun’s bright face, it is safe to look without eclipse glasses.
At all times outside totality, eye protection is required throughout the eclipse.
How to take photos safely
Pointing a camera directly at the sun can damage the sensor.
To ensure camera safety, the camera needs a proper solar filter. During the couple of minutes when the sun is 100 percent covered, the filter comes off and you can shoot bare.
The filter should go back on the instant the first bead of sunlight returns.
How can you watch the solar eclipse online?
NASA will livestream the solar eclipse on Wednesday starting at 17:15 GMT.
When will the next total solar eclipse be?
The next total solar eclipse will be on August 2 next year. It will cross southern Spain, North Africa, Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Italy’s Po river runs low as drought threatens farms and water supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:54:33 UTC
23:54:33 KST

At the confluence with the Ticino, boats now sit in shallow, muddy water surrounded by sand, algae and exposed gravel banks. The Po River Basin Authority says flows are well below seasonal averages, with levels at several monitoring stations approaching or exceeding records set during the severe drought of 2022.
The Po is vital to northern Italy’s agricultural heartland, including the Food Valley around Parma, where fruit, vegetables and rice depend on its water. Exceptionally low levels are also affecting supplies, with Ansa reporting tanker deliveries to more than 100 municipalities in Piedmont and Lombardy.
Around Pavia, the river has narrowed to a shallow channel, leaving large areas of riverbed exposed and making navigation increasingly difficult for leisure boats and rowing clubs. In the rice-growing Lomellina area, officials warn that the situation could worsen without significant rainfall, forcing farmers to rely increasingly on groundwater and emergency measures.
Further downstream, near Parma, tributaries and irrigation canals serving intensive fruit and vegetable farming are also running low. Farmers report that water rationing is already affecting irrigation schedules, while the basin authority has identified the stretch below Piacenza as particularly vulnerable as falling water levels expose tree trunks and other debris.
In Turin, the Po has been reduced to a slow-moving, algae-covered channel. Municipal crews have been using excavators mounted on barges to clear dense growth of invasive aquatic plants near the city centre. Regional data show that the river’s flow through Turin has fallen by more than half since June, while at the Sant’Antonio island monitoring station downstream, discharge has at times dropped to around a quarter of its normal level.
Officials warn that heat and low water are accelerating algae and invasive species, disrupting navigation and recreation. The prolonged heat has also worsened drought and wildfires across Europe, putting further pressure on water resources.

US and Morocco test a new cruise missile in the desert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:54:18 UTC
23:54:18 KST

- U.S. and Moroccan forces conducted the first live-fire demonstration at AMTEC near Tan-Tan, Morocco, from August 3 to 7, 2026.
- The test involved a low-cost, long-range cruise missile system built by an unnamed U.S. defense technology startup under the Army's Test Range Expansion Initiative.
U.S. and Moroccan forces have proven out a brand-new weapons testing range in North Africa by firing a low-cost, long-range cruise missile across it, the first live-fire event ever held at the site, according to a report by Army Capt. Jordan Beagle of U.S. Africa Command.
The demonstration ran from August 3 to 7 at the Africa Multidomain Training and Experimentation Center, a testing facility located near Tan-Tan in southern Morocco that the U.S. Army has been building out as part of a broader push to open military test ranges to private defense companies faster than the Pentagon’s traditional procurement process normally allows.
The center, known by its acronym AMTEC, is not new territory for U.S.-Morocco cooperation. The two countries have run joint exercises on Moroccan soil for years, including large multinational drills like African Lion, but AMTEC represents something different: a dedicated, standing range where American and Moroccan troops work directly alongside defense industry engineers to test unproven weapons systems in real desert conditions before those systems ever reach a formal Pentagon program of record. The Defence Blog previously reported that AMTEC was named one of four sites nationwide, alongside Dugway Proving Ground in Utah, the West Cibola Range at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, and Camp Grayling in Michigan, chosen under the Army’s Test Range Expansion Initiative to give smaller and newer defense companies access to military-grade testing environments without the legal and bureaucratic overhead that has historically kept them locked out of Pentagon work entirely.
That initiative matters because it addresses a real bottleneck in how the U.S. military buys new weapons. Traditional defense procurement can take years to move a promising prototype from a company’s workshop to a live-fire test on a government range, a delay that has pushed some of the fastest-moving American weapons startups toward commercial investors instead of military contracts. By opening ranges like AMTEC directly to industry partners, the Army is betting it can compress that timeline dramatically, letting a company validate whether its technology actually works in realistic conditions months or years earlier than the standard acquisition pipeline would allow.
The August demonstration put that theory to a real test. U.S. and Moroccan personnel built an expeditionary test site from scratch and carried out a single live-fire event, working alongside engineers and technicians from the unnamed defense industry partner to check communications systems, assess how well the missile’s wings, tires, and launch trolley performed under actual field conditions, and collect weather and targeting data needed to refine the system further. Africa Command’s report did not name the company involved or specify the missile’s exact range, speed, or cost, describing it only as a low-cost, long-range cruise missile system built to offer affordable, scalable precision-strike capability. That kind of system reflects a broader shift underway across Western militaries, where the runaway cost of traditional cruise missiles, often running into the millions of dollars per unit, has pushed governments and private companies alike toward cheaper, mass-producible alternatives that can be fielded in far greater numbers.
Moroccan Col. Zouhair El Hamdani, the Royal Armed Forces officer overseeing coordination of the project, framed the demonstration as the first real step toward a much larger ambition for the facility.
“The vision is to establish AMTEC as a regional hub for innovation, strategic cooperation and industrial development, as well as a center of excellence dedicated to the experimentation, validation, evaluation and development of advanced technologies,” said Moroccan Col. Zouhair El Hamdani, the royal armed forces officer in charge of coordination. “This first live-fire demonstration marks a significant milestone in turning that vision into reality.”
For Morocco, hosting a facility like AMTEC deepens a defense relationship with Washington that has grown steadily over the past two decades, built on joint training, arms sales, and counterterrorism cooperation across the Sahel region. For the U.S. military, gaining reliable access to North African desert terrain adds a testing environment that is difficult to replicate at American ranges, giving engineers a chance to see how equipment performs in heat, sand, and operational conditions closer to those found in parts of the Middle East and Africa where U.S. forces and their partners actually operate.
Air Force Gen. Dagvin R.M. Anderson, the commander of U.S. Africa Command, cast the demonstration in terms of the broader partnership it represents rather than the single missile test itself.
“Morocco’s partnership provides a crucial venue that accelerates readiness for the U.S. joint force and our African partners,” said Air Force Gen. Dagvin R.M. Anderson, commander of U.S. Africa Command.
Anderson added that AMTEC strengthens security cooperation and drives innovation while also demonstrating that trusted partnerships are how the two countries tackle shared security challenges together, a message aimed as much at reassuring African partners of Washington’s long-term commitment to the region as at showcasing new hardware.
Army Col. Michael M. Gacheru, who leads the regional engagement division within Africa Command’s Strategy, Engagement and Programs Directorate, tied the single demonstration to a much longer-term vision for how the U.S. trains and equips forces across the continent.
“The AMTEC live-fire demonstrates where multinational training is headed, integrating emerging technologies with partner forces in realistic operational environments,” said Army Col. Michael M. Gacheru, the regional engagement division chief of Africom’s Strategy, Engagement and Programs Directorate. “As AMTEC continues to evolve in Morocco, we’re expanding advanced training, strengthening interoperability and accelerating innovation alongside our African and international partners. Together, we’re building a more connected, more capable force prepared for tomorrow’s security challenges.”
Africa Command said future testing at the range will expand beyond cruise missiles into long-range fires, autonomous systems, wireless communications, and advanced sensing technologies, positioning AMTEC as a permanent fixture in how the U.S. and Moroccan militaries evaluate new capabilities rather than a one-time proving ground. What remains unclear from Africa Command’s account is which company built the missile tested in Tan-Tan, what it will cost per unit, and when or whether the system will move toward an actual military contract, details that will likely surface as the program advances further.
A single missile test in a stretch of southern Moroccan desert will not by itself change how fast the Pentagon fields new weapons, but it marks the moment a years-long promise, faster access to real testing ground for the companies racing to build cheaper firepower, started producing actual data instead of paperwork.

ISTANBUL, August 11. /TASS/. Turkey’s stance on the application of the Montreux Convention remains firm and unchanged. The nation continues to uphold its commitments to this fundamental treaty governing the Black Sea straits, as confirmed by Huseyin Bagci, head of the Ankara Global Advisory Group, an esteemed analytical center, who spoke to TASS.
"Turkey’s position on compliance with the convention has not wavered since its inception," Bagci emphasized. "We strictly adhere to this document and will maintain this approach in the future. There is no intention to revise this stance."
Similar sentiments were echoed by other local expert circles, who pointed out that following the onset of Russia’s military operation in Ukraine, Ankara closed the Black Sea straits to ships from countries involved in the conflict as well as non-littoral states.
"Turkey believes that the security of the Black Sea should be managed by the coastal nations themselves," they noted. "By strictly complying with the Montreux Convention, Turkey aims to prevent any escalation of tensions in this maritime region."
Omer Celik, spokesperson for Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party, previously conveyed that several NATO allies had approached Ankara seeking possible waivers to the convention. However, he reaffirmed that Turkey remains committed to adhering to the treaty, prioritizing navigational safety in the Black Sea.
Signed in 1936, the Montreux Convention governs navigation through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles straits. According to Article 19, if Turkey is not engaged in a war, the straits are closed to the passage of ships belonging to belligerent or non-coastal states.

NEW DELHI: Climate change is making extreme rainfall events in the Himalayan region more frequent and intense, while human activity is also increasing the risk of disasters, the Centre told the Lok Sabha on Tuesday, as reported by news agency PTI.Minister of state for home affairs Nityanand Rai said assessments by weather experts, scientific institutions and state authorities had found a link between climate change and the worsening intensity and frequency of extreme rainfall events in the Himalayas.The response came to a question on whether climate change and unscientific construction were contributing to the rising incidence of cloudbursts and other disasters in Himachal Pradesh.Rai cited findings of a Multi-Sectoral Central Team (MSCT), which was formed to examine the increasing frequency and severity of cloudbursts, flash floods, landslides and extreme rainfall in the state. The MSCT is examining the causes behind the increase in extreme weather events, including the geographical and ground conditions of the worst-hit areas and data provided by various government agencies. It will also recommend long-term steps to reduce the impact of such disasters, Rai said.
The Centre said faster snowmelt was another factor contributing to increased runoff in high-altitude areas. Rapid melting can send large volumes of water into already vulnerable mountain terrain, increasing downstream flows.The government also flagged moraine instability as a factor behind off-season slope failures and heavy runoff. Moraines are deposits of loose rock, soil and other debris left behind by glaciers, which can become unstable and trigger slope failures and the movement of water and debris.

Groups sue the Trump administration over its targeting of the International Criminal Court
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Human Rights Watch and three other advocacy groups sued the Trump administration on Tuesday to challenge its campaign against the International Criminal Court, arguing that sanctions against ICC judges and prosecutors are undermining the ability to prosecute people responsible for humanity’s worst crimes.
The complaint — filed in the Southern District of New York — says that President Donald Trump’s executive order last year targeting the Hague-based criminal court and the U.S. sanctions issued against a U.N. human rights expert and three Palestinian rights groups represent a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice and should be struck down,” according to a press release.
The lawsuit is the latest example of organizations pushing back on what they call the Trump administration’s efforts to undermine international law and prevent efforts to combat impunity by governments around the world.
“The fact that so many leading human rights and humanitarian organizations have come together to challenge Trump’s unlawful executive order demonstrates the widespread harm it is causing across civil society groups dedicated to bringing those responsible for grave crimes to justice,” said Andrew Loewenstein of Foley Hoag LLP, the lead counsel representing the plaintiffs.
The groups assert that the financial and legal penalties against the ICC have forced them to “curtail a wide range of human rights and legal work in violation of their First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act.”
Other organizations joining the lawsuit are the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights and the Open Society Institute.
The U.S. and Israel are not among the ICC’s member states, and neither nation recognizes the court’s authority. A White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss ongoing litigation, dismissed the lawsuit Tuesday, saying that the ICC’s actions have infringed on the sovereignty and national security of the U.S. and its closest ally, Israel. The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Efforts to retain the global tribunal’s power come as the ICC faces enormous pressure, both internally and from its more than 120 member states. Among those sanctioned by the U.S. last year was Karim Khan, who was the ICC’s chief prosecutor until he was removed from the post last month, nearly two years after sexual misconduct allegations against him first emerged, as detailed in stories by The Associated Press.
The Trump administration had issued those sanctions against Khan and a dozen other ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court has issued for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over the war in Gaza and investigations into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.
“The Trump administration seeks a get out of jail free card for whomever it chooses. And with this case, we say no,” Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch, said during a press conference Tuesday.
Last month, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the U.S. was launching a “sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty.”
In a video message, Rubio said the U.S. would pressure member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organizations that work with the court and ban staff from traveling to the United States. Countries that “enjoy the benefits of the U.S. security umbrella” will be called upon to reject the court’s jurisdiction over U.S. citizens, he added.
Several countries, including U.S.-allied Venezuela, announced they would withdraw from the court shortly after Rubio’s statements and Khan’s removal.

Myanmar’s military has escalated airstrikes against civilians, UN investigation finds
BANGKOK (AP) — Myanmar’s military has increasingly used low-cost aircraft such as motorized paragliders and gyrocopters in escalating aerial attacks that kill civilians in its conflict with armed, anti-government groups, a U.N. investigation said in a report Tuesday.
Separately, a major ethnic armed group fighting the government in Rakhine state said 20 civilians had been killed in strikes by the military so far this month.
Myanmar’s military government did not immediately respond to either the U.N. probe or the allegations by the Arakan Army. In the past, the military has said it only attacks legitimate targets of war, accusing the resistance forces of being terrorists.
The report by the United Nations-established Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, or IIMM, details a yearlong investigation into alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by Myanmar’s military and affiliated militias, as well as the opposition armed groups.
It found that abuses escalated around the country’s army-organized elections in December and January. The IIMM said it observed a notable escalation in aerial attacks in the months preceding the elections and that they have continued unabated afterward, with investigators also documenting a pattern of deliberate arbitrary detention, torture and sexual violence.
The IIMM said civilian casualties are worsened by the military’s increasing use of “double-tap” aerial attacks, in which a second strike follows the first, apparently targeting first responders, people helping the wounded and those trying to flee.
The IIMM said the Myanmar military was increasingly using motorized paragliders — also known as paramotors — as well as gyrocopters and drones to carry out low-altitude airstrikes with unguided explosives.
In several recent incidents in the upper Sagaing region, paramotor pilots allegedly cut their engines as they approached targets, allowing them to glide silently and leaving civilians little or no warning to flee or seek shelter, the report said.
The IIMM’s report came as the Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group fighting the army in Rakhine, said that about 20 civilians were killed and 22 injured in airstrikes across three townships from Aug. 1-11, including one attack involving up to eight aircraft that lasted about an hour.
The military-backed government has not publicly commented on the alleged attacks.
According to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, an independent organization that keeps detailed tallies of arrests and casualties linked to the civil war, more than 8,000 civilians have been killed and more than 31,000 arrested by Myanmar’s security forces since 2021.
The IIMM, which was established by the U.N. Human Rights Council in 2018 to monitor violations of international law in Myanmar, said it gathered evidence from more than 1,600 sources and witnesses that can be used in future prosecutions of those responsible.
“Behind every piece of evidence we collect are people whose lives have been devastated by these crimes,” group leader Nicholas Koumjian said in the report. “Communities across Myanmar are not only living under the constant threat of violence but are also coping with the profound and lasting impact of what they have endured.”
The IIMM said it is also investigating serious crimes allegedly committed by armed groups opposed to the military, including members of the Arakan Army, who have been accused of rape and other sexual violence against Rohingya Muslim women, summary executions, child recruitment and the destruction of mosques in Rakhine.
The report said numerous people were also arrested under an electoral law that carries up to 20 years in prison or the death penalty for acts such as criticizing the elections online or distributing “anti-election” leaflets.
The election was dismissed by the critics as a sham designed to consolidate the military’s grip on power after its 2021 takeover that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering the civil war.

In the Czech Republic, the water level in the Elbe is approaching a historic low
Kyiv • UNN
In the Czech Republic, drought has caused water levels in most rivers to fall to extremely low levels, while small streams have dried up. Due to the shallowing of the Orlík Reservoir, the remains of a 1929 hydroelectric power plant have been exposed.
The hydrological situation in the Czech Republic continues to deteriorate, reaching critical levels, UNN reports, citing Radio Prague.
Details
According to the latest data from the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute, water levels in the vast majority of monitored watercourses have fallen significantly below long-term average figures. Extremely low hydrological indicators have been recorded across most of the country, and a number of small streams have dried up completely. A critical situation is also being observed in the country's key waterways.
In particular, the water level in the Elbe River is approaching its historic minimum for the entire period of regular observations. On the Vltava River, regulation of the reservoir system has made it possible to partially stabilize the situation; however, in the area of the city of České Budějovice, the figures have also reached their lowest recorded level. The extreme decline in water volumes in the Orlík Reservoir has exposed historic sites: the remains of the former hydroelectric power plant in Dubrava, built in 1929 and flooded in the 1960s during the creation of the reservoir, have appeared on the surface.
In addition to surface waters, the negative trend is also affecting underground sources, where a steady decline in groundwater levels is being recorded, directly affecting the water levels in wells. According to the medium-range weather forecast, no conditions for a change in the situation or an improvement in the hydrological conditions are expected in the coming days.

Eleven kilometres of breaststroke: the story of a serviceman who took up swimming after a serious injury  – photos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:50:00 EEST
23:50:00 KST

Eleven kilometres of breaststroke: the story of a serviceman who took up swimming after a serious injury – photos
Yurii Brel, a service member from Lviv Oblast, continued his military service after suffering a serious injury in Popasna, Luhansk Oblast, and found a new passion – swimming. He now competes in national and international competitions.
Source: Zhabkolapky, a Lviv-based club for veterans and civilians
Details: Yurii, a native of the city of Sheptytskyi in Lviv Oblast, sustained a serious injury in April 2022 while carrying out a combat mission. He then faced a long period of treatment and rehabilitation. However, he decided to return to military service, while sport helped him recover – including adaptive volleyball, rowing on ergometers and swimming.
Yurii has achieved particular success in swimming – he even represents Ukraine at international competitions.
In 2024, he won medals at the annual United States Air Force and Marine Corps Trials, a sporting competition for wounded service members and veterans. In Las Vegas, Yurii competed in short-distance events – the 50-metre breaststroke and backstroke.
Yurii also became a silver medallist at a Lviv Oblast winter swimming championship for veterans.
That winter, Yurii took part in the Crazy Challenge in Kyiv, where six members of Zhabkolapky took turns to complete a continuous 24-hour swim.
"In total, the team covered 62 kilometres. For each of them, this was their first experience of a 24-hour swim. Over the course of that day, Yura spent four hours and 40 minutes in the water and swam 11 kilometres of breaststroke," the club said.
This summer, Yurii swam five kilometres at the Oceanman Kyiv'26 international open-water competition. Now he is preparing for his next 24-hour challenge, this time in open water.
"At first, sport was part of my recovery after the injury. Now I don't think of it just as rehabilitation anymore. I train, I go to competitions, I set myself new goals. One race ends, and I already want to know what's next. I'd like to swim for 12 hours continuously, but that's a goal I'm setting for next year," Yurii shared.
At Zhabkolapky, they say the club brings together service members and civilians, people with no experience and those tackling their first distances. The organisers say their goal was to create a community that would unite veterans, active soldiers and civilians.
"For me, this is a fundamental part of what we do. After coming back from the military, a former serviceman finds himself back in a civilian environment, but the experience he returns with is markedly different from that of most people around him. At the same time, civilians often don't know how to talk to veterans, they're afraid of saying the wrong thing, or they simply don't have experience of that kind of interaction.
Sport creates a space where this interaction happens naturally. You don't need to sit down at a table specifically to talk about how different we are. We have training, a coach, today's task and the next race we're all preparing for together. We help each other, we compete, we joke, we argue, and we work towards the result together," says club founder Yuliia Rudiuk.
Background: Last year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a law on adaptive sport, which recognises this activity as a separate area of physical activity.

The Hungarian Parliament elected András Baka as the new president
Kyiv • UNN
Former Supreme Court President András Baka became president of Hungary with the support of the "Tisza" party. The opposition "Fidesz" boycotted the vote, calling the change of power illegal.
On Tuesday, Hungary’s parliament elected former Supreme Court President András Baka as the country’s next president, a symbolic step in Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s efforts to dismantle the power centers of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Baka was elected to the largely ceremonial position with the votes of the ruling center-right Tisza party, while members of the opposition Fidesz party did not participate in the vote.
In his speech after taking the oath, Baka criticized the previous government, stating that during Orbán’s rule, “one party captured the state,” the branches of government were not separated, and a functioning system of checks and balances was absent.
However, he noted that the task of building a new future for Hungary “requires both justice and restraint,” adding that the role of the president is to represent the interests of citizens with differing views.
There is one thing we definitely cannot do — we cannot build a new Hungary on revenge
Magyar’s victory in the April election brought an end to Orbán’s 16-year rule. He promised to restore democratic standards and called for the resignation of key officials appointed or elected by Orbán’s party.
The removal of former President Tamás Sulyok was Magyar’s main objective, as he called him Orbán’s “puppet.” Last month, Sulyok signed a constitutional amendment adopted by Tisza that ended his own presidency.
Under this amendment, the new president will remain in office until a new constitution takes effect or for a maximum term of five years.
Parliament deputies from the opposition Fidesz party did not participate in the vote, stating in a statement released earlier that day that Tisza had “arbitrarily and unlawfully terminated” Sulyok’s term and accusing the ruling party of “tyranny.”

Swiss government explains its rejection of food initiative
The Swiss government and parliament have rejected the food security initiative. On Tuesday, Economics Minister Guy Parmelin addressed the media in Bern to explain why the government was recommending voters reject the issue on September 27.
The initiative “For food security – through strengthening sustainable domestic production, more plant-based foods and clean drinking water (Food Initiative)” calls for a higher level of self-sufficiency. The aim is to achieve this through increased cultivation of plant-based foods.
More
The Swiss food security initiative: more sustainable agriculture or ‘vegan diktat’?
The production of animal-based foods – such as meat and eggs – is of great importance in Switzerland, the government notes in its commentary on the proposal. Much of Switzerland’s agricultural land is not suitable for arable farming, but only for use as pasture.
The government points out that, should the proposal be approved, agriculture and food systems would need to be restructured within ten years. This would result in negative environmental impacts being shifted abroad.
